text: The pH at which half of the species is deprotonated is called the {{c1::pKa}}
example: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76) is half acetic acid and half acetate at pH 4.76

text: {{c1::Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)}} occurs when blood sugar is very high and acidic substances called ketones build up to dangerous levels in the body
extra: Develops when the body cannot produce enough insulin
example: A type 1 diabetic who skips insulin arrives with glucose 500 mg/dL, Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath.

text: This is the {{c1::indole}} group
example: Serotonin keeps tryptophan's indole ring, which is why it is called an indolamine

text: Extracellular ligands bind to membrane receptors and {{c1::initiate a response within the cell}}
example: Epinephrine binding the β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptor raises cAMP inside the cell without ever entering it.

text: {{c1::Beta oxidation}} is the process by which fatty acids are oxidized and broken down
extra: It generates multiple molecules of 2 carbon Acetyl-CoA, plus the electron carriers NADH and FADH2
example: Palmitate (16 C) gives 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 NADH and 7 FADH<sub>2</sub>, for about 106 net ATP.

text: The urea cycle takes place in the {{c1::cytosol::part of cell}} and {{c1::mitochondrial matrix::part of cell}} of the {{c1::liver::organ}}
example: Carbamoyl phosphate and citrulline form in liver mitochondria; argininosuccinate and urea form in the cytosol.

text: The 1st messenger in the above example of a G-protein coupled receptor is {{c1::epinephrine}}
example: During a fright, epinephrine docks on liver-cell receptors and cAMP relays the order to release glucose

text: Fatty acid synthesis begins with the transfer of {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} from the mitochondria to the cytosol via the {{c1::citrate shuttle}}
example: After a carb-rich meal, citrate builds up in mitochondria and is exported to supply acetyl-CoA for fat-making.

text: Pyruvate kinase is inhibited by {{c1::ATP}}
example: In a resting, well-fed muscle, plentiful ATP slows pyruvate kinase at glycolysis's last step.

text: Glycogen synthase creates {{c1::α-1,4 glycosidic bonds::... glycosidic bonds}} between molecules of glucose
example: Amylose in potato starch is the same kind of straight α-1,4-linked glucose chain.

text: Phagocytosis is the ingestion of {{c1::large solid materials}}
example: A neutrophil engulfs a whole Staphylococcus aureus bacterium.

text: Embedded proteins are embedded in the {{c1::cell membrane}}
extra: Most likely part of a catalytic complex or involved in cellular communication
example: Prostaglandin H synthase (COX-1), the aspirin target, sits embedded in just one leaflet of the ER membrane.

text: {{c1::Operons}} are found in prokaryotic DNA and contain groups of genes that are regulated together
extra:
The advantage is that a group of genes whose products are all needed for a common function can be transcribed together
Operons contain a promoter, an operator, and structural genes, and are regulated by repressors, activators, and inducers
example: The trp operon's five genes for tryptophan synthesis are switched on and off together

text: A {{c1::negative}} sense RNA strand has a nucleotide sequence complementary to the mRNA that it encodes
extra: Like DNA, this RNA cannot be translated into protein directly. Instead, it must first be transcribed into a positive-sense RNA which acts as an mRNA
example: Influenza and rabies viruses carry negative-sense RNA and must bring their own RNA polymerase.

text: The process that converts acetyl-CoA to a fatty acid is {{c1::fatty acid synthesis}}
example: Fatty acid synthase builds palmitate (16 C) from 8 acetyl-CoA units using NADPH.

text: RNA uses a {{c1::ribose}} sugar and {{c1::uracil::base}} instead of {{c1::thymine::base}}
example: The DNA template 3′-TAC-5′ is transcribed into mRNA 5′-AUG-3′, with U pairing opposite A

text: Triglyceride storage in {{c1::adipose tissue::... tissue}} comprises the principal energy reserve in mammals
example: Fat stores 9 kcal/g versus 4 kcal/g for glycogen, so adipose holds most of the body's fuel.

text: {{c1::Osmosis}} is a form of passive transport and describes the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane
example: Red blood cells placed in pure water swell and burst as water rushes in.

text: Native-PAGE is a polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis method for proteins using {{c1::non-denaturing::denaturing or non-denaturing}} conditions
extra: It is run in the absence of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), which would denature the proteins
example: On native-PAGE hemoglobin runs as an intact α<sub>2</sub>β<sub>2</sub> tetramer; SDS-PAGE splits it into α and β chains.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
This reaction requires {{c1::α-ketoglutarate}}, {{c1::NAD+}}, and {{c1::CoA}} and produces {{c1::succinyl CoA}}, {{c1::NADH}}, and {{c1::CO2}}
example: This is the cycle's second CO<sub>2</sub> release: 5 C α-ketoglutarate becomes 4 C succinyl-CoA.

text: {{c1::Glycogenolysis}} is the breakdown of glycogen
example: During a 400 m sprint, epinephrine triggers muscle glycogenolysis for quick glucose 1-phosphate.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
This reaction requires {{c1::ATP}} and produces {{c1::ADP}}
example: Of glycolysis's 2 invested ATP, this step spends the second, after hexokinase spends the first.

text: A chiral molecule is a type of molecule that {{c1::lacks::lacks or has}} an internal plane of symmetry and has a {{c1::non-superimposable::superimposable or non-superimposable}} mirror image
example: Your hands are chiral: a left glove won't fit your right hand, just as L- and D-alanine can't be superimposed

text: In isoelectric focusing, the gel has a pH gradient and the proteins will migrate through the gel until they reach the pH that matches their {{c1::isoelectric point}}
extra: At the pI, the protein has a neutral charge, so it will no longer be attracted to the anode or the cathode and it will stop migrating
example: Lysozyme (pI about 11) stops near the basic end of the gradient, while pepsin (pI about 1) stops near the acidic end.

text: Reducing sugars have a free {{c1::-OH}} group on the {{c1::anomeric carbon}}
extra:
The anomeric -OH must be free, not attached to any other structure
Example: sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because its anomeric carbons have no free -OH
example: Glucose reduces Cu<sup>2+</sup> in Benedict's reagent to a brick-red Cu<sub>2</sub>O precipitate

text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is turned on when it is {{c1::dephosphorylated::phosphorylated or dephosphorylated}}
extra: The enzyme that removes a phosphate is pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase
example: Insulin after a meal and Ca<sup>2+</sup> in contracting muscle activate PDH phosphatase, switching PDC on.

text: Eukaryotic ribosomes are {{c1::80::#}} Svedberg units
example: Cycloheximide blocks eukaryotic 80S ribosomes, so it stops yeast growth but not bacterial growth

text:
Lineweaver-Burk Plot:
  • X-intercept = {{c1::-1/Km}}
  • Y-intercept = {{c1::1/Vmax}}
  • Ratio indicated by the slope = {{c1::Km/Vmax}}
example: With K<sub>m</sub> = 2 mM and V<sub>max</sub> = 10 µM/s, the line crosses x at −0.5 mM<sup>−1</sup> and y at 0.1 s/µM

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
This reaction requires {{c1::succinyl CoA}}, {{c1::GDP}}, and {{c1::Pi}} and produces {{c1::succinate}}, {{c1::GTP}}, and {{c1::CoA}}
example: The GTP made here can pass its phosphate to ADP via nucleoside diphosphate kinase, giving ATP.

text: This is the monosaccharide {{c1::galactose}}
example: Galactose is the C-4 epimer of glucose, differing only in the orientation of one –OH.

text: {{c1::Helicase::Enzyme}} breaks the hydrogen bonds between nitrogenous bases in order to separate the DNA strands
example: Werner syndrome, a premature-ageing disorder, comes from a defective WRN helicase

text: {{c1::Structural proteins::... proteins}} compose the cytoskeleton, anchoring proteins, and much of the extracellular matrix
extra:
The most common structural proteins are:
Collagen
Elastin
Keratin
Actin
Tubulin
example: Keratin intermediate filaments give hair and nails their toughness

text: {{c1::Northern blotting::... blotting}} is used to detect a specific RNA sequence
example: A Northern blot shows insulin mRNA in pancreas tissue but not in liver tissue.

text: {{c1::Flavoproteins}} are a subclass of electron carriers that are derived from riboflavin
extra: They contain FAD or FMN as prosthetic groups
example: Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) is a flavoprotein carrying covalently bound FAD.

text: Branching enzyme creates branches with {{c1::α-1,6 glycosidic bonds::... glycosidic bonds}}
example: Branching enzyme moves a segment of about 7 glucoses to make a branch every 8–12 residues.

text: Glycolysis requires {{c1::2::#}} ATP and produces {{c1::4::#}} ATP
extra: A net gain of 2 ATP
example: Hexokinase and PFK-1 each spend 1 ATP; phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase each make 2 per glucose.

text: Complex II in the ETC is also known as {{c1::succinate dehydrogenase}}
extra:
Complex II removes two hydrogens from succinate and adds them to FAD to make FADH2
The result is, succinate is oxidized to fumarate and FAD is reduced to FADH2
FADH2 is then oxidized back to FAD
example: Malonate, a succinate look-alike, competitively inhibits Complex II, blocking succinate → fumarate.

text: Beta oxidation starts with the oxidation of {{c1::acyl-CoA}}
example: MCAD deficiency blocks this first step for medium chains, causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in fasting infants.

text: The {{c1::fluid mosaic model::... model}} accounts for the presence of lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates in a dynamic, semisolid plasma membrane that surrounds cells
extra: It explains various observations regarding the structure of functional cell membranes
example: Frye and Edidin (1970): in fused mouse-human cells, surface proteins intermixed within 40 minutes

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::phosphoglycerate mutase}}
example: It shifts the phosphate of 3-phosphoglycerate from carbon 3 to carbon 2.

text:
The citric acid cycle produces:
  • {{c1::ATP}}
  • {{c1::NADH}}
  • {{c1::FADH2}}
  • {{c1::CO2}}
example: Per glucose, two turns make 2 GTP/ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> and 4 CO<sub>2</sub>.

text: The citric acid cycle sends electrons to the electron transport chain within the electron carriers {{c1::NADH}} and {{c1::FADH2}}
example: Per glucose, the cycle's 6 NADH and 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> supply about 18 ATP (6 × 2.5 + 2 × 1.5).

text: Complex III in the ETC is also known as {{c1::cytochrome reductase}}
extra: Cytochrome is reduced
example: Antimycin A blocks Complex III, stopping electron flow to cytochrome c.

text: A low pH will cause amino acids to be {{c1::fully protonated}}
example: At pH 1, glycine exists as <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH, with a net charge of +1

text: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme of the citric acid cycle, is inhibited by {{c1::ATP}} or {{c1::NADH}}
example: In a resting, well-fed cell, high ATP and NADH slow isocitrate dehydrogenase and the whole cycle.

text: A {{c1::coenzyme}} is an organic molecule that is required by some enzymes
example: Pyruvate dehydrogenase needs NAD<sup>+</sup> (from niacin, B<sub>3</sub>) and thiamine pyrophosphate (from B<sub>1</sub>)

text: {{c1::Post-translational modifications}} are modifications that occur to a protein after it has been fully formed in translation
extra: PTMs can happen at any step of the protein lifespan. The most common PTM is phosphorylation
example: Proinsulin is cleaved into insulin and C-peptide after translation

text: The {{c1::lac operon}} contains genes that code for proteins that transport lactose into the cytosol and digest it into glucose
extra:
The glucose is then used to make energy
The lac (lactose) operon is found in E. coli and some other bacteria
example: LacY permease imports lactose and LacZ (β-galactosidase) splits it into glucose and galactose

text: The DNA backbone is held together by {{c1::phosphodiester bonds::... bonds}}
extra:
Form between the sugar and the phosphate groups
Nucleotide bases are held together by hydrogen bonds
example: The restriction enzyme EcoRI cuts DNA by hydrolysing backbone phosphodiester bonds at GAATTC

text: {{c1::Glycosphingolipids}} are a subtype of glycolipids and contain a sphingosine, fatty acid, and a sugar unit
extra:
Example: Cerebroside, which contains 1 sugar group
Cerebroside Structure:

text: {{c1::Tight junctions}} in cell membranes prevent solutes from leaking into the space between cells via a paracellular route, but do not provide intercellular transport
example: Tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells form the blood–brain barrier.

text: Glycolysis requires {{c1::2::#}} NAD+ and produces {{c1::2::#}} NADH
example: In a sprinting muscle, lactate dehydrogenase reoxidises those 2 NADH so glycolysis can keep running.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::aldolase}}
example: Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance, with hypoglycaemia after eating fruit.

text: The urea cycle connects to the citric acid cycle using the compounds {{c1::oxaloacetate}} and {{c1::fumarate}}
example: Fumarate released by argininosuccinate lyase becomes malate, then oxaloacetate, the 'Krebs bicycle'.

text: All chiral amino acids except cysteine have {{c1::(S)}} configuration
example: L-alanine is (S), but L-cysteine is (R): its sulfur makes –CH<sub>2</sub>SH outrank –COOH

text: An inducible operon under normal conditions is {{c1::bonded to a repressor}}
extra:
Inducible operons are turned on when an inducer pulls the repressor from the operator site
Example: lac operon is an inducible operon

text: If a C16 fatty acid is completely processed by beta oxidation, {{c1::8::#}} acetyl-CoA molecules will be produced
example: Stearic acid (C<sub>18</sub>) would give 18 ÷ 2 = 9 acetyl-CoA.

text: The citric acid cycle sends electrons to the {{c1::electron transport chain}}
extra: The electron transport chain converts ADP to ATP
example: Each turn of the citric acid cycle hands 3 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub> to the electron transport chain.

text: An operon {{c1::inducer}} is a small molecule that triggers expression of a gene or operon
extra: Example: The lac operon is considered an inducible operon because its default state is to be turned off (repressed), but can be turned on in the presence of the inducer allolactose

text:
The citric acid cycle occurs in the following parts of the cell:
  • Eukaryotes: {{c1::mitochondrial matrix}}
  • Prokaryotes: {{c1::cytoplasm}}
extra: Example of a eukaryotic cell:
example: E. coli, which has no mitochondria, runs the citric acid cycle in its cytoplasm.

text:
The Michaelis–Menten equation is:
{{c1::}}
example: If [S] = 3K<sub>m</sub>, v = V<sub>max</sub> × 3/(1 + 3) = 0.75 V<sub>max</sub>

text: {{c1::Glycolysis}} is the process in which one glucose molecule is broken down to form two molecules of pyruvic acid
example: A sprinter's leg muscle splits each glucose into 2 pyruvate, netting 2 ATP.

text: In prokaryotic translation, the 30S ribosome subunit attaches to the {{c1::Shine-Dalgarno sequence}}, which positions the start codon
extra: It lays down N-formylmethionine in the P site of the ribosome
example: In E. coli, the Shine-Dalgarno sequence AGGAGG sits about 8 nucleotides upstream of the AUG

text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is turned off when it is {{c1::phosphorylated::phosphorylated or dephosphorylated}}
extra: The enzyme that adds a phosphate is pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase
example: High NADH and acetyl-CoA during fat burning activate PDH kinase, switching PDC off.

text: {{c1::Saponification}} is the ester hydrolysis of triacylglycerols using a strong base like NaOH or KOH
example: Boiling animal fat with lye (NaOH) gives glycerol and sodium fatty-acid salts such as sodium stearate: soap

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Histidine}}
example: The proximal histidine (His F8) of haemoglobin binds directly to the iron of each haem group

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::phosphofructokinase (PFK)}}
example: Fructose-6-phosphate + ATP → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the committed step of glycolysis.

text: {{c1::Polycistronic}} mRNA is prokaryotic mRNA that encodes several proteins
extra: Multiple translation sites lead to different gene products being created
example: The lac operon's single mRNA encodes three proteins: lacZ, lacY and lacA

text: {{c1::Cellulose}} is the main structural component for plant cell walls
example: Cotton fibre is nearly pure cellulose, β-1,4-linked glucose that humans cannot digest.

text: Endergonic reactions {{c1::require::require or release}} energy
example: Making ATP from ADP + P<sub>i</sub> needs about +30.5 kJ/mol, so cells couple it to oxidising food

text: Ketone bodies form via ketogenesis due to excess {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} in the liver during a prolonged starvation state
example: On day 3 of a fast, oxaloacetate is used for gluconeogenesis, so liver acetyl-CoA becomes ketones.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
This reaction requires {{c1::H2O}}
example: Fumarate + H<sub>2</sub>O → L-malate, adding H and OH across the C=C double bond.

text: Emulsification of lipids is aided by {{c1::bile salts}}
extra: Emulsification increases the surface area of the lipid, which permits greater enzymatic interaction and processing
example: When a gallstone blocks the bile duct, fat goes undigested and stools turn pale and greasy.

text: {{c1::Voltage-gated channels::... channels}} open within a range of membrane potentials
example: Voltage-gated Na<sup>+</sup> channels in an axon fly open when the membrane depolarises to about −55 mV

text: The {{c1::proton-motive force::... force}} is the proton electrochemical gradient generated by the electron transport chain across the inner mitochondrial membrane
example: Uncoupling protein 1 in brown fat lets protons leak back, burning the proton-motive force as heat.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Proline}}
extra:
Pro, P
Hydrophobic
Typically found in β-pleated sheets at the turns
"Kinky"
example: Prolyl hydroxylase needs vitamin C to turn proline into collagen's hydroxyproline, so scurvy weakens collagen

text: {{c1::Active transport::... transport}} requires energy from ATP or from an existing favorable gradient of another ion (not the solute being transported)
extra: Moves solutes against their concentration gradient
example: The stomach's H<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> ATPase spends ATP to pump H<sup>+</sup> into a lumen near pH 1.

text: A/an {{c1::sphingomyelin}} is a type of sphingolipid found in animal cell membranes, especially in the membranous myelin sheath that surrounds some nerve cell axons
example: In Niemann-Pick disease, missing sphingomyelinase lets sphingomyelin pile up in neurons and the liver

text: Fatty acid synthesis begins with the transfer of acetyl-CoA from the {{c1::mitochondria::cell part}} to the {{c1::cytosol::cell part}} via the citrate shuttle
example: After a sugary meal, liver cells export acetyl-CoA (as citrate) to the cytosol to make palmitate.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase}}
example: GAPDH turns glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate into 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, making glycolysis's NADH.

text: In translation, {{c1::termination}} will occur when the codon in the A site is a stop codon
extra: Release factor places a water molecule on the polypeptide chain and thus releases the protein
example: Reading 5′-…GCC UAA-3′, the chain ends at Ala once UAA enters the A site

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Leucine}}
example: Leucine zippers: leucines every seventh residue let two α-helices of Fos and Jun zip together on DNA

text:
PCR cycle steps and temperatures:
  1. {{c1::Denaturation}} at {{c1::96::#}} °C
  2. {{c1::Annealing}} at {{c1::55 - 65::#}} °C
  3. {{c1::Extension}} at {{c1::72::#}} °C
example: A thermocycler repeats 96 → 60 → 72 °C about 30 times, doubling the target sequence each cycle.

text: {{c1::Glycosylation}} is the chemical addition of a carbohydrate
example: Blood type A adds N-acetylgalactosamine and type B adds galactose to the same red-cell H antigen

text: Lineweaver-Burk plots are double reciprocal plots of 1/v vs. 1/[S], so the x-intercept is {{c1::-1/Km}} and the y-intercept is {{c1::1/Vmax}}
example: A point at [S] = 4 mM and v = 2 µM/s is plotted at 1/[S] = 0.25 mM<sup>−1</sup> and 1/v = 0.5 s/µM

text: {{c1::Cadherins::Type of proteins}} are calcium dependent glycoproteins that hold similar cells together
example: Loss of E-cadherin lets carcinoma cells detach from their neighbours and metastasise

text: The genetic code is considered {{c1::degenerate}} because multiple codons can code for the same amino acid
example: Leucine is encoded by six codons: UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA and CUG

text: Gluconeogenesis is the process in which {{c1::pyruvic acid}} is converted to {{c1::glucose}}
example: A person fasting for 24 hours relies on liver gluconeogenesis once glycogen stores are nearly used up.

text:
Acetyl-CoA can be formed from the following three sources:
  • {{c1::Amino acids}}
  • {{c1::Pyruvic acids}}
  • {{c1::Fatty acids}}
example: In a fasting liver, most acetyl-CoA comes from fatty acids rather than glucose-derived pyruvate.

text: A saturated fatty acid has {{c1::no::#}} double bonds in its tail and is {{c1::less::more or less}} fluid
example: Saturated stearic acid (18:0) melts at 69.6 °C, while unsaturated oleic acid (18:1) melts at 13.4 °C

text: A/an {{c1::ganglioside}} is a molecule composed of a glycosphingolipid with one or more sialic acids linked on the sugar chain
extra: A component of the cell membrane that modulates cell signal transduction events, and appears to concentrate in lipid rafts
example: In Tay-Sachs disease, missing hexosaminidase A lets GM2 ganglioside build up in neurons

text: Step 4 of β-oxidation: {{c1::thiolysis}}
extra:
The acyl-CoA undergoes thiolytic cleavage of the thioester
An acetyl-CoA molecule is broken off of the acyl-CoA
example: Thiolase cuts 3-ketoacyl-CoA with a fresh CoA-SH rather than water, hence the name thiolysis.

text: The protein complex that performs pyruvate decarboxylation and converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is {{c1::pyruvate dehydrogenase complex}}
example: Thiamine (B<sub>1</sub>) deficiency in alcoholics cripples PDC, so pyruvate piles up as lactate.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
This reaction requires {{c1::ADP}} and produces {{c1::ATP}}
example: 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate + ADP → 3-phosphoglycerate + ATP, the first ATP glycolysis earns.

text: A/an {{c1::hydrolase::type of enzyme}} catalyzes cleavage with the addition of H2O
example: Lactase splits lactose plus H<sub>2</sub>O into glucose and galactose in the small intestine

text: {{c1::Western blotting::... blotting}} is used to detect a specific protein in a sample
example: Probed with an anti-actin antibody, a Western blot of muscle lysate shows a single band at 42 kDa.

text: The rate limiting enzyme in the citric acid cycle is {{c1::isocitrate dehydrogenase}}
example: Ca<sup>2+</sup> released during muscle contraction activates isocitrate dehydrogenase, speeding the cycle.

text: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme of the citric acid cycle, is activated by {{c1::ADP}} or {{c1::NAD+}}
example: When the ETC rapidly reoxidises NADH, the high NAD<sup>+</sup>/NADH ratio speeds isocitrate dehydrogenase.

text: High-density lipoproteins (HDL) are considered {{c1::good::good or bad}} because they {{c1::pick up extra cholesterol and return it to the liver}}
example: Regular aerobic exercise raises HDL and is linked to lower heart-disease risk.

text:
Glycolysis, glycogenolysis, and fatty acid synthesis all occur in the {{c1::cytoplasm::part of cell}}
Pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and beta oxidation all occur in the {{c1::mitochondria::part of cell}}
example: Glucose is split in the cytoplasm, then its pyruvate enters the mitochondrion to be burned to CO<sub>2</sub>.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Tyrosine}}
extra:
Tyr, Y
Polar Neutral
Aromatic
Tyrosine is the precursor to catecholamines
example: Thyroid hormones T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub> are built from iodinated tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin

text: {{c1::Glucose transporters}} are transport proteins that move glucose across the cell membrane
example: GLUT1 keeps glucose flowing into red blood cells and across the blood–brain barrier.

text: The {{c1::2°::1°, 2°, 3°, or 4°}} structure of proteins is the local folding of neighboring amino acids including α-helices and β-pleated sheets
extra: Stabilized by hydrogen bonding
example: In prion disease, the normal α-helix-rich PrP refolds into β-sheet-rich PrP<sup>Sc</sup>

text: The 2° structure of proteins is stabilized by {{c1::hydrogen bonds}}
example: In keratin's α-helix, each backbone C=O hydrogen-bonds to the N–H four residues along.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::phosphoglucose isomerase}}
example: It converts glucose-6-phosphate (an aldose) into fructose-6-phosphate (a ketose).

text: The term antiport is used during membrane transport when two particles flow in {{c1::opposite directions}}
example: The cardiac Na<sup>+</sup>/Ca<sup>2+</sup> exchanger brings 3 Na<sup>+</sup> in while pushing 1 Ca<sup>2+</sup> out.

text: Step 2 of fatty acid synthesis: {{c1::Condense}}
extra: Malonyl-CoA condenses with acetyl-CoA, kicking off a CoA and CO2
example: Acetyl (2 C) + malonyl (3 C) → acetoacetyl-ACP (4 C), with the extra carbon leaving as CO<sub>2</sub>.

text: When pyruvate undergoes pyruvate decarboxylation, it is converted to {{c1::Acetyl-CoA}}
example: Each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO<sub>2</sub> and makes one NADH as it becomes acetyl-CoA.

text: A/an {{c1::lipase::type of enzyme}} catalyzes the hydrolysis of fats
example: Pancreatic lipase splits dietary triglycerides into free fatty acids and monoglycerides in the gut

text: A/an {{c1::homotropic effector::... effector}} is an allosteric regulator that is also the substrate
extra: Example: O2 is a homotropic allosteric regulator of hemoglobin

text: Phospholipids contain a {{c1::hydrophilic}} head and {{c1::hydrophobic}} tails
extra:
Hydrophilic = polar; hydrophobic = nonpolar
The backbone may be glycerol or sphingosine
example: Phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) has a polar choline-phosphate head and two fatty-acid tails

text: Low-density lipoproteins (LDL) are considered {{c1::bad::good or bad}} because they {{c1::have a high amount of cholesterol which they deliver to tissues}}
example: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (defective LDL receptors) can cause heart attacks in childhood.

text: The DNA double helix has a diameter of {{c1::20::#}} angstroms
extra:
purine + pyrimidine = uniform width
purine + purine = too wide
pyrimidine + pyrimidine = too narrow
example: At 2 nm wide, the DNA helix is 50,000 times narrower than a 100 µm human hair

text:
In competitive inhibition:
  • Vmax: {{c1::has no change}}
  • Km: {{c1::goes up}}
example: Statins raise HMG-CoA reductase's apparent K<sub>m</sub>, yet a flood of HMG-CoA could still reach V<sub>max</sub>

text: The {{c1::active site::part of enzyme}} is the site of catalysis
example: Chymotrypsin's active site holds Ser195, His57 and Asp102, which cut peptide bonds after aromatic residues

text: A/an {{c1::heterotropic effector::... effector}} is an allosteric regulator molecule that is different from the substrate
example: CTP, not the substrate aspartate, binds ATCase's regulatory subunits and inhibits it

text: A {{c1::zwitterion}} is a molecule whose positive and negative charges cancel out, so its net charge is zero
example: At blood pH 7.4, glycine exists mainly as <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>

text: {{c1::α-helices}} are clockwise coils around a central axis and are a common {{c1::2°::1°, 2°, 3°, or 4°}} protein structure
example: Hair α-keratin is a right-handed α-helix with 3.6 amino acids per turn

text: Step 3 of β-oxidation: {{c1::oxidation}}
extra:
A hydrogen is removed and donated to NAD+
This means NAD+ is reduced to NADH
example: 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase turns the β-OH into a ketone, giving 3-ketoacyl-CoA and NADH.

text: A/an {{c1::transferase::type of enzyme}} moves a functional group from one molecule to another
example: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) moves an amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate

text: {{c1::Blotting}} is a method of transferring fragments of protein, DNA, or RNA that have been separated via electrophoresis and applying them to a blotting membrane
extra: You can then visualize the fragments with a colored stain
example: Proteins from an SDS-PAGE gel are transferred onto a nitrocellulose sheet so a labelled antibody can find them.

text: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme of the citric acid cycle, is activated by {{c1::ADP}} and inhibited by {{c1::ATP}}
extra: High ADP means the system is low on ATP and the citric acid cycle is needed to create more ATP
example: During a sprint, ATP is spent and ADP rises, speeding isocitrate dehydrogenase.

text: {{c1::Glycoside formation}} is the basis for building complex carbohydrates and requires the anomeric carbon to link to another sugar
example: Lactose links C-1 of galactose to C-4 of glucose by a β-1,4 glycosidic bond

text: The Nernst equation is used to calculate {{c1::cell potential}} in non-standard conditions
extra: It accounts for varying temperature and concentrations
example: For K<sup>+</sup> at 140 mM inside and 4 mM outside, E = 61.5 log(4/140) ≈ −95 mV.

text: The stereochemistry of the α-carbon in all eukaryotic amino acids (except glycine) is {{c1::L}}
example: Proteins are built from L-alanine; D-alanine turns up instead in bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan

text:
The nitrogenous bases in DNA and RNA:
  • {{c1::Guanine}}
  • {{c1::Cytosine}}
  • {{c1::Adenine}}
  • {{c1::Thymine (DNA only)}}
  • {{c1::Uracil (RNA only)}}
example: The DNA coding sequence 5′-ATG-3′ appears in mRNA as 5′-AUG-3′, with U in place of T

text: {{c1::Cell Adhesion Molecules}} allow cells to bind to other cells or surfaces
example: Neutrophils use integrins to grip ICAM-1 on inflamed vessel walls before squeezing out into infected tissue

text: {{c1::Nucleic acids}} are polymers of nucleotides
extra: Include deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA)
example: The haploid human genome strings about 3 billion nucleotide pairs into 23 DNA molecules

text: {{c1::Deoxy sugars}} are sugars that have had a hydroxyl group replaced with a hydrogen atom
example: Deoxyribose in DNA lacks ribose's 2′-OH, carrying just an H at C-2′

text:
The genes in the lac operon will be expressed if the following two conditions are met:
  • {{c1::Lactose is available}}
  • {{c1::Glucose is low}}
extra: When lactose is available, the inducer (allolactose) binds to the repressor and the repressor detaches from the DNA:When glucose is low, the activator, catabolite activator protein (CAP), binds to the DNA:
example: E. coli in milk with no glucose turns lac on; add glucose and expression drops despite the lactose

text: {{c1::Promoters}} are regions of DNA that initiate transcription of a particular gene
extra: Are within 25 base pairs of the transcription start site
example: The TATA box, about 25–30 bp upstream of the start site, is where TFIID binds to begin transcription

text: {{c1::Okazaki fragments}} are short, newly synthesized DNA fragments that are formed on the lagging template strand during DNA replication
example: Bacterial Okazaki fragments run 1,000–2,000 nucleotides; eukaryotic ones only 100–200

text: Glycolysis is the process in which one glucose molecule is broken down to form {{c1::two molecules of pyruvic acid}}
example: Red blood cells, lacking mitochondria, rely on glycolysis alone, turning each glucose into 2 pyruvate, then lactate.

text: Prokaryotes have {{c1::1::#}} origin(s) of replication and eukaryotes have {{c1::multiple::#}} origin(s) of replication
example: E. coli copies its whole genome from one origin (oriC), while a human cell fires tens of thousands

text: {{c1::Prostaglandins}} are lipid compounds that are signaling molecules and regulate cAMP levels
extra:
Affect the following functions:
Smooth muscle contraction
Body temperature
Sleep-wake cycle
Fever
Pain
example: Aspirin and ibuprofen block COX, so less prostaglandin is made and fever and pain fall

text: A/an {{c1::oxidoreductase::type of enzyme}} catalyzes REDOX reactions that involve the transfer of electrons
example: Lactate dehydrogenase passes electrons from NADH to pyruvate, making lactate and NAD<sup>+</sup>

text: The pentose phosphate pathway occurs in the {{c1::cytosol::part of cell}}
example: In a liver cell's cytosol, the PPP makes NADPH right where fatty acid synthase needs it.

text: The precursor to steroid hormones is {{c1::cholesterol}}
example: Adrenal cells cut cholesterol's side chain to make pregnenolone, then cortisol and aldosterone

text: In glycogenolysis, glycogen phosphorylase removes single glucose molecules by breaking {{c1::α-1,4 glycosidic bonds::... glycosidic bonds}}
example: Glycogen phosphorylase uses P<sub>i</sub> to release glucose 1-phosphate, stopping 4 residues from a branch.

text: {{c1::Ketogenic amino acids::... amino acids}} are amino acids that can be converted into acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies
extra: A product of protein catabolism
example: Leucine and lysine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids.

text: A/an {{c1::missense mutation::... mutation}} produces a codon that codes for a different amino acid
example: Sickle-cell anaemia: GAG → GTG changes codon 6 of β-globin from glutamate to valine

text: At high temperatures, cholesterol will {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}} fluidity
extra: At high temperatures, cholesterol decreases membrane fluidity by immobilizing a few methylene groups in the fatty acid tails of the lipids
example: During a 40 °C fever, cholesterol keeps membranes from becoming overly fluid and leaky.

text: The resting potential of most cells is between {{c1::-40}} and {{c1::-80}} mV
example: A typical neuron rests at about −70 mV.

text: The {{c1::inner::inner or outer}} mitochondrial membrane surrounds the mitochondrial matrix, where the citric acid cycle produces electrons used in the ETC
example: NADH made by malate dehydrogenase in the matrix hands its electrons to Complex I in the inner membrane.

text: {{c1::DNA primase::Enzyme}} catalyzes the synthesis of the RNA primer
example: In E. coli, primase (DnaG) lays down an RNA primer about 10 nucleotides long for each Okazaki fragment

text: {{c1::Waxes}} in cell membranes provide waterproofing and defense for the cell
extra: Present in very small amounts, if at all. They are most prevalent in plants
example: The waxy cuticle on a cabbage leaf makes rainwater bead up and roll off.

text: {{c1::Adipocytes}} are cells used for storage of triacylglycerol deposits
example: Each white adipocyte is mostly one big triacylglycerol droplet that squeezes its nucleus to the edge

text: The two main enzymes in glycogenesis are {{c1::glycogen synthase}} and {{c1::branching enzyme}}
example: Andersen disease (branching enzyme deficiency) makes long, unbranched glycogen that damages the liver.

text: {{c1::Postprandial}} means after eating a meal
extra: Postprandial state = fed state
example: A 2-hour postprandial glucose test measures blood sugar two hours after a meal.

text: The citric acid cycle is also known as the {{c1::Krebs cycle}} or the {{c1::tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle}}
extra: It is called the tricarboxylic acid cycle because citric acid contains 3 carboxyl groups
example: Hans Krebs described the cycle in 1937 and shared the 1953 Nobel Prize for it.

text: Complex I in the ETC oxidizes {{c1::NADH}} to form {{c1::NAD+}}
extra: NADH gives up 2 electrons
example: Complex I pumps 4 H<sup>+</sup> into the intermembrane space for each NADH it oxidises.

text:
The above reactions are from gluconeogenesis
The conversion of pyruvate to PEP is activated by {{c1::acetyl-CoA}}
example: During a fast, β-oxidation floods the liver with acetyl-CoA, which switches on pyruvate carboxylase.

text: {{c1::Ligand-gated channels::... channels}} open in the presence of a specific binding substance, usually a hormone or neurotransmitter
example: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction opens when ACh binds, letting Na<sup>+</sup> in

text: Glycolysis sends {{c1::glucose 6-phosphate}} to the pentose phosphate pathway
example: Fat cells making triglycerides divert glucose 6-phosphate into the PPP for the NADPH that fatty acid synthesis needs.

text:
Fatty acid synthesis includes the following 5 steps:
  1. {{c1::Attach}}
  2. {{c1::Condense}}
  3. {{c1::Reduce}}
  4. {{c1::Dehydration}}
  5. {{c1::Reduce}}
extra:
ACR DR mnemonic
This adds two new carbon atoms to a fatty acid chain
example: Seven rounds of these 5 steps turn acetyl-CoA into palmitate (16 C), adding 2 C per round.

text: PCR relies on a thermostable DNA polymerase called {{c1::Taq polymerase::... polymerase}}
example: Taq comes from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium from Yellowstone hot springs, so it survives the 96 °C steps.

text: {{c1::Nucleotide excision repair::... repair}} fixes helix-deforming lesions of DNA, such as thymine dimers
extra: A cut-and-patch process that uses excision endonuclease
example: Xeroderma pigmentosum patients lack NER, so sun-induced thymine dimers persist and skin cancers appear

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Glycine}}
extra:
Gly, G
Hydrophobic
The only amino acid that is not chiral
example: Strychnine kills by blocking glycine receptors, the spinal cord's main inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors

text: The {{c1::1°::1°, 2°, 3°, or 4°}} structure of proteins is the linear sequence of amino acids in a peptide
extra: Stabilized by peptide bonds
example: Frederick Sanger sequenced insulin's primary structure first: an A chain of 21 and a B chain of 30 residues

text: In SDS-PAGE, you can add an additional reducing agent called {{c1::2-mercaptoethanol}} to reduce disulfide bonds. This further denatures the protein
example: An IgG antibody (150 kDa) splits into 50 kDa heavy-chain and 25 kDa light-chain bands once 2-mercaptoethanol is added.

text: {{c1::Desmosomes}} bind adjacent cells by anchoring to their cytoskeletons
extra:
Hemidesmosomes are similar, but mainly attach epithelial cells to underlying structures
Found in tissues under intense mechanical stress: cardiac muscle, bladder, gastrointestinal mucosa, epithelium
example: In pemphigus vulgaris, antibodies attack desmosomes and skin cells separate into blisters.

text: {{c1::β-pleated sheets}} are rippled strands that can be parallel or antiparallel and are a common {{c1::2°::1°, 2°, 3°, or 4°}} protein structure
extra: Proline is typically found at the turns in β-pleated sheets
example: Silk fibroin is stacked antiparallel β-sheets, which makes silk strong but hard to stretch

text: {{c1::Secondary active transport::... transport}} harnesses the energy released by one particle going down its electrochemical gradient to drive a different particle up its gradient
example: SGLT1 lets Na<sup>+</sup> flow into gut cells and drags glucose in with it against its gradient.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::fumarase}}
example: Fumarase converts fumarate, a trans alkene, into L-malate, an alcohol.

text: The pentose phosphate pathway produces {{c1::ribose 5-phosphate}} for use in nucleotide synthesis
example: Rapidly dividing tumour cells pull ribose 5-phosphate from the PPP to build DNA nucleotides.

text: {{c1::Anomers}} are a subtype of epimers that differ at the anomeric carbon
example: α-D-glucopyranose and β-D-glucopyranose are anomers, differing only at C-1

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Lysine}}
example: Lysine and leucine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids, broken down to acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate

text: {{c1::Oxygen}} is the final acceptor of electrons in the ETC during aerobic respiration
example: Without enough O<sub>2</sub>, a sprinter's muscle backs up its ETC and turns to lactic acid fermentation.

text: The bulk of chemical lipid digestion occurs in the {{c1::small intestine}} due to pancreatic lipase
example: Orlistat, a weight-loss drug, blocks pancreatic lipase, so dietary fat passes out in the stool.

text: {{c1::Glycolysis}} converts glucose to pyruvate and {{c1::gluconeogenesis}} converts pyruvate to glucose
example: Muscle runs glycolysis during a sprint; the liver runs gluconeogenesis during an overnight fast.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::isocitrate dehydrogenase}}
example: Isocitrate dehydrogenase oxidises isocitrate, releasing the cycle's first CO<sub>2</sub>.

text: The {{c1::α-anomer::... anomer}} has the -OH on the anomeric carbon pointing down
example: Starch and glycogen are chains of α-D-glucose joined by α-1,4 links

text: In gluconeogenesis, the combination of {{c1::pyruvate carboxylase::enzyme 1}} and {{c1::phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase::enzyme 2}} is used to circumvent the action of pyruvate kinase
example: Liver cells turn alanine-derived pyruvate into oxaloacetate, then PEP, spending 1 ATP + 1 GTP per pyruvate.

text: An operon {{c1::repressor}} turns the operon off
extra: The repressor binds to the operator and then blocks the movement of RNA polymerase down the DNA strand
example: When tryptophan is plentiful, Trp-bound TrpR repressor shuts off the trp operon

text: Enzymes {{c1::do not alter::alter or do not alter}} the ∆G or ∆H, and the final equilibrium position
extra: Enzymes only change the rate of reaction
example: Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> about 10<sup>7</sup>-fold but leaves K<sub>eq</sub> unchanged.

text: Phosphofructokinase is inhibited by {{c1::ATP}} and {{c1::citrate}}
example: When citrate piles up in a well-fed liver cell, it signals plenty of fuel and slows PFK-1.

text: Step 2 of β-oxidation: {{c1::hydration}}
extra:
Water is added
–OH is added to the β carbon and –H is added to the α carbon
example: Enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water across the trans C=C, giving L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA.

text: Amino acids are simple organic compounds containing both a {{c1::carboxyl (—COOH)}} group and an {{c1::amino (—NH2)}} group
example: Glycine, H<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH, is the simplest: one amino group and one carboxyl on a single carbon

text: Upon entry into the duodenum, {{c1::emulsification}} occurs, which is the mixing of two normally immiscible liquids; in this case, fat and water
extra: Emulsification increases the surface area of the lipid, which permits greater enzymatic interaction and processing
example: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil in water held together by egg-yolk lecithin.

text:
The three steps in translation are:
  1. {{c1::Initiation}}
  2. {{c1::Elongation}}
  3. {{c1::Termination}}
example: For 5′-AUG GCC UGA-3′: initiation at AUG, elongation adds Ala, termination at UGA

text: {{c1::Gluconeogenesis}} occurs during periods of fasting, starvation, low-carbohydrate diets, or intense exercise
example: Someone on a keto diet eating under 20 g of carbohydrate a day relies on gluconeogenesis for blood glucose.

text: {{c1::Epimers}} are a subtype of diastereomers that differ at exactly one chiral carbon
example: D-glucose and D-galactose are C-4 epimers; D-glucose and D-mannose are C-2 epimers

text: Fructose comes from {{c1::honey, fruit, and sucrose}}
example: Table sugar (sucrose) is split by sucrase into one glucose and one fructose.

text: {{c1::Cooperative binding}} is when the binding of the first molecule of B to A changes the binding affinity of the second B molecule, making it more or less likely to bind
extra: Results in a sigmoidal curve
example: Once haemoglobin binds its first O<sub>2</sub>, its other three haems bind O<sub>2</sub> more readily

text: {{c1::Ketolysis}} regenerates acetyl-CoA for use as an energy source in peripheral tissues
example: During a long fast, the brain converts β-hydroxybutyrate back into acetyl-CoA to fuel its citric acid cycle.

text: This graph shows the activity of a/an {{c1::uncompetitive inhibitor::... inhibitor}}
example: Lithium-treated inositol monophosphatase gives a line parallel to the untreated one, shifted upward

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
This reaction produces {{c1::H2O}}
example: 2-Phosphoglycerate → phosphoenolpyruvate + H<sub>2</sub>O, a dehydration that creates a high-energy enol phosphate.

text: The main function of very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) is to transport fatty acids from {{c1::the liver}} to {{c1::tissues}}
example: After a high-carb meal, the liver packages new triglycerides into VLDL for adipose tissue.

text: The {{c1::citric acid cycle}} is a series of reactions that oxidizes acetyl-CoA
extra: It produces ATP, NADH, FADH2, and CO2
example: Each turn releases 2 CO<sub>2</sub>, matching acetyl-CoA's 2 carbons; this is CO<sub>2</sub> you exhale.

text: {{c1::Ketone bodies}} are produced from acetyl-CoA, mainly in the mitochondrial matrix of liver cells when carbohydrates are so scarce that energy must be obtained from breaking down of fatty acids
example: The liver makes ketones but lacks thiophorase (SCOT), so it cannot burn them itself.

text: A C16 fatty acid will undergo a maximum of {{c1::7::#}} rounds of beta oxidation
example: Stearic acid (C<sub>18</sub>) needs 18 ÷ 2 − 1 = 8 rounds, because the last cut leaves two acetyl-CoA.

text: Orexin {{c1::increases::increases or decreases}} appetite
example: Rats injected with orexin into the hypothalamus eat more food.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Cysteine}}
example: Insulin's A and B chains are held together by disulfide bridges between cysteine residues

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::aconitase}}
example: Fluoroacetate (a rat poison) becomes fluorocitrate, which blocks aconitase and halts the cycle.

text: The term symport is used during membrane transport when two particles flow in the {{c1::same direction}}
example: The kidney's Na<sup>+</sup>-K<sup>+</sup>-2Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransporter (furosemide's target) moves all four ions into the cell together.

text: When the terminal phosphate linkage in ATP is broken using water, {{c1::30::#}} kJ/mol of energy is released
example: Coupling ATP hydrolysis (−30.5 kJ/mol) to glucose + P<sub>i</sub> → G6P (+13.8) makes hexokinase's ΔG°′ −16.7 kJ/mol.

text: The pentose phosphate pathway produces {{c1::NADPH}} and {{c1::pentose}}
extra:
NADPH is used as a reducing agent in metabolism
The pentoses (5-carbon sugars, e.g. ribose) are used in nucleotide synthesis
example: Red blood cells use PPP NADPH to keep glutathione reduced and neutralise H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

text: Body mass index (BMI) = {{c1::\(\frac{weight~in~kg}{(height~in~meters)^2}\)}}
example: A 70 kg adult who is 1.75 m tall has BMI = 70 / 1.75<sup>2</sup> ≈ 22.9 kg/m<sup>2</sup>.

text: A {{c1::nucleosome}} is a segment of DNA wound around a core of eight histone proteins (histone octamer)
example: Each nucleosome wraps 147 bp of DNA about 1.7 turns around two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4

text:
In gel electrophoresis:
  • Small molecules move {{c1::fast::fast or slow}}
  • Large molecules move {{c1::slow::fast or slow}}
extra: Shorter molecules migrate more easily through the pores of the gel
example: A 100 bp DNA fragment runs far ahead of a 5,000 bp fragment on the same gel.

text: The main function of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) is to {{c1::transport cholesterol to tissues}}
example: Cells needing cholesterol for membranes take up LDL through apoB-100 binding the LDL receptor.

text: This is a/an {{c1::beta::alpha or beta}} glycosidic bond
example: Lactose's β-1,4 bond between galactose and glucose needs lactase; without it, lactose intolerance

text: A {{c1::positive::positive or negative}} sense RNA strand is itself an mRNA and can be translated directly into protein
example: Poliovirus and SARS-CoV-2 carry positive-sense RNA that host ribosomes translate as soon as it enters the cell

text:
In gel electrophoresis:
  • {{c1::Agarose}} gel has large pores so it is used to separate nucleic acids
  • {{c1::Polyacrylamide}} gel has small pores so it is better for separating proteins
extra: Nucleic acids are usually larger than proteins
example: A 1,000 bp PCR product is checked on a 1% agarose gel; a 25 kDa protein is run on SDS-PAGE.

text: GLUT-4 is found in {{c1::adipose tissue}} and {{c1::muscle}}
extra: GLUT-4 has a high affinity for glucose
example: After a meal, insulin moves GLUT-4 to the surface of muscle and fat cells to pull in glucose.

text: {{c1::Ion channels}} are membrane-spanning proteins that allow the passage of ions from one side of the membrane to the other
extra:
Types of ion channels:
  • Ungated (always open)
  • Mechanically gated
  • Voltage-gated
  • Ligand-gated
example: CFTR is a Cl<sup>−</sup> channel; its ΔF508 mutation causes cystic fibrosis

text: Gel electrophoresis is a technique commonly used in laboratories to separate charged molecules like DNA, RNA and proteins according to their {{c1::size}} and {{c1::charge}}
extra:
Small molecules move fast
Large molecules move slow
example: Forensic DNA fingerprinting separates DNA fragments on a gel to match a suspect's band pattern.

text: During the initiation of fatty acid synthesis, acetyl-CoA is activated through the synthesis of {{c1::malonyl-CoA}}
example: Acetyl-CoA + HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> + ATP → malonyl-CoA, with biotin as the cofactor.

text: In a {{c1::sugar esterification}}, a sugar reacts with a carboxylic acid or one of its derivatives to form an ester
extra: Sucrose ester, a surfactant and emulsifier, is synthesized from esterification of sucrose and a fatty acid:

text: Calorimeters measure the {{c1::heat generated by an organism}} which can be used to calculate the metabolic rate
example: Lavoisier measured a guinea pig's heat output by how much ice it melted in his ice calorimeter.

text: In eukaryotic translation, the 40S ribosomal subunit attaches to the {{c1::5’ cap}} and scans for the start codon
extra: It lays down methionine in the P site of the ribosome
example: The 40S subunit scans to the first AUG in a Kozak sequence such as GCCACCAUGG.

text: Complex II in the ETC is part of the {{c1::citric acid cycle}}
example: Succinate → fumarate, step 6 of the cycle, happens right in the inner membrane on Complex II.

text: A/an {{c1::phosphatase::type of enzyme}} removes a phosphate group
example: Liver glucose-6-phosphatase strips the phosphate from G6P so free glucose can leave into the blood

text: {{c1::Sphingolipids}} contain a sphingosine backbone
extra:
Protect the cell surface against harmful environmental factors
Many (but not all) sphingolipids are also phospholipids with a phosphodiester bond. These are sphingophospholipids
example: Ceramide, sphingosine plus one fatty acid, is the simplest sphingolipid and seals the skin's outer barrier

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Threonine}}
example: Protein kinase A switches enzymes on or off by phosphorylating the –OH of their serine and threonine residues

text: This is a/an {{c1::alpha::alpha or beta}} glycosidic bond
example: Salivary amylase cuts starch's α-1,4 glucose links, which is why bread tastes sweeter as you chew

text: {{c1::Soap}} is a form of lipid which is a mixture of sodium salts of various naturally occurring fatty acids
example: Lye (NaOH) plus olive oil gives sodium oleate, a soap whose micelles lift grease off dishes.

text: {{c1::Disulfide bonds}} occur when two cysteine molecules are oxidized and create a covalent bond between their thiol groups
example: A perm breaks hair keratin's disulfide bonds with a reducing agent, then reforms them in the curled shape

text: Exergonic reactions {{c1::release::require or release}} energy
example: ATP hydrolysis to ADP + P<sub>i</sub> releases about 30.5 kJ/mol (ΔG°′ ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol)

text: The regulatory enzyme for fatty acid synthesis is {{c1::acetyl-CoA carboxylase}}
extra: It activates acetyl-CoA
example: Insulin and citrate activate acetyl-CoA carboxylase; glucagon and palmitoyl-CoA inhibit it.

text: {{c1::Glycine}} is the only amino acid that is not chiral
example: A glycine solution in a polarimeter shows zero optical rotation, unlike a solution of L-alanine

text: {{c1::Sanger sequencing::... sequencing}} is a method of DNA sequencing based on the selective incorporation of chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides
example: A fragment that ends in ddA at position 15 shows the new strand has A there (so the template has T).

text: The above molecule is known as {{c1::ATP}}
example: A resting adult turns over roughly their own body weight in ATP each day.

text: This is the {{c1::guanidinium}} group
example: Creatine carries a guanidinium group, which muscle phosphorylates to store energy as creatine phosphate

text: This is the monosaccharide {{c1::glucose}}
example: Fasting blood glucose is normally about 70–100 mg/dL.

text:
The isoelectric point formula when there is a basic side chain is:
{{c1::}}
{{c1::Glycogenesis}} converts glucose to glycogen and {{c1::glycogenolysis}} converts glycogen to glucose
example: Between meals, liver glycogenolysis keeps blood glucose near 5 mM; after meals, glycogenesis stores the excess.

text: A/an {{c1::noncompetitive inhibitor::... inhibitor}} binds at the allosteric site, away from the active site
extra: It does not prevent the substrate from binding to the active site
example: Like a doorstop jammed in a hinge: the key still fits the lock, but the door will not open

text: In translation, a succession of {{c1::tRNAs}} add their amino acids to the polypeptide chain as the mRNA is moved through the {{c1::ribosome}} one codon at a time
example: Reading 5′-AUG UUU GGC-3′, tRNAs bring Met, then Phe, then Gly in order

text:
The above reaction is from gluconeogenesis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase}}
example: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate + H<sub>2</sub>O → fructose-6-phosphate + P<sub>i</sub>, undoing the PFK-1 step.

text: The {{c1::3rd base::which base}} in a codon can wobble and break standard Watson-Crick rules but still code for the intended protein
extra:
Wobble is caused by redundancy found in the genetic code
Wobble base pairings are less stable
example: Glycine's codons GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG differ only at the 3rd base, so one tRNA can read several

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::pyruvate kinase}}
example: Pyruvate kinase deficiency starves red cells of ATP and causes haemolytic anaemia.

text: An operon {{c1::promoter}} is the binding site for RNA polymerase, the enzyme that performs transcription
example: Bacterial promoters carry a −10 TATAAT (Pribnow) box where RNA polymerase binds

text: Lipoproteins are named based on their overall {{c1::density}}
extra:
Protein is more dense than triglyceride
The lipoprotein with the most protein is the most dense and is named high-density lipoprotein (HDL)
example: Chylomicrons, mostly triglyceride, are the least dense and float to the top of chilled plasma.

text: Amino acids undergo degradation and send {{c1::NH3}} to the urea cycle
example: In liver failure, NH<sub>3</sub> from amino acid breakdown builds up and causes hepatic encephalopathy.

text: {{c1::Gluconeogenesis}} is the process in which pyruvic acid is converted to glucose
example: In the Cori cycle, lactate from exercising muscle is turned back into glucose by the liver.

text: A/an {{c1::chromatid}} is one half of a chromosome
extra: One of the chromatids is an identical copy of the other
example: A replicated chromosome 1 at metaphase is two sister chromatids joined at the centromere

text: The pentose phosphate pathway converts {{c1::NADP+}} to {{c1::NADPH}}
example: In G6PD deficiency, red cells make too little NADPH and haemolyse after eating fava beans.

text:
The isoelectric point formula when there is a neutral side chain is:
{{c1::}}

Acetyl-CoA feeds into the following two processes:
  • {{c1::Citric acid cycle}}
  • {{c1::Fatty acid synthesis}}
links: Khan Academy · Fatty Acid Synthesis · Khan Academy · Citric Acid Cycle
example: After a carb-heavy meal, excess acetyl-CoA in the liver is turned into palmitate instead of being burned.

text: A/an {{c1::phosphorylase::type of enzyme}} adds a phosphate group from an inorganic phosphate like HPO42− to a substrate
example: Glycogen phosphorylase uses P<sub>i</sub> to cleave glucose off glycogen as glucose-1-phosphate

text: A/an {{c1::competitive inhibitor::... inhibitor}} binds at the active site and thus prevents the substrate from binding
extra: Can be overcome by adding more substrate
example: Methanol poisoning is treated with ethanol, which competes for alcohol dehydrogenase's active site

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Serine}}
example: Sarin nerve gas binds the active-site serine of acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine is never cleared

text: Lipids are {{c1::insoluble}} in water and {{c1::soluble}} in nonpolar organic solvents
example: Olive oil floats on water as a separate layer but dissolves readily in hexane or ether

text: {{c1::Transcription factors}} are proteins that help turn specific genes "on" or "off" by binding to nearby DNA
example: Once cortisol binds, the glucocorticoid receptor enters the nucleus and switches on its target genes

text: Carbohydrates in cell membranes can form a protective {{c1::glycoprotein}} coat
extra: They also function in cell recognition
example: The A and B blood-group sugars on red blood cells are part of this glycoprotein coat.

text: {{c1::Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)}} is a polymer made up of monomers called nucleotides. Long strands form a double helix which runs antiparallel
example: 5′-GGATCC-3′ pairs with 3′-CCTAGG-5′, the two strands running in opposite directions

text: A/an {{c1::isomerase::type of enzyme}} catalyzes the interconversion of isomers
example: Triose phosphate isomerase converts DHAP into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate in glycolysis

text: The ETC creates a {{c1::proton concentration gradient}} that is used to power ATP synthase
extra: Protons are pumped into the intermembrane space so the concentration gradient is across the inner mitochondrial membrane
example: Uncouplers like 2,4-dinitrophenol let protons leak back, so the energy is lost as heat instead of ATP.

text: Complex II in the ETC oxidizes {{c1::succinate}} to form {{c1::fumarate}}
extra: Complex II directly receives FADH2, which does not pass through complex I
example: Each turn of the cycle, 4-carbon succinate loses 2 H to become fumarate, a trans alkene.

text: {{c1::Motor proteins::... proteins}} convert chemical energy into mechanical work by the hydrolysis of ATP
extra:
Common applications:
Muscle contraction
Vesicle movement
Cell motility
Examples:
Myosin
Kinesin
Dynein
example: Kinesin walks synaptic vesicles along axon microtubules toward the nerve terminal, one ATP per 8 nm step

text: {{c1::Isoelectric point}} is the pH at which an amino acid is in zwitterion form
extra: The charges cancel out to make a neutral molecule
example: Glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) is a zwitterion at pH 6 and does not migrate in an electric field

text: The {{c1::3°::1°, 2°, 3°, or 4°}} structure of proteins is the 3-D shape of a single polypeptide chain
extra: Stabilized by hydrophobic interactions, acid-base interactions, hydrogen-bonds, and disulfide bonds
example: Myoglobin is a single chain whose 3° fold buries hydrophobic side chains and cradles one haem

text: A/an {{c1::nonsense mutation::... mutation}} produces a premature stop codon
example: β-globin codon 39 CAG (Gln) → TAG (stop) truncates the chain, causing β<sup>0</sup>-thalassaemia

text: Humans have {{c1::23::#}} pairs of chromosomes, for a total of {{c1::46::#}} chromosomes
example: Down syndrome is trisomy 21: 47 chromosomes instead of 46

text: The citric acid cycle requires {{c1::1::#}} ADP and produces {{c1::1::#}} ATP
example: Per glucose the cycle turns twice, making 2 GTP/ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

text: {{c1::Passive transport::... transport}} is when the molecule moves down its concentration gradient, so no energy is required
example: O<sub>2</sub> diffuses from alveoli into blood with no ATP spent because alveolar P<sub>O2</sub> is higher.

text: The primary structure of nucleic acids is the {{c1::linear sequence of nucleotides}}
example: 5′-ATGC-3′ and 5′-CGTA-3′ contain the same four bases but are different primary structures

text:
Metabolic Pathways Overview
{{c1::}}
example: A sugary snack's glucose can become pyruvate, then acetyl-CoA, then CO<sub>2</sub> in the citric acid cycle or stored fat.

text: Cooperative enzymes display a {{c1::sigmoidal::shape}} curve
extra: Sigmoidal because of the change in activity following initial substrate binding
example: ATCase, the allosteric enzyme of pyrimidine synthesis, gives a sigmoidal rate vs [aspartate] curve

text: The omega end of a fatty acid is the {{c1::methyl::methyl or carboxylic acid}} end
example: In α-linolenic acid, the CH<sub>3</sub> at the tail is the ω carbon, opposite the COOH.

text: Beta oxidation occurs in the {{c1::mitochondrial matrix::part of cell}}
example: Heart muscle, packed with mitochondria, gets most of its ATP from β-oxidation in the matrix.

text: If pH = pI then the amino acid is a {{c1::zwitterion}}
example: Glycine at its pI of about 6.0 exists as <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>.

text: The urea cycle converts {{c1::ammonia}} to urea which is then excreted in urine
extra: Amino acid metabolism produces ammonia which is toxic to the body and must be excreted
example: In ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, ammonia builds up and newborns become lethargic and comatose.

text: A/an {{c1::ligase::type of enzyme}} joins two large biomolecules, often of the same type
example: DNA ligase seals the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand into one continuous strand

text: An irreversible inhibitor is any inhibitor that {{c1::covalently binds}} to the active site of some enzyme, thus eliminating its activity
example: Aspirin acetylates a serine in COX's active site, so platelets lose thromboxane for their 7–10 day lifespan

text: Step 1 of fatty acid synthesis: {{c1::Attach}}
extra: Acetyl-CoA attaches to acyl carrier protein
example: Like a bead clipped onto a string, the acetyl group is loaded onto ACP's phosphopantetheine arm by a thioester.

text: {{c1::Recombinant DNA}} is DNA composed of nucleotides from two different sources, created only in labs
example: Human insulin (Humulin, 1982) is made by E. coli carrying the human insulin gene in a plasmid

text: The two main enzymes in glycogenolysis are {{c1::glycogen phosphorylase}} and {{c1::debranching enzyme}}
example: McArdle disease (muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency) causes cramps during exercise.

text: {{c1::Osmotic pressure}} is the pressure that needs to be applied to a solution to prevent the inward flow of water (prevent osmosis)
extra: Osmotic pressure is used to express the concentration of a solution
example: A 0.1 M glucose solution at 298 K has Π = MRT = 0.1 × 0.0821 × 298 ≈ 2.45 atm.

text:
The four fat soluble vitamins are:
  • {{c1::A}}
  • {{c1::D}}
  • {{c1::E}}
  • {{c1::K}}
example: Eating polar bear liver causes vitamin A poisoning because the fat-soluble vitamin is stored, not excreted

text: {{c1::Glycerophospholipids}} are the same as triacylglycerols except one of the fatty acids is replaced with a phosphate group
example: Swap tristearin's third stearate for phosphate and you get phosphatidic acid, the simplest glycerophospholipid

text: {{c1::Glycogenesis}} is the production of glycogen from sugar
example: After a pasta dinner, the liver and muscles store the extra glucose as glycogen.

text: This graph shows the activity of a/an {{c1::competitive inhibitor::... inhibitor}}
example: Dihydrofolate reductase lines with and without methotrexate cross the y-axis at the same 1/V<sub>max</sub>

text: {{c1::Km}} is the substrate concentration that gives you a reaction rate that is halfway to Vmax
example: Hexokinase (K<sub>m</sub> ≈ 0.1 mM) is half-saturated at far lower glucose than glucokinase (K<sub>m</sub> ≈ 10 mM)

text: {{c1::Centromeres}} are located in the middle of chromosomes and hold sister chromatids together until they are separated during anaphase in mitosis
extra: High GC-content to maintain a strong bond between chromatids
example: Cohesin at the centromere holds sister chromatids together until separase cleaves it at anaphase

text: {{c1::Messenger RNA}} is transcribed from DNA in the nucleus and then travels into the cytoplasm for translation
example: Insulin mRNA is made in a β-cell nucleus, then exits through nuclear pores to ribosomes on the rough ER

text: A Michaelis-Menten curve is {{c1::hyperbolic::shape}}
example: Hexokinase's rate climbs steeply at low glucose, then levels off as it nears V<sub>max</sub>

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Valine}}
example: Sickle-cell anaemia: valine replaces glutamate 6 of β-globin, and its hydrophobic side chain makes HbS clump

text: {{c1::Alternative splicing}} is a regulated process during gene expression that results in a single gene coding for multiple proteins
extra:
In normal gene expression, introns are cut away and exons remain in the sequence
In alternative splicing, a certain exon may be cut out or an intron may stay, so one gene can code for more than one protein
example: The calcitonin gene makes calcitonin in the thyroid but CGRP in neurons by alternative splicing

text: Cholesterol may be obtained through dietary sources or through {{c1::de novo synthesis}} in the liver
example: A strict vegan eats no cholesterol yet still has plenty in their blood because the liver makes it.

text: The glycolysis enzyme pyruvate kinase is irreversible. This is why in gluconeogenesis, pyruvate must first be converted to {{c1::oxaloacetate}} before becoming phosphoenolpyruvate
example: Biotin deficiency (from eating raw egg whites) impairs pyruvate carboxylase and this bypass.

text: Acetyl-CoA contains a high energy {{c1::thioester}} bond that can be used to drive other reactions
example: Citrate synthase uses the energy of acetyl-CoA's thioester to drive its condensation with oxaloacetate.

text:
The isoelectric point formula when there is an acidic side chain is:
{{c1::}}
DNA methylation {{c1::decreases::increases or decreases}} the accessibility of chromatin and stops DNA binding proteins from interacting
example: Methylated CpG islands keep most genes on the inactive X chromosome (Barr body) silent

text: The two major regulatory enzymes in gluconeogenesis are {{c1::pyruvate carboxylase}} and {{c1::fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase}}
example: Glucagon lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, releasing fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase to run gluconeogenesis.

text: {{c1::Disaccharides}} form as a result of a glycosidic bond between two monosaccharide subunits
example: Sucrose is glucose and fructose joined by an α-1,β-2 glycosidic bond

text: {{c1::Glucogenic amino acids::... amino acids}} are amino acids that can be converted into glucose through gluconeogenesis
extra: A product of protein catabolism
example: Alanine from muscle becomes pyruvate and then glucose in the liver (glucose–alanine cycle).

text: DNA polymerase reads the template strand {{c1::3'::# prime}} → {{c1::5'::# prime}} and synthesizes the new strand {{c1::5'::# prime}} → {{c1::3'::# prime}}
example: Reading template 3'-TACG-5', DNA polymerase builds the new strand 5'-ATGC-3'.

text: The {{c1::β-anomer::... anomer}} has the -OH on the anomeric carbon pointing up
example: Cellulose is β-D-glucose joined by β-1,4 links, which humans lack the enzyme to digest

text: {{c1::The central dogma}} states that DNA is transcribed to RNA, which is translated to protein
example: The β-globin gene is transcribed into β-globin mRNA, which ribosomes translate into haemoglobin's β chain

text: SDS-PAGE denatures proteins and separates them solely based on {{c1::mass}}
extra: This allows you to estimate the protein’s molecular mass
example: A 25 kDa protein runs farther down an SDS-PAGE gel than 66 kDa serum albumin, whatever their native charges.

text: A/an {{c1::frameshift mutation::... mutation}} results from a nucleotide addition or deletion, and changes the reading frame of subsequent codons
example: THE FAT CAT ATE THE RAT, minus the first E, reads THF ATC ATA TET HER AT

text: This graph shows the activity of a/an {{c1::noncompetitive inhibitor::... inhibitor}}
example: Halving V<sub>max</sub> from 10 to 5 µM/s doubles the y-intercept from 0.1 to 0.2 s/µM; the x-intercept stays put

text: {{c1::Exons}} are regions of a gene that code for proteins
extra:
Exons exit the nucleus and form mRNA
Introns stay in the nucleus since they are cut out and not included in mRNA
example: The β-globin gene's three exons are spliced together into the mRNA for haemoglobin's 146-residue β chain

text: Three fates of pyruvate (shown above): {{c1::acetaldehyde}}, {{c1::lactate}}, and {{c1::acetyl-CoA}}
extra: Pyruvate can also be converted to oxaloacetate
example: Brewer's yeast sends pyruvate to acetaldehyde, while your sprinting muscles turn it into lactate.

text: {{c1::Denaturation}} is when a protein (or nucleic acid) loses its 4°, 3°, and 2° structures due to breaking non-covalent interactions
example: Frying an egg denatures its albumin, turning the runny clear white solid and opaque

text: DNA {{c1::replication}} is the process of producing an identical replica of a DNA molecule
extra: Occurs in the S (synthesis) phase of the cell cycle
example: A dividing human cell copies about 6 billion base pairs during an S phase lasting roughly 8 hours

text: The {{c1::electron transport chain}} is a series of complexes that transfer electrons from electron donors to electron acceptors via redox reactions
extra: This electron transfer is coupled with the transfer of protons across a membrane to create a proton gradient
example: Electrons pass NADH → Complex I → CoQ → Complex III → cytochrome c → Complex IV → O<sub>2</sub>.

text: The process that converts fatty acid to Acetyl-CoA is {{c1::β-Oxidation}}
example: During a marathon, muscles break stored fatty acids into acetyl-CoA by β-oxidation.

text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is a complex of three enzymes that converts {{c1::pyruvate}} into {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} by a process called pyruvate decarboxylation
example: Its three enzymes, E1, E2 and E3, need five cofactors: TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD<sup>+</sup>.

text: Ribosomes are factories where {{c1::translation (protein synthesis)}} occurs
example: Ribosomes on the rough ER of pancreatic acinar cells translate digestive enzymes like trypsinogen

text: {{c1::Histone acetylation}} increases the accessibility of chromatin and allows DNA binding proteins to interact
example: CBP/p300 acetylates histone H3 lysines at active genes, loosening chromatin for RNA polymerase

text: Complex IV in the ETC is also known as {{c1::cytochrome oxidase}}
extra: Cytochrome is oxidized as it reduces O2 to H2O
example: Cyanide and carbon monoxide kill by blocking Complex IV.

text: The {{c1::4°::1°, 2°, 3°, or 4°}} structure of proteins is the interaction between peptides in proteins that contain multiple subunits
extra: Example: the 4° structure of hemoglobin

text: A {{c1::flippase::enzyme}} is a membrane protein that moves lipids between the two layers of the phospholipid bilayer
example: Flippases keep phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet; when they stop in apoptosis, PS appears outside

text: The N-terminus of a peptide chain is {{c1::positively::positively or negatively}} charged
extra: Due to the –NH3+ group
example: At physiological pH, Gly-Ala carries +1 at its N-terminus and −1 at its C-terminus.

text: Polysaccharides are formed by repeated monosaccharide or polysaccharide {{c1::glycosidic}} bonding
example: Amylose in starch is a chain of hundreds of glucose units joined by α-1,4 glycosidic bonds.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::enolase}}
example: Fluoride in grey-top blood tubes inhibits enolase, stopping glycolysis in the sample.

text: The tertiary structure of nucleic acids is the {{c1::location of the atoms in 3D space}}
example: tRNA's flat cloverleaf folds into a compact L shape, with the anticodon at one tip and the CCA end at the other

text: Single strand binding protein binds to single-stranded DNA and serves to {{c1::prevent annealing of single-stranded DNA into double-stranded DNA}}
example: E. coli SSB tetramers coat the exposed lagging-strand template behind the helicase

text: The 3° structure of proteins is stabilized primarily by {{c1::hydrophobic interactions}}
example: Myoglobin folds with leucine and valine side chains buried in its core, away from water.

text: Simple diffusion is when molecules passively move from an area of {{c1::high::low or high}} concentration to an area of {{c1::low::high or low}} concentration until equilibrium is achieved
example: A drop of food colouring spreads through a glass of still water until the colour is even.

text: {{c1::Proline::Amino acid}} has a rigid cyclic structure and can interrupt 2° protein structure
extra: Proline is "kinky"
example: Collagen's high proline content prevents α-helices, forcing a looser left-handed polyproline helix instead

text: Acyl-CoA must use the {{c1::carnitine shuttle}} to pass through the inner mitochondrial membrane
extra: Acyl-CoA can pass through porins in the outer membrane, but it needs the assistance of carnitine in order to move through the inner membrane
example: In carnitine deficiency, muscles cannot burn long-chain fats, causing weakness and fasting hypoglycaemia.

text: Triacylglycerols and fatty acids act as precursors to {{c1::phospholipids}}
example: Type II pneumocytes build lung surfactant, dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, from palmitic acid

text: Proteins and carbohydrates may move within the membrane, but are slowed by {{c1::their relatively large size}}
example: Bleach a spot of membrane and fluorescent lipids refill it within seconds, labelled proteins far more slowly

text: Step 4 of fatty acid synthesis: {{c1::Dehydration}}
extra:
The –OH group is removed through dehydration, which produces a water molecule
This leaves behind a C=C double bond
example: 3-Hydroxybutyryl-ACP loses water to become crotonyl-ACP, with a trans C=C.

text: A/an {{c1::uncompetitive inhibitor::... inhibitor}} binds only with the enzyme-substrate complex
example: Lithium inhibits inositol monophosphatase uncompetitively, binding only once the substrate is bound

text: Omega fatty acids are classified according to the {{c1::location of the first double bond from the omega end}}
example: Linoleic acid's first double bond is 6 carbons from the methyl end, making it an omega-6.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Glutamate}}
example: Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, acting on NMDA and AMPA receptors

text: During osmosis, water moves from an area of {{c1::low::low or high}} solute concentration to an area of {{c1::high::low or high}} solute concentration
extra: "Water wants to go to where the party is"
example: A cucumber in brine loses water to the salty solution and shrivels into a pickle.

text: The {{c1::induced fit theory::... theory}} states that the enzyme and substrate undergo conformational changes in order to interact fully
example: Hexokinase's two lobes clamp shut around glucose, closing the cleft only after it binds

text: Prokaryotic ribosomes are {{c1::70::#}} Svedberg units
example: Streptomycin targets the 30S subunit of bacterial 70S ribosomes, sparing human cytoplasmic ribosomes

text: FADH2 powers the creation of {{c1::1.5::#}} ATP
example: The 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> from one glucose yield about 2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP.

text: At the first equivalence point in the titration of an amino acid with a neutral side chain, pH = {{c1::pI}}
example: Titrating glycine with NaOH, the first equivalence point falls at pH ≈ 6.0, glycine's pI

text: Pinocytosis is the ingestion of {{c1::liquids}} via vesicles
example: Capillary endothelial cells sip plasma into small vesicles and ferry it across the cell.

text: {{c1::Enzymes}} are reusable catalysts that are unchanged by the reactions they catalyze
extra: Catalyze both the forward and reverse reactions
example: One catalase molecule breaks down millions of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> molecules per second without being used up

text:
The isoelectric point formula when there is no side chain is:
{{c1::}}
GLUT-2 is found in the {{c1::liver}}
extra: GLUT-2 has a low affinity for glucose
example: After a meal, low-affinity GLUT-2 lets hepatocytes take up glucose only when portal blood glucose is high.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Isoleucine}}
example: Isoleucine, leucine and valine are the branched-chain amino acids that build up in maple syrup urine disease

text:
The three major regulatory enzymes in glycolysis are:
  • {{c1::Hexokinase}}
  • {{c1::Phosphofructokinase (PFK)}}
  • {{c1::Pyruvate kinase}}
example: Glucagon in the fasting liver phosphorylates and inactivates pyruvate kinase, slowing glycolysis.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Asparagine}}
example: N-linked glycosylation in the ER attaches sugar chains to the amide nitrogen of asparagine

text: A {{c1::nucleotide}} is a nucleoside with 1 to 3 phosphate groups added
example: ATP is adenosine with three phosphates and AMP is adenosine with one: both are nucleotides

text: {{c1::Antibodies}} are used by the immune system to target a specific antigen, which may be a protein on the surface of a pathogen or a toxin
extra: Antibodies are also known as immunoglobulins
example: Tetanus antitoxin antibodies bind and neutralise tetanus toxin before it reaches nerves

text: When pyruvate converts to acetaldehyde, the next step converts acetaldehyde to {{c1::ethanol}}
example: Brewer's yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae turns acetaldehyde into the ethanol in beer, regenerating NAD+.

text:
Glycolysis overall reaction:
{{c1::Glucose + 2 NAD+ + 2 ADP + 2 Pi}} → {{c1::2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 H2O}}
example: Red blood cells, with no mitochondria, get all their ATP from this reaction: 2 ATP per glucose.

text: {{c1::Vmax}} is the maximum rate at which an enzyme can catalyze a reaction
extra: This is when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate
example: With 1 µmol of enzyme and k<sub>cat</sub> = 100 s<sup>−1</sup>, V<sub>max</sub> = 100 µmol/s; more substrate cannot push it higher

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
This reaction requires {{c1::Pi}} and {{c1::NAD+}} and it produces {{c1::NADH}}
example: Arsenate can stand in for P<sub>i</sub> here, so glycolysis still runs but nets no ATP.

text: A {{c1::nucleoside}} is a 5-carbon sugar plus a nitrogenous base and no phosphate groups
example: Adenosine, adenine plus ribose with no phosphate, is given IV to slow the heart in SVT

text: The {{c1::respiratory quotient}} is the ratio of the volume of carbon dioxide produced to that of oxygen consumed
