example: Burning pure glucose gives RQ = 6 CO<sub>2</sub> / 6 O<sub>2</sub> = 1.0; burning fat gives about 0.7.

text: Enzyme-linked receptors participate in cell signaling through extracellular ligand binding and initiation of {{c1::2nd messenger cascades}}
example: Insulin binds its receptor tyrosine kinase, which autophosphorylates and recruits IRS-1 to start the cascade

text: Chylomicrons transport lipids through the {{c1::lymphatic system::... system}}
example: Chylomicrons enter lacteals and reach the blood via the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver at first.

text: The storage form of glucose in animals is {{c1::glycogen}}
example: A well-fed adult stores roughly 100 g of glycogen in the liver and about 400 g in muscle.

text: Triacylglycerols contain a glycerol attached to 3 fatty acids by {{c1::ester}} bonds
example: Pancreatic lipase hydrolyses the ester bonds of dietary triglycerides to free fatty acids.

text: This is an example of a {{c1::Haworth projection::... projection}}
extra: Haworth projections represent the cyclic structure of monosaccharides with a simple three-dimensional perspective
example: Drawn as a Haworth, β-D-glucopyranose is a flat hexagon with the ring O at back right and the C-1 –OH up

text: {{c1::Lipoproteins}} transport fat molecules throughout the body
example: A fasting lipid panel measures LDL and HDL, two lipoproteins that carry cholesterol in blood.

text: {{c1::Carbohydrates}} are "hydrates of carbon"
extra:
Usually have the formula Cm(H2O)n
Example: Glucose is C6H12O6
H:O ratio is usually 2:1 due to the "hydration" with H2O
Glucose:

text:
The above reaction is from gluconeogenesis
This reaction requires {{c1::H2O}}
example: PEP + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2-phosphoglycerate, the reverse of glycolysis's enolase step.

text: The 1° structure of proteins is stabilized by {{c1::peptide bonds}}
example: Boiling an egg leaves the peptide bonds of albumin intact, so its primary structure survives.

text: {{c1::Exocytosis}} is the process by which the contents of a cell vacuole are released to the exterior
example: Synaptic vesicles fuse with the axon terminal membrane to release acetylcholine into the synapse.

text:
Adenine and Thymine are held together by {{c1::2::#}} hydrogen bonds
Guanine and Cytosine are held together by {{c1::3::#}} hydrogen bonds
extra: Note: RNA has U instead of T
example: A 10 bp all-GC duplex has 30 H-bonds and an all-AT one has 20, so the AT duplex melts at a lower temperature

text: In glycogenolysis, glycogen debranching enzyme breaks branches of glucose molecules off by hydrolyzing {{c1::α-1,6 glycosidic bonds::... glycosidic bonds}}
extra: This creates a single chain of glycogen
example: Cori disease (debranching enzyme deficiency) leaves glycogen with short outer branches.

text: The amino acid sequence of a peptide chain is written {{c1::N}}-terminus to {{c1::C}}-terminus
example: In the dipeptide Ala-Gly, alanine carries the free amino group and glycine the free carboxyl.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Glutamine}}
example: Huntington disease: an expanded CAG repeat adds a long polyglutamine tract to the huntingtin protein

text:
Initiation (start) Codon: {{c1::AUG}}
Termination (stop) Codons: {{c1::UAA}}, {{c1::UGA}}, {{c1::UAG}}
example: 5′-AUG GCC UAA-3′ is read as Met-Ala, then translation stops at UAA

text: {{c1::Mutarotation}} is the spontaneous shift from one anomeric form to another
extra: The straight-chain form is an intermediate
example: A fresh α-D-glucose solution's rotation drifts from +112° to a steady +52.7° as it equilibrates with the β form

text: {{c1::Conjugated proteins}} are complex proteins, such as hemoglobin, consisting of amino acids combined with other substances
example: LDL is a lipoprotein: apolipoprotein B-100 wrapped around cholesterol and triglycerides

text:
In noncompetitive inhibition:
  • Vmax: {{c1::goes down}}
  • Km: {{c1::has no change}}
example: A noncompetitive inhibitor might cut V<sub>max</sub> from 100 to 50 µmol/min while K<sub>m</sub> stays at 4 mM

text: A repressible operon under normal conditions will {{c1::proceed with transcription}}
extra:
Repressible operons are turned off when a corepressor couples with the repressor and this complex binds the operator site
Example: trp operon

text: The 5′ cap and poly-A tail on mRNA {{c1::protect mRNA for translation}}
example: mRNA vaccines carry a 5′ cap and poly-A tail so the injected mRNA survives long enough to be translated

text: Ungated ion channels are {{c1::always::sometimes or always}} open
example: K<sup>+</sup> leak channels stay open at rest, letting K<sup>+</sup> seep out to set the −70 mV resting potential

text: Lipids move freely in the plane of the cell membrane and can assemble into {{c1::lipid rafts}}
example: HIV buds from cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich lipid rafts in the host cell membrane

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::citrate synthase}}
example: Citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA (2 C) to oxaloacetate (4 C) to make citrate (6 C).

text: The {{c1::postabsorptive state::... state}} occurs after digestion and absorption. The body must rely on energy stores such as glycogen for its energy
extra: Postabsorptive state = fasting state
example: By 7 a.m. after an overnight fast, glucagon has the liver breaking down glycogen to hold blood glucose steady.

text: Ketogenesis is the biochemical process through which organisms produce {{c1::ketone bodies}} through breakdown of fatty acids and ketogenic amino acids
example: On a low-carb keto diet, the liver turns fat into acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate.

text: In translation elongation, the new tRNA enters the ribosome at the {{c1::A}} site
extra:
The growing polypeptide chain is transferred from the P site to the A site to meet the new tRNA
Before leaving the ribosome, the tRNA stops in the E site. The order of sites for the tRNA is A-P-E
example: Reading AUG-UUU, Met-tRNA sits in the P site while Phe-tRNA enters the A site

text: A/an {{c1::kinase::type of enzyme}} adds a phosphate group from ATP to a substrate
example: Hexokinase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, trapping it in the cell

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::hexokinase}}
example: In the liver, glucokinase does this job; its high K<sub>m</sub> lets it work mainly after a meal.

text: {{c1::Topoisomerase::Enzyme}} relieves supercoiling (torsional strain) ahead of the replication fork
example: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin kill bacteria by blocking DNA gyrase, a topoisomerase

text: {{c1::DNA polymerase::Enzyme}} adds nucleotides to the growing strand during DNA replication
extra: DNA Polymerase also removes the RNA primer at the end of the strands
example: E. coli DNA polymerase III adds about 1,000 nucleotides per second at each fork

text: A/an {{c1::prosthetic group}} is the attached molecule in a conjugated protein and can be a metal ion, vitamin, lipid, carbohydrate, or nucleic acid
example: Haem, with its Fe<sup>2+</sup>, is the prosthetic group that lets haemoglobin carry O<sub>2</sub>

text: {{c1::Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)}} is a fast and inexpensive technique used to amplify, or make many copies of, a specific target region of DNA in the lab
example: Thirty PCR cycles turn one target copy into 2<sup>30</sup>, about 1 billion, copies.

text: {{c1::Integral proteins::... proteins}} have one or more segments that are embedded in the phospholipid bilayer
example: Bacteriorhodopsin threads seven α-helices through the bilayer and can only be pulled out with detergent.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
This reaction requires {{c1::oxaloacetate}} and {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} and produces {{c1::citrate}} and {{c1::CoA}}
example: Low oxaloacetate in the fasting liver slows citrate synthase, diverting acetyl-CoA to ketone bodies.

text: {{c1::Transcription}} is the first step of gene expression, in which a segment of DNA is copied into RNA by the enzyme RNA polymerase
example: α-Amanitin from death cap mushrooms kills by blocking transcription by RNA polymerase II

text: {{c1::Phosphofructokinase}} is the enzyme that catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis
extra:
After this step, the sugar molecule is committed to completing Glycolysis
Prior to this step, the sugar molecule could have been redirected to be converted to glycogen
example: Insulin after a meal raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which strongly activates PFK-1.

text: Membrane potential is maintained by the {{c1::Na+/K+ pump}} and by {{c1::leak channels}}
example: K<sup>+</sup> leaking out through leak channels is the main reason a neuron rests near −70 mV.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::phosphoglycerate kinase}}
example: It moves a phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP, making glycolysis's first ATP.

text: Long-chain fatty acids are absorbed as micelles and assembled into {{c1::chylomicrons}} for release into the lymphatic system
extra: Short-chain fatty acids are absorbed across the intestine into the blood
example: After a greasy breakfast, chylomicrons turn the lymph in intestinal lacteals milky (chyle).

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::triose phosphate isomerase}}
example: TPI converts DHAP into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, so both halves of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate continue.

text: {{c1::Endocytosis}} is a method of engulfing material into the cells
example: Cells take up LDL cholesterol by receptor-mediated endocytosis in clathrin-coated pits.

text: Galactose comes from {{c1::lactose in milk}}
example: Babies with galactosemia must avoid breast milk and lactose-containing formula.

text: The {{c1::Watson-Crick model::... model}} states that DNA is a double-stranded, helical structure
extra: The two strands are antiparallel
example: Watson and Crick built their 1953 double-helix model using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray Photo 51

text: {{c1::RNA primers}} are short RNA nucleotide sequences that are complementary to the ssDNA and allow DNA replication to start
example: The lagging strand needs a new RNA primer for every Okazaki fragment, so E. coli lays down thousands per genome copy

text: The quaternary structure of nucleic acids is made up of {{c1::interactions of nucleic acids with other molecules}}
extra: Example: DNA interacting with histones to form chromatin

text: The secondary structure of nucleic acids is made up of {{c1::interactions between bases within the same molecule}}
extra:
The secondary structure is responsible for the shape that the nucleic acid assumes
RNA 2° structure has 4 basic elements: loops, helices, bulges, and junctions
example: tRNA folds into a cloverleaf as bases within its single strand pair up into stems and loops

text: A/an {{c1::binding protein::... protein}} is any protein that acts as an agent to bind two or more molecules together
extra:
Examples:
DNA-binding protein
Single-strand binding protein
Telomere-binding protein
example: Serum albumin binds and carries fatty acids, bilirubin and drugs like warfarin in the blood

text: ETC Complex II removes 2 hydrogens from {{c1::succinate}} and adds them to {{c1::FAD}}
extra:
This produces fumarate and FADH2
FADH2 is then oxidized back to FAD
example: FAD stays covalently bound to the enzyme as it picks up succinate's 2 H to become FADH<sub>2</sub>.

text: {{c1::Telomeres}} are at the ends of chromosomes and contain high GC-content to prevent unraveling of the DNA
extra: During replication, telomeres are shortened, but this can be partially reversed by telomerase
example: Human telomeres repeat TTAGGG thousands of times, losing some repeats with every cell division

text:
In uncompetitive inhibition:
  • Vmax: {{c1::goes down}}
  • Km: {{c1::goes down}}
example: With α′ = 2, an uncompetitive inhibitor halves both: K<sub>m</sub> 4 → 2 mM and V<sub>max</sub> 100 → 50 µmol/min

text: {{c1::Enhancers}} are sequences of DNA that function to enhance transcription
extra: Are more than 25 base pairs away from the transcription start site
example: The SV40 viral enhancer boosts transcription of a linked gene even when placed thousands of bases away

text: Complex III in the ETC is the site of the {{c1::Q Cycle}}
example: For every 2 electrons passed to cytochrome c, the Q cycle releases 4 H<sup>+</sup> into the intermembrane space.

text: The {{c1::lock and key theory::... theory}} states that the enzyme and substrate are exactly complementary and fit together like a key into a lock
example: Trypsin's S1 pocket fits only long, positive lysine or arginine side chains, like a lock taking one key

text: A high pH will cause amino acids to be {{c1::fully deprotonated}}
example: At pH 12, glycine exists as H<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>, with a net −1 charge.

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
This reaction requires {{c1::ADP}} and produces {{c1::ATP}}
example: Phosphoenolpyruvate + ADP → pyruvate + ATP, the last ATP-making step of glycolysis.

text: Pyruvate kinase is activated by {{c1::fructose 1,6-bisphosphate}}
example: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate made by PFK-1 primes pyruvate kinase ahead of time (feed-forward activation).

text: The above molecule is an Omega-{{c1::3::#}} fatty acid
extra: The first double bond, counted from the omega end, is located on the 3rd carbon
example: Fish oil's EPA and DHA are omega-3 fatty acids.

text: {{c1::ATP synthase::Enzyme}} uses a proton gradient to power the conversion of ADP to ATP
extra: The electron transport chain generates the proton gradient
example: Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase's F<sub>0</sub> proton channel, halting ATP production.

text: Complex IV in the ETC transfers electrons from {{c1::cytochrome c}} to {{c1::oxygen}}
extra: Produces water and contributes to the proton gradient
example: Four cytochrome c each deliver 1 electron so Complex IV can reduce one O<sub>2</sub> to 2 H<sub>2</sub>O.

text: An operon {{c1::activator}} turns the operon on
extra: Example: lac operon uses catabolite activator protein (CAP)

text: Acetyl-CoA uses the {{c1::citrate shuttle}} to exit the mitochondria
example: ATP-citrate lyase splits exported citrate into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate in the cytosol.

text: {{c1::Suicide inhibition::... inhibition}} is an irreversible form of enzyme inhibition that occurs when an enzyme binds a substrate analog and forms an irreversible complex
extra: Example: Penicillin looks like D-Ala-D-Ala, the normal substrate of bacterial transpeptidase. The enzyme starts catalysis, opens penicillin's β-lactam ring and becomes covalently bound to it, so the cell wall can't be cross-linked. ≠ competitive inhibition: a competitive inhibitor binds reversibly and is outcompeted by more substrate (Km ↑). A suicide inhibitor permanently removes enzyme copies (Vmax ↓).

text: This is the {{c1::imidazole}} group
example: Histamine, released by mast cells in allergy, is decarboxylated histidine and keeps its imidazole ring

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Arginine}}
example: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine into citrulline plus NO, the signal that dilates blood vessels

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Tryptophan}}
example: Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin, melatonin and niacin (vitamin B<sub>3</sub>)

text: Mismatch repair of DNA occurs during {{c1::G2 phase::cell cycle phase}} using the genes MSH2 and MLH1
example: Lynch syndrome (hereditary colon cancer) comes from inherited mutations in MSH2 or MLH1

text: A/an {{c1::lyase::type of enzyme}} catalyzes cleavage without the addition of H2O and without the transfer of electrons
example: Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate in glycolysis

text: {{c1::Oncogenes}} develop from mutations of proto-oncogenes and promote cell cycling; they may lead to cancer
example: A point mutation locks KRAS in its GTP-bound 'on' state, driving most pancreatic cancers

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::succinate dehydrogenase}}
example: Succinate dehydrogenase is the only cycle enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

text: {{c1::Terpenes}} are steroid precursors
example: Squalene, a 30-carbon terpene of six isoprene units, cyclises into lanosterol and then cholesterol

text: {{c1::Zymogens}} are precursors to an enzyme
example: The pancreas secretes trypsinogen, which enteropeptidase in the duodenum cleaves into active trypsin

text: {{c1::Phosphorylation}} is the chemical addition of a phosphoryl group (PO3-) to an organic molecule
example: Phosphorylating Ser14 converts glycogen phosphorylase b into its active a form

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Aspartate}}
example: Aspartate brings the urea cycle's second nitrogen by joining citrulline to form argininosuccinate

text: {{c1::Introns}} are segments of a DNA or RNA molecule which do not code for proteins
extra:
Exons exit the nucleus and form mRNA
Introns stay in the nucleus since they are cut out and not included in mRNA
example: The dystrophin gene is over 99% intron: about 2.2 million bases yield an mRNA of about 14,000

text: DNA is {{c1::negatively::positively or negatively}} charged due to its phosphate backbone
example: In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments always migrate toward the positive electrode (anode)

text: A {{c1::point mutation}} is a mutation in which a single nucleotide base is substituted for another in a sequence of DNA or RNA
extra: Types: silent, nonsense (truncation), missense
example: Factor V Leiden is a single G→A substitution in the F5 gene that makes factor V resist inactivation

text: The citric acid cycle requires {{c1::3::#}} NAD+ and produces {{c1::3::#}} NADH
example: One glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA, so the citric acid cycle yields 6 NADH per glucose.

text: A Svedberg unit (S) is a measure of {{c1::sedimentation rate}}: the tendency of particles to settle out of a fluid
extra:
Depends on both mass and shape
Svedberg units are not additive. Example: prokaryotic 50S and 30S subunits form a 70S ribosome

text: {{c1::Southern blotting::... blotting}} is used to detect a specific DNA sequence
example: In the 1980s, forensic labs matched crime-scene DNA to suspects using Southern blots (RFLP DNA fingerprinting).

text: {{c1::Transmembrane proteins::... proteins}} are a type of integral protein that spans the entire membrane
example: The insulin receptor and the Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> ATPase both span the whole bilayer.

text: ETC complex II {{c1::is not::is or is not}} a proton pump
extra: Since complex II uses FADH2, but is not a proton pump, that means less ATP is formed from FADH2 compared to NADH
example: Complexes I, III and IV pump about 4, 4 and 2 H<sup>+</sup> per electron pair; Complex II pumps none.

text: The pyrimidines in DNA and RNA have {{c1::1::#}} ring(s)
example: CUT the PY: cytosine, uracil and thymine are the single-ring pyrimidines

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::malate dehydrogenase}}
example: Malate dehydrogenase regenerates oxaloacetate, so the cycle can accept the next acetyl-CoA.

text: The Lac operon is a/an {{c1::inducible::repressible or inducible}} operon
extra:
Under normal conditions it is bonded to a repressor
It is turned on when an inducer pulls the repressor from the operator site
example: E. coli on glucose keeps lac off, but moved to lactose-only medium it starts making β-galactosidase

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Methionine}}
example: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), made from methionine and ATP, is the cell's main methyl donor

text: The {{c1::D and L system}} is the convention that is used to designate the configurations of sugars and amino acids relative to glyceraldehyde
extra:
Based on the D- and L- forms of glyceraldehyde
Nearly all carbohydrates in nature are in the D-configuration
example: D-glucose is D because its C-5 –OH points right in the Fischer projection, as in D-glyceraldehyde

text: {{c1::Ribosomal RNA}} makes up the ribosome and is enzymatically active
example: The peptidyl transferase that forms peptide bonds is 23S rRNA, making the ribosome a ribozyme

text: The two main products of beta oxidation are {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} and {{c1::acyl-CoA}}
extra:
Acetyl-CoA is sent to the citric acid cycle
Acyl-CoA is now 2 carbons shorter than before the round of beta oxidation started
example: One round on palmitoyl-CoA (16 C) gives 1 acetyl-CoA plus myristoyl-CoA (14 C).

text:
The 5' cap on mRNA is made up of {{c1::7-methylguanosine}}
The poly-A tail is made up of {{c1::adenine nucleotides}}
example: A typical mammalian mRNA ends in a poly-A tail of roughly 200 adenines.

text: Step 1 of β-oxidation: {{c1::oxidation}}
extra:
Two hydrogens are removed from acyl-CoA and donated to FAD
This means acyl-CoA is oxidized and FAD is reduced to FADH2
example: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase turns palmitoyl-CoA into trans-Δ<sup>2</sup>-hexadecenoyl-CoA, passing 2 H to FAD.

text: This is the monosaccharide {{c1::fructose}}
example: High-fructose corn syrup in soft drinks is about 55% fructose.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex}}
example: Like PDC, it needs thiamine pyrophosphate, so B<sub>1</sub> deficiency impairs it.

text:
The three regulatory enzymes in the citric acid cycle are:
  • {{c1::Citrate synthase}}
  • {{c1::Isocitrate dehydrogenase}}
  • {{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex}}
example: Succinyl-CoA and NADH inhibit α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, a classic case of product inhibition.

text:
The above reaction is from gluconeogenesis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::glucose 6-phosphatase}}
example: Von Gierke disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency) causes severe fasting hypoglycaemia.

text: Phosphofructokinase is activated by {{c1::AMP}}
example: During a sprint, ATP falls, AMP rises, and PFK-1 speeds up glycolysis.

text: The glycolysis intermediate {{c1::glucose 6-phosphate}} feeds into glycogenesis
example: After a meal, liver glucose 6-phosphate becomes glucose 1-phosphate, then UDP-glucose for glycogen.

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Alanine}}
example: In the glucose-alanine cycle, muscle ships its amino nitrogen to the liver as alanine

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::aldolase}}
example: Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (6 C) into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (3 C each).

text: At low temperatures, cholesterol will {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}} fluidity
extra: At low temperatures, cholesterol increases membrane fluidity by preventing fatty acid hydrocarbon chains from coming together and crystallizing
example: Chilled to 4 °C, a cholesterol-rich membrane stays fluid instead of gelling like refrigerated butter.

text: An {{c1::allosteric effector::... effector}} binds at the allosteric site and changes the enzyme's conformation, altering the active site's affinity for substrate (increasing or decreasing activity)
extra:
Positive effectors: activity goes up
Negative effectors: activity goes down
example: 2,3-BPG binds haemoglobin away from the haem sites and lowers its O<sub>2</sub> affinity

text: The brain can derive up to 2/3 of its energy from {{c1::ketone bodies}} during prolonged starvation
example: In prolonged fasting, the brain's glucose use falls from about 120 g/day to about 40 g/day as ketones take over.

text: Hexokinase is inhibited by {{c1::glucose 6-phosphate}}
example: In resting muscle with full glycogen stores, glucose 6-phosphate accumulates and slows hexokinase.

text: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the {{c1::cytosol::part of cell}}
example: Liver and fat-cell cytosol, rich in NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway, host fatty acid synthesis.

text: A/an {{c1::micelle}} can dissolve a lipid-soluble molecule in its fatty acid core
extra:
It then washes away with water because of its shell of carboxylate head groups
Formation of micelles is spontaneous because ΔS > 0: overall entropy increases because there are now more unbound water molecules
example: Bile-salt micelles ferry dietary fats and vitamin A to the intestinal wall for absorption

text:
Eukaryotes have {{c1::multiple::#}} chromosome(s)
Prokaryotes have {{c1::one::#}} chromosome(s)
extra:
The prokaryotic chromosome is circular
Eukaryote:Prokaryote:Note: Plasmids are different from chromosomes and contain DNA that is not essential for survival
example: Humans have 46 linear chromosomes, while E. coli has a single circular one of 4.6 million bp

text: {{c1::Glycerophospholipids}} are phospholipids that contain a glycerol backbone
extra: Make up the cell membrane
example: PIP<sub>2</sub>, a glycerophospholipid, is split by phospholipase C into the messengers IP<sub>3</sub> and DAG

text:
The above reaction is from glycolysis
This reaction requires {{c1::ATP}} and produces {{c1::ADP}}
example: Glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP; the phosphate traps glucose inside the cell.

text: {{c1::Monosaccharides}} are single carbohydrate units
extra: Glucose is the most common monosaccharide
example: Fructose, the sugar in fruit and honey, is a monosaccharide: a single ketohexose unit

text: {{c1::Selectins::Type of proteins}} allow cells to adhere to carbohydrates on the surfaces of other cells and are most commonly used in the immune system
example: E-selectin on inflamed endothelium snags carbohydrate ligands on neutrophils, making them roll

text: {{c1::G protein-coupled receptors}} detect molecules outside the cell then activate internal signal transduction pathways and, ultimately, cellular responses
extra: The 1st messenger ligand initiates the 2nd messenger and the cascade response
example: Rhodopsin in rods is a GPCR: light activates the G protein transducin, which lowers cGMP

text: Very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) are converted to {{c1::intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL)}} and then to {{c1::low-density lipoproteins (LDL)}} before arriving at a tissue
example: As lipoprotein lipase strips triglycerides, a VLDL particle shrinks, grows denser, and becomes IDL, then LDL.

text: {{c1::Facilitated diffusion}} is a form of passive transport that uses transport proteins to move impermeable solutes across the cell membrane
example: GLUT1 carries glucose into red blood cells down its gradient without spending ATP.

text: Glucose has {{c1::6::#}} carbons and pyruvate has {{c1::3::#}} carbons
example: Aldolase is where the split happens: fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (6 C) becomes two 3-carbon trioses.

text: {{c1::Cholesterol}} contributes to membrane fluidity and stability
example: In severe liver disease, excess membrane cholesterol makes red cells rigid, spiky spur cells

text: {{c1::Feedback inhibition::... inhibition}} of an enzyme is when an enzyme is inhibited by high levels of a product from later in the same pathway
example: High ATP, an end product of glycolysis and respiration, inhibits phosphofructokinase-1

text: Steroids contain {{c1::3::#}} cyclohexane ring(s) and {{c1::1::#}} cyclopentane ring(s)
extra: "Three rooms and a garage"
example: Testosterone, cortisol and cholesterol all share this same fused four-ring core

text: Step 3 of fatty acid synthesis: {{c1::Reduce}}
extra: NADPH reduces C=O to C–OH
example: NADPH reduces acetoacetyl-ACP's ketone to give D-3-hydroxybutyryl-ACP.

text: The Q cycle is the process by which electrons travel from {{c1::QH2}} to {{c1::cytochrome c}}
extra: Occurs in complex III of the ETC
example: Ubiquinol carries 2 electrons but cytochrome c takes only 1, so the Q cycle passes them one at a time.

text: A/an {{c1::silent mutation::... mutation}} has no effect on protein synthesis
extra: Usually found in the 3rd base of a codon
example: Changing GGU to GGC still codes glycine, so the protein is unchanged

text: FAD and FMN are the riboflavin-derived prosthetic groups of {{c1::flavoproteins::class of proteins}}
example: Complex I uses FMN to accept NADH's electrons, and Complex II uses FAD.

text: {{c1::HMG-CoA reductase::Enzyme}} is the rate-controlling enzyme of the mevalonate pathway, the metabolic pathway that produces cholesterol
example: Statins such as atorvastatin inhibit HMG-CoA reductase to lower LDL.

text: Complex I in the ETC is also known as {{c1::NADH dehydrogenase}}
extra:
Complex I removes hydrogen from NADH to form NAD+
It is also called NADH Oxidoreductase because when the hydrogen is removed from NADH, electrons are removed with it which makes this a REDOX reaction
example: Rotenone, a fish poison, kills by blocking Complex I.

text: {{c1::Chromatin}} packages DNA into a smaller volume to fit in the cell
extra:
Heterochromatin: Dark, dense, and silent
Euchromatin: Light, uncondensed, and expressed
example: Chromatin packs a human cell's 2 m of DNA into a nucleus only about 6 µm across

text: An operon {{c1::operator}} is a short region of DNA that lies partially within the promoter and interacts with a repressor that controls the transcription of the operon
example: The LacI repressor binds the lac operator, which overlaps the promoter, to block transcription

text: Step 5 of fatty acid synthesis: {{c1::Reduce}}
extra:
NADPH reduces the double bond to make it a single bond
This completes the process of adding 2 new carbon atoms to the fatty acid chain
example: NADPH reduces crotonyl-ACP to butyryl-ACP, a saturated 4-carbon chain.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
This reaction requires {{c1::isocitrate}} and {{c1::NAD+}} and produces {{c1::α-ketoglutarate}}, {{c1::NADH}}, and {{c1::CO2}}
example: 6 C isocitrate becomes 5 C α-ketoglutarate, the lost carbon leaving as CO<sub>2</sub> you exhale.

text: The {{c1::anomeric carbon}} is not a stereocenter in the acyclic form but becomes a stereocenter in the cyclic form
example: Glucose's C-1 is an aldehyde carbon in the open chain but a chiral hemiacetal carbon in the ring

text: {{c1::Apolipoproteins}} are receptor molecules that control interactions between lipoproteins
example: ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, and apoB-100 binds the LDL receptor.

text: Amphoteric molecules can act as either a {{c1::base}} or an {{c1::acid}}
example: Water takes H<sup>+</sup> from HCl to form H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> but gives H<sup>+</sup> to NH<sub>3</sub>, leaving OH<sup>−</sup>

text: {{c1::DNA ligase::Enzyme}} joins DNA strands together by catalyzing the formation of phosphodiester bonds
example: Cloning uses T4 DNA ligase to seal a gene into a plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme

text: {{c1::Triacylglycerols}} are the storage form of fatty acids
example: Triacylglycerol yields about 9 kcal/g, versus about 4 kcal/g for glycogen or protein

text: {{c1::Cyclization}} is when straight-chain carbohydrates form into rings
example: In water, over 99% of glucose exists as the six-membered pyranose ring, its C-5 –OH having attacked C-1

text: The outer mitochondrial membrane is highly permeable to {{c1::metabolic molecules}} and {{c1::small proteins}}
example: Pyruvate and ATP cross the outer membrane freely through porin (VDAC) channels.

text: The pentose phosphate pathway is also known as the {{c1::hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt}}
extra: The pathway allows for carbon atoms from glucose 6-phosphate to take a brief detour (a shunt) before they proceed down the glycolysis pathway
example: Red cells shunt glucose 6-phosphate off for NADPH; its carbons re-enter glycolysis as fructose 6-phosphate.

text: {{c1::Free fatty acids}} are unesterified fatty acids that travel in the bloodstream
example: During a fast, adipose lipolysis releases palmitate into the blood, where it rides on albumin to muscle

text: A/an {{c1::cofactor}} is a metal cation that is required by some enzymes
example: Carbonic anhydrase needs a Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion in its active site to convert CO<sub>2</sub> to bicarbonate

text: The rate limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway is {{c1::glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase}}
extra: This step creates NADPH
example: Primaquine or sulfa drugs trigger haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency.

text:
The above reactions are from gluconeogenesis
The enzymes involved in these two reactions are {{c1::pyruvate carboxylase}} and {{c1::phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK)}}
example: Pyruvate + CO<sub>2</sub> → oxaloacetate (biotin-dependent), then oxaloacetate + GTP → PEP + CO<sub>2</sub>.

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is {{c1::succinyl CoA synthetase}}
example: It makes the cycle's only substrate-level GTP (or ATP) as succinyl-CoA becomes succinate.

text: In plants, energy is stored in the form of {{c1::starch::type of carbohydrate}}
example: Potatoes store energy as starch, a mix of amylose and amylopectin.

text: {{c1::Transfer RNA}} brings amino acids to the ribosome and recognizes the codon on the mRNA using its own anticodon
example: The tRNA with anticodon 3′-UAC-5′ pairs with the start codon 5′-AUG-3′ and carries methionine

text: {{c1::DNA polymerase::Enzyme}} proofreads its work and excises incorrectly matched bases
extra: The daughter strand is identified by its lack of methylation and corrected accordingly
example: Proofreading cuts DNA polymerase's error rate from about 1 in 10<sup>5</sup> to about 1 in 10<sup>7</sup> bases

text: The {{c1::hydrophobic effect}} pushes hydrophobic R groups to the interior of a protein, which {{c1::increases::increases or decreases}} entropy of the surrounding water molecules
extra:
When multiple hydrophobic molecules are in water, the molecules group together spontaneously
The combined molecules have less surface area touching water so fewer water molecules are needed to interact with the hydrophobic surface
This means more water molecules can roam freely which is an increase in entropy
example: Olive oil shaken in water coalesces back into one layer, freeing ordered water and raising its entropy

text: {{c1::Base excision repair::... repair}} fixes nondeforming lesions of the DNA helix such as cytosine deamination by removing the base, leaving an apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site
extra: AP endonuclease then removes the damaged sequence, which can be filled in with the correct bases
example: Uracil-DNA glycosylase removes the U left when cytosine deaminates, leaving an AP site to refill with C

text: This amino acid is {{c1::Phenylalanine}}
example: In phenylketonuria (PKU), phenylalanine hydroxylase fails and Phe builds up, so newborns are screened at birth

text: {{c1::Tumor suppressor genes}} code for proteins that reduce cell cycling or promote DNA repair
extra: Mutated tumor suppressor genes = no brakes
example: TP53 (p53) halts the cell cycle after DNA damage and is mutated in about half of human cancers

text: At the midpoint of a titration, the pH = {{c1::pKa}}
example: Titrating acetic acid with NaOH, the pH reads 4.76 (its pK<sub>a</sub>) once half the acid is neutralised

text: {{c1::Enantiomers}} only come in pairs because they are mirror images while there can be many more than two {{c1::diastereomers}} depending on the number of stereocenters
example: Open-chain aldohexoses have 4 stereocentres, so 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 forms: 8 enantiomer pairs, each with 14 diastereomers

text: The citric acid cycle requires {{c1::1::#}} FAD and produces {{c1::1::#}} FADH2
example: Two turns per glucose give 2 FADH<sub>2</sub>, worth about 3 ATP at 1.5 ATP each.

text: Translation occurs in the {{c1::cytoplasm::part of cell}}, at the {{c1::ribosomes::organelle}}
example: Tetracycline halts bacterial protein synthesis by blocking ribosomes in the cytoplasm

text: Gluconeogenesis takes place in the {{c1::liver::organ}}, {{c1::kidneys::organ}}, and {{c1::intestines::organ}}
example: After an overnight fast, the liver makes most new glucose, and the kidney cortex adds a smaller share.

text: A C16 fatty acid that undergoes complete beta oxidation will produce {{c1::7::#}} NADH and {{c1::7::#}} FADH2
extra: This is because a C16 fatty acid undergoes 7 rounds of beta oxidation and each round produces 1 NADH and 1 FADH2
example: Those 7 NADH and 7 FADH<sub>2</sub> are worth 7 × 2.5 + 7 × 1.5 = 28 ATP.

text:
The Michaelis-Menten reaction scheme is:
{{c1::}}
extra:
E = enzyme
S = substrate
ES = enzyme-substrate complex
k1 = binding of enzyme to substrate, forming ES
k2 = catalytic step that forms product and regenerates free enzyme; the rate-limiting step
example: Sucrase binds sucrose (E + S ⇌ ES), then releases glucose and fructose and is free to bind again (ES → E + P)

text: Peptide bonds link the {{c1::α-carboxyl group::... group}} of one amino acid to the {{c1::α-amino group::... group}} of the next amino acid
example: Glycine and alanine join by one peptide bond to make the dipeptide Gly-Ala, releasing one H<sub>2</sub>O

text: {{c1::Chemiosmosis}} is the movement of ions across a semipermeable membrane, down their electrochemical gradient
extra: An example of this would be the generation of ATP by the movement of H+ across the inner mitochondrial membrane

text:
The above reaction is from the citric acid cycle
This reaction requires {{c1::malate}} and {{c1::NAD+}} and produces {{c1::oxaloacetate}}, {{c1::NADH}}, and {{c1::H+}}
example: Malate + NAD<sup>+</sup> → oxaloacetate + NADH + H<sup>+</sup> makes the cycle's third NADH.

text: NADH powers the creation of {{c1::2.5::#}} ATP
example: The 10 NADH from one glucose yield about 10 × 2.5 = 25 ATP.

text:
L and D indicate {{c1::relative}} configuration
S and R indicate {{c1::absolute}} configuration
example: L-alanine and L-cysteine share the same L arrangement, yet alanine is (S) and cysteine is (R)

text: {{c1::Allolactose}} binds to the lac repressor and makes it change shape so the repressor detaches from the DNA
extra:
When lactose is available, some lactose molecules will be converted to allolactose
This increases the lac operon gene expression
example: IPTG mimics allolactose, binding LacI so labs can switch on lac-driven genes without lactose

text: A/an {{c1::chromosome}} is a deoxyribonucleic acid molecule with part or all of the genetic material of an organism
extra: Eukaryote:Prokaryote:Note: Plasmids are different from chromosomes and contain DNA that is not essential for survival
example: Human chromosome 1, the largest, is a single DNA molecule of about 249 million base pairs

text: {{c1::Chargaff’s rules::... rules}} state that, in DNA, the number of purines equals the number of pyrimidines
extra: This is due to the base pairing of A-T and G-C
example: If a DNA sample is 30% adenine, it is also 30% thymine, leaving 20% guanine and 20% cytosine

text: In {{c1::primary active transport::... transport}}, the energy needed for the transport is derived directly from the breakdown of ATP
example: The Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> ATPase pumps 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out and 2 K<sup>+</sup> in for every ATP it splits.

text: The start codon {{c1::AUG}} codes for {{c1::Methionine::amino acid}}
example: In bacteria the AUG start codon brings in a modified methionine, N-formylmethionine (fMet)

text: The {{c1::absorptive state::... state}} occurs postprandially and is the period in which the gastrointestinal tract is full and anabolic processes dominate
example: An hour after Thanksgiving dinner, insulin drives glycogen, fat and protein synthesis.

text: Catabolism of cellular proteins occurs only under conditions of {{c1::starvation}}
example: A hunger striker loses muscle mass after weeks without food as body protein is burned for fuel.

text: A/an {{c1::acrocentric chromosome::... chromosome}} is one in which the centromere is located near one end of the chromosome and not in the middle
example: Chromosome 21 is acrocentric, which lets it fuse with chromosome 14 in a Robertsonian translocation

text: The purines in DNA and RNA have {{c1::2::#}} ring(s)
example: PURe As Gold: adenine and guanine are purines, a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring

text: {{c1::Gap junctions}} in cell membranes allow for rapid exchange of ions and other small molecules between adjacent cells
example: Gap junctions let ions spread between cardiomyocytes so the heart contracts as one unit.

text: {{c1::Integrins::Type of proteins}} have two membrane-spanning chains and permit cells to adhere to proteins in the extracellular matrix
example: Platelet integrin αIIbβ3 (GPIIb/IIIa) binds fibrinogen to link platelets into a clot

text: {{c1::Post-transcriptional modification}} is the process in eukaryotic cells where primary transcript RNA is converted into mature RNA
example: Before leaving the nucleus, a pre-mRNA gains a 7-methylguanosine cap and a tail of about 200 A's

text: {{c1::Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)}} denatures proteins and gives them a uniform negative charge
example: SDS, the detergent in many shampoos and toothpastes, coats an unfolded protein so it migrates toward the anode.

text: An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) {{c1::depolarizes::depolarizes or hyperpolarizes}} the cell
extra: It makes the inside of the cell more positive, bringing the membrane potential closer to its threshold for firing an action potential
example: Glutamate opening AMPA receptors lets Na<sup>+</sup> in, nudging a neuron from −70 mV toward −55 mV.

text: Red blood cells are also known as {{c1::erythrocytes}}
example: Erythropoietin (EPO), the hormone some cyclists dope with, is named for the erythrocytes it boosts.

text: {{c1::Gestation}} is the period of time between conception and birth
example: Human gestation lasts about 38 weeks from conception; an African elephant's lasts about 22 months

text: The CNS and PNS derive from the {{c1::ectoderm::germ layer}}
example: Neural crest cells, from ectoderm, form the dorsal root ganglia and the adrenal medulla.

text: {{c1::Peristalsis}} is the contraction and relaxation of muscles that propels food down the gut tube
example: Peristalsis lets astronauts swallow food in zero gravity.

text: The {{c1::glomerulus}} is a network of capillaries located at the beginning of each nephron in the kidney
example: In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, inflamed glomeruli leak blood and turn the urine cola-coloured.

text: Epithelial tissue covers {{c1::internal}} and {{c1::external}} surfaces of the body
example: The epidermis covers the outside of the body, and the intestinal lining covers the inside of the gut.

text: {{c1::Ca2+}} enters the presynaptic cell and allows vesicles with neurotransmitters inside to fuse with the axon terminal membrane
extra: The neurotransmitters release into the synaptic cleft
example: A nerve terminal bathed in Ca<sup>2+</sup>-free saline still fires action potentials but releases no acetylcholine.

text: Bile increases the absorption of {{c1::fats}}
extra: Bile is also an important part of the absorption of the fat-soluble substances, such as the vitamins A, D, E, and K
example: A blocked bile duct leaves fat unabsorbed, producing pale, greasy, floating stools.

text: {{c1::Mineralocorticoids}} are a class of corticosteroids and include the hormone {{c1::aldosterone}}
example: In Conn syndrome, an adrenal tumor makes excess aldosterone, causing high blood pressure and low K<sup>+</sup>.

text: Microfilaments make up part of the cell's {{c1::cytoskeleton}}
example: Actin microfilaments form the contractile ring that pinches a dividing animal cell in two during cytokinesis.

text: A {{c1::morula}} is a solid ball of cells resulting from division of a fertilized ovum
example: About 3–4 days after fertilization, the human embryo is a 16-cell morula shaped like a mulberry.

text: In the {{c1::G2 phase::cell cycle phase}}, cells grow and make organelles
example: In G<sub>2</sub>, a cell makes extra mitochondria and the tubulin it will need for the spindle.

text: {{c1::Cortisol}} is a stress hormone released in response to stress and low blood-glucose concentration
example: During a long fast or after a car accident, cortisol rises and raises blood glucose through gluconeogenesis.

text: {{c1::Prions}} are infectious proteins and can trigger misfolding
{{c1::Corticotropin-releasing hormone::... hormone}} stimulates the anterior pituitary to release ACTH
example: Before an exam, stress boosts CRH from the hypothalamus, raising ACTH and then cortisol.

text: Cardiac muscle is under {{c1::involuntary (autonomic)::voluntary or involuntary}} control
example: A sudden fright makes your heart race through sympathetic nerves, without any decision on your part.

text: This is an example of {{c1::stratified columnar}} epithelial tissue
example: Parts of the male urethra and the large ducts of some glands are lined by stratified columnar epithelium.

text: {{c1::Glucagon::Hormone}} causes the liver to convert stored glycogen into glucose
extra: Peptide hormone secreted by alpha-islet cells of pancreas
example: People with diabetes carry glucagon injection kits to rescue a severe hypoglycemic episode.

text:
The two types of agranulocytes are:
  • {{c1::Lymphocytes}}
  • {{c1::Monocytes}}
extra: Agranulocytes have no granules
example: A monocyte that leaves the blood and settles in a tissue becomes a macrophage.

text: {{c1::Hypotonia}}, commonly known as floppy baby syndrome, is a state of low muscle tone
example: A baby with Down syndrome often feels floppy when lifted, slipping through the examiner's hands

text: Blood is considered a {{c1::connective tissue}} because it consists of blood cells surrounded by a nonliving fluid matrix called blood plasma
example: Spun in a centrifuge, blood separates into about 55% plasma (the matrix) and 45% cells.

text: {{c1::X-linked recessive inheritance}} refers to genetic conditions associated with mutations in genes on the X chromosome
example: Hemophilia A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and red-green color blindness are X-linked recessive.

text: {{c1::Obligate anaerobes::type of microorganism}} die in O<sub>2</sub>
example: Clostridium botulinum grows in sealed, oxygen-free cans, producing botulinum toxin.

text: The {{c1::complement system::... system}} enhances the ability of antibodies and phagocytes to clear microbes and damaged cells, promotes inflammation, and attacks the pathogen's cell membrane
extra: Three pathways: classical, alternative and lectin
example: People lacking the membrane attack complex (C5b-C9) get recurrent Neisseria meningitis.

text: In {{c1::telophase::mitosis phase}}, chromosomes decondense, the nuclear membrane forms, and cytokinesis occurs
example: In telophase, each set of 46 chromosomes gets a new nuclear envelope while a cleavage furrow splits the cell.

text: {{c1::Viroids}} are plant pathogens
example: Potato spindle tuber viroid, a tiny naked circle of RNA with no protein coat, deforms potato tubers.

text: {{c1::Calcitonin::Hormone}} is released by the thyroid gland and builds bone
extra:
Increases Ca2+ in bone
Increases Ca2+ excretion from kidneys
Decreases Ca2+ in blood
Decreases Ca2+ absorption in gut
example: Salmon calcitonin nasal spray has been used to treat osteoporosis by inhibiting osteoclasts.

text:
Two layers of the dermis:
  • {{c1::Papillary layer}}
  • {{c1::Reticular layer}}
example: Your fingerprints are ridges of the dermis's papillary layer pushing up into the epidermis above.

text: Ionotropic receptors operate via {{c1::direct::direct or indirect}} neurotransmitter action
extra: Membrane-spanning ion channel proteins that open directly in response to ligand binding
example: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction are ion channels that open the moment ACh binds.

text: {{c1::Hypodermis}} lies between the dermis and underlying tissues and organs. It consists of mostly adipose tissue and is the storage site of most body fat
example: A seal's thick blubber is an enlarged hypodermis that insulates it against icy water.

text: {{c1::Compact}} bone, also known as cortical bone, is a dense material used to create much of the hard structure of the skeleton
example: The hard shaft of the femur is a thick tube of compact bone.

text: {{c1::Mucus}} that is made in your nose, throat and lungs traps bacteria, viruses, and dust
extra: In respiratory system, mucus is propelled upward by cilia via mucociliary escalator
example: The thick mucus you blow out during a cold carries trapped viruses and dead white cells.

text: {{c1::T4::Thyroid hormone}} is a precursor to {{c1::T3::thyroid hormone}}
extra:
T4 = thyroxine
T3 = triiodothyronine
Regulates metabolism
Made from iodine and tyrosine
example: Levothyroxine (synthetic T<sub>4</sub>) is given for hypothyroidism and is converted to T<sub>3</sub> in tissues.

text: The {{c1::duodenum}} is the first part of small intestine and the site of the majority of chemical digestion
example: The duodenum is only about 25 cm long, yet most chemical digestion happens there.

text: {{c1::Translocation}} is a chromosomal mutation in which a segment of DNA is swapped with a segment of DNA from another chromosome
example: A Robertsonian translocation joining chromosomes 14 and 21 can cause inherited Down syndrome

text: {{c1::Nondisjunction}} is when homologous chromosomes (anaphase I) or sister chromatids (anaphase II/mitosis) fail to separate properly
extra: Results in aneuploidy
example: Nondisjunction of chromosome 21 gives an egg two copies, so fertilization yields trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

text: The brain and spinal cord make up the {{c1::central}} nervous system
example: A stroke in the brain and a spinal cord injury both damage the central nervous system.

text: {{c1::Mesoderm::Germ layer}} develops into musculoskeletal system, circulatory system, gonads, and adrenal cortex
extra: “Move-oderm”: Involved in moving things such as muscles, RBC, steroids
example: The heart, the kidneys, and red blood cells all come from mesoderm.

text: The {{c1::parasympathetic}} nervous system controls our rest and digest functions
extra: Remember P for Parasympathetic: "Relaxing and having a Piña colada on beach"
example: After a big Thanksgiving dinner, your heart rate slows and your gut gets busy digesting the meal.

text: The trachea branches into two primary {{c1::bronchi}}
extra:
One bronchus leads to the left lung, the other bronchus leads to the right lung
Ciliated epithelium collects debris in the trachea and bronchi
example: The right main bronchus feeds the three-lobed right lung, and the left feeds the two-lobed left lung.

text: The main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain is {{c1::GABA}}
example: Benzodiazepines like diazepam (Valium) boost GABA-A receptors, calming anxiety and causing drowsiness.

text:
Normal blood pressure range:
{{c1::}}
example: A reading of 118/78 mmHg is normal; 145/95 mmHg is hypertension.

text: {{c1::Ligaments}} attach bones to other bones
example: The ACL connects the femur to the tibia and often tears when a soccer player pivots on a planted foot

text: Skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by {{c1::lower::upper or lower}} motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem
example: Polio destroys lower motor neurons in the spinal cord's anterior horn, causing flaccid paralysis

text: Fetal hemoglobin has a {{c1::greater::greater or lesser}} affinity for O2 than adult hemoglobin
example: Fetal hemoglobin is half-saturated at about 19 mmHg O<sub>2</sub>, adult hemoglobin at about 27 mmHg.

text: {{c1::Free nerve endings}} in the skin can detect temperature, mechanical stimuli (touch, pressure, stretch) or pain (nociception)
example: The burning pain of touching a hot stove is picked up by free nerve endings.

text: If your body needs more oxygen, then 2,3-BPG levels will {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}}
extra: 2,3-BPG causes heme to release its O2. If your body is low on O2, then 2,3-BPG increases so more O2 is unloaded to the tissues
example: A climber who spends a few days at high altitude raises red cell 2,3-BPG so tissues get more O<sub>2</sub>.

text: {{c1::Duplication}} is a chromosomal mutation in which a segment of DNA is copied multiple times
example: Ancient duplications of one globin gene gave rise to the separate α- and β-globin gene families

text: {{c1::Seminal vesicles}} and the {{c1::prostate gland}} make alkaline fluid to help sperm survive the acidic environment of the female reproductive tract
example: Semen at pH about 7.5 briefly neutralizes the vagina's pH of about 4, so sperm are not killed.

text: A polarized membrane has an electrical {{c1::potential difference}} across the cell membrane
example: An AA battery holds a 1.5 V potential difference; a resting neuron's membrane holds about 70 mV.

text: {{c1::Macrophages}} ingest pathogens and present them on MHC-II
example: Alveolar macrophages in the lungs engulf inhaled bacteria such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

text: Skeletal muscle {{c1::is::is or is not}} striated
example: Under a microscope, a biceps fibre shows alternating light (I) and dark (A) bands.

text: The {{c1::hypothalamus::brain structure}} is in charge of homeostasis and the 4 F’s
extra:
Links the nervous system to the endocrine system (via the pituitary) and regulates the autonomic nervous system

Hormone pathway: Hypothalamus → hypophyseal portal → anterior pituitary
example: On a hot day, the hypothalamus senses your rising temperature and triggers sweating and skin vasodilation.

text: {{c1::Episomes}} are plasmids that integrate into the genome
example: The F plasmid can integrate into the E. coli chromosome, creating an Hfr strain.

text:
The posterior pituitary stores the following two hormones which are synthesized by the hypothalamus:
  • {{c1::Oxytocin}}
  • {{c1::Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)}}
example: Alcohol inhibits ADH release, which is why drinking beer makes you urinate more

text: In males with an X-linked recessive mutation, the mutation {{c1::will::will or will not}} be expressed
extra: This is because males only have one X chromosome
example: A man whose single X carries the hemophilia A allele has hemophilia.

text: {{c1::Multipotent}} stem cells can develop into multiple specialized cell types
extra: Most adult stem cells are multipotent stem cells
example: Hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow make red cells, white cells, and platelets, but not neurons.

text: The {{c1::axial skeleton::... skeleton}} includes the skull, vertebral column, ribcage, and hyoid bone
example: A rib fracture from a car crash is an injury to the axial skeleton.

text: Crossing over occurs in {{c1::prophase I::meiosis phase}}
example: Human oocytes finish crossing over in prophase I before birth, then pause there for decades until ovulation.

text: In the thymus, T cells undergo {{c1::positive}} selection (they mature only if they can respond to antigen presented on MHC) and {{c1::negative}} selection (self-reactive T cells undergo apoptosis)
extra: T-cell maturation is facilitated by thymosin
example: A T cell whose receptor binds strongly to self-insulin shown in the thymus dies by apoptosis (negative selection).

text: Unlike microfilaments and microtubules, intermediate filaments such as keratin and desmin do not participate in {{c1::cell motility}}
example: Keratin filaments anchor skin cells together at desmosomes, while actin filaments drive a crawling white blood cell.

text: In humoral (adaptive) immunity, {{c1::B cells}} are responsible for generating antibodies to specific antigens
extra: Require stimulation from helper T-cells
example: After a hepatitis B vaccine, B cells make anti-HBs antibodies, which a blood test measures to confirm immunity.

text:
The colon has the following four segments:
  • {{c1::Ascending}}
  • {{c1::Transverse}}
  • {{c1::Descending}}
  • {{c1::Sigmoid}}
example: Diverticulitis most often affects the sigmoid colon, causing lower-left abdominal pain.

text: Gram-negative bacteria stain {{c1::pink / red::color}} and have a {{c1::thin::thick or thin}} wall
extra: Wall is made of peptidoglycan
example: E. coli loses crystal violet through its thin wall and shows pink from the safranin counterstain.

text: White blood cells are formed in the {{c1::bone marrow}}
extra: Both red and white blood cells are formed in the bone marrow
example: Chemotherapy that damages bone marrow drops the white cell count and raises infection risk.

text: The transfer of antibodies to an individual is considered {{c1::passive immunity::... immunity}}
The diluting segment of the nephron, in the outer medulla, is named for the active reabsorption of {{c1::salt}} at this site
example: Filtrate leaves the thick ascending limb at about 100 mOsm/L, more dilute than plasma at about 300.

text: A/an {{c1::antibody}} is a blood protein produced in response to a specific antigen
example: After strep throat, the body makes antibodies against streptococcal antigens such as streptolysin O (the ASO titre).

text: After processing in the stomach, food particles are now called {{c1::chyme}}
extra: Chyme exits through pyloric sphincter and enters the duodenum
example: A few hours after lunch, the stomach has turned a sandwich into a soupy, acidic chyme.

text: The {{c1::canaliculi}} are small channels that link together the lacunae in bones
example: Osteocytes sealed in lacunae pass nutrients to their neighbours through canaliculi, like tunnels between rooms

text: {{c1::Genetic drift}} is when the composition of the gene pool changes as a result of chance
example: In a population of 10 plants, a white-flower allele can vanish just because its carriers happen to die in a flood

text:
The fat soluble vitamins are:
  • {{c1::A}}
  • {{c1::D}}
  • {{c1::E}}
  • {{c1::K}}
extra: They are absorbed through the lacteals in the villi
example: Polar bear liver is toxic to eat because it stores huge amounts of fat-soluble vitamin A.

text: {{c1::Bone marrow}} produces the cellular elements of the blood, including platelets, red blood cells and white blood cells
example: Doctors sample red marrow from the hip's iliac crest in a bone marrow biopsy to check blood-cell production

text: Hyperpolarization occurs because K+ channels are {{c1::slow to close}}
extra: K+ continues to exit the cell even though resting potential was already reached
example: K<sup>+</sup> channels stay open after −70 mV is reached, so the voltage sinks toward K<sup>+</sup>'s equilibrium of about −90 mV.

text: Aldosterone {{c1::raises::raises or lowers}} blood pressure
example: A patient with an aldosterone-secreting adrenal tumour (Conn syndrome) has high blood pressure and low K<sup>+</sup>.

text: Beta-islet cells of the pancreas release {{c1::insulin}}
example: After you eat a bagel, rising blood glucose triggers beta cells to release insulin.

text:
The Na+/ K+ Pump moves Na+ and K+ in the following amounts and directions:
  • {{c1::3::amount}} Na+ {{c1::out of::direction}} the cell
  • {{c1::2::amount}} K+ {{c1::into::direction}} the cell
extra:
Mnemonic:
3-2-1 NOKIA
3 Na+ Out
2 K+ In
1 ATP used
Pumps ions against their concentration gradient
Helps to restore the concentration gradient and restore the resting potential across the cell membrane
example: Digoxin blocks the Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump in heart cells, raising intracellular Na<sup>+</sup> and contraction strength.

text: The {{c1::proximal convoluted tubule::part of nephron}} is the site of bulk reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, soluble vitamins, salt, and H2O
example: In a healthy person the PCT reabsorbs essentially all filtered glucose, so urine contains none.

text:
The process of fertilization involves the following 4 steps:
  1. {{c1::Sperm binding}}
  2. {{c1::Acrosome reaction}}
  3. {{c1::Cortical reaction}}
  4. {{c1::Genetic transfer}}
example: In sea urchin eggs, the cortical reaction lifts a fertilization envelope that blocks other sperm

text:
Air pathway:
Nasal/oral cavities → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → {{c1::alveoli}}
example: Emphysema from smoking destroys alveolar walls, leaving less surface for gas exchange.

text: Prokaryotic cells reproduce via {{c1::binary fission}}
example: Under ideal conditions E. coli splits by binary fission about every 20 minutes.

text: The {{c1::punctuated equilibrium theory::... theory}} considers evolution to be a very slow process with intermittent rapid bursts of evolutionary activity
example: Fossil trilobites show species unchanged for millions of years, then abruptly replaced by new forms

text: The {{c1::posterior pituitary::brain structure}} releases oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
extra: It is the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland
example: Damage to the posterior pituitary after head trauma can stop ADH release, causing diabetes insipidus.

text: The cells in an electrical synapse are connected by {{c1::gap junctions}}
extra: There is a direct physical connection between the presynaptic neuron and the postsynaptic neuron through which ions flow
example: Heart muscle cells pass ions through gap junctions, so a wave of excitation spreads and they contract in sync.

text:
Osteoblasts {{c1::build::build or resorb}} bone
Osteoclasts {{c1::resorb::build or resorb}} bone
example: PTH activates osteoclasts to resorb bone and raise blood Ca<sup>2+</sup>; calcitonin inhibits them

text: Ghrelin will {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}} hunger
extra:
Ghrelin increases hunger
Leptin decreases hunger
example: Ghrelin rises just before your usual lunchtime, making you hungry as the meal approaches.

text: {{c1::MHC-II}} displays exogenous antigen to helper CD4+ T-Cells
example: A macrophage that ate Mycobacterium displays its peptides on MHC-II to a CD4+ helper T cell.

text: The {{c1::Purkinje fibers}} carry the contraction impulse from both the left and right bundle branch to the myocardium of the ventricles
example: Purkinje fibres conduct at about 4 m/s, the fastest in the heart, so the ventricular wall contracts almost at once.

text: Identical twins are {{c1::monozygotic}}
example: One zygote that splits into two embryos gives twins with identical DNA and the same sex.

text: {{c1::Directional selection::... selection}} is a mode of natural selection in which one extreme phenotype is favored over other phenotypes, causing the allele frequency to shift over time in the direction of that phenotype
example: Galápagos finch beaks grew deeper after the 1977 drought left mainly large, hard seeds

text: {{c1::Total lung capacity}} is the amount of air in the lungs after taking the deepest breath possible
example: A healthy adult male's total lung capacity is about 6 L.

text: GPCRs are integral membrane proteins that possess {{c1::seven::#}} membrane-spanning domains or transmembrane helices
example: Rhodopsin, the light receptor in rods, crosses the membrane 7 times like every GPCR.

text:
Female egg pathway:
{{c1::}}
extra: Note: If unfertilized, the egg will leave through the cervix and vagina, otherwise it implants into the uterus as an embryo
example: In an ectopic pregnancy, the embryo implants in the fallopian tube instead of reaching the uterus.

text: Mucous cells produce {{c1::bicarbonate}}-rich mucus to protect stomach wall from acid
example: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen thin the protective mucus-bicarbonate layer, so heavy use causes stomach ulcers.

text: The {{c1::appendicular skeleton::... skeleton}} includes the limbs, pectoral girdle, and pelvis
example: A broken collarbone (clavicle) from a fall is an injury to the pectoral girdle of the appendicular skeleton.

text: Evaporation of sweat from the skin surface has a cooling effect due to {{c1::evaporative cooling}}
extra: As each drop of sweat evaporates, it takes a bit of body heat away with it
example: Evaporating 1 L of sweat removes about 2,400 kJ (~580 kcal) of heat from the body.

text: {{c1::Ependymal cells}} form the barrier between cerebrospinal fluid and interstitial fluid of the CNS
example: Ependymal cells line the brain's ventricles, and modified ependymal cells of the choroid plexus make CSF.

text: {{c1::Cell differentiation}} is when a cell acquires the structures and functions of a specialized cell
example: A committed myoblast differentiates by making actin and myosin and fusing into a multinucleate muscle fiber.

text: Cortisol increases blood sugar by {{c1::activating gluconeogenesis}}
example: Patients on long-term prednisone often develop high blood sugar (steroid-induced hyperglycaemia).

text: At the {{c1::G<sub>1</sub>}} checkpoint, cells choose whether or not to divide
example: A skin cell with UV-damaged DNA halts at the G<sub>1</sub> checkpoint until the damage is repaired.

text: {{c1::Astrocytes}} form the blood-brain barrier
extra: They help control solutes moving from bloodstream to nervous tissue
example: Dopamine cannot cross the blood–brain barrier, so Parkinson's patients take L-DOPA, which can.

text: “Thick skin” is found only on {{c1::the palms of the hands}} and the {{c1::soles of the feet}}
example: The ridged skin of your fingertips, used for fingerprints, is thick skin and never grows hair.

text: {{c1::Melatonin::Hormone}} regulates sleep / wakefulness and controls the circadian rhythm
example: Travelers take melatonin pills to reset their body clock after a flight across several time zones.

text: A low pH means a {{c1::low::high or low}} heme affinity for O2
extra:
H+ is an inhibitor of heme, so it causes the heme to release its O2
This is called the Bohr Shift. The oxygen saturation curve will shift right in response to a low pH (high H+ concentration)
example: In diabetic ketoacidosis, acidic blood lowers hemoglobin's O<sub>2</sub> affinity and shifts the dissociation curve right.

text: {{c1::Stratum lucidum}} is the epidermis layer that is only found in thick skin
example: A skin biopsy from the sole shows a stratum lucidum; one from the forearm does not.

text:
Air pathway:
Nasal/oral cavities → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → {{c1::bronchioles}} → alveoli
example: During an asthma attack, smooth muscle around the bronchioles constricts and causes wheezing.

text: {{c1::LH::Hormone}} is a gonadotropin that induces ovulation
extra:
Luteinizing Hormone
Released from the anterior pituitary
example: Home ovulation tests detect the LH surge in urine, which triggers ovulation about 24–36 hours later.

text:
Cardiac output equation:
{{c1::}}
extra: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume
example: A heart rate of 70 beats/min × a stroke volume of 70 mL gives a cardiac output of 4.9 L/min.

text: {{c1::Chemical digestion}} is the enzymatic cleavage of chemical bonds such as the peptide bonds of proteins or the glycosidic bonds of starches
example: Lipase hydrolysing the ester bonds of a triglyceride into fatty acids and monoglycerides is chemical digestion.

text: {{c1::Disaccharidase::Enzyme}} is a brush-border enzyme that breaks down maltose, isomaltose, lactose, and sucrose into monosaccharides
example: Sucrase, a disaccharidase, splits table sugar (sucrose) into glucose and fructose.

text: Chief cells secrete {{c1::pepsinogen}} and {{c1::gastric lipase}}
example: Pepsinogen from chief cells turns into active pepsin only when it meets stomach acid.

text: A {{c1::blastula}} is a hollow sphere of cells, called blastomeres, that implants in the endometrial lining
example: A human blastocyst begins implanting in the endometrium about 6–7 days after fertilization.

text: {{c1::Aminopeptidase::Enzyme}} is a brush-border enzyme that removes the N-terminal amino acid from peptides
example: Aminopeptidase clips the N-terminal glycine off the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Val, leaving Ala-Val.

text: {{c1::Testosterone::Hormone}} is the primary male sex hormone and is an anabolic steroid
extra: Produced by the testes in men and the ovaries in women, with a small amount from the adrenal cortex
example: Anabolic steroid abuse by athletes builds muscle but can shrink the testes by suppressing LH.

text: Type {{c1::1::#}} diabetes is a chronic condition in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin
extra: Glucose is not able to enter cells
example: A 10-year-old whose immune system destroys her beta cells needs daily insulin injections.

text: Humoral immunity is immunity provided by {{c1::antibodies}}
extra: Kills antigens while they are floating around in the fluid (humor)
example: Antibodies against tetanus toxin circulating in the blood neutralise the toxin before it reaches nerves.

text: {{c1::Ossification}} is the process of laying down new bone material by cells called osteoblasts
example: A teenager's growth plates ossify and close by the late teens, ending growth in height

text: The pancreatic {{c1::acinar cell::... cell}} is the functional unit of the exocrine pancreas. It synthesizes, stores, and secretes digestive enzymes
extra:
Pancreatic juices contain bicarbonate, pancreatic amylase, pancreatic peptidases, and pancreatic lipase
The juices flow into the duodenum
example: In acute pancreatitis, enzymes leaking from acinar cells raise blood lipase and amylase levels.

text: Bone tissue is also known as {{c1::osseous}} tissue
example: Osteoporosis thins osseous tissue, so an older woman's hip can break in a simple fall

text: A/an {{c1::G-protein coupled receptor}} is a membrane receptor that interacts with a special protein called a G-protein
example: Cholera toxin locks the G<sub>s</sub> protein in its active state, so intestinal cAMP stays high and causes diarrhea.

text: {{c1::Alveoli}} are sacs where gas exchange occurs
example: Roughly 300–500 million alveoli give the lungs about 70 m<sup>2</sup> of gas-exchange surface.

text: Inhalation is considered a/an {{c1::active process::... process}}
extra: Because the diaphragm must contract for inhalation
example: A spinal cord injury above C3 paralyses the diaphragm, so the patient cannot inhale without a ventilator.

text:
The following enzymes are found in the {{c1::duodenum}}:
  • Disaccharidases
  • Aminopeptidase & Dipeptidase
  • Enteropeptidase
example: A lactose-intolerant adult lacks lactase, a disaccharidase on the duodenal brush border.

text: GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release {{c1::FSH}} and {{c1::LH}}
example: At puberty, pulses of GnRH from the hypothalamus raise FSH and LH, starting sperm and egg development.

text: cAMP signaling is turned off when {{c1::phosphodiesterase::enzyme}} breaks the ring of cAMP and turns it into AMP
extra: It is no longer cyclic
example: Caffeine and theophylline inhibit phosphodiesterase, so cAMP lingers longer in cells.

text: cAMP, Ca2+, and inositol phosphates are {{c1::common 2nd messengers}}
example: Acetylcholine on salivary gland cells raises IP<sub>3</sub>, which releases Ca<sup>2+</sup> from the ER to drive secretion.

text: {{c1::Neurulation}} results in the formation of the neural tube, which gives rise to both the spinal cord and the brain
example: Spina bifida results when the neural tube fails to close; folic acid in pregnancy lowers the risk

text: {{c1::Memory T-cells}} serve a similar function to memory B-cells and, at a second encounter with a pathogen, will work to mount a faster and stronger immune response than the first time
extra: The term antigen-experienced T-cell is also used
example: Someone who had chickenpox as a child stays protected for decades, partly through memory T cells.

text: {{c1::Oogenesis}} is the production of female gametes
example: One primary oocyte yields a single mature ovum plus polar bodies, while one spermatocyte yields four sperm.

text: The main mechanism of adaptive evolution (proposed by Darwin) is {{c1::natural selection}}
example: Peppered moths turned mostly dark in sooty industrial England because birds ate the pale ones

text: The {{c1::distal convoluted tubule::part of nephron}} is responsive to aldosterone and is a site of salt reabsorption and waste product excretion just like the PCT
example: Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide block NaCl reabsorption in the DCT to lower blood pressure.

text: {{c1::Expiratory reserve volume}} is the volume of additional air that can be forcibly exhaled following normal exhalation
example: Squeezing out extra air to blow up a balloon after a normal breath out uses your expiratory reserve volume (~1.2 L).

text: The {{c1::ascending limb of the loop of Henle::part of nephron}} is permeable to salt but not to H2O
extra: Therefore, salt is reabsorbed both passively and actively
example: Furosemide blocks the Na<sup>+</sup>-K<sup>+</sup>-2Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransporter of the thick ascending limb, causing strong diuresis.

text: Smooth muscle is under {{c1::involuntary (autonomic)::voluntary or involuntary}} control
example: You can't will your pupils to widen; the iris's smooth muscle answers only to light and autonomic signals.

text: At a chemical synapse, an action potential triggers the presynaptic neuron to release {{c1::neurotransmitters}}
extra: These molecules bind to receptors on the postsynaptic cell and make it more or less likely to fire an action potential
example: A spike reaching a motor neuron's axon terminal releases acetylcholine, making the muscle fiber twitch.

text: The {{c1::descending limb of the loop of Henle::part of nephron}} is permeable to H2O but not salt
extra: Therefore, as the filtrate moves into the more osmotically concentrated renal medulla, water is reabsorbed from the filtrate
example: As filtrate runs down the descending limb, losing water raises it from about 300 to about 1,200 mOsm/L.

text:
The "four F's" regulated by the hypothalamus:
  • {{c1::Fighting}}
  • {{c1::Fleeing}}
  • {{c1::Feeding}}
  • {{c1::Fucking}}
example: A lesion of the lateral hypothalamus makes a rat stop eating, while a ventromedial lesion makes it overeat.

text: {{c1::Movable}} joints are strengthened by ligaments and contain a synovial capsule
example: The knee is a synovial joint, held together by the ACL and other ligaments

text: Leptin will {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}} hunger
extra:
Ghrelin increases hunger
Leptin decreases hunger
example: Mice lacking leptin (ob/ob mice) never feel full and become massively obese.

text: {{c1::Merkel cells}} are mechanoreceptors essential for light touch sensation
example: Merkel cells in your fingertips let you make out the fine dots of Braille.

text: This is an example of {{c1::cocci (sphere)::shape}} bacteria
example: Staphylococcus aureus (grape-like clusters) and Streptococcus (chains) are cocci.

text: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine are examples of {{c1::catecholamines}}
extra:
They are neurohormones important in the stress response
Released by the adrenal medulla
example: An EpiPen injects epinephrine to reverse anaphylaxis from a peanut allergy.

text: During inspiration, {{c1::contraction::contraction or relaxation}} of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles expands the thoracic cavity and lung volume
extra:
Due to this increase in volume, the pressure is decreased
The pressure gradient between the atmosphere and the thoracic cavity allows air to rush into the lungs; inhalation occurs
example: As the diaphragm contracts it flattens downward, like pulling back a syringe plunger to draw air in.

text: The {{c1::medulla oblongata}} is the primary respiratory control center
extra: It is part of the brainstem
example: An opioid overdose suppresses the medulla's respiratory centre, so the person stops breathing.

text: This is an example of {{c1::stratified cuboidal}} epithelial tissue
example: The ducts of sweat glands are lined by stratified cuboidal epithelium.

text: A/an {{c1::allergic reaction}} occurs when the immune system overreacts to a harmless substance known as an allergen
example: Peanut proteins, harmless to most people, can trigger life-threatening anaphylaxis in someone who is allergic.

text: {{c1::Ectoderm::Germ layer}} develops into the nervous system, skin, hair, nails, mouth, and anus
extra: “Attract-oderm”: Skin and hair are things people are attracted to
example: The lens of the eye and the enamel of your teeth both form from ectoderm.

text: {{c1::Secretin}} and {{c1::Cholecystokinin (CCK)}} are hormones in the duodenum that stimulate the release of pancreatic juices and bile, which aid in digestion
example: Fatty, acid-soaked chyme from a cheeseburger triggers both CCK (for the fat) and secretin (for the acid).

text: Myoglobin has a much {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} oxygen affinity than hemoglobin
extra: This means it can bind more securely to the oxygen compared to hemoglobin
example: Myoglobin's P<sub>50</sub> is about 2-3 mmHg versus about 27 mmHg for hemoglobin, so it pulls O<sub>2</sub> off Hb in muscle.

text: The {{c1::Hershey-Chase experiment::... experiment}} confirmed DNA is what contains genetic material
example: Phages labelled with <sup>32</sup>P put radioactivity inside bacteria; <sup>35</sup>S-labelled protein coats stayed outside

text: This is an example of {{c1::simple squamous}} epithelial tissue
example: The walls of the lung alveoli, where O<sub>2</sub> diffuses into blood, are simple squamous epithelium.

text: {{c1::Capillaries}} have walls only 1 cell thick, made of a single layer of endothelium
extra: Easy diffusion of gases (O2, CO2) and waste (NH3, urea)
example: Alveolar O<sub>2</sub> crosses a barrier only about 0.5 µm thick to reach the blood.

text: {{c1::Glial cells}} surround neurons and provide support and insulation
example: Glioblastoma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults, arises from glial cells, not neurons.

text: {{c1::TSH::Hormone}} stimulates the thyroid to produce thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which stimulate metabolism
extra:
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Released from the anterior pituitary
example: In Graves' disease, antibodies mimic TSH and overstimulate the thyroid, causing weight loss and heat intolerance.

text: In {{c1::metaphase::mitosis phase}}, chromosomes meet in middle of the cell
extra: Metaphase = "meet in middle" at the metaphase plate
example: Karyotypes are photographed from metaphase cells, when chromosomes are lined up and most condensed.

text: In sickle cell anemia, the amino acid {{c1::Glu}} is replaced by {{c1::Val}}
extra: Hemoglobin aggregates into insoluble fibers
example: A single GAG→GTG point mutation at codon 6 of the β-globin gene turns HbA into sickling HbS.

text:
Urine pathway:
Bowman's space → proximal convoluted tubule → descending limb of the loop of Henle → ascending limb of the loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → {{c1::collecting duct}} → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra
example: Lithium can make the collecting duct unresponsive to ADH, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

text: DNA is replicated in the {{c1::S phase::cell cycle phase}}
example: A human cell enters S phase with 46 chromosomes of one chromatid each and leaves with 92 chromatids.

text: {{c1::Growth hormone-releasing hormone::... hormone}} stimulates the anterior pituitary to release GH
example: During deep sleep, GHRH pulses from the hypothalamus trigger the night's largest GH release.

text: Pulmonary veins are {{c1::oxygenated::oxygenated or deoxygenated}}
example: Pulmonary veins are the only veins in an adult that carry oxygen-rich blood.

text: {{c1::White::Color}} skeletal muscle fibers are fast-twitch and carry out anaerobic metabolism
example: The white breast meat of a chicken is fast-twitch muscle built for brief bursts of flapping.

text: Type {{c1::2::#}} diabetes is a chronic condition in which insulin receptors become desensitized and are not responsive to insulin
extra: Glucose is not able to enter cells
example: An obese 55-year-old with high blood glucose despite high insulin levels is started on metformin.

text:
The esophagus is under the following control:
  • Top third: {{c1::somatic control}}
