  • Middle third: {{c1::both somatic and autonomic control}}
  • Bottom third: {{c1::autonomic control}}
extra:
Top third has skeletal muscle
Middle third has combo of both skeletal and smooth muscle
Bottom third has smooth muscle
example: In achalasia, the smooth-muscle lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax, so swallowed food sticks.

text: The Griffith experiment showed that bacteria can get DNA through a process called {{c1::transformation}}
extra: Griffith experiment with mice (R strain safe, S strain deadly)
example: Lab E. coli take up a plasmid carrying an ampicillin-resistance gene by transformation

text: The {{c1::larynx}}, also called the voice box, is a hollow, tubular structure connected to the top of the windpipe (trachea)
extra: Only air passes through the larynx; the epiglottis covers it during swallowing
example: The Adam's apple is the thyroid cartilage of the larynx, which becomes more prominent in men after puberty.

text: {{c1::Natural killer cells}} are a type of lymphocyte that can recognize and kill cancer cells or other cells that have been infected
extra: They do not attack invading organisms directly; they destroy the body's own cells that have become cancerous or been infected with a virus
example: NK cells kill virus-infected cells that hide from T cells by switching off MHC-I, a trick herpesviruses use.

text: The pancreas is connected to the duodenum via the {{c1::pancreatic ducts}}
example: A gallstone stuck where the pancreatic duct joins the bile duct can block it and cause pancreatitis.

text: Conjugation is the transfer of genetic material via a/an {{c1::conjugation bridge}}
example: An F+ E. coli cell passes a copy of its F plasmid to an F− cell through a sex pilus.

text: {{c1::Opsonization}} is a term that refers to an immune process where pathogens are targeted for destruction by an immune cell known as a phagocyte
extra: Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction
example: Antibody-coated pneumococci are readily eaten by neutrophils, though their capsule otherwise resists phagocytosis.

text: The {{c1::proximal convoluted tubule::part of nephron}} is the site of secretion for H+, K+, NH3, and urea
example: Probenecid blocks PCT secretion of penicillin, keeping the antibiotic in the blood longer.

text: The {{c1::smooth::smooth or rough}} ER is involved in detox and also in lipid formation
example: Liver cells expand their smooth ER after repeated barbiturate use, speeding drug detoxification.

text: {{c1::Melanin}} is produced by {{c2::melanocytes}} and protects skin from DNA damage caused by UV radiation
example: People with albinism have normal melanocytes but cannot make melanin, so they sunburn easily.

text: Oxygen binds to the {{c1::iron}} atom inside a heme group
example: Carbon monoxide binds the heme iron about 200 times more tightly than O<sub>2</sub>, blocking oxygen transport.

text: Microtubules help the cell {{c1::resist}} compression forces
example: Like tent poles holding up a tent, microtubules keep a cell from being squashed out of shape.

text: Epinephrine is a/an {{c1::catecholamine}}
extra:
Also known as adrenaline
Produced by the adrenal medulla
Increases HR
Increases BP
example: A surge of epinephrine during a near car crash makes your heart pound and your hands shake.

text: The {{c1::I-band}} is a light band on each side of the Z line comprising a region of the sarcomere where thin (actin) filaments are not overlapped by thick (myosin) filaments
example: When a biceps contracts, its I-bands shrink as actin slides over myosin

text: A {{c1::steroid hormone::... hormone}} is a steroid that acts as a hormone
extra:
Derived from lipids and lipid soluble
Examples: estrogen, progesterone, testosterone

text: The amplitude of an action potential is {{c1::independent::dependent or independent}} of the amount of current that produced it
example: A light touch and a hard pinch both give spikes peaking near +40 mV; the pinch just fires them more often.

text: The kidneys are two bean-shaped organs that help the body pass waste as urine and also help {{c1::filter blood before sending it back to the heart}}
example: The kidneys filter about 180 L of plasma a day but excrete only about 1.5 L of urine.

text: {{c1::Paracrine}} signaling is when a cell produces a signal to induce changes in nearby cells
example: At a bee sting, mast cells release histamine that makes nearby blood vessels dilate and leak.

text: {{c1::Agglutination}} is when pathogens clump together into insoluble complexes
example: Mixing type A blood with anti-A antibodies makes the red cells clump, the basis of blood typing.

text: {{c1::Inversion}} is a chromosomal mutation in which a segment of DNA is reversed
example: A chromosome segment ABCDEF that becomes ABEDCF has had its CDE section inverted

text: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes into the {{c1::duodenum}}
extra:
α-islet cells release glucagon
β-islet cells release insulin
example: Pancreatic lipase and trypsinogen flow through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum to digest a meal.

text: {{c1::Cardiac::Type}} muscle is an involuntary, striated muscle that constitutes the main tissue of the walls of the heart
example: Cardiac muscle in a resting adult contracts about 100,000 times a day without tiring.

text: Depolarization occurs when {{c1::Na+}} ions flow in
extra: This increases the charge inside the cell and results in depolarization of the cell membrane
example: Tetrodotoxin from pufferfish blocks Na<sup>+</sup> channels, so neurons cannot depolarize and victims are paralyzed.

text: The main excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS is {{c1::glutamate}}
example: After a stroke, excess glutamate overexcites neurons through NMDA receptors and kills them (excitotoxicity).

text: Blood in the umbilical vein is {{c1::oxygenated::oxygenated or deoxygenated}}
example: The single umbilical vein carries O<sub>2</sub>-rich blood from the placenta toward the fetal liver and ductus venosus.

text: 2,3-BPG causes heme to {{c1::release}} O2
extra: Creates a right shift just like a low pH would
example: Stored blood-bank red cells lose 2,3-BPG, so freshly transfused cells hold O<sub>2</sub> tightly and unload it poorly at first.

text: {{c1::Z-lines}} define the boundary of each sarcomere
example: As a muscle contracts, the Z-lines of each sarcomere are pulled closer together

text: {{c1::Cell determination}} is when a cell commits to becoming a certain type of cell
example: Late-gastrula newt cells fated to be brain still form neural tissue when transplanted to the belly region.

text: {{c1::Pluripotent}} stem cells can be any cell except those found in placental structures
example: Inner cell mass cells (embryonic stem cells) can form any body cell but not the placenta.

text: ADH {{c1::increases::increases or decreases}} blood pressure
example: In septic shock, vasopressin (ADH) is infused to constrict vessels and raise a dangerously low blood pressure.

text:
Three ways a synaptic signal is terminated:
  • {{c1::Breakdown}} by enzymes
  • {{c1::Reuptake}} by the presynaptic neuron
  • {{c1::Diffusion}} out of the cleft
example: Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, so dopamine lingers in the synaptic cleft.

text: {{c1::T-lymphocytes (T-cells)}} are white blood cells that circulate around the body, scanning for cellular abnormalities and infections
extra:
Examples include:
Helper T-cells
Cytotoxic T-cells
Suppressor T-cells
Memory T-cells
example: HIV destroys CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells; a count below 200 cells/µL defines AIDS.

text: {{c1::Cholecystokinin (CCK)}} stimulates bile release from the gallbladder, release of pancreatic juices, and promotes satiety
example: Feeling full after a rich, fatty meal is partly CCK signalling satiety to the brain.

text: Osteons consist of concentric bone layers called {{c1::lamellae}}
example: Lamellae ring each Haversian canal like the growth rings of a tree

text: Striated muscle tissue is a muscle tissue that features repeating functional units called {{c1::sarcomeres}}
example: When a sarcomere contracts, the H-zone and I-band shrink while the A-band keeps its length.

text: The binding of oxygen to hemoglobin can be characterized as {{c1::cooperative}}
extra: When one O2 molecule binds to one of the four heme groups in a hemoglobin, it becomes more likely that the remaining sites will bind to O2
example: CO bound to one heme raises the other hemes' O<sub>2</sub> affinity, so CO-poisoned blood unloads O<sub>2</sub> poorly.

text:
Air pathway:
Nasal/oral cavities → pharynx → larynx → {{c1::trachea}} → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
example: A patient on long-term ventilation breathes through a tracheostomy, a tube placed through the neck into the trachea.

text: CO2 and H+ will trigger the heme group to {{c1::release}} its O2
extra:
CO2 and H+ allosterically inhibit hemoglobin
This means O2 is released near lots of CO2 or in acidic sites, which is where respiration is happening and O2 is needed
example: In an exercising thigh muscle, rising CO<sub>2</sub> and lactic acid make hemoglobin unload more O<sub>2</sub>.

text: The hemoglobin dissociation curve is {{c1::sigmoidal::shape}} and the myoglobin dissociation curve is {{c1::hyperbolic::shape}}
example: At a PO<sub>2</sub> of 20 mmHg, myoglobin is still about 90% saturated while hemoglobin is only about 35%.

text: A/an {{c1::homozygous}} genotype has two of the same alleles
example: A person with blood type O has genotype ii, homozygous for the i allele

text: Electrical synapses are {{c1::faster::faster or slower}} than chemical synapses
example: The crayfish escape reflex uses electrical synapses, so the tail flips with almost no synaptic delay.

text: A cell will enter {{c1::G0 phase::cell cycle phase}} if it does not need to divide
example: Mature neurons and heart muscle cells sit in G<sub>0</sub> and essentially never divide.

text: {{c1::Bacteriophages}} are viruses that infect bacteria, using a tail sheath to inject DNA / RNA
example: Hershey and Chase used phage T2 to show it injects its DNA, not its protein, into E. coli.

text: Innate immunity consists of defenses that are always active and {{c1::non-specific::specific or non-specific}}
example: A neutrophil engulfs Staphylococcus and E. coli alike on first contact, with no prior exposure needed.

text: The number of complete sets of chromosomes in a cell is referred to as the {{c1::ploidy}} of a cell
example: Human body cells are diploid (2n = 46), sperm and eggs are haploid (n = 23), and bread wheat is hexaploid.

text: {{c1::Recombination frequency}} is the likelihood of two alleles being separated during crossing over in meiosis
example: If 17 of 100 offspring show recombinant phenotypes, the recombination frequency is 17%

text:
Pathway of sperm during ejaculation:
{{c1::
SEVE(N) UP mnemonic
}}
example: A vasectomy cuts the vas deferens, so sperm from the epididymis never reach the ejaculatory duct.

text: Alpha-islet cells of the pancreas release {{c1::glucagon}}
example: During an overnight fast, alpha cells release glucagon to keep blood glucose from falling.

text: {{c1::Transformation}} is when bacteria take up genetic material from the environment
extra: Griffith experiment with mice (R strain safe, S strain deadly)

text: Deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae enters the {{c1::right}} atrium of the heart
example: Blood returning from your legs through the inferior vena cava, at a PO<sub>2</sub> of about 40 mmHg, empties into the right atrium.

text:
Digestive pathway:
{{c1::oral cavity}} → {{c1::pharynx}} → {{c1::esophagus}} → {{c1::stomach}} → {{c1::small intestine}} → {{c1::large intestine}} → {{c1::rectum}}
example: A swallowed coin, tracked on X-rays, moves from esophagus to stomach to intestines and is passed within days.

text: The granules in a granulocyte cause {{c1::inflammation that kills bacteria and fungi}}
example: Neutrophil granules release myeloperoxidase, which makes bleach (HOCl) to kill engulfed bacteria.

text: {{c1::P50}} is the oxygen pressure when 50% of hemoglobin has an oxygen bound
example: Normal adult hemoglobin has a P<sub>50</sub> of about 27 mmHg.

text: The {{c1::anterior pituitary::brain structure}} releases hormones that regulate stress, growth, reproduction, and lactation
extra: Anterior lobe of the pituitary gland
example: A pituitary adenoma secreting excess GH in adults causes acromegaly, with enlarged hands and jaw.

text: The parathyroid gland's primary function is to maintain the body’s {{c1::Ca2+}} and {{c1::phosphate}} levels so that the nervous and muscular systems can function properly
extra: It is a collection of four parathyroid glands located on the back of the thyroid
example: Accidental removal of the parathyroids during thyroid surgery drops blood Ca<sup>2+</sup>, causing tetany.

text: Pulmonary arteries are {{c1::deoxygenated::oxygenated or deoxygenated}}
example: Pulmonary arteries are the only adult arteries carrying O<sub>2</sub>-poor blood, at a PO<sub>2</sub> of about 40 mmHg.

text: B cells mature into {{c1::plasma cells}} that produce antibodies
example: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells that floods the blood with one identical antibody.

text: {{c1::Deletion}} is a chromosomal mutation in which a large segment of DNA is lost
example: Cri-du-chat syndrome: losing part of chromosome 5's short arm causes a cat-like cry in infants

text: Several major ideas about evolution came together in the early 20th century to form the modern synthesis model of evolution, including {{c1::genetic variation}}, {{c1::natural selection}}, and {{c1::Mendelian inheritance}}
example: Rock pocket mice: a dark-fur Mc1r mutation spreads on black lava because owls miss dark mice

text: The {{c1::M-line}} is the middle of a sarcomere
example: In a 2.5 µm sarcomere, the M-line sits 1.25 µm from each Z-line

text: {{c1::Adrenergic receptors::... receptors}} are a class of G protein-coupled receptors that are targeted by catecholamines like norepinephrine and epinephrine
example: Albuterol activates β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors in the airways to open them during an asthma attack.

text: Implantation begins with {{c1::apposition}} of the blastocyst at the uterine epithelium, generally about 2-4 days after the morula enters the uterine cavity
extra: By apposition, the blastocyst has already differentiated into an inner cell mass (embryo) and trophectoderm (placenta)
example: About 6 days after fertilization, the blastocyst loosely contacts the uterine wall before it adheres

text: The kidney regulates pH by adjusting the levels of excreted {{c1::H+}} and reabsorbed {{c1::bicarbonate}}
example: In COPD with chronic CO<sub>2</sub> retention, the kidneys compensate over days by keeping more HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>.

text: {{c1::Veins}} are blood vessels that carry blood toward the heart
extra:
Thin walls with few elastic fibers
Pulsation is absent in veins
example: Varicose leg veins form when vein valves fail and blood pools on its way back to the heart.

text:
{{c1::FSH::Hormone}} effects:
  • Males: triggers spermatogenesis and stimulates Sertoli cells
  • Females: stimulates the development of ovarian follicles
extra:
Follicle-stimulating hormone
Released from the anterior pituitary
example: Early in each menstrual cycle, an FSH rise recruits a group of ovarian follicles, one of which becomes dominant.

text: {{c1::Thyrotropin-releasing hormone::... hormone}} stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH
example: In primary hypothyroidism, low T<sub>4</sub> lets TRH and TSH climb, so the TSH blood test is high.

text: {{c1::Complete dominance::... dominance}} is a form of dominance in heterozygous condition wherein the allele that is regarded as dominant completely masks the effect of the allele that is recessive
example: A Pp pea plant has purple flowers identical to a PP plant

text:
Two of the important proteins in a sarcomere are:
  • {{c1::myosin}}, which forms the thick filament
  • {{c1::actin}}, which forms the thin filament
example: Under a microscope, dark A-bands mark myosin and light I-bands mark actin alone, giving skeletal muscle its stripes

text: Sarcomeres attached end-to-end form {{c1::myofibrils}}
example: Each myofibril in a biceps fibre is a chain of thousands of sarcomeres joined end to end

text: Oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins enters the {{c1::left}} atrium of the heart
example: Blood oxygenated in the lungs to a PO<sub>2</sub> of about 100 mmHg returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

text: Fraternal twins are {{c1::dizygotic}}
example: Two eggs released in one cycle and fertilized by two different sperm can give a boy-girl twin pair.

text: Female chromosome pairs are {{c1::XX::XX or XY}}
example: A human female's karyotype is 46,XX: 22 pairs of autosomes plus two X chromosomes.

text: {{c1::Suppressor T-cells (regulator T-cells)}} down regulate the immune response after an infection and promote self-tolerance
extra:
Treg
They help to distinguish between self and nonself molecules, and by doing so, reduce the risk of autoimmune diseases
example: People with a FOXP3 mutation lack regulatory T cells and develop severe multi-organ autoimmunity (IPEX syndrome).

text: {{c1::Hypermutation}} is the term used to describe mutation of the antigen-binding site (variable region) on an antibody
extra:
Results in varying affinities of antibodies for a specific microbe
5 different isotypes: IgM, IgD, IgG, IgE, IgA
example: After a booster shot, hypermutation in lymph-node B cells yields antibodies that bind the antigen far more tightly.

text: Adaptive immunity consists of defenses that are {{c1::specific::specific or non-specific}} to the invader
extra:
Cell-mediated immune response
Humoral immune response
example: Antibodies made after a measles infection protect against measles for life but do nothing against chickenpox.

text: {{c1::Hematopoiesis}} is the process by which stem cells from bone marrow develop into mature blood cells
example: Your bone marrow makes about 2 million red blood cells every second.

text: {{c1::Cytotoxic T-cells}} respond to antigen on MHC-I and kill virally infected cells
extra:
“Killer cells”
Tc, CTL, or CD8+
example: In hepatitis B, CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells kill infected hepatocytes, causing most of the liver damage.

text: {{c1::Prolactin‐release inhibiting factor}} also known as {{c1::dopamine}} inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary
extra:
A catecholamine
Dopamine is a neurohormone. In the endocrine system it regulates the release of hormones. In the brain, it functions as a neurotransmitter
example: Antipsychotics that block dopamine D<sub>2</sub> receptors can raise prolactin and cause milk discharge.

text: {{c1::Divergent evolution::... evolution}} is the process whereby groups from the same common ancestor evolve and accumulate differences, resulting in the formation of new species
example: The forelimbs of humans, whales and bats evolved from one ancestral limb into arms, flippers and wings

text: Na<sup>+</sup> ions enter the cell through {{c1::voltage-gated Na<sup>+</sup> channels}}
extra: The Na+ concentration gradient is what drives the movement of Na+ ions
example: Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated Na<sup>+</sup> channels, so a dentist's injection stops pain signals from your tooth.

text: The {{c1::arachidonic acid pathway::... pathway}} is a central regulator of the inflammatory response
extra: Arachidonic acid is the precursor to eicosanoids
example: Aspirin and ibuprofen block COX, cutting prostaglandin production from arachidonic acid

text: In {{c1::anaphase::mitosis phase}}, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
example: In anaphase, a human cell's 46 pairs of sister chromatids split into 92 chromosomes headed for the two poles.

text: High blood osmolarity and angiotensin II {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}} thirst
example: After a bag of salty potato chips, rising blood osmolarity sends you reaching for a drink.

text:
Blood pathway:
right atrium → {{c1::tricuspid valve}} → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins → venae cavae → right atrium
example: The tricuspid valve has three cusps, hence its name; the mitral valve has two.

text: {{c1::Induction}} is when a group of cells influence the fate of nearby cells
extra: Mediated by inducers, which are commonly growth factors
example: The optic vesicle induces the overlying ectoderm to form the lens of the eye.

text: Ca2+ enters the presynaptic cell through {{c1::voltage-gated calcium channels}} in the cell membrane
extra: Ca2+ is at a much higher concentration outside the cell. This concentration gradient forces Ca2+ to move into the cell
example: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, antibodies block presynaptic Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels, so less ACh is released and muscles weaken.

text:
As an endocrine gland, the pancreas secretes {{c1::hormones}} to control blood sugar levels
As an exocrine gland, the pancreas secretes {{c1::enzymes}} to break down the proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids in food
extra: Endocrine pancreatic hormones are insulin and glucagon
links: Khan Academy · Endocrine Pancreas · Khan Academy · Exocrine Pancreas
example: In type 1 diabetes only the insulin-making beta cells are destroyed, so the person still digests food normally.

text: This is an example of {{c1::simple cuboidal}} epithelial tissue
example: Kidney tubules and thyroid follicles are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium.

text: {{c1::Parathyroid hormone::Hormone}} stimulates bone breakdown
extra:
Decreases Ca2+ in bone
Decreases Ca2+ excretion from kidneys
Increases Ca2+ in blood
Increases Ca2+ absorption in gut
Activates vitamin D (Calcitriol)
example: A parathyroid adenoma raises PTH, leading to high blood Ca<sup>2+</sup>, bone loss, and kidney stones.

text: Neurons that transmit impulses between other neurons, especially as part of a reflex arc, are called {{c1::interneurons}}
example: In the knee-jerk reflex, an interneuron inhibits the hamstring motor neuron while the quadriceps contracts.

text: In the case of a/an {{c1::autoimmune condition::... condition}}, a self-antigen is recognized as foreign, and the immune system attacks normal cells
example: In type 1 diabetes, T cells destroy the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas.

text: The {{c1::sarcoplasmic reticulum}} forms a cufflike structure surrounding a myofibril and its main function is to store Ca2+
example: Malignant hyperthermia: a RYR1 mutation floods the cytosol with Ca2+ from the SR during anaesthesia

text: {{c1::Antagonistic}} muscle pairs are those whose actions oppose each other
example: The biceps flexes the elbow while the triceps extends it.

text: Muscle contraction begins at the neuromuscular junction, where the efferent neuron releases {{c1::acetylcholine}} which binds to receptors on the sarcolemma and causes depolarization
example: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies block ACh receptors, causing drooping eyelids and weakness

text: The GI tract originates from the {{c1::endoderm::germ layer}}
example: The epithelial lining of the stomach and intestines, and the cells of the liver and pancreas, all come from endoderm.

text: When a membrane is depolarized, the membrane potential becomes more {{c1::positive::positive or negative}} compared to its resting potential
example: A neuron whose membrane goes from −70 mV to −55 mV is depolarizing.

text: Surfactant {{c1::reduces::reduces or increases}} surface tension in the alveoli
extra: Low surface tension is required to prevent collapse of the alveoli
example: Babies born before about 34 weeks often lack surfactant, so their alveoli collapse (respiratory distress syndrome).

text: A {{c1::single twitch}} is the response of a single muscle fiber to one brief stimulus
example: A single electrical pulse to a frog's gastrocnemius in the lab gives one brief contraction

text: Insulin and glucagon are {{c1::peptide hormones::... hormones}}
example: Insulin must be injected because, as a peptide, it would be digested by gut proteases if swallowed.

text: {{c1::Variable expressivity}} is when a phenotype is expressed but to a different degree among individuals with the same genotype
example: In neurofibromatosis type 1, relatives with the same mutation range from a few café-au-lait spots to many tumours

text: The {{c1::AV node}} is the part of the electrical conduction system of the heart that coordinates the top of the heart. It electrically connects the atria and ventricles
example: In complete (third-degree) heart block, the AV node conducts nothing, so atria and ventricles beat independently.

text: The {{c1::pharynx}} connects the mouth to the esophagus
extra: The epiglottis prevents food from entering the larynx
example: Strep throat (pharyngitis) is an infection of the pharynx, the shared passage for food and air.

text: In the Cisternal Maturation Model, cisternae {{c1::evolve and mature}}
extra:
The cis-Golgi matures and becomes the medial-Golgi, then eventually, the trans-Golgi
Vesicles move in retrograde motion
example: Procollagen bundles too large for transport vesicles still cross the Golgi, carried along by maturing cisternae.

text: Urine passes from the kidneys, through the {{c1::ureters}}, then into the bladder
example: A kidney stone stuck in the ureter causes severe flank pain that radiates to the groin.

text: {{c1::Aerotolerant anaerobes::type of microorganism}} do not use O<sub>2</sub> but tolerate it
example: Lactobacillus turns milk into yogurt by fermentation alone, unharmed by the air around it.

text: {{c1::Gastrulation}} is a phase early in the embryonic development of most animals, during which the single-layered blastula is reorganized into a multilayered structure known as the gastrula
example: In the third week of human development, gastrulation forms the ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm

text: In the Vesicular Transport Model, the cis-, medial-, and trans-Golgi cisternae are {{c1::static}} structures
extra: The contents are physically shuttled from each cisterna to the next
example: Like a fixed assembly line: the stations (cisternae) stay put while the product (protein) moves between them.

text: If the blood pH is too low, respiration will {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}}
extra:
Respiration goes up to blow off CO2
Based on Le Châtelier’s Principle, the bicarbonate buffer will shift left to remove H+ which will raise the pH back to normal levels
example: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis breathes deep and fast (Kussmaul breathing) to blow off CO<sub>2</sub>.

text: {{c1::Tropic hormones::... hormones}} are hormones that act on endocrine glands, usually inducing them to secrete other hormones

Blood pathway:
right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → {{c1::left ventricle}} → aortic valve → aorta → arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins → venae cavae → right atrium
example: Long-standing high blood pressure thickens the left ventricle wall (left ventricular hypertrophy).

text: {{c1::Transduction}} is the transfer of genetic material using a bacteriophage
example: Phage P1 accidentally packages a piece of host DNA and carries it into the next E. coli it infects.

text: Red blood cells are formed in {{c1::bone marrow}}
extra: Both red and white blood cells are formed in the bone marrow
example: In adults, red cells are made mainly in the marrow of the pelvis, sternum, ribs, and vertebrae.

text:
Steps of GPCR signaling:
  1. {{c1::Ligand binds to GPCR}}
  2. {{c1::GPCR undergoes conformational change}}
  3. {{c1::Alpha subunit exchanges GDP for GTP}}
  4. {{c1::Alpha subunit dissociates and regulates target proteins}}
  5. {{c1::Target protein (e.g., adenylyl cyclase) produces a 2nd messenger (e.g., cAMP) that triggers a cascade response}}
  6. {{c1::GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP, everything returns to its original place, ready to repeat the sequence}}
example: Glucagon binds its GPCR on a liver cell, G<sub>s</sub> activates adenylyl cyclase, cAMP rises, and glycogen breaks down.

text: {{c1::Secretin::Hormone}} stimulates the release of pancreatic juices and slows motility
example: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum triggers secretin, so the pancreas pours out bicarbonate to neutralise it.

text: {{c1::Adolescence}} begins with puberty, a roughly two-year period of rapid sexual maturation
example: Girls usually begin puberty around age 10–11 with breast budding, boys around 11–12

text: The antigen-binding region of an antibody is the {{c1::tip of the variable region}}
example: An IgG has two identical antigen-binding tips, so one antibody can bridge two viruses together.

text: In the GPCR sequence, cAMP is a second messenger and {{c1::triggers a response inside the cell}}
example: In liver cells, cAMP activates protein kinase A, which sets off glycogen breakdown into glucose.

text: The {{c1::thyroid gland}} is in the neck, below the Adam's apple, and secretes T3 and T4, which regulate metabolism
extra:
T4 = Thyroxine
T3 = Triiodothyronine
Also helps regulate calcium homeostasis
example: Iodine deficiency makes the thyroid swell into a goiter as it struggles to make T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub>.

text: {{c1::Langerhans cells}} are antigen-presenting cells in skin
example: Langerhans cells pick up nickel from a cheap earring and trigger allergic contact dermatitis.

text: {{c1::Helper T-cells}} activate cytotoxic T-cells and macrophages to attack infected cells, or they stimulate B-cells to secrete antibodies
example: Helper T cells release IL-2, which drives cytotoxic T cells to multiply against a virus.

text: During exhalation, the diaphragm muscles {{c1::relax::contract or relax}}
extra: There is an elastic recoil of the lung tissue which causes a decrease in volume
example: At the end of a quiet breath out you simply let go: the diaphragm relaxes and domes back up with no effort.

text: {{c1::Microglia}} digest waste in CNS
example: After a stroke, microglia act as the brain's macrophages and engulf the dead neurons.

text: Skeletal muscle is under {{c1::voluntary (somatic)::voluntary or involuntary}} control
example: You can choose to blink or smile, both done by skeletal muscle.

text: Retroviruses have single-stranded {{c1::RNA}} genomes
extra: Reverse transcriptase is needed to make DNA
example: HIV is a retrovirus: its ssRNA genome is copied into DNA that integrates into a T cell's chromosome.

text: Smooth muscle is considered smooth because {{c1::it does not have the striations }}
example: A slide of intestinal smooth muscle shows spindle-shaped cells with no light and dark bands.

text: Norepinephrine is a {{c1::catecholamine}} that acts as both a hormone and a neurotransmitter
example: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto heart muscle, and the adrenal medulla also secretes it into the blood.

text: The cell membrane is {{c1::highly}} permeable to K+ and {{c1::slightly}} permeable to Na+
extra: Movement through the leak channels is controlled by concentration gradients
example: Leaking mostly K<sup>+</sup>, a neuron rests at −70 mV, near K<sup>+</sup>'s −90 mV equilibrium, far from Na<sup>+</sup>'s +60 mV.

text: {{c1::Viral}} genomes may be made of DNA or RNA and may be single or double stranded
example: Herpesviruses have dsDNA, parvovirus ssDNA, rotavirus dsRNA, and influenza ssRNA genomes.

text: The {{c1::pharynx}} is part of both the digestive and respiratory systems and it is called the "throat"
extra:
Both food and air pass through the pharynx
Air is warmed and humidified
example: The tonsils sit in the walls of the pharynx, guarding the passage shared by air and food.

text: Muscles relax when {{c1::acetylcholine}} is degraded by {{c1::acetylcholinesterase}}, terminating the signal and allowing Ca2+ to return to the sarcoplasmic reticulum
example: Sarin nerve gas inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so muscles cannot relax and go into spasm

text: {{c1::Oxytocin}} stimulates uterine contractions and milk ejection (let-down) among other functions
extra:
Produced in the hypothalamus
Released from the posterior pituitary
example: Doctors give Pitocin, synthetic oxytocin, to start or strengthen labor contractions.

text: Myelinated sheaths make up the {{c1::white::white or grey}} matter in the brain
example: The corpus callosum, the white-matter bridge between the hemispheres, is made of myelinated axons.

text: The {{c1::cecum}} is the first part of the large intestine and is an outpocketing that accepts fluid from the small intestine
extra: Site of attachment of the appendix
example: Appendicitis pain settles in the lower right abdomen, where the cecum and its appendix sit.

text: {{c1::Totipotent}} stem cells have the potential to develop into any cell found in the human body
example: Splitting a 2-cell embryo can yield identical twins because each blastomere is totipotent.

text: {{c1::Transverse tubules (T-tubules)}} are extensions of the cell membrane that penetrate into the center of skeletal and cardiac muscle cells
example: T-tubules carry an action potential deep into a fibre so even its central myofibrils contract at once

text: The {{c1::bicarbonate buffer}} is by far the most important buffer for maintaining acid-base balance in the blood
example: Normal blood holds about 24 mEq/L of HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, keeping pH between 7.35 and 7.45.

text: The adrenal cortex releases {{c1::cortisol}} and {{c1::aldosterone}}
extra: Sits along the perimeter of the adrenal gland (top of kidney)
example: John F. Kennedy had Addison disease, in which the adrenal cortex makes too little cortisol and aldosterone.

text: {{c1::Pepsin::Enzyme}} breaks down proteins in the stomach
example: Pepsin starts breaking down the protein in a steak while it sits in your acidic stomach.

text: In a {{c1::lytic}} bacteriophage life cycle, virions are made until the cell lyses
extra: Viruses enter cells and use the cell to make copies of themselves, often destroying the cell in the process
example: Phage T4 fills an E. coli cell with new phages, then bursts it open to release them.

text: Hemoglobin has four polypeptide chains (tetramer), each combined with an {{c1::iron::element}}-containing heme group
example: Iron-deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding leaves too little iron to build heme.

text: The {{c1::sympathetic}} nervous system controls our fight or flight response
example: Seeing a bear on a trail makes your pupils dilate, your heart race, and your digestion pause.

text: Skeletal muscle is {{c1::multinucleated::nucleation}}
example: Each skeletal muscle fibre forms when hundreds of myoblasts fuse, so it holds hundreds of nuclei.

text: {{c1::Autocrine signaling}} is when the cell secretes a hormone or chemical messenger that binds to a receptor on itself
example: Activated T cells secrete IL-2, which binds IL-2 receptors on those same T cells and drives their proliferation.

text: The molecular clock model states that the degree of difference in the genome between two species is related to the {{c1::amount of time}} since the two species broke off from a common ancestor
example: Human and chimp DNA differ by only about 1%, matching a split roughly 6–7 million years ago

text: {{c1::The law of segregation}} states that two alleles of each gene become separated and only one allele from each parent will be passed to the offspring
example: A Pp purple-flowered pea plant puts P into half its gametes and p into the other half.

text: {{c1::Progesterone}} maintains and protects the endometrium
extra:
“Estrogen establishes and progesterone protects the endometrium”
Progesterone responds to LH
example: After ovulation, the corpus luteum's progesterone keeps the endometrium ready; when it falls, menstruation starts.

text: {{c1::Periosteum}} is a thin membrane that covers many of the bones in your body
example: A kick to the shin hurts sharply because the tibia's periosteum, just under the skin, is full of pain nerves

text: The sarcolemma maintains a/an {{c1::membrane potential}} much like a neuron does
example: A resting skeletal muscle fibre sits at about −90 mV, close to a neuron's −70 mV

text: A/an {{c1::plasmid}} is a small prokaryotic DNA molecule separate from chromosomal DNA
extra: Often, the genes carried in plasmids provide bacteria with genetic advantages, such as antibiotic resistance
example: Scientists insert the human insulin gene into a plasmid so E. coli makes human insulin.

text: {{c1::Red::Color}} skeletal muscle fibers are slow-twitch and carry out oxidative phosphorylation
extra: The red color is from myoglobin, which binds oxygen
example: The dark meat of a chicken's legs is red, slow-twitch muscle used for standing all day.

text: The {{c1::gut microbiota}} is a community of microorganisms that live in the digestive tracts
extra: These microorganisms produce vitamin K and biotin (vitamin B7)
example: Newborns lack the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, so they get a vitamin K shot at birth.

text: {{c1::Action potential}} is the mechanism by which electrical signals travel through the nervous system
example: An action potential travels a myelinated motor axon at about 100 m/s, crossing a 1 m leg nerve in 10 ms.

text:
The four phases of Mitosis:
  1. {{c1::Prophase}}
  2. {{c1::Metaphase}}
  3. {{c1::Anaphase}}
  4. {{c1::Telophase}}
extra:
Acronym: PMAT
Note: Interphase precedes mitosis, it is not part of mitosis
example: On an onion root-tip slide you can spot cells caught in each of prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

text:
Urine pathway:
{{c1::Bowman's space}} → {{c1::proximal convoluted tubule}} → {{c1::descending limb of the loop of Henle}} → {{c1::ascending limb of the loop of Henle}} → {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}} → {{c1::collecting duct}} → {{c1::renal pelvis}} → {{c1::ureter}} → {{c1::bladder}} → {{c1::urethra}}
example: A urinary tract infection usually climbs the pathway in reverse, from urethra to bladder to kidney.

text: The {{c1::pleural cavity (or space)}} is a thin fluid-filled space between the two pleurae of each lung
example: In a pneumothorax, air leaks into the pleural space and the lung collapses.

text: ADH is a hormone that increases permeability of the {{c1::collecting duct}} to H2O, which {{c1::increases::increases or decreases}} H2O reabsorption
extra: Results in higher BP and lower blood osmolarity. The urine will be concentrated
example: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels into collecting duct cells, so a dehydrated person makes dark, concentrated urine.

text: The {{c1::SRY gene::gene}} is responsible for initiation of male sex determination and codes for testis-determining factor (TDF)
example: An XX person whose X carries a translocated SRY gene develops testes (XX male syndrome).

text: In heterozygous females with an X-linked recessive mutation, the mutation {{c1::will not::will or will not}} be expressed
extra: Females have two X chromosomes, so the mutation is carried but not expressed. The normal X chromosome will be expressed because this is a recessive trait
example: Queen Victoria carried the hemophilia allele without the disease but passed it to her son Leopold.

text: Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption in the {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}} and {{c1::collecting duct}}, thereby increasing H2O reabsorption and raising blood pressure
example: Amiloride blocks the ENaC Na<sup>+</sup> channels that aldosterone upregulates in the collecting duct.

text: Parietal cells secrete {{c1::HCl}} and {{c1::intrinsic factor}}
extra: Intrinsic factor is needed for vitamin B12 absorption
example: Omeprazole blocks the parietal cell H<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump, cutting stomach acid in reflux disease.

text: {{c1::Skeletal::Type}} muscle provides support and is involved with movement, blood propulsion, and thermoregulation
example: Calf muscle contractions while walking squeeze the leg veins, pushing blood back toward the heart.

text:
The 7 taxonomic ranks in order:
  1. Most specific: {{c1::Species}}
  2. {{c1::Genus}}
  3. {{c1::Family}}
  4. {{c1::Order}}
  5. {{c1::Class}}
  6. {{c1::Phylum}}
  7. Broadest: {{c1::Kingdom}}
extra: King Phillip Came Over From Great Spain
example: Humans: Homo sapiens, genus Homo, Hominidae, Primates, Mammalia, Chordata, Animalia

text: When the {{c1::stretch reflex::... reflex}} is activated, the stretched muscles and the supporting muscles are contracted while the antagonist muscles are inhibited (relaxed)
extra: The stretch reflex (myotatic reflex) is a muscle contraction in response to stretching within the muscle
example: Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, which contracts while the hamstrings relax: the knee jerk

text: A virus is a nonliving particle containing {{c1::protein}} and {{c1::DNA or RNA}} that can infect a living cell
example: Tobacco mosaic virus is a single RNA strand wrapped in a protein coat, with no cytoplasm or ribosomes.

text: {{c1::Inspiratory reserve volume}} is the volume of additional air that can be forcibly inhaled following normal inhalation
example: Gasping in extra air before diving underwater, on top of a normal breath, uses your inspiratory reserve volume (~3 L).

text: {{c1::Hyporeflexia}} refers to below normal or absent reflexes
extra:
It can be detected through the use of a reflex hammer
It is the opposite of hyperreflexia
example: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy often abolishes the ankle-jerk reflex

text: {{c1::Pleural membranes}} allow the lungs to easily move within the body cavity with minimal friction from other organs
example: In pleurisy, inflamed pleurae rub against each other, making every breath sharply painful.

text:
The stomach has the following four parts:
  • {{c1::Fundus}}
  • {{c1::Body}}
  • {{c1::Antrum}}
  • {{c1::Pylorus}}
extra: The enzyme pepsin chemically breaks down proteins
example: In infant pyloric stenosis, a thickened pylorus blocks the stomach outlet, causing projectile vomiting.

text: The {{c1::collecting duct::part of nephron}} has variable permeability, which allows reabsorption of the right amount of H2O depending on the body’s needs
extra: Responsive to both aldosterone and ADH
example: After you drink a litre of water, ADH falls, the collecting duct stays watertight, and you pass pale, dilute urine.

text: The {{c1::founder effect}} is the loss of genetic variation that occurs when a new population is established by a very small number of individuals
example: The Pennsylvania Amish have high rates of Ellis–van Creveld syndrome, traced to a few founders

text: {{c1::Convergent evolution::... evolution}} is the process whereby organisms that are not closely related will independently evolve similar traits as a result of having to adapt to similar environments or ecological niches
example: Sharks (fish) and dolphins (mammals) independently evolved streamlined bodies and fins

text: K+ concentration is higher {{c1::inside::inside or outside}} the cell
example: K<sup>+</sup> is about 140 mM inside a neuron but only about 5 mM outside.

text: {{c1::Parallel evolution::... evolution}} is the independent evolution of similar traits, starting from a similar ancestral condition
example: Freshwater sticklebacks in separate lakes independently evolved reduced armour plates from the same marine ancestor

text: In prokaryotes, the electron transport chain takes place in the {{c1::cell membrane::cellular component}}
example: E. coli pumps protons out across its plasma membrane and makes ATP with ATP synthase in that membrane.

text:
Blood pathway:
right atrium → tricuspid valve → {{c1::right ventricle}} → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins → venae cavae → right atrium
example: The right ventricle wall is about a third as thick as the left, since it pumps only to the nearby lungs.

text: {{c1::Cartilage}} is a connective tissue that is firm but flexible and connects bones together
example: Costal cartilage joins the ribs to the sternum, letting the chest flex as you breathe

text: 2,3-BPG has no effect on {{c1::myoglobin::hemoglobin or myoglobin}}
extra: BPG works by binding in the space between the subunits in hemoglobin. Myoglobin has just one monomer, so BPG does not affect it
example: At high altitude, rising 2,3-BPG unloads more O<sub>2</sub> from hemoglobin but leaves muscle myoglobin unchanged.

text: The {{c1::lymphatic system}} transports lymph, a fluid containing infection-fighting white blood cells, throughout the body
extra:
Equalizes fluid distribution
Transports fats and fat-soluble compounds in chylomicrons
example: Breast cancer spreads first to the armpit lymph nodes because lymph from the breast drains there.

text: {{c1::Endocrine}} signaling releases signals into the bloodstream, which carries them to target cells in distant parts of the body
example: Insulin released by the pancreas travels in the blood to act on muscle and fat cells.

text: A/an {{c1::heterozygous}} genotype has two different alleles
example: A sickle-cell carrier has genotype HbA/HbS: one normal and one sickle allele

text:
Three skin layers:
  • Outer: {{c1::epidermis}}
  • Middle: {{c1::dermis}}
  • Inner: {{c1::hypodermis (subcutaneous layer)}}
example: An insulin injection passes through the epidermis and dermis into the fatty hypodermis.

text: {{c1::Hydrostatic pressure::... pressure}} moves fluid out of a capillary and into the interstitial fluid
example: At the arterial end of a capillary, about 35 mmHg of blood pressure pushes fluid out into the tissues.

text: {{c1::Villi}} are small finger-like projections of tissue which increase the surface area of the intestine
extra:
The capillary bed absorbs water-soluble nutrients
The lacteal absorbs fat and sends it to the lymphatic system
example: When celiac disease flattens the villi, the lost surface area leaves nutrients such as iron poorly absorbed.

text: Repolarization occurs when {{c1::K+}} ions exit the neuron
example: Tetraethylammonium blocks K<sup>+</sup> channels, so the action potential stays depolarized much longer.

text: {{c1::Chromosomal mutations::... mutations}} are much larger than nucleotide mutations and affect whole segments of DNA
example: The Philadelphia chromosome in leukaemia moves a huge DNA segment between chromosomes 9 and 22, not one base

text: {{c1::Pacinian corpuscles}} are nerve endings in the skin responsible for sensitivity to vibration and pressure
example: Feeling your phone buzz in your pocket is detected by Pacinian corpuscles.

text:
Blood pathway (including valves), starting in the right atrium:
{{c1::right atrium}} → {{c1::tricuspid valve}} → {{c1::right ventricle}} → {{c1::pulmonary valve}} → {{c1::pulmonary artery}} → {{c1::lungs}} → {{c1::pulmonary veins}} → {{c1::left atrium}} → {{c1::mitral valve}} → {{c1::left ventricle}} → {{c1::aortic valve}} → {{c1::aorta}} → {{c1::arteries}} → {{c1::arterioles}} → {{c1::capillaries}} → {{c1::venules}} → {{c1::veins}} → {{c1::venae cavae}} → {{c1::right atrium}}
example: A leg-vein clot rides the vena cava through the right heart into the pulmonary artery, lodging in the lungs.

text: {{c1::Dominant}} alleles only require one copy in order to be expressed
example: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant: one mutant HTT copy is enough to cause it

text: {{c1::Meissner's corpuscle}} is a type of nerve ending in the skin that is responsible for sensitivity to light touch
example: Feeling a feather brush lightly across your fingertip uses Meissner's corpuscles.

text:
Blood pathway:
right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → {{c1::mitral valve}} → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins → venae cavae → right atrium
example: In mitral valve prolapse, the valve bulges back into the left atrium, producing a mid-systolic click.

text: The jejunum and ileum of the small intestine are primarily involved in {{c1::absorption}}
example: The terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B<sub>12</sub>, so removing it in Crohn's disease surgery causes B<sub>12</sub> deficiency.

text: {{c1::Codominance}} is when both alleles are simultaneously expressed in the heterozygote
example: Blood type AB: I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup> red cells display both A and B antigens

text: The kidney (one of three portal systems, with the hepatic and hypophyseal) has {{c1::two capillary beds in series}}. They connect the arteries to the veins inside the nephron
extra: The two capillary beds are the glomerular and peritubular capillaries
example: Glomerular capillaries run at about 60 mmHg to filter; peritubular capillaries downstream, about 13 mmHg to reabsorb.

text: The A-band contains both actin and myosin. It is the only part that {{c1::maintains a constant size during contraction}}
example: A 1.6 µm A-band stays 1.6 µm even as its sarcomere shortens from 2.5 to 2.0 µm

text: The {{c1::mitral valve::... valve}} is between the left atrium and the left ventricle
extra: Oxygenated blood passes through
example: Rheumatic fever most often damages the mitral valve, causing mitral stenosis years later.

text: Frequency summation is the addition of {{c1::multiple simple twitches}} before the muscle has a chance to fully relax
example: Holding a heavy grocery bag needs rapid nerve firing so twitches fuse into a steady contraction (tetanus)

text: {{c1::Estrogen::Hormone}} develops the female reproductive tract and thickens the uterine wall
extra:
“Estrogen establishes and progesterone protects the endometrium”
Estrogen responds to FSH
example: After menstruation, rising estrogen from growing follicles rebuilds and thickens the endometrium.

text: Vibrissae are {{c1::nose hairs}}
extra: They trap large particles of dust that might otherwise be inhaled
example: Vibrissae are the hairs you can see just inside your nostrils, the ones some people trim.

text: A/an {{c1::spirometer}} measures the volume of air being exhaled or inhaled
example: An asthmatic blowing into a spirometer shows a reduced FEV<sub>1</sub>, the volume exhaled in the first second.

text: {{c1::ACTH::Hormone}} stimulates the production and release of cortisol
extra:
Adrenocorticotropic Hormone
Released from the anterior pituitary
example: A pituitary tumor making excess ACTH drives cortisol overproduction in Cushing disease.

text: In the term G-protein, the "G" refers to {{c1::the fact that they bind GTP and GDP }}
extra:
GTP = guanosine triphosphate
GDP = guanosine diphosphate
example: Ras is a small G protein: switched on when bound to GTP and off when bound to GDP.

text: {{c1::Trypsin::Enzyme}} catalyzes the hydrolysis of peptide bonds which breaks down proteins into smaller peptides
example: Trypsin cuts proteins on the carboxyl side of lysine and arginine residues.

text: Cell bodies and dendrites (unmyelinated) make up the {{c1::grey::white or grey}} matter in the brain
example: The cerebral cortex, the brain's outer layer, is grey matter packed with neuron cell bodies.

text: In some patients, stroking the sole of the foot produces extension (dorsiflexion) of the big toe, often with extension and abduction ("fanning") of the other toes. This abnormal response is termed the {{c1::extensor plantar reflex}}, or {{c1::Babinski reflex}}
example: After a stroke damaging the corticospinal tract, stroking the patient's sole makes the big toe point up

text: The {{c1::farther apart::closer together or farther apart}} two alleles are on the same chromosome, the more likely they are to assort independently
example: Genes 50 map units apart on one chromosome assort as if they were on different chromosomes

text: {{c1::Synaptic pruning}} refers to the process by which extra neurons and synaptic connections are eliminated in order to increase the efficiency of neuronal transmissions
extra: Synaptic pruning is thought to help the brain transition from childhood to adulthood
example: The teenage prefrontal cortex loses unused synapses while keeping those used for practised skills like piano

text: {{c1::Obligate aerobes::type of microorganism}} require O<sub>2</sub>
example: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe, so it favors the oxygen-rich upper lobes of the lungs.

text: {{c1::Genotype}} is the combination of alleles one has at a given locus
example: A pea plant's genotype at the seed-colour locus can be YY, Yy or yy

text: {{c1::Insulin::Hormone}} signals liver, muscle, and fat cells to take in glucose from the blood
extra: Peptide hormone secreted by beta-islet cells of pancreas
example: Insulin moves GLUT4 transporters to the surface of muscle and fat cells so they take up glucose.

text:
The outer pleural membrane is the {{c1::parietal membrane::... membrane}}
The inner pleural membrane is the {{c1::visceral membrane::... membrane}}
example: Pleurisy pain comes from the parietal pleura, which has pain fibres; the visceral pleura on the lung has none.

text: RBCs and WBCs are both formed in {{c1::bone marrow}}
example: A bone marrow transplant for leukaemia replaces the source of both red and white blood cells.

text: Interphase includes {{c1::G<sub>1</sub>, S, and G<sub>2</sub> phases::cell cycle phases}}
extra: Phase where the cell spends most of its life
example: In a typical 24-hour human cell cycle, about 23 hours are interphase and only about 1 hour is mitosis.

text: The H-zone contains only {{c1::myosin}} filaments
example: In a fully contracted muscle the H-zone almost disappears as actin slides in from both sides

text: Mendel's {{c1::law of independent assortment::law of ...}} states that the alleles of two (or more) different genes get sorted into gametes independently of one another
example: A YyRr pea plant makes YR, Yr, yR and yr gametes in a 1:1:1:1 ratio

text: {{c1::Venules}} are very small blood vessels that bring blood from capillary beds to the veins
example: In inflammation, white blood cells squeeze out of the blood into tissue mainly at postcapillary venules.

text: {{c1::Neurotransmitters}} are stored in synaptic vesicles and are released when Ca2+ enters the axon terminal in response to an action potential
example: Each synaptic vesicle at the neuromuscular junction holds a quantum of several thousand acetylcholine molecules.

text: At the {{c1::G2}} checkpoint, the cell will check that the DNA has replicated correctly
example: A cell whose DNA was broken by radiation is held at the G<sub>2</sub> checkpoint instead of entering mitosis.

text: A/an {{c1::interferon::type of protein}} interferes with viral replication and dispersion
extra: Given off by virally infected cells
example: Interferon-α has been given as a drug to treat chronic hepatitis B and C.

text: During muscle contraction, shortening of the sarcomere occurs as myosin heads bind to the exposed sites on actin, forming {{c1::cross bridges}} and pulling the actin filament along the thick filament
example: Like a tug-of-war team pulling a rope hand over hand, myosin heads grab, pull and regrab actin toward the M-line

text: {{c1::Fine motor::... motor}} skill is the coordination of small muscles in movements; usually involving the synchronisation of hands and fingers with the eyes
example: A 9-month-old picking up a Cheerio between thumb and index finger (pincer grasp)

text:
Urine pathway:
Bowman's space → proximal convoluted tubule → {{c1::descending limb of the loop of Henle}} → ascending limb of the loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra
example: Desert kangaroo rats have very long loops of Henle, letting them make extremely concentrated urine.

text: {{c1::Diastole}} is the period of the cardiac cycle that encompasses ventricular relaxation
extra:
AV valves are open
Semilunar valves are closed
Chambers fill with blood
example: Diastolic pressure, the 80 in a 120/80 reading, is the arterial pressure while the ventricles relax and fill.

text: When multiple presynaptic neurons release neurotransmitters at the same time and trigger an action potential, it is known as {{c1::spatial summation}}
example: Three presynaptic neurons each giving a 5 mV EPSP at once lift a −70 mV cell to its −55 mV threshold.

text: {{c1::Smooth::Type}} muscle forms the supporting tissue of blood vessels and hollow internal organs, such as the stomach, intestine, and bladder
example: Smooth muscle in the uterine wall contracts to push a baby out during labour.

text: The pineal gland secretes {{c1::melatonin::hormone}}
extra: Located in the epithalamus, tucked into a groove between the two thalamus halves
example: The pineal gland releases melatonin when it gets dark, so levels peak in the middle of the night.

text: {{c1::Estrogen::Hormone}} is the primary female sex hormone and leads to the development of secondary sexual characteristics
extra:
Produced by the ovaries
Regulates the menstrual cycle and decreases milk production
“Estrogen establishes; progesterone protects the endometrium”
example: At puberty, rising estrogen drives breast development and widening of the hips.

text: Each {{c1::myocyte}} contains many myofibrils
example: One long, multinucleated skeletal muscle cell holds hundreds to thousands of myofibrils

text: Most of the skin can be classified as {{c1::thin::thick or thin}} skin
example: Hair grows only from thin skin, so the skin of your scalp and forearms is thin skin.

text: Peroxisomes {{c1::break down}} material
example: Peroxisomes break down very-long-chain fatty acids, which pile up in adrenoleukodystrophy.

text: Fertilization occurs in the {{c1::fallopian tube}}
example: Sperm usually meet the egg in the ampulla, the widest part of the fallopian tube, within a day of ovulation.

text: {{c1::Cilia}} function together using their wave-like motion to move mucus up and away from the lungs and back into the throat
extra: This is the mucociliary escalator
example: In Kartagener syndrome, immotile cilia can't clear mucus from the lungs, causing repeated chest infections.

text: {{c1::Schwann cells}} make myelin in PNS
example: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, the immune system attacks Schwann cell myelin, causing ascending weakness.

text: {{c1::Mechanical digestion}} is the physical breakdown of large food molecules into smaller particles
example: Chewing a carrot and the stomach churning food are both mechanical digestion; no chemical bonds are broken.

text: {{c1::Prolactin::Hormone}} stimulates milk production
extra: Released from the anterior pituitary
example: Prolactin stays high while a mother breastfeeds, keeping her milk production going.

text: {{c1::Vital capacity}} is the difference between minimum and maximum volume of air in the lungs
extra: This is the maximum amount of air a person can expel from the lungs after a maximum inhalation
example: With a total lung capacity of 6 L and a residual volume of 1.2 L, vital capacity is 6 − 1.2 = 4.8 L.

text: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) promotes {{c1::increased::increased or decreased}} water retention and {{c1::decreased::increased or decreased}} plasma osmolarity
extra:
Increases blood pressure
Produced in the hypothalamus
Released from the posterior pituitary
example: Alcohol suppresses ADH, which is why drinking beer makes you urinate more.

text: {{c1::CCK}} stimulates the gallbladder to release bile into the biliary tree
extra:
CCK = Cholecystokinin
CCK is released by the duodenum
example: Gallstone pain often strikes shortly after a fatty meal, when CCK makes the gallbladder squeeze.

text:
A pregnancy is divided into the following trimesters:
  • First trimester is from week {{c1::1}} to the end of week {{c1::12}}
  • Second trimester is from week {{c1::13}} to the end of week {{c1::26}}
  • Third trimester is from week {{c1::27}} to {{c1::the end of the pregnancy}}
example: A woman 20 weeks pregnant is in her second trimester, halfway to a 40-week due date

text: {{c1::Mastication}} is the process by which food is crushed and ground by teeth
example: Grinding a carrot between your molars is mastication.

text: The {{c1::osteon}} is the chief structural unit of compact (cortical) bone
extra: Consists of concentric bone layers called lamellae, which surround a long hollow passageway, the Haversian canal
example: A cross-section of the femur's shaft shows thousands of osteons packed like tiny tree trunks

text: The {{c1::gallbladder}} stores and concentrates bile
example: When the gallbladder concentrates bile too far, cholesterol can crystallise into gallstones.

text: The {{c1::Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment::... experiment}} built upon Griffith's experiment and showed that DNA is what caused the bacterial transformation
extra: This brought us one step closer to proving that DNA holds our genetic material
example: Adding DNase to the S-strain extract abolished transformation, while protease and RNase did not

text:
"Thin skin" epidermis has the following 4 layers:
  • Outer: {{c1::Stratum Corneum}}
  • {{c1::Stratum Granulosum}}
  • {{c1::Stratum Spinosum}}
  • Inner: {{c1::Stratum Basale}}
example: Dandruff flakes are dead keratinised cells shed from the stratum corneum of the scalp.

text: A/an {{c1::allele}} is a variant form of a gene located at the same position on a chromosome
example: The ABO blood-group gene has three alleles: I<sup>A</sup>, I<sup>B</sup> and i

text: {{c1::Edema}} results when the lymphatic system is overwhelmed and can’t drain excess fluid from tissues
example: After lymph nodes are removed in breast cancer surgery, the arm on that side can swell with lymphoedema.

text: {{c1::Recessive}} alleles require two copies in order to be expressed
example: Cystic fibrosis appears only when a child inherits two mutant CFTR alleles

text: Vasodilation increases blood flow to the skin and helps to {{c1::expel::expel or retain}} heat
example: After a hot run, your face turns red as skin vessels dilate to shed heat.

text: {{c1::Hematocrit}} is the percentage of blood composed of RBCs
example: Severe dehydration raises the hematocrit, because plasma volume falls while the red cell count stays the same.

text: The {{c1::corticobulbar tract::... tract}} connects the cerebral cortex to the motor cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem
extra: A two-neuron path; does not include the oculomotor nerve
example: A motor cortex stroke can weaken the opposite lower face, drooping one corner of the mouth

text: The somatic nervous system is {{c1::voluntary::voluntary or involuntary}}
extra: Associated with the voluntary control of body movements via skeletal muscles
example: Deciding to kick a soccer ball uses the somatic nervous system to contract your leg's skeletal muscles.

text: Shrinking the diameter of blood vessels that supply the skin, a process known as vasoconstriction, reduces blood flow and helps {{c1::retain::expel or retain}} heat
example: In the cold, your toes go white as skin vessels constrict to keep heat in the core.

text: The {{c1::liver::organ}} detoxifies chemicals and converts NH3 to urea
example: In liver failure, ammonia builds up in the blood and causes confusion (hepatic encephalopathy).

text:
Digestive pathway:
oral cavity → pharynx → {{c1::esophagus}} → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum
example: Heartburn is stomach acid backing up into the esophagus, the tube just above the stomach.

text: {{c1::Gross motor::... motor}} skills are large movements a baby makes with his or her arms, legs, feet, or entire body
extra: Crawling, running, and jumping are gross motor skills

text: {{c1::Afferent}} neurons ascend the spinal cord and carry sensory information to the brain
example: Touching a hot stove sends a signal along afferent fibers through the dorsal root into the spinal cord.

text: {{c1::Bronchioles}} are the smallest of the branches of the bronchi and they end in {{c1::alveoli}}
example: In bronchiolitis, RSV infects babies' bronchioles and clogs the tiny airways leading to the alveoli.

text: The {{c1::corticospinal tract::... tract}} is a white-matter motor pathway from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord that controls movements of the limbs and trunk
extra: Terminates on lower motor neurons and interneurons in the spinal cord
example: A stroke in the left motor cortex paralyses the right arm and leg because the corticospinal tract crosses in the medulla

text: Semen is a combination of {{c1::sperm}} and {{c1::seminal fluid}}
example: Sperm make up only about 2–5% of semen volume; most of the rest comes from the seminal vesicles.

text: Bone, cartilage, tendon, and blood are examples of {{c1::connective}} tissue
example: The Achilles tendon, a dense regular connective tissue, links the calf muscle to the heel bone.

text:
Blood pathway:
right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → {{c1::pulmonary artery::pulmonary ...}} → lungs → {{c1::pulmonary veins::pulmonary ...}} → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins → venae cavae → right atrium
example: Before birth, most blood bypasses the lungs from the pulmonary artery to the aorta through the ductus arteriosus.

text: If your blood osmolarity is {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} than normal, your body reacts to replace this water loss by releasing ADH
extra:
ADH leads to increased water resorption by your kidneys
Osmolarity goes down and blood pressure goes up
example: After a salty meal, rising plasma osmolarity triggers ADH release, so you pass less, darker urine.

text: The {{c1::nephron}} is the functional unit of the kidney
extra: There are 1.3 million nephrons per kidney
example: Diabetes slowly destroys nephrons, which cannot regrow, leading to chronic kidney disease.

text: The {{c1::Golgi apparatus::organelle}} modifies and distributes proteins
example: The Golgi tags enzymes bound for lysosomes with mannose-6-phosphate.

text:
The phases of meiosis:
  1. {{c1::Prophase I}}
  2. {{c1::Metaphase I}}
  3. {{c1::Anaphase I}}
  4. {{c1::Telophase I}}
  5. {{c1::Prophase II}}
  6. {{c1::Metaphase II}}
  7. {{c1::Anaphase II}}
  8. {{c1::Telophase II}}
example: A human spermatocyte runs PMAT twice to make four haploid sperm with 23 chromosomes each.

text: Cardiac muscle is {{c1::uninucleated::nucleation}}
extra: It can sometimes be considered binucleated
example: A cardiac muscle cell is a branched cell with one central nucleus, unlike a multinucleated biceps fibre.

text: In an adrenergic receptor sequence, adenylyl cyclase removes 2 phosphates from {{c1::ATP}} to produce {{c1::cAMP}}
extra: cAMP is a second messenger
example: Adenylyl cyclase cuts pyrophosphate (PP<sub>i</sub>) off ATP and links the remaining phosphate into a ring.

text: A/an {{c1::Punnett square}} is a square diagram that is used to predict the genotypes of a particular cross or breeding experiment
example: A Punnett square for two Aa carriers gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa

text: {{c1::Haversian canals}} contain the blood vessels and nerves of bone and communicate with bone cells through channels called canaliculi
example: A cross-section of compact bone shows each osteon's central Haversian canal holding tiny blood vessels and a nerve

text: {{c1::Dendritic cells}} are antigen-presenting cells in the skin
example: After a mosquito bite, skin dendritic cells pick up the foreign proteins and carry them to the nearest lymph node.

text: {{c1::Platelets}}, also called {{c1::thrombocytes}}, are a component of blood whose function is to react to bleeding from blood vessel injury by clumping, thereby initiating a blood clot
example: Aspirin blocks platelet clumping, so someone taking it daily bleeds longer from a small cut.

text: Delta-islet cells of the pancreas release {{c1::somatostatin}}
example: A somatostatinoma of delta cells suppresses insulin, causing diabetes, gallstones, and fatty stools.

text: A/an {{c1::synapse}} is a junction between two nerve cells
example: The human brain has roughly 100 trillion synapses linking its neurons.

text: The primary neurotransmitter at neuromuscular junctions is {{c1::acetylcholine}}
example: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing droopy eyelids.

text:
Air pathway:
{{c1::Nasal/oral cavities}} → {{c1::pharynx}} → {{c1::larynx}} → {{c1::trachea}} → {{c1::bronchi}} → {{c1::bronchioles}} → {{c1::alveoli}}
example: Inhaled air passes about 23 generations of branching airways between the trachea and the alveoli.

text: {{c1::Immovable}} joints are fused together to form sutures
example: The sutures joining the skull's parietal bones are immovable joints

text: Gene–environment interaction is when {{c1::two different genotypes}} respond to environmental variation in different ways
example: Children with PKU develop intellectual disability on a normal diet but not on a low-phenylalanine diet

text: {{c1::Somatostatin (GHIH)::Hormone}} inhibits GH and also leads to lower insulin and lower glucagon
extra:
Growth Hormone-Inhibiting Hormone
Peptide hormone secreted by delta-islet cells of pancreas
example: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, treats acromegaly by suppressing GH release.

text: A {{c1::shunt}} is a hole or a small passage that allows fluid to move from one part of the body to another
extra: Example: Shunt vessels connect an artery directly to a vein so the blood skips the capillaries

text: {{c1::Cell-mediated (cytotoxic) immunity::... immunity}} produces an immune response that does not involve antibodies
extra: It involves the activation of phagocytes, T-cells, and the release of cytokines in response to an antigen
example: A positive TB skin test, a firm red bump 48-72 h after injection, is a T-cell reaction, not an antibody one.

text:
White blood cells (leukocytes) come in five major types that are divided into the following two groups:
  • {{c1::Granulocytes}}
  • {{c1::Agranulocytes}}
example: Neutrophils are granulocytes; lymphocytes are agranulocytes.

text: {{c1::Phenotype}} is the observable manifestation of a genotype
example: Pea plants with genotypes YY and Yy share the same yellow-seed phenotype

text: A/an {{c1::capsid}} is the protein shell of a virus
example: HIV's cone-shaped capsid is built from many copies of the p24 protein.

text: Na+ concentration is higher {{c1::outside::inside or outside}} the cell
example: Na<sup>+</sup> is about 145 mM outside a neuron but only about 15 mM inside.

text: GnRH is produced by the {{c1::hypothalamus}} and acts on the {{c2::anterior pituitary}} to trigger FSH and LH release
example: People with Kallmann syndrome make no GnRH, so FSH and LH stay low and puberty does not start.

text: The law of segregation occurs in {{c1::anaphase I::meiosis phase}}
example: In anaphase I of a Pp pea plant cell, the homolog carrying P and the one carrying p go to opposite poles.

text: {{c1::Spongy}} bone, also known as cancellous bone or trabecular bone, is a very porous type of bone located at the ends of the long bones (the epiphyses), with harder compact bone surrounding it
example: Bone marrow biopsies are taken from the spongy bone of the hip (iliac crest), where red marrow fills the spaces.

text: {{c1::Systole}} is the part of the cardiac cycle during which some chambers of the heart muscle contract after refilling with blood
extra:
AV valves are closed
Semilunar valves are open
Blood pumps from the chambers into the arteries
example: Systolic pressure, the 120 in a 120/80 reading, is the arterial pressure while the ventricles contract.

text: {{c1::Skin}} is a physical barrier and secretes antimicrobial enzymes like defensins
example: Burn patients who lose large areas of skin are at high risk of Pseudomonas infection.

text: During muscle contraction, Ca2+ binds to {{c1::troponin}}, causing a shift in tropomyosin and exposure of the myosin-binding sites on the actin filament
example: Ca<sup>2+</sup> binds troponin C; once the SR pumps Ca<sup>2+</sup> back, tropomyosin re-covers actin and the muscle relaxes

text: {{c1::Efferent}} neurons exit the spinal cord and bring signals from the brain to the muscles and glands
example: Motor neurons leaving the ventral horn carry the command that makes your biceps contract.

text: Aldosterone increases {{c1::sodium}} reabsorption; water follows osmotically, so blood volume rises without a net change in blood osmolarity
extra: This forces more fluid into the blood and raises BP
example: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone, so the kidney excretes more Na<sup>+</sup> and water and blood pressure falls.

text: The hepatic portal system delivers {{c1::deoxygenated::oxygenated or deoxygenated}} blood to the {{c1::liver::organ}} to be detoxified further before it returns to the heart
example: Swallowed morphine reaches the liver through the portal vein first, so much of it is broken down (first-pass effect).

text: The resting membrane potential (voltage) of a cell is approximately {{c1::-70}} mV
example: A resting motor neuron reads about −70 mV, while a resting cardiac ventricular cell sits near −90 mV.

text: The skeletal system is derived from the {{c1::mesoderm::germ layer}}
example: The femur, its cartilage, and the muscles that move it all arise from mesoderm.

text: {{c1::Temporal summation}} occurs when one presynaptic neuron fires repeatedly in rapid succession and the combined signals trigger an action potential
example: One presynaptic neuron firing three 5 mV EPSPs in quick succession lifts a −70 mV cell to its −55 mV threshold.

text: When the membrane potential is depolarized during an action potential, it reaches a peak of around {{c1::+40}} mV
example: A neuron's voltage swings from −70 mV to +40 mV at the peak, a jump of 110 mV in about 1 ms.

text: {{c1::Glucocorticoids}} are a class of corticosteroids and include the hormone {{c1::cortisol}}
example: Prednisone, a synthetic glucocorticoid, is prescribed to suppress inflammation during an asthma flare.

text: {{c1::Lysosomes}} are the demolition and recycling center
example: In Tay-Sachs disease, a missing lysosomal enzyme (hexosaminidase A) lets GM2 ganglioside pile up in neurons.

text:
Hormones can be grouped into three main types:
  • {{c1::Peptide hormones}}
  • {{c1::Amine hormones}}
  • {{c1::Steroid hormones}}
example: Insulin is a peptide hormone, epinephrine an amine hormone, and cortisol a steroid hormone.

text: {{c1::Direct hormones::... hormones}} act directly on the target tissue or organ
{{c1::Lysozyme}} is an antimicrobial enzyme that forms part of the innate immune system
extra: Found in tears and saliva
example: Lysozyme, discovered by Alexander Fleming in his own nasal mucus, digests the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.

text: {{c1::Synovial}} fluid lubricates the joints and permits smooth movement
example: Healthy knee synovial fluid is viscous like egg white, letting cartilage surfaces glide with almost no friction

text: This is an example of {{c1::simple columnar}} epithelial tissue
example: The small intestine lining, which absorbs nutrients, is simple columnar epithelium.

text: {{c1::Oligodendrocytes}} make myelin in CNS
example: Multiple sclerosis destroys oligodendrocyte myelin in the brain and spinal cord, slowing nerve signals.

text: The {{c1::amine hormones::... hormones}} are relatively small hormones derived from the amino acids tyrosine and tryptophan
example: Melatonin is made from tryptophan, while epinephrine and T<sub>4</sub> are made from tyrosine.

text: The {{c1::large intestine}} absorbs H2O and salts, and forms feces
example: When stool moves slowly through the colon, it loses extra water and becomes hard (constipation).

text: In muscles, {{c1::creatine phosphate}} is what adds a phosphate group to ADP, forming ATP
example: A sprinter's first ~10 seconds of a 100 m dash run largely on creatine phosphate

text: {{c1::Stabilizing selection::... selection}} is a type of natural selection in which the population mean stabilizes on a particular non-extreme trait value
example: Human babies of about 3–4 kg survive best, while very small or very large newborns fare worse

text: The primary function of red blood cells is to {{c1::carry oxygen}}
extra: RBCs contain hemoglobin to carry oxygen
example: In severe anaemia, too few red cells carry oxygen, so the person gets breathless climbing stairs.

text: {{c1::Androgens}} are a group of hormones that play a role in male traits and reproductive activity
extra: They are steroid hormones and are converted to testosterone and estrogen in the gonads
example: Excess adrenal androgens in congenital adrenal hyperplasia cause ambiguous genitalia in newborn girls.

text: A/an {{c1::chemical synapse::type of synapse}} communicates using chemical messengers (neurotransmitters)
example: At a chemical synapse, serotonin crosses a cleft about 20 nm wide to bind receptors on the next neuron.

text: Smooth muscle is {{c1::uninucleated::nucleation}}
example: Each spindle-shaped smooth muscle cell in the bladder wall has a single central nucleus.

text: {{c1::Ovaries::Organs}} are controlled by FSH and LH
example: The mid-cycle LH surge around day 14 triggers the ovary to release an egg.

text:
Air pathway:
Nasal/oral cavities → {{c1::pharynx}} → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
example: Strep throat is an infection of the pharynx (pharyngitis) by Streptococcus pyogenes.

text: {{c1::Memory B cells}} form after a primary infection and produce an accelerated, more robust antibody response upon re-infection
example: A second measles exposure years after vaccination triggers antibodies within days, so the person never falls ill.

text: {{c1::Enteropeptidase::Enzyme}} is a brush-border enzyme that activates trypsinogen to make trypsin
example: Infants lacking enteropeptidase cannot activate trypsin and fail to thrive from protein malabsorption.

text: {{c1::Dipeptidase::Enzyme}} is a brush-border enzyme that breaks apart dipeptides (bound pairs of amino acids)
example: Aspartame, a dipeptide (Asp-Phe methyl ester), is split by peptidases into aspartate and phenylalanine.

text: The main function of {{c1::atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)}} is to lower the blood pressure by promoting excretion of water and sodium
example: A large IV saline infusion stretches the atria, which release ANP to dump the extra salt and water in urine.

text: During the {{c1::G1 phase::cell cycle phase}}, cells synthesize mRNA and proteins
extra:
Prepares the cell for the later steps leading to mitosis
G1 stands for "Gap 1"
example: A liver cell in G<sub>1</sub> makes the mRNA and proteins, like cyclin D, it needs before copying its DNA.

text: {{c1::Juxtacrine}} signaling is when a cell signals another cell that is directly adjacent or attached
example: Notch receptors on one cell bind Delta ligands on the membrane of the neighboring cell it touches.

text: The {{c1::SA node}} is the heart's natural pacemaker
example: The SA node fires about 60 to 100 times a minute, setting a normal resting heart rate.

text: {{c1::Incomplete dominance::... dominance}} is a form of intermediate inheritance in which one allele for a specific trait is not completely expressed over its paired allele
example: Crossing red and white snapdragons gives pink-flowered offspring

text: The {{c1::adrenal glands}} are endocrine glands located above the kidneys and they produce a variety of hormones
example: A sudden scare makes your adrenal medulla release epinephrine, raising your heart rate

text: The {{c1::sarcolemma}} is a cell membrane that encloses each muscle cell
