example: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, missing dystrophin lets the sarcolemma tear during contraction

text:
Air pathway:
Nasal/oral cavities → pharynx → larynx → trachea → {{c1::bronchi}} → bronchioles → alveoli
example: An inhaled peanut usually lodges in the right main bronchus, which is wider and more vertical than the left.

text: In neurological terms, {{c1::fasciculations}} are the spontaneous firing of a motor unit
extra:
With fasciculation, only one or few of these units fire
Fasciculations can be caused by something as simple as drinking too much caffeine
example: Patients with ALS show visible fasciculations rippling under the skin of the arms and tongue

text: {{c1::Penetrance}} is the proportion of individuals carrying a particular variant of a gene that also express an associated trait
example: If 80 of 100 people carrying a mutant allele show the disease, its penetrance is 80%

text: {{c1::Ruffini endings}} are responsible for the sensation of the stretch of your skin
example: Sensing your skin stretch as you bend your fingers around a cup uses Ruffini endings.

text: Immunization induces {{c1::active immunity::... immunity}}, the activation of B-cells that produce antibodies
example: The MMR vaccine makes your own B cells produce measles antibodies that last for decades.

text: The stomach has a pH of about {{c1::2}}
example: Stomach acid at pH 2 is about as acidic as lemon juice, 100,000 times more acidic than pure water (pH 7).

text: {{c1::Troponin::protein}} is bound to {{c1::tropomyosin::protein}}; together they regulate actin–myosin interactions
example: In a relaxed biceps, tropomyosin blocks actin's myosin-binding sites, held in place by troponin until Ca<sup>2+</sup> arrives

text: In a/an {{c1::lysogenic}} bacteriophage life cycle, the virus DNA is embedded into the host DNA
example: Bacteriophage lambda inserts its DNA into the E. coli chromosome as a prophage and lies dormant.

text: {{c1::Mast cells}} release cytokines and granules that contain chemical molecules to create an inflammatory cascade
extra: Important for wound healing and defense against pathogens via the inflammatory response
example: A mosquito bite turns into an itchy red bump as skin mast cells degranulate.

text: In a/an {{c1::electrical synapse::... synapse}}, there is a direct physical connection (gap junctions) between the presynaptic neuron and the postsynaptic neuron
extra: Electrical current in the form of ions flow between the cells
example: The crayfish tail-flip escape reflex uses electrical synapses, so the signal crosses with almost no delay.

text: {{c1::Membrane potential}} is an electrical potential difference between the inside and outside of a cell
extra: Measured as the voltage between one electrode inside and one outside the plasma membrane
example: A microelectrode inside a squid giant axon reads about −70 mV relative to the seawater bath.

text: Myoglobin contains {{c1::one::#}} heme group
example: A myoglobin molecule carries at most one O<sub>2</sub>; a hemoglobin molecule carries up to four.

text: A {{c1::peptide hormone::... hormone}} is a hormone that consists of amino acids
extra:
Water soluble
Examples: insulin, glucagon, leptin, ADH, oxytocin

text: G-cells secrete {{c1::gastrin}}
extra: A peptide hormone that increases HCl secretion and gastric motility
example: A gastrin-secreting tumour (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) causes excess acid and multiple ulcers.

text: This is an example of {{c1::bacilli (rod)::shape}} bacteria
example: Escherichia coli and Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) are rod-shaped bacilli.

text: The {{c1::rough::smooth or rough}} ER makes proteins from mRNA
example: Antibody-secreting plasma cells are packed with rough ER.

text: {{c1::Piloerection}} is the erection or bristling of hairs due to the involuntary contraction of small muscles at the base of hair follicles that occurs as a reflexive response cold
example: A cat facing a dog puffs up its fur, the same reflex that gives you goosebumps.

text: The {{c1::adrenal medulla}} is the principal site of the conversion of tyrosine into the catecholamines
extra: The adrenal medulla is located at the center of the adrenal gland, surrounded by the adrenal cortex which sits on top of the kidneys
example: A pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal medulla, floods the blood with epinephrine, causing spikes in blood pressure.

text: {{c1::Hemoglobin}} is found inside RBCs and it carries oxygen
example: Each gram of hemoglobin carries about 1.34 mL of O<sub>2</sub>, so 15 g/dL holds ~20 mL O<sub>2</sub> per 100 mL of blood.

text: Centrioles contain 9 triplets of {{c1::microtubules}} and organize the spindle fibers that pull {{c1::chromosomes}} apart
example: Colchicine blocks microtubule assembly, so the spindle never forms and dividing cells stall in metaphase.

text: {{c1::Hyperpolarization}} is when the membrane potential dips below the resting potential
extra: While hyperpolarized, the neuron is in the relative refractory period: a greater-than-normal stimulus is needed to trigger a second action potential
example: After a spike, a neuron dips to about −80 mV before settling back to −70 mV.

text: {{c1::Endoderm::Germ layer}} develops into the GI tract, respiratory tract, endocrine glands, bronchi, bladder, and stomach
extra: “In-doderm”: Things that are inside
example: The lining of the gut, the liver, the pancreas, and the thyroid gland all come from endoderm.

text: {{c1::Disruptive selection::... selection}} favors organisms with extreme traits over those with intermediate traits, driving a population apart
example: African seedcracker finches have either small or large beaks for soft or hard seeds; medium beaks lose out

text: The {{c1::ductus arteriosus}} is a shunt that allows blood from the right ventricle to bypass the fetus's non-functioning lungs
extra: It connects the main pulmonary artery to the proximal descending aorta in a fetus
example: Indomethacin can close a patent ductus arteriosus in a premature baby by blocking prostaglandins.

text: {{c1::ATP}} binds to the myosin head, allowing it to release from actin
example: Rigor mortis: after death no ATP is made, so myosin heads stay locked onto actin

text: The nucleolus makes {{c1::ribosomes}}
example: Fast-growing cancer cells often show large, prominent nucleoli that churn out ribosomes.

text: If the blood pH is too high, respiration will {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}}
extra:
Respiration goes down, trapping CO2
Based on Le Châtelier’s Principle, the bicarbonate buffer will shift right to add more H+ which will lower the pH
example: A patient who vomits repeatedly loses stomach acid, becomes alkalotic, and breathes more slowly and shallowly.

text: Fetal hemoglobin has a {{c1::lower::higher or lower}} P50 because of its high affinity for oxygen
extra: P50 is the oxygen pressure when 50% of hemoglobin has an oxygen bound
example: Fetal hemoglobin's P<sub>50</sub> is about 19 mmHg, versus about 27 mmHg for adult hemoglobin.

text: Male chromosome pairs are {{c1::XY::XX or XY}}
example: A human male's karyotype is 46,XY, and the SRY gene on his Y chromosome triggers testis development.

text: The hemoglobin dissociation curve is {{c1::sigmoidal::shape}}
extra: Sigmoidal because once a single O2 is bound, the other 3 hemes quickly bind their own O2 molecule
example: Hb stays about 90% saturated as PO<sub>2</sub> falls from 100 to 60 mmHg, then plunges to about 35% at 20 mmHg.

text: The {{c1::detrusor muscle}} is the muscular lining of the bladder; it relaxes to store urine and contracts during urination
example: Oxybutynin, an anticholinergic, relaxes the detrusor to treat an overactive bladder.

text: {{c1::Histamine}} is released by mast cells and causes blood vessels to dilate, increasing blood flow and cell trafficking to an area of infection
example: Antihistamines such as cetirizine block histamine to calm the red, swollen hives of an allergy.

text: The nervous system outside the brain and spinal cord is the {{c1::peripheral}} nervous system
example: The sciatic nerve running down your leg and the vagus nerve to your heart are part of the PNS.

text:
{{c1::MHC-I}} glycoproteins are present on all nucleated cells
{{c1::MHC-II}} glycoproteins are present on specialized antigen-presenting cells (APCs), including macrophages, dendritic cells, and B cells
example: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus and shows no MHC-I, while every liver cell does.

text: {{c1::Foramen ovale}} is a shunt that allows blood to bypass the fetal lungs
extra: In the wall between the left and right atria of a fetus
example: If the foramen ovale fails to seal after birth it stays open as a patent foramen ovale, found in about 1 in 4 adults.

text: The main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord is {{c1::glycine}}
example: Strychnine blocks glycine receptors in the spinal cord, causing uncontrolled muscle spasms.

text: Blood in the umbilical artery is {{c1::deoxygenated::oxygenated or deoxygenated}}
example: The two umbilical arteries carry CO<sub>2</sub>-rich blood from the fetus's internal iliac arteries to the placenta.

text: In muscle contraction, depolarization spreads down the sarcolemma to the T-tubules, triggering the release of {{c1::Ca2+}}
example: Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia by blocking Ca<sup>2+</sup> release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

text: {{c1::Long bones::... bones}} are hard, dense bones that provide strength, structure, and mobility
extra: Some bones in the fingers are classified as long bones, even though they are short in length
example: The femur, the body's longest bone, is the classic long bone

text: The {{c1::tricuspid valve::... valve}} is between the right atrium and the right ventricle
extra: Deoxygenated blood passes through
example: IV drug users often get tricuspid valve endocarditis, as injected bacteria hit that valve first.

text:
Pathway of electrical conduction in the heart:
{{c1::}}
example: Each beat starts in the SA node, pauses ~0.1 s at the AV node, then races down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.

text: An inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) {{c1::hyperpolarizes::depolarizes or hyperpolarizes}} the cell
extra: It keeps the membrane potential of the postsynaptic neuron below threshold for firing an action potential
example: GABA opens Cl<sup>−</sup> channels, and Cl<sup>−</sup> flowing in pulls the neuron's voltage further below threshold.

text:
The three types of granulocytes are:
  • {{c1::Neutrophils}}
  • {{c1::Eosinophils}}
  • {{c1::Basophils}}
extra:
-phil = granulocytes
Part of the innate immune system
example: The pus in an infected cut is mostly dead neutrophils.

text: {{c1::Crossing over}} is when two chromosomes of a homologous pair exchange segments with each other
example: A maternal chromosome carrying A and B swaps a segment with its paternal partner carrying a and b, giving Ab and aB.

text: In eukaryotes, the electron transport chain takes place in the {{c1::inner mitochondrial membrane::cellular component}}
example: The cristae folds of the inner membrane give a heart muscle cell's mitochondria huge area for the ETC.

text: {{c1::Hair follicle receptors}} are mechanoreceptors that send sensory (afferent) impulses to the CNS when hair moves
example: Brushing a feather across just the tips of your arm hairs is felt even though it never touches your skin

text: The {{c1::bulbourethral gland}} makes viscous fluid to clean out the urethra
example: The clear pre-ejaculate fluid released during arousal comes from the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.

text: {{c1::Sarcomeres}} are the functional units of muscle and are composed of long, fibrous proteins as filaments that slide past each other when a muscle contracts or relaxes
example: A biceps fibre shortens during a curl because thousands of its sarcomeres, lined up in series, all shorten

text: {{c1::Gonads}} are glands that produce gametes (sex cells) and sex hormones
The cell membrane's resting potential is maintained by the fact that there are {{c1::more::more or less}} K+ leak channels than Na+ leak channels
extra: More K+ leaves the cell than Na+ enters, so the inside stays negative
example: Because the resting membrane is far more K<sup>+</sup>-permeable, a neuron rests near −70 mV, close to K<sup>+</sup>'s −90 mV.

text: The {{c1::trachea}} is a hollow tube that connects the larynx to the bronchi of the lungs. It is also called the windpipe
extra: Ciliated epithelium collects debris in the trachea and bronchi
example: C-shaped rings of cartilage hold the trachea open; you can feel them at the front of your neck.

text: Myoglobin stores and releases oxygen in {{c1::muscle tissue}}
example: Sperm whale muscle is so rich in myoglobin it looks almost black, storing O<sub>2</sub> for long dives.

text: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) does not have β subunits, so {{c1::2,3-BPG}} has less of an effect on it
extra: This is why fetal hemoglobin has a greater affinity for O2 compared to adult hemoglobin
example: HbF (α<sub>2</sub>γ<sub>2</sub>) pulls O<sub>2</sub> away from the mother's HbA across the placenta.

text: Gram-positive bacteria stain {{c1::purple::color}} and have a {{c1::thick::thick or thin}} wall
extra: Wall is made of peptidoglycan/lipoteichoic acid
example: Staphylococcus aureus holds crystal violet in its thick peptidoglycan wall and looks purple.

text: Bile is made in the {{c1::liver}} and stored in the {{c1::gallbladder}}
example: After gallbladder removal, people still make bile, but it drips steadily into the intestine instead of being saved.

text: {{c1::Arterioles}} are tiny branches of arteries that lead to capillaries
example: Arterioles in your skin constrict in the cold, which is why your fingers turn pale.

text: This is an example of {{c1::stratified squamous}} epithelial tissue
example: The epidermis of the skin and the lining of the esophagus are stratified squamous epithelium.

text: Mitosis and cytokinesis occur in the {{c1::M phase::cell cycle phase}}
example: A dividing onion root-tip cell in M phase shows condensed chromosomes, then a cell plate splitting it in two.

text:
Hormones produced by the anterior pituitary:
{{c1::}}
example: A prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma causes milk discharge and missed periods

text: {{c1::Transposons}} are DNA sequences that can change their position within a genome
example: McClintock's 'jumping genes' moving in and out of a pigment gene give maize kernels their speckled colors.

text: {{c1::Endorphins}} are released from the anterior pituitary and decrease pain
example: Endorphins bind the same μ-opioid receptors as morphine to blunt pain.

text: {{c1::Luteinizing Hormone (LH)}} induces ovulation in females and, in males, it initiates the production of testosterone
example: In men, LH acts on Leydig cells in the testes, which respond by making testosterone.

text: {{c1::Adaptive radiation}} is the relatively fast evolution of many species from a single common ancestor
extra: Adaptive radiation generally occurs when an organism enters a new area and different traits affect its survival
example: Darwin's finches: one mainland ancestor gave rise to over a dozen Galápagos species with different beaks

text: The {{c1::external::internal or external}} urethral sphincter is made of skeletal muscle and is under voluntary control
example: Holding your urine on a long car ride until you reach a restroom uses the external urethral sphincter.

text: {{c1::Arteries}} are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart
extra:
Thick muscular tube
Elasticity allows for recoil and helps propel blood forward
example: You can feel the radial artery pulse at your wrist because the artery wall stretches with each heartbeat.

text: {{c1::Red blood cells::... blood cells}} have no nucleus, mitochondria, or organelles
example: Lacking mitochondria, red blood cells make all their ATP by glycolysis and never use the O<sub>2</sub> they carry.

text: A recessive allele is only expressed if an organism is {{c1::homozygous}} for it (both alleles are recessive)
example: PKU appears only in children homozygous for the recessive PAH allele

text: Eukaryotic cells reproduce via {{c1::mitosis}}
example: A skin cell divides by mitosis into two identical daughter cells with 46 chromosomes each.

text: K<sup>+</sup> leaves the cell through {{c1::voltage gated K<sup>+</sup> channels}} and {{c1::leak channels}}
example: During repolarisation, K<sup>+</sup> rushes out through voltage-gated channels, taking the neuron from +30 mV back toward −70 mV.

text: When two genes are close together on the same chromosome, they {{c1::do not assort independently}} and are said to be linked
example: Morgan's fruit-fly genes for body colour and wing size sit close on one chromosome and are mostly inherited together

text: Shivering is small, rapid contractions of {{c1::skeletal::type}} muscle that generate heat by expending energy
example: Teeth chattering on a cold day is shivering of the skeletal jaw muscles.

text: The small intestine is lined with {{c1::villi}}, which are covered with {{c1::microvilli}}
example: In celiac disease, gluten flattens the villi and microvilli, so nutrients are poorly absorbed.

text: The {{c1::internal::internal or external}} urethral sphincter is made of smooth muscle and is under involuntary (autonomic) control
example: In males, the internal urethral sphincter closes during ejaculation so semen does not enter the bladder.

text: This is an example of {{c1::transitional}} epithelial tissue
example: The bladder is lined by transitional epithelium, which stretches as the bladder fills with urine.

text: {{c1::Residual volume}} is the amount of air that remains in a person's lungs after fully exhaling
extra: Some air must stay in the lungs to keep the alveoli from collapsing
example: Even after you blow out every last bit of air, about 1.2 L stays in your lungs.

text: {{c1::G-Protein Coupled Receptor (GPCR)}} is a membrane receptor that transfers a signal from outside the cell to the inside of the cell
extra: About 50% of all modern drugs target GPCRs
example: Epinephrine binding the β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic GPCR outside a cell raises cAMP inside it.

text: {{c1::Tidal volume}} is the volume of air inhaled and exhaled in a normal breath
example: A resting adult moves about 500 mL of air in and out with each quiet breath.

text: This is an example of {{c1::spirilla (spiral)::shape}} bacteria
example: Helicobacter pylori, the spiral-shaped bacterium behind stomach ulcers, corkscrews through gastric mucus.

text: {{c1::Embryogenesis}} is the process by which the embryo forms and develops
example: A human zygote divides into a 16-cell morula by about day 3–4 after fertilization

text: Blood pressure is sensed and maintained by {{c1::baroreceptors}} and {{c1::chemoreceptors}}
example: When you stand up quickly and BP dips, carotid sinus baroreceptors sense it and your heart rate rises within seconds.

text: White blood cells are also known as {{c1::leukocytes}}
example: Leukaemia, a cancer of white blood cells, takes its name from the same leuko- (white) root.

text: {{c1::Tyrosine::Amino acid}} is the precursor to catecholamines
extra: Tyrosine is converted into catecholamines in the adrenal medulla
example: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine → norepinephrine → epinephrine.

text:
Air pathway:
Nasal/oral cavities → pharynx → {{c1::larynx}} → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
extra: Larynx is the "voice box"
example: Shouting at a concert can inflame the vocal cords in the larynx (laryngitis) and leave you hoarse.

text: {{c1::Clonus}} is a series of involuntary, rhythmic, muscular contractions and relaxations
example: Sharply dorsiflexing the foot of a patient with a spinal cord injury sets off repeated rhythmic ankle beats

text: {{c1::Muscle spindles}} are stretch receptors within the body of a muscle that primarily detect changes in the length of the muscle
example: When your head drops as you doze off, neck muscle spindles sense the stretch and jerk it back up

text: The myoglobin oxygen saturation curve is hyperbolic because {{c1::it only has one heme group and cannot exhibit cooperative binding}}
example: Like a Michaelis-Menten enzyme, myoglobin's saturation climbs steeply at low PO<sub>2</sub> and then levels off, with no lag.

text: {{c1::Genetic leakage}} is when genes flow from one species to another via hybrid offspring
{{c1::Virions}} are individual virus particles found outside cells
example: A sneeze sprays influenza virions that drift through the air until they reach a new host's cells.

text: The {{c1::bundle of His}} transmits impulses from the AV node to the ventricles
example: The bundle of His is the only electrical path through the insulating fibrous ring between atria and ventricles.

text: {{c1::Gonadotropin-releasing hormone::... hormone}} stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH
extra:
GnRH
Produced by the hypothalamus
example: In Kallmann syndrome GnRH is missing, so FSH and LH stay low and puberty does not start.

text: {{c1::MHC-I}} displays endogenous antigen to cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells
example: A flu-infected airway cell shows viral peptides on MHC-I, and a CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell kills it.

text: In {{c1::prophase::mitosis phase}}, the DNA condenses, centrioles migrate to opposite poles, and microtubules form
example: In prophase, a human cell's loose chromatin condenses into 46 visible X-shaped chromosomes.

text:
Thermoregulation is accomplished through:
  • {{c1::Sweating}}
  • {{c1::Piloerection}}
  • {{c1::Shivering}}
  • {{c1::Vasodilation / Vasoconstriction}}
example: Stepping out into winter air, you get goosebumps and start to shiver.

text: {{c1::Tendons}} attach bones to muscles
example: The Achilles tendon attaches the calf muscles to the heel bone (calcaneus)

text: The {{c1::liver}} synthesizes bile, albumin and clotting factors
example: Patients with cirrhosis bruise and bleed easily because the liver makes too few clotting factors.

text: The {{c1::vasa recta::structure}} and {{c1::loop of Henle::structure}} flow in opposite directions, creating a countercurrent multiplier system that allows maximal reabsorption of water
example: Without the vasa recta's countercurrent flow, blood would wash out the medulla's ~1,200 mOsm/L salt gradient.

text: A study that looks at the interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental events is looking at {{c1::gene-environment interaction}}, not epigenetics
example: Caspi found maltreated boys with low-activity MAOA were far more likely to become antisocial

text: The nucleoid region is found in {{c1::prokaryotes::eukaryotes or prokaryotes}} and contains {{c1::DNA}}
example: E. coli packs its single circular 4.6 Mb chromosome into a nucleoid with no membrane around it.

text: Cartilage is {{c1::avascular}} and {{c1::aneural}}
extra:
Avascular: no blood vessels
Aneural: no nerves
example: Worn knee cartilage in osteoarthritis barely regrows because no blood vessels bring repair cells

text: White blood cells are primarily involved in {{c1::immune responses}}
extra: Recognizing and neutralizing invaders such as bacteria and viruses
example: A bacterial pneumonia can raise the white blood cell count from about 7,000 to over 15,000 per µL.

text: This is an example of {{c1::pseudostratified columnar}} epithelial tissue
example: The trachea is lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium that sweeps mucus upward.

text: {{c1::Osmotic pressure::... pressure}} moves fluid into the blood vessel
example: Children with kwashiorkor have too little plasma albumin, so fluid stays in the tissues and the belly swells.

text: {{c1::Growth hormone::Hormone}} stimulates growth and cell reproduction
extra:
Also known as somatotropin
Released from the anterior pituitary
example: Robert Wadlow, the tallest man on record (2.72 m), grew from excess GH secreted by his pituitary.

text: Cardiac muscle cells are connected with {{c1::intercalated discs}} that contain {{c1::gap junctions}}
example: Gap junctions let an impulse from the SA node spread cell to cell so the atria contract together.

text: Aldosterone is a hormone synthesized in the adrenal cortex in response to {{c1::angiotensin II}} or high {{c1::[K+]}}
example: In a dehydrated hiker, the renin-angiotensin system makes angiotensin II, which prompts aldosterone release.

text: Hardy–Weinberg equation: {{c1::p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1}}
example: If a recessive allele has q = 0.1, carriers are 2pq = 2(0.9)(0.1) = 0.18, or 18%

text: The {{c1::ovaries}} have follicles that produce ova
example: A newborn girl's ovaries hold about 1–2 million primordial follicles, each with a primary oocyte.

text: {{c1::Facultative anaerobes::type of microorganism}} toggle between aerobic and anaerobic
example: E. coli respires aerobically with O2 but switches to fermentation in the oxygen-poor gut.

text: Metabotropic receptors operate via {{c1::indirect::direct or indirect}} neurotransmitter action
extra:
Neurotransmitter binding triggers a signaling pathway, which may indirectly open or close channels
Metabotropic receptors are not themselves ion channels
example: Muscarinic ACh receptors in the heart act through a G protein that opens K<sup>+</sup> channels and slows the heart rate.

text: The oral cavity is where salivary {{c1::amylase::enzyme}} and {{c1::lipase::enzyme}} start the chemical digestion of food
extra: Mastication breaks the food down to small pieces which are formed into a bolus and swallowed
example: A cracker held on your tongue for a minute starts tasting sweet as salivary amylase cuts starch into maltose.

text:
A dihybrid cross, shown above, will result in the following phenotypic ratios:
  • Expressed AB: {{c1::9/16::.../16}}
  • Expressed Ab: {{c1::3/16::.../16}}
  • Expressed aB: {{c1::3/16::.../16}}
  • Expressed ab: {{c1::1/16::.../16}}
extra:
9:3:3:1
Dihybrid cross means a cross involving two traits and each parent organism is heterozygous for both of the traits.
example: Mendel's RrYy × RrYy peas: 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow, 32 wrinkled green

text: The G protein is classified as a heterotrimeric protein because {{c1::it is made up of 3 subunits: α, β, γ}}
example: When glucagon activates G<sub>s</sub>, it splits into a GTP-bound α<sub>s</sub> subunit and a βγ pair.

text:
Total capacitance of capacitors in series:
{{c1::}}
extra: In series, the total capacitance is always less than the smallest individual capacitance.
example: Two 4 µF capacitors in series: 1/C = 1/4 + 1/4, so C = 2 µF

text:
Electrostatic force between two charges:

{{c1::}}
example: Two 1 µC charges 1 m apart repel with F = (9 × 10<sup>9</sup>)(10<sup>−6</sup>)(10<sup>−6</sup>)/1<sup>2</sup> = 0.009 N

text:
Dilution of a solution:
{{c1::}}
example: Diluting 100 mL of 6 M HCl to 600 mL gives 6 × 100/600 = 1 M

text:
Gravitational force between two masses:

{{c1::}}
example: Doubling the Earth–Moon distance would cut their gravitational pull to 1/2<sup>2</sup> = 1/4

text:
Molarity:

{{c1::}}
example: 58.5 g NaCl (1 mol) made up to 0.5 L of solution gives 1/0.5 = 2 M

text:
Gravitational potential energy between two masses:

{{c1::}}
example: Moving a satellite twice as far from Earth's centre halves |U|, making U less negative

text:
Cell potential:

{{c1::}}
example: Zn–Cu galvanic cell: E° = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V

text:
Molality:

{{c1::}}
example: 1 mol NaCl (58.5 g) dissolved in 2 kg of water is 1/2 = 0.5 m

text:
Initial velocity in the x direction (projectile motion):

{{c1::}}
example: A ball launched at 20 m/s at 60° has v<sub>x</sub> = 20 cos 60° = 10 m/s

text:
Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas:

{{c1::}}

Units of the newton:
{{c1::}}
example: A 100 g apple weighs about 1 N: 0.1 kg × 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> ≈ 1 kg·m/s<sup>2</sup>

text:
Displacement from initial velocity, acceleration and time:

{{c1::}}
example: A cart starting from rest at 2 m/s<sup>2</sup> for 4 s travels ½(2)(4<sup>2</sup>) = 16 m

text: Avogadro's number = {{c1::6.02 × 1023}}
example: 18 g of water (1 mol) holds 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> H<sub>2</sub>O molecules

text:
Ideal gas law:
{{c1::}}
example: 1 mol of gas at 273 K and 1 atm fills V = (1)(0.0821)(273)/1 ≈ 22.4 L

text:
Torque:

{{c1::}}
example: Pushing a door with 20 N at 90°, 0.5 m from the hinge, gives τ = 0.5 × 20 = 10 N·m

text:
Units of the ohm:
{{c1::}}
example: A resistor passing 2 A under 10 V has R = 10 V/2 A = 5 Ω

text:
Osmotic pressure:

{{c1::}}
extra:
i = van't Hoff factor
M = molarity
R = gas constant
T = temperature in kelvin

text:
Power:

{{c1::}}
example: A climber doing 600 J of work in 3 s outputs P = 600/3 = 200 W

text:
Centripetal force:

{{c1::}}
example: A 2 kg ball swung at 3 m/s on a 1 m string needs F = 2(3<sup>2</sup>)/1 = 18 N

text:
Potential energy stored in a capacitor:

{{c1::}}
example: A defibrillator's 100 µF capacitor at 2,000 V stores ½(10<sup>−4</sup>)(2000<sup>2</sup>) = 200 J

text:
Speed of light in a vacuum:
{{c1::}}
example: Sunlight reaches Earth in about 500 s: 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> m ÷ 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s

text:
Units of the pascal:
{{c1::}}
example: A 1 N force spread over 1 m<sup>2</sup> is 1 Pa; atmospheric pressure is about 101,000 Pa

text:
Faraday's constant:
{{c1::}}
example: Plating 1 mol of Cu<sup>2+</sup> as copper takes 2 mol e<sup>−</sup>, or 2 × 96,485 ≈ 193,000 C

text:
Mole fraction:

{{c1::}}
example: A mix of 2 mol N<sub>2</sub> and 3 mol He has X<sub>He</sub> = 3/5 = 0.6

text:
Work done on a gas by an outside force:

{{c1::}}
extra: Work done on the gas = −(pressure) × (change in volume)
example: Compressing a gas by 0.002 m<sup>3</sup> at 100 kPa: W = −(10<sup>5</sup>)(−0.002) = +200 J on the gas

text:
Kinetic energy:

{{c1::}}
example: A 2 kg ball at 3 m/s has KE = ½(2)(3<sup>2</sup>) = 9 J

text:
Electric field created by a point charge (magnitude):

{{c1::}}
example: A 1 nC charge creates E = (9 × 10<sup>9</sup>)(10<sup>−9</sup>)/1<sup>2</sup> = 9 N/C at 1 m

text:
Electric potential at a distance from a point charge:

{{c1::}}
example: A 1 nC charge gives V = (9 × 10<sup>9</sup>)(10<sup>−9</sup>)/3 = 3 V at 3 m

text:
Root-mean-square current of alternating current:

{{c1::}}
example: An AC current peaking at 10 A has I<sub>rms</sub> = 10/√2 ≈ 7.1 A

text:
Total resistance of resistors in parallel:
{{c1::}}
extra: In parallel, the total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.
example: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6, so R = 3 Ω

text:
Period of a wave:
{{c1::}}
example: 60 Hz alternating current has a period T = 1/60 ≈ 0.017 s

text:
Units of the farad:
{{c1::}}
example: A capacitor holding 2 C at 1 V is 2 F; typical circuit capacitors are only microfarads

text:
Thin lens equation:
{{c1::}}
extra:
f = focal length
di = distance of image
do = distance of object
example: An object 30 cm from a lens with f = 10 cm: 1/d<sub>i</sub> = 1/10 − 1/30, so d<sub>i</sub> = 15 cm

text:
pH from proton concentration:

{{c1::}}
example: Lemon juice with [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ 10<sup>−2</sup> M has pH = −log(10<sup>−2</sup>) = 2

text:
Gibbs free energy from enthalpy, entropy and temperature:

{{c1::}}
extra: Change in Gibbs free energy = (change in enthalpy) − (temperature) × (change in entropy)
example: Ice melting at 298 K: ΔG = 6.0 kJ − 298(0.022 kJ/K) ≈ −0.56 kJ, so it is spontaneous

text:
Magnetic force on a moving point charge:
{{c1::}}
example: A 2 C charge moving at 3 m/s perpendicular to a 4 T field feels F = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 N

text:
Final velocity from initial velocity, acceleration and displacement:

{{c1::}}
example: A ball dropped from rest falls 5 m: v<sup>2</sup> = 0 + 2(10)(5) = 100, so v = 10 m/s

text:
Work:

{{c1::}}
example: Pushing a box 5 m with 10 N along its motion does W = 10 × 5 = 50 J

text:
Elastic potential energy:

{{c1::}}
extra: Elastic potential energy = ½ × (spring constant) × (stretch or compression of the spring)2
example: A spring with k = 200 N/m compressed 0.1 m stores ½(200)(0.1<sup>2</sup>) = 1 J

text:
Energy of a photon:

{{c1::}}
extra:
E = energy of a photon
h = Planck's constant
c = speed of light
λ = wavelength
f = photon frequency
example: A 500 nm photon has E = hc/λ = (1.99 × 10<sup>−25</sup> J·m)/(5 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m) ≈ 4.0 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J

text:
Arrhenius equation:
{{c1::}}
extra:
k = rate constant
A = frequency factor
Ea = activation energy
R = gas constant
T = temperature in K
example: Refrigerating milk at 4 °C slows spoilage because a lower T shrinks the rate constant k

text:
Observed frequency in the Doppler effect:

{{c1::}}
extra:
General form: f' = f(v ± vo)/(v ∓ vs)
Top signs when moving toward; bottom signs when moving away.
example: A 500 Hz siren approaching at 20 m/s (v = 340 m/s) sounds like 500 × 340/320 ≈ 531 Hz

text:
Gravitational potential energy at height h:

{{c1::}}
example: A 2 kg book on a 1.5 m shelf has U = 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J

text:
Gas constant:
{{c1::R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K)}}
example: At 298 K, RT = 8.314 × 298 ≈ 2,480 J/mol, about 2.5 kJ/mol

text:
Magnetic force on a current-carrying wire:
{{c1::}}
example: A 2 m wire carrying 5 A perpendicular to a 0.1 T field feels F = 5 × 2 × 0.1 = 1 N

text:
Density of water:
{{c1::}}
example: A 2 L bottle of water has a mass of about 2 kg

text:
Normal force on an object on an inclined plane:

{{c1::}}
example: A 10 kg box on a 60° ramp has N = 10 × 10 × cos 60° = 50 N

text:
Magnification of a lens:

{{c1::}}
example: An object 10 cm from a lens imaged 30 cm behind it has m = −30/10 = −3: inverted and 3× larger

text:
Units of the volt:
{{c1::}}
example: A 9 V battery gives each coulomb of charge 9 J of energy

text:
Henderson–Hasselbalch equation:
{{c1::}}
example: An acetate buffer with equal acid and base (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76) has pH = 4.76 + log 1 = 4.76

text:
Units of the watt:
{{c1::}}
example: A 60 W bulb uses 60 J of energy every second

text:
Units of the ampere:
{{c1::}}
example: A current of 3 A moves 3 C of charge past a point every second

text:
Force from mass and acceleration:

{{c1::}}
example: A 2 kg cart pushed at 3 m/s<sup>2</sup> feels F = 2 × 3 = 6 N

text:
Force of friction on an object on an inclined plane:

{{c1::}}
example: A 10 kg box on a 60° ramp with μ = 0.2 feels 0.2 × 100 × cos 60° = 10 N of friction

text:
Newton's third law:
{{c1::}}
example: When you push a wall with 50 N, the wall pushes back on you with 50 N

text:
Electric field between the plates of a capacitor:

{{c1::}}
example: A 12 V capacitor with plates 2 mm apart has E = 12/0.002 = 6,000 V/m

text:
Boiling point elevation:

{{c1::}}
example: 1 m glucose (i = 1) raises water's boiling point by 1 × 0.512 × 1 ≈ 0.51 °C

text:
Heat of a phase change (heat of transformation):

{{c1::}}
extra:
Heat = mass × (latent heat)
Latent heat is the enthalpy change of an isothermal phase change.
A separate formula is needed because ΔT = 0 during a phase change; q = mcΔT would wrongly give q = 0.
example: Melting 10 g of ice takes q = 10 × 334 J/g = 3,340 J with no temperature change

text:
Pressure:
{{c1::}}
extra:
Pressure = force / area
A fluid exerts pressure on the walls of its container and on objects placed in it.
example: A 600 N person standing on two 0.02 m<sup>2</sup> soles exerts 600/0.04 = 15,000 Pa

text:
Component of gravity along an inclined plane:

{{c1::}}
extra: Mnemonic: "sin is sliding down the slide."
example: A 10 kg box on a 30° ramp feels 10 × 10 × sin 30° = 50 N pulling it down the slope

text:
Sound intensity level (β, in decibels):

{{c1::}}
example: A sound 1,000 times threshold intensity has β = 10 log(1000) = 30 dB

text:
Beat frequency of two sound waves with different frequencies:

{{c1::}}
example: Tuning forks at 440 Hz and 444 Hz produce |444 − 440| = 4 beats per second

text:
Capacitance from plate area and separation:

{{c1::}}
example: Plates of 1 m<sup>2</sup> 1 mm apart: C = (8.85 × 10<sup>−12</sup>)(1)/0.001 ≈ 8.9 nF

text:
Total capacitance of capacitors in parallel:
{{c1::}}
extra: Capacitances in parallel add, giving a larger total capacitance.
example: A 2 µF and a 3 µF capacitor in parallel total 2 + 3 = 5 µF

text:
Units of the joule:
{{c1::}}
example: Lifting a 1 N apple 1 m straight up takes 1 N × 1 m = 1 J of work

text:
Planck's constant, h:
{{c1::}}
example: A photon of frequency 10<sup>15</sup> Hz has E = (6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup>)(10<sup>15</sup>) = 6.63 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J

text:
Buoyant force:

{{c1::}}
extra:
If FB > mobjectg (weight), the object floats.
If FB < mobjectg (weight), the object sinks.
example: A 0.01 m<sup>3</sup> block fully under water feels F<sub>B</sub> = 1000 × 0.01 × 10 = 100 N

text:
Wavelength of a standing wave in a pipe closed at one end:
{{c1::}}
example: A 0.5 m pipe closed at one end has a fundamental λ = 4 × 0.5 = 2 m

text:
Resistance of a material:

{{c1::}}
extra:
ρ = resistivity
L = length of the resistor
A = cross-sectional area
example: A 10 m copper wire (ρ = 1.7 × 10<sup>−8</sup> Ω·m) of 1 mm<sup>2</sup> has R = (1.7 × 10<sup>−8</sup>)(10)/10<sup>−6</sup> = 0.17 Ω

text:
Centripetal acceleration:

{{c1::}}
example: A car at 10 m/s on a 50 m-radius curve has a<sub>c</sub> = 10<sup>2</sup>/50 = 2 m/s<sup>2</sup>

text:
Initial velocity in the y direction (projectile motion):

{{c1::}}
example: A ball launched at 20 m/s at 30° has v<sub>y</sub> = 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s

text:
Density:
{{c1::}}
example: A 10 cm<sup>3</sup> piece of gold with mass 193 g has density 193/10 = 19.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>

text:
Force of friction:

{{c1::}}
example: A 10 kg box (N = 100 N) on a floor with μ<sub>k</sub> = 0.3 feels 0.3 × 100 = 30 N of friction

text:
Weight (force of gravity) from mass and gravitational acceleration:

{{c1::}}
example: A 70 kg person weighs 70 × 9.8 ≈ 686 N on Earth

text:
Index of refraction:
{{c1::}}
example: Light moves at 2.25 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s in water, so n = 3.00/2.25 ≈ 1.33

text:
Freezing point depression:

{{c1::}}
example: 1 m NaCl (i = 2) lowers water's freezing point by 2 × 1.86 × 1 = 3.72 °C

text:
Heat absorbed or released by a system with a temperature change:

{{c1::}}
example: Warming 100 g of water by 10 °C takes q = 100 × 4.18 × 10 = 4,180 J

text:
Charge stored in a capacitor from capacitance and voltage:

{{c1::}}
extra: Charge = capacitance × (voltage across the capacitor)
example: A 10 µF capacitor charged to 5 V stores Q = (10 × 10<sup>−6</sup>)(5) = 50 µC

text:
Root-mean-square voltage of alternating current:

{{c1::}}
example: US outlets supply 120 V<sub>rms</sub>, which means a peak of 120 × √2 ≈ 170 V

text:
Total resistance of resistors in series:
{{c1::}}
extra: Resistances in series add, giving a larger total resistance.
example: 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω resistors in series total 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω

text:
Final velocity from initial velocity, acceleration and time:

{{c1::}}
example: A car at 5 m/s accelerating at 2 m/s<sup>2</sup> for 3 s reaches 5 + 2 × 3 = 11 m/s

text:
Electric potential energy of a charged particle:

{{c1::}}
example: A +2 C charge at a point where V = 5 V has U = 2 × 5 = 10 J

text:
Change in internal energy of a system (W = work done by the system):

{{c1::}}
example: A gas absorbing 100 J of heat while doing 40 J of work gains ΔU = 100 − 40 = 60 J

text:
Absolute pressure in a fluid at depth h:

{{c1::}}
extra: Absolute pressure = (pressure at the fluid's surface) + (pressure due to the fluid's weight)
example: 10 m underwater: P = 101 kPa + (1000)(9.8)(10) Pa ≈ 199 kPa, about 2 atm

text:
Rydberg formula:
{{c1::}}
extra: Used to determine the wavelength of light emitted or absorbed after an electron moves between energy levels
example: Hydrogen's n = 3 → 2 drop gives 1/λ = R(1/4 − 1/9), the red 656 nm H-alpha line

text:
Hooke's law:
{{c1::}}
extra:
Force exerted by the spring = −(spring constant) × (displacement of the spring)
The negative sign means the spring force opposes the spring's displacement.
example: A spring with k = 100 N/m stretched 0.05 m pulls back with F = −100 × 0.05 = −5 N

text:
Volumetric flow rate:

{{c1::}}
extra: The volume of fluid that passes a point per unit time.
example: Blood at 30 cm/s through a 3 cm<sup>2</sup> aorta flows Q = 3 × 30 = 90 mL/s ≈ 5.4 L/min

text:
Heat of reaction from product and reactant enthalpies:

{{c1::}}

Wavelength of a standing wave in a pipe open at both ends:
{{c1::}}
example: A 0.5 m pipe open at both ends, like a flute, has a fundamental λ = 2 × 0.5 = 1 m

text:
Ohm's law:
{{c1::}}
example: A 9 V battery across a 3 Ω resistor drives I = 9/3 = 3 A

text:
Snell's law:
{{c1::}}
example: Light entering glass (n = 1.5) from air at 30° to the normal: sin θ<sub>2</sub> = 0.5/1.5, so θ<sub>2</sub> ≈ 19.5°

text: A Lewis base is a substance that {{c1::donates a pair of electrons}}
example: NH<sub>3</sub> donates its lone pair to BF<sub>3</sub>, forming the adduct F<sub>3</sub>B–NH<sub>3</sub>

text: The {{c1::equivalence point}} is the point at which equivalent amounts of acid and base have reacted
example: 25 mL of 0.1 M HCl reaches equivalence after 25 mL of 0.1 M NaOH (2.5 mmol each)

text: The sum of the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is {{c1::zero::#}}
example: In H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0, so S = +6

text: Planck’s Constant (h) = {{c1::6.626 × 10<sup>-34</sup> J•s}}
example: Green light at 6 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz carries E = hf ≈ 4 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J per photon

text: If temperature goes up, the rate constant goes {{c1::up::up or down}} and the reaction speed goes {{c1::up::up or down}}
extra: This is because the exponent gets closer to 0. The exponent becomes less negative
example: Milk lasts longer in a 4 °C fridge than on the counter because its spoilage reactions slow down

text: He is {{c1::diamagnetic::diamagnetic or paramagnetic}}
example: Like He (1s<sup>2</sup>), Be (1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>) is diamagnetic since every electron is paired

text: A reaction is at equilibrium if Q = {{c1::K<sub>eq</sub>}}
example: If K = 4 and the measured Q = 4, the concentrations stop changing because forward and reverse rates match

text: Buffering capacity is a measure of the ability of a buffer to {{c1::resist changes in pH}}
example: A 1 M acetate buffer neutralizes ten times as much added HCl as a 0.1 M one for the same pH drop

text: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a substance that {{c1::donates H+}}
extra: An Arrhenius acid and Brønsted acid both donate H+
example: In NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>, water is the acid, donating H<sup>+</sup> to NH<sub>3</sub>

text: In an electrochemical cell, current flows from the {{c1::cathode::anode or cathode}} to the {{c1::anode::anode or cathode}}
example: In a Zn–Cu cell, conventional current runs through the wire from the copper strip to the zinc strip

text: The presence of nonvolatile solute particles in a liquid solvent results in a/an {{c1::reduction::increase or reduction}} of the vapor pressure above a liquid
example: Seawater evaporates more slowly than fresh water because dissolved salt lowers its vapor pressure

text: According to the {{c1::Bohr Model::... Model}}, electrons orbit the nucleus in orbits that have a set size and energy
example: Bohr's hydrogen levels E<sub>n</sub> = −13.6 eV/n<sup>2</sup> give −13.6 eV at n = 1 and −3.4 eV at n = 2

text: The {{c1::reaction quotient (Qc)}} is a measure of the relative amounts of products and reactants present in a reaction at a given time
extra: Exclude pure solids and liquids
example: For N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub>, Q = [NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2</sup>/([N<sub>2</sub>][H<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3</sup>) at any moment

text: If Qsp is {{c1::less than::less than, greater than, or equal to}} Ksp then the solution is unsaturated so no precipitate will form
example: [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = [Cl<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−6</sup> M gives Q<sub>sp</sub> = 10<sup>−12</sup> < 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>: no AgCl forms

text: The electronic geometry of an atom with 4 electron groups is {{c1::tetrahedral}}
example: H<sub>2</sub>O has four electron groups, so its electronic geometry is tetrahedral though its shape is bent

text: Speed of Light (c) = {{c1::3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s}}
example: A radio signal crosses the 3.8 × 10<sup>8</sup> m to the Moon in about 1.3 s

text: An {{c1::empirical}} formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
example: Glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O

text:
Change in Gibbs free energy of a redox reaction in nonstandard conditions, as a function of Q:
{{c1::}}
example: ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol and Q = 1,000 at 298 K: ΔG = −11.4 + 17.1 = +5.7 kJ/mol, so it runs in reverse

text: Nonpolar bonds have a ΔEN that is {{c1::less than 0.5}}
example: A C–H bond has ΔEN = 2.55 − 2.20 = 0.35, so it counts as nonpolar

text: {{c1::Enthalpy (H)}} is a measure of the potential energy of a system found in intermolecular attractions and chemical bonds
example: Burning methane turns bond energy into heat: ΔH = −890 kJ/mol

text: The electronic geometry of an atom with 2 electron groups is {{c1::linear}}
example: BeCl<sub>2</sub>: two electron groups around Be give a linear, 180° shape

text: An Arrhenius base is a substance that {{c1::produces OH-}}
example: NaOH dissolving in water releases Na<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup>

text: A/an {{c1::covalent}} bond is the sharing of electrons between two atoms
example: In H<sub>2</sub>, two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons

text: A/an {{c1::chelate}} is a compound with a central cation bonded to the same ligand in multiple places
example: EDTA grips Pb<sup>2+</sup> at six sites, which is how it treats lead poisoning

text: Galvanic cells are also known as {{c1::voltaic cells}}
example: An AA alkaline battery is a galvanic (voltaic) cell

text: {{c1::Coordinate covalent}} bonds are when a single atom provides both bonding electrons
extra: Most often found in Lewis acid-base chemistry
example: In NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, nitrogen's lone pair supplies both electrons of its bond to H<sup>+</sup>

text: Any free element (including homonuclear diatomics like O<sub>2</sub>) has an oxidation number of {{c1::0::#}}
example: In Fe metal, Cl<sub>2</sub> gas and S<sub>8</sub>, every atom has oxidation number 0

text: If Q < K<sub>eq</sub>, then the reaction will move to the {{c1::right}}
example: If K = 10 and Q = 2, the reaction makes more product until Q reaches 10

text:
For a first order reaction:
  • Rate Law: {{c1::}}
  • Integrated Rate Law: {{c1::}}
example: <sup>14</sup>C decay is first order: half of what remains decays every 5,730 years

text: Galvanic cells house {{c1::spontaneous::spontaneous or non-spontaneous}} reactions
example: A Zn–Cu Daniell cell runs on its own at E° = +1.10 V and can light a bulb

text: A basic buffer is a mixture of a {{c1::weak base}} and {{c1::its conjugate salt}}
example: Ammonia mixed with ammonium chloride holds the pH near 9.25

text: The azimuthal quantum number for this orbital is {{c1::0 = s orbital}}
example: Hydrogen's single electron sits in a spherical 1s orbital (l = 0)

text: The graph above shows the titration curve of a {{c1::strong acid}} with a {{c1::strong base}}
example: HCl titrated with NaOH: a steep jump with the equivalence point at pH 7

text:
Intermolecular forces in order of strength (hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole forces, London dispersion forces):
{{c1::}}
example: Water (H bonds) boils at 100 °C, HCl (dipole-dipole) at −85 °C, CH<sub>4</sub> (dispersion) at −162 °C

text: In element notation, Z is the {{c1::atomic number}}
example: Every carbon atom has Z = 6 (6 protons), whether it is <sup>12</sup>C or <sup>14</sup>C

text: Anions are ions with a {{c1::negative}} charge
example: Chlorine gains one electron to become the anion Cl<sup>−</sup> (chloride)

text: The graph above shows the titration curve of a {{c1::weak acid}} with a {{c1::weak base}}
example: Acetic acid titrated with ammonia: a shallow curve with no sharp jump near pH 7

text: If ΔG < 0, the reaction will be {{c1::spontaneous}}
example: Iron rusting in moist air (ΔG < 0) happens on its own, though slowly

text: pK<sub>b</sub> = {{c1::-log(K<sub>b</sub>)}}
example: Ammonia: K<sub>b</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>, so pK<sub>b</sub> = 4.74

text: Na+, K+, NH4+, and NO3- are {{c1::always::sometimes or always}} soluble
example: NaNO<sub>3</sub>, KCl and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl all dissolve readily in water

text: If a reaction has a positive ∆H and positive ∆S, then it will be {{c1::spontaneous::spontaneous or non-spontaneous}} at {{c1::high::high, low, or all}} temperatures
extra:
"High" = above the crossover T, where ∆G = 0: T = ∆H / ∆S. Above it, T∆S > ∆H, so ∆G < 0 (spontaneous). Below it, non-spontaneous.
Example (ice melting): ∆H ≈ +6.0 kJ/mol, ∆S ≈ +22 J/mol·K → T ≈ 6000/22 ≈ 273 K (0 °C). Melts on its own above 0 °C, not below. (Convert kJ → J first!)

text: The maximum number of electrons in a single energy level in terms of principal quantum number = {{c1::2n2}}
extra:
Example: What is the maximum number of electrons that can be in the second energy level?
2n2 = 2(22) = 8 electrons

text: In element notation, A is the {{c1::mass number}}
example: Carbon-14 has A = 14: 6 protons + 8 neutrons

text: If an electron moves to a closer orbital, a photon is {{c1::emitted}}
extra:
If n goes up, a photon is absorbed
If n goes down, a photon is emitted
example: Hydrogen's n = 3 → n = 2 drop emits the red 656 nm Balmer line

text:
Periodic trend for ionization energy:
{{c1::}}
example: Helium has the highest first ionization energy (2,372 kJ/mol); caesium among the lowest (376 kJ/mol)

text: In {{c1::decomposition}} reactions, a single reactant breaks down
example: 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>, the fizz when peroxide is poured on a cut

text: CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> is {{c1::insoluble}} except with Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, and Mg<sup>2+</sup>
example: PbCrO<sub>4</sub> (chrome yellow pigment) is insoluble, while K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> dissolves

text: {{c1::Zeff}} is the attractive positive charge of nuclear protons acting on valence electrons
extra: Zeff is always less than the total number of protons present in a nucleus due to the shielding effect from other electrons in the atom
example: Sodium's 3s electron feels Z<sub>eff</sub> ≈ 11 − 10 = +1, since 10 core electrons shield it

text:
Periodic trend for electronegativity:
{{c1::}}
example: Fluorine (4.0) is the most electronegative element; caesium (0.79) is one of the least

text: Ionic bonds have a ΔEN that is {{c1::greater than 1.7}}
example: NaCl has ΔEN = 3.16 − 0.93 = 2.23, so its bond is ionic

text: Diamagnetic materials are {{c1::repelled}} by an external magnetic field
extra: All electrons are paired and have opposing spins ↑↓
example: A live frog has been levitated in a strong magnetic field because its water is diamagnetic

text: A/an {{c1::neutralization}} reaction is when an acid and base react to form water and salt
extra: A type of double-replacement reaction
example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O

text: {{c1::Vaporization}} is the phase change from liquid to gas
example: Sweat evaporating off your skin on a hot day

text: If an electron moves to a farther orbital, a photon is {{c1::absorbed}}
extra:
If n goes up, a photon is absorbed
If n goes down, a photon is emitted
example: Hydrogen's electron absorbs a 10.2 eV (122 nm) photon to jump from n = 1 to n = 2

text: The bond angle of an sp<sup>3</sup> hybridized atom is {{c1::109.5°}}
example: Methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) is tetrahedral, with H–C–H angles of 109.5°

text: The endpoint of a titration is when {{c1::the indicator reaches full color}}
example: In an HCl–NaOH titration with phenolphthalein, the endpoint is the first drop that leaves a lasting colour

text: The graph above shows the titration curve of a {{c1::strong acid}} with a {{c1::weak base}}
example: NH<sub>3</sub> titrated with HCl: the equivalence point falls below pH 7 because NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is acidic

text: The bond angle of an sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized atom is {{c1::120°}}
example: BF<sub>3</sub> is trigonal planar, with 120° F–B–F angles

text:
Change in Gibbs free energy of a redox reaction in standard conditions, as a function of Keq:
{{c1::}}
extra:
ΔG° = standard change in Gibbs free energy
R = universal gas constant, 8.31 J/(K·mol)
T = temperature in kelvin

text: An acidic buffer is a mixture of a {{c1::weak acid}} and {{c1::its conjugate salt}}
example: Acetic acid mixed with sodium acetate holds the pH near 4.74

text: A/an {{c1::supercritical}} fluid is one in which the density of gas = density of liquid
extra: No distinction between those two phases
example: Supercritical CO<sub>2</sub> (above 31 °C and 73 atm) is used to decaffeinate coffee

text: The {{c1::electromotive force (EMF)}} is the maximum potential difference between two electrodes of a galvanic or voltaic cell
extra: Also known as the cell potential
example: A Daniell (Zn–Cu) cell has an EMF of 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V

text:
For BaSO4(s) ⇌ Ba2+(aq) + SO42-(aq), the solubility product constant is
Ksp = {{c1::[Ba2+][SO42-]}}
example: For CaF<sub>2</sub>(s) ⇌ Ca<sup>2+</sup> + 2F<sup>−</sup>, K<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>][F<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup>

text: The elements in the groups labeled with ? are known as {{c1::transition metals}}
example: Iron, the oxygen-binding metal in haemoglobin, is a transition metal

text: The orbital hybridization of an atom with 5 electron groups is {{c1::sp3d}}
example: The sulfur in SF<sub>4</sub> (four bonds, one lone pair) is sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridized

text: If Qsp is {{c1::greater than::less than, greater than, or equal to}} Ksp then the solution is supersaturated so a precipitate will form
example: [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = [Cl<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−3</sup> M gives Q<sub>sp</sub> = 10<sup>−6</sup> > 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>: AgCl precipitates

text: Cations are ions with a {{c1::positive}} charge
example: Sodium loses one electron to become the cation Na<sup>+</sup>

text: The {{c1::Pauli Exclusion Principle::... Principle}} states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers
extra: That means, for paired electrons, one must be +1/2 spin and the other -1/2 spin
example: Helium's two 1s electrons share n = 1, l = 0, m<sub>l</sub> = 0 but differ in m<sub>s</sub> (+½ vs −½)

text: Phenolphthalein is colorless up to a pH of {{c1::8.2}} and becomes purple
example: Titrating HCl with NaOH, phenolphthalein stays colourless until the first drop past equivalence pushes pH above 8.2

text: {{c1::Ionic}} bonds are formed by the complete transfer of valence electron(s) between atoms
extra: Usually formed between an element with a low ionization energy and an element with a high electron affinity
example: Na gives its 3s electron to Cl, forming Na<sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> (table salt)

text: The elements in the group labeled with ? are known as {{c1::alkaline earth metals}}
example: Calcium, the mineral in bones and milk, is an alkaline earth metal that forms Ca<sup>2+</sup>

text:
Approximate electronegativity values of H, C, N, O, and F:
{{c1::}}
example: In a C–O bond the difference 3.5 − 2.5 = 1.0 makes it polar, with δ<sup>−</sup> on oxygen

text: The orbital hybridization of an atom with 2 electron groups is {{c1::sp}}
example: The carbon in CO<sub>2</sub> has two electron groups (two C=O bonds) and is sp hybridized

text: {{c1::Pi}} bonds are formed by lateral (side-by-side) overlap of atomic orbitals
extra: The 2nd and 3rd bonds in double and triple bonds are pi bonds
example: Ethylene's C=C is one sigma bond plus one pi bond from side-by-side overlap of 2p orbitals

text:
Periodic trend for electron affinity:
{{c1::}}
example: Across row 3, Na releases about 53 kJ/mol on gaining an electron while Cl releases 349 kJ/mol

text:
For a second order reaction:
  • Rate Law: {{c1::}}
  • Integrated Rate Law: {{c1::}}
example: 2NO<sub>2</sub> → 2NO + O<sub>2</sub> is second order, with rate = k[NO<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2</sup>

text:
The redox reaction above, balanced in acidic solution:
{{c1::}}
example: MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 5e<sup>−</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O balances O with H<sub>2</sub>O and H with H<sup>+</sup>

text: The elements in the group labeled with ? are known as {{c1::halogens}}
example: Chlorine in bleach and fluorine in toothpaste fluoride are halogens

text: pK<sub>a</sub> = {{c1::-log(K<sub>a</sub>)}}
example: Acetic acid: K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>, so pK<sub>a</sub> = 4.74

text: [OH<sup>-</sup>] = {{c1::10<sup>-pOH</sup>}}
example: A pOH of 4 means [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−4</sup> M

text:
The redox reaction above, balanced in basic solution:
{{c1::}}
example: MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 3e<sup>−</sup> → MnO<sub>2</sub> + 4OH<sup>−</sup> uses OH<sup>−</sup> in place of H<sup>+</sup>

text: The elements in the groups labeled with ? are known as {{c1::rare earth metals}}
example: Neodymium, a lanthanide, makes the strong magnets in earbuds and electric motors

text:
Periodic trend for atomic size:
{{c1::}}
example: Down group 1, atoms grow from Li to Na to K to Rb to Cs as each row adds an electron shell

text: SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> is {{c1::soluble}} except with Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Sr<sup>2+</sup>, Ba<sup>2+</sup>, Pb<sup>2+</sup>, Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>, and Ag<sup>+</sup>
example: BaSO<sub>4</sub> is insoluble enough to swallow as an X-ray contrast agent, while Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dissolves

text: {{c1::Molar solubility}} is the number of moles of a substance that can be dissolved per liter of solution before the solution becomes saturated
example: AgCl (K<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>) has molar solubility √(1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>) ≈ 1.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M

text:
Signs (+, −, or 0) in the table above for each type of electrochemical cell:
{{c1::}}
example: A phone battery while charging is an electrolytic cell: E<sub>cell</sub> < 0 and ΔG > 0

text: The oxidation state of oxygen in a compound is {{c1::-2::#}}, except for peroxides like H2O2, and Na2O2, in which the oxidation state for O is {{c1::-1::#}}
example: In CO<sub>2</sub>, O is −2; in BaO<sub>2</sub>, a peroxide, O is −1

text: Phase changes from gas → liquid → solid are {{c1::exothermic::endothermic or exothermic}}
extra: These reactions release heat energy
example: Steam condensing on skin releases its heat of vaporization, so steam burns worse than 100 °C water

text: The elements in the group labeled with ? are known as {{c1::noble gases}}
example: Neon glows in signs and helium fills party balloons, both unreactive noble gases

text: {{c1::Sigma}} bonds are formed by head-on overlapping between atomic orbitals
example: The H–H bond in H<sub>2</sub> is a sigma bond from head-on overlap of two 1s orbitals

text: The electronic geometry of an atom with 6 electron groups is {{c1::octahedral}}
example: BrF<sub>5</sub> has six electron groups: octahedral geometry, square pyramidal shape

text: {{c1::London dispersion}} forces are temporary attractive forces created when a temporary dipole induces a dipole in a neighboring molecule
extra: The weakest intermolecular force
example: Fleeting induced dipoles hold nonpolar Br<sub>2</sub> molecules together as a liquid at room temperature

text: A neutralization reaction is when an acid and a base react to form {{c1::water}} and {{c1::a salt}}
extra: H+ ions and OH- ions combine to generate water
example: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2KOH → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

text: Formal charge = {{c1::valence electrons − dots − sticks}}
extra:
"Dots" are nonbonding electrons
"Sticks" are pairs of bonding electrons
example: N in NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>: 5 valence − 0 dots − 4 sticks = +1

text:
Gibbs free energy from the reaction quotient Q:
  • {{c1::}}
  • {{c1::}}
example: With ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol and Q = 10 at 298 K, ΔG = −5.7 + 5.7 = 0: the system is at equilibrium

text: The {{c1::molecular}} formula shows the exact number of atoms of each element
extra: It is a multiple of the empirical formula
example: Benzene's molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> is six times its empirical formula CH

text:
The units for the rate constant of a first order reaction are
{{c1::}}
example: A first-order reaction with k = 0.1 s<sup>−1</sup> has a half-life of 0.693/0.1 = 6.93 s

text:
Nernst equation:
{{c1::}}
extra:
Used to calculate cell potential in nonstandard conditions
Ecell = cell potential
E°cell = standard cell potential
R = universal gas constant, 8.31 J/(K·mol)
T = temperature in kelvin
n = number of moles of electrons transferred
F = Faraday's constant = 96,485 C/mol
Q = reaction quotient (equals K if reaction is at equilibrium)

text: {{c1::Bond order}} refers to the number of bonds between two atoms (single, double, or triple bond)
example: N<sub>2</sub> (N≡N) has a bond order of 3; O<sub>2</sub> (O=O) has a bond order of 2

text: A/an {{c1::complex ion}} has a metal ion at its center with a number of other molecules or ions surrounding it
example: [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, a Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion ringed by four NH<sub>3</sub> ligands, is deep blue

text:
For a zeroth order reaction:
  • Rate Law: {{c1::}}
  • Integrated Rate Law: {{c1::}}
example: Saturated liver alcohol dehydrogenase clears ethanol at a constant rate, whatever the blood level

text: {{c1::Equilibrium Constant (Keq)}} is the value of the reaction quotient at chemical equilibrium
extra: Exclude pure solids and liquids
example: For H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2HI at about 450 °C, K<sub>eq</sub> = [HI]<sup>2</sup>/([H<sub>2</sub>][I<sub>2</sub>]) ≈ 50

text: Polar bonds have a ΔEN that is between {{c1::0.5}} and {{c1::1.7}}
example: An O–H bond has ΔEN = 3.44 − 2.20 = 1.24, so it is polar covalent

text:
Gibbs free energy from the equilibrium constant Keq:
{{c1::}}
Qsp is the {{c1::reaction quotient}} for a reaction that consists of a solid dissolving in a solution
extra: The reaction quotient for a regular chemical reaction is abbreviated Qc
example: Mixing to give [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = [Cl<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−3</sup> M makes Q<sub>sp</sub> = 10<sup>−6</sup>

text: If a reaction has a negative ∆H and negative ∆S, then it will be {{c1::spontaneous::spontaneous or non-spontaneous}} at {{c1::low::high, low, or all}} temperatures
example: Water freezes on its own only below 0 °C

text: A/an {{c1::REDOX titration::... titration}} is similar in methodology to acid-base titrations, however, these titrations follow transfer of charge
example: Purple KMnO<sub>4</sub> is titrated into Fe<sup>2+</sup> until a faint pink persists, marking all Fe<sup>2+</sup> oxidized

text: A Brønsted-Lowry base is a substance that {{c1::accepts H+}}
example: NH<sub>3</sub> accepts H<sup>+</sup> from water to become NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>

text: {{c1::Kb}} is the equilibrium constant corresponding to the dissociation of a base, BOH, into a hydroxide ion and its conjugate acid
example: Ammonia has K<sub>b</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> for NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>

text: Quantum number {{c1::ms}} is the spin quantum number and gives the {{c1::electronic spin}} of the electron
extra: +1/2 or -1/2
example: In the Stern–Gerlach experiment, silver atoms split into two beams, one for each spin, +½ and −½

text: Quantum number {{c1::n}} is the principal quantum number and gives the electron {{c1::energy level or shell number}}
extra:
1, 2, 3, ...
Except for d- and f-orbitals, the shell # matches the row of the periodic table
example: Sodium's valence electron is in n = 3, matching its place in row 3 of the periodic table

text: Orbits that are farther from the nucleus have {{c1::increased::increased or decreased}} energy
example: A hydrogen electron has −3.4 eV at n = 2, higher than −13.6 eV at n = 1

text: {{c1::Gibbs Free Energy}} combines enthalpy and entropy into a single value and is used to determine the spontaneity of a reaction
extra:
We are only concerned with changes in G, rather than its absolute value
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
example: Ice melting at 25 °C: ΔH > 0, but TΔS is larger, so ΔG < 0 and it happens spontaneously

text: If Q > K<sub>eq</sub>, then the reaction will move to the {{c1::left}}
example: If K = 1 and Q = 5, products convert back to reactants until Q falls to 1

text: Phase changes from solid → liquid → gas are {{c1::endothermic::endothermic or exothermic}}
extra: Gases have more heat energy than liquids and liquids have more heat energy than solids
example: Melting ice absorbs 6.01 kJ/mol, which is why ice chills a drink

text: At the half-equivalence point (midpoint) of a titration, pH = {{c1::pKa}}
example: Halfway to equivalence in a titration of HF (pK<sub>a</sub> 3.17), the pH reads 3.17

text:
In a base:
  • {{c1::blue::red or blue}} litmus paper has no change of color
  • {{c1::red::red or blue}} litmus paper changes its color to {{c1::blue::red or blue}}
example: Soapy water turns red litmus blue

text: {{c1::Freezing}} is the phase change from liquid to solid
example: Water in an ice tray turning to ice at 0 °C in the freezer

text: A/an {{c1::concentration cell}} is a galvanic cell that is comprised of two half-cells with the same electrodes, but differing in concentrations
example: Cu electrodes in 1 M and 0.01 M Cu<sup>2+</sup> give E = (0.0592/2) log 100 = 0.059 V

text: Bromothymol blue is yellow up to a pH of {{c1::6}} and is blue at any pH greater than {{c1::7.6}}
example: Blowing CO<sub>2</sub> through a straw into blue bromothymol blue solution turns it yellow

text: If a reaction has a negative ∆H and positive ∆S, then it will be {{c1::spontaneous::spontaneous or non-spontaneous}} at {{c1::all::high, low, or all}} temperatures
example: 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>(l) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O(l) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) releases heat and makes gas, so it runs at any temperature

text: Protons and electrons have {{c1::different::the same or different}} masses
extra:
Protons and neutrons are both the same mass
Electrons are much smaller
example: A proton (1.67 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg) is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron

text: S<sup>2-</sup> is {{c1::insoluble}} except with Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Sr<sup>2+</sup>, and Ba<sup>2+</sup>
example: Black PbS precipitates from Pb<sup>2+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>, while Na<sub>2</sub>S dissolves

text: The orbital hybridization of an atom with 6 electron groups is {{c1::sp3d2}}
example: The xenon in XeF<sub>4</sub> (four bonds, two lone pairs) is sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridized

text:
ΔH from heats of formation:
{{c1::}}

ΔH from bond dissociation energies:
{{c1::}}

Standard entropy of reaction:
{{c1::}}
Kinetic products are {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} in free energy compared to thermodynamic products and can form at {{c1::lower::higher or lower}} temperatures
example: HBr adding to 1,3-butadiene at −80 °C gives mostly the 1,2-adduct, the kinetic product

text: {{c1::Polyprotic acids}} are specific acids that are capable of losing more than a single proton per molecule
example: Phosphoric acid, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, can lose three protons in turn

text: The elements in the groups labeled with ? are known as {{c1::non-metals}}
example: Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of your body's molecules, are non-metals

text: The {{c1::Rutherford Model::... Model}} states that an atom is mostly empty space, with electrons orbiting a fixed, positively charged nucleus
example: Gold foil experiment: most alpha particles passed straight through, but a few bounced back

text: Weak acids and bases do not completely {{c1::dissociate}}
example: In 0.1 M acetic acid only about 1.3% ionizes, so the pH is about 2.9 rather than 1

text: OH<sup>-</sup> is {{c1::insoluble}} except with Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Sr<sup>2+</sup>, and Ba<sup>2+</sup>
example: Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (milk of magnesia) is insoluble, while NaOH dissolves readily

text: The order of this reaction is {{c1::zeroth order}}
example: If [A] falls 1.0 → 0.8 → 0.6 M in successive minutes, [A] vs time is a straight line

text: The elements in the group labeled with ? are known as {{c1::post-transition metals}}
example: Lead in old water pipes and tin in solder are post-transition metals

text: A/an {{c1::amphoteric species::... species}} is a species that can behave as an acid or a base
example: HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> can gain H<sup>+</sup> (→ H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) or lose one (→ CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>)

text: Standard conditions are {{c1::298}} K, {{c1::1}} atm, {{c1::1}} M
extra:
Standard conditions (298 K) → thermodynamics (ΔG°, ΔH°, E°)
STP (273 K, 1 atm) → gas laws (1 mol = 22.4 L)
example: The Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu standard potential E° = +0.34 V is measured at 298 K, 1 atm and 1 M

text:
The phase diagram with its phases labeled:
{{c1::}}
example: On water's diagram, 25 °C and 1 atm falls in the liquid region; 100 °C at 1 atm sits on the liquid–gas line

text: In an electrochemical cell, a cathode attracts {{c1::cations::anions or cations}} and is always the site of {{c1::reduction::oxidation or reduction}}
example: In a Zn–Cu cell, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to copper metal at the copper cathode

text: Quantum number {{c1::l}} is the azimuthal quantum number and gives the {{c1::3D shape (subshell)}} of an orbital
extra:
0, 1, 2, …, n-1
0 = s orbital
1 = p orbital
2 = d orbital
3 = f orbital
4 = g orbital
example: A 3d electron has l = 2, so its orbital has the cloverleaf d shape

text: {{c1::Reduction potential}} is a measure of the tendency of a chemical species to gain electrons and be reduced
extra: A more positive Ered indicates a greater tendency to be reduced
example: F<sub>2</sub> (E° = +2.87 V) is reduced far more readily than Li<sup>+</sup> (E° = −3.04 V)

text: The azimuthal quantum number for this orbital is {{c1::2 = d orbital}}
example: Iron ([Ar]4s<sup>2</sup>3d<sup>6</sup>) has six electrons in its l = 2 d orbitals

text: {{c1::Colligative properties}} are physical properties of solutions that depend on the concentration of dissolved particles but not on their chemical identity
example: Salting an icy road lowers water's freezing point so the ice melts below 0 °C

text: If Qsp is {{c1::equal to::less than, greater than, or equal to}} Ksp then the solution is saturated and at equilibrium so no precipitate will form
example: Clear solution sitting over undissolved AgCl crystals has Q<sub>sp</sub> = K<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>

text: {{c1::Deposition}} is the phase change from gas to solid
example: Frost forming on a cold car windshield as water vapour turns directly into ice

text: The orbital hybridization of an atom with 4 electron groups is {{c1::sp3}}
example: The nitrogen in NH<sub>3</sub> (three bonds, one lone pair) is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridized

text: The {{c1::standard reduction potential}} is the tendency for a chemical species to be reduced, and is measured in volts at standard conditions
example: Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Cu has E° = +0.34 V; Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Zn has E° = −0.76 V

text: If ΔG > 0, the reaction will be {{c1::non-spontaneous}}
example: Water does not split into H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> on its own (ΔG° = +237 kJ/mol); electrolysis must drive it

text: A Lewis acid is a substance that {{c1::accepts a pair of electrons}}
example: In Friedel–Crafts reactions, AlCl<sub>3</sub> accepts a Cl<sup>−</sup> lone pair to form AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>

text: In a titration, the {{c1::titrant}} (the known solution) is added from a burette to a certain quantity of the {{c1::analyte}} (the unknown solution) until the reaction is complete
example: 0.1 M NaOH is dripped from a burette into vinegar to find how much acetic acid it holds

text: The {{c1::Aufbau Principle::... Principle}} states that electrons will fill the lower energy levels before moving to higher energy orbitals
example: Potassium puts its 19th electron in 4s before 3d because 4s is lower in energy

text:
Cell potential (electromotive force) of an electrochemical cell:
{{c1::}}
example: Zn–Ag cell: E°<sub>cell</sub> = E°<sub>cathode</sub> − E°<sub>anode</sub> = 0.80 − (−0.76) = +1.56 V

text:
In an acid:
  • {{c1::red::red or blue}} litmus paper has no change of color
  • {{c1::blue::red or blue}} litmus paper changes its color to {{c1::red::red or blue}}
example: Lemon juice turns blue litmus red

text:
Universal litmus paper turns:
  • {{c1::red, orange or yellow::colors}} in acids
  • {{c1::green::color}} in neutral solutions
  • {{c1::blue or purple::colors}} in alkalis
example: Vinegar turns universal paper red, pure water turns it green, and household bleach turns it purple

text: The orbital hybridization of an atom with 3 electron groups is {{c1::sp2}}
example: The carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde (H<sub>2</sub>C=O) has three electron groups and is sp<sup>2</sup>

text: The electronic geometry of an atom with 3 electron groups is {{c1::trigonal planar}}
example: SO<sub>2</sub> has three electron groups (two bonds, one lone pair): trigonal planar geometry, bent shape

text: {{c1::Indicators}} are weak acids or bases that display different colors in the protonated and deprotonated forms
example: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base

text: Electrolytic cells house {{c1::non-spontaneous::spontaneous or non-spontaneous}} reactions
example: Electrolysis of molten NaCl needs an external power supply to make Na metal and Cl<sub>2</sub> gas

text: When [A-] = [HA] at the half-equivalence point, log(1) = {{c1::0}}, so pH = {{c1::pKa}}
example: Titrating acetic acid, the pH reads 4.74 when exactly half the acid has been neutralized

text: The maximum number of electrons in a single subshell in terms of the azimuthal quantum number = {{c1::4l + 2}}
extra:
The number of orbitals in a subshell = 2l + 1
With a maximum of 2 electrons per orbital, the maximum number of electrons per subshell = 2(2l + 1) = 4l + 2
Example: For the d subshell, we know the mathematical value for d is l = 2
4l + 2 = 4(2) + 2 = 10 electrons at maximum in the d subshell

text: If ΔG = 0, the reaction will be {{c1::at equilibrium}}
example: Ice and water coexisting at 0 °C and 1 atm, where ΔG for melting is 0

text: The elements in the group labeled with ? are known as {{c1::metalloids}}
example: Silicon, a metalloid, is the semiconductor in computer chips

text: In an electrochemical cell, electrons flow from the {{c1::anode::anode or cathode}} to the {{c1::cathode::anode or cathode}}
example: In a Zn–Cu cell, electrons travel through the wire from the zinc strip to the copper strip

text: The point in phase diagram where all 3 phases exist is known as the {{c1::triple point}}
example: Water's triple point is 0.01 °C and 0.006 atm

text: In an electrochemical cell, an anode attracts {{c1::anions::anions or cations}} and is always the site of {{c1::oxidation::oxidation or reduction}}
example: In a Zn–Cu cell, the zinc anode is oxidized: Zn → Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>

text: {{c1::Reaction order}} is a number that relates the rate of a chemical reaction to the concentrations of the reacting substances
extra: The sum of all the exponents of the concentrations of substances gives the overall order of the reactionIn the above example, the overall order = a + b
example: For rate = k[NO]<sup>2</sup>[O<sub>2</sub>], the reaction is 2nd order in NO and 3rd order overall

text: The elements in the group labeled with ? are known as {{c1::alkali metals}}
example: Sodium dropped in water fizzes and releases H<sub>2</sub>, forming NaOH

text: {{c1::Dipole-dipole}} forces are attractive forces between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another polar molecule
example: The δ+ H of one HCl molecule attracts the δ− Cl of a neighbouring HCl molecule

text:
Principal and azimuthal quantum number labels on the periodic table:
{{c1::}}
example: Bromine (row 4, group 17) has its valence electrons in 4p: n = 4, l = 1

text: Le Châtelier’s Principle states that if a stress is applied to a system, the system {{c1::shifts to relieve that applied stress }}
example: Adding N<sub>2</sub> to N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> shifts it right, making more NH<sub>3</sub>

text: If a reaction has a positive ∆H and negative ∆S, then it will be {{c1::non-spontaneous::spontaneous or non-spontaneous}} at {{c1::all::high, low, or all}} temperatures
example: Photosynthesis (6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>) never runs by itself; it needs light energy

text: The graph above shows the titration curve of a {{c1::weak acid}} with a {{c1::strong base}}
example: Acetic acid titrated with NaOH: the equivalence point sits near pH 8.7 because acetate is basic

text: Weak acids and bases have {{c1::weak::strong or weak}} conjugates
example: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.74) is weak, and its conjugate acetate is a weak base (pK<sub>b</sub> 9.26)

text: The {{c1::net ionic equation::... equation}} is a chemical equation for a reaction which lists only those species participating in the reaction
extra: Does not include spectator ions
example: AgNO<sub>3</sub> + NaCl reduces to Ag<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup> → AgCl(s)

text: A/an {{c1::solution}} is a special type of homogeneous mixture composed of two or more substances
example: Seawater, with NaCl spread evenly through the water

text: [H<sup>+</sup>] = {{c1::10<sup>-pH</sup>}}
example: Stomach acid at pH 2 has [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−2</sup> = 0.01 M

text: The bond angle of an sp hybridized atom is {{c1::180°}}
example: CO<sub>2</sub> and acetylene (HC≡CH) are linear, with 180° angles at the sp carbon
A solution with pH 3 has pOH 14 − 3 = 11

text: The bond angle of an sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> hybridized atom is {{c1::90°}}
example: SF<sub>6</sub> is octahedral, with every adjacent F–S–F angle at 90°

text: Body temperature is approximately {{c1::37°C}}
example: Human cell cultures are incubated at 37 °C to match body temperature

text: Room temperature is approximately {{c1::25°}} Celsius
example: Standard-state tables use 298 K, which is 25 °C room temperature

text: The order of this reaction is {{c1::second order}}
example: If 1/[A] climbs 1 → 2 → 3 M<sup>−1</sup> in successive minutes, 1/[A] vs time is a straight line

text: Bond angles of an sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridized atom are {{c1::90°}} and {{c1::120°}}
example: PCl<sub>5</sub> is trigonal bipyramidal: 120° between equatorial Cl atoms, 90° to the axial ones

text: {{c1::Ionization energy}} is the amount of energy required to remove an electron
example: Removing sodium's 3s electron takes 496 kJ/mol, forming Na<sup>+</sup>

text: The {{c1::half-equivalence point}}, also known as the {{c1::midpoint}}, is the point in the buffering region at which half the analyte has been protonated or deprotonated
example: If 20 mL of NaOH neutralizes a sample of acetic acid, the midpoint is at 10 mL, where pH = 4.74

text: Cl<sup>-</sup>, Br<sup>-</sup>, and I<sup>-</sup> are {{c1::soluble}} except with Pb<sup>2+</sup>, Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>, and Ag<sup>+</sup>
example: AgNO<sub>3</sub> added to NaCl solution forms a white AgCl precipitate

text: {{c1::Solvation}} or {{c1::dissolution}} is the process of dissolving a solute in solvent
example: Water molecules surround each Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> of a salt crystal and pull them apart

text: The sum of the oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion is equal to {{c1::the charge of the ion}}
example: In MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>: Mn + 4(−2) = −1, so Mn = +7
