text: The common ion effect causes solubility to {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}} when adding like ions
example: AgCl dissolves less in 0.1 M NaCl than in pure water because of the extra Cl<sup>−</sup>

text: {{c1::Osmolarity}} is the number of moles of solute particles (osmoles) per liter of solution
example: 1 M NaCl gives 2 osmol/L (Na<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup>); 1 M glucose gives only 1 osmol/L

text: The {{c1::Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle::... Principle}} states that it is impossible to know the momentum and position of an electron simultaneously
example: Pinpointing an electron with a short-wavelength photon gives it a kick that blurs its momentum

text: Hydrogen bonds are most often formed between hydrogen and the following elements: {{c1::O, N and F}}
extra: O-H, N-H, F-H
example: Water's O–H···O hydrogen bonds let it boil at 100 °C, while H<sub>2</sub>S boils at −60 °C

text: Paramagnetic materials are {{c1::pulled into}} an external magnetic field
extra: Contain one or more unpaired electrons with spin ↑
example: Liquid O<sub>2</sub> sticks between the poles of a magnet because of its two unpaired electrons

text: {{c1::Entropy}} is a measure of how much energy has spread out or how spread out energy has become
example: A hot coffee cooling as its heat spreads out into the room

text: The oxidation state of hydrogen in a compound is {{c1::+1::#}}, except for metal hydrides, such as NaH, LiH, etc., in which the oxidation state for H is {{c1::-1}}
example: In HCl, H is +1; in CaH<sub>2</sub>, each H is −1

text: {{c1::Solubility}} is measured in terms of the maximum amount of solute dissolved in a solvent at equilibrium
example: About 36 g of NaCl dissolves in 100 mL of water at 20 °C; any extra stays as crystals

text: Methyl orange is red at a pH less than {{c1::3.1}} and is yellow at a pH greater than {{c1::4.4}}
example: Methyl orange is red in stomach acid (pH 2) and yellow in pure water (pH 7)

text: {{c1::Sublimation}} is the phase change from solid to gas
example: Dry ice (solid CO<sub>2</sub>) shrinks straight into CO<sub>2</sub> gas at room pressure, never leaving a liquid puddle

text: {{c1::Crystalline lattices}} are large, organized arrays of ions

When in a compound, metals have the following oxidation states:
  • Group 1A metals = {{c1::+1::#}}
  • Group 2A metals = {{c1::+2::#}}
example: In NaCl, Na is +1; in MgO, Mg is +2

text: PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> are {{c1::insoluble}} except with Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
example: Limestone (CaCO<sub>3</sub>) and bone's calcium phosphate are insoluble, but Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> dissolves

text: A monatomic ion has an oxidation number equal to {{c1::the charge of the ion}}
example: Fe<sup>3+</sup> has oxidation number +3; Cl<sup>−</sup> has −1

text: Quantum number {{c1::ml}} is the magnetic quantum number and gives the orbital {{c1::sub-type}}
extra:
Integers -l to +l
The orientation of the electron's orbital with respect to the three axes in space, x, y, and z.
example: For l = 1, m<sub>l</sub> = −1, 0, +1, so the 2p subshell has three orbitals

text:
Nernst equation with the constants simplified to a single value:
{{c1::}}
extra:
Used to calculate cell potential in nonstandard conditions
Ecell = cell potential
E°cell = standard cell potential
0.0592 = all constants multiplied or divided
n = number of moles of electrons transferred
Q = reaction quotient (equals K if reaction is at equilibrium)
example: Zn–Cu cell with [Zn<sup>2+</sup>] = 1 M, [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.01 M: E = 1.10 − (0.0592/2) log 100 = 1.04 V

text:
Change in Gibbs free energy of a redox reaction as a function of the standard cell potential:
{{c1::}}
extra:
n = number of moles of electrons transferred
F = Faraday's constant = 96,485 C/mol
E°cell = standard cell potential
example: Daniell cell: ΔG° = −(2)(96,485)(1.10 V) ≈ −212 kJ/mol

text:
Polar molecules are {{c1::hydrophilic::hydro...}}
Nonpolar molecules are {{c1::hydrophobic::hydro...}}
example: Sugar dissolves in tea, while olive oil beads up on water

text: When choosing a titration indicator, you want to select an indicator that changes color in a range close to your {{c1::equivalence point::point on titration curve}}
example: For acetic acid vs NaOH (equivalence pH ≈ 8.7), phenolphthalein (8.2–10) works; methyl orange (3.1–4.4) does not

text: O<sup>2-</sup> is {{c1::insoluble}} except with Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, Sr<sup>2+</sup>, and Ba<sup>2+</sup>
example: Rust (Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) is insoluble, while Na<sub>2</sub>O dissolves (forming NaOH)

text: The equilibrium constant for the autoionization of water, Kw, is {{c1::10-14}} at 25 °C
example: In pure water at 25 °C, [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 10<sup>−7</sup> M, and 10<sup>−7</sup> × 10<sup>−7</sup> = 10<sup>−14</sup>

text: {{c1::Formal charge}} is the charge given to an individual atom within a molecule
example: In NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, the nitrogen atom carries the +1 formal charge

text: A/an {{c1::free radical}} is an atom or molecule with an unpaired electron
example: UV light splits Cl<sub>2</sub> into two Cl• radicals, each with one unpaired electron

text: {{c1::Electron affinity}} is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to the atom
example: Chlorine releases about 349 kJ/mol when it gains an electron to form Cl<sup>−</sup>

text: Ksp is the {{c1::equilibrium constant}} for a reaction that consists of a solid dissolving in a solution
extra: The equilibrium constant for a regular chemical reaction is abbreviated Keq
example: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup> has K<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup> at 25 °C

text: Li is {{c1::paramagnetic::diamagnetic or paramagnetic}}
example: Like Li (1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>1</sup>), Na ([Ne]3s<sup>1</sup>) is paramagnetic with one unpaired electron

text:
Periodic trend for effective nuclear charge:
{{c1::}}
example: Across row 2, Z<sub>eff</sub> rises from Li to F, so fluorine holds its electrons far more tightly

text: {{c1::Electronegativity}} is a measure of how strongly atoms attract electrons
example: In H<sub>2</sub>O, oxygen pulls the shared electrons away from hydrogen, making O partially negative

text: In a 1 molar solution, normality can be thought of as the {{c1::number of protons a molecule of acid can release in solution}}
extra: For example, each molecule of H2SO4 can release two protons in solution, so its normality is 2

text: Van der Waals Forces is a general term that includes {{c1::dipole-dipole}} forces and {{c1::London dispersion}} forces
example: HCl molecules attract by dipole-dipole forces; argon atoms attract only by London dispersion forces

text: In a/an {{c1::neutral}} solution, both red and blue litmus paper have no change in color
example: Pure water or NaCl solution leaves both red and blue litmus unchanged

text: {{c1::Atomic weight}} is the weighted average of the masses of an element's isotopes
extra: Each mass is multiplied by the isotope's natural abundance
example: Chlorine: 0.758(35) + 0.242(37) ≈ 35.5 amu, the value on the periodic table

text: Thermodynamic products are {{c1::lower::higher or lower}} in free energy compared to kinetic products and they are {{c1::more::more or less}} stable
example: At 40 °C, HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene mainly as the more stable 1,4-adduct, the thermodynamic product

text: A/an {{c1::hydrolysis}} reaction uses water to break the bonds in a molecule
example: Sucrase hydrolyses sucrose + H<sub>2</sub>O into glucose + fructose

text: The order of this reaction is {{c1::first order}}
example: If [A] halves every 10 min (1.0 → 0.5 → 0.25 M), ln[A] vs time is a straight line

text: {{c1::Disproportionation}}, also known as {{c1::dismutation}}, is a REDOX reaction where a molecule is transformed into two or more dissimilar products
example: 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>: oxygen at −1 goes to both −2 and 0

text: Strong acids and bases dissociate {{c1::completely::partially or completely}}
example: 0.1 M HCl gives a full 0.1 M H<sup>+</sup>, so its pH is 1

text: The greater the number of bonds (bond order) the {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} the bond strength and the {{c1::shorter::longer or shorter}} the bond
example: C≡C (120 pm) is shorter and stronger than C=C (134 pm), which beats C–C (154 pm)

text: The electronic geometry of an atom with 5 electron groups is {{c1::trigonal bipyramidal}}
example: ClF<sub>3</sub> has five electron groups: trigonal bipyramidal geometry, T-shaped molecule

text: You exclude pure solids and liquids in the reaction quotient and equilibrium constant because {{c1::their effective concentrations stay constant throughout the reaction}}
extra: They are disregarded and their activity is given the value of 1
example: For CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g), K = [CO<sub>2</sub>] alone

text: Raoult's law states that the vapor pressure of a solution is equal to {{c1::the sum of the vapor pressures of each volatile component multiplied by the mole fraction of that component in the solution}}
extra: Raoult's law can be used to calculate the molecular mass of an unknown solute
example: A 50:50 mole mix of benzene (95 torr) and toluene (28 torr) has P = 0.5(95) + 0.5(28) = 61.5 torr

text: A/an {{c1::solvent}} is a liquid that dissolves a solid, liquid or gaseous {{c2::solute}}
example: In seawater, water is the solvent and NaCl is the solute

text: When in a compound, group 7A elements (halogens) have an oxidation state of {{c1::-1::#}} unless combined with an element of greater electronegativity
example: In NaCl, Cl is −1, but in ClO<sub>2</sub> (bonded to more electronegative O) Cl is +4

text:
O is the hydrogen bond {{c1::acceptor::acceptor or donor}}
N is the hydrogen bond {{c1::donor::acceptor or donor}}
extra:
The acceptor must possess a lone electron pair
The donor is usually strongly electronegative
example: In a G–C base pair, guanine's N–H donates a hydrogen bond to cytosine's C=O oxygen, the acceptor

text: Avogadro’s Number = {{c1::6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 1 mol}}
example: 12 g of carbon-12 contains 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> atoms

text: An H<sub>2</sub>O molecule is a bent because {{c1::the lone pair of electrons repulse each other and push the H atoms away}}
example: Water's H–O–H angle is 104.5°, squeezed below methane's 109.5° by oxygen's two lone pairs

text:
The units for the rate constant of a zeroth order reaction are
{{c1::}}
example: A zero-order reaction that uses up 0.02 M of reactant every second has k = 0.02 M·s<sup>−1</sup>

text: {{c1::Hund’s Rule}} states that all orbitals must first have one electron before any orbital can obtain a second electron
example: Nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy three separate p orbitals, one each, with parallel spins

text: The azimuthal quantum number for this orbital is {{c1::3 = f orbital}}
example: Neodymium ([Xe]4f<sup>4</sup>6s<sup>2</sup>) has four electrons in l = 3 f orbitals

text: The azimuthal quantum number for this orbital is {{c1::1 = p orbital}}
example: Carbon's two highest-energy electrons occupy dumbbell-shaped 2p orbitals (l = 1)

text: An Arrhenius acid is a substance that {{c1::produces H+}}
extra: An Arrhenius acid and Brønsted acid both donate H+
example: HCl dissolving in water releases H<sup>+</sup> (as H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) and Cl<sup>−</sup>

text: {{c1::Combustion reactions}} are exothermic reactions in which something reacts with oxygen
example: A gas stove burns methane: CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

text: {{c1::Ka}} is the equilibrium constant corresponding to the dissociation of an acid, HA, into a proton and its conjugate base
example: Acetic acid has K<sub>a</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> for CH<sub>3</sub>COOH ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>

text: The {{c1::complete ionic equation::... equation}} shows all of the ions present in a reaction including spectator ions
example: Ag<sup>+</sup> + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> + Na<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup> → AgCl(s) + Na<sup>+</sup> + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>

text: Titrations of a/an {{c1::polyvalent acid or base}} show multiple buffering regions and equivalence points
example: Titrating H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> with NaOH gives three buffering regions, near pK<sub>a</sub> 2.1, 7.2 and 12.3

text: pK<sub>a</sub> + pK<sub>b</sub> = {{c1::pK<sub>w</sub>}} = {{c1::14::#}}
example: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has pK<sub>a</sub> 9.25, so its conjugate base NH<sub>3</sub> has pK<sub>b</sub> = 14 − 9.25 = 4.75

text:
The units for the rate constant of a second order reaction are
{{c1::}}
example: For rate = k[A]<sup>2</sup>, a rate of 0.4 M/s at [A] = 2 M gives k = 0.1 M<sup>−1</sup>s<sup>−1</sup>

text: Strong acids and bases have {{c1::weak::strong or weak}} conjugates
example: HCl is a strong acid, so Cl<sup>−</sup> is too weak a base to change water's pH

text: {{c1::Fusion}} is the phase change from solid to liquid
example: An ice cube melting into a puddle of water in your hand

text: Based on the size of the M+2 peak, you know this is a mass spectrum of a molecule that contains {{c1::bromine::element}}
extra: Br has a 1:1 ratio relative to the M peak
example: Bromobenzene shows twin peaks of equal height at m/z 156 and 158.

text: sp3 hybridization is {{c1::25%::%}} s character and {{c1::75%::%}} p character
example: Each of methane's four C–H bonds uses an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital that is 1 part s to 3 parts p.

text: Simple distillation can be used if the boiling points are under 150°C and are at least {{c1::25°C::#°C}} apart
example: Diethyl ether (bp 35 °C) and toluene (bp 111 °C) separate cleanly by simple distillation.

text: A strong reducing agent like {{c1::LiAlH4 (LAH)}} is needed to reduce a carboxylic acid or an ester into an alcohol
example: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces ethyl acetate to two molecules of ethanol.

text: An amide functional group has a/an {{c1::carbonyl}} group linked to a/an {{c1::nitrogen}} atom
example: Every peptide bond in a protein, –CO–NH–, is an amide linkage.

text:
Identify the α-carbon
{{c1::}}
example: In butanal, C-2 (next to the CHO carbon) is the α-carbon.

text: In NMR spectroscopy, the multiplicity of a proton signal is given by the n + 1 rule, where n = {{c1::the number of protons on adjacent carbons}}
example: In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br, the CH<sub>2</sub> has 3 neighbouring H, so it appears as a 3 + 1 = 4-line quartet.

text: In a peptide bond, rotation of the C-N bond is restricted due to {{c1::resonance}}
extra: Resonance causes the C-N bond to take on a partial double bond character
example: The peptide C–N bond is 1.32 Å, shorter than a normal C–N single bond (1.47 Å).

text: This is {{c1::carbonic acid::name}}
example: In red blood cells, carbonic anhydrase joins CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O into carbonic acid, H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>

text: Gel-filtration chromatography separates molecules based on their {{c1::size}}
extra:
Also known as size-exclusion chromatography
Smaller molecules enter the porous gel beads causing them to elute slower
Larger molecules do not fit in the pores so they elute faster
example: Size-exclusion chromatography separates IgG antibodies (150 kDa) from myoglobin (17 kDa).

text: {{c1::Gabriel synthesis}} generates an amino acid from potassium phthalimide, diethyl bromomalonate, and an alkyl halide
example: Gabriel synthesis with benzyl bromide as the alkyl halide yields phenylalanine.

text: The substituents on this benzene ring are in {{c1::para}} position
example: Hydroquinone (1,4-dihydroxybenzene) has its two –OH groups para.

text:
Identify the α-hydrogens
{{c1::}}
example: Acetone has six α-hydrogens, three on each methyl.

text: This is {{c1::formaldehyde::name}}
example: Formaldehyde (HCHO) dissolved in water as formalin preserves tissue specimens

text: Alcohols have an {{c1::–OH}} group and use the suffix {{c1::–ol}} or the prefix {{c1::hydroxy-}}
extra: Alcohols have higher priority than double or triple bonds
example: Ethanol is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH; lactic acid is named 2-hydroxypropanoic acid

text: A/an {{c1::amine functional group::... functional group}} is a basic nitrogen atom with a lone pair of electrons
example: Methylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) uses its lone pair to accept H<sup>+</sup>, forming CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>.

text: A secondary substrate with an aprotic solvent will go {{c1::SN2::SN1 or SN2}}
example: 2-Bromobutane with NaI in acetone gives 2-iodobutane with inversion.

text: Polypeptides are made up of multiple {{c1::amino acids}} linked by {{c1::peptide bonds}}
extra: Proteins are large, folded, functional polypeptides
example: Insulin is two polypeptide chains of 21 and 30 amino acids.

text:
Identify the functional group in red
{{c1::}}
extra: Acyl groups are derived by removing one or more hydroxyl groups from an oxoacid (an oxygen-containing acid)
example: The acetyl group, CH<sub>3</sub>C(=O)–, carried by acetyl-CoA is an acyl group.

text: A/an {{c1::Brønsted-Lowry}} acid is a proton donor
example: HCl donates H<sup>+</sup> to water, forming H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>.

text:
Identify the most acidic proton
{{c1::}}
extra:
This is a β-dicarboxylic acid
Note: the COOH O–H protons (pKa ≈ 2.8) are the most acidic; the α-H between the two carbonyls is unusually acidic for a C–H (resonance-stabilized carbanion) but far less acidic than the COOH protons
example: In malonic acid, HOOC–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH, the two O–H protons are the most acidic.

text: The rate law for an SN2 reaction is {{c1::SN2 Rate = k[substrate]1[nucleophile]1}}
example: With k = 0.5 M<sup>−1</sup>s<sup>−1</sup>, 0.2 M CH<sub>3</sub>Br and 0.1 M OH<sup>−</sup>, the rate is 0.01 M/s.

text: When two equivalents of alcohol react with an aldehyde, a/an {{c1::acetal}} is formed
example: Methyl glucoside forms when glucose's hemiacetal C-1 reacts with a second alcohol, methanol.

text: Polar {{c1::protic::protic or aprotic}} solvents are capable of hydrogen bonding
extra: Polar Protic: Acetic Acid, H2O, ROH, NH3
example: Methanol's O–H hydrogen-bonds to anions like F<sup>−</sup>, caging them in a solvent shell.

text: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a {{c1::weak::weak or strong}} reducing agent
extra: It will reduce an aldehyde or a ketone into an alcohol, but will not reduce a carboxylic acid or an ester
example: NaBH<sub>4</sub> in methanol reduces cyclohexanone to cyclohexanol.

text: Cl<sup>-</sup> and Br<sup>-</sup> are {{c1::good::good or bad}} leaving groups
example: Bromide leaves readily from tert-butyl bromide in water, forming the tert-butyl carbocation.

text: This is a/an {{c1::acetyl group::... group}}
example: Acetyl-CoA carries an acetyl group (CH<sub>3</sub>CO–) into the citric acid cycle

text: In an extraction, the {{c1::nonpolar::polar or nonpolar}} layer is the organic layer and dissolves nonpolar compounds
example: In an ether/water extraction, nonpolar naphthalene dissolves in the diethyl ether layer.

text: When hydrogens are on adjacent atoms, they interfere with each other's magnetic environment, causing {{c1::spin-spin coupling}}, also known as {{c1::splitting}}
example: In ethanol, the CH<sub>3</sub> signal is split into a triplet by the two neighbouring CH<sub>2</sub> protons.

text: Alcohols are classified as 1º, 2º, and 3º alcohols according to the number of carbons attached to the {{c1::carbon bearing the hydroxyl group}}
extra: In other words, whether the hydroxyl is bound to a primary, secondary, or tertiary carbon
example: Ethanol is a 1º alcohol, 2-propanol (isopropanol) is 2º, and tert-butanol is 3º

text: {{c1::Enantiomers}} are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable and are mirror images of each other
extra: Same chemical and physical properties, except for rotation of plane polarized light
example: (R)-carvone smells of spearmint while its enantiomer (S)-carvone smells of caraway

text: Based on the size of the M+2 peak, you know this is a mass spectrum of a molecule that contains {{c1::chlorine::element}}
extra: Cl has a 3:1 ratio relative to the M peak
example: Chlorobenzene shows peaks at m/z 112 and 114 in a 3:1 ratio.

text: In a mass spectrum, the M+2 peak shows the relative abundance of either {{c1::81Br}} or {{c1::37Cl}}
extra:
Br: M : M+2 ≈ 1:1
Cl: M : M+2 ≈ 3:1
example: CH<sub>3</sub>Br shows peaks at m/z 94 and 96 of nearly equal height.

text: In an extraction, the {{c1::polar::polar or nonpolar}} layer is the aqueous (water) layer and dissolves compounds with hydrogen bonding or polarity
example: Adding NaOH turns benzoic acid into sodium benzoate, which moves into the aqueous layer.

text: Removal of a proton from the more substituted (and more hindered) α-carbon gives the {{c1::thermodynamic::kinetic or thermodynamic}} enolate
extra: The thermodynamic enolate has the more substituted C=C double bond
example: NaOEt at room temperature favors 2-methylcyclohexanone's enolate at the methyl-bearing C-2.

text: {{c1::Recrystallization}}, also known as {{c1::fractional crystallization}}, is a procedure for purifying an impure compound in a solvent
extra:
The impure compound is dissolved in hot solvent to make a concentrated solution, then cooled
As solubility drops, the desired compound (present in excess) crystallizes out before the impurities
example: Crude benzoic acid dissolved in hot water recrystallizes as pure needles on cooling.

text: {{c1::Absolute configuration::... configuration}} gives the stereochemistry of a compound without having to compare to other compounds
example: Natural L-alanine is (S)-alanine, an assignment made from CIP priorities alone.

text: The {{c1::integration}} is the area under each peak (signal) on the NMR spectrum. It corresponds to the number of protons in that signal
example: Ethanol's <sup>1</sup>H NMR peaks integrate 3:2:1 for its CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub> and OH protons.

text: Multiple bonds are {{c1::less::more or less}} flexible than single bonds
extra: This is because rotation is not permitted in the presence of a π bond
example: Ethane's C–C bond rotates freely, but cis-2-butene cannot twist into trans-2-butene.

text: When one equivalent of alcohol reacts with a ketone, a/an {{c1::hemiketal}} is formed
example: Fructose's C-5 –OH attacks its C-2 ketone, forming a cyclic hemiketal (furanose).

text: {{c1::Transesterification}} is the process of exchanging the R″ group of an ester with the R′ group of an alcohol
extra:
"Transformation of an ester"
Alcohol is the attacking nucleophile
example: Biodiesel is made by transesterifying vegetable-oil triglycerides with methanol.

text: The IR spectroscopy frequency range for C≡C and C≡N triple bonds is {{c1::1900}} - {{c1::2200}} cm-1
example: 1-Hexyne shows a weak C≡C stretch near 2100 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text: The acidity of a carboxylic acid can be decreased by substituents that are electron-{{c1::donating::withdrawing or donating}}
example: Propanoic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.87) is weaker than formic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 3.75).

text: In gas chromatography, the liquid sample is vaporized before separation. Molecules are separated based on their {{c1::polarity}} and {{c1::boiling point}}
extra:
The stationary phase is a thin layer of material applied to the inside of the column
Typically the polarity of the stationary phase matches that of the solute
The mobile phase is an inert gas
example: In GC, pentane (bp 36 °C) elutes before octane (bp 126 °C).

text: The type of bond indicated in this IR spectroscopy chart is {{c1::N-H}}
example: A secondary amine like diethylamine gives a single N–H peak near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text:
Give the number of sigma and pi bonds for each bond order
{{c1::}}
example: Ethyne's C≡C is 1 σ + 2 π bonds, while ethene's C=C is 1 σ + 1 π bond.

text: sp hybridization is {{c1::50%::%}} s character and {{c1::50%::%}} p character
example: Each carbon in acetylene (HC≡CH) is sp, mixing one s with one p orbital.

text: A/an {{c1::enolate anion}} is formed when an α-hydrogen in the molecule of an aldehyde or a ketone is removed
example: LDA pulls an α-H from cyclohexanone, giving its enolate.

text:
The retention factor in thin-layer chromatography is:
Rf = {{c1::\(\frac{distance~the~spot~moved}{distance~the~solvent~front~moved}\)}}
example: A spot that moves 3 cm while the solvent front moves 6 cm has R<sub>f</sub> = 3/6 = 0.5.

text: {{c1::Decarboxylation}} is a chemical reaction that removes a carboxyl group and releases carbon dioxide (CO2)
extra: β-keto acids (including β-dicarboxylic acids) decarboxylate spontaneously when heated
example: Acetoacetate decarboxylates to acetone, which gives diabetic ketoacidosis breath its fruity smell.

text: {{c1::Stereoisomers}} are connected in the same order but differ in 3D orientation
example: cis- and trans-2-butene have the same bonds but differ in how the groups sit around the C=C

text: A methyl substrate cannot undergo an elimination reaction because elimination reactions create {{c1::double bonds between two carbons, C=C}}
extra: There is only one carbon in a methyl so no double bond can be created
example: CH<sub>3</sub>Br with the strong base NaOEt gives only CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, never an alkene.

text: In the mass spectrum, the heaviest ion (the one with the greatest m/z value) is likely to be the {{c1::molecular ion}}
example: Ethanol's molecular ion, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH<sup>+</sup>, appears at m/z 46.

text: Removal of a proton from the less substituted (and less hindered) α-carbon gives the {{c1::kinetic::kinetic or thermodynamic}} enolate
extra: The kinetic enolate has the less substituted C=C double bond
example: LDA at −78 °C deprotonates 2-methylcyclohexanone at the CH<sub>2</sub> (C-6), not at C-2.

text: {{c1::Lewis}} acids are electron acceptors
extra: Contain vacant orbitals or positively polarized atoms
example: BF<sub>3</sub> accepts the lone pair of NH<sub>3</sub> into boron's empty p orbital.

text: A ketone is an internal functional group containing a/an {{c1::carbonyl}} bonded to two {{c1::alkyl chains}}
example: Acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, has its carbonyl between two methyl groups.

text: This is a/an {{c1::benzyl group::... group}}
example: Benzyl alcohol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) carries a benzyl group

text:
When an alcohol is oxidized it becomes one of the following compounds:
  • {{c1::aldehyde}}
  • {{c1::ketone}}
  • {{c1::carboxylic acid}}
extra: Oxidation of an alcohol removes the H and adds a second bond to the O to make a carbonyl
example: Ethanol oxidizes to acetaldehyde, then acetic acid; 2-propanol oxidizes to acetone.

text: {{c1::Strecker synthesis::... synthesis}} and {{c1::Gabriel synthesis::... synthesis}} are two common methods of synthesizing amino acids in the lab
example: A lab can make alanine either way: Strecker from acetaldehyde, or Gabriel using methyl bromide.

text: {{c1::Saponification}} is an ester hydrolysis of triacylglycerols using a strong base like NaOH or KOH
extra: The resulting soaps (fatty acid salts) form micelles in water
example: Heating animal fat with lye (NaOH) yields glycerol and soap, as in traditional soap-making.

text: In redox reactions, the {{c1::oxidized::oxidized or reduced}} molecule loses electrons and the oxidation number increases
example: In Zn → Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>, zinc is oxidized from 0 to +2.

text: A/an {{c1::chiral center}} is a carbon with four different groups attached
example: Alanine's α-carbon bears H, NH<sub>2</sub>, COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>, so it is a chiral center

text: Cyclic amides are called {{c1::lactams}}
example: The β-lactam ring of penicillin is a four-membered cyclic amide.

text: A/an {{c1::micelle}} dissolves nonpolar organic molecules in its interior, and can be solvated with water due to its exterior shell of hydrophilic groups
example: Bile-salt micelles carry dietary cholesterol and fatty acids to the intestinal wall.

text: Multiple bonds are {{c1::stronger::weaker or stronger}} than single bonds
example: A C≡C bond (839 kJ/mol) is stronger than C=C (614 kJ/mol) or C–C (348 kJ/mol).

text: In liquid chromatography, {{c1::silica}} is a common stationary phase while {{c1::toluene}} or another nonpolar liquid is used as the mobile phase
example: A silica column run with a nonpolar solvent elutes orange β-carotene before green chlorophyll.

text: {{c1::Nucleophilicity}} is a term used to describe the strength of a nucleophile
example: Hydroxide (OH<sup>−</sup>) is a stronger nucleophile than neutral water.

text: Carboxylic acids have a high boiling point due to {{c1::hydrogen bonding}}
extra: They often exist as dimers in solution due to the hydrogen bonding
example: Acetic acid (MW 60) boils at 118 °C, while 1-propanol (MW 60) boils at 97 °C.

text: During a filtration, a solid, also known as the {{c1::residue}}, is isolated from a liquid, also known as the {{c1::filtrate}}
example: Pouring coffee through a paper filter leaves the grounds (residue) and yields the coffee (filtrate).

text: sp2 hybridization is {{c1::33%::%}} s character and {{c1::67%::%}} p character
example: Each carbon in ethylene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) is sp<sup>2</sup>, mixing one s with two p orbitals.

text: The largest peak in the mass spectrum, corresponding to the most abundant ion, is called the {{c1::base peak}}
example: In acetone's mass spectrum, the base peak is CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at m/z 43, not M<sup>+</sup> at 58.

text: When a phosphodiester bond is formed, a/an {{c1::pyrophosphate (PPi)}} is released
extra: The pyrophosphate can then be hydrolyzed into two inorganic phosphates (Pi)
example: When DNA polymerase adds dATP to a strand, the α-phosphate joins the chain and PP<sub>i</sub> leaves.

text: Alkenes have a {{c1::double}} bond and use the suffix {{c1::-ene}}
example: Ethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>), the fruit-ripening hormone, has one C=C double bond

text: {{c1::Carboxylic acid}} is the highest priority functional group
extra: This is because it contains 3 bonds to oxygen
example: In 4-oxopentanoic acid, the ketone is demoted to the prefix oxo- because –COOH takes the suffix

text: {{c1::Relative configuration::... configuration}} gives the stereochemistry of a compound relative to the D- and L- forms of glyceraldehyde
extra:
In a Fischer projection, look at the highest-numbered chiral carbon:
–OH on the right → D-sugar
–OH on the left → L-sugar
example: D-Glucose is a D-sugar because its C-5 –OH points right in the Fischer projection.

text: Quantum number ms is the {{c1::spin}} quantum number and gives the {{c1::electronic spin}} of the electron
extra: +1/2 or −1/2
example: The two electrons in helium's 1s orbital have m<sub>s</sub> = +1/2 and −1/2.

text: In NMR spectroscopy, a peak that is shielded appears {{c1::upfield (right)::downfield or upfield}}
example: Cyclohexane's protons are shielded and appear upfield at about 1.4 ppm.

text: {{c1::Electrophiles}} are electron loving
extra: Contain a positive charge or are positively polarized
example: H<sup>+</sup> and the tert-butyl carbocation are electrophiles that seek an electron pair.

text: Cyclic esters are called {{c1::lactones}}
example: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) contains a five-membered lactone ring.

text: {{c1::Oxidation number}} is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were completely ionic
example: In H<sub>2</sub>O, oxygen's oxidation number is −2 and each hydrogen's is +1.

text: A {{c1::carbonyl}} is a carbon-oxygen double bond
example: Urea, (NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O, contains a carbonyl flanked by two nitrogens.

text:
Cis functional groups are on {{c1::the same}} side
Trans functional groups are on {{c1::opposing}} sides
example: cis-2-Butene has both CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the same side of the C=C; trans-2-butene has them on opposite sides.

text: This is {{c1::acetylacetone::name}}
example: Acetylacetone sits mostly in its enol form, stabilized by conjugation and an internal hydrogen bond

text: Ka is the {{c1::acid dissociation}} constant
extra:
An indicator of acid strength
It is the equilibrium constant corresponding to the dissociation of an acid, HA, into a proton and its conjugate base
example: Acetic acid's K<sub>a</sub> of 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> means a 0.1 M solution is only about 1.3% ionized.

text: Quantum number l is the {{c1::azimuthal}} quantum number and gives the {{c1::3D shape (subshell)}} of an orbital
extra:
0, 1, 2, …, n − 1
0 = s orbital
1 = p orbital
2 = d orbital
3 = f orbital
4 = g orbital
example: A 3p electron has l = 1, so it occupies a dumbbell-shaped p orbital.

text: {{c1::Orbital hybridization}} is the idea that atomic orbitals fuse to form newly hybridized orbitals
example: Carbon in methane mixes one 2s and three 2p orbitals into four equivalent sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals.

text: This is {{c1::formic acid::name}}
example: Formic acid (HCOOH) is the acid in ant stings

text: The nitrogen containing functional group shown above is called a/an {{c1::amide}}
extra: Amides are synthesized from a carboxylic acid by replacing the –OH group with an amino group that may or may not be substituted
example: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) carries an amide group, –NHCOCH<sub>3</sub>, on its benzene ring.

text: This compound is named {{c1::propane}}
example: Propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) is the fuel in barbecue gas tanks

text: {{c1::Meso compounds}} have an internal plane of symmetry
extra: Will be optically inactive because the two sides of the molecule cancel each other out
example: meso-Tartaric acid (2R,3S) has two stereocenters yet is achiral, with a mirror plane bisecting its C2–C3 bond.

text: {{c1::Deshielding}} in NMR spectroscopy is when a nucleus' chemical shift is increased due to the removal of electron density, magnetic induction, or other effects
extra: Deshielding is the opposite of shielding
example: The CH<sub>3</sub> of CH<sub>3</sub>F (4.3 ppm) is more deshielded than that of CH<sub>3</sub>I (2.2 ppm).

text: {{c1::Molecular}} orbitals are obtained by combining the {{c1::atomic}} orbitals from the individual atoms that make up the molecule
extra: Molecular orbital theory is able to explain why some bonds between atoms are observed to be in between a single and a double bond. Valence-bond theory, the more traditional theory, cannot explain these "hybridized" bonds
example: MO theory puts two unpaired electrons in O<sub>2</sub>'s π* orbitals, explaining why liquid O<sub>2</sub> sticks to a magnet.

text: Aldehydes and ketones can be protected by converting them into {{c1::acetals}} or {{c1::ketals}}
example: Ethyl acetoacetate's ketone is protected as a ketal so LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces only its ester.

text: This is {{c1::benzaldehyde::name}}
example: Benzaldehyde gives almond extract its flavour

text: Chromatography is a laboratory technique for the separation of a mixture based on {{c1::how fast each component travels through a structure}}
extra:
The mixture is dissolved in a fluid called the mobile phase, which carries it through a structure holding another material called the stationary phase
The various constituents of the mixture travel at different speeds, causing them to separate
example: Paper chromatography separates the colored dyes in black marker ink into distinct bands.

text: In a hydration reaction, water adds to a carbonyl and forms a/an {{c1::geminal diol}}
example: Chloral hydrate, Cl<sub>3</sub>CCH(OH)<sub>2</sub>, forms when water adds to chloral's carbonyl.

text: A carboxylic acid can act as a nucleophile and attack a second carboxylic acid to form a/an {{c1::anhydride}}
example: Two acetic acid molecules condense, losing water, to form acetic anhydride.

text: {{c1::Leaving groups}} are molecular fragments that retain the electrons after heterolysis
extra:
The best LG can stabilize additional charge through resonance or induction
Weak bases make good leaving groups
example: When CH<sub>3</sub>Cl reacts with OH<sup>−</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup> leaves carrying both C–Cl bond electrons.

text: The IR spectroscopy frequency for C=O bonds is {{c1::1750}} cm-1
example: Ethyl acetate shows a strong, sharp C=O peak near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text:
In a mass spectrum, the M : M+2 peak ratio is:
  • {{c1::1:1}} for Br
  • {{c1::3:1}} for Cl
example: Chloromethane shows M at m/z 50 and M+2 at m/z 52 in a 3:1 ratio.

text: This is {{c1::acetone::name}}
example: Acetone, the solvent in nail polish remover, gives the breath in diabetic ketoacidosis its fruity smell

text: {{c1::Keto-enol tautomerization}} refers to a chemical equilibrium between a keto form and an enol
extra:
The keto and enol forms are said to be tautomers of each other
They can be interconverted by moving a hydrogen and a double bond
example: Acetaldehyde, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, interconverts with its enol, vinyl alcohol (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHOH).

text: The substituents on this benzene ring are in {{c1::ortho}} position
example: Catechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene) has its two –OH groups ortho.

text: The hydrogens of a/an {{c1::aldehyde}} group have an NMR range of 9.7 - 10.0 ppm
example: Acetaldehyde's CHO proton appears at about 9.8 ppm.

text:
Acid chloride, amides, anhydrides, carboxylate and esters ranked from most to least reactive in nucleophilic substitution:
{{c1::Acid chloride > Anhydrides > Esters > Amides > Carboxylate}}
example: Acetyl chloride reacts violently with water, while acetamide needs hot acid or base to hydrolyze.

text: This is {{c1::acrolein::name}}
example: Acrolein forms when cooking fat overheats and gives burnt oil its acrid smell

text: The IR spectroscopy frequency range for O-H bonds is {{c1::3000}} - {{c1::3300}} cm-1
example: 1-Butanol's hydrogen-bonded O–H appears as a broad, rounded band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text: In NMR spectroscopy, the {{c1::chemical shift}} is the position on the δ scale (in ppm) where the peak occurs
example: Chloroform's lone proton (CHCl<sub>3</sub>) has a chemical shift of 7.26 ppm.

text: The hydrogens of a/an {{c1::alkyl}} group have an NMR range of 0.7 - 1.9 ppm
example: The CH<sub>3</sub> protons of hexane appear near 0.9 ppm.

text: Strong bases favor {{c1::E2}} reactions
example: tert-Butyl bromide with potassium tert-butoxide gives 2-methylpropene by E2.

text: This is {{c1::benzoic acid::name}}
example: Sodium benzoate, the salt of benzoic acid, is a common food preservative

text: {{c1::SN1::SN1 or SN2}} products are a racemic mixture
extra: In the 2nd step, the nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation from either side, leading to a racemic mixture of products
example: (R)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane in water gives a 50:50 mix of (R)- and (S)-3-methyl-3-hexanol.

text: {{c1::Vinylic}} hydrogens have an NMR range of 4.5 - 6.5 ppm
example: Ethylene's four equivalent hydrogens appear at 5.3 ppm.

text: High Ka = {{c1::strong::strong or weak}} acid
example: HF (K<sub>a</sub> 6.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) is a stronger acid than acetic acid (K<sub>a</sub> 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>).

text: {{c1::Quinones}} are conjugated cyclic diketones but are not aromatic
extra:
Synthesized through oxidation of phenols
Examples:
Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone)
Vitamin K2 (the menaquinones)
example: Oxidizing hydroquinone gives 1,4-benzoquinone, a yellow conjugated cyclic diketone.

text: The term "enol" comes from the fact that it is a/an {{c1::alkene}} that is also a/an {{c1::alcohol}}
example: Vinyl alcohol, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHOH, is the simplest enol.

text:
In E/Z naming of alkenes:
  • Z: highest-priority groups on {{c1::the same}} side(s)
  • E: highest-priority groups on {{c1::opposite}} side(s)
example: In 2-butene each C=C carbon's top group is CH<sub>3</sub> (over H), so cis-2-butene is (Z)-2-butene.

text: The acidity of a carboxylic acid can be enhanced by substituents that are electron-{{c1::withdrawing::withdrawing or donating}}
example: Trichloroacetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 0.7) is far stronger than acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76).

text: A/an {{c1::retro-aldol reaction::... reaction}} is the reverse of an aldol reaction
extra:
The bond between the α- and β-carbon is cleaved
Catalyzed by heat
example: In glycolysis, aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.

text: A reducing agent {{c1::donates::accepts or donates}} electrons and is {{c1::oxidized::oxidized or reduced}} in the process
example: In 2Na + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2NaCl, sodium is the reducing agent and goes from 0 to +1.

text: This Newman projection shows {{c1::anti}} conformation
extra: The carbon attachments are on opposite ends, 180 degrees apart
example: Anti butane, with its two methyl groups opposite each other, is its lowest-energy conformation

text: Fractional distillation is a process by which components in a mixture are separated into different parts (called fractions) according to their different {{c1::boiling points}}
example: Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into gasoline, kerosene and diesel fractions.

text: A/an {{c1::Brønsted-Lowry}} base is a proton acceptor
example: NH<sub>3</sub> accepts a proton from water, becoming NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.

text: Aldehydes have a carbonyl group on the {{c1::terminal::terminal or non-terminal}} carbon
example: Propanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, has its C=O on the end carbon

text: Affinity chromatography separates proteins based on {{c1::their affinity for a specific ligand}}
extra:
Beads are bound to a specific ligand and proteins with a high affinity for that ligand will bind to the beads
Proteins with a low affinity for the ligand will elute first
example: His-tagged proteins bind a Ni<sup>2+</sup> column while untagged proteins wash straight through.

text: Amides are given the suffix {{c1::–amide}}
example: CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> is ethanamide; HCONH<sub>2</sub> is methanamide (formamide).

text: Nitrogen and nitrogen derivatives react with carbonyls to form {{c1::imines}}
example: Retinal binds a lysine of opsin as an imine (Schiff base) in rhodopsin.

text: This is {{c1::styrene::name}}
example: Styrene polymerizes into polystyrene, the plastic of foam cups

text: A primary substrate will go {{c1::SN2::SN1 or SN2}}
extra:
1 step
If you were to do an SN1 reaction on a primary substrate, you'd get a primary carbocation, which is very unstable
example: 1-Bromobutane with NaCN in DMSO gives pentanenitrile by S<sub>N</sub>2.

text: {{c1::Lewis}} bases are electron donors
extra: Contain a lone pair of electrons and are often anions
example: NH<sub>3</sub> donates its lone pair to Ag<sup>+</sup>, forming [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>.

text: Quantum number n is the {{c1::principal}} quantum number and gives the electron {{c1::energy level or shell number}}
extra:
1, 2, 3, ...
Except for d- and f-orbitals, the shell # matches the row of the periodic table
example: Sodium's valence electron sits in n = 3, matching its place in row 3 of the periodic table.

text: The reagents used in acid halide synthesis are {{c1::SOCl2}} and {{c1::PBr3}}
example: Acetic acid + SOCl<sub>2</sub> gives acetyl chloride, SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl.

text: {{c1::Resonance}} is the delocalization of electrons in molecules that have conjugated bonds
example: In acetate, the negative charge is shared over both oxygens, so both C–O bonds have the same length.

text: A secondary substrate with a protic solvent will go {{c1::SN1::SN1 or SN2}}
example: 2-Bromobutane heated in water forms 2-butanol via a secondary carbocation.

text: Aldehydes and ketones are synthesized from alcohols through {{c1::oxidation}}
example: The liver's alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde.

text: Carboxylic acids can be made by the {{c1::oxidation}} of 1° alcohols or aldehydes
example: Wine turns to vinegar as Acetobacter oxidizes ethanol to acetic acid.

text: This is a/an {{c1::acryl group::... group}}
example: Acrylamide (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCONH<sub>2</sub>), which forms polyacrylamide gels for SDS-PAGE, carries an acryl group

text: A/an {{c1::wash}} is the reverse of an extraction: a small amount of solvent that dissolves the impurities is run over the compound of interest
example: Rinsing filtered aspirin crystals with ice-cold water washes away leftover acetic acid.

text: In a typical thin-layer chromatography setup, the spot that moves farthest is the {{c1::nonpolar}} substance and the spot that moves the shortest distance is the {{c1::polar}} substance
extra: The stationary phase is typically silica gel, which is polar
example: On a silica TLC plate run in hexane, biphenyl runs near the solvent front while benzoic acid stays near the baseline.

text: The types of bonds indicated in this IR spectroscopy chart are {{c1::C-H}} and {{c1::C=O}}
example: Acetone's IR spectrum shows C–H stretches just below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a sharp C=O at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text: Esters are given the suffix {{c1::–oate}}
example: CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate).

text: Multiple bonds are {{c1::shorter::shorter or longer}} than single bonds
example: C–C in ethane is 154 pm, C=C in ethene 134 pm, and C≡C in ethyne 120 pm.

text: Ketones have a carbonyl group on a {{c1::non-terminal::terminal or non-terminal}} carbon
example: Butanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, has its C=O on carbon 2

text: This is the {{c1::keto::keto or enol}} form of acetone
extra:
Keto form has a regular ketone or an aldehyde
Enol form contains an alcohol
example: The keto form of acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, is what you buy as nail-polish remover.

text: This is a/an {{c1::acetal}}
extra: A primary carbon with two –OR groups and a hydrogen atom
example: Acetaldehyde + 2 CH<sub>3</sub>OH gives the acetal 1,1-dimethoxyethane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

text: A/an {{c1::redox}} reaction is a reaction with the transfer of electrons from the substance being oxidized to the substance being reduced
example: In Zn + Cu<sup>2+</sup> → Zn<sup>2+</sup> + Cu, zinc hands two electrons to copper.

text:
Geminal diols have their two hydroxyl groups attached to {{c1::the same::the same or adjacent}} carbon(s)
Vicinal diols have theirs attached to {{c1::adjacent::the same or adjacent}} carbon(s)
example: Hydrated formaldehyde, CH<sub>2</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub>, is geminal; ethylene glycol, HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is vicinal.

text: The number 2 in an SN2 reaction refers to the fact that the reaction is {{c1::bimolecular}}
example: Doubling [OH<sup>−</sup>] doubles the rate of CH<sub>3</sub>Br + OH<sup>−</sup>, and so does doubling [CH<sub>3</sub>Br].

text: Polar {{c1::aprotic::protic or aprotic}} solvents do not participate in hydrogen bonding
extra: Polar Aprotic: DMF, DMSO, Acetone, Ethyl Acetate
example: Acetonitrile (CH<sub>3</sub>CN), common in HPLC, is polar but has no O–H or N–H to hydrogen-bond.

text: Peptide Bonds are formed when the {{c1::N-terminus}} of an amino acid nucleophilically attacks the {{c1::C-terminus}} of another amino acid
extra:
Condensation reaction
Can be cleaved hydrolytically using a strong acid or base
example: Alanine's –COOH joined to glycine's –NH<sub>2</sub> gives the dipeptide Ala-Gly plus water.

text: NMR spectra are calibrated using {{c1::tetramethylsilane (TMS)}}, which has a chemical shift of 0 ppm
example: TMS, Si(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>, gives one sharp peak set at 0 ppm, upfield of nearly all organic protons.

text: A weak oxidizing agent like {{c1::pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC)}} must be used for synthesizing aldehydes from alcohols, or else the reaction will continue oxidizing and form a carboxylic acid
example: PCC in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> stops benzyl alcohol at benzaldehyde.

text: {{c1::Amphoteric}} molecules can act as either acids or bases
example: Water accepts H<sup>+</sup> from HCl but donates H<sup>+</sup> to NH<sub>3</sub>.

text: This compound is named {{c1::butane}}
example: Butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) is the fuel in disposable lighters

text: Ion exchange chromatography separates proteins by their {{c1::net charge}}
extra:
The column is filled with charged beads, either positively or negatively charged
Cation exchange: negatively charged beads; negatively charged proteins elute first
Anion exchange: positively charged beads; positively charged proteins elute first
example: At pH 7, positive lysozyme (pI ≈ 11) and negative albumin (pI ≈ 4.7) separate by ion exchange.

text: A/an {{c1::extraction}} combines two immiscible liquids, one of which easily dissolves the compound of interest
example: Shaking brewed tea with dichloromethane pulls the caffeine into the organic layer.

text: The rate law for an SN1 reaction is {{c1::SN1 Rate = k[substrate]1}}
example: With k = 0.01 s<sup>−1</sup> and [substrate] = 2 M, the S<sub>N</sub>1 rate is 0.02 M/s whatever [Nu] is.

text: In NMR spectroscopy, a peak that is deshielded appears {{c1::downfield (left)::downfield or upfield}}
example: The protons of CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (5.3 ppm) appear downfield of those of CH<sub>3</sub>Cl (3.1 ppm).

text: This is {{c1::benzoin::name}}
example: Two benzaldehyde molecules join into benzoin in the cyanide-catalyzed benzoin condensation

text: This compound is named {{c1::pentane}}
example: Pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) boils at 36 °C, so it evaporates quickly from a warm hand

text: A/an {{c1::alkynyl}} hydrogen has an NMR range of 2.5 - 3.0 ppm
example: The lone terminal hydrogen of propyne, HC≡C–CH<sub>3</sub>, is an alkynyl hydrogen.

text:
Identify the acidic proton
{{c1::}}
example: In acetic acid, the O–H proton (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76) is acidic, not the CH<sub>3</sub> protons.

text: In a typical thin-layer chromatography setup, the stationary phase is made up of {{c1::silica gel::substance}} which is {{c1::polar::polar or nonpolar}}
extra: Polar molecules are slowed by the stationary phase. Nonpolar molecules are repelled by the stationary phase and elute first
example: TLC plates are glass or aluminium sheets coated with silica gel (SiO<sub>2</sub>), rich in polar Si–OH groups.

text: {{c1::pKa}} is the pH at which half of the species is deprotonated
example: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76) at pH 4.76 is 50% acetate and 50% acetic acid.

text: {{c1::Chemoselectivity}} is the ability of a reagent or intermediate to react with one group or atom in a molecule in preference to another group or atom in the same molecule
example: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces a ketone to an alcohol but leaves an ester in the same molecule untouched.

text: This is a/an {{c1::carbonate ion::... ion}}
example: Limestone and chalk are calcium carbonate, CaCO<sub>3</sub>

text: Alkanes are named according to the number of {{c1::carbons}} present followed by the suffix {{c1::–ane}}
example: A five-carbon straight-chain alkane is pent- + -ane = pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>)

text: This reaction will go {{c1::SN2::SN1 or SN2}}
extra: The substrate is secondary and acetone is an aprotic solvent
example: 2-Bromopropane with NaCN in DMSO gives 2-methylpropanenitrile by S<sub>N</sub>2.

text: For n number of chiral carbons, there are {{c1::2n}} possible stereoisomers
example: Open-chain glucose has 4 chiral carbons, giving 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 aldohexose stereoisomers

text: {{c1::Isomers}} have the same chemical formula but have a different arrangement of their atoms (connectivity or spatial)
example: Ethanol and dimethyl ether are both C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O

text: {{c1::Gravity filtration::... filtration}} can be used to collect solid product, although generally {{c1::vacuum filtration::... filtration}} is used for this purpose because it is faster
example: A Büchner funnel under vacuum collects recrystallized acetanilide crystals far faster than a gravity funnel.

text: The substituents on this benzene ring are in {{c1::meta}} position
example: Resorcinol (1,3-dihydroxybenzene) has its two –OH groups meta.

text: A distillation separates liquids according to differences in their {{c1::boiling points}}
extra: The liquid with the lowest BP vaporizes first and is collected as the distillate
example: Distilling wine vaporizes ethanol (bp 78 °C) before water (bp 100 °C), making brandy.

text: An {{c1::equatorial bond::... bond}} is a bond which is perpendicular to the axis of the ring
extra: The bond lies along the equator of the chair
example: Methylcyclohexane spends about 95% of its time with the CH<sub>3</sub> equatorial

text: The aldehyde functional group is given the number {{c1::1}} numbering location
example: In 3-methylbutanal, the CHO carbon is C-1 and the methyl sits on C-3.

text: The number 1 in an SN1 reaction refers to the fact that the reaction is {{c1::unimolecular}}
example: Doubling [tert-butyl bromide] doubles the S<sub>N</sub>1 rate; doubling [nucleophile] changes nothing.

text: Nucleophilic addition reactions involve the attack of a nucleophile on the slightly positive {{c1::carbon center}} of a carbonyl group
example: CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr attacks formaldehyde's carbonyl carbon, giving ethanol after acid workup.

text: When one equivalent of alcohol reacts with an aldehyde, a/an {{c1::hemiacetal}} is formed
example: Glucose's C-5 –OH attacks its own C-1 aldehyde, forming the cyclic hemiacetal.

text: This is a {{c1::secondary::primary, secondary, or tertiary}} alcohol
example: Isopropanol (2-propanol), the rubbing alcohol, is a secondary alcohol.

text: This compound is named {{c1::hexane}}
example: Hexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) is the nonpolar solvent used to extract oil from soybeans

text: Keto form is much {{c1::more::more or less}} common than enol form
extra: Can be attributed to the fact that a C=O double bond is significantly more stable (higher bond energy) than a C=C double bond
example: Acetone is over 99.99% keto form at equilibrium.

text: {{c1::Induction}} refers to uneven distribution of charge across a σ bond because of differences in electronegativity
extra: The more electronegative groups a carbonyl-containing compound has, the greater its reactivity
example: In chloromethane, the C–Cl bond pulls electron density, leaving carbon δ+ and chlorine δ−.

text: In a Michael addition, a/an {{c1::enolate}} attacks a/an {{c1::α,β-unsaturated carbonyl}}, creating a bond
example: The enolate of diethyl malonate adds to the β-carbon of methyl vinyl ketone.

text: This compound is named {{c1::methane}}
example: Methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) is the main component of natural gas

text: This is a/an {{c1::ketal}}
extra: A secondary carbon with two –OR groups
example: Acetone + 2 CH<sub>3</sub>OH gives the ketal 2,2-dimethoxypropane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

text: {{c1::Conformational isomers::... isomers}} differ by rotation around a single σ bond
example: Ethane's staggered and eclipsed forms interconvert just by spinning about the C–C bond

text: This is a {{c1::primary::primary, secondary, or tertiary}} alcohol
example: Ethanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is a primary alcohol.

text: A/an {{c1::racemic}} mixture is a 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers
extra: Not optically active because the light rotations cancel out
example: Thalidomide was sold as a racemic 50:50 mix of its (R) and (S) enantiomers.

text: This is a/an {{c1::carboxyl group::... group}}
example: Every amino acid, glycine included, carries a carboxyl group (–COOH)

text: Increased ring strain in a molecule can make it {{c1::more::more or less}} reactive
example: Ethylene oxide's strained three-membered ring opens readily with water, unlike ordinary ethers.

text: In size-exclusion chromatography, large molecules will elute {{c1::first::first or last}}
extra:
Larger molecules do not fit in the pores so they elute faster
Smaller molecules enter the porous gel beads causing them to elute later
example: Thyroglobulin (660 kDa) elutes from a gel-filtration column before cytochrome c (12 kDa).

text: Hydrogen cyanide reacts with carbonyls to form {{c1::cyanohydrins}}
example: Acetone + HCN gives acetone cyanohydrin, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(OH)CN.

text: {{c1::Conjugation}} occurs when single and multiple bonds alternate
extra: This creates a system of unhybridized p orbitals along the backbone of the molecule through which π electrons can delocalize
example: 1,3-Butadiene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>) is conjugated; 1,4-pentadiene is not.

text: {{c1::Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy::... spectroscopy}} measures alignment of nuclear spin with an applied magnetic field
extra:
NMR spectroscopy is useful for determining the structure (connectivity) of a compound, including functional groups
Plotted as frequency vs. absorption energy
example: MRI scanners image the body by detecting the nuclear spin of hydrogen in water.

text: When two equivalents of alcohol react with a ketone, a/an {{c1::ketal}} is formed
example: Cyclohexanone + 2 CH<sub>3</sub>OH (H<sup>+</sup>) gives the ketal 1,1-dimethoxycyclohexane.

text: An aldol nucleophile is the {{c1::enolate}} formed from the deprotonation of the α-carbon
example: In acetaldehyde's aldol, base removes an α-H to form the nucleophile <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO.

text: 1°, 2°, and 3° alcohols are named according to the number of carbons attached to {{c1::the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group::which carbon}}
extra: In other words, whether the hydroxyl is bound to a primary, secondary, or tertiary carbon
example: In 2-butanol, the –OH carbon bonds to two other carbons, making it a 2° alcohol.

text: {{c1::Phosphoric acid}} is sometimes referred to as a phosphate group or inorganic phosphate
example: ATP hydrolysis releases ADP and P<sub>i</sub> (HPO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>).

text: The aldol electrophile is a/an {{c1::aldehyde}} or {{c1::ketone}}
example: In the acetone–benzaldehyde aldol, benzaldehyde's carbonyl is the electrophile attacked by acetone's enolate.

text: {{c1::Steric hindrance}} describes when a reaction cannot proceed (or significantly slows) because substituents crowd the reactive site
example: Neopentyl bromide reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 extremely slowly, even though it is a primary halide.

text: A mass spectrometer ionizes atoms and molecules with a high-energy electron beam and then deflects the ions through a magnetic field based on the {{c1::mass-to-charge ratio (\(\frac{m}{z}\))}} of the ion
extra: The mass spectrum of a sample shows relative abundance of each ion on the y-axis and \(\frac{m}{z}\) along the x-axis
example: CO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ions (m/z 44) curve less in the magnetic field than H<sub>2</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ions (m/z 18).

text: An {{c1::axial bond::... bond}} is a bond which is parallel to the axis of the ring
extra: "Straight up and down"
example: Axial groups on a cyclohexane chair clash with the other axial groups on the same face (1,3-diaxial strain)

text: This compound is known as a/an {{c1::phenol}}
extra:
Benzene ring with –OH group attached
Named for the relative position of the –OH groups
example: Phenol, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, was Lister's carbolic acid antiseptic.

text: Both linear and cyclic anhydrides are given the suffix {{c1::anhydride}}
example: (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O is acetic anhydride; the cyclic one from succinic acid is succinic anhydride.

text: Carboxylic acids use the suffix {{c1::–oic acid}}
extra: Salts are named with the suffix –oate
example: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH is propanoic acid; its sodium salt is sodium propanoate.

text: Low pKa = {{c1::strong::weak or strong}} acid
example: HCl (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −7) is a far stronger acid than acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.76).

text: This is the {{c1::enol::keto or enol}} form of acetone
extra:
Enol form contains an alcohol
Keto form has a regular ketone or an aldehyde
example: Acetone's enol, CH<sub>2</sub>=C(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> (prop-1-en-2-ol), is a trace tautomer.

text: This is an example of {{c1::Fischer esterification}}
extra: Treatment of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst forms an ester and eliminates H2O
example: Acetic acid + ethanol with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives ethyl acetate and water.

text: DMSO is polar {{c1::aprotic::protic or aprotic}}
extra: Dimethyl sulfoxide is polar aprotic because it does not participate in hydrogen bonding
example: DMSO is a common solvent for S<sub>N</sub>2 reactions such as bromoethane + NaCN → propanenitrile.

text: Optical activity is the ability of a molecule to {{c1::rotate}} plane-polarized light
example: Sucrose has a specific rotation of +66.5°, so it turns plane-polarized light clockwise.

text: {{c1::Organic phosphates}} are carbon containing compounds that also have phosphate groups
extra:
The most notable examples are nucleotide triphosphates (ATP or GTP) and DNA
ATP Structure:
example: Glucose-6-phosphate, made by hexokinase in the first step of glycolysis, is an organic phosphate.

text: Amides are derivatives of carboxylic acids in which the {{c1::hydroxyl}} group has been replaced by a/an {{c1::amine or ammonia}}
example: Replacing benzoic acid's –OH with –NH<sub>2</sub> gives benzamide.

text: {{c1::Carboxylic acid}} functional groups contain a carbonyl and a hydroxyl group connected to the same carbon
extra: They are always terminal groups
example: Acetic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, is the carboxylic acid that makes vinegar sour.

text: Alkynes have a {{c1::triple}} bond and use the suffix {{c1::–yne}}
example: Ethyne (HC≡CH) is the acetylene burned in welding torches

text: An oxidizing agent {{c1::accepts::accepts or donates}} electrons and is {{c1::reduced::oxidized or reduced}} in the process
example: In 2Na + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2NaCl, Cl<sub>2</sub> is the oxidizing agent and goes from 0 to −1.

text: This is a/an {{c1::carboxylate ion::... ion}}
example: Acetate (CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>) is the carboxylate ion left when acetic acid loses H<sup>+</sup>

text: {{c1::Aldehydes}} have the suffix -al
extra:
Aldehydes take their name from their parent alkane chains
The -e is removed from the end and is replaced with -al
example: Ethane becomes ethanal (acetaldehyde); propane becomes propanal.

text: {{c1::Aliphatic}} compounds are hydrocarbon compounds containing carbon and hydrogen joined together in straight chains, branched chains, or non-aromatic rings
extra:
Aliphatic amino acids are Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Pro
Met can also be considered aliphatic
example: Hexane, isobutane and cyclohexane are aliphatic; benzene is not.

text: Vacuum distillation is used if the boiling points are over 150 °C, to prevent degradation of the product. The vacuum {{c1::lowers the air pressure}}, which decreases the boiling point of the liquid
example: Glycerol (bp 290 °C) is vacuum-distilled so it does not decompose near its normal boiling point.

text: Bonding orbitals are created by overlap of atomic orbitals of the {{c1::same::same or opposite}} sign
example: Same-sign, side-by-side overlap of two carbon p orbitals forms ethylene's π bond.

text: This is {{c1::acrylic acid::name}}
example: Acrylic acid polymerizes into the polyacrylate gel that absorbs liquid in disposable diapers

text: KMnO4, Na2Cr2O7, K2Cr2O7 and CrO3 are {{c1::oxidizing::oxidizing or reducing}} agents that can form carboxylic acids
extra: Note: PCC is weak and stops oxidizing at the aldehyde
example: Jones reagent (CrO<sub>3</sub> in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) oxidizes 1-butanol to butanoic acid.

text: {{c1::Ubiquinone}} is a biologically active quinone that acts as an electron acceptor in complexes I, II, and III of the electron transport chain
extra:
Also called coenzyme Q
It is reduced to ubiquinol
example: Complex II hands electrons from succinate (via FADH<sub>2</sub>) to ubiquinone.

text: An aldol is a/an {{c1::aldehyde}} plus a/an {{c1::alcohol}}
example: Two acetaldehydes combine to form 3-hydroxybutanal, the original aldol.

text: -OH is a {{c1::bad::good or bad}} leaving group
example: Ethanol reacts with HBr only after H<sup>+</sup> turns –OH into –OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, which leaves as water.

text: The hydrogens of a/an {{c1::aryl}} group have an NMR range of 6.5 - 8.0 ppm
example: Benzene's six equivalent hydrogens give one peak at 7.3 ppm.

text: An SN1 reaction has {{c1::two::#}} step(s)
extra:
Step 1: The LG leaves, forming a carbocation
Step 2: The nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation from either side, leading to a racemic mixture of products
example: In 2-chloro-2-methylpropane hydrolysis, Cl<sup>−</sup> leaves first, then water attacks the carbocation.

text: {{c1::SN2::SN1 or SN2}} reactions lead to inversion of stereochemistry
extra: The nucleophile must perform a backside attack, which leads to inversion of stereochemistry
example: (R)-2-Bromobutane with OH<sup>−</sup> gives (S)-2-butanol by S<sub>N</sub>2.

text: In anion exchange chromatography, the beads are {{c1::positively::positively or negatively}} charged and this causes {{c1::positively::positively or negatively}} charged proteins to elute first
example: At pH 7, positively charged lysozyme passes straight through a DEAE (anion exchange) column.

text: An aldol condensation starts with a/an {{c1::aldol addition}} to create a/an {{c1::aldol}}
extra:
Then it undergoes a dehydration to give a conjugated enone (α,β-unsaturated carbonyl)
Very common in the production of pharmaceuticals and perfumes
example: Acetaldehyde's aldol, 3-hydroxybutanal, loses water on heating to give crotonaldehyde (but-2-enal).

text: In a mass spectrum, the {{c1::M+1}} peak is a small peak 1 m/z unit to the right of the molecular ion peak
extra:
Reflects the natural abundance of 13C (1.1%)
Example: an M+1 peak 4.4% as intense as the M peak means 4.4/1.1 = 4 carbons

text: This is a/an {{c1::formyl group::... group}}
example: N-formylmethionine, the first amino acid of bacterial proteins, has a formyl group on its amine

text: In chromatography, the mobile phase is typically {{c1::nonpolar}} and this causes {{c1::nonpolar}} molecules to elute faster
example: With hexane as the mobile phase, nonpolar naphthalene runs ahead of polar benzyl alcohol.

text: In redox reactions, the {{c1::reduced::oxidized or reduced}} molecule gains electrons and the oxidation number decreases
example: In Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Cu, copper is reduced from +2 to 0.

text: Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules are rules for {{c1::naming stereoisomers}}
extra: Priority goes to the attached atom (on the chiral carbon or double-bonded carbon) with the highest atomic number
example: CIP ranking names the two CHBrClF enantiomers (R) and (S), with Br > Cl > F > H.

text: The types of bonds indicated in this IR spectroscopy chart are {{c1::O-H}} and {{c1::C-O}}
example: Ethanol's IR spectrum shows a broad O–H near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C–O stretch near 1050 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text: An aldehyde is a terminal functional group containing a/an {{c1::carbonyl}} bonded to at least one {{c1::hydrogen}}
example: Formaldehyde (H<sub>2</sub>C=O) has two hydrogens on its carbonyl carbon.

text: {{c1::Diastereomers}} are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable and are not mirror images of each other
example: D-Glucose and D-galactose are diastereomers that differ only at C-4.

text: A/an {{c1::ester}} is a carboxylic acid derivative where –OH is replaced with -OR
example: Isoamyl acetate, the ester that gives bananas their smell, has –OR where acetic acid had –OH.

text: {{c1::Constitutional (structural) isomers::... isomers}} have identical chemical formulas but differ structurally
extra: They share only a molecular formula and have different physical and chemical properties
example: Butane and isobutane are both C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> but boil at −1 °C and −12 °C

text: The hydrogens of a/an {{c1::carboxylic acid}} group have an NMR range of approximately 11.0 - 12.0 ppm
example: Acetic acid's –COOH proton appears near 11.4 ppm.

text: The two categories of {{c1::configurational isomers::... isomers}} are enantiomers and diastereomers
extra: Can only change from one form to another by breaking and reforming bonds
example: (R)- and (S)-alanine are enantiomers; D-glucose and D-galactose are diastereomers

text: Acetic acid is polar {{c1::protic::protic or aprotic}}
extra: Polar protic because it participates in hydrogen bonding
example: Acetic acid's –COOH groups hydrogen-bond so strongly that the acid forms dimers even as a vapor.

text: SN2 reactions prefer {{c1::methyl and primary}} substrates
extra:
It is easy for the nucleophile to attack the carbon because the carbon is accessible (less steric hindrance)
The reaction can proceed in 1 step
example: Iodomethane and 1-bromobutane react readily with CN<sup>−</sup> by S<sub>N</sub>2; tert-butyl bromide does not.

text: An S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction has {{c1::one::#}} step(s)
extra:
The nucleophile attacks at the same time as the LG leaves
The nucleophile must perform a backside attack, which leads to inversion of stereochemistry
example: I<sup>−</sup> attacks bromomethane's carbon as Br<sup>−</sup> departs, in a single concerted step.

text: The IR spectroscopy frequency for N-H bonds is {{c1::3300}} cm-1
example: A primary amine like ethylamine shows two N–H spikes near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text: A tertiary substrate with a protic (or aprotic) solvent will go {{c1::SN1::SN1 or SN2}}
extra:
2 steps
There is too much steric hindrance for the nucleophile to attack the carbon while the leaving group is still there, so the LG must leave first
The products will be a mixture of SN1 and E1
example: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane in ethanol forms an ether via a tertiary carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1).

text: Alcohols can be converted to {{c1::mesylates}} or {{c1::tosylates}} to make them better leaving groups for nucleophilic substitution reactions
example: Treating ethanol with TsCl in pyridine gives ethyl tosylate, which NaCN then displaces easily.

text: The IR spectroscopy frequency range for C=C bonds is {{c1::1600}} - {{c1::1680}} cm-1
example: 1-Hexene shows a C=C stretch near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

text: KMnO<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> are {{c1::strong::weak or strong}} oxidizing agents
extra: They oxidize a 1° alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid (a 2° alcohol to a ketone)
example: Old breathalyzers used acidified orange dichromate, which turned green (Cr<sup>3+</sup>) as it oxidized ethanol.

text: This is {{c1::acetophenone::name}}
example: Acetophenone (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>) is the simplest aromatic ketone

text: Quantum number ml is the {{c1::magnetic}} quantum number and gives the orbital {{c1::sub-type}}
extra:
Integers from −l to +l
Gives the orientation of the orbital with respect to the x, y and z axes
example: For l = 1, m<sub>l</sub> = −1, 0, +1 gives the three orbitals p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub> and p<sub>z</sub>.

text: This reaction will go {{c1::SN1::SN1 or SN2}}
extra: The substrate is secondary and CH3OH is a protic solvent
example: 2-Bromopropane in methanol gives 2-methoxypropane via a secondary carbocation.

text: The "SN" in SN1 and SN2 reactions refers to {{c1::nucleophilic substitution}}
example: CH<sub>3</sub>Br + OH<sup>−</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>OH + Br<sup>−</sup>: a nucleophile swaps in for the leaving group.

text: In chromatography, the stationary phase is typically {{c1::polar}} and this causes {{c1::polar}} molecules to elute slower
example: On silica, polar benzoic acid travels more slowly than nonpolar naphthalene.

text: In nucleophilic acyl substitution a {{c1::nucleophile}} displaces the {{c1::leaving group}}
extra:
The nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, opening the carbonyl and forming a tetrahedral intermediate
The carbonyl reforms, kicking off the leaving group
example: In ethyl acetate + OH<sup>−</sup>, hydroxide displaces ethoxide to give acetate and ethanol.

text: {{c1::Phosphodiester bonds::... bonds}} make up the backbone of DNA
example: In the dinucleotide ApG, a phosphodiester joins A's 3′ carbon to G's 5′ carbon.

text: Strecker synthesis generates an amino acid from a/an {{c1::aldehyde}}
example: Strecker synthesis turns formaldehyde into glycine and acetaldehyde into alanine.

text: Imines can tautomerize to form {{c1::enamines}}
extra: Tautomerization is a reaction which involves simple proton transfer
example: CH<sub>3</sub>CH=NCH<sub>3</sub> shifts a proton to become the enamine CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–NHCH<sub>3</sub>.

text: {{c1::Infrared spectroscopy::... spectroscopy}} measures absorption of infrared light, which causes molecular vibration such as stretching, bending, twisting, and folding
extra:
Based on this it is possible to determine the functional groups that make up the molecule
Plotted as % transmittance vs. wavenumber (\(\frac{1}{λ}\))
example: IR tells cyclohexanol from cyclohexanone: one shows a broad O–H band, the other a sharp C=O peak.

text: This is {{c1::acetaldehyde::name}}
example: Liver alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO)

text: Aldol addition is a powerful way to create a {{c1::carbon-carbon}} bond
example: In gluconeogenesis, aldolase joins DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

text: Aldehydes are usually {{c1::more::more or less}} reactive toward nucleophilic additions than ketones because of both steric and electronic effects
example: Formaldehyde in water is almost fully hydrated, while acetone barely forms its hydrate.

text: Phosphoric acid is an excellent buffer because it contains three hydrogens, each with {{c1::a unique pKa}}
extra: The wide variety in pKa values allows phosphoric acid to act as a buffer over a large range of pH values
example: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> has pK<sub>a</sub> values of about 2.1, 7.2 and 12.3.

text: Amines are classified as 1º, 2º, and 3º amines according to the number of carbons attached to the {{c1::nitrogen atom}}
example: Methylamine is 1º, dimethylamine is 2º, and trimethylamine (the fishy smell) is 3º

text: {{c1::Ultraviolet spectroscopy::... spectroscopy}} measures the absorption of UV light, which causes movement of electrons between molecular orbitals
extra: UV spectra are plotted as percent transmittance or absorbance vs. wavelength
example: DNA absorbs UV most strongly at 260 nm, which labs use to measure DNA concentration.

text: {{c1::Alkanes}} are hydrocarbons in which all carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds
example: Octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) in gasoline has only C–C single bonds

text: In cation exchange chromatography, the beads are {{c1::negatively::positively or negatively}} charged and this causes {{c1::negatively::positively or negatively}} charged proteins to elute first
example: At pH 7, negatively charged albumin flows straight through a CM-cellulose (cation exchange) column.

text: Antibonding orbitals are created by overlap of atomic orbitals of the {{c1::opposite::same or opposite}} signs
example: Out-of-phase overlap of two H 1s orbitals gives H<sub>2</sub>'s σ* orbital, with a node between the nuclei.

text:
In a Fischer projection:
  • Vertical lines go to the {{c1::back}} of the page
  • Horizontal lines {{c1::come out of the}} page
extra:
Vertical lines are like dashes
Horizontal lines are like wedges
example: In D-glyceraldehyde, the horizontal H and OH point toward you, while CHO and CH<sub>2</sub>OH point away.

text: {{c1::High-performance liquid chromatography::... chromatography}} relies on pumps to pass a pressurized liquid solvent containing the sample mixture through a column filled with a solid adsorbent material
extra: This gives HPLC higher resolving power
example: Hospitals use HPLC to measure HbA1c by separating glycated from non-glycated hemoglobin.

text: This is a {{c1::tertiary::primary, secondary, or tertiary}} alcohol
example: tert-Butanol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH, is a tertiary alcohol.

text: The hydrogens of a/an {{c1::methyl ketone}} have an NMR range of 2.0 - 2.4 ppm
example: Acetone's six CH<sub>3</sub> protons give a single peak at about 2.1 ppm.

text: This Newman projection shows {{c1::gauche}} conformation
extra: The carbon attachments are 60 degrees apart
example: Gauche butane is about 3.8 kJ/mol less stable than anti because its methyl groups crowd each other

text: This functional group is called a/an {{c1::carbonyl group}}
example: Acetone, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O, has a carbonyl group on its central carbon

text: This Newman projection shows {{c1::eclipsed}} conformation
extra: Less favorable because it forces more interactions between the front and back attachments, creating more strain
example: Fully eclipsed butane, methyl directly over methyl, is its highest-energy conformation

text: Treatment of a 1° alcohol with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) leads to the formation of a/an {{c1::aldehyde}}
extra: Any stronger oxidizing agent will oxidize the alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid
example: PCC oxidizes 1-propanol to propanal without going on to propanoic acid.

text: Diols contain two {{c1::hydroxyl}} groups
example: Ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol), the antifreeze, has two –OH groups

text: {{c1::Ketones}} use the suffix -one and the prefixes oxo- or keto-
extra:
Ketones take their name from their parent alkane chains
The ending -e is removed and replaced with -one
example: Propane becomes propanone (acetone); 3-oxobutanoic acid names its ketone with the oxo- prefix.

text: {{c1::Alcohols}} use suffix –ol or prefix hydroxy-
extra:
Contains an –OH group
Alcohols have higher priority than double or triple bonds
example: In HOCH<sub>2</sub>COOH, the –OH is named as a prefix: hydroxyacetic acid (glycolic acid).

text: A/an {{c1::nucleophile}} contains lone pairs of electrons or pi bonds and is “Nucleus-loving”
example: Cyanide (CN<sup>−</sup>) uses its carbon lone pair to attack bromoethane.

text: {{c1::Hydroxyquinones}} are produced by oxidation of quinones
extra: Adds a variable number of hydroxyl groups
example: Lawsone (2-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone), the dye in henna, is a hydroxyquinone.

text: This is {{c1::acetic acid::name}}
example: Vinegar is about 5% acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH)

text: {{c1::Laminar flow::... flow}} is smooth and orderly
example: Honey poured slowly from a spoon falls in one smooth, unbroken stream.

text: {{c1::Conductors}} are a type of material that allows the flow of charge
example: Copper house wiring carries current because its free electrons move easily.

text: Electric potential energy {{c1::increases::increases or decreases}} when like charges move closer together or when opposite charges move apart
example: Ionizing an atom costs energy because pulling an electron away from the nucleus raises potential energy.

text: A {{c1::confidence interval}} gives an estimated range of values which is likely to include an unknown population parameter
example: A poll reports 52% ± 3% support, a 95% confidence interval of 49% to 55%.

text: Light is a {{c1::transverse wave::... wave}}
extra: Light is a transverse wave because its components vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation
example: Polarized sunglasses can block light vibrating in one plane, which only a transverse wave allows.

text: Slope = \(\frac{{{c1::rise}}}{{{c1::run}}}\)
example: A line rising 6 units over a run of 2 units has slope 6/2 = 3.
A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s has KE = ½(2)(6<sup>2</sup>) = 36 J.

text: This is an example of {{c1::alpha}} decay
Electric field strength in a capacitor: {{c1::}}
example: A capacitor with 100 V across plates 0.01 m apart has a field of E = V/d = 10,000 V/m.

text: {{c1::Electrical potential}} is the potential energy of a unit charge in any electric field
extra:
Different points in the space of an electric field surrounding a source charge will have different electrical potential values
