Note: Electric potential is not the same as electric potential difference. Electric potential difference, also called voltage, is the difference of electric potentials of two different points
example: 1 m from a +1 μC point charge, the potential is V = kQ/r = 9 × 10<sup>3</sup> V.

text: Poiseuille’s law determines the {{c1::rate}} of laminar flow
extra:
At constant flow, ΔP ∝ 1/r4 (an inverse fourth-power relationship)
Q = flow rate
P = pressure
r = radius
η = fluid viscosity
L = length of tubing
example: Halving a blood vessel's radius cuts laminar flow to 1/16 at the same pressure difference.

text: {{c1::Torque}} is a twisting force that causes rotation
example: Pushing a door perpendicularly with 20 N, 0.8 m from the hinge, gives 16 N·m of torque.

text: Angular Frequency (ω) also known as radial or circular frequency, measures {{c1::angular displacement}} per {{c1::unit time}}
example: A wheel spinning once per second has ω = 2π rad/s ≈ 6.28 rad/s.

text:
Use scientific notation shortcuts to adjust the above number so the coefficient is 3.14:
{{c1::}}
extra: LARS: Left Add, Right Subtract

text:
Effect of pipe width on fluid velocity:
  • Narrow passages: {{c1::fast::fast or slow}}
  • Wider passages: {{c1::slow::fast or slow}}
extra: Continuity equation
example: Putting your thumb over the end of a garden hose makes the water shoot out faster.

text: A normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 is called a/an {{c1::standard normal distribution}}
example: A z-score of 1.96 on the standard normal curve marks off the top 2.5% of values.

text: {{c1::Lorentz force::... force}} is the sum of the electrostatic and magnetic forces acting on a body
example: In a velocity selector, a proton passes straight only when the electric force qE balances the magnetic force qvB.

text: {{c1::Translational equilibrium::... equilibrium}} occurs in the absence of any net forces acting on an object
example: A car cruising at a steady 60 km/h on a straight road is in translational equilibrium.

text:
Cohesion refers to the clinging of {{c1::like::like or unlike}} molecules
Adhesion refers to the clinging of {{c1::unlike::like or unlike}} molecules
extra: Capillary action occurs when the adhesive forces to the wall are stronger than the cohesive forces between the liquid molecules
example: Water beads up on a waxed car (cohesion) but wets and creeps up a clean glass wall (adhesion).

text: A {{c1::confounding variable::... variable}} is one that influences both the dependent variable and independent variable, causing a spurious association
example: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because hot weather drives both.

text: The relationship in this graph is {{c1::logarithmic}}
example: Loudness in decibels grows logarithmically with sound intensity: 10× the intensity adds only 10 dB.

text: Capillary action occurs when the {{c1::adhesive forces::... forces}} to the wall are stronger than the {{c1::cohesive forces::... forces}} between the liquid molecules
extra:
The wall of the container just above the water surface attracts water molecules upwards through the force of adhesion
In capillary action, adhesion > cohesion
example: Water rises up a narrow glass capillary tube and wicks up a paper towel dipped in a spill.

text: log<sub>b</sub>(b) = {{c1::1}}
example: log<sub>10</sub>(10) = 1 and ln(e) = 1.
A 10 cm × 10 cm square of gauze covers 100 cm<sup>2</sup>.

text: Electric potential energy {{c1::decreases::increases or decreases}} when like charges move apart or when opposite charges move closer together
example: Two protons released near each other fly apart, turning potential energy into kinetic energy.

text: The law of reflection states that the angle of reflection is {{c1::equal::less than, greater than, or equal to}} to the angle of incidence
example: A laser hitting a mirror 30° from the normal reflects at 30° on the other side of the normal.

text: For an object inside the focal point of a (convex) converging lens, the image is {{c1::virtual}} and {{c1::upright}}
example: A magnifying glass held close to a stamp shows an enlarged, upright stamp.

text: {{c1::Index of refraction}} is a dimensionless number that describes how fast light propagates through a material
example: Water's n of 1.33 means light travels at 3 × 10<sup>8</sup>/1.33 ≈ 2.25 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s in it.

text: {{c1::Internal validity::... validity}} refers to how well an experiment is done, especially whether it avoids confounding variables that affect the measurements
example: A coffee and cancer study that ignores smoking, which goes along with coffee drinking, has poor internal validity.

text: In a data set, the {{c1::median}} is the middle number; found by ordering all data points and picking out the one in the middle
extra: Or, if there are two middle numbers, take the mean of those two numbers
example: The median of 3, 7, 1, 9, 5 is 5 (ordered: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

text: {{c1::Clinical significance}} refers to the usefulness or importance of experimental findings to patient care or patient outcomes
example: A drug that lowers systolic pressure by only 1 mmHg, even with p < 0.001, has little clinical significance.

text: {{c1::Half-life}} is the amount of time required for half of a sample of radioactive nuclei to decay
extra: Or, the time it takes to reduce the radioactivity of a substance by half
example: Of 100 g of iodine-131 (half-life about 8 days), 25 g remains after 16 days.

text: {{c1::Work}} is the process by which energy is transferred from one system to another
example: Pushing a crate with a 10 N force for 5 m transfers 50 J of energy to it.

text: {{c1::Temperature}} is the average kinetic energy of the particles that make up a substance
example: Gas molecules at 600 K have twice the average kinetic energy of the same gas at 300 K.

text: This is a {{c1::concave::concave or convex}} mirror
extra: Light rays converge at a single point called the focal point
example: The inside of a spoon and a shaving mirror are concave mirrors.

text:
Estimating log:
log(A x 10B) ≈ {{c1::B + 0.A}}
example: log(2 × 10<sup>5</sup>) ≈ 5 + 0.2 = 5.2, close to the exact 5.30.

text: Displacement is path {{c1::independent::dependent or independent}}
example: Running one full lap of a 400 m track gives a displacement of 0 m.

text: The {{c1::independent variable::... variable}} is the variable that is changed or controlled in a scientific experiment
example: In a study of caffeine dose and reaction time, the caffeine dose is the independent variable.

text: The electromagnetic spectrum is the range of {{c1::frequencies}} and {{c1::wavelengths}} found in electromagnetic waves
example: It runs from radio waves longer than a football field to gamma rays smaller than an atom.

text: This distribution is {{c1::right::left or right}} skewed, also known as {{c1::positively::negatively or positively}} skewed
example: Household income: most families earn modest amounts while a few very high earners stretch the tail right.

text: Newton's third law: {{c1::For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction}}
example: A swimmer pushes backward on the pool wall and the wall pushes the swimmer forward just as hard.

text: {{c1::Paramagnetic materials::... materials}} possess some unpaired electrons and become weakly magnetic in an external magnetic field
example: Liquid O<sub>2</sub>, with two unpaired electrons, clings between the poles of a strong magnet.

text: This is an example of {{c1::gamma}} decay
This distribution is {{c1::left::left or right}} skewed, also known as {{c1::negatively::negatively or positively}} skewed
example: Scores on an easy exam: most students score above 90, while a few low scores stretch the tail left.

text:
cos(30º) = {{c1::\(\frac{\sqrt 3}{2}\) ≈ 0.9}}
sin(30º) = {{c1::\(\frac{1}{2}\)}}
example: A 10 N force at 30° above the horizontal has a vertical part of 10 sin 30° = 5 N.

text: {{c1::Frequency (f)}} is the number of cycles a wave makes per second
example: A tuning fork playing concert A vibrates 440 times each second, a frequency of 440 Hz.

text:
Speed of sound by medium:
  • Fastest: {{c1::solid}}
  • Middle: {{c1::liquid}}
  • Slowest: {{c1::gas}}
example: Sound travels about 5,960 m/s in steel, 1,480 m/s in water and 343 m/s in air.

text: {{c1::Mass}} is a measure of the inertia of an object; its amount of material
example: A 10 kg bowling ball has the same 10 kg mass on the Moon as on Earth.

text: {{c1::Amplitude}} is the maximum displacement of a wave from its rest position
extra: The maximum point is called a crest. The minimum point is called a trough
example: A rope wave that rises 5 cm above and dips 5 cm below its rest line has an amplitude of 5 cm.

text: A {{c1::between-group design::... design}} is an experiment with two or more groups of subjects, each tested with a different factor at the same time
example: One group gets caffeine and a separate group gets placebo before the same memory test.

text: {{c1::Chemical potential energy::... energy}} is the energy stored in the bonds of compounds
example: Glucose stores energy in its bonds that cellular respiration releases to make ATP.

text: {{c1::Traveling waves::... waves}} have continuously shifting points of maximum and minimum displacement so that the peak of the wave "travels" forward
extra: Example: Ocean waves travel over a long distance. As opposed to standing waves that would appear to stay in one spot

text: No {{c1::heat}} is exchanged in an adiabatic process
example: Air pumped quickly into a bike tire heats up because the compression is too fast for heat to escape.

text: Every charge generates a/an {{c1::electric field}}, which can exert forces on other charges
example: A proton's electric field pushes a nearby proton away and pulls a nearby electron toward it.

text: {{c1::Gravity}} is the attractive force between two objects as a result of their masses
example: Gravity between the Earth and the Moon keeps the Moon in orbit.
A chessboard has 8 × 8 = 64 squares.

text: The {{c1::social desirability bias::... bias}} is a type of response bias that is the tendency of survey respondents to answer questions in a manner that will be viewed favorably by others
example: Survey respondents underreport how much alcohol they drink and overreport how often they vote.

text: A {{c1::moderating variable::... variable}} is one that influences the strength of a relationship between two other variables
example: Caffeine boosts alertness more in people who rarely drink coffee; habitual use moderates the effect.

text: {{c1::Potential energy::... energy}} is a type of energy an object has because of its position
extra: The energy stored within a system
example: A boulder perched on a cliff edge holds energy by its position that is released if it falls.
log(1) = 0, so a solution with [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1 M has a pH of 0.

text: This is a {{c1::convex::concave or convex}} mirror
extra: The focal point is on the inside of the mirror, even though the light rays never go to that side
example: A car's passenger-side mirror and the back of a spoon are convex mirrors.

text: Based on the Doppler effect, the perceived frequency will be {{c1::lower::higher or lower}} than the emitted frequency when the source and detector are moving away from each other
example: A race car's engine note drops in pitch as it speeds away from the stands.

text: The {{c1::coulomb}} is the unit of charge
extra: The amount of charge in one ampere-second
example: A 2 A current flowing for 3 s moves 6 C of charge.

text: Speed is a {{c1::scalar::vector or scalar}} and includes only the {{c1::magnitude of velocity (rate of change of distance)}}
example: A car going 25 m/s around a circular track has constant speed but changing velocity.

text: The {{c1::Hawthorne effect}} is when the behavior of subjects is altered simply by knowing that they are being studied
example: Hawthorne Works employees raised their output whenever they were observed, whatever the lighting change.

text: {{c1::Period (T)}} is the number of seconds it takes to complete a cycle
extra:
It is the inverse of frequency
Period is a measure of time
Wavelength is a measure of length
example: A 50 Hz wave has a period of 1/50 = 0.02 s.

text: Laminar flow occurs at {{c1::low::high or low}} Reynolds numbers
extra:
ρ = density of fluid
V = velocity
L = diameter of pipe
μ = dynamic viscosity of the fluid
Reynolds number is dimensionless
example: Honey oozing slowly through a straw has a very low Reynolds number and flows smoothly.

text: {{c1::Fluorescence}} is the emission of light by a substance that has absorbed light or other electromagnetic radiation
extra: The emitted light has lower energy and higher wavelength
example: Under a black light, a highlighter absorbs UV and glows with longer-wavelength visible light.

text: In water, every additional 10 meters of depth adds approximately {{c1::1 atm}} to Ptotal
example: A scuba diver at 30 m feels about 1 + 3 = 4 atm of total pressure.

text: {{c1::Scalars}} are quantities that have only a magnitude
example: Mass (2 kg), temperature (37 °C), time (5 s) and energy (500 J) are scalars.

text: Damping is a decrease in {{c1::amplitude}}
example: A swing left alone makes smaller and smaller arcs as friction and air resistance drain its energy.

text: {{c1::Selection bias::... bias}} is the bias introduced by the selection of individuals, groups or data for analysis in such a way that proper randomization is not achieved
extra: The sample obtained is not representative of the population
example: The 1936 Literary Digest poll predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt by sampling car and phone owners.

text: {{c1::Nuclear fission}} occurs when a large nucleus splits into smaller nuclei
example: In a reactor, uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into barium and krypton nuclei.

text: {{c1::Basic science research::... research}} occurs in a lab and does not include human subjects
extra: Basic science research is often the best type for demonstrating causality because the experimenter has the highest degree of control over the experimental conditions
example: Testing how a new compound inhibits purified HIV protease in test tubes.

text: Field lines show the activity of a {{c1::positive::positive or negative}} test charge
extra:
Field lines represent the electric field vectors for a charge: they point away from a positive charge and toward a negative charge
The field is stronger where the field lines are closer together
example: Near a lone electron, field lines point inward, the way a positive test charge would be pulled.

text: In our circulatory system, or any closed fluid system, as total cross-sectional area increases, velocity {{c1::decreases::increases or decreases}}
example: Blood moves fastest in the aorta and slowest in the capillaries, whose total cross-section is far larger.

text: Fluids can exert {{c1::perpendicular}} forces but not shear forces
example: Water at rest presses straight out on a fish tank's walls but cannot resist being stirred sideways.

text:
cos(60º) = {{c1::\(\frac{1}{2}\)}}
sin(60º) = {{c1::\(\frac{\sqrt 3}{2}\) ≈ 0.9}}
example: A 10 N pull at 60° above the horizontal has a horizontal part of 10 cos 60° = 5 N.

text: {{c1::Detection bias::... bias}} arises from educated professionals using their knowledge in an inconsistent way by searching for an outcome disproportionately in certain populations
example: Women on estrogen got more uterine exams for bleeding, inflating how often endometrial cancer was found in them.

text: {{c1::Interference}} describes the ways in which waves interact in space to form a resultant wave
example: Two pebbles dropped into a pond send out ripples that overlap into a pattern of tall and flat spots.

text: Archimedes’ principle: an object placed in a fluid experiences a buoyant force equal to the {{c1::weight of the fluid displaced by the object}}
extra:
If FB > mobjectg (weight), the object floats
If FB < mobjectg (weight), the object sinks
example: A 1 L block fully under water displaces 1 kg of water and feels about 10 N of buoyant force.

text: {{c1::Nuclear fusion}} occurs when small nuclei combine into larger nuclei
example: The Sun fuses hydrogen nuclei into helium, releasing energy from the mass lost.

text: A {{c1::research sample}} is a group of people, objects, or items taken from a larger population for measurement
extra: The sample should be representative of the population so that findings can be generalized from the sample to the population as a whole
example: 500 adults with type 2 diabetes recruited from five clinics to stand in for all US adults with diabetes.

text:
The FINER mnemonic for formulating research questions checks whether the research is:
  • {{c1::feasible}}
  • {{c1::interesting}}
  • {{c1::novel}}
  • {{c1::ethical}}
  • {{c1::relevant}}
example: A trial that needs 10 million patients followed for 50 years fails the FINER check for feasibility.

text: {{c1::Resonance}} is when one object vibrating at the same natural frequency of a second object forces that second object to vibrate
example: An opera singer holding a wine glass's natural frequency can make it vibrate until it shatters.

text: For a convex mirror, the image will always be {{c1::virtual}} and {{c1::upright}}
example: A store's security mirror shows a shrunken, upright view of the whole aisle.

text: A {{c1::mediating variable::... variable}} is one that explains the relationship between the two other variables
example: Education raises income, which in turn improves health; income mediates education's effect on health.

text:
Units for joule
{{c1::}}
extra:
Joules are units of energy
A joule is the amount of work you do when you exert a force of 1 newton to move an object a distance of 1 meter (1 newton meter or Nm)
example: Lifting a 1 kg book 1 m takes 1 kg × 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> × 1 m ≈ 9.8 kg·m<sup>2</sup>/s<sup>2</sup> = 9.8 J.

text: {{c1::Gravitational potential energy::... energy}} is the potential an object has to do work as a result of being located at a particular position in a gravitational field
example: A 2 kg book on a 1.5 m shelf has U = mgh = 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J (g ≈ 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>).

text: {{c1::Validity}}, also known as {{c1::accuracy}}, is the degree to which the measurements of an experiment are true and accurate
extra: This is not the same as reliability, which is the extent to which a measurement gives results that are very consistent
example: A scale that reads 70 kg for a person who truly weighs 70 kg gives a valid, accurate measurement.

text: A {{c1::histogram}} is a chart representing a frequency distribution; the heights of the bars represent observed frequencies
example: Bars showing how many students scored 60–69, 70–79 and 80–89 on an exam.

text:
Solve the above expression using scientific notation shortcuts:
{{c1::}}
extra: Raise the coefficient to the power of the outside exponent then multiply the two exponents together

text: Surface tension is created by {{c1::cohesive forces::... forces}}
example: A water strider walks across a pond without breaking the water's surface.

text:
Work done during expansion or compression of a gas:
{{c1::}}
example: A gas expanding by 2 L against a constant 1 atm does 2 L·atm ≈ 203 J of work on its surroundings.

text: {{c1::Capacitors}} have the ability to store and discharge electrical potential energy
example: A defibrillator's capacitor builds up charge, then discharges it through the heart in milliseconds.

text: Sound propagates through all forms of matter but not through {{c1::a vacuum}}
extra: Fastest through solids, followed by liquids, and slowest through gases
example: A ringing bell inside a glass jar goes silent as the air is pumped out.

text: A/an {{c1::electric dipole}} is a separation of positive and negative charges
extra: The simplest example of this is a pair of electric charges of equal magnitude but opposite sign, separated by some (usually small) distance
example: A water molecule, with a partial negative O and partial positive H atoms, is an electric dipole.

text: The {{c1::dependent variable::... variable}} is the variable that is measured (the outcome) in a scientific experiment
example: In a study of caffeine dose and reaction time, reaction time is the dependent variable.

text: A/an {{c1::magnetic field}} is a region around a magnetic material or a moving electric charge within which the force of magnetism acts
extra: Unit is the tesla (T)
example: Earth's magnetic field, about 5 × 10<sup>-5</sup> T at the surface, swings a compass needle north.

text: {{c1::Thermal equilibrium::... equilibrium}} is when systems have the same average kinetic energy and thus the same temperature.
example: A thermometer in a cup of tea stops changing once it and the tea reach the same temperature.

text: {{c1::Dispersion}} is when various wavelengths of light separate from each other
extra: Dispersion occurs because the index of refraction is different for each color
example: A prism splits white light into a rainbow, bending violet more than red.

text: {{c1::Kinetic energy::... energy}} is the energy of motion, observable as the movement of an object
example: A 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s has KE = ½(2)(3<sup>2</sup>) = 9 J.

text: Volumetric flow rate is the volume of fluid that passes per {{c1::unit time}}
extra:
Flow rate = volume / time
Or, flow rate = (velocity) × (cross-sectional area)
A = cross-sectional area
v = velocity
example: A faucet that fills a 10 L bucket in 20 s has a flow rate of 0.5 L/s.

text: The {{c1::placebo effect}} is an improvement in a patient's condition after a fake treatment, simply because the patient expects it to help
extra: Example: an inactive substance such as sugar, distilled water, or saline solution
example: A patient's headache eases after a sugar pill she believes is a strong painkiller.
Tripling a car's speed raises its kinetic energy 3<sup>2</sup> = 9-fold.

text: Beta-positive (β+) decay is the decay of a {{c1::proton}} into a {{c1::neutron}}
extra: It emits a positron and a neutrino
example: Fluorine-18, the tracer in PET scans, undergoes β<sup>+</sup> decay into oxygen-18.

text: The probability of {{c1::dependent}} events changes depending on the outcomes of other events
example: Drawing two aces without replacement: 4/52 for the first, then 3/51 for the second.

text:
The four tenets of medical ethics are:
  • {{c1::Beneficence}}
  • {{c1::Nonmaleficence}}
  • {{c1::Respect for patient autonomy}}
  • {{c1::Justice}}
example: A competent Jehovah's Witness who refuses a blood transfusion has that choice honoured under autonomy.

text: {{c1::Voltage}} is the electric potential difference between two points in an electrical field
extra: The greater the voltage, the greater the flow of electrical current
example: A AA battery keeps a 1.5 V potential difference between its two terminals.

text: A {{c1::cohort study::... study}} is a longitudinal study that samples a cohort, performing a cross-section at intervals through time
example: The Framingham Heart Study has followed town residents since 1948 to track heart disease risk factors.

text: For a concave mirror, if the object is very close to the mirror (inside the focal point) then the image will be {{c1::virtual}} and {{c1::upright}}
example: A shaving mirror held close to your face shows it enlarged and upright.

text: {{c1::Resistance}} is the opposition that a substance offers to the flow of electrons
example: A 10 Ω resistor lets only 1 A through when 10 V is applied across it.

text:
cos(90º) = {{c1::0}}
sin(90º) = {{c1::1}}
example: A force perpendicular to the motion (θ = 90°) does no work, since W = Fd cos 90° = 0.

extra: LARS: Left Add, Right Subtract

text: The relationship in this graph is {{c1::quadratic}}
example: Distance fallen from rest follows d = ½gt<sup>2</sup>, so doubling the time quadruples the distance.

text: The critical angle is the angle of incidence that offers an angle of refraction of exactly {{c1::90::#}} degrees
example: For light going from glass (n = 1.5) into air, sin θ<sub>c</sub> = 1/1.5, so θ<sub>c</sub> ≈ 42°.

text: {{c1::Reflection}} is the rebounding of incident light waves at a medium’s boundary
example: Seeing your face on a calm lake is light rebounding off the water's surface.

text: {{c1::Ecological validity}} refers to the extent to which the findings of a research study are able to be generalized to real-life settings
example: A memory study using shopping lists in a real supermarket beats nonsense syllables in a lab for ecological validity.

text: Gauge pressure = {{c1::absolute pressure::... pressure}} − {{c1::atmospheric pressure::... pressure}}
extra: It's the reading a pressure gauge shows; it is zero-referenced to atmospheric pressure, so a reading of 0 atm means no pressure beyond atmospheric
example: A tire at 3 atm absolute pressure reads 3 − 1 = 2 atm on a tire gauge.

text: cos(θ) = {{c1::\(\frac{adjacent}{hypotenuse}\)}}
example: In a 3-4-5 right triangle, the angle opposite the 3 side has cos θ = 4/5 = 0.8.

text: Light absorption is the process by which light is absorbed and converted into {{c1::energy}}
extra:
An electron can jump from a lower-energy to a higher-energy orbit by absorbing a photon of light
The photon's energy (E = hf) must equal the energy difference between the orbits
example: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and uses that energy to drive photosynthesis.

text: {{c1::Absolute pressure}} is the sum of all pressures at a certain point within a fluid
extra: Absolute pressure = (pressure at the surface of the fluid) + (pressure due to the fluid's weight)
example: At 10 m underwater, absolute pressure is about 1 atm (air) + 1 atm (water) = 2 atm.

text: Current-carrying wires create magnetic fields that are {{c1::concentric circles}} surrounding the wire
example: Iron filings sprinkled around a vertical current-carrying wire line up in rings centred on the wire.

text: Isobaric processes have constant {{c1::pressure}}
example: Gas heated in a cylinder under a freely sliding piston expands while its pressure stays fixed.

text: Sound waves are {{c1::longitudinal waves::... waves}}
extra: Sound waves are longitudinal waves because particles of the medium through which the sound is transported vibrate parallel to the direction that the sound wave moves
example: A loudspeaker cone pushes air back and forth, sending compressions and rarefactions to your ear.

text: {{c1::Refraction}} is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another
extra: The speed of light changes depending on index of refraction of the medium. This speed change causes refraction
example: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface.

text: Snell's law: {{c1::}}
example: Light entering glass (n = 1.5) from air at 30° bends to sin θ = 0.5/1.5, so θ ≈ 19.5°.

text: The {{c1::interquartile range}} (midspread, or middle 50%) is the difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles, i.e. between the upper and lower quartiles
example: If Q3 = 80 and Q1 = 60 on an exam, the IQR is 80 − 60 = 20 points.

text: A/an {{c1::dipole moment}} is a measure of the separation of positive and negative electrical charges within a system
extra: It is the product of charge (q) and separation distance (d)
example: Polar HCl, with its electrons pulled toward Cl, has a dipole moment, while nonpolar H<sub>2</sub> has none.

text: Conservative forces are path {{c1::independent::dependent or independent}}
extra:
Work depends only on the object's displacement (start and end points)
Examples: gravity and electrostatic forces
In the diagram, only the work along the green line counts; the roundabout path does not matter
example: Raising a 1 kg box 2 m by the stairs or by the elevator changes its potential energy by the same ~20 J.

text: Pressure is {{c1::equal::equal or varying}} in every direction in a fluid at a given depth
extra: If it were not equal, the fluid would flow
example: A diver's eardrums feel the same pressure at 10 m whether the diver faces up, down or sideways.

text: When a set of outcomes is {{c1::exhaustive}}, there are no other possible outcomes
example: Rolling a die: the outcomes 1 through 6 are exhaustive, since one of them must occur.

text: In an experiment, a result has {{c1::statistical significance}} if it is unlikely to have occurred by chance
example: A drug that lowers blood pressure more than placebo with p = 0.01, below α = 0.05, is statistically significant.

text: If a person has a disease but the medical test doesn't pick it up, this is a type {{c1::2::#}} error
extra: Type 2 error = false negative
example: A rapid strep test reads negative in a child who actually has strep throat.

text: Ultrasound uses high frequency sound waves to compare the {{c1::relative densities}} of tissues in the body
extra: Doppler Ultrasound is used to determine the flow of blood within the body
example: On a fetal ultrasound, dense bone shows up bright white while amniotic fluid looks black.

text: Magnification of a lens: {{c1::}}
example: An object 10 cm from a lens that forms an image 30 cm away has m = −30/10 = −3 (inverted, 3× larger).

text: {{c1::Radioactive decay}} is when an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by emitting radiation, such as an alpha particle or beta particle
example: Radon-222 gas seeping into basements decays by emitting alpha particles.
Moving 4 times farther from a light source cuts its intensity to 1/4<sup>2</sup> = 1/16.

{{c1::}}
extra: Calculate the square root of the coefficient then divide the exponent by 2

text: This is an example of {{c1::β+}} decay
{{c1::Acceleration}} is the vector representation of the change in velocity over time
example: A car going from 0 to 27 m/s in 9 s accelerates at 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

text: {{c1::Transverse waves::... waves}} are oscillations where particles are displaced perpendicular to the wave direction
extra: Light is a transverse wave because its components vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation
example: Flicking one end of a rope up and down sends a hump travelling horizontally along it.

text: A normal distribution has a bell shape, the mean and median are {{c1::equal::equal or unequal}}, and {{c1::68%::%}} of the data falls within 1 standard deviation
example: IQ scores (mean 100, SD 15): about 68% of people score between 85 and 115.

text: Specific heat is the amount of energy necessary to {{c1::raise the temperature of one gram of substance by 1° C or 1 K}}
extra: Remember, temperature is average kinetic energy
example: Raising 10 g of water by 5 °C takes q = mcΔT = 10 × 4.18 × 5 ≈ 209 J.

text: Newton's first law: {{c1::An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by a nonzero net force}}
example: A hockey puck slides across frictionless ice at constant velocity until a stick or the boards stop it.

text: The junction rule states that the sum of the currents flowing into a junction is {{c1::equal to::greater than, less than, or equal to}} the sum of the currents flowing out of that junction
example: If 5 A flows into a junction and 3 A leaves along one branch, 2 A must leave along the other.

text: sin(θ) = {{c1::\(\frac{opposite}{hypotenuse}\)}}
example: In a 3-4-5 right triangle, the angle opposite the 3 side has sin θ = 3/5 = 0.6.

text: Bernoulli’s equation: {{c1::}}
extra: The sum of all forms of energy in a fluid flowing along an enclosed path is the same at any two points in the path
example: Faster air over the curved top of an airplane wing has lower pressure than the air below, giving lift.

text: For an object outside the focal point of a convex (converging) lens, the image is {{c1::real}} and {{c1::inverted}}
example: The eye's lens forms a real, inverted image of the world on the retina.

text:
Solve the above expression using scientific notation shortcuts:
{{c1::}}
extra: Make the exponents the same before adding or subtracting the coefficients

text: Young’s double-slit experiment shows the {{c1::constructive}} and {{c1::destructive}} interference of waves that occur as light passes through parallel slits
extra: Results in minima (dark fringes) and maxima (bright fringes) of intensity
example: Laser light through two slits 0.1 mm apart paints alternating bright and dark stripes on a wall.

text:
Strings fixed at both ends and pipes open at both ends support standing waves with length:
{{c1::}}
extra: Length of the string or open pipe = (some multiple of wavelengths) / 2
example: A 1 m guitar string fixed at both ends has a fundamental wavelength of 2L = 2 m.

text: The Doppler effect is a shift in the perceived {{c1::frequency}} of a sound when the source of the sound and its detector are moving relative to one another
example: An ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches and drops in pitch as it passes.

text: {{c1::Diamagnetic materials::... materials}} possess no unpaired electrons and are slightly repelled by a magnet
example: A live frog can be levitated in a very strong magnetic field because its water is diamagnetic.

text:
Wave speed:
{{c1::}}
extra:
v = wave speed
f = frequency
λ = wavelength
example: A 440 Hz sound with a 0.78 m wavelength travels at v = fλ = 440 × 0.78 ≈ 343 m/s.
A gross is a dozen dozen: 12 × 12 = 144 eggs.

text: {{c1::Efficiency}}
extra: The ratio of the machine’s work output to work input when non-conservative forces are taken into account
example: A pulley system that takes in 200 J of work and puts out 150 J is 75% efficient.

text: {{c1::Total internal reflection}} is when light cannot be refracted out of a medium and is instead reflected back inside the medium
extra: Occurs when light moves from a medium with a higher index of refraction to a medium with a lower index of refraction with a high incident angle
example: Fibre-optic endoscopes carry light along bent glass fibres by total internal reflection.

text: The loop rule states that the sum of all the electric potential differences (voltages) around a loop is {{c1::zero::#}}
extra: The sum of voltage sources is always equal to the sum of voltage drops
example: In a loop with a 12 V battery and two resistors, if one resistor drops 8 V the other must drop 4 V.

text: {{c1::Constructive interference::... interference}} occurs when waves are exactly in phase with each other
extra: The amplitude of the resultant wave is equal to the sum of the amplitudes of the two interfering waves
example: Two speakers playing the same tone in phase sound louder where their crests line up.

text: The Rydberg formula is used to predict the {{c1::wavelength}} of light emitted or absorbed after an electron moves between energy levels
example: For hydrogen, the n = 3 → n = 2 transition gives the 656 nm red H-alpha line.

text: When an electron falls from a higher-energy to a lower-energy orbit, it {{c1::emits a photon of light}}
extra: This is light emission
example: A neon sign glows red as excited electrons drop to lower levels and emit photons.

text: Light will be refracted when passing from one medium to another if the two mediums have different {{c1::indexes of refraction}}
example: A Pyrex rod dipped in vegetable oil of the same index seems to vanish because light does not bend.

text: In the Bohr model, when an electron absorbs a photon, its energy level (n) goes {{c1::up::up or down}}
extra: Farther orbits = more energy held by the electron
example: A hydrogen electron that absorbs a 10.2 eV photon jumps from n = 1 to n = 2.

text: The Coulomb's law proportionality constant (in air) is k = {{c1::9.0 x 109 N • m2 / C2}}
extra: The units on k are such that when placed into the Coulomb's Law equation the units on charge (Coulombs) and the units on distance (meters) will be canceled, leaving a Newton as the unit of force
example: Two 1 C charges 1 m apart would repel with F = (9.0 × 10<sup>9</sup>)(1)(1)/1<sup>2</sup> = 9.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> N.

text: {{c1::Electrolytic conduction}} is the movement of free ions under electric field
example: In salt water, Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions migrate to opposite electrodes to carry current.

text: {{c1::Translational research::... research}} connects basic science research to clinical research
example: Taking a compound that shrank tumours in mice into its first human safety trial.

text: {{c1::Intensity}} (power per unit area) is perceived as how loud a sound is
extra:
It is based on a wave’s amplitude
Intensity will decrease over distance. For example, a loud sound is not as loud if you hear it from far away.
example: A 120 dB rock concert carries 10<sup>6</sup> times the intensity of 60 dB normal speech.

text: tan(θ) = {{c1::\(\frac{opposite}{adjacent}\)}}
example: In a 3-4-5 right triangle, the angle opposite the 3 side has tan θ = 3/4 = 0.75.

text: Isothermal processes have constant {{c1::temperature}}
example: A gas slowly compressed in a cylinder sitting in a large water bath stays at the bath's temperature.

text: {{c1::Weight}} is the force experienced by a given mass due to the gravitational attraction to the Earth
example: A 70 kg person weighs 70 × 9.8 = 686 N on Earth but only about 113 N on the Moon.

text:
Tangent in terms of sine and cosine:
tan(θ) = {{c1::\(\frac{y}{x}\)}} = {{c1::\(\frac{sin(θ)}{cos(θ)}\)}}
Ammeters are inserted in series in a circuit and measure {{c1::current}}
example: To measure a bulb's current, you break the circuit and wire the ammeter in line with the bulb.

text: This is a {{c1::convex}} lens, also known as a {{c1::converging}} lens
example: A magnifying glass is a converging lens that can focus sunlight onto a hot point.
A 3-4-5 right triangle works because 3<sup>2</sup> + 4<sup>2</sup> = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5<sup>2</sup>.

text: A {{c1::bimodal distribution::... distribution}} has two different modes, which appear as distinct peaks (local maxima)
example: Restaurant customer counts peak at lunch and again at dinner, giving two humps.

text: A {{c1::research population}} is a well-defined collection of individuals or objects known to have similar characteristics
example: All adults in the United States who have type 2 diabetes.

text: {{c1::Mutually exclusive}} is a statistical term describing two or more events that cannot possibly coincide
example: A single die roll cannot be both a 2 and a 5.

text: {{c1::Metallic conduction}} is the flow of current due to movement of electrons
example: Electrons drifting through the copper wires of a lamp cord carry its current.

text: Newton's second law: {{c1::Any acceleration is the result of a nonzero net force}}
example: A 2 kg cart pushed with a 6 N net force accelerates at 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

text: {{c1::Insulators}} are a type of material that resists the movement of charge
example: The rubber coating on a power cord keeps charge from reaching your hand.

text: Sound is produced when something {{c1::vibrates}}
extra: The vibrating body causes the medium (water, air, etc.) around it to vibrate
example: A struck tuning fork's prongs vibrate and push on the air to make its tone.

text: {{c1::Heat of transformation}} is the amount of energy required for a phase change of a substance
extra:
Temperature does not change during the transformationQ = heat transferred during the phase change
m = mass
HL = latent heat or heat of transformation
example: Melting 10 g of ice at 0 °C takes 10 g × 334 J/g = 3,340 J while the temperature stays at 0 °C.

text: {{c1::Open systems::... systems}} will exchange both energy and matter with their surroundings
example: A pot of boiling water without a lid takes in heat from the stove and loses steam to the room.

text:
Pipes closed at one end support standing waves with length:
{{c1::}}
extra: Length of the closed pipe = (some odd multiple of wavelengths) / 4
example: A 0.25 m pipe closed at one end has a fundamental wavelength of 4L = 1 m.

text: Distance is path {{c1::dependent::dependent or independent}}
example: Driving a 10 km winding road between two towns 6 km apart covers 10 km of distance.

text: {{c1::Skewed distributions::... distributions}} have differences in their mean, median, and mode
example: House prices in a city: a few mansions pull the mean above the median, which sits above the mode.

text: {{c1::Heat}} is energy transfer between two objects at different temperatures
extra: It occurs until the two objects come into thermal equilibrium (reach the same temperature)
example: An ice cube held in your warm hand melts as heat flows from your skin into the 0 °C ice.

text: {{c1::Isolated systems::... systems}} do not exchange matter or energy with surroundings
example: An ideal sealed, perfectly insulated thermos exchanges neither heat nor matter with the room.

text: A {{c1::cross-sectional study::... study}} is an observational study that analyzes data collected at one point in time across a sample population
example: A one-time survey of 5,000 adults recording how many of them currently smoke.

text: The intensity of a sound (perceived as loudness) is dependent on the sound wave's {{c1::amplitude}}
example: Plucking a guitar string harder makes bigger vibrations and a louder note at the same pitch.

text: {{c1::Partially constructive / destructive interference::... interference}} occurs when two waves are not quite perfectly in or out of phase with each other
extra: The displacement of the resultant wave is equal to the sum of the displacements of the two interfering waves
example: Two 1 cm waves 90° out of phase combine into a wave of about 1.4 cm, between 0 and 2 cm.

text: Gamma (γ) decay is the emission of a {{c1::gamma}} ray, made up of {{c1::photons}}
extra: Converts a high-energy nucleus into a more stable nucleus
example: Technetium-99m emits gamma rays used for medical imaging as it settles into technetium-99.

text: If a medical test says someone has a disease, but the person actually does not, this is a type {{c1::1::#}} error
extra: Type 1 error = false positive
example: A mammogram flags cancer in a healthy woman, leading to an unnecessary biopsy.

text: {{c1::Current}} is the flow of electric charge
extra:
By convention, current is the direction positive charge would move
In reality, only electrons move in a circuit, opposite to the conventional direction (toward higher voltage)
example: A 2 A current means 2 C of charge passes any point in the wire each second.

text: {{c1::Closed systems::... systems}} will exchange energy but not matter with their surroundings
example: A capped bottle of water in the freezer loses heat but no water.

text: Pitch is our perception of {{c1::frequency}}
example: An 880 Hz tone sounds one octave higher than a 440 Hz tone.

text: {{c1::Ferromagnetic materials::... materials}} possess some unpaired electrons and become strongly magnetic in an external magnetic field
example: An iron nail stroked with a magnet becomes a magnet itself and can pick up paper clips.

text:
x = {{c1::cos::cos or sin}}
y = {{c1::sin::cos or sin}}
example: At 60° on the unit circle, the point is (cos 60°, sin 60°) = (0.5, 0.87).

text: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that consist of an oscillating {{c1::electric field::... field}} and an oscillating {{c1::magnetic field::... field}}
extra: The two fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation of the wave
example: Sunlight crosses the vacuum of space as linked electric and magnetic field oscillations.

text:
Maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron (photoelectric effect):
{{c1::}}
example: A 5 eV photon hitting a metal with a 2 eV work function ejects electrons with KE<sub>max</sub> = 3 eV.

text: {{c1::Electron capture}} is a process that unstable atoms can use to become more stable
extra: An electron in an atom's inner shell is drawn into the nucleus where it combines with a proton, forming a neutron and a neutrino
example: Potassium-40 can capture an inner-shell electron and become argon-40.

text: Diffraction is the bending and spreading out of light waves as they pass through a {{c1::narrow slit}}
example: Laser light through a hair-thin slit spreads into a wide central band flanked by fainter fringes.

text: The ethics of clinical research requires {{c1::equipoise}}, which is a state of genuine uncertainty on the part of the clinical investigator regarding which treatment is "better" for the study participant
extra: Should the investigator discover that one treatment is of superior therapeutic merit, he or she is ethically obliged to offer that treatment
example: CAST halted its flecainide and encainide arms in 1989 once the drugs proved to raise death rates, ending equipoise.

text: {{c1::Resistors}} are conductive materials with a moderate amount of resistance that slow down electrons without stopping them
example: A resistor placed in series with an LED limits the current so the LED does not burn out.

text: Test charges will move spontaneously in whichever direction results in a {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}} in their electrical potential energy
example: An electron released between capacitor plates drifts toward the positive plate, lowering its potential energy.

text:
Protons have a {{c1::positive::+ or -}} charge
Electrons have a {{c1::negative::+ or -}} charge
extra: Both protons and electrons possess the fundamental unit of charge (e = 1.60 × 10-19 C)
example: A Na<sup>+</sup> ion has 11 protons but only 10 electrons, giving it a net +1 charge.
Doubling the distance from a point charge cuts the force to 1/2<sup>2</sup> = 1/4.

text: Potential energy stored in a capacitor: {{c1::}}
example: A 2 μF capacitor charged to 100 V stores ½CV<sup>2</sup> = ½(2 × 10<sup>-6</sup>)(100<sup>2</sup>) = 0.01 J.

text: For vector addition, use the {{c1::tip-to-tail}} method, or you can break the vector into its component parts and use the {{c1::Pythagorean Theorem}}
extra: Tip-to-Tail Method:Pythagorean Theorem Method:
example: Walking 3 m east then 4 m north gives a 5 m resultant displacement (3<sup>2</sup> + 4<sup>2</sup> = 5<sup>2</sup>).

text: In the visible spectrum, {{c1::red::color}} has the largest wavelength
extra: Mnemonic: ROY G BIV
example: Red light is about 700 nm, longer than green (about 530 nm) or blue (about 470 nm).
A square plot 11 m on each side covers 121 m<sup>2</sup>.

text: Hydraulic machines operate based on the application of Pascal’s principle to generate {{c1::mechanical advantage}}
example: A 100 N push on a 1 cm<sup>2</sup> piston lifts 10,000 N on a 100 cm<sup>2</sup> piston in a car lift.

text: A/an {{c1::force}} is any push or pull that has the potential to result in an acceleration
example: Kicking a 0.5 kg soccer ball with a 50 N force accelerates it at 100 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

text: x = logb(y) can also be written {{c1::y = bx}}
example: log<sub>10</sub>(1000) = 3 because 10<sup>3</sup> = 1000.

text: In the visible spectrum, {{c1::violet::color}} has the smallest wavelength
extra: Mnemonic: ROY G BIV
example: Violet light is about 400 nm, while red light is about 700 nm.

text: {{c1::Viscosity}} is a measure of a fluid’s internal friction
example: Honey pours far more slowly than water because its viscosity is much higher.

text: Velocity is a {{c1::vector::vector or scalar}} and includes both {{c1::magnitude}} and {{c1::direction}}
example: A car moving 25 m/s north has a different velocity from one moving 25 m/s south.

text: {{c1::Friction}} is a force that opposes motion as a function of electrostatic interactions at the surfaces between two objects
extra:
Static friction = stationary object
Kinetic friction = sliding object
example: Static friction between tires and road keeps a car parked on a hill from sliding.

text: {{c1::Longitudinal waves::... waves}} are oscillations where particles are displaced parallel to the wave direction
extra: Sound waves are longitudinal waves because particles of the medium through which the sound is transported vibrate parallel to the direction that the sound wave moves
example: Pushing one end of a stretched Slinky in and out sends compressions along its length.

text: {{c1::External validity::... validity}} refers to the ability of a study to be generalized to the population that it describes
example: A drug tested only on men aged 20 to 30 may not generalize to elderly women.

text:
The Hill criteria include the following 9 principles used to provide evidence of a causal relationship between a presumed cause and an observed effect:
  • {{c1::Temporality}}
  • {{c1::Plausibility}}
  • {{c1::Consistency}}
  • {{c1::Strength of association}}
  • {{c1::Dose response}}
  • {{c1::Specificity}}
  • {{c1::Coherence}}
  • {{c1::Experiment}}
  • {{c1::Analogy}}
example: Heavier smokers get more lung cancer (dose response), and smoking comes before the cancer (temporality).

text: {{c1::Solids}} maintain their shape regardless of their container
example: An ice cube keeps its cube shape whether it sits in a bowl or a glass, until it melts.

text: {{c1::Electrical potential energy}} is the amount of work required to bring a test charge from infinitely far away to a given position in the vicinity of a source charge
example: Bringing a +1 μC charge to 1 m from a +1 μC source takes kq<sub>1</sub>q<sub>2</sub>/r = 9 × 10<sup>-3</sup> J of work.

text: This graph is an example of {{c1::exponential}} decay
extra:
The rate of decay is directly proportional to the amount presentn = # of undecayed nuclei
n0 = # of undecayed nuclei at t = 0
λ = known decay constant
example: A drug with a 6 h half-life falls from 80 mg to 40, 20 and then 10 mg over 18 hours.

text: {{c1::Vectors}} are physical quantities that have both magnitude and direction
extra: Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force
example: A plane flying 250 m/s due west has a velocity vector; the 250 m/s alone is a scalar speed.

text: {{c1::Antinodes}} are points of maximum oscillation
extra: Found in standing waves when there are two waves with constructive interference
example: The midpoint of a guitar string vibrating at its fundamental swings the farthest.

text:
cos(0º) = {{c1::1}}
sin(0º) = {{c1::0}}
example: A rope pulling a sled horizontally (θ = 0°) puts all its force forward: F cos 0° = F and F sin 0° = 0.

text: {{c1::Standing waves::... waves}} oscillate in time but the peak amplitude profile does not move in space
extra: Produced by the constructive and destructive interference of two waves of the same frequency traveling in opposite directions in the same space
example: A plucked guitar string vibrates in place, bulging in the middle without the bulge moving along it.

text: The apparent frequency might be higher, lower, or equal to the emitted frequency when the two objects are moving in the same direction. It depends on their {{c1::relative speeds}}
example: A car following an ambulance at the same speed hears the siren at its true, unshifted frequency.

text: For a concave mirror, if the object is farther than the focal point, the image will be {{c1::real}} and {{c1::inverted}}
example: Looking into the bowl of a spoon held at arm's length shows you upside down.

text: {{c1::Electrical potential energy::... energy}} is the energy between two charged particles
example: Pushing two protons closer together raises their electrical potential energy because they repel.

text: The {{c1::range}} of a set of numbers is the highest number minus the lowest number
example: For 4, 9, 15 and 22 the range is 22 − 4 = 18.

text: Coulomb’s law gives the magnitude of the {{c1::electrostatic force vector}} between two charges
example: Doubling the distance between two charges cuts the electrostatic force between them to one quarter.

text: A {{c1::positive control::... control}} is a group in an experiment that receives a treatment with a known result, and therefore should show a particular change during the experiment
extra: It is used to control for unknown variables during the experiment and to give the scientist something to compare with the test group
example: When testing a new antibiotic, a plate given penicillin should kill susceptible bacteria, proving the assay works.

text:
Ammeter vs. voltmeter vs. ohmmeter
  • Ammeter: measures current; placed in {{c1::series}}; ideal resistance {{c2::≈ 0}}
  • Voltmeter: measures voltage; placed in {{c1::parallel}}; ideal resistance {{c2::≈ ∞}}
  • Ohmmeter: measures resistance; placed {{c1::across the isolated element (circuit off)}}; {{c2::self-powered by its own battery}}
extra: Why: an ammeter must not drop voltage in the branch it measures, and a voltmeter must not draw current away from it. An ohmmeter drives its own small current and applies R = V/I.
example: A 3 V battery across a 6 Ω resistor: the series ammeter reads 0.5 A and the parallel voltmeter reads 3 V.

text: The Venturi tube demonstrates that as cross-sectional area decreases from point 1 to point 2, the linear speed must {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}}
extra:
The average height of the horizontal tube remains constant, so pgh remains constant at points 1 and 2
As the dynamic pressure increases, the absolute pressure must decrease at point 2, causing the column of fluid sticking up from the Venturi tube be to be lower at point 2
example: Water flowing from a 4 cm<sup>2</sup> section into a 2 cm<sup>2</sup> section doubles its speed (A<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub>).

text: The Reynolds number is used to check whether the flow is {{c1::laminar}} or {{c1::turbulent}}
extra:
Laminar flow occurs at low Reynolds numbers
ρ = density of fluid
V = velocity
L = diameter of pipe
μ = dynamic viscosity of the fluid
Reynolds number is dimensionless
example: Fast blood flow through a narrowed aortic valve raises the Reynolds number enough to turn it turbulent.

text: A {{c1::process function::... function}} describes the pathway from one equilibrium state to another
example: Taking a gas from (1 L, 2 atm) to (2 L, 1 atm) does 2 L·atm of work expanding first, 1 L·atm dropping pressure first.

text: The emission and absorption spectra of a substance tell us {{c1::what elements are found in the substance}}
extra: The spectrum of light emissions and absorptions from a particular substance
example: A flame test's bright yellow-orange glow reveals sodium in a sample.

text: The number which appears most often in a set of numbers is called the {{c1::mode}}
example: In the set 2, 3, 3, 5, 8 the mode is 3.

text: {{c1::Displacement (x)}} refers to how far a point is from the equilibrium position, expressed as a vector quantity
extra: The term can apply to any measure of length including amplitude and wavelength
example: A mass on a spring pulled 3 cm below its rest point has a displacement of 3 cm downward.

text: log(A<sup>B</sup>) = {{c1::B•log(A)}}
example: Pure water with [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-7</sup> M has log(10<sup>-7</sup>) = −7 log(10) = −7, so pH 7.

text: Pascal’s principle states that pressure applied to a fluid will be distributed {{c1::undiminished}} throughout the entire volume of the fluid
extra: A pressure change at any point in a fluid is transmitted throughout the fluid such that the same change occurs everywhere
example: Squeezing a sealed toothpaste tube anywhere raises the pressure throughout, pushing paste out the cap.

text: Nodes are points where there is no {{c1::oscillation}}
extra: Found in standing waves when there are two waves with destructive interference
example: The two fixed ends of a plucked guitar string are nodes that never move.

text: The work function is the minimum energy necessary to {{c1::eject an electron from a given metal}}
example: Sodium's work function is about 2.3 eV, so a 2 eV photon cannot eject an electron from it.

text: {{c1::Hypothesis tests}} use a known distribution to determine whether the null hypothesis can be rejected
example: A t-test checks whether a drug group's lower blood pressure versus placebo is bigger than chance.

text: When all the light rays have electric fields with equal intensity but constantly rotating direction, this light is called {{c1::circularly polarized light}}
extra: Circularly polarized light is created by exposing unpolarized light to special pigments or filters
example: RealD 3D movie glasses use circularly polarized lenses, so the image holds up when you tilt your head.

text: The {{c1::standard deviation}} is a measure that is used to quantify the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of data values
example: Test scores 70, 70, 70 have an SD of 0; scores 50, 70, 90 have the same mean but a much larger SD.

text:
Opposite charges exert {{c1::attractive}} forces
Like charges exert {{c1::repulsive}} forces
example: Two balloons rubbed on your hair push each other apart but are pulled back toward your hair.

text: Based on the Doppler effect, the perceived frequency will be {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} than the emitted frequency when the source and detector are moving toward each other
example: A train horn sounds higher than its true pitch the whole time the train races toward you.

text: log(A x B) = {{c1::log(A) + log(B)}}
{{c1::Dielectric materials::... materials}} are insulators placed between the plates of a capacitor that increase capacitance by a factor equal to the material’s dielectric constant, κ
example: Filling the gap with glass of κ = 5 turns a 2 μF capacitor into a 10 μF capacitor.

text: A {{c1::case–control study::... study}} is an observational study in which two existing groups that differ in outcome are compared on the basis of a supposed causal attribute
example: Doll and Hill (1950) compared past smoking in lung cancer patients with that of patients without cancer.

text:
Wave types: two independent ways to classify
By whether the pattern moves
  • Traveling: peaks and troughs {{c1::move through space}}
  • Standing: peaks stay in place, with fixed {{c1::nodes and antinodes}}
By direction of particle displacement
  • Transverse: {{c2::perpendicular}} to propagation (e.g. {{c2::light / EM waves}}, a plucked string)
  • Longitudinal: {{c2::parallel}} to propagation (e.g. {{c2::sound}})
extra: The two pairs combine freely: a standing wave on a guitar string is transverse, and a standing wave in an organ pipe is longitudinal (sound). A standing wave forms when two identical waves travel in opposite directions and interfere.
example: A stadium wave is a traveling transverse wave: fans move up and down while the pattern moves sideways.

text: The threshold frequency is the minimum light frequency necessary to {{c1::eject an electron from a given metal}}
extra: This frequency is just able to eject electrons without giving them additional energy
example: Red light is below sodium's threshold frequency, so it ejects no electrons however bright the lamp.

text: {{c1::Power}} is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred
example: Doing 100 J of work in 2 s takes 50 W; doing the same work in 4 s takes only 25 W.

text: \(log(\frac{A}{B})\) = {{c1::log(A) − log(B)}}
When objects are placed outside the focal length of a convex lens or concave mirror, the image is always {{c1::real}}
example: A projector's converging lens throws a real image of the slide onto a screen.
Shrinking the distance between two charges to 1/7 raises the force between them 7<sup>2</sup> = 49-fold.

text: Voltmeters are inserted in parallel in a circuit to measure {{c1::voltage}}
example: To measure a bulb's voltage, you clip the voltmeter's two leads across the bulb's terminals.

text: A {{c1::state function::... function}} is a property that depends only on the present state of a system, not on how that state was reached
extra: Examples: pressure, density, temperature, volume, enthalpy, internal energy, Gibbs free energy, entropy
example: Water warmed from 20 °C to 50 °C on a stove or in a microwave ends with the same internal energy.

text:
cos(45°) = {{c1::\(\frac{\sqrt 2}{2}\) ≈ 0.7}}
sin(45°) = {{c1::\(\frac{\sqrt 2}{2}\) ≈ 0.7}}
example: A ball launched at 10 m/s at 45° has horizontal and vertical speeds of about 7 m/s each.

text: According to the venturi effect, the velocity of a fluid passing through a constricted area will {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}} and its static pressure will {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}}
example: A perfume atomizer blows fast air across a tube, lowering its pressure and drawing liquid up.

text: {{c1::Rotational equilibrium::... equilibrium}} occurs in the absence of any net torques acting on an object
example: A seesaw balances with a 30 kg child 2 m from the pivot opposite a 60 kg adult at 1 m.

text: {{c1::Wavelength (λ)}} is the distance between two crests or two troughs of a wave
example: Green light has a wavelength of about 530 nm, while FM radio waves are about 3 m long.

text:
Solve the above expression using scientific notation shortcuts:
{{c1::}}
extra: Divide the coefficients then subtract the exponents

text: {{c1::Turbulent flow::... flow}} is rough and disorderly
example: Smoke from a candle breaks into chaotic, swirling eddies a few centimetres above the wick.

text:
Steps of the scientific method:
  1. Initial: {{c1::formulate a hypothesis}}
  2. Intermediate: {{c1::test that hypothesis}}
  3. Final: {{c1::provide results for further testing of the hypothesis}}
example: Hypothesize that caffeine improves recall, test it in a randomized trial, then publish for others to replicate.

text: This is an example of {{c1::β-}} decay
This is a {{c1::concave}} lens, also known as a {{c1::diverging}} lens
example: Glasses that correct nearsightedness (myopia) use diverging lenses.

text:
Solve the above expression using scientific notation shortcuts:
{{c1::}}
extra: Multiply the coefficients then add the exponents

text: The {{c1::photoelectric effect}} is the ejection of an electron from the surface of a metal in response to light
example: UV light shone on a negatively charged zinc plate knocks out electrons and discharges it.

text: An {{c1::outlier}} is a data point that differs significantly from other observations
example: In salaries of $40k, $45k, $50k and $2 million, the $2 million is an outlier.

text: A/an {{c1::equipotential}} line is a line on which the potential at every point is the same
extra:
Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to electrical field lines
No work is done when a charge moves along an equipotential line
example: Every point 1 m from an isolated point charge has the same potential, forming a spherical equipotential.

text: Free body diagrams are representations of the {{c1::forces}} acting on an object
example: A book resting on a table has two arrows: its weight mg down and the normal force up.

text: A {{c1::histogram}} presents numerical data, whereas a {{c1::bar graph}} shows categorical data
example: Exam-score bins form a histogram; counts of students by favourite colour form a bar graph.

text: Isovolumetric processes have constant {{c1::volume}}
example: Heating gas in a sealed, rigid steel tank raises its pressure but does no P-V work.

text: {{c1::Plane polarized light waves}} are light waves in which the vibrations occur in a single plane
example: Glare reflected off a lake is mostly horizontally polarized, which polarized sunglasses block.

text: {{c1::Destructive interference::... interference}} occurs when waves are exactly out of phase with each other
extra: The amplitude of the resultant wave is equal to the difference in amplitude between the two interfering waves
example: Noise-cancelling headphones play an inverted copy of outside noise so the two waves cancel.

text: Non-conservative forces are path {{c1::dependent::dependent or independent}}
extra:
They cause dissipation of mechanical energy from a system
Examples: friction and air resistance
example: Dragging a crate between the same two points loses more energy to friction along a winding 20 m path than a straight 5 m one.

text: The relationship in this graph is {{c1::exponential}}
example: Bacteria doubling every 20 minutes: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 cells.

text: Alpha (α) decay is the emission of an alpha particle, which is a {{c1::helium}} nucleus
example: Uranium-238 emits an alpha particle and becomes thorium-234.

text: Images with a concave lens are always {{c1::virtual}} and {{c1::upright}}
example: Seen through a nearsighted person's glasses, objects look smaller and upright.

text: {{c1::Elastic potential energy::... energy}} is created when stretching or compressing an elastic object
extra: Elastic potential energy = ½ × (spring constant) × (degree of stretch or compression)2
example: A spring with k = 100 N/m stretched 0.2 m stores ½(100)(0.2)<sup>2</sup> = 2 J.

text: For vector subtraction, you must change the {{c1::direction}} of the subtracted vector and then do a tip-to-tail addition
example: To find 5 m/s east − 3 m/s west, flip it to 3 m/s east and add: 8 m/s east.

text: x = ln(y) can also be written {{c1::y = ex}}
example: ln(7.39) ≈ 2 because e<sup>2</sup> ≈ 7.39.

text: A {{c1::negative control::... control}} group is a group in which no response is expected
extra: It is the opposite of the positive control, in which a known response is expected
example: When testing a new antibiotic, a bacterial plate treated with sterile water should show no killing.

text: Beta-negative (β-) decay is the decay of a {{c1::neutron}} into a {{c1::proton}}
extra: With emission of an electron (the β- particle is an electron) and an antineutrino
example: Carbon-14 undergoes β<sup>-</sup> decay into nitrogen-14 as a neutron turns into a proton.

text: Capacitance in terms of charge (coulombs) and voltage (volts): {{c1::}}
example: A capacitor holding 6 μC of charge at 3 V has C = Q/V = 2 μF.

text: The relationship in this graph is {{c1::curvilinear}}
example: Yerkes-Dodson law: performance rises then falls as arousal increases, an inverted U.

text:
Energy of a photon:
{{c1::}}
extra:
E = energy of a photon
h = Planck's constant
c = speed of light
λ = wavelength
f = frequency
example: A 620 nm photon has E = hc/λ = 1240 eV·nm / 620 nm = 2 eV.

text: The significance of a statistical finding is determined by comparing the {{c1::p-value}} to the selected significance level
extra: A significance level of 0.05 is commonly used
example: A drug trial gives p = 0.03, below α = 0.05, so the effect is called statistically significant.

text:
Mechanical advantage of an inclined plane:
{{c1::}}
example: A 10 m ramp rising 2 m gives a mechanical advantage of 10/2 = 5.

text: When a scientist repeats an experiment with a different group of people or a different batch of the same chemicals and gets very similar results then those results are said to be {{c1::reliable}} or {{c1::precise}}
example: A blood pressure cuff that reads 120/80, 121/80 and 120/79 on three tries is reliable.

text: The average of a set of numbers is called the {{c1::mean}}
example: The mean of 2, 4 and 9 is 15/3 = 5.

text: Ohmmeters are used to measure the {{c1::resistance}}
extra: Inserted around a resistive element; they are self-powered and have negligible resistance
example: A multimeter on its ohm setting, clipped across a disconnected 100 Ω resistor, reads about 100 Ω.

text: A {{c1::within-subject design::... design}} is an experimental design in which all participants are exposed to every treatment or condition
extra:
Controls for individual variation by comparing a subject's scores in one condition to the same subject's scores in other conditions
So, the subject serves as its own control
example: Each participant takes a memory test once after caffeine and once after placebo, on different days.

text: Resistance of a material: {{c1::}}
extra:
ρ = resistivity
L = length of resistor
A = cross-sectional area
example: Doubling a wire's length doubles its resistance; doubling its cross-sectional area halves it.

text: {{c1::Fluids}} are substances that flow and conform to the shape of their containers
extra: This includes liquids and gases
example: Water poured into a vase and air pumped into a balloon both take the shape of their container.

text: The probability of {{c1::independent}} events does not change based on the outcomes of other events
example: Each coin flip has a 1/2 chance of heads, even after five heads in a row.

text: Specific gravity is the ratio of {{c1::an object's density}} to {{c1::water's density}}
example: Ice at 0.92 g/cm<sup>3</sup> has a specific gravity of 0.92, so it floats with about 92% submerged.

text: {{c2::Feeding and eating}} disorders involve {{c1::distress/disability from behavioral abnormalities related to food}}
extra:
anorexia nervosa = not eating enough
bulimia nervosa = binge eating then vomiting
example: Pica: a child who repeatedly eats dirt and paint chips.

text: Dopamine is produced in the {{c1::arcuate nucleus}}, {{c1::substantia nigra}}, and {{c1::VTA}}.
example: Cocaine blocks reuptake of dopamine released by VTA neurons into the nucleus accumbens.

text: {{c2::Delusions}} are {{c1::false fixed beliefs not explainable by culture that hold true despite obvious evidence that they aren't true}}
example: A man insists his wife has been replaced by an identical impostor, whatever evidence he is shown (Capgras).

text: The cognitive component of attitude is {{c1::how thoughts/knowledge about something influence our attitude}}
{{c2::The corticobulbar tract}} is when {{c1::UMN's of the cerebral cortex synapse on the brainstem}}
example: Corticobulbar fibres drive the facial nucleus, so a cortical stroke can droop the opposite lower face.

text: {{c1::Independent stressors}} are {{c2::stressors that occur without the person's influence}}
{{c2::Dependent personality}} disorder includes individuals who are {{c1::submissive and clingy}}
extra: example: people who stay in physically abusive relationships
example: A 30-year-old who still has her mother choose her clothes, meals and job.

text: {{c2::Substance-Related and Addictive}} disorders involve {{c1::distress/disability from abnormal use of substances that affect mental function}}
example: A man keeps drinking heavily despite losing his job and his licence to drunk-driving charges.

text: Full term is between {{c1::37}} and {{c1::42}} weeks
extra:
preterm is before 37 weeks
postterm is after 42 weeks
example: Due dates are set at 40 weeks after the last period, in the middle of the term window.

text: In the brain, {{c1::white}} matter is on the inside and {{c1::grey}} matter is on the outside
example: A brain slice shows a thin grey cortical rim over deep white tracts such as the corpus callosum.

text: The physiological needs of Maslow's hierarchy are {{c1::essentials to survive like food, water, breathing, and sleep}}
example: A shipwrecked sailor's first concern is finding drinking water.

text: Temperament can include {{c1::emotional reactivity}}, {{c1::shyness}}, and {{c1::sociability}}
example: A toddler who hides behind her mother at every new face shows a shy temperament.

text: Neuropeptide Y in humans stimulates the {{c1::feeding}} circuit, blocking {{c1::satiety}}
example: Injecting NPY into a rat's hypothalamus makes it keep eating even when already full.

text: Acetylcholine is released by {{c1::LMNs}} and {{c1::the ANS}}
example: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release from LMNs, causing flaccid paralysis.

text:
Nociceptors and thermoceptors travel in {{c1::slow::Fast/Slow}} neurons
Position/Vibration/Touch travel in {{c1::fast::Fast/Slow}} neurons
example: Touching a hot stove: you feel the contact instantly, but the burning pain arrives a moment later.

text:
Origin of acetylcholine in the brain: {{c1::basal forebrain::Generally}}
Specifically: {{c1::nucleus basalis & septal nuclei::Specifically}}
example: Alzheimer's disease destroys nucleus basalis of Meynert neurons, depleting the cortex of acetylcholine.

text: The factors that regulate our intake of food, sex, and drugs include {{c1::biological}} factors and {{c1::sociocultural}} factors
example: Ghrelin makes you hungry before lunch (biological), yet you still eat cake at a party when full (sociocultural).

text: GABA inhibits a neuron by allowing {{c1::Cl-}} to enter the neuron and this {{c1::hyperpolarizes}} the cell
example: Benzodiazepines like diazepam boost GABA<sub>A</sub> Cl<sup>-</sup> flow, calming anxiety and stopping seizures.

text:
Nature vs. nurture (how a person's behavior develops):
  • Nature: {{c1::genes and hereditary factors}}
  • Nurture: {{c1::environmental variables}}
example: Identical twins raised apart in the Minnesota Twin Study shared many traits, pointing to nature.

text: {{c2::The theory of planned behavior}} states that we {{c1::consider our intentions and implications of our actions before we decide to behave}}
example: Before buying a car, you weigh the cost, your family's opinion and whether you can afford the payments.

text: {{c1::Glutamate}} is the {{c2::most common excitatory neurotransmitter}}
example: Excess glutamate released after a stroke overexcites neurons to death (excitotoxicity).

text: The ego is {{c1::unconscious and conscious}} and seeks {{c1::long term gratification}}
extra: it is involved in perceptions, thoughts, and judgement
example: Instead of buying a car on impulse, you save for a year and buy it outright.

text: {{c1::Serotonin}} modulates mood, sleep, eating, and dreaming
example: SSRIs like fluoxetine (Prozac) raise synaptic serotonin to treat depression.

text:
{{c2::Borderline personality}} disorder includes individuals who:
  • {{c1::have unstable relationships}}
  • are {{c1::emotionally unstable}}
  • {{c1::have a variable self-image}}
  • are {{c1::impulsive}}
extra: Example: displays characteristics of a stereotypical teenager.
example: A woman idolizes a new friend one week, rages that the friend betrayed her the next, then cuts herself.

text: {{c1::Heredity}} is passing traits from parents/ancestors to offspring through genes
example: A child of a parent with Huntington's disease has a 50% chance of inheriting it.

text: {{c2::Psychoticism}} is {{c1::the degree of nonconformity or social deviance}}
example: A person who ignores social rules, acts impulsively and shows little empathy scores high in psychoticism.

text: {{c1::Reinforcing effect}} is when we want to constantly stimulate the brain by using drugs
example: Cocaine floods the nucleus accumbens with dopamine, so users want to take it again and again.

text: The dominant brain hemisphere for most people is the {{c1::left::right/left}} hemisphere
example: About 95% of right-handers process language in the left hemisphere.

text: {{c1::Calcium}} is an indicator of Chelation
extra: Chelation means "to grab" or "to bind." When EDTA is injected into the veins, it "grabs" heavy metals and minerals such as lead, mercury, copper, iron, arsenic, aluminum, and calcium and removes them from the body. Except as a treatment for lead poisoning, chelation therapy is controversial and unproved.
example: EDTA chelates Ca<sup>2+</sup>, so blood drawn into purple-top EDTA tubes cannot clot.

text: {{c1::Phobias}} are {{c2::when an individual is irrationally afraid of a specific object or situation}}. This is an example of {{c2::focused anxiety}}.
extra: Phobias can be debilitating (fear of leaving the house) or allow for a normal life (fear of snakes)

text: Testosterone and estrogen are hormones that mediate {{c1::libido}}, among other functions
extra: Testosterone is also associated with aggressive behavior
example: Men on testosterone-lowering therapy for prostate cancer commonly report a reduced sex drive.

text: {{c2::Central}} traits are {{c1::less dominant than cardinal, such as honesty, sociability, and shyness}}
example: A friend who is kind and witty in most situations, though not every single one.

text: {{c1::Seasonal affective disorder::... disorder}} is a type of depression that's related to changes in seasons
extra: Typically the patient is depressed during winter
example: A Minnesotan who becomes sad and sleeps more every November, improving with spring or light therapy.

text: The forebrain becomes the {{c1::cerebrum (telencephalon) and diencephalon (thalamus/hypothalamus)}}
example: The olfactory bulbs and cerebral hemispheres both arise from the telencephalon.

text: Etiology: {{c1::The manner of causation}}
example: The etiology of scurvy is a lack of vitamin C.

text: {{c1::Skinner::scientist}} and {{c1::Pavlov::scientist}} are associated with the behaviorist theory
example: Pavlov's dogs salivated at a bell; Skinner's rats pressed a lever for food pellets.

text: Infants develop from {{c1::head}} to {{c1::toe}}
extra: Example: infants can lift their heads before they can crawl

text: {{c1::Altruism}} is {{c2::a mature defense mechanism where individuals gain pleasure, satisfaction, and fulfillment from helping others}}
example: After her daughter was killed by a drunk driver, Candy Lightner founded Mothers Against Drunk Driving.

text: {{c1::The corpus callosum}} connects the two cerebral hemispheres
example: Split-brain patients cannot name an object flashed only to the left visual field.

text: Delusions of persecution are {{c1::false beliefs that other people are out to get them.}}
extra:
Often vague and bizarre ideas and plots
Example: the Martians are trying to poison me with radioactive particles in my tap water

text:
The neurotic defense mechanisms include:
  • {{c1::intellectualization}}
  • {{c1::rationalization}}
  • {{c1::regression}}
  • {{c1::repression}}
  • {{c1::displacement}}
  • {{c1::reaction formation}}
example: Forgetting a traumatic car crash (repression) or being extra sweet to a rival you resent (reaction formation).

text: The higher functions of the nervous system include {{c1::cognition}}, {{c1::emotions}}, and {{c1::consciousness}}
example: Solving a chess puzzle, feeling joy at winning and being aware that you are playing.

text: {{c1::Motivation}} is the purpose, or driving force, behind our actions
example: Hunger drives you to the fridge; wanting a promotion drives you to work late.

text: {{c2::Reflexes}} are {{c1::sensory and motor nerve loop responses without thinking}}
{{c1::Bipolar I disorder}} is when {{c2::an individual has had at least one manic episode, with or without major depressive episodes}}
example: A student with one week-long manic episode needing hospital has bipolar I, even with no depression.

text: In the spinal cord, {{c1::grey}} matter is on the inside and {{c1::white}} matter is on the outside
example: A spinal cord cross-section shows a butterfly-shaped grey core ringed by white tracts.

text: The {{c1::internal capsule}} contains the corticospinal tract
example: A small lacunar stroke in the internal capsule causes pure weakness of the opposite face, arm and leg.

text: The {{c1::nigrostriatal}} pathway is associated with motor planning and purposeful movement
example: Parkinson's disease: loss of nigrostriatal dopamine causes tremor, rigidity and a shuffling gait.

text: The superego is our {{c1::moral conscience}} and is {{c1::conscious and unconscious}}
example: You feel guilty after lying to a friend, even though nobody ever found out.

text:
Biological factors related to {{c1::schizophrenia}} include:
  • Genetic factors
  • Birth trauma
  • Marijuana use
  • Family history
example: An identical twin of someone with schizophrenia has about a 50% risk, versus about 1% in the general population.

text: A {{c1::trait}} is a relatively stable characteristic of a person that causes individuals to consistently behave in certain ways
example: Someone high in honesty returns a lost wallet whether or not anyone is watching.

text: A {{c1::Freudian slip}} is an unintentional error in speech or memory regarded as revealing subconscious feelings
extra: Example: a financially stressed patient says "please don't give me bills" instead of "pills".
