text: {{c1::The behaviorist theory of personality::Theory}} believes that {{c2::personality is the result of learned behavior patterns based on environment.}}
extra: All individuals begin as blank slates and environment completely determines behavior/personality
example: A child praised every time he shares grows into a generous adult.

text: The central nervous system includes {{c1::the brain}} and {{c1::spinal cord}}
example: Multiple sclerosis attacks myelin in the brain and spinal cord, damaging the CNS.

text:
The negative symptoms to schizophrenia include:
  • {{c1::blunted emotions}}
  • {{c1::loss of enjoyment}}
  • {{c1::avolition}}
  • {{c1::lack of speech}}
extra:
avolition = reduction/inability to persist in goal-directed behavior (loss of motivation)
mnemonic: BALL
Blunted emotion, Avolition, Lack of Speech, Loss of Enjoyment
example: A patient sits for hours with a blank face, answers in single words and no longer showers or works.

text: Merkel cells detect {{c1::texture}} and {{c1::pressure}}
example: Reading Braille with a fingertip depends on Merkel cells.

text:
Diathesis-stress model: {{c1::Some people are predisposed to having a specific mental illness}}
However, {{c1::many illnesses will never manifest because of a positive environment}}
example: Twins share a genetic risk for depression, but only the one who loses a job and a marriage develops it.

text: {{c2::Hypomania}} is {{c1::a mild form of mania}} and is associated with {{c1::times of high productivity and energy}}
example: A man sleeps 4 hours a night for several days, feels great and finishes a month's work, without needing hospital.

text:
Physical abnormalities in individuals with depression include:
  • {{c1::decreased activity in frontal lobe}}
  • {{c1::increased activity in limbic structures}}
  • {{c1::abnormal cortisol levels}}
example: Many depressed patients have high cortisol that fails to drop after a dexamethasone suppression test.

text: Free nerve endings detect {{c1::pain}}
example: Stubbing a toe fires free nerve endings that signal sharp pain.

text: Obsessions are {{c1::thoughts that occur involuntarily and are often unwelcome}}
extra: Ex. obsession with hands being dirty, compulsion to wash them many times a day.

text:
The cerebellum functions:
  • {{c1::coordinate movement}}
  • {{c1::aid in proprioception w/ muscle spindles}}
  • {{c1::helps balance}}
  • {{c1::fine motor function}}
example: A drunk driver fails the finger-to-nose test because alcohol impairs the cerebellum.

text:
The mature defense mechanisms include:
  • {{c1::humor}}
  • {{c1::sublimation}}
  • {{c1::suppression}}
  • {{c1::altruism}}
example: Joking about your breakup (humor) or volunteering at a shelter after a loss (altruism).

text: The {{c1::palmar grasp}} reflex is when {{c2::children close their hands on anything that comes in their palm}}
example: A newborn grips a parent's finger so tightly it can briefly support its own weight.

text: Cluster C personality disorders include {{c1::avoidant}}, {{c1::dependent}}, and {{c1::obsessive-compulsive personality disorder}}
example: A man who cannot pick his own clothes without asking his partner (dependent).

text: {{c1::Depressive}} disorders are {{c2::distress/disability from abnormally negative mood.}}
extra: Mood is not emotion: mood is long-term and not necessarily related to events.
example: Major depressive disorder: weeks of sadness, poor sleep and lost appetite with no clear trigger.

text: GABA primarily acts on the {{c1::brain}}
example: Alcohol enhances brain GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors, causing sedation and slurred speech.

text: {{c2::Orientation behaviors}} are used to {{c1::regulate spatially in the environment}}
extra: Example: a bug moving toward light

text: {{c1::Identification}} is the middle level of conformity. Here a person changes their public behaviour and their private beliefs, but only while they are in the presence of the group
example: A teen uses her soccer team's slang and opinions at practice but drops them at home.

text: {{c1::Panic disorders::Illness}} are {{c2::when an individual has sudden bursts of sheer panic and intense fear that are recurrent and unexpected (often without any trigger), followed by persistent worry about having more attacks}}
extra: Some situations warrant high levels of panic (e.g. a break-in), but people with panic disorder panic over little things to an abnormal degree.
example: Out of nowhere in a grocery line, a man's heart races and he fears he is dying; now he dreads the next attack.

text: {{c1::Galant}} reflex is when {{c2::a baby's skin is stroked, the baby moves to the side it was stroked}}
example: Stroking along one side of a face-down baby's spine makes its hips swing toward that side.

text: {{c1::The Reticular Activating System}} is required for {{c2::consciousness}} and is used to {{c2::diffuse the projection of glutamate into the cerebral cortex}}
example: A small brainstem stroke hitting the RAS can leave a patient in a coma despite an intact cortex.

text: According to Freud, the two instinctual drives that motivate human behavior are {{c1::the libido}} and {{c1::the death instinct}}
example: Freud would see falling in love as the libido and starting a bar fight as the death instinct.

text:
Lewy body disease, caused by build-up of Lewy bodies, is associated with:
  • {{c1::less motor abnormalities from basal ganglia dysfunction}}
  • {{c1::more cognitive dysfunction (loss of function from cerebral cortex)}}
It is separate from Parkinson's.
example: Robin Williams' autopsy revealed diffuse Lewy body disease.

text: {{c1::Sucking}} reflex is when {{c2::a baby will suck on any object in its mouth}}
example: A newborn starts sucking as soon as a pacifier touches the roof of its mouth.

text: Phenylketonuria is a {{c1::genetic}} disorder
example: Newborn heel-prick screening catches PKU; a low-phenylalanine diet prevents intellectual disability.

text: Dopamine produced in the substantia nigra helps control {{c1::motor planning}} and {{c1::purposeful movement}}
example: L-DOPA replaces dopamine lost from the substantia nigra, easing Parkinson's tremor and slowness.

text: {{c1::Social potency}} is defined as social dominance or interpersonal power and a desire to make an impact on others
extra: MPQ = Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire
example: A student who always takes charge of group projects and persuades others scores high on social potency.

text: {{c1::Gestalt psychologists}} believed that it was not possible to understand human behavior by breaking it down into parts, so people must be viewed as a whole
example: A triangle drawn with gaps in its sides is still seen as one whole triangle (closure).

text: {{c1::Selective mutism}} is an {{c2::anxiety disorder characterized by difficulty speaking in social situations but developmentally normal in terms of language and communication}}
example: A girl who chats freely at home but stays completely silent at school.

text: The death instinct drives {{c1::aggressive behaviors fueled by unconscious wish to die/hurt oneself or others}}
example: Freud would read a man's habit of picking fights he cannot win as an unconscious death wish.

text:
The symptoms of major depressive disorder include:
  • {{c1::Suicidal thoughts}}
  • {{c1::Interests decreased}}
  • {{c1::Guilt}}
  • {{c1::Energy decreased}}
  • {{c1::Concentration decreased}}
  • {{c1::Appetite disturbance}}
  • {{c1::Psychomotor changes}}
  • {{c1::Sleep disturbances}}
example: A widower who for 3 weeks sleeps all day, has lost 5 kg, cannot focus at work and feels worthless.

text:
Brain structure and function can be analyzed simultaneously using:
  • {{c1::functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)}}
  • {{c1::positron emission tomography (PET) scans}}
example: An fMRI during a word task shows Broca's area lighting up on an anatomical image of the brain.

text: {{c2::Displacement}} is {{c1::a neurotic defense mechanism where a person displaces anger from someone else onto a safer target::psych definition}}
extra: Example: a mother who is mad at her husband gets mad at her child instead

text: Gray matter is mostly {{c1::neuron somas}}
example: The cerebral cortex looks grey because it is packed with neuron cell bodies.

text: Depression is likely a combination of {{c1::biological}} and {{c1::psychosocial}} factors
example: A woman with a family history of depression becomes depressed after losing her job.

text:
D.I.D is common in individuals who:
  • {{c1::have a history of child abuse}}
  • {{c1::have undergone extreme life stress}}
extra: life stress can cause a persons conscious awareness to dissociate from painful memories
example: A woman severely abused as a young child later loses hours of time while another identity takes over.

text: {{c2::A personality trait}} is a {{c1::stable predisposition towards a certain behavior}}
example: A conscientious person reliably arrives early for work, class and appointments.

text: Delusions of control are {{c1::beliefs that ones thoughts or actions are being controlled by outside, alien forces.}}
extra: example: The CIA has tapped into my brain and is controlling my thoughts

text:
Incentive theory focuses on {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} reinforcement
Drive-reduction theory focuses on {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} reinforcement
example: You eat dessert because it tastes good (incentive) but drink water to end thirst (drive reduction).

text: {{c1::fMRI}} analyzes {{c2::amounts of oxygenated vs deoxygenated blood in the brain to figure out what regions are active}}
example: Viewing faces makes the fusiform face area light up on fMRI as oxygenated blood rushes in.

text:
Steps of zygote development
{{c1::1 cell → 2 cell → 4 cell → 8 cell → 16 cell → morula (32 cell) → blastocyst → gastrula → neurula}}
example: A human embryo is a morula around day 3–4 and a blastocyst ready to implant by about day 5–6.

text: {{c2::OCD}} is characterized by {{c1::obsessions}} and {{c1::compulsions}}
extra:
obsessions: unwanted repetitive thoughts
compulsions: unwanted repetitive actions
example: A man checks that the stove is off 20 times before leaving, afraid the house will burn down.

text: {{c2::Heritability}} is {{c1::the percentage of variation of traits due to genes}}
example: Height has h<sup>2</sup> of about 0.8: roughly 80% of height variation in a population comes from genetic differences.

text: {{c2::Cognitive dissonance}} is {{c1::the discomfort experienced when holding 2 or more conflicting cognitions (ideas, beliefs, values, etc)}}
example: Festinger and Carlsmith: people paid $1 to call a dull task fun later rated it more enjoyable than those paid $20.

text: {{c1::Catatonic schizophrenia}} includes {{c2::extremes of behavior}}
extra:
A former DSM-IV subtype; DSM-5 removed schizophrenia subtypes and treats catatonia as a specifier.
Examples: cannot speak, cannot move, erratic movements, repeating words.

text:
The functions of the frontal lobe:
  • {{c1::executive function}}
  • {{c1::impulse control}}
  • {{c1::long-term planning}}
  • {{c1::motor function (primary motor cortex)}}
  • {{c1::speech production (broca's area)}}
example: Phineas Gage became impulsive and rude after an iron rod pierced his frontal lobe.

text: {{c2::Histrionic personality}} disorder includes individuals who {{c1::are very attention seeking}}, {{c1::display emotions outwardly}}, and {{c1::wear bright clothes}}
example: A woman who wears flashy outfits, speaks dramatically and sulks whenever she is not the centre of attention.

text: {{c1::Factor analysis}} is a statistical method that {{c2::categorizes and determines major categories of traits}}
example: Raymond Cattell used factor analysis to reduce thousands of trait words to 16 personality factors.

text: Hypertonia is {{c1::increased tone of skeletal muscles}}
example: A stroke patient's elbow resists passive straightening, then suddenly gives way like a clasp-knife.

text: Hypochondriac: {{c1::A person who is abnormally anxious about their health}}
example: A man who reads every headache as a brain tumour despite repeatedly normal scans.

text: Ruffini endings detect {{c1::stretching}}
extra: mnemonic: If you stretch your luck, you get ruffed up
example: Ruffini endings sense the skin stretching over your knuckles as you make a fist.

text: The hindbrain becomes the {{c1::pons}}, {{c1::medulla}}, and {{c1::cerebellum}}
example: The medulla's breathing centre and the cerebellum's balance control both develop from the hindbrain.

text: The {{c1::superego}} functions to {{c2::strive for perfection}} and {{c2::inhibit sexual and aggressive impulses and replace them with morality}}; it {{c2::does not need instant gratification}}. It is {{c2::unconscious and conscious::unconscious or conscious}}.
example: You feel guilty about keeping extra change a cashier gave you by mistake, so you go back and return it.

text: The {{c1::Myers Briggs Personality Test}}, associated with {{c1::Carl Jung::psychologist}}, {{c2::characterizes individuals in one of 16 personality types based on personality traits::what it does}}
example: An INTJ is introverted, intuitive, thinking and judging.

text: {{c2::Schizoid personality}} disorder includes individuals who are {{c1::emotionally detached in relationships and show little emotion}}
example: A man who lives alone, has no friends and is indifferent to both praise and criticism.

text: {{c1::Cognitive distortions}} are ways that our mind convinces us of something that isn't really true
extra:
All-or-Nothing Thinking / Polarized Thinking
Overgeneralization
Mental Filter
Disqualifying the Positive
Jumping to Conclusions – Mind Reading
Jumping to Conclusions – Fortune Telling
Magnification (Catastrophizing) or Minimization
Emotional Reasoning
Should Statements
Labeling and Mislabeling
Personalization
Control Fallacies
Fallacy of Fairness
Fallacy of Change
Always Being Right
Heaven’s Reward Fallacy
example: After one bad exam a student thinks 'I'll never get into med school', an overgeneralization.

text: {{c1::Delirium}} is {{c2::reversible episodes of cognitive/higher brain problems}} caused by {{c2::drugs or blood abnormalities}}
example: An elderly patient with a UTI becomes confused overnight and clears once antibiotics treat the infection.

text: {{c1::The cognitive approach towards motivation}} states that {{c2::thought processes dictate motivation and thus drive our behavior}}
example: A student studies hard because she expects good grades will earn her a medical school place.

text: Role-playing can change attitude as a result of {{c1::our behavior and carrying out a role.}}
extra:
Internalizing the role and carrying out behavior accordingly
Example: Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment

text: {{c2::Synaptic pruning}} is {{c1::breaking down connections between certain neurons and focusing resources on the ones we use the most}}
extra: occurs early in adolescence and then decreases later in adolescence
example: A teen who practises violin daily keeps those circuits strong while unused connections are trimmed away.

text: CAT scans analyze brain structure using {{c1::X-ray images of the brain}}
example: An emergency CT scan shows fresh blood from a brain bleed as a bright white patch.

text: Adler and Horney's theory of personality states that our unconscious is motivated by {{c1::social urges}}
example: Adler's inferiority complex: a small, sickly child strives to excel at sports to compensate.

text: Adrenal medulla secretes {{c1::catecholamines}}
example: A pheochromocytoma floods the blood with epinephrine and norepinephrine, causing episodic hypertension.

text:
Biological factors influencing drug intake:
{{c1::family predisposition}} and {{c1::chemical imbalances}}
Sociocultural factors influencing drug intake:
{{c1::curiosity}}, {{c1::coping}}, {{c1::peer pressure}}
example: A teen with an alcoholic parent (biological) starts drinking because friends at parties do (peer pressure).

text:
LMN signs:
  • {{c1::atrophy}}
  • {{c1::fasciculations}}
  • {{c1::hypotonia}}
  • {{c1::hyporeflexia}}
example: A baby with spinal muscular atrophy is floppy and areflexic, with thin muscles and a twitching tongue.

text: {{c1::Projection}} is {{c2::an immature defense mechanism where an individual attributes unwanted thoughts and feelings onto another person. }}
extra: Example: after failing a test and feeling stupid, you call your dog "stupid" and "dumb"

text:
{{c2::Somatic symptom}} disorder is when:
  • {{c1::mental disorders manifest physical symptoms}}
  • {{c1::people spend excessive time/energy worrying about their symptoms}}
example: A woman's chronic stomach pain consumes her days; she keeps seeing new doctors despite normal tests.

text: {{c1::Alogia}} is {{c2::a symptom common in schizophrenics that is the lessening of speech fluency and productivity}}
example: Asked how his weekend was, a patient replies only 'fine' and says nothing more.

text: The function of upper motor neurons (UMN's) is to {{c1::control lower motor neurons}}
example: A motor cortex stroke leaves spinal LMNs intact but without UMN commands, so the opposite arm is weak and spastic.

text:
The identities in people with DID:
  • {{c1::are in denial of the other personalities' existence}}
  • {{c1::have different emotional responses}}
  • {{c1::have different mannerisms}}
example: One identity is a timid adult who speaks softly; another is a defiant teenager who swears and smokes.

text: {{c1::Dissociative}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability from abnormalities of identity or memory}}
extra: Examples: dissociative identity disorder (formerly multiple personality disorder), dissociative amnesia, depersonalization/derealization disorder.
example: Dissociative fugue: after a crisis a man travels to another city, takes a new name and cannot recall his past.

text: {{c1::Cheyne-Stokes breathing}} is a crescendo then descrescendo of breathing followed by a stop in breathing
example: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is seen in severe heart failure or after a stroke, often during sleep.

text: {{c1::Rooting}} reflex is when {{c2::an infant turns their head when their cheek is stroked}}
extra:
allows for orientation to mothers nipple/bottle
disappears around 4 months
example: A hungry newborn turns toward a finger brushed against her cheek, mouth open, searching for the nipple.

text:
{{c2::The prototype willingness model}} states that behavior is a function of:
  • {{c1::past behavior}}
  • {{c1::attitudes}}
  • {{c1::subjective norms}}
  • {{c1::intentions}}
  • {{c1::willingness to engage in a specific behavior}}
  • {{c1::models/prototyping}}
extra: Mnemonic: P A W S I M (possum)
example: A teen who drank before, sees drinkers as cool role models and is offered beer at a party is likely to drink.

text: In {{c1::reflex arcs}}, interneurons in the spinal cord relay information back to the source of the stimulus while simultaneously routing it to the brain
example: Touching a hot stove: your hand jerks back before your brain registers the pain.

text: The cluster A personality disorders are {{c1::paranoid}}, {{c1::schizoid}}, and {{c1::schizotypal}}
example: A man who assumes coworkers are plotting against him and reads insults into harmless remarks (paranoid).

text:
Opponent-process model:
  • {{c1::Accounts for a wide range of behavior}}
  • {{c1::What goes up must come down}}
example: The pleasant high of a night of drinking is followed by a hangover's irritability.

text: {{c2::Secondary}} traits are {{c1::preferences or attitudes}}
extra: Example: liking music, not eating meat

text: Endorphins function to {{c1::block pain sensations}}
example: Morphine mimics endorphins at mu-opioid receptors to block pain.

text: The {{c1::cerebral cortex::brain structure}} is the outer layer of neural tissue of the cerebrum
extra: Four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital
example: The cortex is only about 2–4 mm thick but is folded into gyri and sulci to fit inside the skull.

text: The door-in-the-face phenomenon is {{c1::following up a large request with a more reasonable one so the subject complies}}
example: Cialdini: students refused to counsel delinquents for 2 years but then agreed to chaperone them on a zoo trip.

text:
The cluster B personality disorders include:
  • {{c1::antisocial}}
  • {{c1::borderline}}
  • {{c1::histrionic}}
  • {{c1::narcissistic}} personality disorder
example: A man who craves constant praise and belittles anyone who outshines him (narcissistic).

text: {{c2::Neuroticism}} is {{c1::the degree of emotional stability}}
example: Someone who panics and cries over a minor criticism scores high in neuroticism.

text:
There are four things we do to reduce cognitive dissonance:
  • {{c1::Attitude change}}
  • {{c1::Behavior change}}
  • {{c1::Perceptual change}}
  • {{c1::Attribution change}}
example: A smoker who knows smoking kills tells herself the health risks are exaggerated.

text: Parathyroid glands regulate {{c1::calcium levels}}
example: Accidental removal of the parathyroids in thyroid surgery causes low Ca<sup>2+</sup> and muscle cramps (tetany).

text: {{c2::Covert behaviors}} are {{c1::behaviors that are not observable}}
example: Silently working out a tip in your head, or daydreaming during a lecture.

text: {{c1::Sublimation}} is a mature defense mechanism where you channel negative/unacceptable energy to positive/socially acceptable energy
extra: Example: someone with violent tendencies may take up boxing to cope

text: {{c1::Trauma/Stressor-Related}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability that occurs after stressful/traumatic events}}
example: Adjustment disorder: a student becomes depressed and cannot function for weeks after his parents divorce.

text:
The 4 ways we reduce cognitive dissonance are:
  • {{c1::modifying cognitions}}
  • {{c1::trivializing}}
  • {{c1::adding cognitions}}
  • {{c1::denying facts}}
extra: example: a smoker learns that smoking leads to cancer
example: A smoker told about lung cancer says his grandfather smoked daily and lived to 95 (adding cognitions).

text: Prolactin secretion is inhibited by {{c1::dopamine}}
example: Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist, shrinks prolactinomas and stops milk discharge.

text:
Simple traits = {{c1::linked to specific genes}}
Complex traits = {{c1::controlled by group of genes and/or environment}}
example: Cystic fibrosis follows one gene (CFTR); height depends on hundreds of genes plus nutrition.

text: Serotonin is released to the {{c1::cerebral cortex}} and {{c1::many other parts of the nervous system}}
example: Raphe serotonin reaches the cortex to shape mood and the spinal cord to dampen pain signals.

text: {{c1::Lesion studies}} involve {{c2::destroying areas of the brain and then studying the resulting changes in behavior}}
extra: Example: Phineas Gage's personality changed after an iron bar damaged his frontal lobe (he was reportedly kind beforehand); not an intentional study, but it shows how brain damage reveals a region's function
example: Rats with lesions of the ventromedial hypothalamus overeat and become obese.

text:
Function of medulla oblongata:
{{c1::regulates autonomic activity of heart and lungs}}
example: An opioid overdose kills by suppressing the medulla's breathing centre.

text: Dopamine produced in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) controls {{c1::the mesolimbic (reward) pathway}}
example: Winning a bet triggers a dopamine burst from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens.

text: {{c2::Extroversion}} is the {{c1::degree of sociability}}
example: The guest who chats with everyone at a party and leaves feeling energized.

text:
The four lobes of the cerebral cortex:
  • {{c1::frontal}}
  • {{c1::parietal}}
  • {{c1::occipital}}
  • {{c1::temporal}}
example: A blow to the back of the head, over the occipital lobe, can make a person see stars or lose vision.

text: {{c2::Trait theory}} describes {{c1::personality}} in terms of {{c1::patterns of behavior}}
example: Describing a friend as outgoing and organized sums up how she usually behaves.

text: {{c1::Factitious disorder}}, also called {{c1::Munchausen syndrome}}, is {{c2::when patients want to be sick and falsify symptoms to get diagnosis/treatment}}.
example: A nurse secretly injects herself with insulin to cause low blood sugar and get admitted to hospital.

text: Hyporeflexia is {{c1::decreased muscle stretch reflex}}
example: Tapping the patellar tendon of a patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome produces little or no knee jerk.

text: Atrophy is {{c1::loss of skeletal muscle volume}}
example: After ulnar nerve injury, the hand's interosseous muscles waste, leaving hollows between the metacarpals.

text: The love needs of Maslow's hierarchy are needs for {{c1::belonging, love, and acceptance from friends/family}}
example: A new college student joins a club to make friends and feel she belongs.

text: Polycystic kidney disease is a {{c1::genetic}} disorder
example: A man whose father has autosomal dominant PKD has a 50% chance of inheriting the kidney cysts.

text: The embryo becomes a fetus at {{c1::10}} weeks after the last menstrual period
example: If a woman's last period began on 1 March, her embryo becomes a fetus around 10 May (70 days later).

text:
The functions of the occipital lobe:
{{c1::visual processing}}
example: A stroke in the left occipital lobe wipes out the right half of the visual field in both eyes.

text: {{c2::Adolescence}} is {{c1::the transition period between childhood and adulthood}}
example: A 15-year-old going through puberty while working out her own identity, per Erikson.

text:
The physiological features of Alzheimer's disease include:
  • {{c1::cerebral atrophy}}
  • {{c1::loss of neurons}}
  • {{c1::build-up of amyloid plaques between cells}}
  • {{c1::neurofibrillary tangles of protein tau within neurons}}
example: Auguste Deter, Alois Alzheimer's first patient, showed plaques and tangles at her autopsy in 1906.

text:
Major motor milestones:
  • 2-4 months → {{c1::heads up / chest up}}
  • 2-5 months → {{c1::roll over}}
  • 5-8 months → {{c1::sit up}}
  • 5-10 months → {{c1::stand w/ support}}
  • 6-11 months → {{c1::pull up to standing position}}
  • 7-12 months → {{c1::able to crawl}}
  • 7-13 months → {{c1::can walk while holding furniture}}
  • 10-14 months → {{c1::can stand on their own}}
  • 11-15 months → {{c1::walk alone}}
example: A typical baby sits unsupported at about 6 months and takes first steps alone around 12 months.

text: Teratogen: {{c1::Agent or factor that causes malformation of an embryo}}
example: Thalidomide taken in pregnancy around 1960 caused babies to be born with severely shortened limbs.

text: {{c1::Social phobias}} are {{c2::fears of different social situations that are not easy to avoid}} and are associated with {{c2::people avoiding places where they may be judged/involve situations that lead to embarrassment}}.
extra: Example: intense fear of being scrutinized by others, or shyness
example: A student eats lunch in a bathroom stall to avoid being watched in the cafeteria.

text:
{{c2::The attitude to behavior process model::theory}}:
{{c1::event triggers attitude}} → {{c1::attitude and outside knowledge determine behavior}}
extra: Example: Tommy believes junk food is unhealthy because relatives have heart disease, so he avoids chips, soda and candy.

text: {{c1::Cortical cooling}} will cool down neurons until they stop firing during lesion studies
example: Cooling a patch of a monkey's visual cortex silences it, and vision there returns once it is rewarmed.

text: The two most common {{c2::inhibitory}} neurotransmitters are {{c1::GABA}} and {{c1::Glycine}}
example: Strychnine poisoning blocks glycine receptors, causing violent muscle spasms.

text: The libido is our instinctual desire to {{c1::survive}}, {{c1::procreate}}, and {{c1::grow}}
example: A young couple deciding to start a family reflects the libido's drive to procreate.

text: Glutamate allows {{c1::Na+}} to enter the neuron and this {{c1::depolarizes}} the cell which creates an action potential
example: Glutamate binding AMPA receptors lets Na<sup>+</sup> rush in, pushing a neuron from −70 mV toward threshold.

text: {{c1::Conversion}} disorder is {{c2::a somatic symptom disorder where their are ONLY neurological symptoms}}
extra: example: inability to swallow, inability to speak, seizures, paralysis
example: A soldier develops sudden leg paralysis with no nerve damage just before he is due to return to combat.

text: People with Parkinson's have clumps of {{c1::Lewy bodies}} in the {{c1::dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra}}
example: Under the microscope, Lewy bodies are round pink clumps of α-synuclein inside nigral neurons.

text: Hyperreflexia is {{c1::an increase in the muscle stretch reflexes}}
example: After a spinal cord injury, a light tap on the knee makes the leg kick out forcefully.

text: Illness anxiety disorder: {{c1::Patients focus more on being ill than on actual somatic symptoms}}
example: A woman with no symptoms keeps booking tests, convinced she has cancer.

text: {{c1::Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability from psychosis}}.
example: A man hears voices commenting on his actions and believes the TV is sending him secret messages.

text: Maslow and Rogers believed the central feature of our personality is {{c1::self-concept}}: {{c1::all our thoughts and feelings about ourselves (our answer to 'Who am I?')}}
example: Answering 'Who am I?' with 'a caring nurse, a runner and a shy person' describes your self-concept.

text: {{c1::Eros}} is {{c2::our life drive associated with health, safety, and sex.}}
example: Eating well, exercising and seeking a romantic partner reflect Eros.

text: {{c2::Contralateral control}} is that {{c1::the left brain controls the right side of the body and right brain controls the left side of the body}}
example: A stroke in the left motor cortex paralyses the right arm and leg.

text: {{c1::Serotonin}} is released from {{c2::raphe nuclei}}, which are located {{c2::all over the brainstem}}.
example: MDMA (ecstasy) floods synapses with serotonin released from raphe neuron terminals.

text: {{c1::Moro}} reflex is {{c2::an infant's startle reaction where they fan out their arms}}
extra:
Disappears by 4–6 months
Mnemonic: Moro → Goro (arms fanned out)
example: A loud clap or a sudden drop makes a newborn fling out its arms, then pull them in and cry.

text: {{c2::Adoption studies}} are used to {{c1::compare adopted children to their biological family and adoptive family}}
extra: Helps in environment vs genetics debates
example: In Kety's Danish adoption study, schizophrenia tracked with biological, not adoptive, relatives.

text: Hypotonia is {{c1::decrease in tone of skeletal muscle}}
extra:
LMN sign
Tone is how contracted a muscle is when the person is relaxed
example: An infant with spinal muscular atrophy feels floppy, like a rag doll, when lifted.

text: {{c1::Type theory::... theory}} is the belief that an individual's personality can be quantified into a few unique categories
extra:
Ancient Greek humors
Sheldon’s somatotypes
Divisions into Type A and Type B
Myers-Briggs Type Indicator
example: Sheldon would class a muscular, athletic build as a mesomorph, predicted to be bold and assertive.

text: {{c1::Rationalization}} is {{c2::a neurotic defense mechanism that involves making yourself believe you were not at fault}}
extra:
Can involve false logic and false reasoning
Example: I had to cheat on the test because the professor made it impossible

text: The {{c1::dopamine receptor D4 (DRD4) gene::... gene}} is known to regulate traits such as motivation and thrill seeking, and is also associated with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and addictive and risky behavior
example: Carriers of the long 7-repeat DRD4 allele tend to score higher on novelty seeking.

text: The minimum justification principle states that {{c1::when someone does something with minimal justification, it creates dissonance}}
extra:
Example: buying something you didn't really need
Example: saying "yeah, I wanted to do that" after doing something you didn't really want to do

text: Jeffrey Gray's {{c1::biopsychological theory}} of personality proposes a behavioral approach system (BAS) and a behavioral inhibition system (BIS)
extra:
BAS: regulates appetitive motives (moving toward something desired)
BIS: regulates aversive motives (moving away from something unpleasant)
example: The BAS pulls a student toward a fun party; the BIS holds her back for fear of failing tomorrow's exam.

text: {{c2::Denial}} is {{c1::a pathological defense mechanism where a person pretends something hasn't happened}}.
extra: Example: a person with breast cancer denies that they have it

text: The {{c1::amygdalae}} are almond-shaped groups of nuclei in the temporal lobes that help process memory, decision-making and emotional reactions
example: Patient S.M., with both amygdalae destroyed, felt no fear when handling snakes and spiders.

text: {{c2::Somatic symptom and related}} disorders involve {{c1::distress/disability from symptoms similar to illnesses accompanied by excessive/disproportionate thoughts, feelings, or behaviors about them (with or without a diagnosed medical condition)}}
extra: Example: someone has abdominal pain caused by stress but no physical signs.

text: The self-esteem needs of Maslow's hierarchy include needs to {{c1::feel confident}}, {{c1::recognize achievements}}, and {{c1::feel competent in your skills}}
example: Earning a promotion and being praised by your boss for a job well done.

text: The biologic theory of personality believes that {{c1::important components of personality are inherited/determined by genes}}
example: In the Minnesota study, identical twins raised apart showed strikingly similar personalities.

text: {{c1::Passive aggression}} is {{c2::an immature defense mechanism where you passively express anger towards someone}}
extra: Example: your roommate leaves a pile of dishes, then invites you to a bar; you reply, "I would, but I have a TON of dishes to do today for some reason!"

text:
The functions of the parietal lobe:
  • {{c1::somatosensation (somatosensory cortex)}}
  • {{c1::spatial processing, orientation, and manipulation}}
example: A right parietal stroke can leave a patient ignoring the left side of the plate (hemineglect).

text: Cognitive therapy (CT): {{c1::Identify and change unhealthy thinking, problematic behavior, and distressing emotional responses}}
example: A patient who thinks 'everyone hates me' learns to test that thought against the evidence.

text: {{c1::Body dysmorphic disorder::... disorder}} is characterized by having an unrealistic negative evaluation of one’s appearance
example: A man of normal appearance who spends hours a day checking a 'huge' nose others barely notice.

text: {{c1::Mental disorders}} are {{c2::abnormalities of the mind that cause distress or disability}}
example: Major depression that leaves someone unable to work and withdrawn from friends.

text: Abnormalities of LMN's can cause {{c1::lower motor neuron signs}}
example: A cut peripheral nerve leaves the muscle it supplies weak, floppy and wasting.

text: {{c2::Temperament}} is {{c1::the innate component of personality}} and is {{c1::persistent as an individual ages}}
example: Kagan's highly reactive infants were more likely to be shy, cautious children years later.

text: Puberty causes brain changes in the {{c1::prefrontal cortex}}, {{c1::limbic system}}, and {{c1::corpus callosum}}
example: The corpus callosum thickens through adolescence, speeding communication between the hemispheres.

text:
Steps to muscle stretch reflex (knee jerk):
  1. {{c1::somatosensory neurons (afferent) in muscle spindles synapse in spinal cord after stimulus}}
  2. {{c1::axon sent back out LMN (efferent) to contract muscle}}
  3. {{c1::muscle on top of leg contract (quadricep), muscle on bottom of leg inhibited (hamstring)}}
example: A tap just below the kneecap kicks the lower leg forward before you decide to move.

text:
Characteristics of learned behaviors:
  • {{c1::non-inherited}}
  • {{c1::extrinsic}}
  • {{c1::permutable}}
  • {{c1::adaptable}}
  • {{c1::progressive}}
example: A dog learns to sit on command for treats and can later be retrained to lie down instead.

text: {{c1::Suppression}} is {{c2::a mature defense mechanism where unwanted thoughts are consciously and deliberately pushed out of awareness but can be accessed later}}
example: Deciding not to think about an argument until your exam is over, then dealing with it afterwards.

text: Basal ganglia has an important role in {{c1::motor function}}, {{c1::cognition}}, and {{c1::emotion}}
example: Huntington's disease destroys the caudate, causing jerky movements, dementia and mood changes.

text:
Stages of the sexual response cycle (developed by {{c1::Masters and Johnson}}):
  1. {{c2::excitement}}
  2. {{c2::plateau}}
  3. {{c2::orgasm}}
  4. {{c2::resolution}}
example: Heart rate and breathing rise in excitement, peak at orgasm and return to baseline in resolution.

text: {{c1::Social psychology}} is the branch of psychology that analyzes the situational approach to behavior and emphasizes the influence of social phenomena and interactions with each other
example: In Asch's line studies, people went along with an obviously wrong group answer about a third of the time.

text: Schizophrenia is caused by a combination of {{c1::genetics}} and {{c1::environment}}
example: If one identical twin has schizophrenia, the other has it only about half the time.

text: {{c2::Cardinal}} traits are traits that {{c1::dominate your personality}}
example: Ebenezer Scrooge's greed shapes almost every choice he makes.

text: The {{c1::biopsychosocial}} approach to mental health looks {{c2::at psychological, social, and biological factors to determine causes of mental disorders}}
extra: ex: Is someone depressed because of their environment?
example: A man's depression traced to family history (bio), negative thinking (psycho) and a recent job loss (social).

text: Low dopamine is associated with {{c1::parkinson's disease}}
example: MPTP in a 1980s batch of designer 'synthetic heroin' destroyed users' nigral dopamine neurons, causing Parkinsonism.

text: {{c2::Dopamine}} release in the {{c2::tuberoinfundibular}} pathway inhibits {{c1::prolactin}} release in the {{c1::pituitary}}
example: Haloperidol blocks D<sub>2</sub> receptors in this pathway, raising prolactin and causing galactorrhea.

text: The reticular formation is {{c1::neuron somas scattered throughout the brainstem}}
example: The serotonin-making raphe nuclei lie within the brainstem's reticular formation.

text: {{c1::Intellectualization}} is {{c2::a neurotic defense mechanism that involves taking the intellectual aspect and detaching it from the emotional aspect of a situation.}}
example: Told she has cancer, a woman talks only about survival statistics and treatment protocols, showing no emotion.

text: The basic functions of the nervous system include {{c1::motor function}}, {{c1::senses}}, and {{c1::automatic(reflexes) functions}}
example: Walking (motor), feeling a hot pan (senses) and a knee-jerk (reflex) are all basic functions.

text: Autism spectrum disorder is associated with issues of {{c1::social}} and {{c1::communication}} skills
example: A toddler who avoids eye contact, does not respond to her name and rarely points or gestures.

text: {{c1::Phrenology}} is the outdated belief that each brain area is devoted to a specific personality trait, thought, or emotion, and that developed areas grow and create bumps on the skull
example: Franz Gall felt skull bumps with his fingers to judge traits such as benevolence or combativeness.

text:
In twin/adoption studies, a weak genetic component would show:
  • Identical twins {{c1::=::= or ≠}} fraternal twins
  • Identical twins raised together {{c1::≠::= or ≠}} identical twins raised apart
  • Adopted children = {{c1::adoptive::biological or adoptive}} parents
example: An adopted child raised in Tokyo speaks Japanese like the adoptive parents, whatever the biological parents speak.

text: The behavioral component of attitude is {{c1::how we act or behave toward something}}
extra: Example: I avoid spiders when I see one (behavior).

text: {{c1::Reaction formation}} is {{c2::a neurotic defense mechanism where someone goes beyond denial and begins behaving in the opposite way to which they think or feel}}
extra: Example: a person hiding same-sex attraction adopts a harsh anti-gay attitude to convince themselves of their heterosexuality

text: The two classification systems of mental health are {{c1::ICD-10}} and {{c1::DSM-5}}
example: A US psychiatrist diagnoses depression with DSM-5 criteria but bills insurance with an ICD-10 code such as F32.

text: Histamine is released from the {{c1::hypothalamus}} to the {{c1::cerebral cortex}}
example: First-generation antihistamines like diphenhydramine enter the brain and cause drowsiness.

text: {{c1::Obsessive-Compulsive and Related}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability from obsessions or compulsions}}
example: Hoarding disorder: a woman fills her home with old newspapers she cannot bring herself to throw away.

text: {{c1::Oxidopamine}} destroys dopamine and norepinephrine neurons to model Parkinson's disease in lesion studies
example: Injecting oxidopamine (6-OHDA) into one side of a rat's substantia nigra produces Parkinson-like motor deficits.

text: {{c1::Surface}} traits of personality are very obvious and can be easily identified by other people, whereas {{c1::source}} traits are less visible to other people and appear to underlie several different aspects of behavior
example: Cattell: frequent party-going is a surface trait arising from the deeper source trait of social boldness.

text:
People with depression have a decreased level of:
  • {{c1::serotonin}}
  • {{c1::norepinephrine}}
  • {{c1::activity in the mesolimbic pathway}}
  • {{c1::activity in prefrontal cortex}}
example: SSRIs such as sertraline and SNRIs such as venlafaxine treat depression by raising serotonin and norepinephrine.

text: Glycine primarily acts on the {{c1::spinal cord}}
example: Tetanus toxin blocks glycine release in the spinal cord, causing lockjaw and rigid spasms.

text: {{c2::The reality principle}} states that {{c1::when individuals become mature, they sacrifice short term reward and replace it with long term gratification}}
example: In the marshmallow test, children who waited about 15 minutes got two marshmallows instead of one.

text: Dopamine produced in the arcuate nucleus {{c1::controls prolactin release::function}}
example: A tumour compressing the pituitary stalk blocks arcuate dopamine, so prolactin rises (stalk effect).

text: Personality is believed to be {{c1::constant::ever-changing or constant}} over a person's lifetime
example: Someone outgoing in high school is usually still outgoing at their 30-year reunion.

text: {{c1::Fixation}} is when an adult is stuck in one of Freud's developmental stages
extra: Example: someone fixated at the oral stage might show oral traits such as smoking or being overly talkative

text: The {{c1::house money effect}} states that after a prior gain, people become more open to assuming risk since the new money is not treated as one's own
extra: It's the tendency of individual investors to take on greater risks when investing with profits attained
example: A gambler up $500 at blackjack bets it all on one hand because it feels like the casino's money.

text: {{c1::Amotivation}} is the lack of motivation
extra: Very similar to avolition, which is usually described as a negative symptom of schizophrenia
example: A student who sees no point in school stops attending class and does not care about failing.

text: {{c1::Co-rumination}} is excessively discussing and dwelling on problems and negative feelings with a roommate/partner/friend, which can increase the likelihood of depression spreading between them
example: Two roommates spend every night rehashing their breakups, and both grow more depressed.

text: Humanists believe humans strive for {{c1::self-actualization}}
example: Maslow named Abraham Lincoln and Eleanor Roosevelt as examples of self-actualized people.

text: {{c1::Thanatos}} is {{c2::our death drive associated with self-destructive and harmful behaviors}}
example: A man who keeps binge drinking and driving recklessly after several crashes shows Thanatos at work.

text: The foot-in-the-door phenomenon is {{c1::that humans have a tendency to agree to small actions first and eventually comply to larger ones.}}
example: Freedman and Fraser: homeowners who first signed a petition were far likelier to later accept a big yard sign.

text: The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) is a nucleus in the {{c1::hypothalamus}} whose neurons produce {{c1::ADH & oxytocin::x2}}
example: A suckling baby triggers PVN oxytocin release, which ejects milk from the breast.

text:
The four types of defense mechanisms are:
  • {{c1::pathological}}
  • {{c1::immature}}
  • {{c1::mature}}
  • {{c1::neurotic}}
example: Denial (pathological), projection (immature), repression (neurotic), humor (mature).

text: Clonus is {{c1::rhythmic contractions of antagonist muscles}}
example: Sharply dorsiflexing a stroke patient's foot makes the ankle beat rhythmically several times.

text: Delusions of grandeur are {{c1::beliefs that one is a famous/important figure or that they have a super power}}
example: A patient insists he is Jesus Christ and can heal the sick by touch.

text: {{c1::Personality}} is the unique combination of patterns that influence behavior, thought, motivation, and emotion in a human being
example: One person reliably cracks jokes at parties while another stays quiet, across years and settings.

text: In {{c1::the theory of planned behavior::theory}}, intentions are based on {{c2::attitudes}}, {{c2::subjective norms}}, and {{c2::perceived behavioral control}}
extra:
Attitudes: toward the behavior (e.g. I like to study)
Subjective norms: what others think of the behavior (e.g. my friends don't like to study)
Perceived behavioral control: how easy or hard the behavior is (e.g. I work 50 hours this week, so I can't study as much)

text: Cluster B personality disorders are associated with {{c1::dramatic, emotional, and erratic traits}}
example: A woman who swings from idolizing to hating a partner and threatens self-harm when he leaves (borderline).

text: Personality disorders are categorized into {{c1::cluster A}}, {{c1::cluster B}} and {{c1::cluster C}}
example: Paranoid is cluster A (weird), borderline is cluster B (wild), avoidant is cluster C (worried).

text: {{c1::Avoidant personality}} disorder includes individuals who {{c2::feel inadequate and try to avoid putting themselves in situations where they can be criticized}}
extra: This doesn't mean they don't wish they could hang out with everyone
example: A woman longs for friends but declines every invitation for fear of being judged.

text: Puberty begins at approximately {{c1::13}} y/o in males and {{c1::11}} y/o in females
example: A girl's breast budding often begins around 10–11, while a boy's voice usually breaks around 13–14.

text: A {{c2::repressed memory}} is a memory that is {{c1::unconsciously blocked due to it being associated with high levels of stress}} and is commonly associated with individuals who have {{c1::PTSD}}
example: A combat veteran cannot recall the ambush in which his friends were killed.

text: {{c2::Paranoid personality}} disorder includes individuals {{c1::with profound distrust and suspicion of other people}}
example: A man refuses to tell coworkers his birthday, sure they will use it against him.

text: {{c2::Traits}} are {{c1::distinguishing qualities and characteristics that compose us}}
example: A person's brown eyes, height and shyness are all traits.

text: Inhibition of CCK may lead to {{c1::eating without feeling full}}
example: Rats given a CCK receptor blocker eat larger meals before they stop.

text: Positive feedback is when {{c1::the output of a process further stimulates (amplifies) that same process}}
example: During labour, oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, which push the baby down and trigger more oxytocin release.

text: Carl Rogers believed that Maslow's hierarchy {{c1::described qualities that are nurtured early in life}} and that {{c1::self-actualization is a constant growth process nurtured in growth-promoting climates}}
example: A child raised by warm, accepting parents keeps growing toward her potential well into adulthood.

text: Epinephrine and norepinephrine maintain {{c1::wakefulness}} and mediate the {{c1::fight / flight responses}}
example: A surge of adrenaline when a car swerves toward you raises your heart rate and sharpens alertness.

text: {{c1::Neurotransmitters}} are released by neurons to carry a signal
example: Acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction makes a skeletal muscle contract.

text: According to Hans Eysenck, {{c1::extraverts::introverts or extraverts}} seek excitement and social activity in an effort to heighten their arousal level, whereas {{c1::introverts::introverts or extraverts}} tend to avoid social situations in an effort to keep such arousal to a minimum
example: An extravert unwinds at a loud party; an introvert recharges at home with a book.

text: Brain function can be analyzed by {{c1::electroencephalogram (EEG)}} and {{c1::magnetoencephalogram (MEG) (SQUIDS)}}
example: EEG and MEG catch the brain's response to a sound within milliseconds of it playing.

text: The pathological defense mechanisms include {{c1::denial}}
example: An alcoholic insists he has no drinking problem despite losing his job over it.

text: Cortical reaction is when {{c1::calcium floods into the cell after acrosome reaction to prevent other sperm from binding and increase metabolism of zygote}}
example: If cortical granules fail to release, two sperm can enter the egg, giving a triploid zygote.

text: {{c2::Parkinson's disease}} is associated with {{c1::motor abnormalities}} and {{c1::mental dysfunctions}}
extra:
Motor abnormalities: tremor, abnormal gait, poor balance, stiff muscles
Cognitive symptoms develop later
example: Michael J. Fox was diagnosed with Parkinson's at 29 after noticing a twitch in his little finger.

text: {{c1::The 5 factor model of personality::Theory}} believes that {{c2::there are 5 big personality traits that include openness, conscientiousness, extroversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism}}
example: A tidy, punctual student who plans every week ahead scores high in conscientiousness.

text: The immature defense mechanisms include {{c2::projection}} and {{c2::passive aggression}}
extra: mnemonic: it is immature to say pp
example: Accusing your partner of cheating when you cheat (projection); 'forgetting' a coworker's message (passive aggression).

text:
Monozygotic twins share {{c1::100}}% of genes
Dizygotic twins share {{c1::50}}% of genes
example: The first successful kidney transplant (1954) worked because donor and recipient were identical twins.

text: {{c1::Neuroleptics::medication}}: relieve only positive symptoms and worsen or maintain negative symptoms
example: Haloperidol quiets hallucinations but leaves a patient's flat affect and apathy untouched.

text: {{c1::The situational approach to behavior}} states that {{c2::behavior is dependent on a particular situation we are placed in}}
example: A loud, joking student becomes quiet and formal during a job interview.

text: {{c2::Narcissistic personality}} disorder includes individuals who {{c1::have huge egos}} and {{c1::need admiration/praise}}
example: A manager who demands constant praise, takes credit for others' work and cannot handle criticism.

text: {{c2::Elimination}} disorders involve {{c1::distress/disability from urinating or defecating at inappropriate times or places}}
example: Enuresis: a 7-year-old who still wets the bed several nights a week.

text: {{c1::Mania}} is a state of high optimism, euphoria, poor judgement, etc
example: A woman awake for 3 days spends $20,000 on a sports car, convinced she is about to become a pop star.

text: A person with {{c1::dissociative amnesia}} can’t recall past experiences
example: A soldier who cannot remember a deadly ambush he survived, though his other memories are intact.

text: {{c1::Affect}} is how mood is displayed to others, such as crying.
example: At a funeral, a widow's sad mood shows in her affect: tears, slumped posture and a quiet voice.

text: Teenagers express {{c2::poor judgement}} as a result of {{c1::an underdeveloped prefrontal cortex}}
example: A 16-year-old takes far more driving risks with friends in the car than when driving alone.

text: {{c1::Cranial nerves::... nerves}} arise from the brain and are distributed to the head, neck, and face
example: The facial nerve (CN VII) lets you smile and close your eyes.

text: Cluster A personality disorders are classified by {{c1::odd and eccentric traits}}
example: A loner who believes in telepathy and dresses oddly (schizotypal).

text: Jung's theory of the collective unconscious states that personality is influenced by {{c1::archetypes}}
example: The hero, the wise old man and the mother figure recur in myths across unrelated cultures.

text: {{c1::The drive reduction theory}} AKA {{c1::drive theory}} states that {{c2::motivation focuses on drives and needs to maintain homeostasis}}
example: Being dehydrated creates thirst, which drives you to drink until fluid balance is restored.

text: Two techniques to help analyze brain {{c1::structure::Structure or Function}} are {{c2::computerized axial tomography (CAT)}} and {{c2::magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)}}
example: MRI reveals the white matter plaques of multiple sclerosis; a CT scan shows a skull fracture.

text: MRI analyzes brain structure using {{c1::radio waves exposed to a magnetic field to analyze signals released as atoms realign with the magnetic field}}
example: Patients with older pacemakers or metal fragments often cannot have an MRI because of its strong magnet.

text: The {{c1::Id}} is the {{c2::reservoir of psychic energy}} and {{c2::seeks instant gratification of internal needs or external stimulation}}. It is {{c2::unconscious::unconscious or conscious}}.
example: A hungry toddler grabs a cookie off a stranger's plate the moment he sees it.

text:
Characteristics of innate behavior:
  • {{c1::inherited}}
  • {{c1::intrinsic}}
  • {{c1::stereotypic}}
  • {{c1::inflexible}}
  • {{c1::consummate}}
example: A greylag goose rolls a displaced egg back with the same motion every time, even if the egg is removed mid-roll.

text: The safety needs of Maslow's hierarchy are needs for {{c1::security and protection, including financial safety, health, and property}}
example: Buying health insurance and locking your doors at night.

text: Alzheimer's is a degenerative brain disorder linked to a loss of {{c1::acetylcholine}} in neurons that link to the {{c1::hippocampus}}
extra: Alzheimer's is a type of dementia and causes memory loss
example: Donepezil, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, boosts acetylcholine to ease Alzheimer's memory loss.

text: Hans Eysenck's three dimensions of personality include {{c1::psychoticism}}, {{c1::extroversion}}, and {{c1::neuroticism}}
example: An anxious, shy rule-follower: high neuroticism, low extroversion, low psychoticism.

text: {{c2::Intrinsic motivation}} is {{c1::motivation driven by internal rewards}}
extra: Example: doing something because you enjoy doing it
example: Practising guitar for hours because you love playing, with no audience and no pay.

text: {{c1::Lower motor neurons (LMN)}} are {{c2::efferent neurons of the PNS that go from the spinal cord to a muscle to control it}}
example: A ventral horn motor neuron whose axon leaves the cord to make the biceps contract.

text: {{c2::Dissociative identity disorder}} is {{c1::when two or more distinct personalities exist in a single body}}
example: Chris Costner Sizemore, the real woman behind The Three Faces of Eve, switched among distinct personalities.

text: Persistent depressive disorder is dysthymia for at least {{c1::2}} years that doesn’t meet criteria for major depressive disorder
extra: PDD is a mild but long-term form of depression
example: A woman who has felt low, tired and pessimistic most days for 3 years without a major depressive episode.

text: Upper motor neurons are found in {{c1::the cerebral cortex}} and synapse on {{c1::LMNs in the brainstem or spinal cord}}
example: Betz cells in the primary motor cortex send axons down to LMNs in the spinal cord.

text: Since brain structures build on top of each other as we evolve, the inner brain contains {{c1::older structures that regulate basic needs}}
example: The medulla, among the oldest brain parts, keeps a person breathing even in a deep coma.

text: Fertilization occurs at week {{c1::2}} after last menstrual period
example: In a 28-day cycle, ovulation and fertilization happen around day 14 after the last period began.

text: The main neurotransmitters in the {{c2::peripheral}} nervous system are {{c1::acetylcholine}} and {{c1::norepinephrine}}
example: ACh from the vagus nerve slows the heart; norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves speeds it up.

text: Someone in a dissociative fugue will lose awareness of their {{c1::identity}} or other important autobiographical information and also engages in some form of {{c1::unexpected travel}}
example: A man vanishes from home and turns up weeks later in another city under a new name, unaware of his past.

text: {{c1::Social anxiety}} disorder involves irrational anxiety/fear from everyday interactions
example: A student who skips class presentations and avoids parties for fear of embarrassing herself.

text: {{c1::The principle of aggregation}} states that {{c2::the effects of an attitude are more apparent when we look at average behavior instead of isolated acts}}
example: A pro-environment person may drive one day, but over a year recycles and cycles far more than average.

text: {{c1::Neurons}} are the basic working unit of the brain: specialized cells that transmit information to other nerve cells, muscle, or gland cells
example: A spinal motor neuron sends a signal down its axon that makes a leg muscle contract.

text: {{c1::The pleasure principle}} states that {{c2::humans behave to gain pleasure or avoid pain}}
example: A child eats candy and refuses vegetables simply because candy tastes good.

text:
Stages of Maslow's hierarchy of needs, from bottom to top:
  • {{c1::physiological}}
  • {{c1::safety}}
  • {{c1::love}}
  • {{c1::self esteem}}
  • {{c1::self actualization}}
example: Food, then a safe home, then friends, then a promotion, then writing the novel you always dreamed of.

text: {{c1::Dependent stressors}} are {{c2::stressors that are, at least in part, due to an individuals characteristics or behaviors}}
example: Getting fired after repeatedly arriving late, or a breakup caused by your own constant arguing.

text:
Gross motor skills involve {{c1::large::large vs small}} muscles
Fine motor skills involve {{c1::small::large vs small}} muscles
example: Kicking a ball uses gross motor skills; picking up a Cheerio with a pincer grasp uses fine motor skills.

text: Thyroid gland regulates {{c1::body metabolism}}
example: Graves' disease makes the thyroid overactive, causing weight loss, heat intolerance and a racing heart.

text: Carl Rogers believed that growth is nurtured when {{c1::an individual is genuine}} and {{c1::through acceptance}}
extra:
genuine = open and revealing about themselves without fear of being wrong
acceptance = positive regard for others and open up and learn without fear of others looking at us differently
example: A therapist who admits her own mistakes and accepts a client's anger without judging helps the client grow.

text: {{c1::Projective identification}} is when {{c2::a person targeted with projection can start believing and having thoughts of the attributes projected on to them}}.
extra: Example: you feel stupid, so you call someone else stupid, and over time they begin to feel stupid

text: The 3 main types of innate behavior are {{c1::reflexes}}, {{c1::orientation behaviors}}, and {{c1::fixed-action patterns (FAP)}}
example: Knee-jerk (reflex), a moth flying toward a lamp (orientation), a goose rolling back a stray egg (FAP).

text: Social psychology focuses on the interactions between {{c1::individuals}} and {{c1::their environment}}
example: In Milgram's study, 65% of ordinary people gave the maximum 450 V shock when an experimenter insisted.

text: {{c2::Schizotypal personality}} disorder includes individuals with {{c1::odd beliefs and magical thinking}}
example: A woman who believes she can read strangers' minds and wears a cape to the grocery store.

text: Fasciculations are {{c1::involuntary twitches of skeletal muscle}}
example: In ALS, ripples of twitching are visible under the skin of the tongue and arms.

text: Inherited traits are {{c1::traits passed down from parents to children}}
Pathological defense mechanisms are defense mechanisms that {{c1::distort reality}}
example: A man told he has terminal cancer insists he is perfectly healthy and signs up for a marathon.

text: The muscle stretch reflex causes a muscle to {{c1::contract after it is stretched too far to protect it}}
example: A tap on the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, which contracts in a knee jerk.

text: The three components that shape our attitude are {{c1::affective}}, {{c1::behavioral}}, and {{c1::cognitive}}
example: Liking dogs (affective), adopting one (behavioral), and believing dogs are loyal (cognitive).

text:
Functions of reticular formation:
  • {{c1::aids in alertness}}
  • {{c1::aids sleep/wake cycle}}
  • {{c1::helps filter information to the thalamus}}
  • {{c1::some autonomic functions}}
example: You sleep through traffic noise but wake instantly to your baby's cry as the reticular system filters input.

text: {{c1::Sleep-wake}} disorders result in {{c2::distress/disability from sleep related issues}}
extra: includes insomnia, breathing-related sleep disorders, abnormal behaviors during sleep
example: Obstructive sleep apnea: a man who snores stops breathing repeatedly at night and is exhausted all day.

text: Depression is influenced by {{c1::biological}}, {{c1::psychological}}, and {{c1::sociocultural/environmental}} factors
example: Genetic risk (biological), negative thinking (psychological) and poverty (sociocultural) combine to trigger depression.

text: {{c1::Regression}} is {{c2::a neurotic defense mechanism that involves acting like a baby in stressful situations}}
extra:
Not necessarily a baby, but an earlier stage of development
Example: teens may giggle uncontrollably in a stressful situation with the opposite sex

text: Delusions of reference are {{c1::when a neutral environmental event is believed to have a special/personal meaning}}
extra: ex: Believing a remark heard on TV is directed specifically at the person watching

text:
Problems with adoption studies include that:
  • {{c1::there is usually incomplete info about biological families}}
  • {{c1::that adoption typically isn't random (matched with someone similar to biological family)}}
example: Agencies often place a child with a family of similar race and class to the birth parents.

text:
{{c1::The humanistic theory::Theory}}, developed by {{c1::Carl Rogers::Psychologist, client-centered therapy}}, focuses on the ideas that:
  • {{c2::behavior is conscious}}
  • {{c2::humans are inherently good}}
  • {{c2::we are self-motivated to improve}}
  • that we have {{c2::free will}}
example: A Rogerian therapist reflects a client's feelings with unconditional positive regard, trusting the client to grow.

text: Symptoms of depression include {{c1::feelings of hopelessness}} and {{c1::loss of interest in activities}}
example: A former keen runner stops running entirely and says nothing will ever get better.

text: The embryonic mesencephalon becomes {{c1::the midbrain}}
example: The superior and inferior colliculi and the substantia nigra all arise from the mesencephalon.

text: Autism spectrum disorder is not a {{c1::birth defect}}
example: Unlike a cleft lip seen at birth, autism shows up later as delayed speech and poor eye contact in a toddler.

text: {{c1::Haloperidol}} is an antipsychotic drug medication used to treat schizophrenia
example: Haloperidol blocks dopamine D<sub>2</sub> receptors, easing hallucinations but risking tardive dyskinesia.

text: The function of behavior is to {{c1::keep homeostasis}}
example: Feeling cold, you put on a jacket to bring your body temperature back toward 37 °C.

text: The #1 reason individuals reach out for mental health services is {{c1::depression}}
example: About 1 in 6 US adults will have major depression at some point in their life.

text: {{c1::Tonic neck}} reflex is when {{c2::a baby's head is turned, the arm on that side straightens while the other arm bends}}
example: A newborn lying with head turned right takes a fencer's pose: right arm straight, left arm bent.

text: PVN neurons project directly to the {{c1::posterior pituitary}} and release {{c1::oxytocin or vasopressin::x2}}
example: Dehydration after a marathon triggers vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary to conserve water.

text: {{c1::Behavioral genetics}} looks at {{c2::the genetic component to behavior}}
example: Twin studies estimate the heritability of ADHD at about 70–80%.

text: The {{c1::ego}} functions to {{c2::mediate between the innate desires of the id and the perfection-seeking superego}}. It is {{c2::unconscious and conscious::unconscious or conscious}}.
example: Craving cake, you decide to have a slice after dinner rather than stealing one now or refusing it forever.

text:
Aspects of {{c2::knowledge acquisition}} in social cognitive theory:
  • {{c1::attention}}
  • {{c1::memory}}
  • {{c1::imitation}}
  • {{c1::motivation}}
extra:
Mnemonic: AM I Motivated?
Example: to learn to draw a star, you need enough attention, the memory to remember it, the ability to imitate it, and the motivation to do it.

text: The {{c1::biomedical}} approach to mental health focuses {{c2::on biology and physical abnormalities}}
extra: ex: Abnormalities of the cells in the brain might be causing a mental disorder
example: Treating depression with an SSRI because it is attributed to low serotonin.

text: {{c2::Attitude}} is {{c1::a learned tendency to evaluate things in a certain way}}
extra: evaluate people, issues, events, objects, etc
example: After years of hearing that vegetables are healthy, you come to rate salads favourably.

text: High dopamine is associated with {{c1::schizophrenia}}
example: Chlorpromazine, the first antipsychotic, eases hallucinations by blocking dopamine D<sub>2</sub> receptors.

text: {{c2::Generalized anxiety disorder}} describes a person who {{c1::has a general state that is tense and uneasy to a degree that influences their life. It also must last for 6 months or more.}}
example: A mother who for a year has worried daily about money, her kids' safety and her health, unable to relax.

text: {{c2::Anxiety}} disorders are {{c1::distress/disability from abnormal worry or fears}}. Examples include {{c1::generalized anxiety disorder}} and {{c1::panic disorder}}
example: A student who has worried constantly about grades, health and money for over 6 months has GAD.

text: {{c1::Fixed-action patterns}} are {{c2::sequences of coordinated movement performed without interruption}}
extra:
Similar to a reflex but more complicated
Example: any prey-sized movement near a mantis elicits a strike that, once initiated, cannot be altered

text: {{c1::Expectancy-value theory::... theory}} states that the amount of motivation for a task is based on the expectation of success and the value of that success
example: A student who believes she can ace organic chemistry and needs it for med school studies hard for it.

text: Acquired traits are {{c1::learned traits that come from experience with the environment}}
example: Speaking fluent French after years of living in Paris is an acquired trait.

text: {{c2::Personality}} disorders involve {{c1::distress/disability related to personality patterns outside accepted societal norms}}
example: Antisocial personality disorder: a man repeatedly lies, steals and feels no remorse for hurting others.

text:
The brainstem includes the:
  • {{c1::midbrain}}
  • {{c1::pons}}
  • {{c1::medulla oblongata}}
  • {{c1::reticular formation}}
example: A brainstem stroke can cause locked-in syndrome: fully awake but able to move only the eyes.

text: {{c2::Extrinsic motivation}} is {{c1::motivation to do something based on an external reward or to avoid punishment}}
example: Working overtime only for the holiday bonus, or finishing homework just to avoid detention.

text: {{c2::Complex behavior}} is {{c1::a combination of innate and learned behavior}}
extra: Example: an insect innately knows how to fly, but becomes more efficient through learning

text: {{c1::Lewy body dementia}} is a disease associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain
extra: These deposits, called Lewy bodies, affect chemicals in the brain whose changes, in turn, can lead to problems with thinking, movement, behavior, and mood
example: A 72-year-old with fluctuating confusion, vivid visual hallucinations and a Parkinsonian shuffle.

text: {{c1::Self-determination theory::... theory}} is a theory of human motivation and personality and emphasizes 3 universal needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness
example: A nurse who picks her shifts (autonomy), masters IV lines (competence) and bonds with her team (relatedness).

text:
The functions of the temporal lobe:
  • {{c1::sound processing (auditory cortex)}}
  • {{c1::speech perception (wernicke's area)}}
  • {{c1::memory (hippocampus)}}
  • {{c1::emotion (limbic system)}}
extra: mnemonic: Without the temporal lobe, you are a M E S S
example: H.M. could no longer form new memories after surgeons removed both his medial temporal lobes.

text: {{c2::Innate behavioral traits}} are {{c1::genetically programmed behavior present at birth that requires no experience with the environment}}
example: A spider raised in isolation spins its species' typical web on the first try without ever seeing one.

text: Abnormalities in the neural pathways of the {{c1::raphe nuclei}}, {{c1::locus coeruleus}}, and {{c1::VTA}} are implicated in depression
example: SSRIs such as fluoxetine treat depression by boosting serotonin from raphe nuclei neurons.

text: The {{c1::critical period}} and {{c1::sensitive period}} are maturational stages in the lifespan of an organism during which the nervous system is especially sensitive to certain environmental stimuli
extra: "Critical period" also relates to the ability to acquire one's first language
example: Lorenz's goslings imprinted on him during the first hours after hatching and followed him everywhere.

text:
Posterior pituitary hormones:
  • {{c1::ADH (vasopressin)}}
  • {{c1::Oxytocin}}
example: Pitocin, a synthetic oxytocin, is given to induce labour contractions.

text: A problem with twin studies is that {{c1::identical twins are typically treated more similarly than fraternal twins}}
example: Parents dress identical twins alike and expect the same grades from them, inflating their similarity.

text: {{c2::Ethology}} focuses on {{c1::the observation of animal behaviors}}
example: Konrad Lorenz watched goslings imprint on him and follow him around as if he were their mother.

text:
Biological factors for {{c1::bipolar disorders}} include:
  • High norepinephrine
  • Abnormal serotonin
  • Family history
example: A child with a parent who has bipolar I disorder is several times more likely than average to develop it.

text: {{c1::Acetylcholine}} is released from the {{c2::nucleus basalis}} and {{c2::septal nuclei}} in the {{c2::frontal}} lobe
example: Scopolamine, which blocks acetylcholine in the brain, can cause confusion and memory lapses.

text: {{c2::Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs}} states that {{c1::we must satisfy needs from bottom to top, where basic needs are at the bottom}}
example: A starving refugee focuses on finding food before worrying about friendships or self-esteem.

text: {{c1::Behavior}} is {{c2::coordinated internal and external response of an organism to their environment}}
example: A deer hears a twig snap: its heart rate rises and it bolts into the trees.

text: {{c2::Factitious disorder/Munchausen syndrome by proxy}} is {{c1::when one person makes another person look ill so they can take care of them}}.
extra: Can cause serious injury or even death of the person receiving the false care
example: Gypsy Rose Blanchard's mother made her use a wheelchair and feeding tube for illnesses she never had.

text: Pacinian corpuscles detect {{c1::deep pressure}} and {{c1::vibration}}
example: Feeling your phone buzz in your pocket relies on Pacinian corpuscles.

text: {{c1::Hans Eysenck::psychologist}} believed that {{c2::we have 3 dimensions of personality that include all traits.}}
example: Eysenck would rate a calm, rule-following party lover as high extroversion, low neuroticism, low psychoticism.

text: {{c1::Neurocognitive}} disorders involve {{c2::loss of cognitive/other function of the brain after the nervous system has developed}}. They include {{c2::delirium}} and {{c2::dementia}}
example: An 80-year-old with Alzheimer's disease can no longer remember her grandchildren's names.

text: {{c1::EEG}} is {{c2::noninvasive monitoring of the electrical activity of the brain using electrodes on the scalp}}
example: A child with absence seizures shows 3-per-second spike-and-wave bursts on EEG.

text: {{c1::Neurodevelopmental}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability due to abnormality in development of the nervous system}}. Examples include {{c2::autism spectrum disorders}}, {{c2::intellectual disabilities}}, and {{c2::ADHD}}
example: A 7-year-old with ADHD who cannot stay seated in class and keeps blurting out answers.

text: PVN neurons are activated by {{c1::stressful changes}}
example: Facing a public speech activates PVN neurons that release CRH, starting the cortisol stress response.

text: Extensor plantar response is {{c1::when your toes extend up when an object scrapes along your foot, as opposed to the normal response of curling toes down}}
example: A positive Babinski sign is normal in infants under about 1–2 years but signals UMN damage in adults.

text: {{c1::The corticospinal tract}} is {{c2::when UMN's of the cerebral cortex synapse on LMN's in the spinal cord}}
example: A stroke cutting the corticospinal tract in the internal capsule weakens the opposite arm and leg.

text: The {{c1::opponent-process theory::... theory}} views emotions as pairs of opposites. For example, fear/relief or pleasure/pain
extra:
When one emotion is experienced, the other is suppressed
Explains motivation for drug use: as drug use increases, the body counteracts its effects, leading to tolerance and uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms
example: After the terror of a first skydive ends, jumpers feel an intense rush of relief and elation.

text: {{c1::Kainic acid}} is used to destroy cell bodies but leave passing axons alone during lesion studies
example: Kainic acid injected into a rat's hippocampus kills its neurons but spares the axons passing through.

text:
Upper motor neuron signs:
  • {{c1::Hyperreflexia}}
  • {{c1::Clonus}}
  • {{c1::Hypertonia}}
  • {{c1::Extensor Plantar Response}}
example: After a stroke, a patient's arm is stiff, the knee jerk is brisk and the big toe goes up on Babinski testing.

text:
In twin/adoption studies, a strong genetic component would show:
  • Identical twins {{c1::≠::= or ≠}} fraternal twins
  • Identical twins raised together {{c1::=::= or ≠}} identical twins raised apart
  • Adopted children = {{c1::biological::biological or adoptive}} parents
example: Adopted children's adult weight tracks their biological parents' BMI, not their adoptive parents'.

text:
During sex:
  • {{c2::oxytocin::hormone}} {{c1::facilitates bonds and feelings of connectedness after orgasm}}
  • {{c2::prolactin::hormone}} {{c1::relieves sexual arousal after orgasm}}
  • {{c2::endorphins::hormone}} {{c1::produce feelings of euphoria and pleasure}}
example: Cuddling after orgasm feels intimate partly because oxytocin released at climax promotes bonding.

text: The affective component of attitude is {{c1::how we feel or have emotion about something}}
extra: Example: I'm scared of spiders (emotion), and this feeling shapes my attitude toward them.

text: Lower motor neuron cell bodies are located in {{c1::the spinal cord}} and terminate in {{c1::skeletal muscle}}
example: LMNs to the quadriceps have cell bodies in the L2–L4 ventral horn and end on the thigh muscle.

text: A {{c2::drive}} is {{c1::an aroused state caused by survival needs}}
extra: we act to fulfill our biological drives
example: After skipping lunch, hunger sends you straight to the fridge when you get home.

text: {{c1::Humor}} is {{c2::a mature defense mechanism where people express jokes/humor to alleviate feelings }}
example: Joking with nurses about the hospital food while waiting for a frightening biopsy result.

text: {{c2::MEG}} requires {{c1::a large machine and special room}} and records {{c1::magnetic fields produced by electric currents in the brain}}
example: MEG runs inside a magnetically shielded room, with SQUID sensors cooled by liquid helium.

text: {{c1::The evolutionary approach (motivation)}} states that {{c2::instincts play a role in motivation}} and that humans are motivated by {{c2::trying to survive}}
example: An innate fear of snakes and heights motivates avoidance that helped our ancestors survive.

text:
Schizophrenia:
  • {{c2::Mesolimbic::Pathway}} - {{c1::Positive}} effects
  • {{c2::Mesocortical::Pathway}} - {{c1::Negative}} effects
extra: Mesolimbic ↑ DA = positive sx; Mesocortical ↓ DA = negative sx
example: Amphetamine abuse, which floods mesolimbic dopamine, can trigger paranoid hallucinations.

text:
Psychoanalytic theory says that personality is shaped by:
  • {{c1::childhood experiences}}
  • {{c1::unconscious thoughts/desires}}
  • {{c1::feelings}}
  • {{c1::past memories}}
example: A psychoanalyst links a man's distrust of women to unresolved childhood conflict with his mother.

text: Secondary drives stem from {{c1::learning}}
example: Working overtime for money, which you value only because you learned what it buys.

text: Appearance of primitive (infant) reflexes in adults signifies {{c1::serious medical problems}}
example: A grasp reflex returning in an adult can signal frontal lobe damage, as in advanced dementia or stroke.

text: {{c2::A manic episode}} is {{c1::a period of abnormally elevated mood and increased energy}} that lasts at least {{c1::7}} days and can {{c1::be severe enough to cause impairment in functioning}}
example: For 10 days a man barely sleeps, talks nonstop and maxes out credit cards until his family hospitalizes him.

text: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5) categorizes mental disorders based on {{c1::symptoms}}
example: Major depressive disorder requires at least 5 of 9 listed symptoms lasting at least 2 weeks.

text:
Function of pons:
{{c1::regulates waking and relaxing}}
example: Pontine signals switch on REM sleep and the muscle paralysis that stops you acting out dreams.
