text: {{c1::Bipolar and related}} disorders are {{c2::disorders associated with periods of abnormally elevated mood (mania or hypomania), often alternating with abnormally negative (depressive) moods}}
example: A man sleeps 2 hours a night for a week, spends his savings on impulse, then crashes into depression.

text: {{c2::Social Psychology}} looks at {{c1::how individuals think, feel, and behave in social interactions}}
example: Darley and Latané found people were less likely to help in an emergency when more bystanders were present.

text: Compulsions are {{c1::activities that one must do and are often related to obsession}}
extra: Ex. obsession with hands being dirty, compulsion to wash them many times a day.

text: {{c1::PET scans}} {{c2::inject radioactively labeled glucose into the bloodstream to analyze which brain areas are active at a given point of time}}
extra: Active cells will use more glucose
example: FDG-PET shows reduced glucose use in the temporal and parietal lobes in Alzheimer's disease.

text: {{c1::Optimum arousal theory}} states that {{c2::people are motivated to maintain an optimal (moderate) level of arousal}}
extra:
Humans seek an optimal (not maximal) level of arousal; under-aroused people seek stimulation.
Example: people enjoy amusement parks.
example: A bored student puts on music to study but turns it off once a noisy roommate comes home.

text: {{c1::The Hawthorne effect}} is when individuals {{c2::modify or improve an aspect of their behavior in response to their awareness of being observed}}
extra: Example: you work harder when you know your boss is watching

text: The connectome is a {{c1::neural map of the connections within the brain}}
example: The roundworm C. elegans connectome maps all 302 of its neurons and their roughly 7,000 synapses.

text: {{c1::Babinski}} reflex is when {{c2::babies fan their toes outward when their soles are stroked}}
extra: typically disappears before 12 months, if persistent then possible UMN sign
example: Stroking the sole of a 3-month-old makes the big toe go up and the other toes fan out.

text: The self-actualization needs of Maslow's hierarchy include {{c1::reaching one's maximum potential and achieving the most one can be}}
extra: This differs from person to person: each individual has their own ideal to strive toward (e.g. being an ideal parent, artist or athlete).
example: An accountant leaves her job at 50 to become the painter she always wanted to be.

text:
{{c2::Antisocial personality}} disorder is when individuals:
  • {{c1::have little or no regard for others}}
  • {{c1::commit crimes, show no remorse, and are inconsiderate}}
example: A con man swindles elderly people out of their savings and laughs about it afterwards.

text: {{c1::Sexual dysfunction}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability from abnormalities in performance of sexual activities}}
example: Erectile disorder: a man who for months cannot keep an erection and is distressed by it.

text: A {{c2::need}} is {{c1::a lack or deprivation that will energize a drive (aroused state)}}
Agoraphobia: {{c1::Fear of open spaces/crowds}}
example: A woman avoids malls, buses and concerts for fear she could not escape if panic struck.

text: Primary drives are related to {{c1::biological processes}}
example: Thirst after a long run sends you straight to the water fountain.

text: Low serotonin is associated with {{c1::depression}}
example: SSRIs such as sertraline treat depression by raising synaptic serotonin.

text:
Steps to fertilization:
{{c1::sperm binding}}
↓
{{c1::acrosome reaction}}
↓
{{c1::cortical reaction}}
↓
{{c1::genetic transfer}}
example: IVF with ICSI skips sperm binding and the acrosome reaction by injecting one sperm straight into the egg.

text:
Relieve both positive and negative symptoms:
{{c1::Atypical antipsychotic::medication}}
example: Risperidone can ease both hallucinations and social withdrawal in schizophrenia.

text: The peripheral nervous system includes {{c1::everything outside the CNS}}, {{c1::cranial nerves}}, and {{c1::spinal nerves}}
example: Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses the median nerve at the wrist, a PNS nerve.

text:
PTSD is associated with:
  • {{c1::a traumatic event}}
  • {{c1::re-experience of the event}}
  • {{c1::avoidance}}
  • {{c1::unable to function}}
  • {{c1::month or more of symptoms}}
  • {{c1::arousal increased}}
example: A soldier back from combat relives firefights in flashbacks, avoids fireworks and startles easily for 6 months.

text: If the environment is kept 100% the same between individuals with different genes and they exhibit differing traits, then the trait is considered {{c1::100}}% heritable
example: Genetically different wheat strains grown in identical soil, water and light: every yield difference is genetic.

text: Drive-reduction motivation is {{c1::motivation based on the need to fulfill a certain drive}}
Cluster C personality disorders are associated with {{c1::fear and anxiety}}
example: A man turns down a promotion for fear his new coworkers will criticize him (avoidant).

text: {{c1::Swimming}} reflex is when {{c2::infants in water move their legs/arms in a swimming motion and involuntarily hold their breath}}
example: A 3-month-old placed face-down in water paddles its arms and legs and holds its breath.

text: {{c2::Cyclothymic disorder}} is characterized by distinct episodes of {{c1::hypomania}} and {{c1::dysthymia}}
example: For 2 years a man swings between mild highs and low moods that never meet full mania or depression criteria.

text: {{c2::Dementia}} is {{c1::irreversible and progressive episodes of cognitive/higher brain problems}}
example: Alzheimer's disease erodes memory over years, and the lost function never comes back.

text: White matter is mostly {{c1::myelinated axons}}
example: The corpus callosum looks white because its axons are wrapped in fatty myelin.

text: {{c2::Epigenetics}} is {{c1::changes in gene expression that do not involve altering the DNA sequences}}
example: People conceived in the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944-45 showed altered IGF2 methylation six decades later.

text: {{c2::Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)}} is {{c1::when a person has lingering memories and nightmares about a traumatic past event that it impacts their daily lives}}.
extra: Symptoms must persist for more than 1 month after the event
example: A car-crash survivor has nightmares and panics at screeching tyres months after the accident.

text: {{c2::Effort justification}} is an idea that people tend to {{c1::attribute a greater value to an outcome they had to put effort into acquiring or achieving}}
example: Aronson and Mills: women who endured an embarrassing initiation rated a dull discussion group as more interesting.

text: Adrenal cortex secretes {{c1::corticosteroids}}
example: Cortisol, a glucocorticoid from the adrenal cortex, rises during a stressful exam week.

text: Classical twin study compares {{c1::monozygotic and dizygotic twins raised in the same household}}
example: Identical twins share autism far more often than fraternal twins, pointing to strong heritability.

text:
The positive symptoms to schizophrenia include:
  • {{c1::hallucinations}}
  • {{c1::delusions}}
  • {{c1::disorganized speech/thinking}}
  • {{c1::disorganized behavior}}
  • {{c1::catatonic behavior}}
extra: mnemonic: Its POSITIVE to Have 3D Cats
example: A patient hears voices saying he is watched (hallucination) and believes the FBI is tracking him (delusion).

text: Word association testing tests for {{c1::subconscious thoughts or personality traits::x2}}
example: A client who answers the cue word 'mother' with 'smother' may reveal a hidden conflict.

text: {{c1::Arousal}} is the state of being awake and reactive to stimuli
example: A sprinter crouched in the blocks is highly aroused; someone drifting off to sleep has low arousal.

text: Psychological factors in depression include {{c1::learned helplessness}}, {{c1::cognitive distortions}}, and {{c1::attribution}}
example: Seligman's dogs that could not escape shocks later stopped trying even when escape was easy.

text: The two steps to a reflex include the {{c1::afferent (stimulus)}} and {{c1::efferent (response)}}
example: Stepping on a tack: afferent fibres carry the pain in and efferent fibres pull the foot away.

text: The {{c1::functional attitudes theory::... theory}} suggests that beliefs and attitudes are influential to various psychological functions
example: Wearing a pro-environment T-shirt expresses who you are, the ego-expressive function of an attitude.

text: People with Alzheimer's typically lose the brain region called {{c1::the nucleus basalis}}, which is important in {{c1::acetylcholine release}}
example: Donepezil, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, treats Alzheimer's by boosting acetylcholine.

text: The brains of individuals with parkinsons exhibit {{c1::deterioration of the substantia nigra, which is used to produce dopamine}}
extra:
remember from the earlier cards, substantia nigra dopamine is associated with motor function and purposeful movement. (the other regions that produce dopamine are the arcuate nucleus and VTA but that dont matter rn)
ARE YOU MAKING THE CONNECTIONS NOW ON WHY SUBSTANTIA NIGRA DETERIORATION RESULTS IN THE PARKINSONS SYMPTOMS
example: In 1982, users of synthetic heroin tainted with MPTP lost substantia nigra neurons and became parkinsonian.

text:
The physical abnormalities associated with schizophrenia include:
  • {{c1::decreased cerebral cortex size (frontal/temporal)}}
  • {{c1::enlarged fluid filled regions of brain}}
  • {{c1::dopamine abnormalities(elevated)}}
example: An MRI of a patient with schizophrenia shows enlarged lateral ventricles and a thinner frontal cortex.

text: {{c1::The pleasure principle}} states that {{c2::young children (or immature individuals) seek immediate pleasure to avoid suffering. No compromise.}}
{{c1::Affective flattening}} is {{c2::a symptom common in schizophrenics that is the reduction in the range and intensity of emotional expression}}
extra: includes facial expression, eye contact, interpreting body language
example: Told that her mother has died, a patient replies in a monotone with an unchanged, blank face.

text:
Five classic anxiety-related disorders:
  • {{c1::generalized anxiety disorder}}
  • {{c1::panic disorder}}
  • {{c1::phobias}}
  • {{c1::OCD}}
  • {{c1::PTSD}}
extra: DSM-IV grouping; DSM-5 moves OCD and PTSD into their own categories.
example: A veteran with combat flashbacks (PTSD), or someone who cannot board a plane for fear of flying (phobia).

text: {{c1::Obsessive-compulsive personality disorders}} include individuals who are {{c2::focused on life being ordered and for them being in control to the extent it annoys other people}}
extra: Do not confuse with OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder)
example: A manager redoes his team's reports because the margins are not exactly right, and they miss the deadline.

text: Someone with depersonalization / derealization disorder experiences a feeling of detachment from the {{c1::mind and body}} or the {{c1::environment}}
example: Feeling you are watching yourself from outside, as if in a movie, while knowing it is not real.

text:
The right hemisphere is involved in:
  • {{c1::creativity}}
  • {{c1::music}}
  • {{c1::spatial processing}}
  • {{c1::art}}
example: Patients with right-hemisphere damage often struggle to read a map or copy a simple drawing.

text: {{c1::Paraphilic}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability from having sexual arousal to unusual stimuli for a person's culture}}.
extra: Includes arousal to things that cause harm, to children, to nonconsenting adults, or to inanimate objects
example: Voyeuristic disorder: repeatedly spying on unsuspecting people undressing for sexual arousal.

text: Carl Rogers’ {{c1::unconditional positive regard}} involves showing complete support and acceptance of a person no matter what that person says or does
extra: Flows from the humanistic view of personality
example: A therapist stays warm and accepting toward a client who admits to cheating on a partner.

text: {{c1::Stepping}} reflex is when {{c2::infants will start to step when held upright with feet touching flat surface}}
example: Held upright over a table, a 2-week-old lifts one foot after the other as if walking.

text: {{c1::Norepinephrine}} is released in the {{c2::locus coeruleus}}, which is in the {{c2::pons}}.
example: Clonidine quiets the locus coeruleus, easing the jittery hyperarousal of opioid withdrawal.

text: {{c1::Antipsychotics}} can treat anxiety with dementia, OCD and anxiety disorders
extra: Mainly used to manage psychosis (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder); increasingly used for non-psychotic disorders
example: Low-dose risperidone added to an SSRI can help treatment-resistant OCD.

text: Heritability symbol: {{c1::h2}}
example: A twin study reporting h<sup>2</sup> = 0.5 for IQ means half the IQ variance in that sample is genetic.

text: Acrosome reaction is when {{c1::enzymes leak into zona pellucida and digest it}}
example: Acrosin, a protease from the sperm's acrosome, digests a path through the zona pellucida.

text:
Anterior Pituitary hormones:
  • {{c1::FSH}}
  • {{c1::LH}}
  • {{c1::ACTH}}
  • {{c1::TSH}}
  • {{c1::Prolactin }}
  • {{c1::Endorphins}}
  • {{c1::GH}}
example: A prolactinoma in the anterior pituitary causes milk discharge and missed periods.

text: {{c1::Gordon Allport}} believed we have 3 basic categories of traits: {{c2::cardinal traits}}, {{c2::central traits}}, and {{c2::secondary traits}}
example: Mother Teresa's altruism (cardinal), a friend's kindness (central), preferring tea to coffee (secondary).

text: {{c2::Learned behavioral traits}} are {{c1::persistent changes in our behavior that result from experiences}}
example: A child who burns a hand on a hot stove stays careful around stoves from then on.

text: The Id is {{c1::unconscious}} and seeks {{c1::immediate gratification}}
example: A hungry baby screams for milk immediately, no matter who is busy.

text: {{c1::Spinal nerves::... nerves}} arise from the spinal cord and are distributed in the other parts of the body such as the skin, skeletal muscles, and blood vessels
example: The sciatic nerve, formed from the L4–S3 spinal nerves, supplies the back of the thigh and most of the leg.

text: Left hemisphere is involved in {{c1::language}}, {{c1::math}}, and {{c1::logical thinking}}
example: A left-hemisphere stroke often leaves a patient with aphasia, struggling to find words.

text: Dysgraphia is {{c1::a writing disorder}}
example: A child who knows the answer but writes it slowly in cramped, illegible, badly spaced letters.

text: {{c1::Incentive theory::theory}} believes that {{c2::individuals are motivated to engage in behaviors that produce rewards}}
example: Working extra shifts to earn a holiday bonus.

text: {{c1::Gender dysphoria}} is {{c2::distress/disability caused by a person identifying with a gender different from the one they were assigned}}
example: A child assigned male at birth insists for years that she is a girl and is distressed by her body.

text: {{c1::Defense mechanisms}} are {{c2::a way to protect ourselves from unconscious wants, feelings, desires, and impulses}}
extra: a psychological shield against anxiety and discomfort
example: A student who failed an exam insists the test was unfair rather than admit he did not study.

text: {{c1::Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct}} disorders involve {{c2::distress/disability from behaviors that are unacceptably disruptive or impulsive for someone's culture}}
extra:
Inability to control behaviors
Mnemonic: DICC (Disruptive, Impulse-Control, Conduct)
example: Conduct disorder: a teen who repeatedly sets fires, bullies classmates and is cruel to animals.

text: {{c1::Comparative psychology}} is the study of animals in order to find out about humans
example: Harlow's infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother over a wire one that gave milk.

text:
The cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia include abnormalities with:
  • {{c1::attention}}
  • {{c1::organization}}
  • {{c1::planning}}
  • {{c1::thinking}}
  • {{c1::memory}}
example: A patient with schizophrenia cannot follow a recipe's steps or hold a phone number in mind long enough to dial it.

text: The {{c1::midbrain::division of brain}} includes the colliculi, the tegmentum, and the cerebral peduncles
example: The superior colliculus turns your eyes toward a sudden flash; the inferior colliculus relays a sudden sound.

text: Sperm binding occurs when sperm binds to {{c1::the zona pellucida}}
example: Human sperm bind the human zona pellucida but not the zona of a mouse egg.

text: Negative feedback is when {{c1::the output of a process inhibits that same process, maintaining homeostasis}}
example: High blood glucose triggers insulin release; as glucose falls, insulin secretion falls too.

text:
Neuropeptide Y inhibition causes the inhibition of CCK, which limits meal size by:
{{c1::Being released in response to fats/proteins in the duodenum and signaling satiety via the vagus}}
example: After a fatty meal, duodenal CCK makes you feel full before dessert arrives.

text: {{c1::Glutamate::excitatory amino acid NT}} is associated with ↑ cortical arousal
example: Ketamine blocks NMDA glutamate receptors and is used as a general anaesthetic.

text:
Biological factors influencing food intake:
{{c1::hormones such as leptin, orexin, ghrelin, and insulin}}
Sociocultural factors influencing food intake:
{{c1::eating for different occasions, times, desires, and availability}}
example: Rising ghrelin before lunch makes you hungry; eating turkey on Thanksgiving because everyone does is sociocultural.

text: {{c2::Psychoanalytic}} theory is associated with {{c1::Sigmund Freud::Psychologist}}
example: Freud's case of Little Hans traced a boy's fear of horses to unconscious Oedipal fear of his father.

text: Norepinephrine is released to the {{c1::cerebral cortex}} and the {{c1::ANS}}
extra: Released to the ANS less than acetylcholine
example: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto the heart, raising heart rate during exercise.

text: {{c2::Repression}} is {{c1::a neurotic defense mechanism. It is an unconscious process where thoughts are pushed down into the unconscious}}
extra:
example: In the oedipus complex, sexual and aggressive thoughts are pushed into the unconscious
https://www.simplypsychology.org/oedipal-complex.html
example: An adult abused as a child has no conscious memory of the abuse.

text: Prodrome is {{c1::the period before the onset of active psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia, marked by early signs like social withdrawal and declining functioning}}
example: A college student withdraws from friends and lets his grades slide for a year before he first hears voices.

text: {{c1::Bipolar II disorder}} is when {{c2::individuals experience hypomania with at least one major depressive episode. They also never experience a manic episode.}}
example: A woman with recurrent major depression plus a 4-day spell of high energy and little sleep that never impaired her.

text: Dyscalculia is {{c1::a mathematics learning disorder}}
example: A bright student who reads fluently but cannot learn times tables or read the time on a clock.

text: {{c1::Semantic encoding}} is a specific type of encoding in which the meaning of something is encoded as opposed to the sound or vision of it
extra: Semantic encoding is stronger than both acoustic and visual encoding
example: Asking 'is a robin a bird?' gives better recall of 'robin' than asking whether it is printed in capitals.

text: {{c2::Working memory::Type of memory}} includes {{c1::sensory information you actually process}} and consists of {{c1::what you are thinking about in the moment}}.
example: Working out a 15% tip on a $40 bill in your head ($6) while chatting with friends.

text: {{c1::Homeostasis}} is the body's maintenance of a stable internal state (temperature, heartbeat, metabolism, etc.)
example: On a hot day you sweat to keep your core temperature near 37 °C.

text: {{c1::Outpatient}} treatments allow patients to live at home and come in for treatment
example: A patient lives at home and attends a clinic for therapy three evenings a week.

text: Activity in the {{c1::prefrontal cortex::Brain region}} is decreased during REM sleep
extra: This explains why dreams can defy logic, as the prefrontal cortex is responsible for logical thinking
example: In a dream you fly over your school and chat with your late grandmother, and none of it seems odd.

text: {{c2::Proactive}} interference is when {{c1::old information impairs new learning}}
extra:
example: harder to learn new password after using an old one for a long time
Memory hook: Pro pushes forward: the old memory pushes forward and blocks the new one. (Retro reaches back: new wrecks old.)Source: Penn State PSYCH 100 blog, sites.psu.edu (bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/5/109761/files/2019/10/psych-100-blog-2-2.png)

text:
{{c1::Opioids::Drug class}} effects:
  • {{c2::decrease CNS function}}
  • {{c2::decrease HR}}
  • {{c2::decrease BP}}
  • {{c2::act as analgesics}}
  • {{c2::vasodilate}}
example: A heroin overdose patient arrives drowsy with slow breathing, pinpoint pupils and low blood pressure.

text:
Primary role of hypocretin: {{c1::control sleep & arousal}}
Also known as {{c1::orexin}}
example: Loss of the hypothalamic orexin neurons causes narcolepsy with cataplexy.

text: {{c1::The tetris effect}} is when you devote so much time to an activity during the day that it begins to pattern your thoughts, mental images, and dreams.
extra: This is why when you fall asleep after a day at the amusement park you may feel as though you are still riding the rides as you fall asleep

text: Common symptoms of Korsakoff's syndrome include {{c1::severe memory loss}} and {{c1::confabulation}}
extra: Confabulation: patients make up stories to fill in memory gaps
example: Asked about yesterday, a hospitalized Korsakoff patient insists he went fishing with his brother.

text: {{c1::The spotlight model of attention::Model}} states that {{c2::we take info from 5 senses but don't pay attention to everything}}
example: You feel your socks only when you think about them, though touch receptors signal all day.

text: {{c1::Intelligence}} is a mental quality that allows us to learn from experience, solve problems, and use knowledge to adapt to new situations
example: A newcomer to Tokyo works out the subway map and adjusts her commute within a week.

text: {{c1::Episodic}} memory is {{c2::event-related}} memories
{{c1::Free recall}} involves no cues in recalling
example: 'Write down every word you remember from the list,' with no hints given.

text: The {{c1::growth mindset}} attitude towards intelligence states that {{c2::intelligence is changeable if you learn more}}
extra: this mindset praises effort, perseverance, improvement, and strategies
example: Dweck found kids praised for effort ('you worked hard') chose harder puzzles than kids praised as 'smart'.

text: {{c1::Spacing}} is spreading out study sessions instead of cramming to encode information better
example: Studying 1 hour a day for 5 days beats 5 hours the night before the exam.

text: Temporal monotonicity: {{c1::Adding pain at the end of a painful experience will worsen the retrospective evaluation of the experienced pain}}
extra: Example: breaking your leg at the end of a walk across Antarctica is remembered worse than eating delicious cake at the end

text: {{c1::Spearman's Theory of General Intelligence}} states that {{c2::there is one general intelligence that depends on a g-factor}}
extra:
The g factor stands for general intelligence.
People who are intelligent in one area tend to be intelligent in other areas.
example: Spearman saw that schoolchildren's grades in Classics, French and math all correlated positively.

text:
The three things that influence our ability to multitask:
  • {{c1::Task similarity}}
  • {{c1::Task difficulty}}
  • {{c1::Practice}}
extra:
more similar the tasks, the harder it is
more difficult the tasks, the harder it is
more practice doing the tasks, the easier it is
example: Walking while talking is easy, but reading while listening to a podcast is hard, as both are verbal.

text: {{c1::Transdermal entry::Method of drug entry}} is when a drug is absorbed through the skin
example: A nicotine patch on the upper arm releases nicotine through the skin over 24 hours.

text: {{c2::Retroactive}} interference is when {{c1::new learning impairs old information}}
extra:
example: writing your new address a bunch makes it harder to remember your old address
Memory hook: Retro reaches back: the new memory reaches back and wrecks the old one. (Pro pushes forward: old blocks new.)Source: Penn State PSYCH 100 blog, sites.psu.edu (bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.psu.edu/dist/5/109761/files/2019/10/psych-100-blog-2-2.png)

text: The fastest route of drug entry is {{c1::IV injection}}
extra: Inhalation is close behind (lungs → heart → brain in seconds).
example: An IV drug has 100% bioavailability, entering the bloodstream at once with no absorption step.

text: {{c1::Meditation}} is training to self-regulate your attention and awareness
example: Sitting 10 minutes each morning focusing on your breath, gently returning whenever your mind wanders.

text: Treatments for insomnia include {{c1::medication}}, {{c1::psychological training}}, and {{c1::lifestyle changes}}
example: A doctor prescribes zolpidem (Ambien) short-term while the patient starts CBT for insomnia.

text: {{c1::Drowsiness}} is the state just before falling asleep or after waking up.
example: Eyelids drooping as you read in bed, just before you drift off.

text: {{c1::Electroencephalograms (EEGs)}} can measure brain waves
example: Scalp electrodes on a sleep-lab patient record the slow, high-amplitude delta waves of N3 sleep.

text: Cognitive bias: a {{c1::tendency to think a certain way}}
extra: Causes deviations from a standard of rationality or good judgment
example: Confirmation bias: a voter reads only news that supports the candidate she already likes.

text: {{c1::Selective attention}} is the ability to {{c2::maintain attention while being presented with interfering stimuli}}
example: In the Stroop task you say 'blue' for the word RED printed in blue ink, ignoring what it reads.

text: {{c1::Inhalation::Method of drug entry}} is breathing or snorting or smoking
example: An asthmatic puffs an albuterol inhaler so the drug reaches the airways directly.

text: {{c1::Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)::Treatment method}} is psychological treatment for drug addiction.
example: A smoker learns to spot the thought 'I need a cigarette to relax' and replace it with a walk.

text: {{c1::Change-blindness}} is {{c2::failing to notice a change in the environment as a result of selective attention}}
example: In Simons' door study, about half the people giving directions missed that the stranger had been swapped.

text: {{c1::Insight}} is the "aha moment" of problem solving
example: Köhler's chimpanzees suddenly stacked boxes to reach bananas hung out of reach.

text:
Opioids are {{c1::synthetic (fentanyl)::Natural/Synthetic}}
Opiates are {{c1::natural (morphine, from the opium poppy)::Natural/Synthetic}}
example: Codeine and morphine come straight from the poppy; fentanyl and methadone are made in a lab.

text: IQ scores are scaled so the average person scores {{c1::100}}
example: With a standard deviation of 15, about 68% of people score between 85 and 115.

text: {{c1::Directed attention}} is when attention is focused sustainably on a single task
example: A surgeon keeps her focus on a three-hour operation without drifting.

text: Hypnosis is an example of an {{c1::induced state of consciousness}}
example: A hypnotherapist's slow countdown leads a smoker into a relaxed, focused trance before quit suggestions.

text: {{c1::Hallucinogens::Drug Class}} can be used to help in {{c2::PTSD}} treatment
extra: This can allow individuals to visualize and come to terms with painful memories
example: In trials, MDMA-assisted therapy reduced PTSD symptoms more than the same therapy with a placebo.

text:
{{c1::The means-end analysis}} is when we:
  • {{c2::break down large problems into smaller problems}}
  • {{c2::tackle the problem that has the most difference between the current state and goal state}}
extra: Example: when planning a trip to a new country, the biggest problem is getting there, so you book a plane ticket first.

text:
MDMA (ecstasy) effects:
  • Neurotransmitters: {{c1::↑ serotonin (main), plus ↑ NE and DA}}
  • Physiological: {{c1::↑ HR, BP, and body temperature (hyperthermia)}}
  • Psychological: {{c1::euphoria, feelings of connectedness, mild perceptual distortions}}
  • Long-term: {{c1::damage to serotonin-releasing neurons}}
example: A raver on MDMA dances for hours in a hot club, overheats and collapses with heatstroke.

text: According to Freud, the literal meaning of our dream is known as {{c1::manifest content}}
extra: Example: a monster is chasing you.

text:
Concrete operational stage:
  • occurs between ages {{c1::7-11}}
  • associated with {{c1::conservation}}, {{c1::empathy}}, and {{c1::math skills}}
extra: conservation is when kids can tell that a short glass and a tall glass can have the same amount of water despite different heights.
example: A 9-year-old knows a clay ball squashed flat still holds the same clay, and can work out 7 × 8 = 56.

text: {{c1::Inpatient}} treatment requires residence at a hospital or treatment facility
example: A patient spends 28 days living at a residential rehab centre with round-the-clock staff.

text: {{c1::Hypnagogic hallucinations}} are hearing/seeing things that aren't there during N1 sleep
extra: they typically can be very frightening
example: Falling asleep, you hear someone call your name or see a shadowy figure that isn't there.

text: {{c2::The information processing model::Model}} states that we {{c1::get inputs from environment}}, {{c1::process the inputs}}, and {{c1::output decisions}}.
example: A driver sees a red light (input), recognizes it means stop (processing), and brakes (output).

text:
In the reward pathway, {{c2::dopamine}} acts on the:
  • {{c1::amygdala}}
  • {{c1::nucleus accumbens}}
  • {{c1::prefrontal cortex}}
  • {{c1::hippocampus}}
extra: Mnemonic: We are all PHANs of dopamine
example: With cake: amygdala feels joy, hippocampus stores the moment, accumbens wants more, PFC attends to it.

text: Sigmund Freud stated that dreams are {{c1::unconscious thoughts and desires that need to be interpreted}}
example: Freud would read a dream of a train entering a tunnel as a disguised sexual wish.

text: Serotonin is associated with {{c1::feelings of satiation}}
extra: This is why serotonin goes down in the reward pathway: you keep wanting more reward and are never satisfied.
example: Fenfluramine, which releases serotonin, was sold as a diet drug because it made people feel full.

text: A faster route of drug entry means {{c1::more addictive potential::effect}}
example: Smoked crack reaches the brain faster than snorted powder cocaine and is more addictive.

text: One sleep cycle typically lasts {{c1::90 minutes::Time}}
example: Over 7.5 hours of sleep you pass through about 5 cycles (5 × 90 min = 450 min).

text: The retrieval cue of priming is {{c1::prior activation of nodes/associations without our awareness}}
extra: example: reading a story about rabbits, then someone mentions the word HAIR. You are more likely to think HARE.

text:
{{c2::Hallucinogens}} are drugs that:
  • {{c1::distort}} perceptions
  • {{c1::dilate}} pupils
  • {{c1::heighten}} sensations
  • {{c1::increase}} connectedness
  • cause {{c1::mood swings}}
example: On LSD, a user sees the carpet pattern swirl and feels the music as colours.

text: {{c1::L.L. Thurstone's Theory of Primary Mental Abilities::Theory}} states that {{c2::there are 7 distinct primary mental abilities rather than one general (g) factor}}
extra:
Mnemonic: LL Cool J (Thurstone) and his 7 primary abilities
Thurstone's 7 primary mental abilities:
  • Verbal comprehension
  • Word fluency
  • Number facility
  • Spatial visualization
  • Associative memory
  • Perceptual speed
  • Reasoning
vs. Gardner: Thurstone's abilities come from factor analysis of test scores, are mostly academic and still correlate; Gardner's intelligences are broader (musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal) and claimed to be independent.
example: A student can excel at spatial visualization yet lag in word fluency, two separate abilities on Thurstone's list.

text: {{c1::Syntax}} is how words are put together in sentences
example: 'The dog bit the man' and 'The man bit the dog' use the same words but word order changes the meaning.

text: {{c1::Opioids::Drug class}} can act like an analgesic to reduce perception of pain
example: After surgery, a morphine drip lets a patient sit up without feeling the incision pain.

text: {{c1::Assimilation}} is when we {{c2::incorporate new information into an existing schema}}
example: A toddler who knows 'doggy' calls the first cat she sees a 'doggy' too.

text: The retrieval cue of state-dependency states that {{c1::you can remember things better when you are in the same mood you encoded the information}}
extra: Example: if you learn something drunk, you will remember it better drunk

text: {{c1::Encoding specificity}} is enhanced memory when {{c2::recalling information takes place under same conditions as learning}}
extra: Example: you do better on a test taken drunk if you studied drunk

text: {{c1::Explicit}} memories are {{c2::facts/events you can clearly describe}}
example: Telling a friend what you ate at your 18th birthday dinner.

text: {{c1::Attention}} is when you {{c2::focus/concentrate on something at the exclusion of other stimuli in the environment}}
example: Reading this card, you ignore the hum of the air conditioner and the feel of your chair.

text:
The order within a sleep cycle goes from
{{c1::N1 → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM → N1}}
example: Fall asleep at 11 p.m. and the first REM period typically arrives around 12:30 a.m., 90 minutes later.

text:
Relapse is more likely to occur when:
  • {{c1::the substance is more addictive}}
  • {{c1::patients encounter things that they associate with the drug}}.
example: A former smoker lights up again when she smells smoke at the bar where she used to smoke.

text: {{c1::Pegword system}} is verbal anchors linking words that rhyme with the number they rhyme with to encode better
example: One is a bun, two is a shoe: picture a bun stuffed with milk cartons and a shoe full of eggs.

text: {{c1::Confirmation bias}} is {{c2::actively seeking out information that supports one's own beliefs}}
example: A voter who only watches news channels that back their party and skips the ones that criticize it.

text: {{c1::Deductive::Deductive or Inductive}} reasoning starts with rules, then forms conclusions
example: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal.

text: {{c1::Wernicke's area::Brain region}} is involved in {{c2::language comprehension}} and is located in the {{c2::temporal}} lobe
example: After a left temporal-lobe stroke, a patient with normal hearing cannot follow the command 'touch your nose'.

text: The common depressant drugs are {{c1::alcohol}}, {{c1::barbiturates}}, and {{c1::benzodiazepines}}
example: Phenobarbital (a barbiturate) and diazepam (a benzodiazepine) both boost GABA<sub>A</sub> signalling, like alcohol.

text: {{c1::False information}} causes inaccurate recollections of an event
extra: Example: participants watched a car stop at a yield sign. Those later given a description that falsely mentioned a stop sign were more likely to claim the car stopped at a stop sign.

text:
{{c1::Broadbent's early selection theory}} proposed that stimuli
{{c2::go into a sensory register}} → {{c2::selective filter}} → {{c2::perceptually processed}} → {{c2::conscious}}
extra: Problem: if unimportant stimuli are filtered out, you should not be able to hear your name in a crowd (cocktail party effect).
example: At a party, the filter passes your friend's voice and blocks other chatter before any meaning is processed.

text: The Nativist perspective is supported by the fact that {{c1::all languages share universal grammar}}
extra: Since all languages share same grammar (verb,noun,adj) then language must be innate
example: Children of pidgin speakers turn the pidgin into a creole with full grammar within one generation.

text: The {{c1::fixed mindset}} attitude towards intelligence states that {{c2::intelligence is biologically set and unchanging}}
example: A student fails a calculus test, decides 'I'm just not a math person', and stops studying.

text: {{c1::Schemas}} are {{c2::mental-models/frameworks used to organize and interpret new information}}
example: Your 'restaurant' schema tells you to wait to be seated, order, eat, then pay the bill.

text: {{c1::Conjunction fallacy}} is when {{c2::people tend to think the probability of two events occurring together is higher than just one}}
extra: Example below: one event alone is always at least as likely as both events occurring together.
example: Linda, a former activist, is rated likelier to be a 'feminist bank teller' than simply a 'bank teller'.

text: {{c1::The dual coding hypothesis}} states that it is easier to remember words associated with images.
example: The word 'elephant' is easier to recall than 'justice' because it brings an image to mind.

text: LSD effects: causes {{c1::hallucinations}} by acting as a serotonin ({{c1::5-HT<sub>2A</sub>}}) receptor {{c1::agonist}}
example: A user on LSD sees trails behind moving hands and colours bleeding into each other.

text: {{c1::Lexicon}} is the complete set of meaningful units in a language
example: Your mental dictionary of words like 'dog' and 'run' and parts like the suffix '-ed' is your lexicon.

text: The brain maintains homeostasis when taking drugs by {{c1::attempting to counteract their effects}}
extra: Example: If amphetamines increase HR, your brain will try to decrease your HR

text: {{c1::The serial position effect}} states that {{c2::we are better at remembering things at the beginning and end of a list}}
example: Asked to recall a 15-item grocery list, you remember 'milk' (first) and 'eggs' (last) best.

text: {{c2::The Interactionist approach::Theory}}, associated with {{c2::Vygotsky}}, believes that {{c1::biological and social factors must interact for children to learn language}}
extra: children WANT to communicate with adults, so it motivates them to learn language
example: A toddler points at a dog, her father says 'Yes, a dog!', and her urge to share attention turns into a new word.

text: {{c1::Priming}} is where {{c2::exposure to one stimulus affects our response to a future stimulus}}.
extra: example: we are primed to respond to our name
example: After reading the word 'doctor', you recognize 'nurse' as a word faster than 'butter'.

text: Nicotine acts in the nervous system as {{c1::an acetylcholine receptor agonist::where it binds}}
example: Nicotinic receptors, named for nicotine, are the ion channels ACh opens at the neuromuscular junction.

text: Heritability of intelligence is studied through {{c1::twin studies}}
extra:
do identical twins have same intelligence raised together vs apart?
what about fraternal twins raised together vs apart?
example: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart found identical twins raised separately still had very similar IQs.

text: {{c1::Semantic networks}} are {{c2::concepts organized in your mind as connected ideas}}
extra: Closely related ideas are closer together; less closely related ideas are further apart
example: Hearing 'fire engine' quickly brings 'red', 'truck' and 'siren' to mind, but not 'banana'.

text: {{c1::Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence::Theory}} states that {{c2::there are 3 independent intelligences (creative, analytical, and practical) that are based on real world success}}
extra: mnemonic: The CPA was STERN towards the orphan
example: Brazilian child street vendors did sums almost perfectly while selling but often failed them on school-style tests.

text: The {{c1::left::Right or Left}} hemisphere of the brain is involved in language
example: About 95% of right-handers process language in the left hemisphere, so a left-sided stroke often causes aphasia.

text:
Preoperational stage characteristics:
  • Occurs between ages {{c1::2-6/7}}
  • Associated with:
    • {{c1::pretend play}}
    • {{c1::egocentrism}}
    • {{c1::beginning to understand symbols}}
    • {{c1::beginning to talk}}
extra: Egocentrism: children can only understand things from their own point of view. Example: a child sitting in front of you watching TV doesn't understand that you can't see it.
example: A 4-year-old holds a banana to her ear and pretends it is a phone to talk to grandma.

text: {{c1::Piaget::Theorist}} believed that {{c2::once children could think a certain way, they developed language to describe those thoughts::view of language}}
extra: Example: children in the preoperational stage develop words like "gone" or "away" to reflect object permanence

text: {{c1::Cued recall}} involves extra clues to help in recall
example: Remembering 'banana' from the list once told 'it was a yellow fruit'.

text: A/an {{c1::mental set}} is a framework for thinking about a problem
extra: It can be shaped by habit or by desire
example: After solving water-jar problems with one long formula, Luchins' subjects missed a far simpler solution.

text: Participants taking longer to read a word because it is emotionally charged is called {{c1::interference}}
example: In an emotional Stroop task, a combat veteran names the ink colour of 'BOMB' slower than that of 'TABLE'.

text:
The common stimulants include:
  • {{c1::caffeine}}
  • {{c1::amphetamines}}
  • {{c1::methamphetamines}}
  • {{c1::MDMA}}
  • {{c1::cocaine}}
  • {{c1::nicotine}}
example: An 8-oz cup of coffee holds about 95 mg of caffeine, the world's most widely used stimulant.

text: {{c1::Benzodiazepines}} are a type of medication known as tranquilizers. Familiar names include Valium and Xanax
example: Lorazepam (Ativan), another benzodiazepine, is given before an MRI to calm a claustrophobic patient.

text: Korsakoff's syndrome is associated with individuals who are {{c1::malnourished}} or {{c1::alcoholics}}
example: A man who has drunk a bottle of vodka a day for 20 years while barely eating develops Korsakoff's.

text: The two types of cues that direct our attention are {{c1::exogenous}} and {{c1::endogenous}} cues.
example: A sudden flash grabs your eyes (exogenous), while an arrow pointing left tells you where to look (endogenous).

text: The {{c1::cocktail party effect::... effect}} is the ability to focus one's attention on a particular stimulus while filtering out a range of other stimuli (noise)
example: At a loud wedding reception you follow your friend's story while tuning out the band and other chatter.

text: In iconic memory experiments, the {{c1::whole report technique::... technique}} requires participants to recall as many elements from the original visual display as possible
extra: The partial report condition requires participants to identify a subset of the characters from the visual display using cued recall
example: Sperling flashed a 3×4 letter grid for 50 ms; under whole report people named only about 4 of the 12 letters.

text: {{c1::Crystallized IQ}} is the ability to use {{c2::acquired knowledge}} and {{c2::experience}}
example: A 70-year-old retired history teacher dominating a trivia night on world history and vocabulary.

text: Analytical intelligence is {{c1::the ability to solve well defined problems}}
example: Scoring high on the SAT math section, where every problem has one right answer.

text: {{c1::Shadowing task}} is an experiment where {{c2::people are told to repeat everything said in one ear and ignore the other}}.
example: Cherry's listeners shadowed one ear and never noticed the ignored ear switch from English to German.

text: The buildup of {{c1::acetaldehyde}} causes symptoms such as nausea, headache, facial flushing and internal organ damage
example: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so a patient who drinks gets flushing and nausea from acetaldehyde.

text: The SCN does not secrete melatonin itself; it signals the {{c1::pineal gland}}, which releases melatonin in response to {{c2::darkness}}
extra: Light on the retina → SCN → suppresses pineal melatonin release. Darkness → melatonin rises → sleepiness.
example: Scrolling a bright phone at midnight delays melatonin release and makes falling asleep harder.

text: {{c1::Substance-induced disorders::Disorder}} are conditions that are caused by substances.
example: Weeks of heavy meth use trigger paranoid psychosis, a substance-induced psychotic disorder.

text: {{c2::Theta waves::Brain wave}} are slower/lower frequency waves that are associated with {{c1::drowsiness}} and {{c1::right after falling asleep}}
example: As your head bobs during a dull late-night lecture, your EEG shifts to theta waves.

text: In the reward pathway, the nucleus accumbens mediates {{c1::reward/pleasure (motivating reward-seeking action)}}
extra: Example: Let's move our hand and take another bite of this cake.

text: {{c1::Daydreaming}} is the state of being awake, but more relaxed and not as focused.
example: Staring out the window during a lecture, imagining your next vacation.

text: {{c1::Methadone}} activates opiate receptors slowly and dampens the high to aid in addiction treatment
example: With methadone occupying his opioid receptors, a patient who slips and uses heroin feels little high.

text: {{c1::Chunking}} is grouping information into categories to remember it better
extra: example: group your shopping list into categories

text: Insight about a problem can often be achieved through {{c1::incubation}}
extra: Incubation is setting a problem aside for a while until you understand it, like sleeping on it and seeing the solution the next day.

text: {{c1::Inattentional blindness}} is when {{c2::we aren't aware of things in our visual field when our attention is directed elsewhere in that field}}
extra: Example: the "count the passes" video, in which viewers miss a gorilla strolling through

text: {{c1::Vigilance}}, also termed sustained concentration, is defined as the ability to maintain concentrated attention over prolonged periods of time
extra: During this time, the person attempts to detect the appearance of a particular target stimulus
example: A radar operator scanning a screen for hours to catch the rare blip of an enemy plane.

text: {{c1::Belief perseverance}} is {{c2::maintaining a belief despite new information that firmly contradicts it}}
extra: Example: believing evolution is false despite overwhelming evidence

text: Active chemical in marijuana is {{c1::THC}}
example: Dronabinol, a synthetic THC pill, is prescribed to curb chemotherapy nausea and boost appetite.

text: {{c2::Global aphasia}} is when an individual {{c1::has a damaged Broca's and Wernicke's area}}
example: A large left middle cerebral artery stroke can wreck both areas, leaving a patient unable to speak or understand.

text: If the corpus callosum is severed, the individual is considered {{c1::split-brained}}
example: Sperry and Gazzaniga studied epilepsy patients whose corpus callosum was cut to stop seizures spreading.

text: {{c1::Morphology}} is the structure of words in a language
example: 'Unhappiness' breaks into three morphemes: un- + happy + -ness.

text: Intelligence is dependent on both {{c1::genetics}} and {{c1::environment}}
example: PKU is genetic, but a low-phenylalanine diet from birth prevents the intellectual disability it causes.

text: {{c1::Positive priming}} is when prior exposure to a stimulus speeds of processing by simply experiencing the stimulus
example: Having seen 'elephant' on a list earlier, you complete 'ele___' with 'elephant' faster.

text: {{c2::Consciousness}} is the awareness of our {{c1::self}} and {{c1::environment}}
example: Right now you notice both your own tiredness and the hum of the fridge across the room.

text: The neurotransmitter associated with the reward pathway is {{c1::dopamine}}
example: A slot-machine win triggers a dopamine burst in the nucleus accumbens, making you want to play again.

text:
{{c1::Nicotine::Drug}} effects:
  • {{c2::increase HR}}
  • {{c2::increase BP}}
  • {{c2::acetylcholine receptor agonist}}
  • {{c2::disrupt sleep}}
  • {{c2::suppress appetite}}
example: Smokers who quit often gain a few kilograms once nicotine's appetite suppression is gone.

text:
The cognitive abilities that decline with age are:
  • {{c1::recall}}
  • {{c1::episodic memory}}
  • {{c1::processing speed}}
  • {{c1::divided attention}}
  • {{c1::prospective memory}}
extra: Mnemonic: You will DECLINE if you aren't PREP'D
example: A 75-year-old forgets to take his evening pills and reads a menu slowly, yet still aces the crossword.

text: When the {{c2::arcuate fasciculus}} is damaged, an individual has {{c1::conduction aphasia}}
example: A stroke patient speaks and understands normally but cannot repeat 'no ifs, ands, or buts'.

text: {{c1::The framing effect}} is {{c2::where people decide on options based on whether they are presented with positive or negative connotations}}
example: Patients choose surgery more often when told '90% survive' than '10% die', though the odds are identical.

text: Melatonin is secreted by the {{c1::pineal gland}}
example: The pineal gland releases melatonin as evening falls; travelers take melatonin pills to fight jet lag.

text: Broca's aphasia is a {{c1::non-fluent::Fluent or Non-Fluent}} form of aphasia
example: Broca's patient Leborgne understood speech but could say only one syllable, 'tan'.

text: {{c1::Algorithms}} are a problem-solving method that uses a {{c2::logical step-by-step approach that is guaranteed to find the correct solution eventually}}
extra:
Not the quickest way to solve problems, but you will always find the correct solution.
Example: Rubik's cube algorithms always reach a solved state, even though the cube could be solved in fewer turns.

text: Multitasking is {{c1::less::more/less}} efficient than working on a single task
example: Drivers on a hands-free phone call react more slowly to brake lights than undistracted drivers.

text: {{c1::Misleading information}} is phrasing things in such a way that it leads your recall in a certain direction
extra: Example: after watching a car crash, participants asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" (rather than "hit") each other were more likely to recall broken glass, though there was none.

text: {{c1::Exogenous cues}} are cues that {{c2::capture our attention without us having to tell ourselves to look for them}}
extra: Example: bright colors, loud noises

text:
The 4 main types of brain waves are:
  • {{c1::alpha}}
  • {{c1::beta}}
  • {{c1::delta}}
  • {{c1::theta}}
example: Beta while solving a math problem, alpha resting with eyes shut, theta as you doze, delta in deep sleep.

text: {{c1::Procedural memory}} is long-term memory for actions or habits (riding a bike)
example: A pianist plays a memorized piece while chatting, her fingers finding the notes on their own.

text: The information processing model is driven by {{c1::bottom-up::Top-down or Bottom-up}} processing
extra: It is stimulus-driven: it requires an input from the environment.
example: You detect edges, a red colour and a round shape, then piece them together into an apple.

text: {{c1::Emotional intelligence}} is the ability to perceive, understand, use and manage emotions in interactions with others
example: A manager notices an employee's rising frustration in a meeting and calmly defuses it.

text: {{c1::Covert orienting}} is the act of bringing the spotlight of attention on an object or event without body or eye movement
example: Looking straight at your teacher while secretly watching your crush out of the corner of your eye.

text:
The four routes of drug entry include:
  • {{c1::oral}}
  • {{c1::injection}}
  • {{c1::inhalation}}
  • {{c1::absorption through skin/mucous membranes}}
extra:
Ex: nicotine patch (skin), snorting cocaine (nasal mucosa).
Fastest: IV injection (inhalation close behind). Slowest: oral.

text: {{c1::The sensory register}} is a temporary register of all information your senses are taking in
example: Driving past, every billboard, horn and smell briefly registers, but most fades before you notice it.

text: {{c2::Ill-defined}} problems are problems with {{c1::an ambiguous starting and end point}}
example: Deciding which career to pursue or how to write a great novel.

text: {{c1::Caffeine::Drug}} effects: {{c2::inhibits adenosine receptors}} and can {{c2::disrupt sleep}}
example: A coffee at 4 p.m. still blocks adenosine at bedtime, since caffeine's half-life is about 5 hours.

text: {{c2::Psychoactive}} drugs can alter our {{c1::consciousness}} and {{c1::perception}}
example: Psilocybin from 'magic mushrooms' makes colours vivid and minutes feel like hours.

text: {{c1::Proximal stimuli::Type of stimuli}} are the patterns of stimuli from objects and events that reach your senses
extra: example: the light that hits your retina

text: {{c1::Long-term potentiation (LTP)}} is when {{c2::connections between neurons strengthen to improve recall/memory}}
example: Bliss and Lømo found brief high-frequency stimulation of rabbit hippocampus boosted responses for hours.

text: {{c1::Strong Linguistic Determinism}} AKA {{c1::Sapir-Whorfian Hypothesis}} states that {{c2::language completely determines thoughts}}
extra: example: Hopi tribe of Arizona (USA) doesn't have grammatical tense so they don't think about time in the same way we do

text: The first three stages of the sleep cycle are called {{c1::non-rapid eye movement sleep}}, while the fourth stage is called {{c1::rapid-eye movement sleep (REM)}}
example: You pass through NREM stages N1, N2 and N3 first; the first REM period starts about 90 minutes after sleep onset.

text:
Symptoms of Wernicke's encephalopathy:
  • {{c1::poor balance}}
  • {{c1::abnormal eye movements}}
  • {{c1::mild confusion}}
  • {{c1::memory loss}}
extra:
Mnemonic: I want a Bacon, Egg and Cheese, Mom
(balance, eye movements, confusion, memory)
example: A heavy drinker in the ER who staggers, has jerky eyes (nystagmus) and does not know where he is.

text: {{c1::Prosody}} is concerned with how the way something is said influences its meaning
example: 'Oh, great' means delight said brightly, but annoyance said flatly after spilling coffee on your shirt.

text: {{c1::Neglect syndrome}} occurs when damage to the brain causes a patient to {{c2::fail to be aware of items to one side of space}}.
example: Asked to copy a clock, a patient with right parietal damage draws only the numbers on its right half.

text:
People with sleep deprivation are more susceptible to:
  • {{c1::poor memory}}
  • {{c1::poor attention}}
  • {{c1::obesity}}
  • {{c1::depression}}
example: After an all-nighter, a student forgets much of what she studied and snacks more the next day.

text: {{c1::Fixation}} is {{c2::getting stuck on a wrong approach to a problem::problem solving definition}}
example: In Luchins' water-jar task, people keep using the long B − A − 2C formula even when A − C would work.

text: Even after memory decay, you can tell someone has learned something before by how quickly they {{c1::relearn the information}}
extra: This retained memory foundation is called savings: it exists even when the person can't recall the information.
example: Relearning high-school Spanish takes weeks, though it first took years and you now recall almost none.

text: The can't-happen-to-me bias is also known as {{c1::normalcy bias}}
example: Residents ignore a hurricane evacuation order because past storms never flooded their street.

text: {{c1::Recognition}} is a type of retrieval (distinct from recall) that involves identifying previously learned information when it is presented
extra:
Recognition is the easiest way to retrieve information.
Example: I show you a list and ask, "Was bacon or peanut butter on the list?" and you say bacon.

text: In split-brain individuals, if an image is in their left visual field, they can {{c1::pick up the object/draw it}} with their left hand but cannot {{c1::name the object}}
example: Flashed 'key' in the left visual field, a split-brain patient says he saw nothing, yet his left hand picks out a key.

text: {{c1::Acute}} withdrawal lasts {{c2::a few weeks}} and has {{c2::many physical withdrawal symptoms}}
example: In the first week off heroin, a user has sweats, vomiting, diarrhoea and goosebumps.

text: Cannabis (marijuana) can act as a {{c1::hallucinogen}}, {{c1::depressant}}, or {{c1::stimulant}}
example: One joint leaves one user sleepy and calm and another anxious with a racing heart.

text: {{c1::Semantics}} is the association of meaning with a word
example: Knowing that 'bank' can mean the side of a river or a place that holds your money.

text: {{c1::Source amnesia}} is when you can remember a piece of information but can't remember where it came from
example: You know octopuses have three hearts but can't recall where you learned it.

text: If you go through a period of not having a drug, you experience {{c1::withdrawal}}
example: A heavy coffee drinker who skips her morning cup has a pounding headache by noon.

text: {{c1::Acronym}} is an encoding technique where each letter of a word you know stands for something
extra: Example: SNoW DRoP for blotting techniques

text:
{{c1::Stimulants}} are drugs that:
  • {{c2::excite the CNS}}
  • {{c2::increase HR}}
  • {{c2::increase BP}}
  • {{c2::dilate pupils}}
extra:
Typical stimulants:
  • Amphetamines, incl. methamphetamine (increase DA/NE release)
  • Cocaine (blocks DA/NE/5-HT reuptake)
  • Ecstasy / MDMA (stimulant + hallucinogen)
  • Caffeine
  • Nicotine
example: After a line of cocaine, a user's pulse races past 120 and his pupils go wide.

text: Wernicke's and Broca's areas are connected by a bundle of nerve fibers called the {{c1::arcuate fasciculus}}
example: Repeating a phone number you just heard relies on the arcuate fasciculus linking the two areas.

text: {{c1::Source monitoring}} is being able to {{c2::recall the source of a piece of information}}
example: Correctly remembering you read a drug fact in your pharmacology textbook, not on TikTok.

text:
{{c1::The resource model of attention}} states that:
  • {{c2::attention is a limited resource}}
  • {{c2::humans are bad at multitasking}}
example: Students who text during a lecture score lower on a quiz about it than classmates who don't.

text: {{c2::Cocaine}} blocks the reuptake of {{c1::dopamine}}, {{c1::serotonin}}, and {{c1::norepinephrine}}.
example: Cocaine leaves dopamine lingering in nucleus accumbens synapses, giving a short, intense euphoria.

text: LSD acts on {{c1::serotonin}} neurotransmission
example: LSD mimics serotonin at 5-HT<sub>2A</sub> receptors, so just 100 µg can cause hours of hallucinations.

text: The {{c1::cognitive economy principle::... principle}} refers to the simplicity and relevance of a cognitive categorization scheme or representation
example: 'Has wings' is stored once under BIRD rather than separately under canary, robin and sparrow.

text: {{c1::Overt orienting}} is the act of bringing the spotlight of attention on an object or event by moving the body to maximize sensory impact
extra: mnemonic: You have to move your body OVER (overt)
example: Turning your head and eyes toward a honking car to see where the sound came from.

text: Agraphia is the {{c1::inability to write}}
example: After a left parietal stroke, a lawyer can still read and speak but can no longer write a grocery list.

text:
Cognitive behavioral therapy addresses {{c1::cognitive}} and {{c1::behavioral}} components to addiction.
Benefits of CBT:
  • {{c1::more positive thoughts}}
  • {{c1::coping mechanisms}}
  • {{c1::long lasting results}}
example: A drinker learns to swap 'one drink won't hurt' for calling a friend, a skill that lasts after therapy ends.

text: {{c1::Neglect syndrome}} is a neuropsychological condition in which damage to the right parietal lobe causes a person to completely ignore the left side of their world, and even the left side of their body
example: After a right parietal stroke, a man eats only the right half of his plate and shaves only the right side of his face.

text: The cognitive abilities that improve with age are {{c1::semantic memory}}, {{c1::crystallized IQ}}, and {{c1::emotional reasoning}}
example: A 70-year-old beats her grandson at crosswords thanks to a lifetime of vocabulary.

text: {{c1::Hierarchical semantic network}} is the idea that we store concepts from broad categories to lower order categories
example: Collins and Quillian found 'a canary is an animal' takes longer to verify than 'a canary is a bird'.

text: REM sleep is important for {{c1::memory consolidation}} and {{c1::forming episodic memories}}
example: Rats deprived of REM sleep after learning a maze remember the route worse the next day.

text: Receptive aphasia is a {{c1::fluent}} aphasia
example: A Wernicke's patient answers 'How are you?' with fluent nonsense like 'The blue fork drove my sister.'

text: {{c1::Delta waves::Brain wave}} are associated with {{c2::deep sleep}} and {{c2::comas}}
example: A child in deep N3 sleep who can't be roused by a parent shows high-amplitude delta waves.

text: Nativists believe language is {{c1::innate}}
example: Deaf children in Nicaragua with no language model created Nicaraguan Sign Language on their own in the 1980s.

text:
{{c2::Benzodiazepine::Drug}} effects:
  • {{c1::enhance the brain's response to GABA}}
  • {{c1::induce sleep}}
  • {{c1::reduce anxiety}}
example: A nervous flyer takes alprazolam (Xanax) before boarding and dozes off soon after takeoff.

text: {{c1::Retrieval}} is {{c2::pulling something out of long-term memory and bringing it into conscious memory}}
example: Pulling the steps of glycolysis back up during the MCAT, months after studying them.

text: Hindsight bias: {{c1::The inclination, after an event has occurred, to see the event as having been predictable}}
extra: Example: "I knew I should've guessed those lottery numbers!"

text: Flynn effect: {{c1::The growth of IQ in each generation}}
example: Average IQ scores rose about 3 points per decade in the 20th century, so tests had to be re-normed.

text: Practical intelligence is {{c1::the ability to solve ill-defined problems}}
extra:
Ability to apply analytical and creative intelligence to real life scenarios
Street smarts
example: A store manager who talks an angry customer down and keeps the sale, though she struggled in school.

text: People that undergo hypnotism are typically {{c1::more susceptible to suggestion}} and exhibit {{c1::alpha waves::brain waves}}
example: A hypnotized volunteer told his arm is weightless lets it float up, while his EEG shows alpha waves.

text: Alcohol is a CNS {{c1::depressant}}
example: Alcohol boosts GABA<sub>A</sub> signalling, so a few drinks slow reaction time and slur speech.

text: {{c1::Circadian rhythms}} are regular body rhythms across a 24-hour period
example: Cortisol peaks each morning shortly after waking and falls to its lowest around midnight.

text: {{c1::N2 stage sleep::Sleep stage}} is associated with {{c2::theta waves}}, {{c2::sleep spindles}}, and {{c2::K-complexes}}
example: A door slams and the N2 sleeper's EEG shows a large K-complex, yet she sleeps on.

text: The N1 stage of sleep is dominated by {{c1::theta waves::Brain waves}}
example: Dozing off on a bus, you're in N1 with theta on the EEG when a pothole jolts you awake.

text: {{c1::Vygotsky::Theorist}} believed that {{c2::language and thought are independent but converge through development::view of language}}
example: A preschooler talks herself through a puzzle aloud ('blue piece here'), speech that later becomes silent thought.

text: The problem solving method with the highest chance of error is {{c1::intuition}}
example: Picking a multiple-choice answer because it 'feels right' instead of working the problem out.

text: In Piaget's {{c1::sensorimotor stage (0-2)::... stage}}, the child manipulates the environment to meet physical needs through circular reactions
extra: Object permanence develops at the end of this stage
example: A baby accidentally shakes a rattle, likes the sound and shakes it again and again.

text: During hypnosis, {{c1::false memories}} can form: memories that {{c2::are shaped by the hypnotist's expectations, even when the hypnotist does not intend it}}
example: A hypnotist asking 'Did you hear a loud noise that night?' can leave a witness 'remembering' one.

text: Retrograde amnesia is {{c1::inability to recall previously encoded information}}
example: After a concussion in a car crash, a driver cannot remember the hour before the accident.

text: {{c1::Methadone}} is a synthetic opioid used to {{c2::help in addiction and getting individuals off opioids}}
example: A former heroin user takes a daily oral methadone dose at a clinic to prevent withdrawal without a high.

text: In the reward pathway, the amygdala controls {{c1::emotion}}
extra: Example: I love this cake. I am happy eating this cake.

text: {{c1::Intoxication}} is when a drug enters the body and exerts its effects
extra:
Intoxication is specific to the drug type
alcohol = drunk
weed = high

text: MDMA is also known as {{c1::Ecstasy}} or {{c1::Molly}}
example: Ecstasy usually means a pressed MDMA pill; Molly is sold as MDMA powder or crystals.

text:
Formal operational stage:
  • occurs between ages {{c1::12+}}
  • associated with {{c1::abstract thinking}}, {{c1::reasoning through consequences}}, and {{c1::moral reasoning}}
extra: children begin to think like adults at this stage and continue to develop that overtime
example: A 15-year-old solves for x in algebra and debates whether lying is ever morally justified.

text: {{c1::Wernicke's aphasia::Disorder}} is when people {{c2::have trouble comprehending language as a result of temporal lobe damage but are still able to speak}}
example: A patient chats fast and fluently but cannot follow 'close your eyes', unaware anything is wrong.

text: {{c1::Galton's idea of hereditary genius::Idea}} states that {{c2::human ability is hereditary}}
example: Galton's Hereditary Genius (1869) noted that eminent British judges and scientists often had eminent relatives.

text: {{c1::Insomnia}} is persistent trouble falling asleep or staying asleep
example: A stressed accountant lies awake until 2 a.m. most nights during tax season.

text: {{c1::Heuristics}} are {{c2::mental shortcuts to find solutions to problems faster}}
extra: Example: when guessing a password, you guess someone's birthday to cut down on random guesses

text:
During N2 sleep, {{c1::K-complexes}}:
  • {{c2::suppress cortical arousal to keep you asleep}}
  • {{c2::aid in consolidating declarative/explicit memories}}
extra: They are the reason you won't wake up if someone lightly touches you. Your brain recognizes the touch as non-threatening and keeps you asleep

text: The phonological loop is where {{c1::verbal information}} is processed, including {{c1::any words or numbers}}
example: Silently repeating a 7-digit phone number to yourself while you look for a pen.

text: {{c1::Decision making}} is when we make a judgement of the desirability/probability of a certain outcome
example: Choosing between two job offers by weighing a likely promotion at one against higher pay at the other.

text: {{c1::Korsakoff's syndrome::Disease}} is caused by {{c2::a lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine)}}
example: Hospitals give thiamine to malnourished drinkers before IV glucose to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

text: {{c1::An overdose}} can occur when you take your normal dose of a drug under new conditions, without your body preparing for it
example: Siegel's heroin-tolerant rats given a large dose died twice as often in an unfamiliar room (64% vs 32%).

text: Behaviorists believe language is {{c1::just conditioned behavior}}
example: A toddler says 'cookie' and is handed one, so saying 'cookie' gets reinforced.

text: {{c1::Phonology}} is the actual sound of a language
example: English treats 'r' and 'l' as different sounds (rice vs lice), while Japanese does not.

text:
{{c1::Treisman's Attenuation Theory}} states that stimuli
{{c2::enter the sensory register}} → {{c2::attenuator}} → {{c2::perceptual process}} → {{c2::conscious}}
extra:
The attenuator replaces the selective filter: the attended message is processed more fully than the unattended message.
Mnemonic: Treisman aTTenuates
example: Treisman's shadowers briefly followed the story into the ignored ear when it switched sides mid-sentence.

text: {{c1::Fluid intelligence}} is the ability to {{c2::reason quickly and abstractly, such as when solving novel logic problems}}
example: Solving a never-before-seen pattern puzzle on Raven's Progressive Matrices.

text: Anterograde amnesia is {{c1::inability to encode new memories}}
example: After his hippocampi were removed, patient H.M. could not form new long-term memories.

text: {{c2::Conduction aphasia}} is associated with {{c1::normal function of Broca's and Wernicke's area independently}} but {{c1::problems when they have to work together}}
extra: Patients can speak and comprehend, but have great trouble repeating something they were just told
example: A patient follows conversation and speaks fluently but repeats 'the cat sat on the mat' as 'the cap sat on the hat'.

text: {{c1::Self-referencing}} is tying new information to yourself to remember it better
example: You remember the word 'generous' better after asking yourself whether it describes you.

text: Alzheimer's is associated with {{c1::a buildup of amyloid plaques in the brain::cause}}
example: People with Down syndrome carry an extra APP gene on chromosome 21 and build up amyloid plaques early.

text: {{c1::Rote rehearsal}} is saying the same thing over and over to remember it better
example: Repeating 'manzana means apple' ten times in a row before a Spanish quiz.

text: The Nativist perspective (language) believes that during development {{c1::there is a critical period where the language acquisition device is most active between birth to age 8-9}}
example: Genie, isolated until age 13, learned many words but never mastered grammar.

text:
Infants in the sensorimotor stage gather information through:
  • {{c1::senses (sight, smell, taste, touch)}}
  • {{c1::motor function (learn how to move your body around)}}
example: A 9-month-old mouths every new toy and bangs it on the table to learn what it is.

text: {{c1::Ebbinghaus::Psychologist}} was the first person to look at decay in human memory
extra:
Dashed: forgetting without review. Solid blue: each review resets recall and slows the decay (spaced repetition).
Source: Wikimedia Commons — Ebbinghaus2.jpg (public domain); forgetting-curve graph © Taalhammer, taalhammer.com/the-forgetting-curve-hermann-ebbinghaus/
example: Ebbinghaus memorized nonsense syllables like 'DAX' and forgot over half of them within a day.

text: The {{c1::Stanford-Binet intelligence scales}} are designed to measure five factors of cognitive ability: fluid reasoning, knowledge, quantitative reasoning, visual-spatial processing, and working memory
extra: Theoretically, the Stanford-Binet test measures a person's ability to learn
example: A child scoring 130 on the Stanford-Binet sits two standard deviations above the mean of 100 (SD 15).

text: {{c1::Synaptic plasticity}} is change that occurs at synapses, the junctions between neurons that allow them to communicate
example: In Kandel's Aplysia, repeated shocks strengthened sensory-to-motor synapses, so the gill withdrew harder.

text: We use heuristics in decision making to {{c1::make quick decisions based on prior knowledge}}
extra:
Example: asked which is riskier, a shark attack or a fireworks accident, most people say shark attack because vivid media examples (like Jaws) are easy to recall.
Fireworks accidents are actually riskier.

text:
{{c1::Amphetamines/Methamphetamines}} effects:
  • {{c2::release DA, NE, and 5-HT}}
  • {{c2::block DA/NE/5-HT reuptake}}
  • {{c2::cause feelings of euphoria}}
example: A meth user feels a surge of euphoria and energy and stays awake for days on a binge.

text: Evolutionary biologists believe dreams are {{c1::a threat simulation to prepare for the real world}}
example: Dreaming of being chased by a predator lets you rehearse escape without any real danger.

text: The quicker you are able to switch or “shift” your thinking from one dimension (e.g. color of an object) to another (e.g. shape of an object), the greater your level of {{c1::cognitive flexibility}}
example: On the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, quickly switching from sorting by colour to sorting by shape when the rule changes.

text: In the reward pathway, the prefrontal cortex controls {{c1::attention}}
extra: Example: I am putting my attention on this cake I'm eating.

text:
The four classes of psychoactive drugs include:
  • {{c1::depressants}}
  • {{c1::stimulants}}
  • {{c1::hallucinogens}}
  • {{c1::opiates/opioids}}
example: Alcohol (depressant), cocaine (stimulant), LSD (hallucinogen) and heroin (opioid).

text: N3 sleep, also called {{c1::slow-wave sleep}}, is marked by {{c1::delta}} waves. It is the stage in which consolidation of {{c1::declarative}} memory takes place, and the stage of behavioral parasomnias such as {{c1::sleepwalking/sleeptalking}}
example: A child sleepwalks to the kitchen an hour after bedtime, during N3, and remembers nothing next morning.

text: {{c1::The basal forebrain::Brain structure}} is {{c2::the main cholinergic (acetylcholine) output of the central nervous system}}
example: In Alzheimer's disease, loss of basal forebrain neurons (nucleus basalis of Meynert) cuts cortical acetylcholine.

text: REM sleep is also called {{c1::paradoxical sleep}} because {{c2::it has brain activity similar to being awake}}
example: During REM, the EEG looks like someone solving a puzzle, yet the sleeper's limbs are paralyzed.

text: {{c2::Obstructive sleep apnea}} is when {{c1::our airways are obstructed while sleeping to where our airflow gets blocked for a short period of time}}
extra: Example: excess neck tissue blocking the airway
example: An obese man who snores loudly, gasps for air at night and dozes off at his desk.

text: {{c1::Oral drug entry::Method of drug entry}} is ingesting something
example: Swallowing an ibuprofen tablet, which must pass through the gut and liver before reaching the blood.

text: Nicotine is a CNS {{c1::stimulant::stimulant or depressant}}
example: A smoker's morning cigarette raises heart rate and sharpens alertness within seconds.

text: Creative Intelligence is {{c1::the ability to adapt to new situations}} and {{c1::generate novel ideas}}
example: 3M's Art Fry turned a 'failed', weakly sticking glue into the Post-it Note.

text: {{c1::The method of loci}} is imagining moving through an imaginary place with visual representations of topics to be remembered
example: A memory champion places each card of a shuffled deck along a walk through her childhood home.

text: {{c1::Dementia}} is a term for decline in {{c2::memory}} and {{c2::cognitive functions}} to the point of interfering with daily life
example: A grandmother who gets lost driving to her own church and can no longer pay her bills.

text: {{c1::Representativeness heuristic}} is a {{c2::decision making heuristic where choices are based on the most representative answer based on prototypes}}
example: Shy, tidy 'Steve' is guessed to be a librarian, not a farmer, though farmers vastly outnumber librarians.

text: Indications of sleep apnea include {{c1::snoring}} and {{c1::morning fatigue after full night sleep}}
example: His wife complains of his loud snoring, and he wakes after 8 hours in bed still exhausted.

text: {{c1::Convergent thinking}} is the ability to give the "correct" answer to standard questions that do not require significant creativity
extra:
Example: most school tasks and standardized multiple-choice tests
It is the opposite of divergent thinking

text:
Theories of intelligence:
  • {{c1::Spearman}}: one general intelligence (g factor)
  • {{c1::Thurstone}}: 7 primary mental abilities
  • {{c1::Gardner}}: 7–9 independent multiple intelligences
  • {{c1::Sternberg}}: triarchic (analytical, creative, practical)
  • {{c1::Cattell}}: fluid vs. crystallized intelligence
extra:
Fluid = solving new problems, declines with age. Crystallized = accumulated knowledge, stable or rises with age.
Spearman's g has the most research support.
example: A gifted violinist who struggles with algebra fits Gardner's model better than Spearman's single g.

text: {{c2::Universalism}} is the idea that {{c1::thoughts determine language completely}}
extra: example: the Dani of New Guinea have only 2 color words (dark/light) yet perceive and remember colors as well as English speakers (Rosch)

text: The intelligence theory most heavily backed by research is {{c1::Spearman's Theory of General Intelligence}}
example: The WAIS reports one full-scale IQ because a single g factor explains much of the overlap among its subtests.

text: Implicit memory includes {{c1::priming}}, {{c1::procedural memory}}, and {{c1::habits}}
example: Typing your password by finger habit without being able to say the characters aloud.

text: {{c1::Post-acute}} withdrawal has {{c2::less physical symptoms}} and {{c2::more emotional/psychological symptoms}}
example: Months after quitting alcohol, a man no longer shakes but still battles anxiety, poor sleep and irritability.

text: The {{c1::gambler's fallacy}} is the mistaken belief that if something happens more frequently than normal, it will happen less frequently in the future (or vice versa)
example: After 5 reds in a row at roulette, a gambler bets on black, believing it is due.

text: The central executive is used to {{c1::coordinate the visuo-spatial sketchpad and the phonological loop}}
example: While driving with GPS, the central executive juggles the road ahead and the spoken turn directions.

text: Korsakoff's syndrome and Wernicke's encephalopathy are NOT {{c1::progressive}}
extra: They do not keep worsening like Alzheimer's if thiamine is given; Wernicke's is often reversible with prompt thiamine, but Korsakoff's memory loss is often permanent.
example: Eye-movement palsies in Wernicke's often clear within hours of IV thiamine, while Alzheimer's only worsens.

text: {{c1::Broca's area::Brain region}} is involved in {{c2::speech production}} and is located in the {{c2::frontal}} lobe
example: Broca's patient 'Tan' could say only the syllable 'tan'; his autopsy showed a left frontal lobe lesion.

text: {{c1::Source monitoring errors}} are when you can recall a piece of information but attribute it to the wrong source by mistake
example: You retell a joke to the very friend who told it to you, sure you heard it on a podcast.

text: {{c1::Functional fixedness}} is the tendency to use objects only in the way they are normally utilized
extra: Creates barriers to problem-solving
example: In Duncker's candle problem, people fail to see the box of tacks as a shelf for the candle.

text: Most dreaming occurs during {{c1::REM sleep::sleep stage}}
example: A sleeper woken while their eyes dart under closed lids usually recalls a vivid dream.

text: {{c2::Well-defined}} problems are problems with {{c1::a clear starting and end point}}
