example: Solving 2x + 3 = 11 has a clear start and a single correct end: x = 4.

text: {{c1::Beta waves::Brain Wave}} are associated with {{c2::alertness/concentration}}
example: Your EEG shows fast, low-amplitude beta waves while you work through an MCAT passage.

text:
Group meetings can be categorized into three main steps:
  1. {{c1::Acceptance}}
  2. {{c1::Surrender}}
  3. {{c1::Active involvement}}
extra:
1. Acceptance: acknowledge that addiction is a problem you can't control on your own
2. Surrender: give yourself up to a higher power and accept help offered through that power and the group
3. Active involvement: take part in meetings and activities to help yourself and other addicts
example: Alcoholics Anonymous's 12 steps begin with admitting powerlessness over alcohol.

text: {{c1::Cross tolerance}} is when {{c2::you are tolerant to a novel drug because of a similar CNS pathway to a drug you are already tolerant for}}
example: A heavy drinker needs more benzodiazepine sedation for surgery, since both drugs act on GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors.

text: The knew-it-all-along effect and creeping determinism are also known as {{c1::hindsight bias}}
example: After the underdog wins the Super Bowl, fans insist they always knew the upset was coming.

text: Anomia is the {{c1::inability to name things}}
example: Shown a comb, a patient says 'it's the thing you run through your hair' but cannot come up with 'comb'.

text: According to Freud, the hidden meaning of our dream is known as {{c1::latent content}}
extra: Example: a monster chasing you could represent your job pushing you out.

text: Amphetamine blocks {{c1::dopamine}} reuptake
example: Adderall (amphetamine) keeps more dopamine in the synapse, helping a student with ADHD focus.

text: {{c1::Crystallized intelligence}} involves using acquired knowledge and skills
example: Answering a WAIS general-information question such as 'What is the capital of France?'

text: The visuo-spatial sketchpad is where {{c1::visual}} and {{c1::spatial}} info are processed
example: Mentally picturing your kitchen to count how many cupboard doors it has.

text:
Signs of a substance-use-disorder:
  • {{c1::Using increasingly large amounts}}
  • {{c1::Stronger Cravings}}
  • {{c1::Failing life obligations}}
  • {{c1::Withdrawal}}
example: A drinker who needs more each week, misses work, and gets the shakes without alcohol.

text: The two stages to withdrawal are {{c1::acute}} and {{c1::post-acute}}
example: A recovering heroin user has sweats and cramps for two weeks, then months of low mood and cravings.

text: {{c1::Joint attention}} is the focusing of attention on an object by two separate individuals
example: A mother points at a dog and her toddler looks at it too, both attending to the same thing.

text: {{c1::Problem solving}} is when we move from a current state to a goal state
example: Your car won't start (current state) and you must still get to work by 9 am (goal state).

text: The {{c1::modified semantic network}} model says concepts are linked by how related they are (not a strict hierarchy), so links differ between people based on their experience
extra:
Collins & Loftus (1975)
Revises the hierarchical Collins & Quillian model. Shorter links = stronger associations. Activating one concept primes its neighbors (spreading activation).
example: People verify 'a robin is a bird' faster than 'a penguin is a bird', which a strict hierarchy cannot explain.

text: The two types of memory interference are {{c1::retroactive}} and {{c1::proactive}}
example: Learning Spanish then Italian: Spanish intrudes on Italian (proactive); Italian muddles Spanish (retroactive).

text: {{c1::Intramuscular::Method of drug entry}} is when a drug is delivered through a needle in the muscle
example: An EpiPen injects epinephrine into the outer thigh muscle during anaphylaxis.

text: LSD, peyote, mescaline, and ketamine are considered {{c1::hallucinogens}}
example: A person on LSD may see walls breathing and colours swirling for hours.

text: {{c1::Inductive::Deductive or Inductive}} reasoning starts with evidence, then forms conclusions
example: Every swan you have seen is white, so you conclude all swans are white.

text: Implicit memory is {{c1::unconscious::conscious or unconscious}}
example: H.M. improved at mirror-tracing each day yet never remembered having practised.

text: The three most important retrieval cues are {{c1::priming}}, {{c1::context}}, and {{c1::state-dependency}}
example: Taking an exam in the same room where you studied is the context cue at work.

text: Long-term memory includes {{c1::explicit}} AKA {{c1::declarative}} and {{c1::implicit}} AKA {{c1::non-declarative}} memory
example: Recalling your graduation day is explicit; typing without looking at the keys is implicit.

text: {{c1::Autobiographical memory}} is a memory system consisting of episodes recollected from an individual's life
example: Recalling your first day of college: where you lived, who you met and how nervous you felt.

text: Prospective memory is {{c1::remembering to do things in the future}}
extra: Picture of a prospector, for prospective memory
example: Remembering to buy milk on the way home or to take a pill at 8 pm tonight.

text: Babies need {{c1::more::more or less}} sleep than adults
example: A newborn sleeps about 16 hours a day, roughly twice an adult's 8.

text: The {{c1::memory consolidation theory::... theory}} of dreams states that we use our dreams to sort out the problems and stresses of our day
example: A student anxious about tomorrow's exam dreams that night of getting lost on the way to the test.

text: {{c1::Tolerance}} is when you get used to a drug so you need more of it to achieve the same effect
example: A coffee drinker who once felt wired on one cup now needs three to feel awake.

text: {{c1::Sleep apnea}} is when you stop breathing while sleeping; your body wakes up just long enough to gasp for air, then falls back asleep without you realizing it
example: A heavy man with a thick neck stops breathing 30 times an hour at night and is treated with CPAP.

text: People who regularly meditate {{c1::have more control over their attention::effect of regular meditation}}
example: A daily meditator notices her mind drifting in a lecture sooner and brings it back to the speaker.

text: {{c1::Hypnic jerks}} are muscle twitches you sometimes experience as you fall asleep
extra:
Often feels like a sudden falling sensation as you drift off
Involuntary (myoclonic) twitches during the transition into N1 sleep; harmless and very common.
example: Just as you doze off on the couch, your leg kicks and you jolt awake feeling you missed a step.

text:
Common effects of depressants include:
  • {{c1::decreased CNS activity}}
  • {{c1::decreased HR}}
  • {{c1::decreased BP}}
  • {{c1::decreased processing speed}}
  • {{c1::vasodilation at low concentrations/vasoconstriction at high concentrations}}
example: After several drinks, a man's speech slurs, his reactions slow and his face flushes from vasodilation.

text: {{c1::Barbiturates::Drug}} are used to {{c2::induce sleep}} and {{c2::reduce anxiety}}

Sensorimotor stage characteristics:
  • between ages {{c1::0-2}}
  • associated with {{c1::object permanence}} and {{c1::stranger anxiety}}
extra: Object permanence: infants realize objects still exist when they can't see them
example: A 10-month-old cries when a stranger holds her and lifts a blanket to find a hidden toy.

text:
The order of Piaget's stages of development is:
  1. {{c1::sensorimotor}}
  2. {{c1::preoperational}}
  3. {{c1::concrete operational}}
  4. {{c1::formal operational}}
extra: Mnemonic: Some Pussy Cats Fart (S, P, C, F)
example: A baby plays peekaboo, a 4-year-old plays pretend, a 9-year-old grasps conservation, a teen argues hypotheticals.

text: {{c3::Vygotsky}} believed in the idea that children develop language {{c1::by interacting with adults who already know the language}}. This is called {{c2::socialization}}
example: A toddler learns new words as her father names the animals while they read a picture book together.

text: The least effective encoding strategy is {{c1::rote rehearsal}}
example: Repeating a word list 20 times yields worse recall than linking each word to a vivid image.

text: {{c1::Decay}} is when we can't recall a piece of information anymore
example: Years after high school, you can no longer recall the French vocabulary you once knew.

text: Dyssomnias are conditions that make it difficult to {{c1::fall asleep, stay asleep, or avoid sleep}}
example: A stressed student lies awake for hours most nights before exams (insomnia).

text: {{c2::Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligence::Theory}} states that {{c1::there are 7-9 independent intelligences}}
extra:
Mnemonic: picture 7–9 spaced-out stones in a garden (Gardner's independent intelligences)
Gardner (Frames of Mind, 1983): intelligence is a set of relatively independent abilities, not one general IQ:
  • Linguistic
  • Logical-mathematical
  • Spatial
  • Bodily-kinesthetic
  • Musical
  • Interpersonal
  • Intrapersonal
  • Naturalistic (added 1999)
  • Existential (proposed, tentative)
example: Mozart (musical) and Michael Jordan (bodily-kinesthetic) each excel in a different one of Gardner's intelligences.

text: {{c1::Accommodation}} is when we {{c2::create new schemas or adjust our schemas to incorporate new information}}
example: After hearing the cat meow and seeing it refuse to fetch, the toddler forms a separate 'kitty' schema.

text: {{c1::Injection::Method of drug entry}} is intravenous entry
example: A nurse pushes IV morphine into a hand vein, and pain relief begins within minutes.

text: {{c1::Attentional capture}} occurs when attention is attracted by the motion of an object or stimulus
example: A mouse darting across the kitchen floor instantly grabs your attention.

text: Alzheimer's patients initially begin with {{c1::trouble with short term memory}} that progresses into {{c1::problems with long-term memory}}
example: A patient first forgets where she parked this morning; years later she cannot recall her own wedding.

text:
Exogenous cues are driven by {{c1::bottom-up}} processing
Endogenous cues are driven by {{c1::top-down}} processing
example: A fire alarm yanks your attention bottom-up; scanning a crowd for a friend's red coat is top-down.

text:
Iconic memory is {{c1::what you see}} and lasts {{c1::half a second}}
Echoic memory is {{c1::what you hear}} and lasts {{c1::a few seconds}}
example: Asked 'What did I just say?' while zoning out, you can still replay the last few words from echoic memory.

text: IQ stands for {{c1::intelligence quotient}}
example: An 8-year-old with a mental age of 10 has a ratio IQ of 10 ÷ 8 × 100 = 125.

text: Aphasia is {{c1::any disorder that involves language}}
example: After a left-hemisphere stroke, a patient can no longer find words or follow spoken instructions.

text: The mesolimbic pathway includes the {{c1::nucleus accumbens}}, {{c1::amygdala}}, and {{c1::hippocampus}}
example: Walking past his old bar, a former drinker recalls the nights there and feels a surge of craving.

text: {{c1::Sleep spindles}} are {{c3::bursts of brain activity}} during N2 sleep to {{c2::inhibit certain perceptions}} and to {{c2::maintain a tranquil state}}
extra: Spindles and K-complexes are the hallmarks of N2 sleep. Spindles are also linked to memory consolidation.
example: People with more sleep spindles sleep through louder noises, like a door slamming down the hall.

text: MDMA can act as a {{c1::stimulant}} or {{c1::hallucinogen}}
example: At a rave, MDMA keeps a user dancing all night while the lights and music feel intensely vivid.

text: {{c1::Substance-use-disorders::Disorder}} occur when using a drug causes {{c2::serious impairment of functioning in life, work, school, home, etc.}}
example: A student keeps using cannabis daily even as he fails his classes and loses his job.

text: {{c1::Distal stimuli::Type of stimuli}} are {{c2::objects and events out in the world around you}}
example: A real oak tree standing 50 metres away across the park is a distal stimulus.

text: {{c1::Negative priming}} is when prior exposure to a stimulus unfavorably influences the response to the same stimulus
example: Ignore a red 'A' while naming a green 'B'; if 'A' is the target on the next trial, you name it slower.

text: {{c2::Phosphodiesterase}} decomposes {{c1::cAMP}} → {{c1::AMP}}
example: Theophylline inhibits phosphodiesterase, so cAMP stays high and airway smooth muscle relaxes in asthma.

text: The can't-happen-to-me bias {{c1::causes people to underestimate both the possibility of a disaster occurring and its possible effects}}
extra: Example: "The coronavirus won't get ME sick"

text: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus regulates circadian rhythms largely via the hormone {{c1::melatonin::hormone}}
example: Bright phone light at night signals the SCN to hold back melatonin, so you fall asleep later.

text: {{c1::Spreading activation}} says that all ideas in the brain {{c2::are connected and that pulling up one memory can also activate similar memories}}
extra:
Example: saying animal activates mammal and bird, etc.
This makes it easier to retrieve other information related to animal

text: Signs of drug addiction include {{c1::tolerance}} and {{c1::needing drug to feel normal}}
example: A man who once got high on one pill now takes four just to stop shaking and feel normal.

text: People with Wernicke's aphasia can {{c1::produce language}} but have trouble {{c1::comprehending language}}
example: Asked to point to the window, a Wernicke's patient keeps talking fluently but points to the door.

text: {{c1::Caffeine}} is the only drug we can't develop substance-use disorder for
example: DSM-5 diagnoses caffeine intoxication and withdrawal but lists caffeine use disorder only for further study.

text: REM sleep contains {{c1::alpha, beta, and dyssynchronous (similar to beta) waves::Brain Waves}}
example: A sleep tech sees fast, awake-looking waves on the EEG while the sleeper's eyes dart under closed lids.

text: {{c1::Broca's aphasia::Disorder}} is when people {{c2::have trouble producing speech as a result of damage to the language production centers of the brain}}
example: Asked about his weekend, a patient slowly forces out 'Walk... dog... park', knowing exactly what he means.

text: {{c2::Central sleep apnea}} is {{c1::sleep apnea without obstruction but rather problems with the brains control system for breathing}}
example: A patient on high-dose opioids stops breathing during sleep with an open airway because brainstem drive falls.

text: In the reward pathway, the hippocampus controls {{c1::memory}}
extra: Example: Where am I right now eating this cake? Who am I with? Let's remember this time.

text: {{c2::Alpha waves::Brain wave}} are associated with {{c1::daydreaming}}
example: Sitting with eyes closed, relaxed but awake, your EEG fills with alpha waves.

text: The {{c1::trial + error}} method of problem solving is {{c2::taking random guesses until something works}}
example: Thorndike's cats in puzzle boxes pawed at random until they happened to hit the latch that opened the door.

text: {{c1::Flashbulb memories}} are {{c2::very vivid memories formed during an emotionally arousing event}}
example: Many Americans can describe exactly where they were when they heard about the 9/11 attacks.

text: {{c1::The nativist perspective::Idea}}, associated with {{c1::Noam Chomsky}}, states that {{c2::children are born with an innate ability to learn language because we all have a language acquisition device}}
example: Children everywhere say things they never heard, like 'I goed', applying a grammar rule nobody taught them.

text: Inattention is {{c1::bad::good/bad}} for memory
extra: Attention is needed for encoding. Information you don't attend to never gets encoded into long-term memory (encoding failure), so it can't be retrieved later. Example: a lecture you zoned out of.

text: Operation span testing tests for {{c1::the capacity of working memory}}
example: Check '(8 ÷ 2) + 1 = 5?' then memorize a word; after several such pairs, recall the words in order.

text: The three injection types shown above: {{c1::Intramuscular}}, {{c1::Subcutaneous}}, {{c1::Intradermal}}
extra:
Intramuscular: deep into the muscles
Subcutaneous: into the fat layer underneath the skin
Intradermal: into the dermis which is the skin layer underneath the epidermis
example: A flu shot goes intramuscular into the deltoid, insulin subcutaneous, and a TB skin test intradermal.

text: {{c1::Sleep}} is the state of not being aware of yourself or the world around you
example: A deeply asleep roommate doesn't notice you walk in and switch on the light.

text: People with Broca's aphasia can {{c1::understand language}} but have trouble {{c1::producing language}}
example: A Broca's patient follows 'pick up the pen' perfectly but can only answer 'Yes... pen... good'.

text: Nicotine is a CNS stimulant that acts as an {{c1::acetylcholine}} agonist
example: Nicotine binds nicotinic ACh receptors on VTA dopamine neurons, driving the reward of smoking.

text: Posner and Snyder described an action as automatic if {{c1::the action did not affect other mental activities}}
example: A skilled driver chats with a passenger while steering, since driving no longer draws on attention.

text:
Marijuana effects:
  • impairs {{c1::motor function}}
  • heightens {{c1::sensations}}
  • disrupts {{c1::short-term memory}}
  • reduces {{c1::pain}}
extra: Active ingredient: THC, which acts on cannabinoid receptors. Also increases appetite.
example: After smoking, a user forgets what he said a minute ago and fumbles a set of tossed keys.

text: {{c1::Asymmetry}} in spreading activation occurs because of STDP (Spike Time Dependent Plasticity)
example: Saying the alphabet forward is effortless but backward is slow, because the links were strengthened in one order.

text: {{c1::Intuition}} is {{c2::relying on instinct to solve problems}}
example: A chess grandmaster glances at the board and 'feels' the right move before calculating it.

text: Materialists observe {{c1::what happens in the brain when people think/speak/write}}
example: Using fMRI to watch Broca's area light up while a volunteer names pictures aloud.

text:
The cocktail party effect is an example of an {{c1::endogenous}} cue.
It is the ability to {{c1::concentrate on our name when it is called, even in crowds}}
example: Deep in conversation at a party, you suddenly catch your name spoken across the room.

text: {{c1::Motivational interviewing}} involves working with patients to {{c2::find intrinsic motivation to change}}.
extra: Very focused and goal directed therapy.
example: A counsellor asks a smoker what quitting would mean for her kids, so she voices her own reason to stop.

text: {{c1::Semantic}} memory is remembering simple facts like meanings of words
example: Knowing that Paris is the capital of France without recalling when you learned it.

text: In split-brain individuals, if an image is in their right visual field, they can {{c1::name the object}} but cannot {{c1::pick up the object/draw it}} with their left hand
example: Flashed 'ring' in the right visual field, the patient says 'ring', but his left hand cannot find the ring by touch.

text:
{{c1::Divided attention}} occurs when {{c2::an individual must perform two tasks which require attention simultaneously}}
This theory also states that attention is a {{c3::limited resource}}, so you switch between tasks rather than multitasking
example: Texting while driving, your attention flips between screen and road, so you miss a light turning red.

text: The sensory register includes {{c1::iconic}} and {{c1::echoic}} memory
example: A sparkler's glowing trail in the dark is iconic memory; replaying a half-heard question is echoic.

text: {{c1::The Learning (behaviorist) theory::Theory}}, associated with {{c1::BF Skinner}}, states that language {{c2::is acquired through operant conditioning}}
extra: Example: a child says "mama" because every time they say it, their mom praises (reinforces) them

text: {{c1::Dopamine}} is produced in the {{c2::ventral tegmental area::brain region}} in the midbrain for use in the mesolimbic system
example: Cocaine and opioids both boost dopamine sent from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens.

text: {{c1::Binet's idea of mental age::Idea}} compares how children perform at a specific age compared to the average intelligence performance for that age
example: A 6-year-old who passes the tasks most 8-year-olds pass has a mental age of 8.

text: {{c1::Word salad}} is the meaningless speech produced by people with Wernicke's aphasia
example: 'I called my mother on the television and the door did not understand the spoon, you know.'

text: Addiction can be explained by both {{c1::genetic}} and {{c1::environmental}} factors
example: Twin studies put the heritability of alcohol addiction near 50%, with environment explaining the rest.

text: Post-acute withdrawal usually lasts {{c1::two years::time frame}}
example: Someone who quits opioids in January 2024 may still have mood swings and cravings into 2026.

text: {{c1::The availability heuristic}} is a decision making heuristic where choices are based on {{c2::quick, easily accessible examples}}
example: After a plane crash makes the news, people drive instead of fly, though driving is far deadlier per mile.

text: {{c1::Encoding}} is {{c2::transferring information from the working memory to long-term memory}}
example: Rehearsing a new friend's name until you can still recall it the next week.

text:
Effect of caffeine on cAMP: {{c1::Inhibits phosphodiesterase (enzyme) that breaks down cAMP}}
So: {{c1::Caffeine leads to more cAMP activity}}
example: With PDE blocked by caffeine, the cAMP made after an adrenaline surge lasts longer, keeping PKA active.

text: Cocaine users typically experience {{c1::a crash}} after use
example: Hours after a cocaine binge, a user feels exhausted and depressed and craves more.

text: The {{c1::spotlight model of attention}} describes how our focus of attention is analogous to the beam of a spotlight; the moveable spotlight is directed at one location and everything within its beam is attended and processed preferentially, while information outside the beam is unattended
example: While you watch the goalkeeper, a player swap on the far sideline goes unprocessed.

text: {{c1::The episodic buffer}} acts as a connector for information to be stored in long-term memory
example: Remembering a friend's story binds her words, her face and the café into one episode.

text: Working memory AKA {{c1::short-term memory}}
example: Holding a Wi-Fi password in mind just long enough to type it in.

text: {{c1::Pragmatics}} is the branch of linguistics that deals with the context in which language is used
example: 'Can you pass the salt?' is heard as a request, not as a question about your arm strength.

text: Caffeine inhibiting the breakdown of cAMP leads to ↑ {{c1::Glutamate}} production
extra: cAMP pretty much leads to more activity and energy production
example: After a double espresso, extra glutamate release in the cortex leaves you alert and jittery.

text: {{c1::Wernicke's encephalopathy}} is a precursor to Korsakoff's syndrome
example: An alcoholic brought to the ER staggering, confused and with nystagmus later develops lasting amnesia if untreated.

text: {{c1::Narcolepsy}} is when individuals can't help themselves from falling asleep
example: A man with narcolepsy falls asleep mid-sentence at dinner, and his knees buckle when he laughs.

text: {{c2::MDMA}} can damage {{c1::neurons that produce serotonin}}
extra: These are serotonergic neurons (e.g. in the raphe nuclei). The damage is clearly shown in animals and suggested in heavy human users, and may contribute to later mood and memory problems.
example: PET scans of heavy ecstasy users show fewer serotonin transporters than those of non-users.

text: {{c1::Cortisol::Hormone}} promotes wakefulness
example: Cortisol peaks about 30 minutes after you wake up (the cortisol awakening response).

text: Parasomnias are conditions that cause {{c1::abnormal movements or behaviors during sleep}}
example: A child sits up screaming an hour after falling asleep and remembers nothing the next morning (night terror).

text: {{c1::Sensory memory::... memory}} and {{c1::short term memory::... memory}} are transient and based on neurotransmitter activity
example: Without rehearsal, a phone number you just heard fades from short-term memory in about 20 seconds.

text: The most common form of dementia is {{c1::Alzheimer's Disease::disease}}
example: Ronald Reagan's Alzheimer's typifies the disease behind roughly 60–70% of all dementia cases.

text:
{{c1::Executive attention}} is attention involved in:
  • {{c2::goal directed behavior}}
  • {{c2::monitoring internal conflicts}}
  • {{c2::anticipating the effects of behavior}}.
example: A dieter notices the urge to grab a donut, weighs it against her goal, and reaches for an apple.

text:
{{c1::Deutsch and Deutsch's Late Selection Theory::Theory}} states that stimuli
{{c2::enter the sensory register}} → {{c2::perceptual process}} → {{c2::selective filter}} → {{c2::conscious}}
extra:
Problem: processing all incoming information before filtering it would take too much energy.
Mnemonic: The Dutch pay attention to everything, so everything is perceptually processed.
example: MacKay: 'river' played to the ignored ear made listeners hear 'bank' in the attended ear as a riverbank.

text: Melodic Intonation Therapy works best with {{c1::Non-fluent aphasia}}
example: A Broca's aphasia patient who can't say 'I want water' can sing the phrase to a familiar tune.

text: Slowest method of drug entry is through {{c1::oral methods::Method of drug entry}}
example: A swallowed pain pill takes 30 to 60 minutes to work, versus seconds for an IV dose.

text: {{c1::Working backwards}} is when we start with a goal and use it to suggest connections back to the current state
example: Solving a paper maze by starting at the exit and tracing a path back to the entrance.

text: {{c1::Linguistic determinism}} is the idea that {{c2::language has influence on thoughts}}
example: Russian speakers, with separate words for light and dark blue, tell those shades apart faster than English speakers.

text: {{c1::The activation synthesis hypothesis}} states that dreams are {{c2::just our brain interpreting random neural impulses from the brainstem (pons)}}
extra: Since the impulses are random, dreams might not have any meaning.
example: Random pons firing that signals motion gets woven by the cortex into a dream of falling off a cliff.

text: Interactionists place heavy emphasis on {{c1::interconnection of environmental cues and innate biology in regards to language}}
example: A baby's built-in babbling becomes words only as caregivers talk back and name the things she points to.

text: {{c1::Weak linguistic determinism}} AKA {{c1::relativism}} states that {{c2::language influences thoughts}} and {{c2::we think in ways based on how our language is structured}}
extra: Example: English speakers who read "the girl pushed the boy" tend to picture the girl on the left; Hebrew speakers picture it reversed, since Hebrew reads right to left

text: The retrieval cue of context states that {{c1::it is easier to remember something if you are in the same environment you encoded it in}}
extra: example: studying in the same room you take a test can improve recall

text: {{c1::A crash}} can occur when the brain, cued by a usual drug routine, preemptively counteracts a drug that is then not taken
extra:
Conditioned compensatory response: drug cues make the body oppose the drug in advance, pushing it below homeostasis.
Example: daily 9 a.m. cocaine. At 9 a.m. the brain pre-lowers its baseline, so a skipped dose means a crash.
Flip side: the usual dose in a new setting gets no compensation, which raises overdose risk.

text: The cognitive abilities that are stable with age include {{c1::implicit memory}} and {{c1::recognition}}
example: A 90-year-old still ties her shoelaces fluently and picks out familiar faces in old photos.

text: {{c1::Endogenous cues::Type of cue}} require {{c2::internal knowledge to understand the cue.}}
example: A 'Gate B12 →' sign at the airport steers your attention only because you can read it.

text: {{c1::Relapse}} is when a patient slips back and returns to a drug they were addicted to
example: Six months sober, a man starts drinking again after a stressful week at work.

text: Adverse side effects of {{c2::barbiturates}} include reduced {{c1::memory}}, {{c1::judgement}}, and {{c1::concentration}}
example: A patient on phenobarbital forgets appointments and struggles to follow a long conversation.

text: Explicit memory includes both {{c1::semantic}} and {{c1::episodic}} memory
example: Knowing the Eiffel Tower is in Paris is semantic; recalling your own trip to see it is episodic.

text: Opiates and opioids can cause death by {{c1::respiratory depression}}
extra: Examples: heroin, morphine, opium, oxycodone and hydrocodone
example: Naloxone reverses a heroin overdose by restoring breathing within minutes.

text: Consciousness ranges from {{c1::alertness}} to {{c1::sleep}}
example: A student is alert in a morning exam, daydreaming by noon, and drowsy, then asleep, by midnight.

text: The {{c1::anchoring and adjustment heuristic::... heuristic}} is when people start with an implicitly suggested reference point (the "anchor") and then make adjustments to it to reach their estimate
example: Asked if Gandhi died before or after age 140, people then guess he died older than those asked about age 9.

text: In the reward pathway, when dopamine {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}, serotonin {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
example: During a binge, dopamine spikes while serotonin's satiety signal falls, so you keep eating chips.

text:
Three phenomena that can occur during {{c2::N1 sleep::Sleep stage}} are:
  • {{c1::hypnagogic hallucinations}}
  • {{c1::the tetris effect}}
  • {{c1::hypnic jerks}}
example: Drifting off after hours of Tetris, you see falling blocks, then your leg jerks you awake.

text: {{c1::Implicit}} memory is when previous experiences aid the performance of a task without conscious awareness of previous experiences.

Memory decay can be caused by:
  • {{c1::not encoding the memory well enough}}
  • {{c1::not retrieving it for a while}}
example: Cranial nerves crammed once and never reviewed are gone by the time you sit the MCAT.

text: Means of production: {{c1::how we produce goods}}
example: A Manchester mill owner in Marx's day owned the looms; his workers owned only their labour.

text:
Demographic Transition Model:
Stage 5:
  • {{c2::Malthusian}} Theorem:
    {{c1::We run out of resources, causing a high mortality rate}}
  • {{c2::Anti-Malthusian}} Theorem:
    {{c1::Couples only want 0-1 children}}
example: Japan, where deaths now outnumber births and the population has been shrinking since about 2010.

text: Older adults and society separate; assumes people become more self-absorbed as they age: {{c1::Disengagement theory}}
example: A 78-year-old steps down from the church board to spend quiet time reflecting, and a younger member takes over.

text:
Functionalist view of cities:
  • {{c1::They have important functions}}
  • {{c1::Slice of culture and diverse population}}
  • {{c1::Also have crime and other disruptions to society}}
example: New York supplies jobs, hospitals and museums for millions, though it also has crime and traffic.

text: Megalopolis: {{c1::many connected metropolises}}
example: Japan's Taiheiyō Belt, linking Tokyo, Nagoya and Osaka.

text: Urbanization: {{c1::rural → urban areas}}
example: China's urban share rose from about 20% in 1980 to over 60% by 2020 as farmers moved to cities.

text:
Demographic Transition Model:
Stage 3:
  • Death rates {{c1::↓::↑ or ↓}}
  • Population is {{c1::slowly Growing::Growing or Shrinking}}
  • Birth rates {{c1::↓::↑ or ↓}}
example: India, where the fertility rate fell from about 5 in the 1970s to about 2 today.

text: Vertical mobility: {{c1::move up or down the social hierarchy}}
extra: Example: a restaurant manager becomes CEO of a fast-food company; the old CEO is demoted to janitor

text: A {{c1::ghetto}} is a part of a city in which members of a minority group live, typically as a result of social, legal or economic pressure
extra: Ghettos are often known for being more impoverished than other areas of the city
example: The Warsaw Ghetto, where Nazi Germany walled in over 400,000 Jews in 1940.

text: Gender schema theory: {{c1::cognitions regarding what constitutes a sex identity}}
example: A boy shown a picture of a male nurse later remembers it as a female nurse.

text: Internal migration: {{c1::move within same country}}
example: A family moving from Detroit to Houston for oil-industry jobs.

text: Population transfer: {{c1::group is forcefully moved from territory}}
{{c1::Migration}} is the movement of people from one location to another
example: The Great Migration moved about 6 million Black Americans from the rural South to Northern cities (1910–1970).

text:
Conflict theory on cities:
  • {{c1::Source of inequality}}
  • {{c1::Entertainment center for the wealthy}}
example: Manhattan's luxury penthouses and Broadway shows sit a few miles from the poverty of the South Bronx.

text: {{c1::Birth and mortality rate}} is usually measured as the number of births or deaths per 1000 people per year
example: A town of 50,000 with 600 births a year has a birth rate of 600 ÷ 50 = 12 per 1,000.

text: World-systems theory: {{c1::importance of the world as a unit rather than individual countries}}
example: Wallerstein's view: coffee grown cheaply in Ethiopia enriches roasters and retailers in the U.S. and Europe.

text: The gender schema theory proposes that children learn gender roles from their {{c1::culture}}
example: A boy who learns from TV ads that 'trucks are for boys' walks straight past the doll aisle.

text:
Class system:
  • {{c1::allows for degree of social mobility}}
  • {{c1::Often by education}}
example: A first-generation college graduate from a factory-worker family in the U.S. becomes a lawyer.

text: Urban decline: {{c1::as people move out of city centers, city can fall into disrepair}}
example: Detroit shrank from about 1.8 million people in 1950 to under 700,000 by 2020, leaving abandoned houses.

text: Linguistic isolation: {{c1::communities who are isolated may develop own language}}
example: Gullah, a creole spoken by isolated Black communities on the Sea Islands of South Carolina and Georgia.

text: Dependency theory: {{c1::3rd World countries are stuck supplying raw materials to core countries}}
extra: Their position as raw-material suppliers to more developed countries keeps them from becoming developed
example: Congo mines about 70% of the world's cobalt but exports it raw, while richer nations profit from the batteries.

text: Intersectionality theory: {{c1::calls attention to how identity categories intersect in systems of social stratification}}
extra: Example: being a woman and being Black
example: In DeGraffenreid v. GM, analyzed by Crenshaw, GM hired white women and Black men but not Black women.

text: Social capital: {{c1::network of relationships among people who live and work in a particular society, enabling that society to function effectively}}
example: A job seeker lands an interview because a former teammate refers her to the hiring manager.

text: Cohorts are also known as {{c1::groups}}
example: Everyone who finished high school in 2020 forms a cohort shaped by the COVID-19 pandemic.

text:
Meritocracy:
  • {{c1::social position based off merit and achievement}}
  • {{c1::Work hard for what you earn}}
extra:
Birth/parental background doesn't matter
Extreme social mobility; equal opportunity
example: Imperial China's civil service exams let commoners who scored highest become government officials.

text:
{{c1::Baby Boomers}} are from 1946–1964
Large population in the US
extra: Post-WWII; currently leaving the work force
example: Bill Clinton, born in August 1946, is one of the first Baby Boomers.

text:
Poverty magnet:
  • {{c1::people dragged away from the core part of society}}
  • {{c1::Experience social exclusion}}
example: A family evicted for unpaid rent loses its address, so the parents struggle to get jobs or open a bank account.

text: Social Networks can improve your {{c1::health}}
example: Holt-Lunstad's meta-analysis found strong social ties raise the odds of survival by about 50%.

text: {{c1::Morbidity}} is the burden or degree of illness associated with a given disease
example: Diabetes carries heavy morbidity through blindness, kidney failure and amputations, even when it is not fatal.

text: Suburbanization: {{c1::movement away from cities to get a larger home}}
example: Levittown, NY, built from 1947, drew families out of New York City into cheap houses with yards.

text: {{c1::Prevalence}} is the number of cases of a disease per population
example: If 300 of a town's 10,000 residents currently have diabetes, the prevalence is 300 ÷ 10,000 = 3%.

text: Fecundity: {{c1::the potential reproductive capacity of a female}}
example: A healthy woman could biologically bear over a dozen children, though the U.S. fertility rate is about 1.6.

text: Skeptical perspective: {{c1::globalization process is separated and regionalized::regarding globalization}}
extra: Third World countries aren’t being integrated into the global economy with the same benefits
example: Most EU countries trade chiefly with other EU members, a regional bloc rather than one global market.

text: Fertility, migration and mortality all affect the {{c1::growth}} rate
example: Japan's population shrinks because deaths outnumber births and few immigrants arrive.

text: Rational choice theory: {{c1::people compare pros and cons of different courses of action and choose the one they think is best for themselves}}
example: A student skips a party because the grade boost from studying outweighs one evening of fun.

text: TNCs: {{c1::Multinational/Transnational corporations}}
example: Toyota, based in Japan, builds cars in factories in the U.S., Thailand and Brazil.

text: Relative deprivation theory: {{c1::you don't have what you deserve}}
example: Educated but jobless young Tunisians, watching elites prosper, sparked the 2011 Arab Spring protests.

text: Glass ceiling effect: {{c1::women/minorities are poorly represented in higher positions in companies}}
example: Women run only about 1 in 10 Fortune 500 companies.

text: {{c1::Functionalism::...ism}} states that social stratification is necessary and results from the need for those with special intelligence, knowledge, and skills to be a part of the most important professions and occupations
example: Surgeons earn more than cashiers, functionalists say, to lure scarce talent into long, hard training.

text: Concentration segregation: {{c1::a group occupies a small, dense share of the urban area}}
extra:
Concentration of people into different residential groups
Example: Latino, Black, Jewish neighborhoods
example: Manhattan's Chinatown packs tens of thousands of Chinese Americans into a small, dense corner of Lower Manhattan.

text: {{c1::Power}} is the capacity to influence people
example: A CEO who can lay off 1,000 workers with a single memo holds power over them.

text:
{{c1::Activist}} movements aim to change some aspect of society
{{c1::Regressive/Reactionary}} movements resist change
extra: Example: activists want legal weed; regressives want it to stay illegal

text:
Absolute poverty:
  • {{c1::if you go below, survival is threatened}}
  • {{c1::Independent of location}}
example: A family that cannot afford enough food to keep its children from starving, whether in Chad or Chicago.

text: {{c1::Social}} networks include peer, family and community networks
example: A new mother leans on her sister (family), coworkers (peer) and a church group (community).

text: Horizontal mobility: {{c1::move within the same class}}
extra: Example: an accountant switches to a different accounting company

text: {{c1::Social exclusion}} is a sense of powerlessness when individuals feel alienated from society
example: A long-term homeless man shut out of jobs, housing and voting stops trying to take part in society.

text: Urban renewal: {{c1::revamping old parts of cities to become better}}; can lead to {{c1::gentrification}}
example: New York's abandoned elevated rail line became the High Line park, and nearby Chelsea rents soared.

text: {{c1::Incidence}} is the number of new cases of a disease per population at risk
example: If 50 of 10,000 at-risk people catch flu this month, the monthly incidence is 50 ÷ 10,000 = 0.5%.

text: Life course theory: {{c1::a holistic perspective focused on developmental processes across a person's life}}
extra: As people live longer, changing biological processes affect social processes
example: Tracing how a woman's childhood poverty, teenage schooling and adult job together shape her health at 70.

text: {{c1::Age stratification}} refers to the hierarchical ranking of people into age groups within a society. It could also be defined as a system of inequalities linked to age
example: A 16-year-old cannot vote or rent a car, while a 70-year-old may be nudged into retirement.

text: Resource mobilization theory: {{c1::access to resources affecting social movements}}
example: The Montgomery bus boycott ran on Black churches' money, meeting halls and volunteer carpools.

text: Spatial mismatch: {{c1::opportunities for low-income people in segregated communities may be present but farther away/hard to access}}
extra: Gap between where people live and where opportunities are
example: Jobs move to suburban office parks, but inner-city residents without cars cannot reach them by bus.

text: Dependency ratio: {{c1::people aged 0–14 and 65+ (not in the labor force) compared to the number of people aged 15–64}}
example: 30 million people aged 0–14 or 65+ and 60 million aged 15–64 give a dependency ratio of 30 ÷ 60 = 50%.

text: {{c1::Demographics}} are characteristics of a population such as race, ethnicity, gender, age, education, profession, occupation, income level, and marital status
example: The U.S. Census records each resident's age, sex, race and Hispanic origin.

text: Centralization segregation: {{c1::segregation + clustering in a central area}}
extra:
All of one group concentrated in 1 area
Example: Compton, Harlem

text: People try to maintain the same basic structure throughout their lives: {{c1::Continuity Theory}}
example: A lifelong bridge player keeps her weekly game and Sunday church routine after retiring at 70.

text: Modernization theory: {{c1::all countries go from traditional → modern societies}}
example: Rostow predicted every country would pass, as Britain had, from farming villages to industrial mass consumption.

text: Relative poverty: {{c1::relative income of people whose incomes are so low in their own society they’re being excluded from society}}
extra:
Not about survival
About 60% of the median income; rises as the median income rises
example: A U.S. family with a TV and a car that cannot afford the school trips or home internet classmates take for granted.

text: Cosmopolites: people {{c1::drawn to city due to cultural benefits and convenience}}
example: A young artist moves to Paris for its museums, theatres and walkable cafés.

text:
False consciousness:
  • {{c1::awareness of yourself and your interests only}}
  • {{c1::Failure to recognize the state of class relations}}
example: A low-wage worker votes to cut taxes on the rich, believing he will be rich himself someday.

text:
Incipient stage of a social movement
{{c1::Public takes notice of the situation that they consider to be a problem::Explain}}
example: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) made the public notice pesticide damage, sparking the environmental movement.

text: Organized information about the order of actions appropriate to a familiar situation; what we expect men and women to do: {{c1::Gender script}}
example: At a wedding, the bride is walked down the aisle while the groom waits at the altar.

text:
Demographic Transition Model
Stage 4
  • Birth rates are {{c1::↓::↑ or ↓}}
  • Death rates are {{c1::↓::↑ or ↓}}
  • Population is {{c1::Large::Large or Small}}
example: The United States or France, with low birth and death rates and a large, stable population.

text:
Race: socially defined category based on {{c1::physical differences between people}}
Ethnicity: socially defined category based on {{c1::shared cultural factors}}
example: A Nigerian and a Jamaican may both be classed as Black (race) yet differ in ethnicity.

text: Population dynamics: {{c1::how population grows and shrinks over time}}
example: Ireland's population fell from about 8 million in 1841 to about 4.5 million by 1901 through famine and emigration.

text:
Demographic Transition Model:
Stage 1:
  • {{c1::↑::↑ or ↓}} Birth rates
  • {{c1::↑::↑ or ↓}} Death rates
  • Overall population remains {{c1::fairly stable}}
example: Pre-industrial England before about 1750, when many babies were born but many died young.

text: Agender: {{c1::rejecting gender categories}}
example: A person who says they simply have no gender at all.

text: Social reproduction: {{c1::transmission of social benefits/inequality from one generation to the next}}
extra: Example: children of rich parents end up wealthy; children of poor families have less access to education and opportunities and grow up poor
example: Children of Ivy League alumni get legacy admission boosts, passing elite status to the next generation.

text:
Semi-periphery countries (world-systems theory):
  • {{c1::middle group between core and periphery}}
  • {{c1::Developed, but not dominant in international trade}}
example: Brazil builds its own Embraer jets yet relies heavily on exporting soybeans and iron ore.

text:
Hyperglobalist perspective:
  • {{c1::the world is becoming more interconnected}}
  • {{c1::Countries are not separated from one another as they used to be}}
example: A teenager in Lagos streams the same Netflix show, on the same day, as one in Seoul.

text: {{c1::Fertility rate}} is the average number of children born to a woman during her lifetime in a population
example: South Korea's fertility rate fell to about 0.72 in 2023, far below the replacement level of 2.1.

text:
World-systems theory divides the world into 3 types of countries:
  • {{c1::Core}}
  • {{c1::Periphery}}
  • {{c1::Semi-Periphery}}
example: The United States (core), Brazil (semi-periphery) and Chad (periphery).

text: Activity theory: {{c1::successful elderly people maintain the social and physical activities of their earlier years}}
extra: When certain activities are lost, those social interactions need to be replaced so the elderly stay engaged and maintain morale and well-being
example: A retired teacher who starts volunteering at the library to replace the contact she lost with her classroom.

text: {{c1::GI (Greatest) Generation}} is from 1901-1924
example: John F. Kennedy, born in 1917, served in WWII as part of the Greatest Generation.

text: Example: men offering to take a woman's coat or pay the dinner check → {{c1::Gender scripts}}
{{c1::Millennials}} are from the 1980s–2000s, also known as {{c1::Generation Y}}
example: Someone born in 1990 who remembers dial-up internet and job-hunted through the 2008 recession.

text: Demographic transition: shift from {{c1::↑::↑ or ↓}} birth & death rates to {{c1::↓::↑ or ↓}} birth & death rates, {{c1::as country becomes industrialized}}
example: Sweden went from high birth and death rates around 1800 to low ones by the 1930s as it industrialized.

text:
Exurbs:
  • {{c1::beyond suburbs}}
  • {{c1::Prosperous areas outside the city where people live and commute to work}}
example: Loudoun County, Virginia, where well-paid workers live on large lots and drive an hour into D.C.

text: The {{c1::Always-On Generation}} is from 2004 onward
example: A child born in 2010 who learned to swipe an iPad before she could read.

text:
Caste system:
  • {{c1::very little social mobility}}
  • {{c1::Role is determined}}
example: In traditional India, a boy born a Dalit was barred for life from becoming a temple priest.

text: Genderqueer: {{c1::don't identify as either male or female}}
example: Someone who feels their gender falls outside the categories 'man' and 'woman' altogether.

text: Social stratification: {{c1::society's categorization of people in SES, power, income, occupation, etc.}}
example: In the U.S., the top 10% of households hold about two-thirds of all wealth.

text:
Looks at human development as a constant process from birth to death = {{c1::Life Course Theory}}
Successful elderly people maintain the social and physical activities of their earlier years = {{c1::Activity Theory}}
People try to maintain the same activities as they age = {{c1::Continuity Theory}}
Successful elderly people disengage from society as they age to become more introspective = {{c1::Disengagement Theory}}
example: A widower who retires and gradually quits his clubs to reflect alone fits disengagement theory.

text: Transformationalist perspective on globalization: {{c1::}}
extra:
There are interconnecting relationships through indirect power
Globalization is complex
Flow of culture is bidirectional
example: K-pop flows from South Korea to the West while Hollywood films flow back into Seoul.

text: The {{c1::Affordable Care Act (ACA)}} attempts to increase health insurance coverage rates and reduce the cost of health care
example: Under the ACA, young adults can stay on a parent's health plan until age 26.

text: Racialization: {{c1::ascribing racial identities to a group that doesn't identify with that label}}
example: Muslims of many nationalities being treated in the West as a single race after 9/11.

text: Age stratification theory: {{c1::behavior is defined based on our age group. Our age group defines how we act.}}
extra: Example: a 95-year-old is unlikely to go sky-diving, since that is not normal behavior for that age

text: Gentrification: {{c1::improving an area ↑ property value, driving out the poor}}
example: Tech workers moved into San Francisco's Mission District, rents soared and long-time Latino families were priced out.

text: Gender-fluid: {{c1::moving across gender}}
example: A person who feels more like a man some weeks and more like a woman other weeks.

text: Intergenerational mobility: {{c1::change in social class between generations}}
extra: Example: parents started at the bottom; their child is now at the top
example: A janitor's daughter grows up to become a surgeon.

text: Pluralism: {{c1::encourages racial and ethnic variation}}
example: Switzerland recognizes four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.

text:
Symbolic interactionism on cities:
  • {{c1::Strong cultural values}}
  • {{c1::Different perspectives of urban life}}
example: A lifelong New Yorker sees the subway as lively, while a rural tourist sees it as dirty and dangerous.

text:
Ill-health magnet:
  • {{c1::drags people away from society}}
  • {{c1::Can't participate due to health}}
example: A man disabled by severe multiple sclerosis loses his job and stops going to church and his clubs.

text: Discrimination magnet: {{c1::certain groups face discrimination based on race/gender/sexual orientation, etc.}}
example: Identical résumés named 'Emily' or 'Greg' got 50% more callbacks than ones named 'Lakisha' or 'Jamal'.

text: Research perspective that considers how experiences earlier in life affect outcomes later in life: {{c1::Life Course Theory}}
example: The ACE study found adults abused or neglected as children have higher rates of heart disease decades later.

text: Cisgender: {{c1::same biological sex and gender identity}}
example: A person assigned female at birth who identifies as a woman.

text: {{c1::Social class}} is a category of people with shared socioeconomic characteristics
example: A nurse and a teacher with similar incomes, degrees and neighbourhoods both belong to the middle class.

text: Internal colonialism: {{c1::minority group is segregated and exploited}}
example: Apartheid South Africa confined Black South Africans to 'homelands' and used them as cheap mine labour.

text: {{c1::Medicaid}} covers patients in significant financial need
example: A single mother earning below 138% of the federal poverty line in an expansion state qualifies for Medicaid.

text: Core countries (world-systems theory): {{c1::strong central government with enough tax to support it}}
The {{c1::Silent Generation}} is from 1925–1945
extra:
Older than Baby Boomers
Born during the Great Depression
example: Martin Luther King Jr., born in 1929, belongs to the Silent Generation.

text:
Urban complex of 44 million people in NYC area from Boston to DC:
{{c1::Megalopolis}}
example: Amtrak's Northeast Corridor runs through Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington, D.C.

text: A key marker for healthcare systems: {{c1::maternal mortality rate}}
example: Black U.S. mothers die from pregnancy-related causes at nearly 3 times the rate of white mothers.

text: Third gender: {{c1::cultures that recognize non-binary gender}}
example: The hijra of India, recognized as a legal third gender by India's Supreme Court in 2014.

text: {{c1::Globalization}} is the process of integrating a global economy with free trade and tapping of foreign labor markets
example: An iPhone designed in California is assembled in China from parts made in Japan and South Korea.

text: Periphery countries (world-systems theory): {{c1::relatively weak government}}; depend on {{c1::core countries and TNCs}}
Non-binary: {{c1::not identifying with any specific gender}}
example: A person who asks coworkers to use they/them pronouns instead of he or she.

text: {{c1::Spatial inequality}} is social stratification across territories
example: Life expectancy can differ by more than 10 years between rich and poor neighbourhoods of the same city.

text: Rural rebound: {{c1::people getting sick of cities and moving back out to rural areas}}
example: During COVID-19, many remote workers left San Francisco and New York for small towns in Vermont and Idaho.

text: Population growth rate = {{c1::(Births − Deaths + Immigrants − Emigrants) per 1000 population}}
example: 20 births, 8 deaths, 3 immigrants and 5 emigrants per 1,000: 20 − 8 + 3 − 5 = 10 per 1,000, or 1% growth.

text: Sexual Orientation refers to a pattern of {{c1::sexual}} and/or {{c1::romantic/emotional}} attraction
example: A bisexual woman feels sexual and romantic attraction to both men and women.

text: Transgender: {{c1::biological sex and gender identity don't match}}
example: A person assigned male at birth who identifies and lives as a woman.

text: Racial formation theory: {{c1::racial identities are constructed by social/economic/political forces}}
extra: Society, not biology, creates the concept of "races"
example: Irish and Italian immigrants were not seen as 'white' in 19th-century America but later came to be.

text: City vs. metropolis: the {{c1::metropolis has more people::which has more people?}}
example: Ithaca, NY (about 30,000 people) vs the Chicago metropolitan area (about 9 million).

text:
Demographic Transition Model:
Stage 2:
  • Population {{c1::Rises::Rises or Falls}}
  • Death rates {{c1::↓::↑ or ↓}}
  • Birth rates are {{c1::High::High or Low}}
example: Niger today, where vaccines and clean water cut deaths but women still average more than 6 children.

text: Intragenerational mobility: {{c1::change in social class within a person's lifetime}}
extra: Example: started at the bottom, now at the top
example: Howard Schultz grew up in Brooklyn public housing and later became CEO of Starbucks.

text:
Social rewards, status, position are awarded to individuals based on their own ability to work is:
{{c1::Meritocracy}}
example: A Singapore civil servant promoted for exam results and job performance rather than family ties.

text:
Class consciousness:
  • {{c1::awareness of your class and the interests of your class as a whole}}
  • {{c1::Solidarity with class}}
example: Striking UAW autoworkers in 2023 saw themselves as one class of workers united against the Big Three.

text: A {{c1::gender role}} is a social role: the behaviors and attitudes considered acceptable, appropriate or desirable for people based on their actual or perceived sex
example: The expectation that women stay home with the children while men work as breadwinners.

text: {{c1::Generation Z}} is from 1995–2003
example: Someone born in 1998 who got her first smartphone in middle school.

text: {{c1::Medicare}} covers people greater than 65 years old, those with end-stage renal disease, and those with ALS
example: A 67-year-old retiree and a 40-year-old on dialysis for kidney failure both qualify for Medicare.

text: Cultural capital: {{c1::non-financial social assets that promote social mobility beyond economic means}}
extra:
How cultured you are
Respected in society and implies high status
example: A student raised on classical music and fine dining impresses an elite law-firm interviewer over dinner.

text: Mass society theory: {{c1::skepticism about groups involved in social movements; says they form only for people seeking refuge from mainstream society}}
extra:
Members seen as dysfunctional, irrational and dangerous
Examples: Nazism, fascism, Stalinism

text: {{c1::Prestige}} is a term that describes the respect and importance tied to specific occupations or associations
example: Physicians and firefighters rank near the top of occupational prestige polls, while janitors rank far lower.

text: Environmental justice: {{c1::looks at the fair distribution of the environmental benefits and burdens within society across all groups}}
example: Flint, Michigan, a mostly Black city, was left drinking lead-contaminated water from 2014.

text:
Index of dissimilarity:
  • {{c1::0 = Perfect distribution (integration)}}
  • {{c1::100 = total Segregation}}
Political isolation: {{c1::segregated communities are politically weak because their political interests don't overlap with other communities}}
example: A segregated poor neighbourhood cannot stop a highway being built through it, as its votes don't sway the council.

text: The {{c1::dimensional approach::... approach}} to emotion refers to how people experience their emotions. Emotions are measured in terms of dimensions such as arousal (high/low) and valence (positive/negative)
extra: As opposed to discrete emotion theory which is the claim that there is a small number of core emotions
example: Anger rates high arousal and negative valence; contentment rates low arousal and positive valence.

text: Perception of annoyance occurs in the {{c1::cingulate cortex::Brain area}}
example: A mosquito buzzing in your ear all night triggers annoyance processed in the cingulate cortex.

text: The three emotional/behavioral effects of stress are {{c1::anger}}, {{c1::anxiety}}, and {{c1::addiction}}
example: A stressed executive snaps at staff, lies awake worrying, and starts drinking nightly.

text:
Sympathetic nervous system effects:
  • {{c1::dilate pupils}}
  • {{c1::decrease salivation}}
  • {{c1::increase RR}}
  • {{c1::increase HR}}
  • {{c1::increase blood glucose}}
  • {{c1::increase adrenaline and norepinephrine}}
  • {{c1::decrease digestion}}
example: A hiker who meets a bear has a pounding heart, dry mouth, fast breathing and wide pupils.

text: {{c1::Stress}} is the process by which we {{c2::appraise and cope with environmental threats and challenges}}
example: A student appraises a looming exam as a challenge and copes by making a study plan.

text: {{c1::Eustress}} is {{c2::a positive type of stress when a situation is challenging but motivating}}
example: Nerves before your first marathon push you to train harder and run faster.

text: {{c1::Meaning-focused coping}} is when a person copes with a stressor by {{c2::trying to derive meaning from it}}
example: Candy Lightner founded MADD after a drunk driver killed her daughter.

text: {{c1::Distress}} is {{c2::a negative type of stress that builds up over time and is bad for your body}}
example: Years of caring for a parent with dementia while working full time wear down a caregiver's health.

text:
The exhaustion phase of GAS is when individuals have:
  • {{c1::run out of resources to handle stress}}
  • {{c1::have weakened immune systems}}
example: After months of nonstop overtime, a nurse catches every cold going around.

text: The two stages to the appraisal theory of stress are {{c1::primary appraisal}} and {{c1::secondary appraisal}}
example: Facing a bear, you first judge 'this is a threat', then ask 'can I escape it?'

text:
The 7 universal emotions are:
  • {{c1::Happiness}}
  • {{c1::Surprise}}
  • {{c1::Sadness}}
  • {{c1::Fear}}
  • {{c1::Disgust}}
  • {{c1::Contempt}}
  • {{c1::Anger}}
example: Ekman found the isolated Fore of Papua New Guinea recognized Western faces showing happiness, sadness and anger.

text: The three components of emotion are {{c1::physiological}}, {{c1::cognitive}}, and {{c1::behavioral}}
extra:
physiological: heart rate increase, muscle tenses, etc
cognitive: enjoying the party because you like parties
behavioral: facial expression, language
example: Seeing a spider: your heart races, you think 'it's dangerous', and you scream and back away.

text: {{c1::The Appraisal theory of stress::Theory}}, associated with {{c1::Lazarus::Psychologist}}, states that {{c2::stress arises less from physical events and more from assessment/interpretation of the stressor}}
example: Two students get the same B: one panics that med school is over, the other shrugs it off.

text: {{c1::Secondary appraisal}} is {{c2::the evaluation of an individuals ability to cope with a stressor}}
example: After judging a pop quiz a threat, you ask whether you studied enough to handle it.

text:
Multiple approach-avoidance conflict:
  • {{c1::Internal mental debate}}
  • {{c1::Weighs pros and cons for situations}}
example: Choosing among three med schools that each trade off cost, location and prestige.

text:
{{c2::↓}} activity in the {{c3::R}} hemisphere = {{c1::Euphoria}}
{{c2::↓}} activity in the {{c3::L}} hemisphere = {{c1::Depression}}
example: After a right-hemisphere stroke, a patient may seem oddly cheerful and unconcerned about his paralysis.

text: Both positive and negative emotions are processed in the {{c1::orbitofrontal cortex}}
example: Winning money and losing money in a gambling task both activate the orbitofrontal cortex.

text: The endocrine response to stress includes {{c1::releasing catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine)}} and {{c1::releasing cortisol}}
extra:
Catecholamines are released by the adrenal medulla
Cortisol is released by the adrenal cortex
example: Before a final exam, a student's cortisol and epinephrine levels both spike.

text:
Two brain areas associated with disgust:
  • {{c1::Insula::x2}}
  • {{c1::Basal ganglia}}
example: Smelling spoiled milk or watching someone gag in disgust activates the insula.

text: The only sense that bypasses the thalamus is {{c1::olfaction}}
example: The smell of coffee goes from the olfactory bulb straight to olfactory cortex with no thalamic relay.

text:
Stress can lead to:
  • {{c1::hypertension}}
  • {{c1::heart disease}}
  • {{c1::diabetes}}
  • {{c1::reproductive issues}}
  • {{c1::immune problems}}
example: Dementia caregivers in Kiecolt-Glaser's study took 24% longer to heal a small skin wound.

text:
{{c1::The prefrontal cortex::Brain region}} is responsible for:
  • {{c2::higher-order functions}}
  • {{c2::executive control}}
  • {{c2::problem solving}}
  • {{c2::decision making}}
  • {{c2::how you act in social situations}}
example: Phineas Gage became impulsive and rude after an iron rod pierced his prefrontal cortex.

text: {{c1::The stress reaction}} is the {{c2::physical and emotional response to stress}}
example: Before a big presentation, your hands shake, your stomach knots and you feel a wave of dread.

text: The behavioral components to emotion include {{c1::body language}} and {{c1::facial expressions}}
example: Crossing your arms and scowling when a coworker takes credit for your work.

text: One major emotional response to stress is {{c1::depression}}
example: After months of unemployment and debt, a man stops enjoying hobbies and sleeps most of the day.

text: The cognitive component of emotion involves {{c1::how you feel about something}}
{{c1::Emotion}} is a state of mind, or feeling, that is subjectively experienced based on circumstances, mood, and relationships
example: Feeling joy when an acceptance letter arrives, or grief when a pet dies.

text: {{c1::Primary appraisal}} is when you {{c2::assess stress in your present situation}}.
extra: three types of appraisal are irrelevant, positive, or negative
example: When the professor announces a pop quiz, you first ask whether it threatens your grade.

text: The part of the nervous system that is responsible for rest / digest is the {{c1::parasympathetic nervous system}}
extra: Remember P for Parasympathetic: "Relaxing and having a Piña colada on beach"
example: After a big Thanksgiving dinner, your heart rate slows and your stomach gets busy digesting.

text: {{c2::The amygdala::Brain region}} is involved with {{c1::emotion}}, {{c1::aggression}}, and {{c1::fears}}
example: Patient S.M., whose amygdalae were destroyed, felt no fear while handling live snakes.

text: {{c1::Low effort syndrome}} is a coping mechanism where people have the tendency to exert minimal effort to escape stressful social and economic circumstances
extra:
common in minority students to try and not be discriminated against by the dominant culture for trying and then failing.
Would rather just not try than look stupid failing while trying
example: A worker who sees no path to promotion does the bare minimum rather than risk trying and failing.

text:
Type A individuals are {{c1::easily angered, aggressive, and competitive}}
Type B individuals are {{c1::easy going}}
example: A Type A executive honks at slow drivers and works through lunch; a Type B colleague strolls to the park.

text: {{c1::The Limbic System}} is a set of structures in the brain that {{c2::play an important role in regulating emotions}}
example: Fear rising when a snake appears on a hiking trail is driven by limbic structures like the amygdala.

text: {{c1::Maladaptive}} coping strategies relieve symptoms temporarily but don't address the root cause of the stress
extra: While adaptive coping methods improve functioning, a maladaptive coping technique will just reduce symptoms and maintain or strengthen the disorder
example: Drinking wine every night to forget work stress while the workload keeps piling up.

text: {{c1::Social coping}} is when one deals with stress by seeking social support
example: After a breakup, a student calls her best friend to talk it through.

text: {{c2::The thalamus}} is the {{c1::sensory relay station that directs sensory nerves to appropriate brain regions}}
example: Light hitting the retina is relayed through the thalamus's lateral geniculate nucleus to the visual cortex.

text: The resistance phase of GAS is when individuals have {{c1::very high cortisol}}, {{c1::high BP and RR}}, and {{c1::flee/huddle}}
example: Weeks into caring for a sick parent, a caregiver keeps going on high cortisol, always on edge.

text: Avoidance-avoidance conflict: {{c1::2 options and both are unappealing}}
Many consider {{c1::daily hassles::stressor}} to be the most important form of stress
example: Sitting in traffic, losing your keys and a slow Wi-Fi connection pile up into daily stress.

text:
{{c1::James-Lange}} Theory of Emotion
{{c2::event
↓
physiological response
↓
interpretation of physiological response
↓
emotion
}}
extra:
mnemonic: J/L one apart on the alphabet, so physiological response first then emotion
example: A man, who is allergic to bees, encounters a bee. The man’s heart beat increases, he starts sweating, and he then interprets these physiological changes as the emotion fear
example: William James: we feel sorry because we cry and afraid because we tremble, not the reverse.

text: {{c1::Learned helplessness}} is when {{c2::a person suffers from a sense of powerlessness due to persistent failure or loss of control of a situation}}
example: Seligman's dogs, after inescapable shocks, stopped trying to escape even when escape was possible.

text:
The limbic system is composed of the:
  • {{c1::hypothalamus}}
  • {{c1::amygdala}}
  • {{c1::thalamus}}
  • {{c1::hippocampus}}
example: The thalamus relays the sight of a growling dog, the amygdala fires fear, the hypothalamus raises heart rate.

text: {{c1::Kluver-Bucy syndrome::Syndrome}} is caused by {{c2::destruction of the amygdala}} and results in {{c2::hyperorality}}, {{c2::hypersexuality}}, and {{c2::disinhibited behavior}}
example: Klüver and Bucy's monkeys, after temporal lobe removal, mouthed objects and lost their fear of snakes.

text: {{c1::Discrete emotion theory::Theory}} is the claim that there is a small number of core, discrete emotions
example: Ekman's six basic emotions, such as fear and disgust, are treated as distinct, universal categories.

text: The alarm phase of GAS is when {{c1::stress kicks in}} and {{c1::the heart races}}
example: Your heart pounds the instant a car swerves into your lane.

text:
6 universal emotions:
  • {{c1::happiness}}
  • {{c1::sadness}}
  • {{c1::fear}}
  • {{c1::disgust}}
  • {{c1::anger}}
  • {{c1::surprise}}
example: A smile reads as happiness to both a Tokyo commuter and a remote Fore villager.

text: {{c1::Paul Ekman}} founded {{c2::the 6 universal basic emotions that anyone can identify}}
example: Ekman found the isolated Fore people of Papua New Guinea recognised Western facial expressions.

text: In stressed individuals, the {{c1::anterior cingulate::brain region}} stops responding to {{c2::serotonin}}
extra: leads to inability to experience pleasure
example: A burned-out resident no longer enjoys her favourite meals, music or friends.

text:
{{c1::Lazarus}} Theory of Emotion
{{c2::
Event
↓
Labelling event (appraisal)
↓
Emotion + Physiological Response
}}
extra:
mnemonic: Lazarus must Label the event before emotion or PR
example: Wolf is running at you. You label this even as threatening. You simultaneously sweat, increase HR, and feel the emotion of Fear.

text:
{{c1::Cannon-Bard}} Theory of Emotion
{{c2::
Event
↓
Physiological Response + Emotion at same time
}}
extra:
mnemonic: C/B next to eachother in alphabet, so physiological response + emotion at same time
example: Man is allergic to bees encounters a bee. At the same time, the mans heartbeat increases, he starts sweating, and feels fear.

text: General adaptation syndrome was developed by {{c1::Hans Selye}}
example: Selye's stressed rats all showed the same triad: enlarged adrenals, shrunken thymus and stomach ulcers.

text: Cortisol is released in response to stress and low blood-glucose concentration. It increases blood sugar by {{c1::activating gluconeogenesis}}
example: During an overnight fast, cortisol helps the liver make new glucose from amino acids and glycerol.

text:
{{c1::The hypothalamus::Brain region}} functions include:
  • {{c2::regulating the autonomic nervous system}}
  • {{c2::endocrine system (pituitary)}}
  • {{c2::controlling biological drives like hunger, sleep, thirst, sex, etc}}
example: Lesioning a rat's ventromedial hypothalamus makes it overeat and become obese.

text: Individuals with a damaged hippocampus have {{c1::old memories but can't make new ones}}
example: H.M., after surgery removed much of both hippocampi, recalled his childhood but not people met minutes before.

text: {{c1::Transformational grammar}} refers to the different ways that words can be arranged to convey the same information
example: 'The dog chased the cat' and 'The cat was chased by the dog' say the same thing in two word orders.

text: Approach-avoidance conflict: {{c1::An action has both undesirable and desirable outcomes}}
Maladaptive coping mechanisms include {{c1::overcompensation}}, {{c1::surrendering}}, and {{c1::avoidance}}
example: Skipping every class after failing a quiz is avoidance.

text: The recognition of facial expressions associated with sadness has been linked to the {{c1::subcallosal cingulate}}
extra: I looked sad when the Sub Called me Cingul
example: Viewing a photo of a tearful, downcast face activates the subcallosal cingulate.

text: One of the best coping mechanisms for stress is {{c1::social support}}
extra: helps people see they are not alone and improves perceived control and optimism
example: A widow who joins a grief support group copes better than one who grieves alone.

text: The tend and befriend response involves the hormone {{c1::oxytocin}}
example: Under stress, a woman's rising oxytocin nudges her to phone a close friend for support.

text: {{c1::Lexical access}} refers to identifying a word and connecting it to its meaning, which has been stored in long-term memory
example: Reading the letters 'apple' and instantly recalling that it names a crunchy red fruit.

text: {{c1::Coping}} refers to efforts to manage stress
example: A student facing finals makes a study schedule and jogs each evening to keep stress in check.

text: Secondary appraisal evaluates {{c1::an individual's ability to cope with a stressor based on level of harm, threat, and challenge}}
example: A new intern asks herself whether she has the skills to survive her first 28-hour call shift.

text: {{c1::Perceived control}} is the belief that an individual has control over a stressor
example: In Langer and Rodin's study, nursing-home residents given a plant to care for and choices lived longer.

text: {{c1::Complex emotions::... emotions}}, such as grief, regret and jealousy, have highly variable appearances and compositions
example: Grief shows as sobbing in one mourner, numb silence in another and anger in a third.

text: {{c1::Alexia (acquired dyslexia)}} is defined as an acquired impairment affecting reading ability
example: After a left occipital stroke, a professor can still write a letter but cannot read it back.

text:
The four categories of stressors are:
  • {{c1::significant life changes}}
  • {{c1::catastrophic events}}
  • {{c1::daily hassles}}
  • {{c1::ambient stressors}}
example: Hurricane Katrina is a catastrophic event; a traffic jam is a daily hassle.

text: The three stages to {{c1::general adaptation syndrome}} are {{c2::alarm}}, {{c2::resistance}}, and {{c2::exhaustion}}
example: Finals week: an adrenaline rush on day one, grinding through week two, then catching a cold right after.

text: Stressors can trigger the body's {{c1::sympathetic nervous system}} and {{c1::endocrine response}}
example: Hearing footsteps behind you at night quickens your heart and floods you with adrenaline and cortisol.

text:
Parasympathetic nervous system effects:
  • {{c1::pupils constrict}}
  • {{c1::increased salivation}}
  • {{c1::decreased RR}}
  • {{c1::decreased HR}}
  • {{c1::increase glucose storage}}
  • {{c1::decreased adrenaline}}
  • {{c1::increased digestion}}
example: After a big Thanksgiving dinner, your heart rate slows and your gut busily digests the meal.

text: {{c1::Adaptive}} coping strategies involve confronting problems directly, appraising them realistically, changing unhealthy emotional reactions and preventing adverse effects on the body
example: A student who fails a midterm meets the professor and builds a weekly study plan.

text: {{c1::Childhood apraxia of speech (CAS)}} is a speech disorder in which a child's brain has difficulty coordinating the complex oral movements needed to create sounds into syllables, syllables into words, and words into phrases
extra: Typically, muscle weakness is not to blame for this speech disorder
example: A 4-year-old can say 'ba' on its own but says 'banana' differently each time he tries.

text: {{c1::Neustress}} is {{c2::neutral stress when exposed to something that doesn't directly affect you}}
example: Hearing on the news about an earthquake in a country you have no ties to.

text: The {{c1::Yerkes-Dodson}} Law states that {{c2::people perform best when they are moderately aroused}}
example: A student with mild pre-exam nerves outscores both a bored classmate and a panicking one.

text: {{c1::Proactive coping}} is when {{c2::one reduces stress of a situation by anticipating a stressor and preparing for it }}
example: A student who knows finals are in May starts a study schedule in March.

text: {{c1::Apraxia}} is a motor disorder caused by damage to the brain in which the individual has difficulty with the motor planning to perform tasks or movements when asked
example: A stroke patient cannot wave goodbye on command, though his arm is not weak and he waves spontaneously.

text: Stimulation of the amygdala results in {{c1::anger}}, {{c1::violence}}, and {{c1::fear}}
example: Electrically stimulating a cat's amygdala makes it hiss, arch its back and attack.

text: {{c1::General adaptation syndrome}} explains how stressors do not have specific responses, they all generate the same general physical stress response
extra: 3 stages of stress: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
example: Selye's rats showed the same ulcers and enlarged adrenal glands whether exposed to cold, injury or toxins.

text: Darwin hypothesized that emotions are {{c1::expressed as an innate ability that allowed individuals to act in ways that gave them a better chance of survival}}.
example: A dog baring its teeth in anger warns a rival off before a costly fight.

text: {{c2::The tend and befriend response::Response}} is {{c1::the idea that humans respond better to stress when they have a support system}}.
example: During a hurricane, a mother gathers her children close and calls neighbours to band together.

text: Double approach-avoidance conflict: {{c1::2 options, both appealing and unappealing}}
extra: Example: deciding whether to study for school or for the MCAT

text: Destruction of the amygdala results in a {{c1::mellowing}} effect
example: Wild rhesus monkeys become tame and placid after their amygdalae are lesioned.

text: Anger has been associated with the {{c1::left superior temporal sulcus}}
example: Viewing an angry, scowling face engages the left superior temporal sulcus.

text: {{c1::Moods}} typically last longer than emotions
extra: Moods are more generalized than emotions
example: Road rage at a driver who cuts you off fades in minutes, but a grumpy mood can last all day.

text:
{{c1::Schachter-Singer}} Theory of Emotion
{{c2::
Event
↓
Physiological Response + Identify Reason for the Response
↓
Emotion
}}
extra: mnemonic/example: A SINGER who thinks she sucks performs at a concert. When it is over everyone claps. The singer's heart beat increases and at the same time she recognizes the clapping as people thinking she is a good singer. This makes her label the emotion as happiness :)
example: Schachter and Singer's epinephrine-injected subjects felt euphoric beside a giddy stooge, angry beside an irate one.

text: {{c1::The hippocampus::Brain region}} is involved in {{c2::converting short term memory to long term memory}}
example: Recalling next week the flashcards you study today depends on the hippocampus consolidating them.

text: Approach-approach conflict: {{c1::2 options and both are appealing}}
