example: Choosing between acceptances to two dream medical schools.

text: The physiological components to emotion are {{c1::how your body reacts to certain emotions}}

The left hemisphere of the cerebral cortex evokes {{c1::positive}} emotions
The right hemisphere of the cerebral cortex evokes {{c1::negative}} emotions
example: Patients with left frontal strokes, losing that hemisphere's positive emotion, often become depressed.

text: {{c1::The stressor}} is the {{c2::threatening/challenging event that causes stress}}
example: Receiving a layoff notice at work is a stressor.

text: The part of the nervous system that is responsible for fight / flight is the {{c1::sympathetic nervous system}}
example: Facing a growling dog, your heart pounds, your pupils dilate and digestion halts.

text:
Four great ways to help manage stress:
  • {{c1::exercise}}
  • {{c1::meditation}}
  • {{c1::religion}}
  • {{c1::cognitive flexibility (change your perspective on the stressor)}}
example: A stressed med student runs three times a week and meditates 10 minutes each morning.

text: In Lazarus' theory of emotion, labeling is based on {{c1::the individual}} and {{c1::cultural differences}}
extra:
some things might be labeled as good/bad for different people and different cultures
this is why some people like skydiving and some don't

text: Fixation at Freud's genital stage leads to {{c1::no adult fixation, meaning person is mentally healthy}}
example: A well-adjusted adult with a steady job and a loving relationship has, per Freud, reached the genital stage.

text: In Freud's psychosexual development, fixation is centered around {{c1::the libido}} and can have {{c1::lifelong effects well into adulthood}}
example: Freud would say a chain smoker's habit reflects libido stuck at the oral stage of infancy.

text:
Freud's {{c2::Anal}} Stage:
  • Age = {{c1::1-3}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::centered around anus ex:toilet training}}, {{c1::develops control/independence}}, {{c1::makes child feel confident}}
example: A 2-year-old proudly using the potty for the first time is in Freud's anal stage.

text: {{c2::Self-image}} is {{c1::what we believe we are / the view we have of ourselves}}
example: A teen looks in the mirror and thinks, 'I'm tall, funny and bad at math'.

text: {{c1::Attribution substitution}} is when individuals must make judgments that are complex but instead substitute a simpler solution or heuristic
example: Asked 'How happy are you with your life?', people answer with how they feel at that moment.

text:
Failure in one of Erikson's stages leads to:
  • {{c1::reduced ability to move onto further stages}}
  • {{c1::unhealthy personality/sense of self}}
example: An infant who never learns to trust may struggle to build intimacy as an adult.

text: {{c2::Self-esteem}} is {{c1::how much value we place on ourselves}}
example: A student who thinks 'I'm a worthwhile person' even after failing a quiz has high self-esteem.

text: {{c1::Attribution}} theory is how we explain behaviors of others around us
example: Seeing a friend snap at a waiter, you wonder whether she's rude or just had a terrible day.

text: {{c2::Self-fulfilling prophecy}} is {{c1::the idea that stereotypes can lead to behaviors that affirm the original stereotypes}}
example: In Rosenthal's Pygmalion study, randomly chosen students labelled 'bloomers' gained more IQ points.

text: Vygotsky's three stages of {{c1::higher mental function}} development are {{c2::more-knowledgeable other}}, {{c2::zone of proximal development}}, and {{c2::language}}
extra:
More-knowledgeable other: learning from a teacher.
Zone of proximal development: the stage between being taught and doing it yourself.
Language: how adults transmit information to children so they can learn.
example: A child learns to tie shoes from her dad, manages with his hints, then talks herself through it alone.

text: {{c1::Social stigma}} is {{c2::the disapproval of, or discrimination against, a person based on perceivable social characteristics that distinguish them from other members of a society}}
extra: commonly related to culture, gender, race, intelligence, and health
example: People with obesity are often seen as lazy and passed over for jobs.

text: Categorical self is the idea that {{c1::even though individuals are separate and distinct, they all exist in the world with others and can be categorized by groups}}
example: A 3-year-old describes herself as 'a girl, 3 years old, who likes dinosaurs'.

text: {{c2::Internal locus of control}} is when {{c1::a person believes they can influence the events/outcomes of their life}}
extra: example: If someone w/ an internal locus of control did bad on a test, they would attribute that to not studying
example: A smoker who believes quitting is up to her signs up for a cessation program.

text: {{c1::Self-concept}} AKA {{c1::self-identity}} is {{c2::how someone thinks about/perceives/evaluates themselves}}
example: A student who sees herself as 'a shy, hardworking future nurse' is describing her self-concept.

text: Prejudice: {{c1::attitudes that prejudge a group}}
extra:
Making the same assumptions about everyone in a group without considering their differences
Example: a CEO doesn't think women are capable of running a team

text: {{c1::Social perception}} is the way by which we generate impressions about people in our social environment
extra: It contains a perceiver, target, and situation
example: Within seconds of meeting a new roommate, you decide she's friendly because she smiled.

text: According to Carl Rogers, the three components of self-concept are {{c1::self-image}}, {{c1::self-esteem/self-worth}}, and {{c1::ideal-self}}
example: A student sees herself as average (self-image), dislikes herself (esteem), and wants to be a surgeon (ideal).

text: The two types of self-efficacy are {{c1::strong}} and {{c1::weak}}
example: One student believes he can master organic chemistry; another assumes he will fail before trying.

text:
Fixation at Freud's oral stage leads to:
  • {{c1::dependency/aggression}}
  • {{c1::mouth-related activities like smoking, biting nails, sucking thumb, and overeating}}
example: An adult who leans on a partner for every decision shows Freud's oral-dependent personality.

text:
A False Consensus is when you think everyone {{c1::agrees with your opinion}}
A Projection Bias is when you think everyone {{c1::has the same beliefs as you}}
example: A student who cheats believes most of his classmates cheat too.

text:
Erikson Stage 5:
  • Crisis = {{c1::identity vs role confusion}}
  • Age = {{c1::12-20}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::Learns roles to occupy as an adult}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::fidelity (seeing yourself as unique)}}
  • Negative outcome = {{c1::role-confusion (don't know what you want to be)}}
extra: Mnemonic: a stickman hits his head and is confused (role confusion).
example: A 16-year-old trying out goth, jock and drama-club personas is working on identity.

text: {{c2::External locus of control}} is when {{c1::a person attributes environmental events/causes to an outcome }}
extra:
attributes outcomes to something outside of their control
example: person w/ external locus of control does bad on a test and they attribute that to hard questions.
example 2: person w/ external locus of control does good on a test and they attribute that to luck/teacher being lenient
example: A man with diabetes who believes fate controls his health stops checking his blood sugar.

text: {{c1::A reference group}} is {{c2::a group an individual compares themselves to for self-evaluation}}
example: A med student judges her MCAT score against her pre-med friends, not the general public.

text: {{c2::Social identity}} is {{c1::the definition/evaluation of oneself based on groups you belong to in your community}}
example: Describing yourself as 'a Packers fan, a Catholic and a medical student'.

text: {{c1::Implicit personality theory::... theory}}: on first meeting someone we pick up on one characteristic and then assume other traits about the person based on it
example: Learning a new colleague is warm, you also assume she is honest and generous.

text:
Freud's {{c2::Phallic}} stage:
  • Age = {{c1::3-6}}
  • Characteristics: {{c1::children discover difference between males/females}}, {{c1::oedipus complex develops}}, {{c1::electra complex develops}}, {{c1::resolved through identification w/ same-sex parent}}
example: A 4-year-old boy announces he will marry his mommy when he grows up.

text: {{c2::Optimism bias}} is {{c1::the belief that bad things can happen to others but not us}}
example: Smokers believe they are less likely than other smokers to get lung cancer.

text: {{c3::George Mead}} developed the idea of {{c1::social behaviorism}}, where {{c2::the mind and self emerge through communication with others}}
example: A child comes to see herself as 'helpful' because her parents keep thanking her for setting the table.

text: {{c1::Hypothesis of relative deprivation}} states that {{c2::there is an upsurge in prejudice/discrimination when people are deprived of something they feel entitled to}}
example: Factory workers who feel passed over for raises blame immigrants for 'taking their jobs'.

text: {{c1::Cognitive bias}} is the tendency to think in certain ways that typically deviates from standard rationality/judgement
example: Buying a lottery ticket because you 'feel lucky' despite 1-in-292-million Powerball odds.

text: The three components to prejudice are {{c1::cognition}}, {{c1::affect}}, and {{c1::discrimination}}
extra:
cognition (stereotype) is the underlying thought, or overgeneralized belief
affect is the emotional component (actual prejudice aspect)
discrimination is the behavioral aspect to act on prejudice
example: Believing immigrants are lazy (cognition), resenting them (affect), and refusing to hire them (discrimination).

text: Freud believed the first {{c1::5}} years of life were crucial in development of personality
example: Freud would trace an adult's stinginess and rigidity to harsh toilet training at age 2.

text:
Social-identity theory holds that we categorize ourselves in a three-step process:
  1. {{c1::Categorize ourselves without realizing}}
  2. {{c1::Identification}}
  3. {{c1::Social comparison}}
example: A new med student labels herself 'pre-clinical', adopts the class's study habits, then ranks her school above rivals.

text:
The four sources of a person's strong/weak sense of self-efficacy:
  • {{c1::Mastery of experience}}
  • {{c1::Social modeling}}
  • {{c1::Social persuasion}}
  • {{c1::Psychological responses}}
example: Watching a classmate like you ace organic chemistry boosts your belief that you can too.

text: According to Mead, the {{c1::self}} is {{c2::the balance between the "I" and the "Me"}}
example: An employee wears a suit to work (Me) but adds bright socks to express herself (I).

text: {{c2::Stereotyping}} is {{c1::attributing a certain thought/cognition to a group of individuals and overgeneralizing}}
extra:
example: people who wear glasses are smarter
can involve race, gender, culture, religion, shoe size, etc
example: Assuming an Asian-American classmate must be good at math.

text: {{c1::The halo effect}} is the idea that people have inherently good/bad natures rather than looking at individual characteristics
example: Thorndike found officers who rated a soldier high in physique also rated him high in intelligence and loyalty.

text: When the just world hypothesis is threatened, we must {{c1::use rational/irrational techniques to make sense of the events to keep the JWH intact}}
example: Hearing of a random assault, people decide the victim 'must have provoked it' to keep the world fair.

text: Implicit bias: {{c1::Unconscious attitudes that affect our understanding, actions and decisions}}
example: Identical résumés with names like Emily got about 50% more callbacks than those with names like Lakisha.

text: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development differ from Freud's in the idea that {{c1::there was plenty of room for growth in an individual's life}}
example: Freud's last stage begins at puberty, but Erikson adds new crises at 40 and 65, so adults keep growing.

text: The {{c1::"In"}} group are people {{c2::we feel connected to with strong interactions}} and the {{c1::"out"}} group are people {{c2::in a group we are not associated with}}
example: To a Red Sox fan, fellow fans are the in-group and Yankees fans the out-group.

text: {{c2::Self-worth}} is {{c1::believing you are worthy, lovable, and necessary to life}}
example: A child who feels loved by her parents even after striking out believes she is worthy.

text: {{c1::Correspondent inference theory::... theory}} refers to when an observer assumes that a person’s behavior matches or corresponds with the person's personality traits
example: Viewers assume an actor who plays a cruel villain must be mean in real life.

text: {{c2::Stigma}} is {{c1::extreme disapproval of a person based on some behavior or quality of that person}}
extra: Examples: physical deformities, deviant personal traits (e.g. drug addiction), or deviation from a group's accepted norms.
example: A man released from prison is shunned by neighbours and rejected by employers.

text:
Freud's {{c2::Genital}} Stage:
  • Age = {{c1::12+}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::strong sexual interests}}, {{c1::focus on needs of others}}, {{c1::establish balance between life areas}}
example: A 16-year-old starts dating while balancing school, friends and a part-time job.

text: {{c2::Ideal-self}} is {{c1::what we wish/aspire to be}}
example: A pre-med pictures herself as a calm, compassionate surgeon.

text: external attribution of behavior depends on {{c1::consistency}}, {{c1::distinctiveness}}, and {{c1::consensus}}
example: All your friends laugh at one comic, at every show, but at no other comic: he's funny.

text:
Freud's {{c2::Latent}} stage:
  • Age = {{c1::6-12}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::exploration}}, {{c1::intellectual pursuits}}, {{c1::social interaction}}
example: A 9-year-old spends recess playing soccer with same-sex friends and memorising dinosaur facts.

text: Locus of control is {{c1::the extent to which people perceive they have control over events in their lives}}
example: One student credits her A to studying; another credits his to an easy teacher.

text: {{c1::Incongruency}} is when the ideal-self does not match the real-self
example: A student who sees himself as lazy but longs to be a disciplined athlete feels anxious.

text: {{c1::Vygotsky's zone of proximal development}} is the range of abilities that an individual can perform with assistance, but cannot yet perform independently
extra: It is the difference between what a learner can do without help and what he or she can do with help from a more knowledgeable other
example: A child who can't ride a bike alone can ride with a parent steadying the seat.

text: Charles Cooley coined the term {{c1::"looking glass self"}}
example: A girl who senses her classmates think she's smart comes to see herself as smart.

text: {{c2::Self-efficacy}} is {{c1::the belief in one's ability to succeed in a situation / execute the courses of action required in a particular situation}}
extra: example: People w/ high self-efficacy believe they can do well on the MCAT

text: Fixation at Freud's phallic stage leads to {{c1::homosexuality}} and {{c1::exhibitionism}}
extra: Exhibitionism: displaying one's genitals in public.
example: Freud would link an adult who exposes himself in public to unresolved conflict from ages 3-6.

text: The social comparison step of social-identity theory involves {{c1::comparing ourselves with other groups to maintain self-esteem}}
example: Badgers fans boost their pride by mocking the rival Gophers.

text: {{c1::Scapegoats}} are a group of people toward whom blame/aggression is directed
After completion of the game stage, Mead believed we developed {{c1::the "I" and "Me"}}
example: A teen wants to dye her hair blue (I) but worries about what her teachers will think (Me).

text: Kohlberg's conventional stage is from age {{c1::8}} to {{c1::13}}
example: A 10-year-old says you shouldn't steal because it's against the law and good kids follow rules.

text: {{c2::Fundamental attribution error}} is when {{c1::an individual assigns too much weight to internal causes rather than external factors when looking at behavior}}
extra: Example: Dan cuts John off on the highway, and John decides Dan is a selfish person. In reality, Dan was late for his flight.
example: In Ross's quiz study, observers rated randomly assigned quizmasters smarter than the contestants.

text:
Erikson Stage 1:
  • Crisis = {{c1::trust vs mistrust}}
  • Age = {{c1::0-1}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::if infants physical/emotional needs not met, might mistrust everyone}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::hope}}
  • Negative outcome = {{c1::mistrust}}
example: A baby whose cries are always answered learns the world is safe and develops hope.

text:
The stages of Mead's social behaviorism:
  1. {{c1::preparatory stage}}
  2. {{c1::play stage}}
  3. {{c1::game stage}}
example: A toddler mimics Dad shaving, a 4-year-old plays doctor, and a 9-year-old plays shortstop knowing every position.

text: {{c2::Internal}} AKA {{c2::dispositional}} attribution is when we infer that an event or behavior is due to {{c1::personal factors such as traits, abilities, or feelings}}
extra: Example: Jacob fell down the stairs because he is clumsy.

text: {{c2::Attribution}} is {{c1::the process of inferring causes of events/behaviors}}
example: Seeing a classmate fail a test, you infer it was because he didn't study.

text: {{c2::Stereotype threat}} is when {{c1::exposure to a negative stereotype surrounding a task can actually cause decrease in the performance of an individual}}
extra:
It threatens performance.
Example: students hear that their group does worse on the MCAT; the resulting anxiety leads them to do worse.
Example: blue and red students perform equally until a negative stereotype about blue students is introduced; then blue students perform worse.
example: In Steele and Aronson's study, Black students scored lower when a test was framed as measuring intelligence.

text:
Erikson Stage 4:
  • Crisis = {{c1::Industry vs Inferiority}}
  • Age = {{c1::6-12}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::teachers play important role in life}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::Competence (greater self-esteem)}}
  • Negative outcomes = {{c1::If child has no competence, they feel inferior}}
example: A 9-year-old praised for a science-fair project develops a sense of competence.

text: The Oedipus complex is when {{c1::boys view fathers as rivals for mother's affection}}
extra: Boys want to possess the mother and replace the father.
example: A 5-year-old boy tells his father to go away so he can cuddle with mommy.

text:
Kohlberg's third stage of moral development:
{{c1::Post-Conventional::Stage}}
  1. {{c1::Do the right thing (even if against the rules)::substage}}
  2. {{c1::Universal ethical standard (your own set of moral guidelines)::substage}}
extra:
Post-conventional:
5. Social contract: laws exist for the greater good but sometimes work against particular people (e.g. Heinz stealing a drug to save a life).
6. Universal ethical principles: people develop their own moral guidelines, which may not fit the law, and act on them despite consequences; few people reach this stage (e.g. Gandhi).
example: Harriet Tubman broke fugitive slave laws to lead enslaved people to freedom.

text:
Kohlberg's theory of {{c2::moral development}} looks at:
  • {{c1::how people develop morals}}
  • {{c1::how moral reasoning changes as people grow up}}
example: Kohlberg asked children whether Heinz should steal a drug to save his dying wife.

text:
Vygotsky believed babies had four elementary functions:
  • {{c1::attention}}
  • {{c1::sensation}}
  • {{c1::perception}}
  • {{c1::memory}}
example: A newborn turning toward her mother's voice already shows attention and sensation.

text:
Stereotype = {{c1::cognitive}}
Prejudice = {{c1::emotional}}
Discrimination = {{c1::behavioral}}
example: Believing women are bad drivers, disliking them for it, and refusing to lend them your car.

text:
Kohlberg's second stage of moral development:
{{c1::Conventional::Stage}}
  1. {{c1::Conform with majority::substage}}
  2. {{c1::Follow the rules::substage}}
extra:
Conventional:
3. Good boy/good girl: authority is internalized but not questioned; being good to be seen as good by others (emphasis on conformity).
4. Law and order: maintaining social order by obeying laws.
example: A teen says Heinz shouldn't steal because the law forbids it and society needs order.

text: {{c1::The devil effect / reverse halo effect}} is the opposite of the halo effect and says that poor first impression can lead us to assume everything about a person is negative
example: After a new hire shows up late on day one, the boss assumes he's also lazy and careless.

text:
Erikson Stage 6:
  • Crisis = {{c1::Intimacy vs Isolation}}
  • Age = {{c1::20-40}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::try to find love and relationships}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::love}}
  • Negative outcome = {{c1::avoiding intimacy leads to loneliness/isolation}}
example: A 27-year-old who marries her partner of five years has resolved intimacy vs isolation.

text: {{c1::Social-identity}} theory splits self-concept into two parts: {{c2::personal identity}} and {{c2::social identity}}
example: 'I'm witty and stubborn' reflects personal identity; 'I'm a Texan and a nurse' reflects social identity.

text: {{c2::Cultural relativism}} is {{c1::assessing a culture by its own standards rather than viewing it through the lens of one's own culture}}
extra:
No absolute right or wrong; different cultures are all valid.
This can falter if a culture violates human rights.
example: An anthropologist accepts eating with the hands as normal in a culture rather than calling it rude.

text: A CEO who doesn't think women are capable of running a team is an example of {{c1::prejudice}}
{{c2::Personal identity}} is {{c1::definition/evaluation of oneself in terms of things unique to each person like personal traits}}
example: Describing yourself as 'creative, stubborn and a night owl'.

text: The Electra complex is {{c1::when girls view their mothers as rivals for their father's affection}}
extra: Girls want to possess the father and see the mother as a rival.
example: A 4-year-old girl insists she will marry Daddy and tells Mom to sit somewhere else.

text: {{c1::Actor-observer bias}} is when {{c2::we attribute our own behavior to external factors but attribute others behavior to internal factors}}
example: You were late because of traffic, but your coworker was late because he's lazy.

text: {{c2::Recency bias}} is {{c1::the idea that people place a lot of emphasis on your recent actions/performances}}
extra: ex: You're only as good as your last game
example: A manager rates an employee poorly in December for one late project despite a strong year.

text:
Three aspects of the covariation model of attribution:
  • {{c1::consistency}}
  • {{c1::distinctiveness}}
  • {{c1::consensus}}
extra:
High consistency of behavior: more likely internal factors.
High distinctiveness: more likely external factors.
High consensus (everyone does the same thing): more likely external factors.
example: Ann fails every Prof X quiz, fails her other classes too, and her classmates pass: the cause is Ann.

text: The physical attractiveness stereotype believes that {{c1::attractive people have more positive personality traits}}
extra:
Jim, our initial overall impression is in the middle. His accounting rating/skills is very high, sales are negative, and leadership is moderately good
Now imagine, he has overall very good impression, even though he has the same actual skillset. We would perceive that the person is much better at other skills not demonstrated. Regardless of evidence, We may perceive he’s actually pretty good at sales instead of below average, We may say he is extra-ordinary in leadership and accounting instead of just good.
example: In Dion's 1972 study, students rated attractive faces as kinder and more likely to succeed.

text:
People with weak self-efficacy will:
  • {{c1::focus on failures}}
  • {{c1::avoid challenging tasks}}
  • {{c1::quickly lose confidence in abilities}}
  • {{c1::believe they lack ability to handle difficult tasks}}
extra:
mnemonic: FALL
F=Focus on failures
A=Avoid challenging tasks
L=Lose confidence
L=Lack ability to take on difficult tasks
example: After one bad chemistry grade, a student drops pre-med, convinced she can't handle science.

text: {{c1::Cultural imperialism}} is {{c2::the deliberate imposition of one's own cultural values on another culture}}
example: Canada's residential schools punished Indigenous children for speaking their own languages.

text:
Mead's stages:
  • Preparatory stage = focused on {{c1::imitation}}
  • Play stage = focused on {{c1::pretend role play}} and {{c1::is more aware of social relationships}}
  • Game stage = focused on {{c1::ability to understand attitudes/beliefs}} and {{c1::realize others can adopt multiple roles}}
extra: Example (preparatory stage): playing with pots and pans while parents cook.
example: A 4-year-old playing 'doctor' with a stuffed bear is in Mead's play stage.

text: The categorization step of social-identity theory involves {{c1::categorizing ourselves into groups like race, job, etc}}
example: A new hire mentally files herself under 'nurse', 'woman' and 'Latina'.

text: {{c1::Socialization}} is the process by which people {{c2::learn the attitudes, behaviors, and values expected by their community/culture}}
example: A child learns to say 'please' and 'thank you' by watching her parents.

text:
Erikson Stage 8:
  • Crisis = {{c1::Integrity vs Despair}}
  • Age = {{c1::65+}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::people contemplate lives and reminisce}} and {{c1::may feel unaccomplished if they didn't complete something}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::wisdom}}
  • Negative outcome = {{c1::if we feel unproductive it leads to despair/dissatisfaction upon death}}
example: An 80-year-old who looks back on her life with satisfaction, not regret, has achieved integrity.

text: The identification step of social-identity theory involves {{c1::adopting the identity of the group and behaving/acting like the category we belong to}}
example: After joining a fraternity, a freshman starts wearing its letters and using its slang.

text:
Erikson Stage 3:
  • Crisis = {{c1::Initiative vs Guilt}}
  • Age = {{c1::3-6}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::child feels secure in abilities to lead others and play}} and {{c1::they ask questions}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::purpose (in what they do/decisions)}}
  • Negative outcome = {{c1::if ability to lead/ask questions is controlled, they develop guilt(feel like they are a nuisance)}}
example: A 4-year-old who organises a pretend tea party and directs her friends shows initiative.

text: People with an authoritarian personality are {{c1::very prejudiced}}
example: Adorno's F-scale linked rigid obedience to authority with anti-Semitism and ethnocentrism.

text: According to Mead, the {{c1::"I"}} is {{c2::the response to the me}} and is associated with {{c2::non-conformity to societal views}} and {{c2::spontaneity}}
extra: Example: the "I" thinks "I could go to college, travel for a few years, or just get a job", not conforming to normal societal views.

text: Difference between self-worth and self-esteem is {{c1::self-esteem is being confident in yourself while self-worth is feeling that you are worthy/lovable/necessary to life}}
extra: can be confident in your own abilities (self-esteem) without necessarily feeling like you are loved/needed (self-worth)
example: A star surgeon confident in her skills (high self-esteem) may still feel unloved and unneeded (low self-worth).

text: Kohlberg's postconventional stage is from age {{c1::13}} through {{c1::adulthood}}
example: Martin Luther King Jr. broke segregation laws he believed violated universal justice.

text: {{c2::Out-group derogation}} is {{c1::when we are super friendly to our in group but are NOT friendly to the out group and discriminate against them}}
extra: This happens when we feel the out group is threatening to undermine a groups success
example: In Robbers Cave, the Eagles burned the rival Rattlers' flag and the groups raided each other's cabins.

text: Nigrescence model: {{c1::The process of becoming Black}}
extra: Journey toward an integrated racial identity
example: A racist encounter jolts a Black student into immersing herself in Black history and culture.

text: When you look at an individual's behavior from both an internal and external POV, you are considered a {{c1::neutral judge}}
extra: Most people don't weigh internal and external factors equally; they focus on internal ones, hence the fundamental attribution error.
example: A juror who weighs both a defendant's temper and the provocation he faced acts as a neutral judge.

text: Kohlberg's preconventional stage is from age {{c1::3}} to {{c1::7}}
example: A 5-year-old says stealing is wrong because you'll get a time-out.

text: {{c1::Primacy bias}} is the idea that {{c2::first impression is more important than later data}}
example: In Asch's study, 'intelligent, industrious... envious' was rated better than the same traits in reverse.

text: {{c1::Self-serving bias}} is when {{c2::we attribute our own success to internal factors but attribute failures to external factors outside our control}}
extra: this is to maintain our self-esteem and feel better about ourselves
example: A student credits her A to her brilliance but blames her F on an unfair test.

text: {{c2::In-group favouritism}} is when {{c1::we are friendly/favour people in our "in" group but are neutral to "out" group individuals}}
example: A manager hires a candidate from her own alma mater over an equally qualified stranger.

text: The {{c1::sociocultural theory of development::Theory}} stresses the interaction between developing people and the culture in which they live
extra: It looks at the important contributions that society makes to individual development
example: A Maya girl in Guatemala learns weaving by working beside her mother at the loom.

text:
Kohlberg's first stage of moral development:
{{c1::Pre-conventional::Stage}}
  1. {{c1::Avoid punishment::substage}}
  2. {{c1::Seek reward::substage}}
extra:
Pre-conventional (pre-adolescent):
1. Obedience and punishment: reasoning is based on physical consequences; rules are obeyed to avoid punishment.
2. Individualism and exchange: recognizes there is not just one right view handed down by authorities.
example: A child says Heinz shouldn't steal the drug because he'll go to jail.

text:
{{c2::Self-stigma}} is when:
  • {{c1::individuals internalize all negative stereotypes, prejudices, and discriminatory experiences they've had}}
  • {{c1::may begin to feel rejected by society and avoid interacting with society}}
extra: Example: someone with HIV/AIDS who feels the social stigma may deny the condition, lose self-esteem, become depressed, and isolate themselves from work, education, and other social activities.
example: A man with schizophrenia comes to believe he is dangerous and stops applying for jobs.

text: {{c2::Fundamental attribution error}} is when {{c1::individuals attribute character too strongly to explain someones actions}}
extra: Example: Bill cuts off Jill in traffic and Jill decides he is a selfish person, when in reality he is just running late for his flight.
example: Jones and Harris's readers judged a pro-Castro essay's writer pro-Castro even knowing the stance was assigned.

text:
Erikson Stage 2:
  • Crisis = {{c1::Autonomy vs Shame}}
  • Age = {{c1::1-3}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::children develop independence, ex: walk away from mom}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::will (independence)}}
  • Negative outcome = {{c1::if overly controlled, child feels inadequate}}
example: A 2-year-old insisting 'I do it!' while dressing herself is building autonomy.

text: {{c1::Frustration aggression hypothesis}} states that {{c2::someone getting frustrated can lead to prejudice}}
extra: Frustration turns into aggressive impulses. If they can't be directed at the source (e.g. an employer) without risk, the aggression is rechanneled elsewhere, often toward minorities.
example: Hovland and Sears found lynchings in the US South rose as cotton prices fell.

text: {{c1::Ethnography}} is the study of particular people and places
example: Margaret Mead lived in Samoa to study the lives of adolescent girls.

text:
Freud's {{c2::oral}} stage:
  • Age = {{c1::0-1}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::libido centered around mouth}}, {{c1::infant derives pleasure via oral stimulation}}, {{c1::baby develops sense of trust/comfort}}
example: A 6-month-old who calms only when sucking a pacifier is in Freud's oral stage.

text: Prejudice can arise from displaced {{c1::frustration}} (frustration-aggression hypothesis)
example: After losing his job, a man blames and harasses his immigrant neighbours.

text: The two parts of self-concept are {{c1::existential self}} and {{c1::categorical self}}
example: A baby learns she is separate from her mother (existential), then calls herself 'a girl, age 3' (categorical).

text: Existential self is {{c1::the sense of being separate and distinct from others}}
example: A baby learns she is separate from the world when kicking her legs makes the crib mobile spin.

text: {{c2::The just world phenomenon}} is the idea that {{c1::good things happen to good people and bad things happen to bad people}}
example: Assuming a homeless man must be lazy, since good people don't end up on the street.

text: {{c2::Xenocentrism}} is {{c1::judging another culture as superior to one's own culture}}
example: An American who insists French wine and Japanese cars are always better than domestic ones.

text: {{c1::The looking glass self}} states that {{c2::socialization influences how we perceive ourselves}}
example: A boy repeatedly called a troublemaker by teachers comes to see himself as one.

text:
Erikson Stage 7:
  • Crisis = {{c1::Generativity vs Stagnation}}
  • Age = {{c1::40-65}}
  • Characteristics = {{c1::established, settled down, have a career, families are the center}}
  • Virtue = {{c1::care}}
  • Negative outcome = {{c1::feeling stagnant / unproductive}}
example: A 50-year-old who coaches youth soccer and mentors junior colleagues shows generativity.

text: {{c2::External}} AKA {{c2::Situational}} attribution is when we infer that an event or behavior is due to {{c1::the environment/situation that an individual is in}}
extra: example: Jacob fell down the stairs because they were covered in banana peels

text:
The 5 stages of Freud's psychosexual development are:
  • {{c1::oral}}
  • {{c1::anal}}
  • {{c1::phallic}}
  • {{c1::latent}}
  • {{c1::genital}}
example: A thumb-sucking 6-month-old is in the oral stage; a 2-year-old being potty trained is in the anal stage.

text:
The three steps of the looking glass self:
  1. {{c1::how do I appear to others}}
  2. {{c1::what do others think of me}}
  3. {{c1::revise how we think about ourselves based on the previous 2}}
extra: Key point: we are influenced not by others' actual opinions but by what we imagine their opinions are.
example: A new resident imagines she looks nervous on rounds, assumes the attending finds her weak, and doubts herself.

text:
All 6 of Kohlberg's stages in order:
  1. {{c1::avoid punishment}}
  2. {{c1::seek reward}}
  3. {{c1::conform}}
  4. {{c1::follow the rules}}
  5. {{c1::do the right thing even if its against the rules}}
  6. {{c1::universal ethical standard}}
extra: mnemonic: Avoid Sea Creatures From Rivers (right thing) Upstate
example: Why not cheat? A child: 'I'd get caught' (stage 1); a teen: 'it breaks the school rules' (stage 4).

text: Fixation at Freud's anal stage leads to problems with {{c1::orderliness and messiness}}
example: An adult who alphabetises his spice rack and panics at clutter is 'anal-retentive', per Freud.

text: Fixation at Freud's latent stage leads to {{c1::no adult fixation at all}}
example: There is an 'oral' smoker and an 'anal' neat freak, but no 'latent' adult personality type.

text: According to Mead, the {{c1::"Me"}} is {{c2::the part of you society sees}} and is associated with {{c2::conformity to societal views}}
extra: Example: the "Me" thinks "I should go to high school, then college, then get a job", conforming to societal views.

text:
{{c2::Ethnocentrism}} is:
  • {{c1::judging someone else's culture from a position of your own culture}}
  • {{c1::viewing our own culture to be superior to that of others}}
example: An American tourist calls eating insects in Thailand 'disgusting and backward'.

text: Social stigma is fueled by {{c1::stereotypes}}, {{c1::prejudices}}, and {{c1::discrimination}}
example: The belief that mentally ill people are violent fuels fear of them and refusal to rent to them.

text:
People with strong self-efficacy will:
  • {{c1::recover quickly from setbacks}}
  • {{c1::have strong interest}}
  • {{c1::enjoy challenges}}
  • {{c1::have strong sense of commitment}}
example: After a low practice score, a confident pre-med retakes the test eager to improve.

text: Vygotsky believed higher mental functions developed from {{c1::teachers (parent, teacher, older sibling, etc.)}} and included {{c1::independent learning}} and {{c1::thinking}}
extra: Example: a parent helps you solve a puzzle so next time you can do it yourself.

text: {{c2::Self-control}} is the ability to {{c1::control our impulses}} and {{c1::delay gratification}}
example: Saving each paycheck for a car next year instead of spending it on takeout tonight.

text: {{c1::Dishabituation}} is {{c2::a renewed response to previously habituated stimulus}}
extra: Example: you habituate to the feel of a cotton sweater on bare skin. If you take it off and put it back on, you feel the previously habituated stimulus again.

text: {{c1::Albert Bandura}} is associated with social-cognitive theory and the bobo doll experiment
example: In Bandura's 1961 study, kids who saw an adult hit a Bobo doll with a mallet later did the same.

text: {{c2::Counterconditioning (AKA stimulus substitution)}} is {{c1::conditioning of an unwanted behavior or response to a stimulus into a wanted behavior or response by the association of positive actions with the stimulus}}
example: Mary Cover Jones eased little Peter's fear of rabbits by feeding him treats as a rabbit was brought closer.

text: The two types of {{c1::non-associative learning}} are {{c2::sensitization}} and {{c2::habituation}}
example: After a car alarm startles you, you jump at every small noise for the next hour (sensitization).

text: Simple innate behaviors include {{c1::reflexes}}, {{c1::taxis}}, and {{c1::kinesis}}
example: A moth flying toward a porch light is showing a taxis (phototaxis).

text: {{c2::Instinctual drift}} is {{c1::the tendency of an animal to revert to instinctive behaviors that interfere with a conditioned response}}
extra: Example: Skinner's former students Keller and Marian Breland tried to teach a raccoon to put tokens in a piggy bank; instead it drifted to its instinctive behavior of rubbing the tokens in its paws, as it does with food.

text: {{c2::Fixed-ratio}} is when a reinforcement occurs {{c1::after a fixed number of responses}}
extra: Example: a car salesman gets a bonus for every 5 cars he sells.

text: {{c2::Non-associative}} learning is learning where no {{c1::punishment/reward}} is occurring with an increase/decrease of response
example: The sea slug Aplysia withdraws its gill less after repeated gentle touches, with no reward involved.

text: The two types of aversive control are {{c1::escape}} and {{c1::avoidance}}
example: Leaving a party once the music gets painfully loud is escape; skipping the party to dodge the noise is avoidance.

text: Continuous reinforcement, when compared to partial reinforcement, {{c1::teaches behaviors more quickly but is less resistant to extinction when reinforcement stops::explain differences }}
example: People give up on a broken vending machine after one try but keep pulling a slot machine after many losses.

text: Cialdini's liking principle of influence: {{c1::People are easily persuaded by other people that they like}}
example: Tupperware parties sell well because guests buy from a friend who is hosting.

text:
When a response is unconditioned, it means it is {{c1::innate}}
When a response is conditioned, it means it is {{c1::learned}}
example: Blinking at a puff of air is innate; flinching at the sound of a dentist's drill is learned.

text: {{c1::Taste aversion}} is {{c2::when you eat something because you like it, but then stop eating it because you become sick (have a bad experience)}}
extra:
Classical conditioning.
Example: you like cilantro but get sick after a meal with it and start hating it, even if the chicken actually caused the sickness. The body links sickness to food rather than other features of the environment, so the association is learned quickly.
example: Garcia's rats drank saccharin water, were made nauseous by radiation, and avoided saccharin after one pairing.

text: {{c1::Aversive conditioning}} is {{c2::pairing a habit one wishes to break with an unpleasant stimulus to stop a particular behavior}}
extra: Example: shocking a smoker every time they smoke. The shock (UCS) causes pain (UCR); once smoking is associated with the shock, smoking (CS) alone produces pain (CR).
example: Disulfiram (Antabuse) makes drinkers vomit after alcohol, pairing drinking with nausea.

text: {{c1::Perceived behavioral control}} refers to a person's ability to carry out intentions to perform a certain behavior
example: A smoker who believes she can resist cravings is more likely to follow through on her plan to quit.

text: {{c1::Associative}} learning is when one event is connected to another event
example: Your dog runs to the kitchen whenever it hears the can opener.

text: Mirror neurons are {{c1::neurons that fire when an animal performs an act or when the animal observes the same action}}
example: A macaque's premotor neurons fire both when it grabs a peanut and when it watches a researcher grab one.

text: {{c2::Variable-interval}} is when a reinforcement occurs {{c1::after a variable amount of time}}
extra: example: car salesman gets bonus on random days

text: Complex innate behaviors include {{c1::fixed action patterns}}, {{c1::migration}}, and {{c1::circadian rhythms}}
example: A greylag goose rolls a stray egg back to its nest and finishes the motion even if the egg is taken away.

text: {{c2::Social-cognitive}} theory views behavior as being an interaction between {{c1::cognition}}, {{c1::environment}}, and {{c1::behavior}}
example: A teen who believes he is good at math studies more, earns his teacher's praise, and grows more confident.

text: {{c2::Non-associative}} learning is {{c1::when an organism is repeatedly exposed to one type of stimulus}}
example: A sea slug (Aplysia) poked repeatedly withdraws its gill less and less.

text: {{c1::Reciprocal determinism}} is the interaction between a person's {{c2::behaviors}}, {{c2::personal factors}}, and {{c2::environment}}
example: A shy student avoids parties, so she gets fewer invitations, which deepens her shyness.

text:
The elaboration likelihood model explains:
  • {{c1::how attitudes are formed}}
  • {{c1::how likely they are to be changed}}
example: A voter persuaded by a candidate's policy details keeps the view longer than one swayed by a celebrity endorsement.

text: {{c2::Discrimination}} is {{c1::when you learn to discern between differing stimuli and act accordingly::in terms of stimuli}}
extra: Example: you don't want to respond to a gunshot the same way you'd respond to a loud drum set.
example: A dog salivates to the bell paired with food but not to a bell of a different pitch.

text: {{c1::The peripheral route of persuasion}} is when {{c2::you look at superficial/non-verbal cues that aid in persuasion to change your attitude}}.
example: Buying a sneaker because LeBron James wears it in the ad.

text: {{c2::Shaping}} is {{c1::learning through successively reinforcing behaviors that approximate the target behavior}}
example: Skinner taught pigeons to turn a full circle by rewarding a slight head turn, then larger and larger turns.

text: {{c2::Systematic desensitization}} is {{c1::when someone is taught to replace feelings of anxiety with relaxation, usually to aid in phobias}}
extra: Example: a therapist teaches a person with a spider phobia relaxation techniques, then introduces spiders gradually (a picture, then a caged spider, then a free spider) until spiders are associated with relaxation.

text: {{c1::The learning-performance distinction}} states that {{c2::there is a difference between learning a behavior and actually performing the behavior. }}
extra:
A behavior can be learned without actually performing the behavior
Shown in the bobo doll experiment, as some kids did not beat up the doll
example: Kids who saw a model punished for hitting Bobo didn't copy him, until offered a reward to do so.

text: {{c1::Temptation}} is when a desire conflicts with values/long-term goals
extra: Example: being tempted to eat candy while trying to lose weight.

text: {{c2::Operant conditioning}} focuses on {{c1::the relationship between behavior and their consequences and how the consequences influence behavior}}
example: A child praised for cleaning her room starts cleaning it more often.

text: {{c2::A neutral stimulus}} is {{c1::a stimulus that can be sensed but doesn't produce any sort of reflex like salivation}}
example: Before conditioning, a white rat caused Little Albert no fear.

text: Classical conditioning ultimately occurs when {{c1::a neutral stimulus is able to elicit the same response as an unconditioned stimulus}}
example: After repeated pairings, Little Albert cried at the sight of the white rat alone.

text: {{c1::The central route of persuasion}} is when {{c2::your attitude change depends on quality of arguments by the persuader}}.
example: A buyer compares crash-test ratings and fuel economy before choosing a car.

text: Secondary reinforcers are {{c1::things learned to be reinforcers that usually require a pairing with primary reinforcer to have value}}
example: A dog trained with clicks paired with treats will later work for the click sound alone.

text: {{c2::Negative punishment}} is when {{c1::something is taken away to decrease tendency of a behavior}}
extra: Example: mom takes away her kid's phone for misbehaving, to decrease that behavior.

text: A {{c1::stimulus}} is anything that stimulates your senses
example: The smell of fresh bread drifting from a bakery is a stimulus.

text: {{c2::Negative reinforcement}} is when {{c1::something is taken away to increase the tendency of a behavior}}
extra:
example: loud buzzing noise goes away when you put your seatbelt on
take away buzzing to increase tendency of putting on seatbelt

text: Cialdini's reciprocity principle of influence: {{c1::People tend to return a favor}}
example: Hare Krishnas handed travellers a free flower, then asked them for a donation.

text: An unconditioned stimulus is {{c1::a stimulus that elicits an unconditioned response}}
example: A puff of air to the eye makes you blink without any learning.

text: The two routes of the elaboration likelihood model are the {{c1::central}} and {{c1::peripheral}} routes
example: Buying a laptop after comparing specs is central; buying it because a famous athlete uses it is peripheral.

text: Examples of {{c1::associative}} learning include {{c2::classical and operant conditioning}}
example: A rat learns that pressing a lever delivers a food pellet.

text: The three main characteristics that impact persuasion are {{c1::message characteristics}}, {{c1::source characteristics}}, and {{c1::target characteristics}}
example: A toothpaste ad has a dentist (source) give a two-sided argument (message) to busy parents (target).

text: {{c1::Generalization}} is {{c2::the tendency for a stimulus similar to a conditioned stimulus to elicit a conditioned response}}
extra:
This allows us to make appropriate responses to similar stimuli.
Example: a cell phone ringtone elicits the same salivation in dogs as the original bell.
example: Little Albert came to fear a white rabbit and a Santa Claus mask, not just the rat.

text: The marshmallow test is a famous experiment that involved telling kids {{c1::they would get 2 marshmallows if they didn't eat the first one for 15 minutes}}
extra: Those who waited tended to have better life outcomes when followed up 10 years later.
example: Mischel's preschoolers covered their eyes or sang to themselves to keep from eating the marshmallow.

text: {{c2::Habituation}} is when {{c1::response to a stimulus decreases over time}}
extra:
Loss of response to repeated stimuli.
Example: curing a phobia by repeated exposure to the feared object until the emotional response decreases.
example: You stop noticing the refrigerator's hum a few minutes after walking into the kitchen.

text: Aversive control is when behavior is motivated by {{c1::a threat or something unpleasant}}
example: A student studies every night only to avoid failing the class and losing her scholarship.

text: The two information processing routes in the elaboration likelihood model are {{c1::central route of persuasion}} and {{c1::peripheral route of persuasion}}
example: One voter reads the candidates' tax plans; another picks the one who seems most likable.

text: {{c1::Classical AKA Pavlovian conditioning}} is a learning process in which {{c2::an innate response to a potent stimulus comes to be elicited in response to a previously neutral stimulus by pairing a neutral and potent stimulus}}
example: Little Albert came to fear a white rat after it was paired with a loud clanging noise.

text: {{c2::Implosive therapy}} is a technique to {{c1::aid in phobias by heavily increasing anxiety so individuals can see their fear is irrational}}
extra: Example: putting a person with a spider phobia in a room with thousands of spiders, so that facing the fear and surviving shows it is irrational. This produces a lot of anxiety.

text: Conditioned memory: {{c1::Memory formed based on association between 2 things}}
example: Feeling queasy at the smell of tequila after once getting sick on it.

text: {{c2::Positive reinforcement}} is when {{c1::something is added to increase tendency of a behavior}}
extra: Example: getting a gas card for safe driving makes you more likely to drive safely.

text: {{c1::Extinction burst}} is when {{c2::an animal no longer receives regular reinforcement, so the original behavior spikes as a last-ditch effort to gain reinforcement}}
extra:
Example: a pigeon trained to peck a button for food pecks frantically when the button is turned off, then pecks less often.
Example: a baby cries louder when mom doesn't respond right away, then stops when this fails.

text: {{c1::Habituation}} is when an individual tunes out a stimulus
example: You stop noticing the ticking of a wall clock after a few minutes.

text: Persuasion is {{c1::a method for attitude/behavior change}}
example: A public health ad showing a smoker's blackened lungs convinces a viewer to quit.

text: {{c2::Fixed-interval}} is when a reinforcement occurs {{c1::after a fixed amount of time}}
extra: Example: a car salesman gets a paycheck every 2 weeks, no matter how many cars he sells.

text: {{c2::Operant extinction}} occurs when {{c1::a response by an organism is no longer being reinforced}}
extra: Example: you teach your dog to sit by giving it treats; when you stop giving treats, it stops sitting when asked.

text: Operant conditioning is associated with {{c1::B.F. Skinner::psychologist}}
example: Skinner's box: a rat learns to press a lever because each press delivers a food pellet.

text:
{{c1::Central::central/peripheral}} processing produces a lasting attitude change
{{c1::Peripheral::central/peripheral}} processing creates a temporary attitude change
example: A smoker who weighs the lung-cancer data stays quit, while one swayed by a celebrity's ad relapses within weeks.

text: A conditioned stimulus is {{c1::a previously neutral stimulus that now elicits the same response as the unconditioned stimulus}}
example: The whine of a dentist's drill, once paired with pain, now makes you tense on its own.

text: Operant conditioning is also known as {{c1::instrumental conditioning}}
example: Thorndike's cats escaped a puzzle box faster over repeated trials because escaping earned them food.

text: {{c2::The elaboration likelihood model for persuasion}} is a {{c1::cognitive approach to the why/how of persuasion}}
example: Petty and Cacioppo's students judged an exam proposal by its arguments if it affected them, by its source if not.

text: Insight learning is {{c1::the sudden realization ("aha" moment) of a problem's solution, often after a period of no progress}}
extra: Example: using previously learned math skills to solve a problem.
example: Köhler's chimpanzees, after failed attempts, suddenly stacked crates to reach bananas hung out of reach.

text: {{c2::Spontaneous recovery}} is when {{c1::an old, previously extinguished, conditioned stimulus elicits a conditioned response}}
example: A dog whose bell-salivation was extinguished salivates to the bell again after a day's rest.

text: {{c2::Social cognitive theory}} postulates {{c1::that people learn how to behave and shape attitudes through observing the behaviors of others, social factors, and environment}}.
extra: Example: Bobo doll experiment, in which children imitated adults who hit the doll

text: Primary reinforcers are {{c1::things that are innately satisfying/desirable}}
example: A thirsty rat presses a lever for drops of water with no training needed to value the water.

text: {{c2::Sensitization}} is {{c1::increase in responsiveness to a repeated stimulus}}
example: A dripping faucet at night grows more irritating with every drip.

text: Cialdini's commitment and consistency principle of influence: {{c1::If people commit to something, they relate it to their self-image and tend to follow through}}
example: Residents who first agreed to display a small safe-driving sign later accepted a huge lawn billboard.

text: The most effective reinforcement schedule is {{c1::variable-ratio}}
example: Slot machines pay out after an unpredictable number of pulls, so gamblers keep playing for hours.

text: {{c2::Variable-ratio}} is when reinforcement occurs {{c1::after an average number of responses has occurred}}
extra:
Variable number of responses.
Example: a car salesman gets a bonus after selling 5 cars, then 3, then 7, then 6, then 4 (average 5).
Example: slot machine.

text: A {{c1::token economy}} is a system of behavior modification based on systematic reinforcement of a target behavior; the reinforcers are tokens that can be exchanged for other reinforcers (e.g. prizes)
example: A psychiatric ward gives patients tokens for making their beds, redeemable for snacks or TV time.

text: {{c1::Tyranny of choice}} is when too many choices lead to dissatisfaction in choice
example: In Iyengar and Lepper's jam study, shoppers offered 24 jams bought far less often than those offered 6.

text: Cialdini's authority principle of influence: {{c1::People will tend to obey authority figures}}
example: In Milgram's study, 65% of participants delivered the maximum 450-volt shock when told to.

text: Continuous reinforcement is when {{c1::for each behavior, there is a reward}}
example: A vending machine delivers a snack every single time you insert the right coins.

text: {{c2::Avoidance behaviors}} are reinforced by {{c1::the removal of painful/undesirable stimuli as a result of preemptively avoiding them}}
extra:
negative reinforcement
ex: A fire alarm allows you to avoid a fire
example: A rat learns to cross the shuttle box when a warning tone sounds, before the shock ever arrives.

text: {{c1::Observational learning}} is {{c2::learning through watching and imitating others.}}
example: A toddler copies her mother by chatting into a toy phone.

text: {{c1::Extinction}} is when {{c2::a conditioned stimulus no longer elicits a conditioned response}}
extra: Example: you ring the bell many times and never give the dog meat; the dog stops salivating to the bell.

text: {{c2::Positive punishment}} is when {{c1::something is added to decrease the tendency of a behavior}}
extra:
example: giving a speeding ticket to decrease tendency to speed
add speeding ticket to decrease likelihood of speeding(behavior) again

text:
When listener interest, motivation, and importance are low, then we enter {{c1::peripheral}} processing
When listener interest, motivation, and importance are high, then we enter {{c1::central}} processing
extra:
Central: the listener cares about the topic.
Peripheral: the listener doesn't care about the topic.
example: A shopper indifferent to cars picks one for its catchy jingle, while a car enthusiast compares crash-test data.

text:
{{c2::Ego-depletion}} is the idea that:
  • {{c1::self-control is a limited resource}}
  • {{c1::if you use too much self control on one task, it will limit the ability to use it on future tasks}}
example: In Baumeister's study, people who resisted cookies and ate radishes then quit an unsolvable puzzle sooner.

text: {{c2::Escape conditioning}} occurs when {{c1::individuals must escape an unpleasant stimulus once it has occurred}}
extra:
The animal learns a behavior that terminates an aversive stimulus; this is negative reinforcement, since a bad stimulus is taken away.
Example: finding a way out of a building on fire.
example: A rat in a shuttle box learns to jump the barrier as soon as the floor shock on its side begins.

text: Presentation of a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus is known as a {{c1::trial}}
example: Each time Pavlov rang the bell and then gave meat powder counted as one trial.

text: Individuals are more likely to develop phobias towards {{c1::things that impacted our ancestors}} than {{c1::things that are actually dangerous in the real world now}}
extra: example: more likely to have phobias of snakes, spiders, and heights than to have phobias of cars and electrical outlets, even though the latter are probably more dangerous in todays society

text: Cialdini's scarcity principle of influence: {{c1::Perceived scarcity will generate demand}}
extra: Example: "For a limited time only, there is a 20% discount! Buy now!"

text: Latent learning is {{c1::when learned behavior is not expressed until required}}
example: Tolman's rats explored a maze unrewarded, then made as few errors as trained rats once food was added.

text: Cialdini's social proof principle of influence: {{c1::People will do things that they see other people are doing}}
example: Sitcom laugh tracks make viewers laugh more at the jokes.

text: Study testing a causal relationship between the independent and dependent variables, with participants randomly assigned to groups: {{c1::Experimental study}}
extra: Between-subjects and within-subjects designs are common experimental designs
example: Randomly assigning 100 students to caffeine or placebo before a memory test to see if caffeine improves recall.

text: Participants are randomly assigned to an experimental group and take part in only one group: {{c1::Between-subjects design}}
example: Half the participants study in silence and half with music, and each person experiences only one condition.

text:
Examples of self-report studies:
  • {{c1::Survey}}
  • {{c1::Questionnaire}}
  • {{c1::Poll}}
extra: Participants are asked about their feelings, attitudes, beliefs, etc.
example: A Gallup poll asking 1,000 adults how many hours they sleep each night.

text: A moderating variable affects {{c1::the strength of the relationship between 2 variables}}
extra:
Example: gender may change how strongly watching sad videos is related to crying
Moderators include location, gender, race, religion, etc.

text: Reconstructive bias: {{c1::Our memories are not as accurate as we think}}, especially under {{c1::stress}}
example: Loftus's subjects asked how fast cars "smashed" later recalled broken glass that was never in the film.

text: Test-retest reliability: {{c1::A high positive correlation between the first and second administration of a test}}
example: A personality test given twice, 2 weeks apart, yields scores that correlate at r = 0.90.

text: Counting the times a kid pushes other kids over to measure aggression is an example of {{c1::operationalization}}
example: Defining "stress" as a participant's salivary cortisol level is another operationalization.

text: {{c1::Social desirability bias::Bias}}: subjects report behavior in accordance with social norms
extra: Subjects want to appear socially acceptable
example: A patient tells his doctor he exercises 4 days a week when he really manages 1.

text:
All variables examined are continuous:
{{c1::Regression}}
example: Predicting systolic blood pressure from age and BMI, both measured on continuous scales.

text: A correlation coefficient that is below -1 is likely the result of an {{c1::error by the experimenter}} when computing the correlation between 2 variables
example: A reported r = −1.3 between study hours and errors must be a calculation mistake, since r runs from −1 to +1.

text: 3×2 factorial design: {{c1::3 levels of the first variable crossed with 2 levels of the second variable}}
example: Testing 3 caffeine doses (0, 100, 200 mg) in both sleep-deprived and rested people gives 3 × 2 = 6 groups.

text: Internal validity asks: {{c1::Was the research done "right"}}?
example: A drug study with no placebo group cannot tell whether patients improved from the drug or just with time.

text: +/- 1 SD = {{c1::~68% (about 2/3)}} of the sample (normal distribution)
extra:
68–95–99.7 rule (normal distribution only):
±1 SD ≈ 68%
±2 SD ≈ 95%
±3 SD ≈ 99.7%
example: With IQ mean 100 and SD 15, about 68% of people score between 85 and 115.

text: {{c1::Reliability}}: the degree to which an assessment tool produces stable, consistent and replicable results
example: A scale that shows 70.0 kg each time you step on it within a minute is reliable.

text: Clinical trial: {{c1::highly controlled interventional study}}
example: A phase III trial gives 3,000 patients a new statin or a placebo and tracks heart attacks for 5 years.

text: Ecological validity asks: {{c1::Can the findings be generalized beyond the present situation?}}
example: A memory test using random word lists in a quiet lab may not predict recalling a grocery list in a busy store.

text: Cross-sectional study: {{c1::look at a group of different people at one moment in time}}
extra: Example: past smoking habits and current lung cancer diagnoses
example: Testing the vocabulary of 5-, 10- and 15-year-olds all on the same day.

text: Counterbalancing: {{c1::A way of controlling for order effects in a repeated measure design}}
extra: Participants receive the same conditions in different orders, so order cannot act as a confounding variable
example: Half the subjects do the easy task then the hard one; the other half do the hard task first.

text: Embedded field studies: {{c1::When researchers pose as participants}}
example: Rosenhan's researchers faked hearing voices to get admitted to psychiatric hospitals and recorded staff behavior.

text: Vehicle control: {{c1::You want to observe the group when the IV is not present}}
extra: Example: the experimental group gets the drug in saline; the vehicle control group gets saline only

text: {{c1::Reciprocal relationship::Relationship}}: cause ⇌ effect
example: Depression reduces exercise, and less exercise in turn worsens depression.

text: Discriminant validity: {{c1::Things that aren't related are not related}}
example: Scores on a new anxiety scale should barely correlate with scores on a spelling test.

text: Network analysis: {{c1::Investigating social structures through networks and graphs}}
example: Mapping who texts whom in a high school shows a few students linking otherwise separate friend groups.

text:
What is Content Validity?
Does it {{c1::cover all aspects}} of what it's supposed to {{c1::measure?}}
example: A final biology exam that asks only about genetics lacks content validity for the whole course.

text: Observational study that looks back at past information to find a link between past events and current outcomes: {{c1::Retrospective study}}
extra:
Example: reviewing the medical records of people with Alzheimer's disease to find past risk factors
Helps identify potential risk factors for disease
example: Checking old birth records of adults with schizophrenia to see whether more of them were born in winter.

text: The split-half method tests whether {{c1::all parts of the test contribute equally to what is being measured}}
example: Scores on the odd-numbered items of a 40-item anxiety test are correlated with scores on the even-numbered ones.

text: A t-test {{c1::compares the mean of a dependent variable between 2 groups (2 levels of one independent variable)}}
extra: Dependent variable is obtained through measurement
example: Comparing mean exam scores of students who slept 8 hours versus 4 hours uses a t-test.

text: {{c1::Attrition bias::Bias}}: research subjects dropping out
example: In a 2-year smoking-cessation study, most of the people who drop out are those who relapsed.

text: Study that follows groups of people forward in time to see how their behavior influences future outcomes: {{c1::Prospective study}}
extra:
Example: following nurses to relate stress, smoking and exercise to long-term health outcomes
Looks into the future; retrospective studies look into the past

text: A prospective cohort study follows a group of individuals {{c1::forward over a period of time into the future}}
extra: Example: follow middle-aged truck drivers who vary in smoking habits to test whether 20-year lung cancer incidence is highest in heavy smokers, then moderate smokers, then nonsmokers
example: The Nurses' Health Study enrolled nurses in 1976 and has tracked their diet, habits and diseases ever since.

text: Positive control: a treatment with a {{c1::known result}}
extra: Confirms that the methodology and equipment being used work
example: A PCR run includes a sample known to contain the target DNA to confirm the reaction works.

text: External validity asks: {{c1::Can the results be generalized to other situations}}?
extra: Needs a random, representative sample and realistic settings (tight lab control can ↓ external validity)
example: A sleep study run only on college students in a lab may not apply to night-shift nurses at home.

text: Discriminant validity is also known as {{c1::divergent validity}}
example: An extraversion questionnaire whose scores do not track IQ scores shows divergent validity.

text: Study that uses both qualitative and quantitative measures: {{c1::Mixed-method research design}}
extra: Example: rate a product on a 1–10 scale, then interview people who rated it poorly for their qualitative opinion

text: Reliability: {{c1::Consistent results with repeated experiments}}
example: Five repeated glucose readings from the same blood sample all come out near 95 mg/dL.

text: {{c1::Comparative}} studies aim to make comparisons across different countries or cultures
example: Hofstede surveyed IBM employees in over 50 countries to compare cultures on individualism.

text:
When all variables are categorical:
{{c1::Chi-square}}
example: Testing whether men and women differ in preferring cats, dogs or neither uses a chi-square test.

text: Temporal confounds: {{c1::time-related confounding variables}}
example: Mood improves during a 6-month therapy study partly because winter turns to spring mid-study.

text: Test validity: how {{c1::good}} the test is
example: A driving test that checks only parallel parking is a poor test of overall driving ability.

text: Self-Report studies have {{c1::validity}} problems
example: Survey respondents claim to have voted more often than official turnout records show they did.

text: Regression: used when {{c1::all variables examined are continuous}}
example: Predicting adult height in cm from childhood calcium intake in mg/day uses regression.

text: {{c1::Demand characteristics}} occur when {{c2::participants in an experiment change their behavior to try and act how they think the experimenter wants them to behave}}
extra:
The change in behavior can be conscious or unconscious.
Example: in the Stanford prison experiment, the guards may have thought Zimbardo wanted them to mistreat the prisoners, so they did.
example: Orne's subjects kept doing pointless addition sheets for hours, assuming the experimenter had a reason.

text: {{c1::Internal validity}}: whether the results of a study properly demonstrate a causal relationship between two variables
extra: A confounding variable hurts internal validity
example: In a coffee and memory study, the coffee group also slept more, so sleep rather than coffee may explain the gain.

text:
Correlation: {{c1::how related 2 things are in a positive or negative sense}}
  • r = 1: {{c1::perfect positive correlation}}
  • r = −1: {{c1::perfect negative correlation}}
  • r = 0: {{c1::no correlation}}
extra: Unlike regression, makes no assumption about which variable influences the other
example: Temperature in °C and °F correlate at r = 1, since one is an exact linear function of the other.

text: Observational study that determines only whether a relationship exists between two variables (does not prove causation): {{c1::Correlational study}}
extra:
Predictor variable: analog of the independent variable
Criterion variable: analog of the dependent variable
example: A survey finds people who sleep less report more anxiety, without showing which causes which.

text: {{c1::Projection bias::Bias}}: researchers imposing their own beliefs onto subjects
example: A researcher who hates commuting assumes every participant finds their commute stressful.

text: Population validity asks: {{c1::Can the results be generalized to other populations of people?}}
example: Findings from a study of only male undergraduates may not hold for older women.

text:
Type I error = false {{c1::positive}}
Type II error = false {{c1::negative}}
example: Telling a man he is pregnant is a type I error; telling a visibly pregnant woman she isn't is type II.

text: Criterion validity: whether the test itself is {{c1::valid}}
extra: Is the test able to predict a certain outcome?
example: A new depression scale is checked against psychiatrists' clinical diagnoses of the same patients.

text: {{c1::Validity}}: how well an experiment measures what it is trying to measure
example: Measuring intelligence by head circumference gives consistent numbers but is not a valid measure.

text: Observational study: {{c1::the researcher is unable to control the assignment of groups}}
example: Researchers cannot assign people to smoke, so they compare lung health in people who already do or don't.

text: Retrospective chart studies {{c1::examine past charts}}
example: Reviewing 500 past ER charts to see how often chest-pain patients were given aspirin.

text: Null hypothesis: {{c1::There is no relationship between 2 variables}}
example: H<sub>0</sub>: students who drink coffee and students who don't have the same mean exam score.

text: Quasi-experimental design: {{c1::measure outcomes for program participants and non-program participants without random assignment}}
example: Comparing test scores of students who chose to join an after-school tutoring program with those who did not.

text: Chi-square: used {{c1::when all variables are categorical}}
extra: Qualitative data that can be observed and recorded as a category
example: Testing whether vaccinated and unvaccinated people differ in flu (yes/no) rates uses a chi-square test.

text: Reactivity: {{c1::Influencing what is being observed}}
extra: Example: a researcher posing as a patient in a mental hospital could influence what they are trying to observe
example: Hawthorne factory workers became more productive simply because they knew they were being studied.

text: {{c1::Face validity}}: the degree to which a layperson taking a cursory look at an experiment agrees that it measures what it claims to measure
example: A depression questionnaire asking "Do you often feel sad?" plainly looks like it measures depression.

text: P-value under 0.05 = {{c1::Significant}}
example: A drug trial with p = 0.03 lets researchers reject the null that the drug works no better than placebo.

text: {{c1::Researcher bias::Bias}}: bias due to bad experimental design
extra: Scientists performing the research influence the results to portray a certain outcome; research should stay neutral
example: A researcher testing her new teaching method gives it only to her strongest students.

text: Convergent validity: measures that are supposed to be {{c1::related}} are {{c1::related}}
example: Scores on a new anxiety scale correlate strongly with scores on the established Beck Anxiety Inventory.

text: Validity = {{c1::accuracy}}
example: A bathroom scale that reads 5 kg too heavy every time is consistent but not valid.

text:
Practice effect: {{c1::Performance improves over repeated testing/trials due to practice and familiarity}}
Opposite: {{c1::fatigue effect: performance ↓ with time due to boredom or fatigue}}
example: Reaction times speed up over the first 20 trials of a task, then slow by trial 200 as boredom sets in.

text: Concurrent validity: whether the test holds up against a {{c1::benchmark test}}
example: A new 5-minute IQ test shows concurrent validity if its scores match the full WAIS given the same day.

text: Negative control: a control group that is {{c1::not expected to produce results}}
extra:
Example: placebo, saline solution
Confirms that there is no confounding variable
example: A PCR tube with water instead of DNA should show no band; a band there means contamination.

text:
Two-tailed t-test: {{c1::possibility of relationship in both directions}}
One-tailed t-test: {{c1::possibility of relationship in one direction}}
extra:
In short: Two-tailed = "Is A different from B?" (either direction). One-tailed = "Is A bigger than B?" or "Is A smaller than B?", one direction picked in advance; a difference the other way doesn't count.
Two-tailed: H0: X = Y; Ha: X ≠ Y (difference in either direction). α is split between both tails (0.025 each for α = 0.05).
One-tailed: H0: X ≤ Y; Ha: X > Y (or the reverse), only the predicted direction. All of α is in one tail, so significance in that direction is easier to reach.
example: Testing whether a drug changes heart rate is two-tailed; testing whether it lowers heart rate is one-tailed.

text:
Similar to T-test, but for 3+ groups:
{{c1::ANOVA}}
example: Comparing mean weight loss across keto, vegan and Mediterranean diet groups uses one ANOVA.

text: A case-control study is an {{c1::observational study::study type}} used to find a {{c1::risk factor (association, not causation)}}
extra: 2 groups differing in outcome are compared
example: Doll and Hill compared lung cancer patients with matched controls and found far more smokers among the patients.

text:
What is Social desirability bias?
{{c1::How people respond to research questions}}
example: Survey respondents underreport how much alcohol they drink so they seem responsible.

text: Linear regression: {{c1::degree of dependence between 1 variable and another}}
extra: Scatter plot; one-way influence of 1 variable on another
example: A fitted line shows each extra hour of study raises exam scores by about 5 points.

text: Selection bias: bias arising from {{c1::how people are chosen to participate}}
example: The 1936 Literary Digest poll sampled car and phone owners and wrongly predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt.

text: A mediating variable explains {{c1::why 2 things are related}}
extra: Example: "Whenever I watch TV at night, I feel tired the next morning." Not getting enough sleep mediates the relationship between watching TV and being tired.

text: {{c1::Criterion validity}}: whether a variable is able to predict a certain outcome
extra: Example: SAT scores predicting first-year college GPA

text:
How related 2 things are in a positive or negative sense:
{{c1::Correlation}}
example: Shoe size and reading ability correlate positively in children because both rise with age.

text: Cohort study: {{c1::following groups sorted by exposure forward over time to see who develops the outcome}}
extra:
Example: whether smoking is associated with lung cancer
All cohort studies are longitudinal (same people measured over time), but not every longitudinal study is a cohort study (e.g., tracking the same kids' vocabulary from age 2 to 10, with no exposure groups)
example: The Framingham Heart Study followed town residents for decades to link smoking and cholesterol to heart disease.

text: Prospective chart studies {{c1::look at charts as they come}}
example: Recording each new diabetic patient's HbA1c from their chart at every visit over the next year.

text:
Statistically significant (α = 0.05)?
  • p = 0.0420: {{c1::Yes}}
  • p = 0.69: {{c1::No}}

Generalizing to a theory:
{{c1::Taking time- and place-specific observations to create a universal hypothesis or theory}}
example: Darwin's observations of Galápagos finch beaks grew into the general theory of natural selection.

text: A retrospective cohort study looks {{c1::back at events that have already taken place}}
extra: Example: female nurses who smoke and who do not smoke, compared on cancer
example: Using old employment records to compare later cancer rates in asbestos-exposed and unexposed shipyard workers.

text: {{c1::Test-retest reliability}}: reliability in obtaining similar scores over time
example: An IQ test taken in March and again in April gives the same person scores of 112 and 114.

text: {{c1::Unidirectional relationship::Relationship}}: cause → effect
example: Smoking causes lung cancer, but having lung cancer does not make someone start smoking.

text: Generalizing to a population: {{c1::Inferring the results from a sample and applying it to a population}}
extra: Requires a random sample that is representative of the population
example: Polling 1,000 randomly chosen voters to predict how the whole national electorate will vote.

text: Regression to the mean: {{c1::if first measure is extreme, second measure will be closer to the mean}}
example: Athletes on a Sports Illustrated cover after a career-best season usually play worse the next season.

text: Face validity: {{c1::whether a layperson would say the test appears valid}}
example: A timed typing test looks to anyone like a fair measure of typing skill.

text: Construct validity: whether the test measures {{c1::the construct it is supposed to measure}}
example: An "intelligence" test that really measures English vocabulary has poor construct validity for intelligence.

text:
Compares the mean of a dependent variable between 2 groups (2 levels of one independent variable):
{{c1::T-test}}
example: Comparing mean reaction times of 30 caffeinated and 30 decaf participants uses a t-test.

text: Self-reported information is always vulnerable to {{c1::subjective bias}}
extra: Example: "Yeah, I was benching 400 lbs when I was 16"

text: A longitudinal study gathers data from the {{c1::same subjects repeatedly over a period of time}}
extra: Follows variables over a long period of time to look for correlation
