example: The Dunedin study has retested about 1,000 New Zealanders born in 1972–73 from age 3 into midlife.

text: Experimental study: {{c1::involves manipulation of variables}}
example: Researchers assign rats to 0, 2 or 4 hours of daily running and then measure their maze times.

text: {{c1::External validity}}: whether results can be generalized to other situations or to other people (e.g., from a small study to a larger population)
extra: Subtypes: population validity and ecological validity
example: A drug tested only in men aged 20–30 may not work the same way in elderly women.

text: Operationalization: {{c1::Process of strictly defining variables into measurable factors}}
extra:
Taking a vague term and figuring out a way to measure it
Example: counting how often a child pushes others as a measure of aggression

text: {{c1::Reconstructive bias::Bias}}: poor recollection (especially relevant in retrospective studies)
example: Mothers of babies with birth defects recall more medicines taken in pregnancy than mothers of healthy babies.

text: Inter-rater reliability: {{c1::Consistent when two different people measure the same thing}}
example: Two observers count a child's aggressive acts on the same video and both tally 12.

text: Participant observation: {{c1::Observer participates in ongoing activities and records observations}}
extra: Observer is a "player" in the action
example: A sociologist lives in a neighborhood for years, joining daily life while keeping field notes.

text: Confounding variable: {{c1::Changes in dependent variable may be due to existence of or variations in a third variable}}
extra: The third variable could provide an alternative explanation for the relationship between the variables
example: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together because hot weather drives both.

text:
Degree of dependence between 1 variable and another:
{{c1::Linear regression}}
example: Fitting score = 2 × hours + 60 to study data: 10 hours of study predicts a score of 80.

text: {{c1::Inter-rater reliability}}: the degree to which two different researchers or raters agree in their assessments
example: Two radiologists read the same 100 chest X-rays and agree on 95 of them.

text: Attrition bias: {{c1::Occurs when participants drop out of a long-term experiment or study}}
example: In a 1-year diet trial, most dropouts are people losing no weight, which inflates the average loss.

text: Predictive validity: how well the test can {{c1::predict}} future outcomes
example: The MCAT shows predictive validity if high scorers go on to pass USMLE Step 1 at higher rates.

text: Each participant is exposed to every level of the independent variable (repeated-measures design): {{c1::Within-subjects design}}
extra: Higher power: the same person serves in multiple conditions, which ↓ the individual-difference effects seen in between-subjects designs
example: Each participant takes a memory test once after coffee and once after decaf, on different days.

text: {{c1::Bias}}: failure to be objective
example: A researcher who expects a drug to work rates the treated patients as more improved than the controls.

text: ANOVA: {{c1::similar to t-test, but for 3+ groups}}
example: Comparing mean pain scores across placebo, 200 mg and 400 mg ibuprofen groups uses ANOVA.

text:
Null hypothesis vs. Alternative hypothesis is considered under:
{{c1::Hypothesis testing (any test: t-test, ANOVA, chi-square, etc.)}}
extra: H<sub>0</sub> = no difference/no relationship; H<sub>a</sub> = there is one. Every hypothesis test sets them up the same way: if p < α (usually 0.05), reject H<sub>0</sub>. Chi-square is just one such test (for categorical data); t-tests compare means of 2 groups and ANOVA compares 3+.
example: Drug trial: H<sub>0</sub> says the drug lowers blood pressure no more than placebo; H<sub>a</sub> says it does.

text: +/- 2 SD = {{c1::95%}} of the sample
example: With IQ mean 100 and SD 15, about 95% of people score between 70 and 130.

text:
Randomized controlled trial:
  • {{c1::participants are randomly assigned to the treatment under study or a control}}
  • {{c1::Tests efficacy and side effects}}
extra: Gold standard for a clinical trial
example: The 1954 Salk polio vaccine trial randomly gave children either the vaccine or a placebo injection.

text: A confounding variable correlates with and explains {{c1::BOTH the IV & DV}}
extra: Example: nice roads and clean sidewalks seem related, but a wealthy neighborhood (the confounding variable) explains both

text: Study conducted over a long period of time, usually following a specific cohort of people: {{c1::Longitudinal study}}
extra: Example: tracking heart disease incidence over time while monitoring diet and smoking habits
example: Terman's study followed about 1,500 gifted California children from the 1920s through the rest of their lives.

text: {{c1::The phototransduction cascade}} is the process of turning a rod cell off
example: In light, a rod hyperpolarizes from about −40 mV toward −70 mV and stops releasing glutamate.

text: In order of vibration, the ossicles include the {{c1::malleus (hammer)}}, {{c1::incus (anvil)}} and {{c1::stapes (stirrup)}}
extra:
Path of vibration: tympanic membrane → malleus → incus → stapes → oval window → cochlea
Source: Lars Chittka & Axel Brockmann (PLoS Biol), vectorized by Inductiveload, via , CC BY 2.5Source: Marc Giacone, SVG by Angelito7, via , CC BY-SA 3.0
example: In otosclerosis, bone fixes the stapes in place, so vibration stops at the end of this chain.

text: The {{c1::inferior colliculus::brainstem structure}} is involved in the startle reflex and the vestibulo-ocular reflex
example: Jumping when a balloon pops beside you is a startle reflex the inferior colliculus helps coordinate.

text: In down-regulation of sight, when it is bright outside our pupils {{c1::constrict}} and our rods and cones become {{c1::desensitized}} to light
example: Stepping from a dark theater into noon sun, you squint until your pupils constrict and photoreceptors adjust.

text: {{c1::The sclera}} is the white of the eye and made of thick fibrous tissue.
example: Yellowing of the sclera (scleral icterus) is often the first visible sign of jaundice.

text: Top-down processing uses {{c1::deductive reasoning::type of reasoning}}
example: Knowing stop signs are red octagons, you recognize a snow-covered red octagon as a stop sign.

text: Meissner's corpuscles detect {{c1::light touch}}
example: Reading Braille with a fingertip relies on Meissner's corpuscles.

text: {{c1::Slow-adapting neurons::type of neuron}} fire at the {{c2::beginning of a stimulus and calm down after a while}}
example: You feel your glasses press on your nose when you put them on, then the feeling slowly fades.

text: The opposite of sensory adaptation is {{c1::amplification}}
example: After about 30 minutes in the dark, your eyes become sensitive enough to see faint stars.

text: The three components of feature detection include {{c1::color}}, {{c1::form}}, and {{c1::motion}}
example: A red ball rolling across a lawn: red is colour, round is form, rolling is motion.

text:
Aqueous humor functions in anterior chamber:
  • {{c1::applies pressure to maintain shape of the eyeball}}
  • {{c1::allows nutrients and minerals to supply the cells of the cornea/iris}}
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: The cornea has no blood vessels, so it gets most of its glucose from the aqueous humor.

text: {{c1::Symmetry::Gestalt Principle}} states that the mind perceives objects as being symmetrical and forming around a center point
example: In [ ] { } ( ), the marks are seen as three symmetrical bracket pairs, not six separate marks.

text:
Monocular cues include:
  • {{c1::relative size}}
  • {{c1::interposition}}
  • {{c1::relative height}}
  • {{c1::shading and contour}}
  • {{c1::motion parallax}}
  • {{c1::constancy}}
example: A person blind in one eye can still judge depth from cues like relative size and interposition.

text: The superior olive is located in the {{c1::brain stem}} and its function is to {{c1::localize sound}}
example: A horn on your left reaches your left ear a fraction of a millisecond sooner, telling you where it is.

text: The middle ear is {{c1::the region with the three ossicles}}
example: Childhood ear infections (otitis media) fill the middle ear with fluid behind the eardrum.

text: Bottom up processing is driven by {{c1::data}}
example: Proofreading a list of random letters, where only the ink on the page guides what you see.

text: {{c1::Shading and contour}} is a monocular cue that uses light and shadows to perceive form/depth/contours
extra: Example: a crater or mountain, as shown below.
example: A circle shaded dark at the bottom looks like a bump; flipped upside down, it looks like a dent.

text: {{c1::Correct Rejection}} is when a subject gives a negative answer for no signal
example: An airport screener clears a bag that truly holds no weapon.

text: {{c1::The lens}} bends light so it goes to the back of the eyeball. It focuses light specifically on the {{c2::fovea}}.
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: A cataract clouds the lens, so the image focused on the fovea blurs and reading gets hard.

text: {{c1::Continuity::Gestalt Principle}} states that lines are seen as following the smoothest path
extra: You can see the smooth line here
example: An X is seen as two straight lines crossing, not as two V shapes touching at their tips.

text: Projection areas are areas in the four lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital) of the brain where {{c1::sensory processing}} occurs
example: Touch on your hand is processed in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe.

text: Binocular cues give humans a sense of {{c1::depth}}
extra: This is a result of retinal disparity, which is the fact that each of your eyeballs has a different perspective on the world.
example: 3D movies show each eye a slightly different image so the flat screen seems to have depth.

text: Humans can hear frequencies between {{c1::20 Hz}} and {{c1::20 kHz}}
example: A dog whistle at about 25 kHz is silent to humans but clearly audible to dogs.

text: Unimportant stimuli can also be called {{c1::noise}}
example: At a crowded party, the chatter of other guests is noise against your friend's voice.

text: {{c1::Constancy}} is a monocular cue that states our perception of an object doesn't change even if the image cast on the retina is different.
extra: The three types include size constancy, shape constancy, and color constancy
example: A white shirt looks white both in sunlight and under a dim yellow lamp (color constancy).

text: There is higher resolution in the fovea because {{c1::there are no axons in the way of light entering the cell}}
extra: this is why the fovea dimples in
example: Fixing your gaze on a word lets light reach foveal cones unobstructed, so that word is sharpest.

text: {{c1::The vibrational theory of olfaction}} states that vibrational frequency of a molecule gives that molecule a specific odor.
example: Luca Turin argued that boranes smell like rotten eggs because their B–H bonds vibrate like S–H bonds.

text: Sound waves that pass through the auditory canal will hit the {{c1::tympanic membrane}} AKA {{c1::eardrum}}
example: A doctor uses an otoscope to view the pearly grey tympanic membrane at the end of the ear canal.

text: {{c1::The absolute threshold of sensation}} is the {{c2::minimum intensity of stimulus needed to detect a particular stimulus 50% of the time}}
example: A tone heard on 5 of 10 trials is at the listener's absolute threshold.

text: {{c1::Long::Long/Short}} wavelength ({{c1::low}}-frequency) sound waves penetrate deeper into the cochlea, toward the apex
extra:
Cochlea uncoiled along one axis (x = distance from the base). Each frequency peaks at its own spot: high pitch near the base, low pitch (long λ) deepest, near the apex.
Source: Kern A, Heid C, Steeb W-H, Stoop N, Stoop R (2008), PLoS Comput Biol, via , CC BY 2.5
example: A tuba's low notes peak near the cochlear apex, while a piccolo's high notes peak near the base.

text: The parvocellular pathway has good {{c1::spatial}} resolution but poor {{c1::temporal}} resolution
example: Parvo lets you read a still eye chart in detail but responds poorly to a rapidly flickering light.

text: {{c1::Transduction}} occurs whenever energy is transformed from one form to another
example: Cochlear hair cells convert the mechanical energy of sound vibrations into electrical signals.

text: {{c1::Circumvallate papillae::Papillae}} are located at the {{c2::back}} of the tongue
example: The 8–12 large bumps in a V shape at the back of the tongue are circumvallate papillae.

text:
The steps from light hitting a rod to a signal getting sent to the brain include:
  1. light hits rod
  2. {{c1::rod turns off}}
  3. {{c1::bipolar cell turns on}}
  4. {{c1::retinal ganglion cell turns on}}
  5. {{c1::signal travels to optic nerve}}
  6. signal travels to brain
example: Spotting a faint star at night runs through this rod → bipolar → ganglion cell → optic nerve relay.

text: {{c1::Sensory receptors}} are sensory nerves that respond to stimuli
example: Pacinian corpuscles in your fingertips fire when you feel your phone vibrate.

text: {{c1::Gustducin}} is a protein associated with the sensation of taste
example: When quinine in tonic water binds a bitter receptor, gustducin is the G protein it activates.

text: Visual agnosia: {{c1::Impairment in recognition of visually presented objects::Explain}}
extra:
Not due to a deficit in vision (acuity, visual field, scanning), language, memory or intellect
Often due to damage to the posterior occipital and/or temporal lobes (anterior to primary visual cortex)
example: Sacks's patient Dr. P could describe a glove's parts but not name it, and mistook his wife for a hat.

text: Directly above the cribriform plate is the {{c1::olfactory bulb}}
example: A blow to the head can shear olfactory axons where they rise to the bulb, causing loss of smell.

text: The purpose of the oval window is to {{c1::push fluid through the cochlea}}
extra: this allows fluid to pass over the hair cells and stimulate the sensation of hearing
example: Funnelling the eardrum's force onto the much smaller oval window boosts pressure about 20-fold.

text: Cochlear implants are a surgical treatment that attempts to restore hearing in {{c1::sensorineural hearing loss}} AKA nerve deafness
extra:
The electrode in the cochlea bypasses the damaged hair cells and stimulates the auditory (hearing) nerve directly.
Source: Blausen.com staff (2014), via , CC BY 3.0
example: A child born deaf from hair cell loss can learn to understand speech after a cochlear implant.

text: The cilia in the ear are called {{c1::hair bundles}}
example: Loud noise can splay or snap the hair bundles on cochlear hair cells, causing permanent hearing loss.

text:
The steps to olfaction include:
  1. {{c1::molecule binds to GPCR on olfactory epithelia}}
  2. {{c1::G-protein binds to ion channels}}
  3. {{c1::ion channels open and trigger AP}}
  4. {{c1::AP goes through cribriform plate}}
  5. {{c1::AP reaches glomerulus}}
  6. {{c1::AP activates mitral/tufted cells}}
  7. {{c1::AP synapses in brain}}
example: Humans have about 400 kinds of functional olfactory receptor GPCRs that start this chain.

text: Weber's Law states that {{c1::the JND (ΔI) / initial intensity (I) = k (constant)}}
extra:
The JND is proportional to the initial intensity.
Example: you can tell 2 lb from 2.2 lb but not 5 lb from 5.2 lb; you can tell 5 lb from 5.5 lb.Video: Weber's law and thresholds (Khan Academy MCAT)
example: With k = 0.1, a 100 g weight needs 10 g added to feel heavier, while a 1,000 g weight needs 100 g.

text: {{c1::C fibers::Type of nerve fibre}} are unmyelinated and very small in diameter.
extra:
Memory hook: alphabetical = speed order (A-beta > A-delta > C)
• A-Beta = Big Brush: thickest, most myelin, touch
• A-Delta = Dagger: thin, light myelin, fast sharp pain
• C = Coatless, Crawling: unmyelinated, slow dull ache
Rubbing a stubbed toe: Big Brush closes the gate on Dagger & Crawling (gate control)
example: C fibres conduct at only about 0.5–2 m/s, versus about 35–75 m/s for A-beta fibres.

text: {{c1::Taste buds}} are barrel-shaped structures that consist of many gustatory cells
example: Scalding your tongue on hot coffee dulls taste for days until the damaged taste-bud cells are replaced.

text:
Visual pathway:
{{c1::Eye}} → {{c1::optic nerves}} → {{c1::optic chiasm}} → {{c1::optic tracts}} → {{c1::lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)}} → {{c1::visual radiations}} → {{c1::visual cortex}}
example: A pituitary tumor pressing on the optic chiasm causes loss of both outer (temporal) visual fields.

text: {{c1::The choroid}} is a black, pigmented network of {{c2::blood vessels}} that helps nourish the retina.
example: Red-eye in flash photos is light reflecting off the blood-rich choroid behind the retina.

text:
Light from the right visual field goes to the {{c1::left}} side of the brain
Light from the left visual field goes to the {{c1::right}} side of the brain
example: A stroke in the right occipital lobe leaves a patient blind to the left half of the visual field in both eyes.

text: Photopsin is a biological pigment found in the {{c1::cones}} of the retina
example: Red-green color blindness arises when the gene for one cone photopsin is missing or altered.

text: When off center bipolar cells are turned {{c2::on::on/off}}, this activates {{c1::off center retinal ganglion cells::cell type}}, which send signals to optic nerve and to the brain.
example: A black crow against a bright sky makes the off-center ganglion cells for that spot fire.

text: {{c1::Miss}} is when a subject gives a negative response to a present signal
example: A radiologist reads a mammogram as normal, but the patient actually has a tumor.

text: {{c1::C fibres::Type of nerve fiber}} cause a lingering sense of pain
example: The dull, throbbing ache that lingers after you stub your toe is carried by C fibres.

text:
When tip links are pushed back by endolymph movement, the following cascade occurs:
  1. {{c1::K+ channels open}}
  2. {{c1::Ca2+ channels open}}
  3. {{c1::Neurotransmitter released onto spiral ganglion neurons}}
  4. {{c1::Spiral ganglion cells activated}}
  5. {{c1::Auditory nerve activated}}
  6. {{c1::Signal sent to brain}}
example: Endolymph is K<sup>+</sup>-rich, so K<sup>+</sup> flows into hair cells and depolarizes them, unlike in most neurons.

text: {{c1::The vitreous chamber}} is filled with vitreous humour, which is a jelly-like substance
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: Floaters are small clumps in the vitreous humour that cast moving shadows on the retina.

text: {{c1::Prägnanz (law of simplicity)::Gestalt Principle}} states that our brains organize and reduce reality to its simplest form possible
extra: We see a set of overlapping rings rather than many complex, irregular shapes.
example: A Venn diagram is seen as two overlapping circles, not three oddly curved separate pieces.

text:
Auditory pathway:
Cochlea → vestibulocochlear nerve → {{c1::medial geniculate nucleus}} → auditory cortex
example: A ringing phone's signal relays through the thalamus's MGN before reaching the temporal lobe's auditory cortex.

text: {{c1::The vestibular system::System}} provides the sense of {{c2::balance}} and {{c2::spatial orientation}}
extra: It is located in the inner ear (semicircular canals, utricle, and saccule)
example: An inner-ear infection (labyrinthitis) makes the room seem to spin and throws off your balance.

text: {{c1::Relative height}} is a monocular cue where an object is perceived as being farther away when it is higher in the visual field
example: In a seascape painting, boats painted higher up near the horizon look farther away.

text: {{c1::Convergence}} gives humans an idea of depth based on how much the eyeballs are turned.
extra:
Things far away have less retinal disparity
Things close up have more retinal disparity
example: Your eyes turn inward as you bring a finger toward your nose, signaling that it is near.

text:
The sclera's main functions include:
  • {{c1::Muscle attachment point}}
  • {{c1::Extra layer of protection to eyeball}}
example: The six extraocular muscles, such as the lateral rectus, insert on the sclera to turn the eye.

text: The malleus = {{c1::the hammer}}
extra: Source: Marc Giacone, SVG by Angelito7, via , CC BY-SA 3.0
example: The malleus's handle is attached to the eardrum, so it is the first ossicle to move.

text: {{c1::Law of Past Experiences::Gestalt Principle}} states that under some circumstances visual stimuli are categorized according to past experience
extra: Example: a reader seeing an unfamiliar English word interprets an "L" and an "I" side by side as two letters, rather than using closure to combine them into a "U".

text: {{c1::A subliminal stimulus}} is a stimulus below the absolute threshold of sensation
example: A word flashed on screen for 10 ms, too briefly to be consciously seen.

text: Light is an {{c1::electromagnetic wave}}
example: Visible light (about 400–700 nm) sits between ultraviolet and infrared on the electromagnetic spectrum.

text: The stapes = {{c1::the stirrup}}
extra: Source: Marc Giacone, SVG by Angelito7, via , CC BY-SA 3.0
example: The stapes, about 3 mm long, is the smallest bone in the human body.

text: Prosopagnosia: {{c1::Can't recognize familiar faces}}
example: Oliver Sacks, who had prosopagnosia, once apologized to a bearded man who was his own reflection.

text: Most perception of warmth occurs in the {{c1::Insula}}
example: The warmth you feel stepping into a hot bath is registered in the insular cortex.

text: The {{c1::vestibulo-ocular reflex::... reflex}} keeps the eyes fixed on a single point as the head rotates
example: While you shake your head "no", a sign's words stay steady because your eyes counter-rotate.

text:
Vitreous humor has two functions:
  • {{c1::provide pressure to the eyeball}}
  • {{c1::give nutrients to inside of the eyeball}}
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: In a vitrectomy, surgeons replace removed vitreous with saline or gas so the eyeball keeps its shape.

text: {{c1::The retina}} is the inside, back area of the eye filled with {{c2::photoreceptors}}.
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: A detached retina pulls photoreceptors off their blood supply, causing a 'curtain' over part of vision.

text: Light first hits the eye at the {{c1::Cornea}}
example: A contact lens rests directly on the cornea, the first surface incoming light meets.

text: {{c1::The posterior chamber}} is the area between the back of the iris and the front of the lens
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: During cataract surgery, the artificial lens is placed in the posterior chamber, just behind the iris.

text: The incus = {{c1::the anvil}}
extra: Source: Marc Giacone, SVG by Angelito7, via , CC BY-SA 3.0
example: The incus sits between the malleus and stapes, passing vibration on like the middle link of a chain.

text: {{c1::Photoreceptor (rod) discs}} are stacked membrane structures in the outer segment that contain the photopigment rhodopsin
extra:
Not the optic disc, which is the blind spot where the optic nerve exitsElectron micrographs: (A) rod outer segment, with its stacked discs at the top; (B) close-up of the stacked disc membranes, where rhodopsin sits.
Source: Gilliam et al. 2012 (Cell) and Gunkel et al. 2015 (Structure), via , CC BY 2.5
example: A single rod's outer segment holds roughly 1,000 stacked discs packed with rhodopsin.

text: The {{c1::cribriform plate}} separates the {{c2::olfactory epithelium}} from the {{c2::brain}}
example: A skull fracture through the cribriform plate can leak cerebrospinal fluid out of the nose.

text: {{c1::Opsins}} are photoreceptor proteins made light-sensitive by the chromophore retinal
example: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness because rod opsin needs retinal, made from vitamin A.

text: {{c1::c}} is the symbol for the strategy used in signal detection
example: A smoke detector set to sound at the faintest trace of smoke uses a liberal criterion (low c).

text: Somatosensation of pain is called {{c1::nociception}}
example: Capsaicin in chili peppers activates the heat-pain receptor TRPV1, so spicy food burns.

text: {{c1::Foliate papillae::Papillae}} are located at the {{c2::side}} of the tongue
example: The vertical folds you see on the rear sides of your tongue in a mirror are foliate papillae.

text: In up-regulation of sight, our pupils {{c1::dilate}} and our rods and cones begin to synthesize {{c1::light sensitive molecules}}
example: Walking into a dark movie theater, you can barely see at first but make out the seats after several minutes.

text: {{c1::The semicircular canals}} are filled with {{c2::endolymph}}, which is a fluid that shifts to help detect what direction our head is moving in
extra: Also, since we can determine how quickly the endolymph moves, we can also detect the strength of rotation
example: Turning your head to the right makes endolymph lag in the horizontal canal, bending its hair cells.

text: The parvocellular pathway relies on {{c1::cones::photoreceptor}}
example: Picking out the colours and fine print on a cereal box in daylight relies on cone-fed parvo cells.

text: Bottom up processing uses {{c1::inductive reasoning::type of reasoning}}
example: Piecing together stripes, four legs and a mane to conclude you are looking at a zebra.

text:
The 5 main tastes are:
  • {{c1::bitter}}
  • {{c1::salty}}
  • {{c1::sweet}}
  • {{c1::sour}}
  • {{c1::umami}}
example: Coffee is bitter, chips are salty, honey is sweet, lemon is sour and parmesan is umami.

text: When on center bipolar cells are turned on, they activate {{c1::on center retinal ganglion cells}}, which send signals to the optic nerve.
example: A lit doorway at the end of a dark hallway makes on-center ganglion cells for that spot fire rapidly.

text: The sense that doesn't synapse on to the thalamus is {{c1::olfaction}}
example: Smelling a rose sends signals from the olfactory bulb straight to the olfactory cortex, bypassing the thalamus.

text: The three types of nerve fibers are {{c1::A-beta}} fibres, {{c1::A-delta}} fibres, and {{c1::C}} fibres
extra:
Memory hook: alphabetical = speed order (A-beta > A-delta > C)
• A-Beta = Big Brush: thickest, most myelin, touch
• A-Delta = Dagger: thin, light myelin, fast sharp pain
• C = Coatless, Crawling: unmyelinated, slow dull ache
Rubbing a stubbed toe: Big Brush closes the gate on Dagger & Crawling (gate control)
example: Stubbing a toe: you feel the touch (A-beta), a sharp jolt (A-delta), then a dull ache (C).

text: Olfactory epithelia rely on {{c1::G-Protein Coupled Receptors::receptor type}}
example: Smelling coffee starts with an odorant binding a GPCR that activates G<sub>olf</sub> and raises cAMP.

text: {{c1::The accessory olfactory bulbs}} are not present in humans but allow animals to rely more heavily on pheromones
example: Snakes flick their tongues to carry pheromones to the vomeronasal organ, which feeds the accessory bulb.

text: {{c1::Gustation}} is the sense of taste
example: Tasting the saltiness of a potato chip as Na<sup>+</sup> enters taste receptor cells.

text: A {{c1::glomerulus}} is a destination point for various olfactory cells sensitive to the same molecule
extra:
1 olfactory bulb · 2 mitral cells · 3 cribriform plate · 4 nasal epithelium · 5 glomerulus · 6 olfactory receptor cells. Receptor cells of the same color (same odorant receptor) all converge on the same glomerulus.
Source: Chabacano, after Patrick J. Lynch, via , CC BY-SA 2.5
example: All neurons expressing one receptor type for a banana odorant send their axons to the same glomerulus.

text: Rods have a {{c1::slow::speed}} recovery time, while cones have a {{c1::fast::speed}} recovery time.
extra:
Bright light bleaches rhodopsin in rods. In the dark, rhodopsin regenerates slowly, so full dark adaptation takes ~20–30 min. Cone pigments regenerate fast, so cones recover in ~5–10 min and then plateau.
The curve shows the threshold (dimmest visible light) dropping over time: the first dip is the cones, then the rod–cone break at ~7–10 min, then the slower and deeper dip from the rods.Source: Dgtdsgn, , CC BY-SA 3.0
example: Walking from daylight into a dark cinema, you can't find your seat until your rods recover minutes later.

text: {{c1::Tastant}} is a substance that stimulates the sense of taste
example: Sucrose in a sugar cube is a tastant that triggers sweet receptors.

text: {{c1::Contextual effects}} states that the context in which stimuli are presented and the processes of perceptual organization contribute to how people perceive those stimuli
extra: The H and the A are the same symbol, yet you read them as different letters because of the letters around them.
example: The same ambiguous shape reads as the letter B between A and C but as 13 between 12 and 14.

text: Axons leaving from the temporal region of the retina {{c1::do not::do/do not}} cross over at the optic chiasm
extra: This is to make sure stuff from the right visual field gets processed on the left side of the brain and vice versa
example: An aneurysm pressing the chiasm's outer edge cuts that eye's uncrossed temporal fibres, blinding its nasal field.

text: The single tallest true cilium in a hair bundle is called the {{c1::kinocilium}}
example: Bending the stereocilia toward the kinocilium depolarizes the hair cell; bending away hyperpolarizes it.

text: {{c1::Nociceptive pain::... pain}} is caused by potentially harmful stimuli being detected by receptors around the body
example: Touching a hot stove triggers heat nociceptors in your fingertip and you yank your hand back.

text:
Visual pathway:
Eye → optic nerves → optic chiasm → optic tracts → {{c1::lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)}} → visual radiations → visual cortex
example: A stroke in the left LGN of the thalamus causes loss of the right visual field in both eyes.

text: Visual cues that are a result of humans having two eyes are called {{c1::binocular cues}}
example: Threading a needle is much harder with one eye closed, since binocular cues are lost.

text: {{c1::The fovea}} is a special part of the {{c3::macula}} that is completely covered in {{c2::cones}}
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: To read a word you look straight at it, placing its image on the fovea.

text: The otolithic organs help detect {{c1::linear acceleration}} and {{c1::head positioning}}
example: With eyes closed you still sense a car accelerating forward because the utricle's otoliths lag behind.

text: The inner ear includes {{c1::the cochlea}} and {{c1::semicircular canals}}
example: The dizziness after spinning on an office chair comes from fluid sloshing in the semicircular canals.

text: {{c2::Visual cues}} allow us to {{c1::perceptually organize}}
extra: Perceptual organization is how the brain assembles raw sensory input into a coherent scene of objects with form, depth, motion and constancy. Visual cues such as binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence) and monocular cues (relative size, interposition, linear perspective, shading) make this possible, letting us perceive a 3D world from flat 2D images on the retina.
example: Seeing a stadium crowd as distinct people at different distances, not a flat patchwork of colors.

text: Smell synapses at the {{c1::orbitofrontal cortex}}
example: Judging whether a carton of milk smells spoiled relies on the orbitofrontal cortex.

text: There are no photoreceptors in the {{c1::blind spot::eye region}}
example: Close your left eye, stare at a dot, and a nearby X vanishes when its image lands on the blind spot.

text: {{c1::Closure::Gestalt Principle}} states that objects grouped together are seen as a whole and the mind fills in missing information.
extra: Your mind fills in this triangle even though it is not actually there.
example: The WWF panda logo is seen as a whole panda even though parts of its outline are missing.

text: Tonotopy is the spatial mapping of {{c1::sound frequencies}} that are processed by the brain
example: High-pitched sounds vibrate the basilar membrane near the cochlea's base, low pitches near its apex.

text: Somatosensation of pressure is called {{c1::mechanoception}}
example: Feeling a blood-pressure cuff squeeze tighter around your arm.

text: {{c1::Pheromones}} are chemical signals released by a species to trigger an {{c2::innate response::type of response}} in another member of the species
extra: often linked to mating, fighting, and communication
example: Female silkworm moths release the pheromone bombykol, which attracts males from kilometres away.

text: Umami is the ability to taste {{c1::glutamate}}
example: MSG (monosodium glutamate) gives instant ramen its savory umami taste.

text: {{c1::Kinaesthesia}} is our awareness of the movement of the body.
example: Knowing your arms are swinging upward during jumping jacks, even with your eyes closed.

text: {{c1::Sensory ganglia}} are enlargements along peripheral nerves that transmit signals to the CNS
example: Dorsal root ganglia hold the cell bodies of neurons carrying touch from the skin to the spinal cord.

text: {{c1::Cones::photoreceptor}} detect {{c2::color}} and discern {{c2::high}} levels of detail
example: Telling a ripe red strawberry from an unripe green one in daylight relies on cones.

text: There are {{c1::many more::more or less}} rods than cones
example: The human retina has about 120 million rods but only about 6 million cones.

text: {{c1::Neuropathic pain::... pain}} is pain caused by damage or disease affecting the somatosensory nervous system
example: Shingles can leave burning pain along a dermatome for months after the rash heals (postherpetic neuralgia).

text: {{c1::Bottom up processing::type of processing}} begins with the {{c2::stimulus}} which influences our perception.
example: Facing an unfamiliar abstract painting, you build up its shape from its lines and colors alone.

text: {{c1::Audition}} is our sense of sound
example: Recognizing a friend's voice calling your name across a crowded room.

text: {{c1::Scotopic vision::type of vision}} occurs at levels of very low light
example: Seeing the Milky Way in shades of grey on a moonless night relies on scotopic vision.

text: Hair cells at the apex of the cochlea are activated by {{c1::low}} frequency sounds
example: A bass drum's deep thump vibrates hair cells near the cochlear apex.

text: {{c1::Signal Detection Theory}} looks at how humans make decisions under conditions of {{c2::uncertainty}}.
extra: This is used to discern between important and unimportant stimuli
example: A radiologist deciding whether a faint shadow on a mammogram is a tumor or just noise.

text: When it is dark, rod cells are turned {{c1::on::off or on}}. This {{c2::inactivates::activates or inactivates}} on center bipolar cells and {{c2::activates::activates or inactivates}} off center bipolar cells.
example: A dark shadow on part of the retina keeps those rods on, exciting the off-center bipolar cells there.

text: The magnocellular pathway relies on {{c1::rods::photoreceptor}}
example: Spotting a deer darting across a dark road at night relies on rod-fed magnocellular motion detection.

text: {{c1::The ciliary body}} contains the ciliary muscle and ciliary processes and anchors the suspensory ligaments
example: Shifting focus from a distant tree to your phone uses the ciliary body's muscle.

text: The area in the nostril responsible for olfaction is the {{c1::olfactory epithelium}} which contains {{c1::olfactory sensory neurons}}
example: Sniffing hard draws more air up over the olfactory epithelium at the top of the nasal cavity.

text: {{c1::The pinna::Structure}} is the outer part of the ear
example: An earring hangs from the earlobe, the soft lower part of the pinna.

text: {{c1::The blind spot}} is where the optic nerve connects to the eyeball
example: An ophthalmoscope shows the optic disc as a pale circle where the optic nerve leaves the eye.

text: {{c1::The olfactory bulb}} is {{c2::an extension of the brain that receives axons of olfactory sensory neurons projecting up through the cribriform plate from the olfactory epithelium}}
example: Loss of smell often precedes tremor by years in Parkinson's disease, as early pathology hits the olfactory bulb.

text: {{c1::Photopic vision::type of vision}} occurs at high light levels
example: Reading a book outdoors at noon relies on photopic, cone-driven vision.

text: {{c1::d'}} is the symbol for strength of a signal
extra:
hit > miss (when signal is strong)
miss > hit (when signal is weak)
example: A loud alarm in a quiet room has a high d', while a faint beep in a noisy factory has a low d'.

text: {{c1::Interposition}} is a monocular cue where objects are perceived as being closer when they are in front of something
example: A tree that blocks part of a house looks closer than the house.

text: {{c1::Feature detection}} is breaking down an object into its component features
extra: this helps you make sense of what you are looking at
example: Hubel and Wiesel found cat visual cortex neurons that fire only to lines at a specific angle.

text: {{c2::The otolithic organs}} include the {{c1::utricle}} and {{c1::saccule}}
extra: The utricle and saccule sit in the vestibule of the inner ear and detect linear acceleration and head tilt. Calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths) shift with gravity and bend the hair cells' stereocilia. Rotation is sensed by the semicircular canals instead.Source: Blausen.com staff (2014), , CC BY 3.0
example: An elevator starting upward shifts the saccule's otoliths, signaling vertical acceleration.

text: Dermatome: {{c1::Skin with sensory nerve fibers from a single posterior spinal root ganglion}}
example: The C6 dermatome covers the thumb, so a pinched C6 nerve root causes thumb numbness.

text:
{{c1::Rods::Rods or Cones}} are found in the periphery of the eye
{{c1::Cones::Rods or Cones}} are concentrated in the fovea
example: A faint star is easier to see if you look slightly to its side, letting peripheral rods catch it.

text: The iris is a {{c1::muscle}}
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: The iris holds two smooth muscles: the sphincter pupillae constricts the pupil and the dilator pupillae widens it.

text: Active touch {{c1::uses haptic perception to actively inspect an object}}
extra: Example: picking something up to feel it
example: Reading Braille by sliding your fingertips across the raised dots.

text: {{c1::Anterior chamber}} is a space filled with {{c2::aqueous humour}} in the front of the eye
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: In glaucoma, aqueous humour drains poorly from the anterior chamber, so eye pressure rises.

text: The {{c1::just noticeable difference}} is the threshold at which you're able to {{c2::notice a change in sensation}}
example: Adding one sugar cube to plain tea is noticed, but adding one grain of sugar is not.

text: Light from the right side of the visual field hits {{c1::right nasal retina::retina region}} and the {{c1::left temporal retina::retina region}}
example: A ball tossed from your right lands on the outer (temporal) half of your left eye's retina.

text:
Method of adjustment (method of average error): {{c1::Participants control the stimulus and alter it until it is barely noticeable}}
Then: {{c1::Compare the variable stimuli and the standard stimuli to measure sensitivity}}
example: A subject turns a dial until a comparison tone sounds as loud as a 60 dB standard tone.

text: Light from the left side of the visual field hits the {{c1::left nasal retina::retina region}} and {{c1::right temporal retina::retina region}}
example: A car approaching from your left lands on the inner (nasal) half of your left eye's retina.

text: Light is initially bent at the {{c1::cornea}}
example: LASIK corrects nearsightedness by laser-flattening the cornea so it bends light less.

text: The magnocellular pathway has good {{c1::temporal}} resolution and poor {{c1::spatial}} resolution
example: Magno lets you notice a flicker at the edge of vision without being able to read the text there.

text: {{c1::Gestalt Principles::concept}} try to explain how we {{c2::perceive things the way we do}}
example: Four Pac-Man shapes at the corners make you see a white square that isn't drawn (Kanizsa square).

text: {{c1::Rods::photoreceptor}} detect {{c2::light}} and discern {{c2::low}} levels of detail
example: In a dark bedroom you see the outline of furniture but not its colours, thanks to rods.

text: The two main types of physical pain are {{c1::nociceptive pain::... pain}} and {{c1::neuropathic pain::... pain}}
example: A stubbed toe causes nociceptive pain; burning feet from diabetic nerve damage are neuropathic pain.

text: {{c1::Proprioception}} is the sense of the {{c2::position of the body in space}}
extra: AKA: the sense of where your body parts are in space (balance is the vestibular sense)
example: With your eyes closed you can still touch your nose with a fingertip, as in a field sobriety test.

text: When light hits a rod, {{c1::on center}} bipolar cells are active and {{c1::off center}} bipolar cells are inactive
example: A bright spot of light in a dark room excites on-center bipolar cells for that patch of retina.

text: {{c1::False Alarm}} is when the subject perceived a signal when there was none present
example: You reach for your phone after "feeling" it buzz, but no call or text came in.

text: {{c1::Mesopic vision::type of vision}} occurs at dawn or dusk and involves both rods and cones
example: Driving at dusk, when colours look washed out but shapes are still clear.

text: {{c1::The labeled-line theory::Theory}} states that each sensory receptor binds to a specific stimulus and is directly linked to the brain
example: Pressing gently on a closed eyelid makes you 'see' flashes of light (phosphenes).

text: {{c1::A-beta fibers::Type of nerve fiber}} are fast, thick, and covered in myelin
extra:
Memory hook: alphabetical = speed order (A-beta > A-delta > C)
• A-Beta = Big Brush: thickest, most myelin, touch
• A-Delta = Dagger: thin, light myelin, fast sharp pain
• C = Coatless, Crawling: unmyelinated, slow dull ache
Rubbing a stubbed toe: Big Brush closes the gate on Dagger & Crawling (gate control)
example: The light brush of a feather across your arm is carried by A-beta fibres.

text: The {{c1::threshold of conscious perception}} is the minimum stimulus energy that will create a signal large enough in size and long enough in duration to be brought into awareness
example: A candle flame is barely detectable 30 miles away on a clear, dark night.

text: The {{c1::TRPV1}} receptor allows us to sense {{c2::pain}} and {{c2::temperature}}
example: Capsaicin in chili peppers activates TRPV1, so spicy food feels burning hot.

text: Top-down processing uses {{c1::background knowledge}}, which influences perception. It is also driven by {{c1::theory}} rather than data.
example: You read the same ambiguous symbol as H in "THE" and as A in "CAT".

text: {{c1::Place theory::Theory}} states that our perception of sound depends on where each component frequency produces vibrations along the basilar membrane
extra:
Larger wavelength travels further into cochlea
Smaller wavelength does not travel far into cochlea
example: A 10 kHz tone vibrates the basilar membrane near the base, while a 200 Hz tone vibrates it near the apex.

text: {{c1::Sweet::Taste}}, {{c1::Umami::Taste}}, and {{c1::Bitter::Taste}} cells rely on {{c2::G-Protein Coupled Receptors}}
example: Aspartame tastes sweet by binding the T1R2/T1R3 GPCR, the same receptor that sucrose activates.

text: In response to pain/temperature inducing molecules being released, the TRPV1 receptor will {{c1::change conformation}} and {{c1::eventually lead to an AP signal}}
example: Heat above about 43 °C opens TRPV1, letting Na<sup>+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup> in and triggering an action potential.

text:
Visual cues include:
  • {{c1::depth}}
  • {{c1::form}}
  • {{c1::motion}}
  • {{c1::constancy}}
example: A door looks rectangular even when it swings open and casts a trapezoid on the retina (constancy).

text: The stapes is attached to the {{c1::oval window}}
example: The stapes footplate rocks in the oval window like a piston, pushing on the cochlear fluid.

text: The {{c1::opponent-process theory::... theory}} states that the cone photoreceptors are linked together to form three opposing color pairs: blue/yellow, red/green, and black/white
example: After staring at a red square, you see a green afterimage on a white wall.

text: Sound waves from the pinna get funneled into the {{c1::auditory canal}} AKA {{c1::external auditory meatus}}
example: Earwax builds up in the external auditory meatus and can muffle hearing if it blocks it.

text: {{c1::The ciliary body}} secretes aqueous humor
extra: Note the ciliary muscle and suspensory ligaments.
example: Timolol eye drops treat glaucoma by reducing aqueous humor output from the ciliary body.

text: {{c1::Fast-adapting neuron::type of neuron}} fires {{c2::as soon as a stimulus starts, then stops firing, then starts again when stimulus stops}}
example: Pacinian corpuscles fire when you put on a shirt and when you take it off, but not while wearing it.

text: To deal with constant stimulus, the body will {{c1::down::Up/Down}} regulate sensory receptors
example: After a few minutes in a bakery, the smell of bread fades as olfactory receptors respond less.

text: Hair cells at the base of the cochlea are activated by {{c1::high}} frequency sounds
example: Age-related hearing loss strikes base hair cells first, so high-pitched sounds like birdsong fade first.

text: The iris' main function is to {{c1::contract and dilate to change the size of the pupil}}
example: Shining a penlight into one eye makes the iris contract and the pupil shrink within a second.

text: {{c1::Steric theory of olfaction}} AKA {{c1::shape theory}} states that odors fit into receptors like a lock-and-key
example: Amoore noted that chemically different molecules with a similar compact, round shape all smell like camphor.

text:
The method of limits has 2 types: {{c1::ascending & descending}}
Procedure: {{c1::Start too ↓ and work your way ↑ & vice versa}}
extra: Example: for a minimum sound threshold, start too quiet and gradually get louder until the participant hears it

text: {{c1::Physiological zero}} is a temperature that is felt by the skin as neither warm nor cold
extra: Under ordinary conditions usually falls at about 85° to 90°F
example: After one hand soaks in hot water and one in cold, the same lukewarm bowl feels cold to one and warm to the other.

text: The eardrum's vibrations cause {{c1::the ossicles}} to vibrate
example: When fluid fills the middle ear in an ear infection, the ossicles vibrate poorly and hearing is muffled.

text: Unlike proprioception, kinaesthesia is {{c1::behavioral/conscious}}
extra: Example: "If I move like this, I will hit the baseball."

text: Interaural time difference: {{c1::Difference in the time it takes sound to reach the L vs. R ear}}
example: A sound directly to your right reaches the right ear about 0.6 ms before the left ear.

text: {{c1::Form}} is the shape and boundaries of an object
example: Recognizing a stop sign by its octagon outline before you can read the word STOP.

text: {{c1::Photoreceptors::cell type}} convert light to neural impulses
example: A rod can produce a measurable electrical response to a single absorbed photon.

text: {{c1::Conjunctiva}} is the {{c2::thin layer of cells that lines the inside of your eyelids.}}
example: Conjunctivitis (pink eye) inflames this layer, making the inner eyelids red, itchy and swollen.

text: {{c1::Anosmia}} is the inability to perceive odor
example: Many COVID-19 patients suddenly could not smell their coffee or perfume.

text: {{c1::Similarity::Gestalt Principle}} states that items similar to one another are grouped together by the brain
extra: Our brain organizes these as columns and not rows
example: Fans wearing the same team's jersey in a mixed stadium crowd are seen as one group.

text: {{c2::The magnocellular pathway::Feature detection pathway}} is good at determining {{c1::motion}} and {{c1::depth}}
extra:
Memory hook: Magno = Motion; Parvo = Particulars (detail) & Paint (color)
Picture Magneto (magnocellular) moving things.
example: Catching a fly ball relies on the magnocellular pathway tracking its motion and distance.

text: {{c1::The pupil}} is the opening in the middle of the iris.
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: In a red-eye photo, the flash reflects back out through the pupil, the iris's central opening.

text: {{c1::Rods::Rods or Cones}} are 1000x more sensitive to light than {{c1::cones::rods or cones}}
example: On a dim, starlit night you can see shapes but not colors, because only your rods respond.

text: The semicircular canals contribute to {{c1::dizziness}} and {{c1::vertigo}}
extra: Endolymph doesn't stop moving at the same time we do, so it continues to move and our brain thinks we are still moving even if we are stopped
example: After spinning on an office chair and stopping, the room seems to keep spinning.

text: The three types of papillae that contain taste buds are {{c1::fungiform}}, {{c1::foliate}}, and {{c1::circumvallate}}
extra: Memory hook: "Fun Food Counts", front to back: a mushroom (fungi-form), a leaf (foli-ate, like foliage), and a walled circle (circum-vallate, "wall around"). Filiform is just a thread (filament), so no taste buds.
example: Sugar on the tip of the tongue is tasted by taste buds in fungiform papillae.

text: Somatosensation of position is called {{c1::proprioception}}
example: Typing without looking at your fingers relies on sensing where they are.

text: Somatosensation of temperature is called {{c1::thermoception}}
example: Menthol feels cold because it activates TRPM8, the skin's cold receptor.

text: {{c1::The macula}} is the special part of the retina rich in {{c2::cones}}
extra: The macula still has rods, just many more cones than the rest of the retina.Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: Macular degeneration blurs central vision, making faces and print hard to see while side vision stays.

text: {{c1::Parallel processing}} is focusing on all information (color, form, motion) at the same time
example: Watching a red car speed past, you see its colour, shape and motion all at once.

text: The organ of Corti includes the {{c1::basilar}} membrane and the {{c1::tectorial}} membrane
example: The tallest stereocilia of outer hair cells are embedded in the tectorial membrane, so basilar movement bends them.

text: {{c1::The ciliary muscle}} pulls on suspensory ligaments to change the shape of the lens
example: To read a phone up close, the ciliary muscle contracts, the ligaments slacken and the lens rounds.

text: {{c2::Sour::Taste}} and {{c2::Salty::Taste}} rely on {{c1::ion channels}}
example: Na<sup>+</sup> from table salt flows directly through ENaC channels into salty-taste cells.

text: The purpose of the round window is to {{c1::bulge out as fluid flows through the cochlea}}
example: Like squeezing one end of a water balloon, pressing in at the oval window makes the round window bulge out.

text: {{c1::Filiform papillae}} are located at the center of the tongue and do not contain taste buds
example: The rough, sandpaper feel of a cat's tongue comes from hooked filiform papillae.

text: {{c1::Retinal disparity}} provides a binocular cue that facilitates depth perception
extra: The two eyes have slightly different views because of the space between them; the brain uses this difference to perceive depth
example: Hold a finger close and close each eye in turn: the finger seems to jump sideways.

text: {{c1::Olfaction}} is your sense of smell
example: Smelling smoke and realizing the toast is burning.

text: {{c1::Gate control theory::Theory}} states that non-painful inputs close the 'gates' to painful inputs, preventing pain sensation
extra:
Memory hook: alphabetical = speed order (A-beta > A-delta > C)
• A-Beta = Big Brush: thickest, most myelin, touch
• A-Delta = Dagger: thin, light myelin, fast sharp pain
• C = Coatless, Crawling: unmyelinated, slow dull ache
Rubbing a stubbed toe: Big Brush closes the gate on Dagger & Crawling (gate control)
example: Rubbing your elbow after bumping it eases the pain by sending touch signals that close the gate.

text: {{c1::Hearing adaptation}} involves {{c2::contracting the middle ear muscles (stapedius, tensor tympani) to dampen ossicle vibrations and protect the inner ear}}
example: Bell's palsy can paralyze the stapedius, so ordinary sounds seem painfully loud (hyperacusis).

text: McGurk effect: {{c1::Mouth movements influencing our hearing}}
example: Hearing "ba" while watching lips say "ga" makes most people hear "da".

text: It is impossible for humans to see certain color combinations such as reddish-green or yellowish-blue. This is explained by the {{c1::opponent-process theory::... theory}} of color vision
example: Orange can look reddish-yellow and teal bluish-green, but no color ever looks reddish-green.

text: {{c1::Relative size}} is a monocular cue where closer objects are perceived as being bigger
example: In a photo of two identical cars, the one that looks smaller seems farther away.

text: {{c1::Cornea}} is a {{c2::transparent thick sheet of fibrous tissue that primarily bends light in the eye}}
example: The cornea supplies about two-thirds of the eye's focusing power; the lens supplies the rest.

text: {{c1::The somatosensory homunculus}} is a {{c2::map of your body in your brain}}
extra: It is a topological map of your entire body in the sensory cortex
example: On the homunculus the hands and lips are huge, while the back and trunk are tiny.

text: {{c1::The labelled lines model}} states that each taste bud has 5 axons for each type of taste and sends its signals to the {{c2::gustatory cortex}}
example: A sweet-taste cell signals 'sweet' to the gustatory cortex whether triggered by sugar or by aspartame.

text: The {{c1::two-point threshold}} is the minimum distance necessary between two points of stimulation on the skin such that the points will be felt as two distinct stimuli
example: Two pencil tips 5 mm apart feel like two points on a fingertip but like one point on your back.

text: {{c2::Fungiform papillae::Papillae}} are located at the {{c1::front/anterior}} of the tongue
extra: Memory hook: mushrooms (fungi) pop up in the front yard; the big walled circles (circumvallate) guard the back gate.
example: Blue food dye stains the tongue's surface but leaves fungiform papillae as pink dots on the front.

text: {{c1::Non-adapting}} neurons fire at a constant rate
example: A splinter keeps hurting as long as it stays in, since nociceptors barely adapt.

text: {{c1::Sensation}} requires a {{c2::physical stimulus}} to be converted into a {{c3::neural impulse}}
example: Heat from a stove activates skin thermoreceptors, which fire impulses toward the brain.

text: {{c1::Basilar tuning}} enables the cochlea to differentiate between sounds of varying frequencies
example: The basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base (high pitch) and wide and floppy at the apex (low pitch).

text:
{{c1::The conservative strategy}} is to always say {{c2::no unless 100% sure signal is present.}}
This strategy might result in some {{c3::misses}} but you will get all {{c3::correct rejections}}
example: A juror who votes guilty only with overwhelming evidence lets some guilty people go free (misses).

text: The External/Outer ear is {{c1::from the pinna to the tympanic membrane}}
example: Swimmer's ear (otitis externa) is an infection of the outer ear canal.

text: The fusiform gyrus is part of the {{c1::visual system::System}} and plays a role in high-level {{c1::visual processing & recognition}}
example: The fusiform face area lights up on fMRI when people look at faces rather than houses.

text:
{{c1::The parvocellular pathway::Feature detection pathway}} is good at:
  • {{c2::spatial resolution}}
  • {{c2::determining form}}
  • {{c2::high}} levels of detail
  • {{c2::color}}
extra:
Memory hook: Magno = Motion; Parvo = Particulars (detail) & Paint (color)
mnemonic: Pink Pyramid (form/shape) = Parvocellular Pathway
example: Reading the fine print on a red medicine label relies on the parvocellular pathway.

text: Haptic perception: {{c1::The exploration of objects through touch}}
example: Finding your keys in a dark bag by feeling for their shape and jagged edges.

text: {{c1::Processing}} is the neural transformation of multiple neural signals into a {{c2::perception}}
example: Merging the slightly different images from your two eyes into one 3D view of an approaching ball.

text: {{c1::Olfactory glomeruli}} send sensory signals to {{c2::mitral/tufted cells}}
example: Many olfactory axons converge in one glomerulus onto a few mitral cells, which relay the scent onward.

text: {{c1::Proximity::Gestalt Principle}} states that objects that are close together are grouped together.
example: Six dots spaced as three close pairs are seen as three pairs, not six separate dots.

text: {{c1::Spindles}} located in the muscles send signals to the brain in response to stretching. This allows for {{c2::proprioception}}.
example: Touching your nose with your eyes closed relies on muscle spindles reporting your arm's position.

text: {{c1::Transmission}} is the electrical activation of one neuron by another neuron
example: A retinal bipolar cell releasing glutamate onto a ganglion cell and making it fire.

text: {{c1::The trichromatic theory::Theory}} of color vision states that there are three types of cones that make up color vision
example: Red-green colour blindness arises when the red or green cone type is missing or faulty.

text: Method of constant stimuli: {{c1::A fixed set of stimulus intensities is presented repeatedly in random order to prevent prediction::Explain}}
extra: Example: beeps at several preset volumes presented in random order; threshold = volume detected 50% of the time

text: {{c1::Sensory adaptation}} states that our senses are adaptable and that they can change their sensitivity over time
example: After a few minutes in a bakery you no longer notice the smell of bread.

text:
Auditory pathway:
{{c1::Cochlea}} → {{c1::vestibulocochlear nerve}} → {{c1::medial geniculate nucleus}} → {{c1::auditory cortex}}
example: A tumor of the vestibulocochlear nerve (acoustic neuroma) causes one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus.

text:
The steps to the phototransduction cascade include:
  1. {{c1::light hits cis-retinal and converts it to trans-retinal}}
  2. {{c1::rhodopsin changes shape}}
  3. {{c1::transducin gets released from rhodopsin}}
  4. {{c1::transducin binds to a phosphodiesterase}}
  5. {{c1::phosphodiesterase converts cGMP to GMP}}
  6. {{c1::Na+ channels close as a result of low cGMP}}
  7. {{c1::rod cell becomes hyperpolarized and turned off}}
example: One light-activated rhodopsin activates hundreds of transducin molecules, amplifying a single photon.

text: {{c1::The organ of Corti}} is the hearing receptor organ: it sits on the basilar membrane and contains the hair cells
example: Years of loud music damage the organ of Corti's outer hair cells, causing noise-induced hearing loss.

text: The otolithic organs contain {{c1::calcium carbonate crystals::structure}}, which attach to {{c1::hair cells::cell type}} to trigger action potentials to help determine which way is up/down
extra:
Gravity is essential to this as well
Buoyancy can also have an effect, as this takes place in a viscous gel
example: In BPPV, loose otoliths drift into a semicircular canal, so rolling over in bed triggers vertigo.

text: The lens can change shape with the assistance of {{c1::suspensory ligaments}}
example: Viewing a distant mountain, taut suspensory ligaments pull the lens thin and flat.

text: {{c1::The primary auditory cortex::Brain Region}} receives all information from the cochlea and it is part of the {{c1::temporal}} lobe
example: Hearing your phone ring activates Heschl's gyrus in the superior temporal lobe.

text: Phantom pain: {{c1::Perception of pain in a removed area of the body}}
example: After a leg amputation, a patient feels cramping pain in the missing foot.

text: The optic nerves from each eyeball cross over at the {{c1::optic chiasm}}
example: A pituitary tumor pressing on the optic chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia, loss of both outer visual fields.

text: {{c1::The iris}} gives the eye color and is the muscle used to modulate the size of the pupil
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: Brown eyes have an iris rich in melanin, while blue eyes have an iris with little melanin.

text: To hear a sound, you need {{c1::a pressurized sound wave}} and {{c1::hair cells}}
example: Years of loud concerts can destroy hair cells, so sound waves still arrive but go unheard.

text: On the cilia of olfactory sensory neurons (whose axons project to the olfactory bulb) are {{c1::olfactory chemoreceptors}}
example: Limonene binds chemoreceptors on these cilia, and you perceive it as the smell of oranges.

text: The posterior chamber is filled with {{c1::aqueous humor}}
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: Fluid secreted by the ciliary processes pools here, then flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber.

text: The {{c1::vitreous chamber::eye structure}} is the largest of the three chambers and is located behind the lens and in front of the optic nerve
example: Floaters are bits of debris drifting through the vitreous gel that fills this chamber.

text: {{c1::A-delta fibres::Type of nerve fibre}} are small in diameter with less myelin
extra:
Memory hook: alphabetical = speed order (A-beta > A-delta > C)
• A-Beta = Big Brush: thickest, most myelin, touch
• A-Delta = Dagger: thin, light myelin, fast sharp pain
• C = Coatless, Crawling: unmyelinated, slow dull ache
Rubbing a stubbed toe: Big Brush closes the gate on Dagger & Crawling (gate control)
example: The instant sharp sting of a pinprick travels on A-delta fibres.

text: Stereocilia are connected by {{c1::tip links}}
example: Tip links act like springs that pull ion channels open when stereocilia bend toward the tallest one.

text:
{{c1::The liberal strategy::strategy}} is to always {{c2::say Yes}}.
This strategy might result in some {{c3::false alarms}} but you will get all {{c3::hits}}
example: An airport screener who flags every bag catches every weapon but stops many harmless bags (false alarms).

text:
Psychophysics: the psychological study of the relationship between {{c1::physical stimuli & mental response}}
Example: {{c1::A series of different pitches played for a subject to test which they can detect::Example}}
extra:
Making connections between matter and mind
Humans can detect pitches ranging from 20 to 20,000 Hz
example: Measuring the dimmest light a subject can detect in a completely dark room.

text: {{c1::Hit}} is when a subject responded affirmative when a signal was present
example: A radiologist reports a tumor on a scan, and the biopsy confirms it.

text: All of the points on the {{c1::cone of confusion}} have the same interaural level difference and interaural time difference
example: A clap directly in front of you and one directly behind sound alike, since both reach each ear at the same time.

text: {{c1::Law of Common Fate::Gestalt Principle}} states that humans perceive visual elements that move in the same speed and/or direction as parts of a single stimulus
example: A flock of birds flying the same way at the same speed is seen as one moving group.

text: Visual cues that involve only one eyeball are called {{c1::monocular cues}}
example: Painters create depth on a flat canvas using only monocular cues, like drawing distant trees smaller.

text: Spatial discrimination: {{c1::The ability to perceive 2 individual presses on your skin}}
example: A neurologist touches caliper tips to a fingertip and asks the patient "one point or two?"

text: Horizontal and amacrine cells integrate signals from many nearby retinal cells before they reach the ganglion cells and perform {{c1::edge-sharpening}}
example: Mach bands: a gray stripe looks lighter right where it borders a darker stripe.

text: {{c1::Perception}} is the conscious sensory experience of neural processing
example: Realizing that the warm smell drifting from the kitchen is fresh coffee.

text: The pupil's main function is to {{c1::contract and dilate to modulate the amount of light able to enter the eyeball}}
extra: Source: Rhcastilhos & Jmarchn, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
example: Walking from a sunny street into a dark cinema, your pupils dilate to let in more light.

text:
The absolute threshold of sensation can be influenced by the following:
  • {{c1::Expectations}}
  • {{c1::Experience}}
  • {{c1::Motivation}}
  • {{c1::Alertness}}
example: A mother expecting her baby to cry hears a faint whimper that others in the room miss.

text:
Cochlear implant sound pathway:
{{c1::Sound}} → {{c1::microphone}} → {{c1::transmitter (outside the skull)}} → {{c1::receiver (inside skull)}} → {{c1::stimulator}} → {{c1::cochlea}} → {{c1::electrical impulse}}
example: An implant lets a child with dead cochlear hair cells hear by stimulating the auditory nerve directly.

text: {{c1::Sensory adaptation}} is the change over time of receptor to a constant stimulus
example: You stop feeling your watch on your wrist a few minutes after putting it on.

text: {{c1::Motion parallax}} is a monocular cue that gives a sense of depth through motion: things farther away move {{c2::slower}} and things closer to you move {{c2::faster}}
example: From a moving car, roadside fence posts whip past while distant mountains barely move.

text: Group-produced reduction of individual effort is the idea that {{c1::groups that experience social loafing are less productive and perform poorly}}
extra:
Example: half the group stops trying, so the other half stops trying too
Reduced by making the task harder or ranking performance individually
example: In Latané's study, each person clapped and shouted less loudly as group size grew.

text: {{c1::Socialization}} is {{c2::a life-long process where we learn how to interact with others through learning behavioral norms}}
extra: everything we perceive as NORMAL is learned through socialization
example: A toddler learning to say 'please' and 'thank you' by copying their parents.

text: Solomon Asch's experiment showed that individuals were {{c1::highly likely to conform to social norms, even when the correct answer was painfully obvious, when everyone else chose the wrong answer}}
example: In Asch's line study, about 75% of participants went along with the wrong answer at least once.

text: Many participants in Milgram's experiment felt comfort from {{c1::passing responsibility of actions to others}}
extra: People didn't feel as bad when the experimenter said he would take responsibility for whatever happened

text: {{c1::Conformity}} is {{c2::a tendency for people to bring behaviors in line with group norms}}
example: Turning to face the back of an elevator because everyone else in it is facing that way.

text: Norms are reinforced by {{c1::sanctions}}
example: Being shushed by other moviegoers for talking loudly during a film.

text: {{c1::Deindividuation}} is {{c2::when people behave badly in crowds because the crowd conceals their identity}}
extra:
The presence of a large group decreases guilt and inhibition.
Example: Black Friday shoppers trampling others and stealing because the crowd hides who they are.
Example: people posting things online that they would not say in person because their identity is concealed.
example: In Diener's Halloween study, costumed, anonymous children in groups took extra candy more often.

text: {{c1::Norms}} are {{c2::standards for what behaviors are acceptable/unacceptable and are typically set by groups of individuals}}
example: Waiting in line at a coffee shop instead of cutting to the front.

text: {{c2::Social loafing}} is {{c1::a tendency to put forth less effort in group tasks when individual contributions aren't evaluated}}
extra: Example: in group projects, some members put in less effort because only the group grade matters
example: In Ringelmann's rope-pulling study, each person pulled less hard as the group grew larger.

text: Reciprocity: {{c1::We should repay what others have provided us}}
example: After a free sample at the grocery store, shoppers feel obliged to buy the product.

text: Mass hysteria is {{c1::when a large number of people experience unmanageable delusions and anxiety at the same time}}
extra:
The reaction spreads very quickly and can reach more people through rumors and fears.
Example: news of a coming hurricane induces fear in large numbers of people, who rush to stock up and drive erratically.
example: The 1938 'War of the Worlds' radio broadcast reportedly panicked listeners who believed Martians had landed.

text: {{c1::Diffusion of responsibility}} explains {{c2::the bystander effect}}: individuals feel {{c2::less personal responsibility to take action in larger groups}}
extra:
Small groups do not diffuse responsibility, so you are more likely to intervene.
Example: if you are the only one present who knows CPR, you step in; in a crowd of 200 around a collapsed person, you assume someone else will help.

text: Riots are characterized by {{c1::large number of people engaging in dangerous behavior, such as vandalism/violence/etc, usually as a result of a perceived issue like working conditions, race conflicts, etc}}
extra: Cause of the riot may be legitimate, but the group acts out in ways that are illegal/damaging to society
example: The 1992 Los Angeles riots after the acquittal of police officers who beat Rodney King.

text: Informal sanction = {{c1::unofficially recognized sanction that does not result in specific punishment}}
extra: Examples: compliments from peers, frowns, insults, parents yelling at you.

text: {{c2::Internalization}} is when {{c1::an idea/belief/behavior has been integrated into our own values}}.
extra: Ex: start going to gym to comply with friends, but then might internalize that exercise is good for you and continue the behavior

text: Laws are {{c1::norms based on right/wrong with formal consequences for deviation that may/may not cause outrage}}
extra: Example: streaking on the field at a high school football game gets you arrested, but it may not cause severe outrage; some people are disgusted while others laugh and cheer.
example: Jaywalking is illegal and can bring a fine, yet few people are outraged by it.

text: {{c1::Agents of socialization}} are {{c2::what's used to transmit culture, values, and beliefs.}}
example: Saturday-morning TV ads teaching kids which toys are 'for girls' and which are 'for boys'.

text: {{c2::Compliance}} is when {{c1::individuals perform behaviors to get a reward or avoid punishment typically without questioning why}}
extra:
ex: paying taxes (I will get punished if I don’t pay my taxes).
TSA screenings (nobody likes them, but you won’t be allowed on the plane if you don’t)

text: {{c1::Compliance}} is when someone changes their behavior based on the requests of others
example: Signing a petition because a stranger outside the grocery store asks you to.

text: The bystander effect is stronger in {{c1::large::large or small}} groups
extra: In a large group, each person assumes that with so many people present, someone else will surely take action.
example: In Darley and Latané's seizure study, 85% helped when alone but only 31% when they thought 4 others heard.

text:
Milgram's experiment led to the conclusion that
  • {{c1::regular people will comply with authority figures even if it goes against their moral values}}
  • {{c1::that it is easy to think others are evil and atrocious and that we would never do anything horrible unless misguided}}
example: Most volunteers, ordinary men answering a New Haven newspaper ad, went all the way to 450 V.

text:
Ways to avoid groupthink include:
  • {{c1::bringing in outside opinions}}
  • {{c1::not having leader disclose opinions}}
example: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, Kennedy sometimes left meetings so advisers could debate freely.

text: {{c1::The Theory of Differential Association::Theory}} states that {{c2::deviance is a learned behavior that results from continuous exposure to others who violate norms/laws}}
extra: Example: an athlete who believes cheating is wrong joins a team whose members see steroids, partying, and heckling as the way to succeed and show him how to use drugs. Over time he learns to accept these deviant behaviors.

text: {{c1::Identification}} is when {{c2::individuals act/dress in a certain way to be like someone they respect}}
extra: Ex: football player people admired and bought his jersey, but then he engaged in domestic violence and once it was made public the identification of this player by people dropped significantly.

text: Minority influence: {{c1::Smaller group persuades majority to join their side}}
extra: Example: "Hey, maybe we should legalize all drugs" (Portugal to the rest of the world)
example: In Moscovici's study, two confederates who kept calling blue slides 'green' swayed some of the majority.

text: {{c2::Social facilitation}} is the idea that {{c1::individuals perform differently when in the presence of others vs when they are alone}}
example: Triplett found that cyclists rode faster when racing others than when racing the clock alone.

text: Public conformity is {{c1::when you outwardly change beliefs but internally maintain your core beliefs}}
extra: Example: you agree with the group about the shock collar but still believe treats work better, and use treats when alone
example: In Asch's study, conformity dropped sharply when people wrote their answers privately.

text: Positive sanction = {{c1::a reward for conforming to norms}}
example: A child gets a gold star for sharing toys with classmates.

text: {{c2::Informational influence}} is {{c1::looking to a group for guidance when you don't know what to do and you assume the group is correct}}
example: At a formal dinner, watching which fork the others pick up before choosing yours.

text: Milgram's studies on obedience were heavily influenced by {{c1::the Holocaust}}
extra: Many Nazis said they were "just following orders"
example: Milgram began his studies in 1961, just months after Adolf Eichmann's trial opened in Jerusalem.

text: {{c1::Collective behavior}} is {{c2::the spontaneous, unstructured, and temporary behavior of a group of people in response to the same event/situation}}
example: Thousands of fans flooding the streets to celebrate a World Series win.

text: {{c1::Peer pressure}} is the social influence placed on individuals by others they consider equals
example: A teen tries vaping because classmates at a party are all doing it.

text: {{c2::The bystander effect}} is when individuals {{c1::feel less inclined to take action because of the presence of others in the group}}
example: Kitty Genovese's 1964 murder in New York, reportedly witnessed by 38 neighbours who did not help.

text: Norms vary depending on {{c1::context}}, {{c1::location}}, and {{c1::culture}}
extra:
Example: you yell when something good happens at a baseball game, but not in your office.
Example: people in the USA greet with handshakes, but in Europe a kiss on the cheek is more common.

text: A {{c1::mob}} is {{c2::a group of individuals who are emotional/violent but typically target specific individuals or categories of individuals}}
example: A lynch mob hunting down one specific person accused of a crime.

text: {{c2::Group polarization}} is {{c1::when group-decision making amplifies the original opinion of group members to the point where a stronger decision is adopted}}.
extra: Example: most of the group favors training dogs with treats; after discussion that preference becomes even stronger
example: Jurors who lean toward a large damages award agree on an even larger one after deliberating.

text: Private conformity is {{c1::changing behaviors and opinions to align with a group}}
extra: Example: you leave the group genuinely believing a shock collar is the best way to train a dog
example: After a year with vegetarian roommates, you come to truly believe eating meat is wrong.

text: Fads are {{c1::things that gain popularity quickly, lose popularity quickly, are short lived, and are typically entertaining}}
extra: Examples: the cinnamon challenge, the Harlem Shake.

text: Folkways are {{c1::the mildest type of norm}} and are {{c1::the rules/manners we are supposed to follow}}
extra:
Example: common courtesy to tell your friend their zipper is down.
Not following folkways brings no severe consequences or actual punishment.
example: Saying 'bless you' after someone sneezes.

text: The strongest type of conformity is {{c1::internalization}}
extra: because you actually integrate the idea/belief/behavior into your own set of values
example: Someone who quits smoking because she now truly values her health stays smoke-free even when no one is watching.

text: Informal norms are {{c1::understood norms that are less precise, without specific punishments}}
extra:
These dictate appropriate behavior without the need for written rules.
Deviating from them won't get you thrown in jail, but may lead to a bad reputation.
example: Not standing right next to the only other person in a nearly empty elevator.

text: {{c1::Sanctions}} are {{c2::rewards/punishments for behaviors in accord with or against norms}}
example: A $200 fine for littering, or a bonus for beating a sales target.

text: Negative sanction = {{c1::a punishment for violating norms}}
example: A teen is grounded for breaking curfew.

text: Social facilitation: individuals perform better on {{c1::well-rehearsed and easy}} tasks and worse on {{c1::unpracticed and difficult}} tasks in front of an audience
example: A pro pianist plays better before an audience, while a beginner fumbles a new piece on stage.

text: {{c1::Informational social influence}} is when we {{c2::conform because we feel others are more knowledgeable than us}}.
extra: Ex: when you move to a new place. You would ask people around you (who lived in this place for a longer period) of things to do /places to eat and go along with their suggestions.

text: The three types of collective behavior include {{c1::fads}}, {{c1::mass hysteria}}, and {{c1::riots}}
example: The late-1990s Tamagotchi craze, which faded within a few years, was a fad.

text: {{c1::Normative social influence}} is when we {{c2::do something to gain respect/support of peers outwardly, despite possibly internally believing something else}}
extra: Ex: friends are all obsessed with a certain singer. You tell the group you like the singer as well even if you absolutely hate him/her. You continue to say you like it (or even go to the singers concert)

text: Formal norms are {{c1::established written rules}} and are {{c1::typically strictly enforced}}
example: A school's written dress code banning hats in class, enforced with detention.

text:
