Collective behavior differs from group behavior because:
  • {{c1::collective behavior is time limited while groups last longer}}
  • {{c1::collectives can be open while groups can be exclusive}}
  • {{c1::collectives have loose norms while groups have strong/well-defined norms}}
example: A crowd around a street performer disperses in minutes, while a chess club meets weekly under set rules.

text:
The most important agents of socialization include:
  • {{c1::family}}
  • {{c1::school}}
  • {{c1::peers}}
  • {{c1::mass media}}
extra:
family: learn core beliefs, values, norms, etc
school: teaches life skills and academics, teaches social skills, how to obey authority, etc
peers: develop behaviors, contradict parents, etc
mass media: exposed to a TON of content, exposed to mature content, enforce gender roles and stereotypes
example: A kindergarten teacher teaching children to raise their hands and wait their turn.

text: Deviance does not have to be {{c1::negative}}
extra:
Behaving differently from societal norms is deviant, whether or not it is bad.
Example: most Americans eat meat, so vegans are deviant without being bad.
example: Rosa Parks refusing to give up her bus seat in 1955 was deviant yet admirable.

text: {{c2::Mass psychogenic illness}} AKA {{c2::epidemic hysteria}} is {{c1::mass hysteria that can be a result of psychology where large amounts of individuals believe they have the same illness despite lack of disease}}
extra: Example: after the anthrax attacks in the US there were over 2,000 false alarms; people who believed they had been exposed reported symptoms of anthrax infection.
example: The 1962 Tanganyika laughter epidemic spread among schoolgirls with no physical cause found.

text: The two types of deviance in labeling theory are {{c1::primary}} and {{c1::secondary}} deviance
example: A teen who shoplifts once shows primary deviance; one labelled 'thief' who then steals more shows secondary.

text: {{c1::Symbolic interactionism}} states that {{c2::society is a byproduct of everyday interactions of individuals}} and that {{c2::looking at everyday behaviors}} helps us better understand and define deviance
example: Studying how classmates' eye-rolls and jokes come to mark one student's behaviour as 'weird'.

text: Milgram's shock study was conducted to study {{c1::willingness of participants to obey an authority figure}}
example: Participants were told to give a 'learner' shocks of up to 450 V for wrong answers on a word-pair test.

text: {{c1::Social anomie}} is {{c2::a breakdown of social bonds between an individual and community}}.
example: Durkheim linked anomie to rising suicide rates during sudden economic upheaval.

text: Mores are {{c1::norms based on moral value/belief that usually elicit a strong reaction when violated but still no serious consequences}}
extra: Example: a friend takes off his shirt to show the team logo painted on his chest. You value modesty, so you strongly disapprove, but there are no serious consequences beyond your disapproval.
example: Mocking a stranger's disability draws strong moral disapproval but carries no legal penalty.

text: {{c2::Deviance}} is when {{c1::a norm is violated}}
example: Showing up to a formal job interview in pajamas.

text: {{c1::Labeling theory::Theory}} states that {{c2::a behavior is deviant if people have judged the behavior and labelled it as deviant}}
extra:
Deviance depends entirely on what is acceptable in society.
Example: steroid use in professional sports is labeled deviant because it is unfair, while older men using steroids to boost testosterone are not judged as harshly.
example: In Rosenhan's study, staff recorded a 'schizophrenic' pseudopatient's note-taking as 'writing behavior'.

text:
Positive conformity example: {{c1::following people running out of a building}}
Negative conformity example: {{c1::jumping off a bridge because your friends do}}
example: Teens binge drinking at a party because everyone else is, despite knowing the risks.

text: Formal sanction = {{c1::officially recognized and enforced sanction}}
extra: Example: going to jail for breaking the law.
example: A soldier awarded the Medal of Honor receives a formal positive sanction.

text:
{{c1::Secondary deviance}} is deviance that
  • {{c2::has more serious consequences}}
  • {{c2::has a severe negative reaction that produces a stigmatizing label that results in more deviant behavior}}
extra: Example: teammates label a steroid-using athlete deviant, exclude him from practice, and call him a terrible player. This leads him to use more (and more dangerous) steroids, and the deviant reputation stays with him for the rest of his career.
example: A teen arrested once is branded a 'delinquent' at school, then joins a gang and commits more crimes.

text:
Positive obedience example: {{c1::listening to a firefighter telling you not to enter a burning building}}
Negative obedience example: {{c1::ordinary people obeying the Nazis during WWII}}
example: Leaving the beach when a police officer orders everyone out before a hurricane hits.

text: Taboos are {{c1::behaviors completely forbidden/wrong to where deviation typically results in severe disgust and possible legal action}}

The Stanford prison experiment highlights:
  • {{c1::situational attribution}}
  • {{c1::deindividuation}}
  • {{c1::cognitive dissonance}}
  • {{c1::internalization}}
extra:
Situational attribution: situations can influence our behavior.
Deindividuation: guards saw prisoners as one group addressed by numbers, so mistreating them felt less personal.
Cognitive dissonance: guards justified their harsh behavior as if prisoners deserved it.
Internalization: participants internalized their roles, which shaped their attitudes, cognitions, and behaviors.
example: Zimbardo ended the planned two-week study after only six days as the guards grew abusive.

text:
{{c1::Primary}} deviance is deviance that
  • {{c2::has no big consequences with mild reaction from others}}
  • {{c2::the individual continues to behave the same way without feeling wrong}}
extra: Example: all athletes on a team use steroids, so one player's steroid use is not labeled deviant and goes unnoticed.
example: Underage drinking at a college party that no one notices or punishes.

text: {{c2::Groupthink}} is {{c1::when maintaining harmony among group members is more important than analyzing the problem at hand. Usually in insulated groups with respected leaders.}}
extra: Example: neighbors agree with the leader that a misbehaving dog should be put down rather than argue and cause conflict
example: The 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, where Kennedy's advisers kept their doubts quiet to preserve consensus.

text: {{c1::Obedience}} is following orders and obeying authority
example: In Milgram's study, 65% of participants gave the maximum 450-volt shock when told to continue.

text: {{c2::Normative influence}} is {{c1::when you conform to a group's behavior to be accepted/avoid social rejection, even if you privately disagree}}.
example: Laughing at a joke you don't find funny because all your friends are laughing.

text: {{c1::Social influence}} refers to the way in which individuals change their behavior to meet the demands of a social environment
extra: Social influence theory can also describe the effects of hypnosis
example: Lowering your voice as soon as you walk into a quiet library.

text: {{c2::Strain theory::Theory}} states that {{c1::if an individual is blocked from attaining a culturally accepted goal, they may become frustrated/strained and turn to deviance}}
extra:
Includes individuals who lack legitimate means to achieve success; the opportunity to succeed is not equal for everyone.
Example: an athlete at a school without coaching, equipment, or funding becomes frustrated and tries steroids to level the playing field.
example: A man shut out of good jobs who sells drugs to get rich fits Merton's 'innovation' response.

text:
Secure attachment: the child
  • {{c1::explored when mother was present}}
  • {{c1::cried when she was gone}}
  • {{c1::went to her when she returned}}
example: Leo stacks blocks with Mom nearby, wails when she walks out, then runs to hug her and goes back to playing

text: Normative organizations: {{c1::members come together through shared goals}}

"Look at how I am capable of helping you out because I'm rich as fuck" is an example of what form of altruism?
{{c1::Cost signalling}}
example: A wealthy guest loudly picks up the whole table's $800 dinner bill

text:
Game theory: {{c1::involves intention and reasoning about the behaviors of others::definition}}
Evolutionary game theory: {{c1::decisions without conscious intent::definition}}
example: Poker players bluff by reasoning about each other, but a cuckoo's egg-dumping strategy evolved without any intent

text: The social construction model of expressing emotion states that there is no biological circuitry for emotions since emotions are solely based on {{c1::experience and context}}
example: On Día de los Muertos, families greet the dead with festive joy, unlike the solemn mourning of other cultures.

text:
Authoritarian parenting is associated with {{c1::poorer}} child outcomes
Authoritative parenting is associated with {{c1::better}} child outcomes
example: Baumrind found children of authoritative parents were the most self-reliant and socially competent

text: People in prison or the military are in a {{c1::coercive}} organization
example: A psychiatric patient involuntarily committed to a locked hospital ward

text: Max Weber is primarily associated with {{c1::conflict theory}}, as his theory expands on {{c1::Karl Marx}}
example: A poor but respected priest has high status without wealth, a split Weber used to extend Marx's class model

text: Expressions of confidence or encouragement are a form of {{c1::esteem support}}
example: A coach tells a nervous pitcher, 'You've trained hard, you can strike this guy out'

text:
Insecure (ambivalent/resistant) attachment: the child
  • {{c1::clung to mom when she was present}}
  • {{c1::cried when she was gone}}
  • {{c1::continued to cry when she returned}}
extra: May even resist her or push her away when she returns
example: Ava won't leave Mom's lap to play, wails when Mom exits, and is still sobbing in her arms long after she returns

text: Foraging behavior is driven strongly by {{c1::genetics}} but can also be gained through {{c1::learning}}
example: Drosophila larvae with the rover allele of the for gene roam farther while feeding than sitter larvae

text: {{c1::Status}} describes the position a person occupies in a particular setting
example: Being a 'student' in the lecture hall and a 'daughter' at the family dinner table.

text: Sets of behaviors expected for a specific interaction are called {{c1::social scripts}}
example: A job interview: firm handshake, answer questions, ask one of your own, then thank the interviewer

text: Group foraging: {{c1::animals look for food in groups}}
extra: Example: lions, which can kill more and larger prey

text: Solitary foraging: {{c1::an animal looks for food by itself}}
Foraging: {{c1::the search for food in an animal's environment}}
extra: Animals can't survive or reproduce without it
example: Honeybees flying out to collect nectar and pollen from flowers

text: Dramaturgy: {{c1::when interacting, people are assumed to act in accordance with the expectations of their audience}}
extra: People plan their conduct, want to guide and control how they're seen, and act differently alone than in public
example: Goffman saw hotel staff act deferential in the dining room, then mock the guests back in the kitchen

text: Assortative mating: {{c1::non-random mating where individuals with certain phenotypes tend to mate with each other}}
extra: Example: large animals mate with large animals, small with small
example: Tall people tend to marry tall people more often than chance would predict

text: In Harlow's monkey experiments, the cloth mother acts as a {{c1::secure base}}
extra: Eventually the monkey is comfortable enough to explore the world on its own, because it knows the cloth mother will still be there
example: A toddler at the playground wanders to the sandbox, glancing back to check Mom is still on the bench

text: Disassortative (negative assortative) mating: {{c1::opposite of assortative mating; individuals with different or diverse traits mate}}
example: In Wedekind's 'sweaty T-shirt' study, women preferred the scent of men whose MHC genes differed from theirs

text: {{c1::Gesellschaft}} emphasizes the larger society in which importance is placed on secondary relationships that are based on impersonal ties
extra: Example: one's sense of duty to a society or organization
example: A big-city corporation where coworkers relate mainly through formal, contract-based roles.

text: {{c1::Verbal communication::... communication}} is through spoken, written, or signed words
example: Texting a friend 'running late' is verbal communication even though nothing is spoken.

text: Being a doctor is an {{c1::achieved status::status type}}
example: Becoming an Olympic gold medalist, or even a convicted felon

text: Unintentional discrimination: {{c1::how policies can discriminate unintentionally}}
example: In Griggs v. Duke Power (1971), a diploma requirement for jobs screened out far more Black than white applicants

text: Secondary groups: {{c1::formal, impersonal, temporary relationships based on a limited goal}}
example: Classmates assigned to a semester lab group who stop talking after handing in the final report

text: Perceived similarity: {{c1::Thinking another person (often SO) is similar to them but they aren't actually similar}}
example: A woman believes her husband shares her love of opera, though he secretly finds it boring

text: Businesses and government jobs are examples of {{c1::utilitarian}} organizations
extra: Members are paid for their efforts
example: A Starbucks barista who shows up each shift because she is paid an hourly wage

text: Harlow's monkey experiments showed that {{c1::attachment to the mother is based on comfort}}
example: Monkeys fed only by the wire mother still spent most of each day clinging to the cloth mother

text: Being friendlier toward people who share your last name is an example of {{c1::kin selection}}
example: A father runs into a burning house to save his own son before the neighbour's child

text: Kin selection: {{c1::people act more altruistically toward close kin than toward distant or non-kin people}}
extra: The same holds when people share last names, especially rare last names
example: A woman donates a kidney to her sister but would not give one to a stranger

text: Institutional discrimination: discrimination by {{c1::organizations and institutions}}
example: In the 1930s US banks redlined Black neighbourhoods, refusing mortgages to anyone who lived there

text: Social scripts: {{c1::instructions provided by society on how to act}}
example: At a restaurant you wait to be seated, order from a menu, eat, then pay the bill and tip

text: Oligarchy: {{c1::a small group of people having control of a country, organization or institution}}
example: After 1991, much of Russia's economy came under the control of a handful of billionaire 'oligarchs'

text: Side-effect discrimination: {{c1::one institution/organization/sector can influence another negatively}}
extra:
Institutions (economics, politics, law, medicine, business) are interrelated, so discrimination in one area can affect another
Example: an unfair guilty verdict later costs a Black man a job because of his record

text: The ability of organizations to be unbiased: {{c1::impersonality}}
example: A professor grades exams by student ID number instead of name so favourites can't get extra points

text: A Black man in a small town is affected by the criminal justice system, which affects his economic situation, which affects his access to health care: {{c1::side-effect discrimination}}
example: Underfunded schools in Black neighbourhoods limit job prospects, which then limits access to good health insurance

text: Bats using echolocation to gain information about their environment: {{c1::auto-communication}}
example: Dolphins clicking and listening to the echoes to find fish in murky water

text:
Charities send out small gifts. By helping you out now, they hope you respond by giving them a larger gift in the future. This is an example of what form of Altruism?
{{c1::Reciprocal altruism}}
example: You help a classmate study for organic chemistry, and next semester she shares her physics notes with you

text: Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation: an experiment done to {{c1::assess the type of attachment (secure vs. insecure) an infant has to its caregiver}}
extra:
The child is left in a room with a stranger after the mother leaves
Depends on parenting: sensitive, responsive mothers → secure; insensitive/unresponsive mothers → insecure
example: A 1-year-old who ignores Mom when she comes back into the room is classed as insecure-avoidant

text: Sexual selection: {{c1::natural selection arising through one sex's preference for certain characteristics in individuals of the other sex}}
example: Peahens choose males with the largest, most eye-spotted tails, so peacock tails grew huge over generations

text: Altruism: {{c1::caring about the welfare of other people and acting to help them}}
extra: Beneficial to society and also to individuals
example: In 2007 Wesley Autrey jumped onto New York subway tracks to shield a stranger from an oncoming train

text: A/an {{c1::organization}} is a group with identifiable membership that engages in certain action to achieve a common purpose
example: The American Red Cross, with identifiable volunteers working toward disaster relief.

text: {{c1::Role performance}} refers to carrying out behaviors that are characteristic of a certain role
example: A teacher actually grading papers and leading the class discussion.

text: {{c1::Disorganized attachment::... attachment}} is when the child shows no clear pattern of behavior in response to the caregiver’s absence or presence
extra: Occurs when a caregiver is erratic or abusive
example: In the Strange Situation, a disorganized infant approaches the returning mother, then freezes or backs away.

text: Individual discrimination: {{c1::one person discriminating against another based on a characteristic}}
example: A landlord refuses to rent an apartment to a woman because she wears a hijab

text: McDonaldization: {{c1::policies of fast food organizations have come to dominate other organizations of society}}
extra: Efficiency, calculability, predictability, uniformity and control
example: Universities grading by Scantron multiple-choice exams for speed, countable scores and uniformity

text: Max Weber's impersonality: {{c1::individuals and officials conduct activities in an unbiased manner}}
example: A DMV clerk applies the same vision-test rule to the mayor as to everyone else in line

text: A medical student who adopts a more empathetic approach than usual with a patient is using the {{c1::front-stage self}}
example: A flight attendant smiling warmly at rude passengers throughout a 10-hour flight

text: {{c1::Display rules}} are unspoken rules that govern the expression of emotions
extra: The emotions are universal, so the way in which they are displayed accounts for emotional differences across cultures
example: In Ekman's study, Japanese students masked disgust at a gory film with smiles when an experimenter was present.

text: Max Weber studied the {{c1::structure of organizations::studied what?}}: 5 main characteristics of an ideal bureaucracy, regardless of the organization's goal
example: The IRS fits Weber's ideal: specialized jobs, a hierarchy, written rules, impersonality and merit hiring

text:
Harlow's monkey experiments:
  • {{c1::Wire mother provided food}}
  • {{c1::Cloth mother provided comfort}}
  • Infant monkeys preferred the {{c1::cloth mother}}
extra: Attachment to the mother is based on comfort, not food
example: Frightened by a mechanical toy, Harlow's infant rhesus monkeys ran to the cloth mother, not the wire one

text: Max Weber's employment based on technical qualifications: {{c1::hiring in a bureaucracy is based on a person's qualifications, not favoritism or personal rivalries}}
example: A hospital hires a nurse because she passed the NCLEX and has ICU experience, not because she's the CEO's niece

text: Going from fraternity bro to pre-med gunner is an example of {{c1::role exit}}
example: A soldier discharged after 20 years who learns to see himself as a civilian schoolteacher

text: {{c1::Avoidant attachment::... attachment}} is when a child shows no preference for the caregiver compared to strangers
extra: Occurs when a caregiver has little or no response to a distressed child
example: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, an avoidant toddler ignores the mother when she returns.

text: {{c1::Aggression}} is a physical, verbal, or nonverbal behavior with the intention to cause harm or increase social dominance
example: In Bandura's Bobo doll study, children who watched an adult hit the doll later hit it themselves.

text: A/an {{c1::network}} is an observable pattern of social relationships between individuals or groups
example: Your LinkedIn connections, mapped as who knows whom, form an observable network.

text: Reciprocal altruism: {{c1::people are more cooperative if they will interact with that person again in the future}}
extra: We feel more obliged to help someone who has helped us
example: Vampire bats regurgitate blood meals for roost-mates that fed them on earlier nights

text: Reinforcement-modeling: {{c1::kids model their behavior based on reinforcement}}
extra: Example: parents who give in to a child's temper tantrums get more tantrums in the future

text: {{c1::Autocommunication}} is communication to oneself
example: Keeping a diary that no one but you will ever read

text: {{c1::Monogamy::Mating system}} describes exclusive mating relationships
example: Prairie voles form lifelong pair bonds with one partner, a classic model of monogamy.

text: A student has to write 2 papers, do hundreds of Anki cards, study P/S and finish 9 lab reports in one week: {{c1::role strain}}
example: A parent of three cannot get every child to soccer, piano and tutoring on the same afternoon

text: {{c1::Mating systems::... systems}} describe the way in which a group is organized in terms of sexual behavior
example: In elephant seals, one dominant bull mates with a harem of females, a polygynous mating system.

text: {{c1::Social support::... support}} is the perception or reality that one is cared for by a social network
example: A widower whose friends bring meals and check in weekly after his wife's death.

text: {{c1::Gemeinschaft}} emphasizes community ties in which personal relationships and families are given the most importance
example: A small Amish farming village where everyone knows each other and family ties guide daily life.

text: The {{c1::frustration aggression hypothesis::... hypothesis}} states that aggression is the result of blocking, or frustrating, a person's efforts to attain a goal
example: A driver stuck in traffic for an hour honks and yells at the other drivers.

text: The most powerful predictor of friendships and relationships: {{c1::geographical proximity}}
example: In Festinger's study of MIT student housing, residents befriended next-door neighbours far more than those down the hall

text: {{c1::Nonverbal communication::... communication}} is through means other than the use of words
example: Rolling your eyes at a friend's bad joke signals annoyance without a word.

text: Permissive (indulgent) parenting: {{c1::non-directive and lenient, with few behavioral expectations for the child}}
example: Parents let their 8-year-old skip homework, eat candy for dinner and stay up past midnight

text: Role strain: {{c1::tension within one status when you cannot carry out all of its obligations}}
example: A resident must see 20 patients in a shift yet is also expected to teach every medical student on the team

text: Being a prince of a royal family is an {{c1::ascribed status::status type}}
example: Being of Korean descent or being the youngest child in your family

text: Ascribed statuses: {{c1::statuses you can't change, given from birth}}
example: Being born into India's Brahmin caste

text: Evolutionary game theory: {{c1::game theory applied to evolution; the fitness payoff of a behavioral strategy depends on the strategies of others in the population}}
extra:
Depends on reproduction and environment
Genes for successful strategies become more common in successive generations
example: In the hawk–dove game, aggressive hawks do well when most others are doves but poorly when most are hawks

text: An organization focusing more on its rules than on its overall goal: {{c1::goal displacement}}
extra:
Max Weber
True goals are displaced by too much emphasis on rules
↓ productivity and societal success
example: A hospital turns away a bleeding man at the door because his insurance paperwork is incomplete

text: Evolutionary game theory predicts the availability of {{c1::resources}} and {{c1::social}} behavior
extra: Each individual's strategy depends on the strategies of the other players
example: In Axelrod's repeated prisoner's-dilemma tournaments, the cooperative tit-for-tat strategy scored highest

text: {{c1::Role}} is the term used to describe the thoughts and behavior expected of someone occupying a status
example: A doctor (status) is expected to diagnose, keep confidences and show empathy (role).

text: Homophily: {{c1::People tend to choose relationships with those with similar attributes}}
example: A high-school cafeteria where friend groups cluster by race, grade and sport

text: A guy who says he loves baseball secretly watches cooking shows and hangs out with his cat at home: the {{c1::back stage}} of dramaturgy
example: A teacher who is strict in class eats cereal in pajamas and watches cartoons at home

text: {{c1::Interpersonal attraction}} is the attraction between people which leads to the development of platonic or romantic relationships
example: Next-door dorm neighbours becoming close friends simply because they see each other every day.

text: After Brown v. Board, a girl in an integrated school still doesn't feel welcome in her classroom: {{c1::past-in-present discrimination}}
example: Families shut out of homeownership by 1930s redlining still hold less wealth to pass on today

text: Customer service now making you go through 12 menu options before reaching someone who can help: {{c1::bureaucratization}}
example: Dropping a college class now requires an online form plus signatures from an adviser, instructor and dean

text:
Max Weber's division of labor: {{c1::people are trained to do specific tasks}}
Can lead to {{c1::trained incapacity}}
extra: Trained incapacity: workers are so specialized in their tasks that they lose touch with the overall picture
example: On Ford's assembly line one worker only tightened bolts, never seeing how the whole car came together

text: An organization with a CEO, manager, assistant and intern shows a {{c1::hierarchy of organization}}
example: The Army's chain of command runs private → sergeant → lieutenant → colonel → general

text: Authoritative parenting: {{c1::strict, consistent and loving, but pragmatic and issue-oriented; listens to the child's arguments}}
extra:
Balances responsibility with the rights of the child
Uses discipline
example: Parents set a 10 p.m. curfew, explain why, and agree to 11 p.m. after their teen makes a good case

text: Movie theaters all look and work the same, with the same ticket systems and pre-show entertainment: {{c1::McDonaldization}}
example: Every Starbucks makes a grande latte the same way, in the same cup, at a posted price

text: Master status: {{c1::the status you identify with as the most important}}
extra: Example: a woman feels her role as a mother is more important than her role as a woman

text: Animals use body language, facial expressions, visual displays, scents, and vocalizations to {{c1::communicate}}
extra: Takes place not only between nonhuman animals, but between humans and other animals as well
example: Honeybees perform a waggle dance to show hivemates the direction and distance of food.

text: Bureaucracy: {{c1::rules, structures and rankings that guide organizations}}
example: The US Postal Service, with set job descriptions, written procedures and a chain of command

text: {{c1::Kin selection}} is the evolutionary strategy that favors the reproductive success of an animal's relatives, even at a cost to that animal's own survival
example: A Belding's ground squirrel gives an alarm call that warns relatives but draws predators to itself.

text: In-group: {{c1::the group you are affiliated with based on identification}}
example: A Yankees fan cheering with fellow Yankees fans and booing the Red Sox fans in the stands

text: Iron law of oligarchy: {{c1::any human organization will inevitably become controlled by a ruling elite, no matter how democratic it is at the start}}
example: Michels watched Germany's democratic Social Democratic Party come to be run by a small group of entrenched leaders

text: Utilitarian organizations: {{c1::members are paid/rewarded for their efforts}}
Max Weber's hierarchy of organization: {{c1::each position is under the supervision of a higher authority; not all people in an organization are equal}}
Sharing information or giving advice is {{c1::informational support::form of support}}
example: A second-year medical student tells a first-year which review books helped her pass Step 1

text: Egoism: {{c1::People act based on their own self-interest and welfare}}
example: A man donates to charity only for the tax deduction and the good publicity

text: The form of support that gives someone a sense of social belonging: {{c1::companionship support}}
example: A lonely widower joins a Thursday bowling league and feels he belongs again

text: False consensus: {{c1::We assume everyone else agrees with what we do, even if they do not}}
extra: Example: saying physics sucks and assuming everyone agrees, even though many people like physics

text: Role exit: {{c1::stopping a role previously central to one's identity and establishing a new identity}}
example: A pro athlete retires and rebuilds his identity as a TV sports commentator

text: Watching baseball with friends despite not liking baseball is the {{c1::front stage}} of dramaturgy
example: A job candidate laughs at the interviewer's bad jokes and says she loves teamwork

text: A mother gives in to her child's tantrum, which makes the child more likely to throw tantrums in the future: an example of {{c1::reinforcement-modeling}}
example: A child who gets candy for whining at the checkout whines louder on the next shopping trip

text: Financial support, material goods or services are examples of {{c1::tangible/instrumental}} support
example: Neighbours bring casseroles and drive you to chemotherapy appointments after your cancer diagnosis

text: Homophilous social networks are similar to a {{c1::reference}} group
example: A pre-med who befriends other pre-meds and then judges her own MCAT score against theirs

text: Advertisers depend on the {{c1::mere exposure effect}} to sell products
example: A cereal jingle replayed in every TV ad break makes shoppers reach for that brand

text: Projection bias: {{c1::We assume others share the same beliefs we do}}
example: A vegan host assumes her dinner guests will also prefer a meat-free meal

text: A/an {{c1::peer group}} is a self-selected group formed around shared interests
example: A group of teens who form a band because they all love punk music.

text: Animals communicate with chemical signals called {{c1::Pheromones}}
example: Ants lay a pheromone trail that nestmates follow to a food source

text: School segregation challenged in Brown v. Board of Education: {{c1::institutional discrimination::type of discrimination}}
extra: The Supreme Court ruled that segregated schools aren't equal and that Black students were being mistreated
example: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld laws forcing Black passengers into separate railway cars

text: Primary groups: {{c1::the people closest to you}}
example: Four best friends who have texted every day since kindergarten

text: Front stage (dramaturgy): {{c1::how we act when we are in a social setting}}
example: A lawyer speaking calmly and formally while arguing before a jury

text: Cost signaling: {{c1::helping others to show them you are a big deal, rich or have resources}}
example: A billionaire gives $100 million to a hospital that then names a new wing after him

text: Authoritarian parenting: {{c1::very strict; tries to break the child's will and relies on punishment}}
example: A father grounds his son for a month for questioning curfew and answers every 'why?' with 'because I said so'

text: Preparation for impression management happens in the {{c1::back stage}}
extra: Example: putting on makeup, looking in the mirror and trying different outfits

text: Obese people mating with other obese people is {{c1::assortative mating}}
example: Highly educated people tending to marry other highly educated people

text: Primary group: {{c1::your core social group}}
Organizations achieve maximum efficiency through {{c1::bureaucracy}}
extra: Rules, structures and rankings that guide organizations
example: The DMV's numbered tickets, standard forms and service windows process thousands of licences a day

text: The emotional bond between an infant and its mother (caregiver) is called {{c1::attachment}}
example: A 1-year-old crawls to his mother and clings to her when a loud dog barks

text: Empathy-altruism hypothesis: {{c1::some people are altruistic due to empathy}}
example: Batson's students who felt empathy for 'Elaine' offered to take her electric shocks even when they could just leave

text: Achieved status: {{c1::status you earn yourself after working for it}}
example: Earning a black belt in karate after eight years of training

text: Religious groups or MADD are examples of {{c1::normative}} organizations
extra: Members come together through a shared goal
example: Volunteers who join Habitat for Humanity because they want to build homes for families in need

text:
Max Weber's written rules and regulations: {{c1::the organization is governed by written rules and regulations}}
Can lead to goal displacement: {{c1::rules become more important than the goals of the organization}}
example: A nonprofit spends so much effort on grant-reporting rules that it ends up serving fewer homeless people

text: {{c1::Role set}} is a set of all roles that are associated with one status
example: A professor's status carries the roles of lecturer, researcher, advisor and committee member.

text: Affection, love, trust and caring are examples of {{c1::emotional}} support
example: A friend sits with you and hugs you after your dog dies

text: Similarity bias: {{c1::We will not befriend people different from us}}
extra: We befriend those similar to us
example: Two biology majors who both love hiking and indie music quickly become best friends

text: Trained incapacity: {{c1::workers are so specialized they lose touch with the big picture}}
example: A cardiologist so focused on the heart that he misses his patient's obvious depression

text: {{c1::Mate choice}} is the selection of a mate based on attraction and traits
example: Peahens prefer peacocks with larger tails bearing more eyespots.

text: Past-in-present discrimination: {{c1::how things done in the past, even if no longer allowed, can have consequences for people in the present}}
extra: Example: after Brown v. Board, Black students didn't feel welcome in the classroom

text: Example: Andrew has a set pre-med idea and assumes others share it. This is {{c1::projection bias}}
extra: We assume others share the same beliefs we do

text: Example: I see Milo every day and begin to like Milo more. This is the {{c1::mere exposure effect}}
Impression management: {{c1::our attempt to control how others see us on the front stage}}
extra: There are multiple front stages, and you play a different role in each one
example: Posting only vacation photos and promotions on Instagram, never the bad days

text: Mere exposure effect: {{c1::Repeated exposure to novel people or objects ↑ our liking for them}}
extra: The more often we see something, the more we like it
example: A song you disliked at first grows on you after hearing it on the radio ten times

text: Young babies are happy to be passed around, but around 8 months {{c1::stranger anxiety}} sets in
example: A 9-month-old who used to smile at everyone now screams when a neighbour tries to hold her

text: Obese people mating with lean people is {{c1::disassortative (negative assortative) mating}}
extra: Individuals with dissimilar traits mate more often than expected by random chance
example: White-throated sparrows with white head stripes almost always pair with tan-striped mates

text: Auto-communication: {{c1::an animal gives information to itself}}
Saying a robot has consciousness is an example of {{c1::anthropomorphism}}
example: Saying your dog feels guilty about chewing up your shoes

text: Role conflict: {{c1::conflict between 2+ different statuses}}
extra: The different statuses compete for someone's time
example: A surgeon-mother is paged for an emergency operation during her daughter's school play

text: Discrimination: {{c1::different treatment and harmful actions against members of a group, often minorities}}
example: Jim Crow laws kept Black Americans out of whites-only restaurants, schools and swimming pools

text: {{c1::Cost-signalling}} lets an altruist establish a "better than you" reputation
example: Arabian babblers compete to stand sentinel and feed groupmates, and dominant birds block rivals from helping

text: Bureaucratization: {{c1::process by which organizations become increasingly governed by laws and policy}}
example: A clinic that once took walk-ins now needs a referral, insurance pre-authorization and three intake forms

text: A/an {{c1::social group}} is made up of two or more people with similar characteristics that share a sense of unity
example: Members of a campus Korean Student Association who share a heritage and sense of belonging.

text: Inclusive fitness: {{c1::an organism's own reproductive success plus its contribution to the reproductive success of relatives who share its genes}}
example: A childless aunt who helps raise her nieces still passes on copies of her genes through them

text: Back stage (dramaturgy): {{c1::more private area of our lives, when the act is over}}
example: After a long shift, a nurse kicks off her shoes at home and vents about patients to her roommate

text: Difference between discrimination and prejudice: {{c1::in discrimination, action is taken on the negative attitude}}
example: Disliking Muslims is prejudice; refusing to hire a Muslim applicant is discrimination

text: University administrators don't teach classes and professors aren't responsible for building maintenance: {{c1::division of labor}}
example: In a hospital, phlebotomists draw blood, pharmacists dispense drugs and surgeons operate

text: Juggling extracurriculars, friendships, school, research, clinical experience, volunteering, fraternity life and family relationships: {{c1::role conflict}}
example: A police officer is ordered to arrest his own brother

text: A science professor who doesn't let women into his class is an example of {{c1::individual discrimination}}
example: A manager never promotes employees over 50 because he thinks older workers are slow

text: Random mating: {{c1::all individuals within a species are equally likely to mate with each other}}
example: Wind-pollinated plants in a large field, where pollen lands on any plant regardless of its traits

text: Coercive organizations: {{c1::members don't have a choice about membership}}
Anthropomorphism: {{c1::attributing human characteristics to non-human animals}}
extra: Example: thinking a cat sleeps with you out of love, when it is really after your body heat

text: The {{c1::prisoner’s dilemma}} is when two people act out of their own self-interest, but if they had cooperated, the result would have been even better
example: Two suspects each confess and get 5 years, though both staying silent would have earned each just 1 year.

text: {{c1::Promiscuity}} is the mating system that is characterized by no exclusivity
example: Bonobos mate with many partners in their group without forming lasting pair bonds.

text: Explains how societies change and adapt over time through conflict; two opposing positions merge to create a new society where both are content: {{c1::conflict theory}}
example: Civil rights protests clashing with segregationists produced the 1964 Civil Rights Act

text: {{c1::Micro-cultures}} cannot support people throughout their lifespan
example: A sorority's culture stops shaping a member's daily life once she graduates

text: Normative culture: {{c1::values in line with larger society norms}}
example: Most people wait their turn in line rather than cutting ahead

text: Medicine: a male-dominated field (most heads of doctors and hospitals are men), which creates a disparity in power → {{c1::Feminist theory}}
example: Most hospital CEOs are men even though most US healthcare workers are women

text: Polygamy: {{c1::more than 1 spouse}}
example: Brigham Young, the 19th-century Mormon leader, had dozens of wives

text:
Sick role:
  • {{c1::You're allowed to take a break}}
  • {{c1::But you must try to get well and seek competent medical help; failing to do so is deviant}}
example: A student with flu is excused from class but is expected to see a doctor and take her medicine

text: Medicine: the meanings given to a lab coat or stethoscope shape the doctor–patient interaction → {{c1::Symbolic interactionism}}
example: A patient tells a doctor in a white coat symptoms she would never share with a man in a hoodie

text:
Exogamy: {{c1::Custom of marrying outside a social group}}
Example: {{c1::Xbox player marrying PS4 player}}
example: Incest taboos in every culture require people to marry outside their immediate family

text: Thomas theorem: {{c1::The interpretation of a situation causes the action}}
extra: "If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences"
example: A rumour that a bank will fail makes depositors pull out their cash, so the bank really fails

text: Hidden curriculum: {{c1::learning normative cultural values, socialization, etc.}}
example: Students learn to raise their hands, wait their turn and obey authority, though no class teaches it

text: Heterogamy: {{c1::Marriage between 2 culturally different individuals}}
example: A Jewish American marrying a Hindu woman from India

text: Homogamy: {{c1::Marriage between similar individuals}}
example: Two Catholic lawyers in their 30s from the same city getting married

text: Modernization in terms of religion: {{c1::more information available to the public, less emphasis on religion}}
example: As Ireland modernized, weekly Mass attendance fell from most of the population to a minority

text: Common ownership of production, motivated by what benefits society as a whole and focused on human needs and economic demands: {{c1::Socialism}}
example: The UK's National Health Service, publicly owned and funded so care goes to whoever needs it

text: Polyandry: {{c1::more than 1 husband}}
example: In parts of Tibet and Nepal, brothers have shared a single wife (fraternal polyandry)

text:
What is the purpose of medical systems?
To keep people healthy or a capitalist organization??
{{c1::Rational choice-Exchange theories}}
example: A hospital opens a profitable cardiac wing instead of a money-losing psychiatric ward

text: Illness experience: {{c1::the process of being ill and how people cope with illness}}
extra: Example: a broken wrist makes someone question their life

text: A {{c1::belief}} is something a person considers to be true
example: Believing that the Earth is round or that an afterlife exists

text: Social selection (health selection) hypothesis: an {{c1::individual's health can influence their social mobility and therefore status}}
example: People whose schizophrenia costs them their jobs often drift down into poorer neighbourhoods

text: The division of labor in government and the economy is a {{c1::functionalist::sociological theory}} concept
extra: Everyone is required to have a responsibility in society
example: Durkheim saw farmers, teachers and doctors each filling a role that keeps society running

text: Cam belongs to the dominant religious organization in Iran, which includes most members of society: {{c1::ecclesia}}
example: Nearly everyone in medieval Western Europe belonged to the Catholic Church

text: {{c1::Individualistic}} cultures prioritize the individual over the entire group, valuing independence over identifying with a group
extra: Example: Western Europe and the United States

text: Rational choice theory, independence of irrelevant alternatives: {{c1::adding other options won't affect the previous options' rankings}}
extra: A > B > C and B > X > C, therefore A > B > X > C
example: A diner prefers steak to chicken; when fish is added to the menu, she should still pick steak over chicken

text: Antithesis (dialectic): {{c1::reaction to the thesis; push-back from those unhappy with the status quo}}
example: Factory workers unionize and strike against the owners who set their wages

text: Institutional facts: {{c1::created by social conventions and rely on other facts}}
extra: Example: money depends on the paper we have given value

text: Cultural transmission: {{c1::how culture is learned}}
example: A grandmother teaching her granddaughter to make tamales for Christmas

text: Material culture: {{c1::physical & technological aspects of our daily lives}}
example: Smartphones, cars and the Statue of Liberty

text: Symbolic interactionism: {{c1::focuses on individuals and the significance they put on things in their lives}}
example: A wedding ring is just metal, but to its wearer it stands for lifelong commitment

text: High culture: {{c1::experience of the highest class of society}}
example: Attending the Metropolitan Opera in a tuxedo

text: Conservative view of institutions: {{c1::institutions are natural by-products of human nature}}
example: Seeing the nuclear family as a natural outgrowth of human nature that should be preserved

text: Cultural universals: {{c1::features common to all cultures (every culture has a way of dealing with them)}}
extra: Example: language, illness/medicine/healing, wedding and funeral ceremonies

text:
Perspectives on mass media:
  • {{c1::Functionalist}}: entertainment; agent of socialization and enforcer of social norms
  • {{c1::Conflict}}: portrayal of divisions in society (race/ethnicity, gender, social class)
  • {{c1::Feminist}}: stereotypes and misrepresentation toward the dominant ideology, e.g. gender roles
  • {{c1::Interactionist}}: micro-level; how media shape day-to-day behavior
example: A sitcom can teach manners (functionalist) yet show only rich white families (conflict) and housewife moms (feminist)

text: Microsociology studies {{c1::face-to-face interactions}}
example: Observing how two drivers negotiate who goes first at a four-way stop

text: Macro-level perspective that focuses on gender inequalities inherent to patriarchal capitalist societies: {{c1::feminist theory}}
example: Women do most unpaid housework and childcare while men hold most Fortune 500 CEO jobs

text: Synthesis (dialectic): {{c1::thesis and antithesis creating a new state}}
example: Owners and striking unions settle on an 8-hour workday and a minimum wage

text:
Classless, moneyless community where all property is owned by community:
{{c1::Communism}}
example: Early Israeli kibbutzim, where members shared all property and ate in a common dining hall

text: Cultural assimilation: {{c1::interpenetration and fusion of ethnic minorities into the dominant culture}}
example: Grandchildren of Italian immigrants in the US who speak only English and celebrate Thanksgiving

text: Social dysfunction: {{c1::a process that has undesirable consequences and may reduce the stability of society}}
example: Prohibition in the 1920s fueled bootlegging and organized crime like Al Capone's gang

text: Non-material culture: {{c1::does not include physical objects}}; also called {{c1::symbolic culture}}
example: The American Dream belief that hard work leads to success

text: In a consanguineous kinship, individuals are related by {{c1::blood}}
extra:
Affinal Kinship: Individuals that are related by choice such as in a marriage. Doesn't have to be your own choice
Consanguineous Kinship: Related through blood
example: Your first cousin, who shares a set of grandparents with you

text: Language is defined as spoken or written {{c1::symbols}} combined into a system
example: The letters c-a-t mean a furry pet only because English speakers agree that they do

text: Feminist theory: {{c1::gender oppression}} means women are not only unequal to men but oppressed, subordinated and abused
example: Marital rape was not a crime in all 50 US states until 1993

text: Social facts: {{c1::ways of acting, thinking, and feeling external to the individual that exert social control over them}}
example: Durkheim showed suicide rates are a social fact, staying stable within groups year after year

text:
Conflict theory believes society evolves thru several stages:
{{c1::Feudalism}} → {{c1::Capitalism}} → {{c1::Socialism}}
example: Serfs farming a lord's land gave way to Manchester mill workers, whom Marx expected to seize the factories

text: Culture shock: {{c1::feelings of disorientation when someone encounters unfamiliar cultural practices}}
example: An American in Japan feels lost when tips are refused and everyone removes their shoes indoors

text:
Culture = {{c1::a way of life shared by a group of individuals}}
Society = the {{c1::way people organize themselves}}
example: The United States is a society; baseball, Thanksgiving and English are parts of its culture

text: Brute facts and institutional facts are part of {{c1::weak social constructionism}}
example: A ball crossing the goal line is a brute fact; that it counts as a 6-point touchdown is an institutional fact

text: Intended consequences of institutions: {{c1::Manifest functions}}
extra:
Businesses provide a service
Schools educate people so they can get jobs
Law maintains social order

text: Thesis (dialectic): {{c1::the existing, generally accepted state}}
extra: Example: the thesis was that the bourgeoisie ran factories and the working class provided labor

text: Small societies are held together by {{c1::similarities}}
example: An Amish farming community where everyone shares the same faith, work and customs

text: Polygyny: {{c1::more than 1 wife}}
example: Islamic law allows a man to have up to four wives at once

text: Girl Scouts, college sororities and boarding schools are all examples of a {{c1::micro-culture}}
example: A hospital night-shift crew with its own inside jokes, rituals and slang

text: Feminist theory: {{c1::gender differences}} are socially constructed via the process of socialization
example: Girls given dolls and boys given toy trucks learn gendered interests from early childhood

text: In 19th-century capitalist Europe, the rich upper class was the {{c1::bourgeoisie}} and the poor lower class was the {{c1::proletariat}}
example: Manchester mill owners grew rich while child workers in their factories toiled 12-hour days

text: A/an {{c1::sect}} is a religious group that arose from a split from a larger religion
example: Lutheranism began as a sect after Martin Luther's 1517 protest against the Roman Catholic Church

text: {{c1::Social institutions}} are well-established social structures that dictate certain patterns of behavior or relationships
example: Public schooling, which sets when children learn, what they learn and how they behave in class

text: Conflict theory and functionalism are both {{c1::macro::macro or micro}} sociology
example: Analyzing how unequal school funding across the US keeps poor communities poor

text: Feminist theory: {{c1::structural oppression}} means women's oppression and inequality are due to capitalism, patriarchy and racism
example: A low-wage Black single mother faces barriers from racism, sexism and capitalism at the same time

text: Counterculture: {{c1::a subculture that rejects the larger culture's norms and develops its own norms}}
Religious fundamentalism: a reaction to {{c1::secularization}} that goes back to {{c1::strict religious beliefs}}
example: The 1979 Iranian Revolution replaced the Shah's secular reforms with strict Islamic law

text: Feminist theory: {{c1::gender inequality}} is central to all behavior and organization in society; women's subordination is viewed as an inherent feature
example: In the US, women earn about 82 cents for every dollar men earn

text: Endogamy: {{c1::Marrying within a specific social group}}
example: India's caste system, in which people traditionally marry within their own caste

text: A problem with functionalism: it {{c1::focuses entirely on institutions without regard for the individual}}
example: Functionalism explains how hospitals keep society running but ignores what one patient feels in the ER

text:
Research that calls attention to the ways in which health and disease are conditioned in a social context:
{{c1::Social epidemiology}}
example: In the US, the richest 1% of men live about 15 years longer than the poorest 1%

text: In social philosophy, {{c1::objectification}} is the act of treating a person, or sometimes an animal, as an object or a thing
example: A beer ad that shows only a woman's legs and torso, never her face

text:
4 main points of culture:
  • People {{c1::share}} culture in society
  • Culture is {{c1::adaptive}}
  • Culture {{c1::builds}} on itself
  • Culture is {{c1::transmitted}}
example: Thanksgiving is shared nationwide, has changed over time, grew from harvest feasts and is taught to each generation

text: In large societies there is {{c1::mutual interdependence}} (organic solidarity)
example: A New Yorker relies on strangers to grow her food, deliver her mail and fix her phone

text: Strong social constructionism: {{c1::reality is dependent on language and social habits}}
example: A strong constructionist would say even 'disease' exists only because we name and classify it

text: Rational choice theory: {{c1::people are motivated by money and do what's best to get more goods}}
example: A shopper buys the cheaper of two identical TVs to keep more money for other goods

text: Progressive view of institutions: {{c1::institutions are artificial creations that need to be redesigned if they are not helpful}}
example: Arguing the US health system is a human design that should be rebuilt into universal coverage

text: Rational choice theory, completeness: {{c1::every action can be ranked}}
example: A diner can always rank her options, such as pizza over tacos over sushi, with no pair left uncompared

text: A {{c1::value}} is what a person deems important in life
example: A family that values education saves for years to send its kids to college

text: The norm that human remains should be buried in a cemetery outside the settlement is an example of {{c1::normative culture}}
example: The norm that guests bring a gift to a wedding

text: Conflict theory: most struggles in society happen because of {{c1::conflicts between different social classes}}
example: Factory workers striking against owners for higher wages and safer conditions

text: Lower class united to create {{c1::class consciousness}} as they realized they were being exploited
example: Coal miners form a union after realizing they all share low pay and deadly working conditions

text: A {{c1::monarchy}} is the rule of a king, queen or emperor
example: Saudi Arabia, an absolute monarchy ruled by a king from the House of Saud

text: Ecclesia: {{c1::dominant religious organization that includes most members of society}}
extra: Examples: Lutheranism in Sweden, Islam in Iran

text: Ludwig Gumplowicz expanded on {{c1::Marx}} and proposed that society is shaped by {{c1::war/conquest}}
extra: Cultural and ethnic conflicts lead to dominant groups
example: The Norman conquest of 1066 made the Normans a ruling class over the Anglo-Saxons

text: A {{c1::democracy}} is a form of government in which power is vested in the people and exercised directly by them or by their elected agents under a free electoral system
example: US citizens electing a president every four years

text: {{c1::Gatekeeping theory::... theory}}: when an event occurs, someone decides whether and how to pass the information on to others, such as a friend, an official or a journalist
example: A newspaper editor decides whether a local chemical spill makes the front page or gets cut

text: Rational choice theory, transitivity: {{c1::preferences follow the transitive property}}
extra: A > B and B > C, therefore A > C
example: If you prefer Harvard to Duke and Duke to UCLA, you must prefer Harvard to UCLA

text:
Addresses decision making via cost-benefit analysis:
{{c1::Exchange theory}}
example: A man ends a relationship once its constant arguments cost him more than the companionship gives

text: Exchange theory: {{c1::using rational choices in social interactions}}
extra:
Addresses decision making via cost-benefit analysis
Application of rational choice theory to social interactions
example: A woman stays friends with a coworker because the advice she gets outweighs the time it costs her

text:
Max Weber introduced 3 independent factors of social stratification:
  • {{c1::Class}}
  • {{c1::Status/Prestige}}
  • {{c1::Power}}
example: A lottery winner has class but no prestige; a beloved, poorly paid priest has prestige but little class

text:
Private ownership of production with market economy based on supply/demand:
{{c1::Capitalism}}
example: A privately owned bakery raises bread prices when demand climbs and flour runs short

text: In an affinal kinship, individuals are related by {{c1::choice }}
extra:
Affinal Kinship: Individuals that are related by choice such as in a marriage. Doesn't have to be your own choice
Consanguineous Kinship: Related through blood
example: Your sister's husband is your affinal kin, related through her marriage rather than by blood

text: Focuses on individuals and how they behave, based on the meaning we give to things: {{c1::symbolic interactionism}}
example: A teen sees being handed the car keys as a sign her parents now trust her as an adult

text: Explains how society exists over time, always trying to come to an equilibrium: {{c1::functionalism}}
extra: Example: business institutions had to adapt to the online shopping boom

text: A {{c1::dictatorship}} is an authoritarian form of government ruled by a single leader or group of leaders
extra: Typically has no party or a weak party, little mass mobilization and limited political pluralism
example: North Korea, ruled by the Kim family with no free elections

text: People always take rational actions, weighing costs and benefits to gain the most benefit: {{c1::rational choice theory}}
example: A student skips a party because a better MCAT score is worth more to her than one fun night

text: {{c1::Collectivistic}} cultures emphasize the needs and goals of the group as a whole over the needs and desires of each individual
example: In China and Japan, family duty and group harmony often come before personal ambition

text: Weak social constructionism: social constructs depend on {{c1::brute facts}}, which are the {{c1::most basic and fundamental facts}}
example: That Mount Everest has snow at its summit is a brute fact, true no matter what anyone thinks

text: A/an {{c1::ritual}} is a formal ceremonial behavior that usually includes symbolism
example: Graduates throwing their caps into the air at commencement

text: Secularization: {{c1::weakening of the social and political power of religious organizations}}
example: France's 1905 law separated church and state, ending the Catholic Church's official status

text: {{c1::Patriarchy}} is a social system in which men hold primary power and predominate in roles of political leadership, moral authority, social privilege and control of property
example: Until 2019, Saudi women needed a male guardian's permission to get a passport or travel abroad

text: Functionalism looks at society as a {{c1::whole}} and at how the institutions that make up society adapt to keep it {{c1::stable and functioning}}
example: Durkheim argued crime is functional because punishing it reinforces society's shared norms

text: Example: Chinese children wearing American clothes to fit in with the local culture → {{c1::cultural assimilation}}
{{c1::Social construct}} is a concept that everyone in society agrees to treat a certain way regardless of its inherent value.
The 2 views of institutions: the {{c1::conservative}} view and the {{c1::progressive}} view
example: Same-sex marriage debates pit marriage as a natural institution against marriage as a human creation open to change

text: Doctor-patient interactions or family dynamics are {{c1::micro::macro or micro}} sociology
example: Watching how a nurse and patient negotiate pain medication during one bedside visit

text: {{c1::Multiculturalism}} is the encouragement of multiple cultures within a community to enhance diversity
example: Canada adopted official multiculturalism in 1971, supporting immigrant groups in keeping their languages and traditions

text: Indirect effects of institutions: {{c1::latent::latent or manifest}} functions
extra:
Schools expose students to social connections and new activities
Businesses connect people across society

text: Macrosociology: {{c1::looking at big phenomena that affect big portions of the population}}
example: Studying how the 2008 recession raised unemployment across the entire United States

text: Assumptions we hold about different races, genders and subcultures, which can be dangerous in medicine: {{c1::social constructionism}}
example: In a 2016 study, half of white medical trainees held false beliefs such as Black people having thicker skin

text: Unequal distribution of access to resources in society (e.g., who has access to medical care): {{c1::conflict theory::sociological theory}}
example: Uninsured patients delay care for chest pain while wealthy patients pay for concierge doctors

text:
Explains social phenomena in terms of the meaning that they hold when people interact with one another:
{{c1::symbolic interactionism}}
example: A red rose on Valentine's Day means love only because people share that meaning

text: Applying rational choice theory to social interaction, people behave to maximize their own rewards while minimizing punishments: {{c1::exchange theory}}
example: Two friends keep taking turns hosting dinner as long as each feels the other returns the favor

text: A {{c1::subculture}} is a group of people within a culture that distinguish themselves from the primary culture
example: Goth teens with black clothes and their own music scene who still go to school and follow most norms

text: Culture lag: {{c1::culture takes time to catch up with technological innovations}}, causing {{c1::social}} problems
example: Laws against texting while driving came years after cell phones started causing crashes

text:
When people become ill, medicine ensures they return to functional state so they can become functional to society:
{{c1::Functionalism}}
example: A doctor treats a factory worker's broken arm so he can return to the assembly line in six weeks

text: Explains what society is rather than how it exists or changes; everything is created from the mind of society: {{c1::social constructionism}}
example: US census race categories have changed many times, showing they are socially defined

text:
Knowledge is not real, and only exists because we give it reality through social agreement:
{{c1::Social constructionism}}
extra: Example: the self is a social construct
example: Pluto stopped being a planet in 2006 only because astronomers voted to redefine the word

text: Popular culture: {{c1::patterns of experiences that exist within mainstream normative society}}
extra: Example: attending a game or watching a parade

text:
Looks at stability of society = {{c1::Functionalism}}
How society changes = {{c1::Conflict theory}}
How things are given value = {{c1::Social constructionism}}
How individuals act = {{c1::Symbolic interactionism}}
example: Schools train workers (functionalism), favour the rich (conflict), coin 'gifted' (constructionism), label kids (interactionism)

text: Meso-level culture: {{c1::medium-sized groups}}
extra: Example: communities, organizations, cities, states, clans and tribes
example: New Orleans, with its own jazz, Mardi Gras traditions and Creole food

text: Patients and doctors constructing illness out of ordinary behavior: {{c1::medicalization}}
extra: Example: not sitting still in class does not mean ADD
